This game is a open world delight, 12 hours in and I've barely scratched the surface. It's got all the makings for a great game, an already established story line the writers contribute to and add on to what the movies have already done. Multiple great elements of gameplay, the major two being car combat and hand to hand fighting.
Take the best part of the Arkham Asylum Batman games, the hand to hand combat. Then take the best part of GTA, the driving combat but in a more expansive environment. Don't worry about smashing into a building if you need to do a quick donut to evade an enemy...
Mad Max was one of the original takes on the Post Apocalyptic future, and the game holds true to his (director Baz Luherman) lunatic fringe vision of warlords, gas guzzlers, and sand kings. THe game has a great soundtrack, on par with Skyrim for me, It rises and ebbs according the action in the game, and when its at its hottest, drums pound, choruses chant, and you really feel the adreline.
There are plenty of different cars to choose, and mods to customize the hurt you bring you with metal angel. However you choose to ride out, this game is well worth the money. If you like car combat, id say must have. If you like open world, must have. if you like post apocalypse, must have.

First of all, don't be fooled by my play time. I have played countless hours of this on Xbox. The game is amazing.
The story is great. The characters are great (Tiny Tina <3). The replay value is great. The content is great. The visuals are great. Its just so amazing.... The story is really good and you care about the characters, and when youre done with it, dont worry, tons of sidequests! Want a challenge? Replay the game in a higher difficulty while keeping your guns and gear. Sidequests again! Bored of these? Take on an even higher difficulty with better loot, stronger enemies, rare weapons....I could go on. But, theres more. DLCs? Theres a ton of these. Theyre awesome, they add new gear, new sidequests, new storylines, new areas, so amazing. And the classes are all different and worth trying. The enemies-Oh the enemies....They all have unique attacks, weak points, etc. Shoot a goliath in the head? Their helmet goes off and they attack anyone nearby. Even their friends. And headshots do more damage. Spiderants? Shoot them in the head to stun them and them shoot their butt (weak point) to kill them. Too much psychos? Trip them by shooting their legs. Its so worth learning all the unique patterns and weak spots, they are so useful. The graphics are beautifully cel-shaded, which gives a nice cartoony aspect to the game. The voice acting is sweet. The loot....Its the main point of the game....So much weapons....Basically, you have a bunch of weapons of every time that come with prefixes. Which means you can get the same gun three times, while one has a scope and a bayonnet, the other one has a sight, and the other one has a blade and iron sights. Now, the rare loot....Youre gonna have to farm them...But its worth it. Every. Second. Of. It. You get sick guns that 1. Make you feel awesome for having something so rare 2.Have unique features 3. Are really powerful 4. ITS WORTH IT. You can get anything, from a pistol that shoots 7 exploding bullets in a horizontal line,while only consuming one bullet,to a submachine gun called Baby Maker which reloads by throwing the gun which explodes like a grenade, creating another smaller gun which also explodes, while creating another one in your hand with techy stuff. So.Awesome. Also, the gun making companys. (sorry, i forgot how to spell manifacturors) Each one has special abilities. Jakobs, which fires as fast as you can pull the trigger, tediore, which reloads by throwing the gun which explodes, and making another one in your hand, Maliwan, which creates elemental guns like fire shooting shotguns or acid shooting snipers, and more. This game is a masterpiece. Buy it now.

I really enjoy this game because it's such a simple, compact game that actually has a lot to it and has very large amounts of replayability. You play as a ship from 1 of 4 factions on a randomly generated map (which you can also edit to your desire which is an awesome touch). There are towns throughout the map from which you can take on quests, trade, and even capture for your faction. There are also pirates throughout the world that you must fight as well through your travels. Towns grow as you complete quests for them and along the way you can upgrade your ship. There are actually a lot of stats and customization when it comes to your ship, with different types of crew, sails, captains, etc. I have not come across any bugs personally. The combat it rather simple, just toggle Volley while you circle your enemy. There are upgrades for more powerful means of combat such as gas clouds and such.The graphics aren't the prettiest but they are enjoyable and don't diminish the gameplay. It's actually a rather soothing game in a way and I can see myself losing hours upon hours in it, completing quest after quest. I would rate this 9/10.

Introduction
I bought this game as soon as I finished the first Life is Strange, since I felt like I needed more and could not just let the experience end there.  Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a prequel to the game that came before it, simply titled Life is Strange.  In this game you play as one of the antagonists, from the first game, Chole Price; 3 years before the events of the first game.
Story
I personally like Before the Storm more than the first game, and I really enjoyed the first game.  I feel like 3 episodes was enough to show the story and growth between Chloe and Rachel.  The story of Before the Storm is emotional, captivating and extremely well thought out.  The writers have truly achieved something special with this game.  To see how the relationship between Chloe and Rachel grow is enthralling.  I will not explain any of the plot because there is not a lot to say without spoiling the game, and I feel like the best experience is going in blind.  Although I do recommend playing through the first game before you play through this one, but that is down to personal preference.
Length
To some, 3 episodes does not seem like a lot.  But for what this game is trying to achieve I think it fits.  I feel like if there were more episodes the story might have repeated itself; and to be honest it took me, on average, 3 hours to complete an episode.  That is quite some time.  Once I finished the game I felt like the amount of episodes and the story itself are intertwined.  The story was fantastic and I feel like if they dedicated more time to it then it might have become washed down with unmeaningful dialogue and just filler in terms of story.
Visuals
I will put this out there.  I love the Life is Strange art direction.  It gives the game more of a sense of simpleness and minimalism, but then it changes when you get into a conversation with someone and you see that the depth of the game isn’t to do with the graphics but is about the characters and the story they tell.  The scenery is something that is of importance in this game, since a conversation is not just about what is being said, it is also about where it is being said.  Something emotional said in a field is not going to have the same effect as if it was said at a house party.  Or at least that is my take on it.  Another thing to mention is that, mainly with Chloe and Rachel, the facial animations and overall gestures are far better than the first game, you can see what they are feeling; and that is something that just adds a tad more depth into the game.
Soundtrack
Once again the music used is spectacular.  With a majority of the music used made by the band Daughter.  I once read a comment that said the main menu music sums up Choles life, and once listening to it, I truly believe this; and this is something you do not get from most games.  Of course it is rare when you find a game where the music doesn't fit the setting but on the opposite side it rare to find a game where the music fits so well it almost doesn't seem right.
Mechanics
Now of course Chloe cannot rewind time like Max could in the first game.  So one of the mechanics that was added is called Backtalk, very suiting for Chloe might I add.  Backtalk is a risk/ reward conversation system in which Chloe, well back talks, to get her own way.  The game mentions that you need to listen carefully to what your opponent says and you need to choose a relating response, and you have to do so carefully because if you fail you cannot rewind time and try again like you could in the first game.
Cons
No game is perfect and although I think this game is phenomenal it has its faults.  One thing I will admit before continuing is that the game does not have nearly as much lip syncing issues as it did in the first game.  When playing I felt like some of the characters movements were out of sync, although I knew they weren't I could not stop feeling that way.  For example in one scene you are speaking to one of the characters and he lifts his arms up in confusion/ anger, but this was done with no dialogue the only sound was ambient and I couldn't help but feel like that body language would have worked far better during the conversation itself.  Although I mentioned that the lip syncing problem was not as prominent in this game as it waa the first, there was one scene where I felt like it still was an issue.  It happens during an encounter in Rachel's household.  I am still not sure if it was intentional or if I just feel like I was looking for it since I knew it was a problem in the first game.
That is the end of my review of Life is Strange: Before the Storm.  I am sure I missed out some things, but nothing is perfect.
If you are a fan of the original Life is Strange then you for sure need to buy this game, I believe you will thoroughly enjoy it.
In my review of the first Life is Strange I referred to it being a masterpiece and that I think it  needs to be played by as many people as possible.
I feel the exact same way, and more, about Life is Strange Before the Storm.
Two words, BITTERSWEET MASTERPIECE.

Spec Ops: The Line is an interesting game. It's basically a game about choices, and the deconstruction of those choices making them meaningless, making the player question them. Also it's about showing the player the horror of war and what it can do to a person. The game has a great story, with characters who have personal arcs as the story goes. It's a shame the gameplay is mediocre at best, with a Gears of War like combat system, only not as well implemented.
I recommend this game to those who can look past it's sub-par gameplay aspect, and want to know the story.

Lead a Delta Force squad through Dubai after it's been hit by a storm wall, submerging most of the city under dunes and leaving the populace in violent disarray.
The story hits hard, so hard you want to stop when realizing what you have done, but you push on regardless.
Gameplay feels like Gears of War, but the team cohesion and shouts of the combat zone feel like something more.
The voice acting is all top-notch, making each character personable and the banter between eachother feel real.
Ammunition is as scarce as it should be, so expect to swap weapons and keep moving.
Story choices give healthy replay along with hidden intel to expand the story.
The soundtrack was perfect for the type of game and very enjoyable personally.
Most certainly worth the purchase!

When I first heard of Undertale, I had no interest in playing it. I thought the fanbase was massively cringeworthy and the game was probably uninteresting.
I was correct about the fanbase, but boy was I wrong about the game.
I normally play action/adventure RPG games with the occasional sprinkling of singleplayer FPS. I am not the kind of person to normally go in for conceptual hipster nonsense, and I say that because that's what I thought this game was.
In reality, it has some of the best atmosphere and writing I've seen in a game in a very long time. And above all else, it manages to be heart-rendingly (no pun indended) sad at times and actually funny at other times. Plus, the music is fantastic and the whole package has a level of care I don't often see anymore.
You are doing yourself a disservice if you don't try this game out. And I don't say that lightly.

I've only played this for a few hours, and there is still lots of the game I've yet to see, but I already know that I like it.
There is very little in the way of a tutorial, and nowhere to look up keybinds (although you can assign new keybinds as you go), but once you get past these small obstacles and figure out how to play properly, it is a very fun game. Relaxing, especially in the lower level areas.
The first zone was almost entirely at peace. There were a few pirates to dispatch, but once they were gone, the only other I could encounter pirates there was when I took a mission to hunt one down. Pretty much what you would expect for any MMO starting zone. Enough to get your toes wet, but not enough to overwhelm you.
The second zone opens at level three, although you may want to consider putting off going there until level 5 at least. When you arrive, you cannot do any trading until the zone has been taken from the pirates that are trying to control it. This is basically a small capture the flag event, combined with blasting pirates. Take out pirates and towers, find a captured town or lighthouse, and park up next to it. That's all you need to do to capture it, which will change the allegiance of the town to your own.
Once the zone has been cleared of pirates, trade becomes possible, although be careful. After a while, a small pirate fleet will arrive and try to take the zone back.
Well, that's about as far as I've got, but it is a thoroughly enjoyable game, and I'm looking forward to seeing the rest of it.
Edit:
I had a technical problem, where I couldn't create worlds or join them. Basically made the game unplayable. But, the technical support was brilliant. Mine was an odd problem which ended up having nothing to do with the game itself, but rather one of the Steam DLLs. Michael (the developer) was of great help in finding and fixing the problem with contact and new ideas each day until it was resolved.

Now lets get into the review!

You are playing as captain Walker. a delta force operator who was dropped in Dubai for a mission to find survivers of the failed evacuation of Dubai. but when you and your team reach the outskirts of Dubai everything goes south real fast. You get ambushed and attacked from all sides. And you seem to be landing deep in a ♥♥♥♥♥torm. after a while you find some terrible secrets about Dubai after the sandstorm. your mission just changed: SURVIVE

This is a 3th person shooter with cover based shooting mechanics. The game has some responsive controls and plays very well, you can also command your squad to stun the enemy with flashbangs or kill them from a distance to get you out of pretty messy situations. It is a bit more tactical than most shooters of this genre. You can choose from a variety of weapons do completely destroy your enemies, ranging from pistols to long range rifles. The gameplay ain't anything special but it works well for this game. Jump in and out of cover while you try to dodge bullets and command your 2 comrades in battle.
The game has some really neat graphics and it looks good for a thirdperson shooter. The devs really brought a post-apocalyptic hit by a sandstorm Dubai to life. Destroyed enviroments, broken buildings and snad.. lots and lots of sand. as for the voice acting I have nothing to complain. The voice actors did a good job. The game itself did not suffer from bad framerate and bugs, glitches. nothing to take me out of the game. It is well optimized and there are enough settings to mess around with at the menu.

Pros:
Very fun and highly addictive for someone with a competitive nature.
Very easy to learn if you take the time, no need for a basketball background.
Lots of customization for your player(s) including, clothes, attributes, cards, toys, skills, ceremonies, and freestyles.
Joining a crew is easy and the players in most crews are willing to help.
Almost everything can be bought with in-game currency.
Very easy to find and enter a game.
3 different channels splits up the levels so you aren't playing high levels as a level 1.
8 different character types. (Center, Power Forward, Small Forward, Shooting Guard, Point Guard, Swing, Dual Guard, and Control Tower)
Great events that help you get items otherwise unobtainable.
In game currency is very easy to come by. (You start with something like 40,000 points and you gain 100-300+ per game. Items cost somewhere between 5,000-12,000 and if you want to add attributes to your items it's another like 8,000 I believe)
Cons:
A LOT of annoying and cancerous players who do nothing but shout about how much better they are than you.
If you have a high ping theres almost no way you can play the C, PF, or CT position.
Almost no sign of GMs.
The game is HEAVILY team based. Meaning if your team sucks, you can't solo win.
A lot of players from European and Asian servers play on the North American server and lag terribly.
All of this being said, I've been playing this game since the first installment all the way back when it was made by Sierra. Me and my friend put hundreds of hours into this game back then and after it was sold to GameKiss we stopped playing because the servers were bad. Now that it's back and the server problem has been fixed we love playing with each other again. If you do pick this game up and start playing send me a message in game at either BMxStryker or BMxRebounds or BMxVulcan and I'll do my best to teach you the basics that the tutorial doesn't.

But seriously, suprisingly pretty nice game to play while I'm just trying to kill time.  It has easy and simple controls and mechanics.  Has an RPG element added to it, which I personally love.  You can build colonies, and have faction wars.  You can run cargo and passengers.  In my opinion there are a good amount of things you can do without it getting annoyingly repetitive.  I myself enjoy pirate hunting above all, the combat system is easy and relatively stress free.  Simple button activated skill combined with auto firing cannon sysrems make for easy transitions from exploration to combat.  Combat which can include a great many ships at once.
What I would like from this game?  A better soundtrack for one.  It would be cool to add some shanties(one of my favorite things from Assassin's Creed Black Flag).  I like where they are musically for the most part, but perhaps some more diversity would help immersion?  It's a bit childish, some themes are definitely geared towards a younger play audience, understandably.
Furthermore, REPETITIVE.  Everything, especially the beggining, is very repetitive.  They MUST add a content update for this game to survive.  They need bigger maps, they need more music(as stated above), and some awesome world bosses would be cool as well.
All in all, what I got when I bought it was much better than I expected.  I got it because I enjoy naval combat and what I got was more so than I had previously thought.  I have hopes for a content update so for now, for an on sale price, it was worth it.

Now I only played 2.5 hours of this game, but that is mostly because I got bored of the grind. I might give it another go if I am very bored, but I doubt I will play much longer in it's current state.
Windward has many good points, the game itself is an excellent idea but it grows boring very quickly, even the music was amazing at first until I realized it was just the same two tracks on loop over and over. It got incredibly repetitive.
This game would be fantastic if it was one huge map maybe 10x or 15x the size of the current map size, then everyone on the same map fighting for control. But as it is now you go to one map, clear it out of pirates, do some quests, move on and repeat. It gets tiresome quickly, the progression speed also seems very slow (unless I did something very wrong, but if I did it wasn't explained to me through any form of ingame tutorial). I spent 2.5 hours with this game and got 1 new ship and 3 upgrades for my ship.
Overall, if you don't mind repetitive grinding then go for it. Also if you have friends to play with this game might be more fun, or perhaps some future content patch will make it better. But in it's current state I can't recommend it unless you don't mind blowing 13€ (or your regional equivalent) for a few hours of fun (a trip to the cinema cost the same so why not) until you get bored of the grind.
Short summary of good / bad.
The good:
- Fun concept
- Great UI (most indie games suck, but I was impressed with windward UI)
- Pretty looking game
- Good music (but repetitive very quickly)
- Combat seems interesting and lots of stats if you like numbers.
- Seems to have a lot of customization options through items, even though I didn't get to play with it much.
The bad:
- Extremely repetitive (even the music gets old fast)
- A few bugs (like pirates would spawn in areas I couldn't get to, so impossible to complete quest)
- Very slow progress, I just don't have the time to play a game for 5+ hours to get to the fun stuff. Then I'd rather play a game where I have fun from the start.
As a final note I would like to say this is definitely a game to keep an eye on, if the repetitiveness of the gameplay gets fixed in the future I would be happy to recommend this game.

New graphics engine and new trucks, which is not necessarily good, because I'm honestly struggling to take a liking to these modern models. I wouldn't mind some models from the 80's or 90's being put in, especially since there is not much variety in the offer. There are only 7 brands  and most of them have only 2 models and they are only of the tractor-trailer type. There are no models with a "bed" instead of a trailer. pay attention to trucks in real life and you'll see how much they differ, especially if you live in a country where living standards don't allow every company to have only brand-new models from Europe's biggest producers.
Otherwise, it's same old game, just in new clothes, nothing ground-breaking new.
And the upcoming American Truck Simulator will be even worse, back to the (overdone, tired and boring) USA map for the I-don't-know-which-anymore visit.
My preference would be for the next game to instead take place in a country that we've never been to yet. South America with it's dangerous mountain roads to it's desolate south regions, Africa with everything from excellent tarmac roads to almost unpassable dirt tracks, Asia with everything possible and lastly the iconic Russia. Of all these interesting possibilities the developers sadly decided to reuse the one they've done to death.
In ETS2 there is also too little road hazards (unless you count crashes between AI drivers which are frequent or even AI drivers as road hazard themselves). A bigger variety and randomly-moving would be better.
I would actually rate older titles in the series, Pedal to the Metal, Haulin' and American Long Haul, according to their features much higher than ETS2, even though they take place on that old map.
The games actually LOST content as the series progressed. ETS2 is even more basic in features than the original 18 Wheels of Steel. That one at least had more country roads and you could amuse yourself by asking NPC truckers for weather and cops. ETS2 doesn't have many interesting roads (it's mostly Autobahn and other countries' counteparts) and you can't talk to NPCs. On the other hand it does have much better physics, driving models, some nice mountain sections, controls and of course graphics.
But what is no doubt keeping sales up is the multiplayer mod. It can be very fun to play with friends, especially if you form a convoy of managable size. And now that most of the trolls have been rooted out (that doesn't mean there aren't any left though!) it can be pretty unfrustrating play. Bewarned though, admins are pretty ruthless and, as a side-effect of the troll infestation, ideas have been coming up on forums of more draconic rules, reduced freedom of play and unpleasant features.
But that is not where this game shines. It's not about excitement or grind or trolls, but it's about relaxation and simple joy in driving. I've never played a game that would calm me down like this and that could be this unfrustrating.
If you're one of the people who simply go drive for the simple pleasure of the drive, this game is for you. It will give you 80% of the same feeling and emotions and save you a lot of money on fuel.

I can definitely say that this game is worth the money. This comes from someone who really isn't that big into hunting, and my experience on the subject is limited. I've played hunting games before, but none quite like this. I haven't played a hunting game that I genuinely enjoyed or put hours into. I can see me putting hundreds of hours into this game given that the developers keep working to imrpove it. I'll simplify the review with a standard pros/cons list.
- The game is incredibly beautiful, one of the most stunningly graphical games I've ever played. Seriously. The atmosphere and diversity within the environment is incredible. Your relationship to the world is what makes it special and different. Every piece of grass you step on, every fallen leaf, twig, or branch your brush against seems like an actual object. The sound design also aids this very well. It makes you genuinely feel like you are out in the woods, it's not hard to close your eyes and imagine the breeze of the wind or the calls of the birds/crickets as if you were really there. This game makes me want to go camping or backpacking.
- The gunplay is pretty great. It's one of those games that replicate shooting a gun extremely well, and it's immersive. There's nothing like sighting a buck for three minutes, and finally pulling the trigger as you get the perfect shot. The bang rings out and roars throughout the land, and things become still as the smoke settles and you see that you hit your shot. The different rifles, revolvers, bows, shotguns, and all are pleasant to use and keep things interesting.
- The rating system/trophy score is pretty good, albeit it needs work which I will explain below. It takes into account how large the animal was, whether it had antlers or a unique hide/fur, how well you placed your shot, and with what kind of weapon you used. For example, I would not want to blow up a poor little fox with a 12 gauge. Bad tropy. Shoot a buck with a 12 gauge? Good trophy.
- The tracking system is really good. I would never have thought that I'd have fun tracking a deer I shot poorly for thirty minutes.
- There's a decent variety of animals to hunt (tons of deer, foxes, bison, moose, a few bears, boar, lynxs, coyotes, elk, maybe a few more I'm missing).
- Mulitplayer is fun, and hunting with a buddy can be a great experience.
- Animal behavior is accurate and done exceptionally well. As with the rating system, it does require work. It's sometimes enjoyable to just sit on top of a hill and just watch. I've watched deer, bisons, foxes, and bears without shooting them simply just because it is enjoyable.
- The quest system and the perk/skill trees are done very well.
- The rating system, while good, needs a lot of improvements and tweaking. It doesn't take into account (at least it doesn't show us visually), the size or point-rating of the antlers. The game would benefit from having a trophy room where you can also go back and view all of your top harvests.
- There's a few issues with the penetration of some of the weapons, many are underpowered. The shotguns specifically need fixed. 12 gauge buckshot is too weak, and the spread is almost akin to an unrealistic COD degree. You can shoot a doe with "BUCK"shot who is 20-25 meters in front of you, your shot can be placed perfectly, and she will not fall. Instead you'll have to track her for fourty-sixty meters until you find her dead. IMO that's not acceptable or realistic at all.
- The animals could use some diversity in terms of visuals. If you run into a group of five or six fallow does, they all look almost identicaly except for slight size variations which you can make out. Same with the other animals.
- There's a good number of bugs, I'll be honest. Thankfully none of them are game-breaking, to me they're personally not even considered annoyances. They're just kind of... there. I won't get too in depth, but sometimes when you shoot an animal it just freezes for two seconds before falling. The AI can get stuck sometimes when in tough terrain, but they eventually find their way out. Binoculars can be wonky when you open the map while zoomed in with them. There's plenty.
- The DLC, while worth the money, I am concerned of it becoming just a cash-grab to Expansive Worlds. Medved-Taiga is worth every penny, and I don't regret buying the ATV's or camping equipment. But in my opinion, it's a
game. I shouldn't have to pay for that. I'd love to see some more free content.
- The game needs more activities. Bird hunting? Turkeys, rabbits? Expansive Worlds, the devs, gives us birdshot in the game but if you shoot a bird or rabbit with them it's useless (you don't get any XP/money). Maybe even fishing. As with above, it could use some more content and a larger variety of animals.
- I'm listing bugs twice. They need fixed, and it seems as if the devs don't have communication between them and their playerbase as a top priority. It would be nice to know what they're doing with the game, and what they are considering for its future.
- The UI in the menus could use a bit of polishing. It's pretty complex and I think it could be simplified or easier to navigate.
So that's that. I do honestly and fully believe the pros outweigh the cons, and I don't regret a dime on this game. On a scale of 1-10, I might even be generous enough to give it an 8.1/10. I see me playing this game a lot in the future. That is going to be especially true if the developers polish some of the weak spots, fix the bugs that exist, and add more content to the game. Check it out!

A game of Rogue Legacy is 30% luck, 30% skill, and 40% good planning.
You start as a knight who enters a castle filled with demons, skeletons and monsters. Of course, you inevitably die. However, you're then able to select your heir, who you then will take control of to do the same again. Heirs can have different classes with different stats (knights can take a beating, mages can cast spells, knaves can sneak about, etc.) and with randomly selected traits.
These traits range from the useful (gigantism, hypergonadism etc.) to the disadvantageous (ectomorph, vertigo etc.) to the just sort of funny (hyperchondriac, irritable bowel syndrome etc.). Every single time you die, you select a new heir, which means that gameplay is always changing and no two runs are the same.
The castle is procedurally generated, shaking up the formula every time, and is littered with treasure chests and runes which can be used to upgrade characters. While in the later stages this allows you to customise your playstyle, in the beginning, when you haven't got the skills to collect enough loot, it can get pretty frustrating.
Overall, this is a fun, unique game with several measures put in place to keep things interesting. If you've got some extra money and have an hour or so to kill, I'd say check it out.

Rogue Legacy isn't necessarily a bad game.  It's just not the game for everyone.  I for one, was intrigued by the concept of genetics playing a role in the characters.  And while that is a quintessential element of this game, I feel that it is overshadowed completely by two factors: difficulty and repetitiveness.  First off, the game is EXTREMELY difficult.  One of the hardest games I've ever played.  The enemy patterns are unpredictable at first and as you quickly die, it becomes increasingly difficult to upgrade your weapons or general stats as you don't make enough gold.  This leads me to my next point, the game is repetitive.  Go into the castle, collect gold, die, pray you made enough to upgrade something, go into castle, collect gold, die, pray again...  The castle is randomly generated each time so there is variation, but it all feels the same to me.  Just not the game for me.  Glad I tried it, wasn't happy in the end.

When talking about Spec-ops the line, it is often the setting, characters and story line that is discussed and celebrated. What is often overlooked is that this game boasts some of the tightest, most tactile controls you will find in an action game, let alone a third person shooter. The enemy AI is another phenomenal asset of this game: rarely have I struggled to predict enemy flanking paterns after the, for real, fourth playthrough. The harder difficulty settings are brutal and very satisfying. Weapons are not to plentiful, but each gun is very different from the next.
The cover system is perfect. Rarely does it feel so smooth to run and gun and hop from cover to cover. The team-member mechanics are very interesting and really fun to use.

You may find Spec Ops: The Line a little bit linear, because it is, but the story it's one of the best I've ever encountered, especially in a shooter game. The graphics are still really good for today, and the level design it's a top one! I really recommend playing this game, not because of the gameplay, that isn't extraordinary, but because of the graphics, level design, and the amazing story!

These aren't just mobs spawning they're human beings. Too many times I forget this in other shooters. Some of the plot details are racy and controversial, but I think they're what really set it apart from CoDs/ Battlefields. Controls could be a bit sticky at times, especially when it came to cover and vaulting. You're no bullet sponge either so expect to die...a lot. Seriously, even on normal this one is tough. Soundtrack is killer as well. All in all a refreshing change and well worth the on-sale price. Don't pass this one up!
Without a smidget of irony, this game is art. Not the "pretty color, look at this game, video games are art, guise" stuff, but a truely thought provoking expirence.

A series of dust storms has destroyed much of Dubai, leaving countless civilians stranded. The 33rd Battalion, a United States infantry unit, is sent to provide aid but soon disappears. In a last ditch effort, a three-man Delta Force team is sent in to find out what happened and rescue survivors. As captain of this reconnaissance team it is up to you and your teammates to fight your way across the city and find answers.
Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter where you will find that you are heavily reliant on cover. You have the ability to command your teammates in battle, telling them who to target. Combat is fast paced and fun, albeit a bit generic. My main complaint with combat would be that the AI sometimes feels a bit clumsy, but nothing bad enough to be game breaking.
The game is very story rich and is definitely worth paying attention to. Occasionally you will be forced to make some very difficult decisions. What I liked about this is that there is never really a “right” or “wrong” answer. Unlike some military shooters, this game does not glorify war. Instead it touches on the horrors of war and the profound psychological impact it often has on those who experience it.
The environment is absolutely breathtaking, by far my favorite in any game ever. They did a wonderful job at making Dubai look so ruined yet beautiful, resulting in a few areas where you have to stop just to admire your surroundings.
I realize that this can vary quite a bit from person to person but I was pleasantly surprised by the music used in the game. Quite a few classics including Hendrix and Deep Purple, as well as some more modern but worthwhile bands such as the Black Angels. If that’s not your thing, it’s still worth mentioning that the original score is pretty solid.
I’m normally extremely skeptical of military shooters, but this game is something else entirely and is now considered among my favorite games.  A bit shorter than I would have liked it to be, but still one that I would highly recommend.

At the start of the game, you may be thinking this is just another modern shooter...
By the end of the game, you'll be proven wrong. The story-telling in this game is unmatched.  If you want a game that shows the true, grim side of war, this is that game.
10/10 Masterpiece.

This classic pirate style gameplay is back in full force and now COOP! Vast worlds and large faction battles make this game unique from the rest of the games on the steam Library. Do you wanna help cities grow large and make everyone richer in the region or simply want to defend your home land from invaders this is the game for you.

Impressions:
For years, I've searched for a worthy successor of Sid Meier's Pirates! and this game comes pretty damn close. Foregoing the over the top personality and story elements that immerse you in the Caribbean, this game instead optimizes the combat, navigation and creates massive randomly generated worlds for you to sail around and to blow ships up in. You have skills, both passive and active, which make you a more effective combatant and if you'd rather just play the merchant game, you can sail amongst a massive number of towns building up large sums of gold. Also, the music is ridiculously relaxing in this game and top down sailing has never been so pleasurable. This game is incredibly promising and already a heck of a lot of fun with four different factions to battle between and a large number of ships to sail. You can expect I'll definitely spend some more time in this Age of Sail foray.

It is as it says on the tin, you sail a boat, destroy other boats, trade,  upgrade and fit your boat with increasingly more powerful stuff. It has its moments, but leans on a tendency to be a bit of a grind, at least out of the box. So for those that remember those older sailing ship trading and fighting management games, you're bound to find something you like. It's pricing is, acceptable. But a discount is always nice.
Play with your friends, and if you shouldn't have some (close at hand) find some swashbuckling mates in an online sessions to hook up with.
Went for supplies on the beach after a battle, sunk my own ship. 10/10 would sink again

If you expect a clone of Pirates! or Port Royal you might get disappointed. This game has a different focus and feels closer to Action-RPGs like Diablo or Sacred combined with arena multiplayer kinda like Guild Wards.
You have an inventory just that instead of collecting swords and helms you collect Sails, Crew Members, Cannons, Captains. They have random stats and can be common, rare etc. There's a skill tree that unfortunatly is not very complex and Items have a level requirement.
It's not like Pirates! or others where you can freely travel the map. Well in theory you could however the world is divided in zones and similar to for example Word of Warcraft each zone has a suggested level, so throughout the game you progress from zone to zone and going to a zone with a much higher level will most likely result in your death.
So theres constant progression and because of that there's also grinding. However grinding is much more fun, at least for me, than it is in hack and slays. That is because one thing that fortunately is very similar to pirates! is the combat - positioning and outmanouvering your enemy is key and can help you take down bigger enemies.
You have skills with a cooldown you can use in combat. They are also comparable to action RPGs, for example you can place an AOE effect that places a neon-green fog that will damage every enemy that stays within it. They make combat even more interesting but they also break with the otherwise realistic setting.
The combat mechanics are quite fun. You take cities and other buildings like lighthouses and defensive towers by stayin in a given area as long as no enemy is around. Theres a progress bar that fills over time similar to battlefield. The AI is also decent. You can buy buildings and place them on the map at strategic important positions. If offered the right quest you can even place new cities.
Theres also trading however it's WAY to simple. You can't buy specific units of something, instead you buy one "slot" of something. At the start you have two slots available, later on you can store up to 5 goods. In other games that offer trading you can buy a varieng amount of goods and the price for each ton was re-calculated after each transaction.
If you want to increase profit from trading in this game you mostly do this by equiping better items instead of min/maxing your routes and carefully calculating profit margins.
This game really is mostly a arena PVP game with fun naval combat mechanics (which make grinding much more tolerable) and typical RPG elements. I imagine that PVP is a lot of fun however I have not tried it yet and I could imagine that the progression system makes PVP unfair for new players.

Captain's Log
Day 1.
I am swayed by promises of power into joining the Valiant faction, a faction renowned for its military prowess.
My newly aquired ship resides at the port of Aswall, a small seaside town. The sea calls to me, and I am eager to set sail, but before I head off, I ask a local clerk if he has any assignments for me to carry out. As it turns out, a few passengers are in great hurry to get to the town of Seatoncreek, and I am also tasked with pinpointing the exact location of said town.
This turns out to be easier than expected, as my passengers give me the location of their destination.
After a few final checks, I finally set sail.
My humble sloop, its sailcloth embroidered with the fearful image of a lion's head, drift across the sea. The few islands that pass are blanketed with the snow that fall mercilessly from the heavens. The cold has caused small islands of ice to form on the water's surface, but that does not stop me from reaching my destination.
When I reach the port, I say goodbye to my passengers, who thank me for my services with a purse of coins. Delighted with my day's work, I decide to stay in Seatoncreek for the time being.
Day 2.
A notice board in Seatoncreek tells me of a notorious pirate known as Rasnaris, and about a bounty placed on his head. I decide to take up the hunt.
As I travel south, I pass by a fellow ship of the Valiants. I travel with him for some time, and just when I am about to break formation, a ship flying black sails appears in the distance. I have found Rasnaris.
A battle ensues, with my brave ally taking Rasnaris on head-on. I, on the other hand, unexperienced in battle as I am, decide to stay far away, firing volleys at Rasnaris from afar. After a battle that has us going back up all the way to Seatoncreek, Rasnaris finally begins taking in water, and sinks shortly after. Victory!
Day 3.
I pick up a few missions to ferry cargo to distant towns, and I get to know the local waters a bit better. I also come across a few pieces of floating cargo, that I greedily pick up. After some time, I come across another bounty, this time on a felon known as Kerhen. I decide to hunt him down.
After some sailing, I find Kerhen. There is no time for proper introductions, as cannonballs instantly begin to soar through the air. This time, I am on my own.
My vessel proves to be more well-equipped than Kerhens. He sinks to the bottom of the ocean, and I claim my reward.
Day 4.
I recive notice that a nearby town, Waber, has been capruted by pirates. I head towards it in order to investigate this matter further, and most of all see if I can attempt to recapture it.
The town appears to be unguarded, and I capture it without any interference. As I enter Waber as its saviour, I am told that there are two pirates in the area. For the future safety of the town, I hunt them down and bring them justice.
Day 5.
This region is too peaceful. I crave for the screams of my enemies! I travel to one of the outer regions owned by the Valiant, which, supposedly, has a bit of a pirate problem. I am assured of this fact as I almost immediately come across a pirate settlement protected by a tower. I make short work of the tower and capture the settlement in the name of the Valiant.
Day 6.
I capture more of the pirate scum's settlements. None will stand in the way of the Valiant!
As I get close to yet another one of their pitiful hamlets, I am greeted by two pirate ships. In my hubris, I take them both on. The mistake proves to be almost fatal. I sink the first one without much problems, but my hull has taken quite a few hits, which the late pirate's mate takes advantage of. At first, I try taking him on, only to notice that my hull won't hold. I retreat, hoping that my ship is faster than his. I am in luck, as this proves to be the case.
Fate, however, does not favor me this day, as I run into a large island, preventing my escape. I have to face my adversary.
I sail along the island's shore, hoping that I will, still, be able to outrun him. This time, however, he keeps up, and lines up for a broadside. I quickly and abruptly turn around and sail towards the front of his ship, moving me out of the line of fire. I fire a desperate volley at his ship, which proves to be more effective than I dared to think. The cannonballs rip through his sailcloth and puncture his hull, and he goes down to the bottom of the sea.
Day 7. I have proven my worth to the Valiant. The region is under Valiant control once more. As I set sail for new waters once again, I gaze once more upon the mighty ships stationed in the docks of the more prominent towns. Huge vessels fitted with brass-lined cannons.
Cannons that I, one day, will fire upon the enemies of the Valiant. And woe betide anyone that dares to stand in my way.

Recommendation Bonus if you liked games such as side-scrolling adventuring Castlevanias (Simon's Quest, Symphony of the Night). Recommendation Bonus if want to try Rogue-like games in a platform setting.
Background: This is my second rogue-like game. This game has been hard on me with the random traits and classes only furthering that difficulty and killing my enthusiasm for it. Still, I saw this game had a lot of heart from its developers embedded into the game and that kept me going.
Some points, may be pluses for some, negatives for others, or neutrals.
* Enjoyed the 2D graphical style
* Enjoyed the music overall that sometimes harkened back to that early 90's video game music
Gameplay:
* Side-scrolling platform adventure with RPG elements and permanent death
* Played with a gamepad, did not try to play with keyboard/mouse yet
* Controls may sometimes feel unresponsive when performing two actions simultaneously such as jumping and swinging a sword or moving and swing a sword ~ if you adjust to it, you may sometimes use this lag to your advantage to swing while stepping backwards, but can initially lead to missed swings and/or death by not stopping the enemy's attack
* Fight monsters, avoid traps, explore a single large castle with four major areas, find coin and treasure, gambit with statues or encounters of luck or misfortune, fight bosses to progress the main story, read through the logs of those that ventured the castle before you to piece a greater mystery, die and leave your wealth to your descendants to improve their odds of success before paying the gatekeeper all of your wealth to ensure that to buy upgrades, you will need to have a good money run
* You have access to a standard sword swing, a jumping down stab, a magic attack that is often randomly assigned to your hero at the start and if applicable a class-special ability
* You choose one of three heroes each attempt from a random selection of traits and unlocked classes
* Classes consist of such things as knights who are balanced with the ability to block, barbarians with a large health pool and the ability to shout enemies away, wizards with a large mana pool to use more magic, ninja who can move quick with strong sword attacks, miners who have low combat attributes - but find more gold and can locate chests on the map and more
* Traits can drastically alter gameplay and are randomly selected, such as dwarfism which allows your hero to fit in narrow passages that may avoid some enemies or find treasure, as well as make it easier to dodge, but shorten their sword arm - or hypochondriac where you hero exaggerates how much damage they take, making it difficult to tell how dangerous an enemy really is - or vertigo, that makes the screen upside down and reverse while making half of your controls backwards ~ you may end up with one or more of these traits to make for an interesting, frustrating or nauseating experience
* You can spend the gold of your predecessor to increase health, mana, strength, intelligence, encumbrance limit, unlock new classes, increase the gold found on subsequent playthroughs and more - however, increasing any aspect will raise the price of the others, so you may want to consider the direction you would like to take as you unlock more upgrades
* You can discover equipment recipes and attachable runes in chests or completing challenges, equipment such as a sword that reduces the damage received, armor that allows you to drain health from enemies at the expense of less max health, runes that let you make an extra jump or runes that give you mana when attacking an enemy
* Dungeons are mostly randomized with four major areas that remain in the same general directions - this may result in dungeons that are too brutal for a new player to places too easy for a veteran ~ when exploring, you can hire an engineer-like character to lock the current dungeon design at the expense of much of your earnings, giving you a chance to continue exploring the same setup if you like the layout or if you want another shot at a boss
* Optional Challenge Rooms that do not count toward destroying your game progress ~ using a preset hero against advanced versions of a boss
* New Game Plus with enemies of greater stats ~ have not tried to explore more to see if there may be new enemy types or enemy attack patterns (edit: just finished New Game +1 and +2, the spike of difficulty with new enemy attack patterns created so much screen chaos and bullet hell that I ran to the bosses for safety, I don't have it in me to try New Game +3 or go achievement hunting)
* Easter eggs and references to various sources throughout the game's content, gave it a light-hearted or personal touch
Difficulty:
* The game's difficulty varies greatly based on what hero you have available, your personal play style, what dungeon you're presented with and if fighting a boss, if you're adapted to the overall boss tactics and taking advantage of your class/trait (if applicable) tactics ~ overall, the game is on the harder side and can be rewarding as you clear out areas or go through past locations with greater confidence
* Does not appear to be a guaranteed way to recover health or mana in the castle, leading you to eventually run out of recovery items and die as you make mistakes
* The game auto-saves, so if you're having a bad run and losing health, it's going to remember that, sometimes it can be more convenient to you as the player to accept the sweet embrace of death
* Most deaths were attempting to adapt to boss mechanics, died approximately 118 times over 9.2 hours or approximately one death every 5 minutes ~ the hero that cleared the main story is one hit away from death (edit: 135 times over 14.5 hours and three playthroughs, just going to put this game down now before the amount of screen activity on New Game +3 causes an epileptic seizure)
ESRBish/Content Advisory:
* Some characters are depicted farting with visual trails of their mishaps and may decrease the enjoyment of the curry you're eating
* Some characters see the screen upside down and backwards, which may disorient some players
* There is an image of an 8-bit man sitting on a toilet, could not recall if his genitalia was drawn with three pixels or if it that is part of his first two legs
* There may be some occasional language when reading murals such as "sh*t"
* Some dark themes

I really wanted to like this game. And while it started out with a lot of promise, it would suffer the same flaws as many permadeath games recently released. And let me preface by saying if video games were suicide, I would want the wood chipper, head first. I love punishing games, when they are made by competent people! With that said, right off the bat, your weapon has a horrible delay which is comparable only to Simon Belmont's whip in the first Castlevania on the NES. I would've said the controls were delayed like Dragon's Lair on NES but I'm not that cruel. Not a deal breaker, however, almost three decades later one may think controls might become a tad more responsive. I guess not. The next giant flaw and by far the most ridiculous is that I cannot count the number times an enemy would just spawn underneath my character while he would be standing in a stationary position. Make the game as difficult as you please, just please cut the cheap crap. I would rather the developer just start me with one HP than resort to cheap tricks to depleat health. Sometimes when you enter a room you will be given an objective. Complete the objective and you get to open a treasure chest. Sometimes you'll have five seconds from the time you enter a room to find the chest and open it. Only problem, by the time you glance at the pop up window to see what it says, valuable time has already worn off the clock. Upgrading also looked to be sweet initially but turned out to be an abortion. Just in case you haven't figured out already, you are going to die a lot in this game, which is fine. Sounds great right? Well, it would be if upgrade prices didn't rise every single time you died. It just seems like someone was trying a little too hard to be clever but never hit the epiphany that they really aren't. Let me put it into perspective. Lets say you want to buy a house, but every time you call your real estate agent the price goes up a couple of hundred bucks. Now call dozens of times and watch the price soar. It would get annoying pretty quickly. Was there someone on the development team who was a finance major and wanted to be cute with the game's upgrading system? Inflation is a necessary concept in economics and finance, not in a medieval video game. Oh, and by the way, every time you die death takes all of your money before letting you back into the castle for another run. So, don't think you'll be able to stock pile loot. What's the necessity of talking to death every time you die? Why not just remove all of the money automatically and reduce the dreadful monotony? As far as the good goes, the soundtrack is well done and combat can get pretty intense from time to time. It doesn't sound like it, but his game is teetering on the brink of something great. Iron out the major flaws that ruin the experience and this would be a stellar game. Heck, even removing upgrade inflation would make this game an easy eight.

The gameplay dynamic in Windward goes from calm, controlled and thoughtful (if you're looking for trade routes and quests to build up your towns), to outright mayhem and sudden and repeated death (if you've ventured into a tough pirate region, or a combat instance).
These are some basic facts to know, if you're considering a purchase:
The game begins with creation of a World, somewhat under the control of the creator, in terms of its shape, the challenges it will present, and some other global features.  The world consists of a large number of rectangular regions, each of which contains a procedurally generated terrain and oceans, with a few coastal towns scattered in each. The next decision is to choose your starting faction.  There are several Windward factions, all of which are allies by default, and each comes with a different set of advantages and drawbacks, which are described to you when you're asked to choose: maybe you want to get rich as an Exchange captain, or rampage the seas wiping out pirates with Valiant, or ... the choices are yours.
You will begin in a Challenge Level 0 area (be thankful!) which will be peaceful enough to get familiar with sailing your sloop between ports around the map.  If you haven't watched the introduction video to get a feel for the gameplay, do it now!
Although the game is *all* about sailing, and it's called
, this isn't a sailing ship simulator.  Your craft will make its way directly into the wind, if you like to point it that way, although more slowly.  There's a certain amount of wind variation, but you'll never get a flat calm, nor a storm to sink you.  You have simple controls to speed up, slow down and steer to starboard or to port (right and left, for landlubbers :).  You can even warp backwards at low speed, necessary if you're stuck up some creek, and your hull is taking damage from being aground.
With limited gold at the start, and very much like Commander Jameson in the original Elite, you have few options for climbing to the top: you need to get some weapons, some experience with which to buy talent points, and to build or find more advanced towns which will sell you more advanced ships.
Some reviewers have described the early phases of the game as 'tedious' and 'grinding', and if you're an adrenaline junky who doesn't want to take the time to grow your ship and your XP, you might agree.  For my money, the calm and thoughtful elements are just as absorbing and rewarding as the maniac battles against fleets of pirates.  Make no mistake, though, you will encounter piracy early in the game, and you'll get sunk by gloating pirates often enough to make you want to get back at 'em.
The visual aspect of the game is excellent: the water and landscape are animated, there are flocks of gulls and shoals of fish, the clouds drift across the sky in the direction of the prevailing wind (which, incidentally, changes direction slowly but constantly - sometimes it's better to plan a journey that doesn't take you into the teeth of the wind).  The sound too is well-chosen, with informative sound effects for game events, and music which matches the peacefulness or otherwise of your situation.
Options for single-player play, multi-player on LAN or Internet servers and invitation-only 'instances' all exist, which means that you can be as solitary or gregarious as you wish.  The developer has been very accessible and attentive during Early Access, updating
almost every day for the last six months, and there is a helpful community on the Steam forums to answer your questions.
At the price, you won't find many better ways to spend enjoyable hours with a game.  I thoroughly recommend it.

I am a huge fan of Sid Meier's Pirates! and have been wishing for years that Firaxis would make a new updated version of it. Windward is the closest thing to that game I have seen. Very similar naval battle mechanics to Pirates!, combined with 4 unique factions which cater to different playstyles, add in an MMO esque skill tree system, and an addicting loot/upgrade system and this game provides an incredible amount of entertainment.
All of the maps are generated similar to other sandbox games and roguelikes. meaning there is near endless replay value here. The game can get repetitive as most loot grind games (Diablo, Borderlands) can after a while but since it offers diffrent ways for you to progress, it breaks that monotony up a bit. Get sick of combat? start just doing noncombat trade missions, sick of trading? Just start exploring. Wanna play offline and fight AI pirates? Go for it. Wanna do some PVP large naval battles, hop on a busy server and have at it. Your ship and skills are persistant, meaning whether you are playing offline or on you can still progress your abilities and gear.
One of my only concerns with this game is that I hope the dev (there is only one) keeps working on it and adding to it, because It has the potential to be even better than Pirates! if he expands on his base game.  I highly recommend this game for anyone who was a fan of Pirates! or strategy games and even rpgs, at the very worst it is a good time killer worth 15 bucks easy, but personally I think the sky is the limit for this game.

This game is by far the worst hunting simulator I have ever played. There are dozens of inaccuracies in this game from the firearms to the ammunition to how the animals react. Polyomer tipped ammo is widely known for its increased expansion not superior penetration. Soft-point ammo, which they label as a being the superior expanding ammo will penetrate deeper. In 200 words:
A game generally in the spirit of the movie Fury Road; although this game has nothing directly to do with the movie. The setting is post-apocalyptic; humanity has turned on itself while the game world is populated by those without hope. Surprisingly, however, there are a lot of people around.
The story is entertaining although i wouldn't say too difficult; perhaps thoughtful in the end depending on your point of view. Achievements (if these are your thing) are challenging but based more on time invested than skill. Look deeper and there is black humour to darker elements throughout the game e.g. one Airplane quote, skeletons embracing, references to cannibalism and so on. Game lore (in essence postcards from the past) spread throughout the world are interesting to read and hear Max comment on. Car combat is entertaining.
Down sides? Maybe repetitive combat, decrease in game hardness as you upgrade, you appear to have the only shotgun in the world, lots of stuff to do (drive here do this etc), no death penalty, never really strained for ammo/fuel, instant travel (needed but by-passes game content late game imo).
Would I play the sequel? Yes?

While Windward is a fun single-player experience, it really shines in multiplayer with both local hosting and dedicated servers that let you drop in with your personal ship and join in on the pirate-hunting and faction wars with a community.

Windward is a wonderful little gem. The dev clearly had the discipline not to try and cram all sorts of additional doodads and whizzbangs to try and pad out the game, which, combined with actually using the Early Access platform in the manner one would expect it to be used, has resulted in a game with pleasing core gameplay and a smooth, customiseable experience that can be as casual or psychotically unfair as you want it to be.
At the time of release Windward concentrates on the core basics of it's gameplay; sailing and fighting. Sailing around the map is a weirdly pleasant experience for the most part, since the game throws realism overboard and makes controlling your ship easy and forgiving. Let's face it, people like the aesthetic and theme of the Age of Sail, but you don't want to be struggling to get your bloated wooden whale around the place. Instead, Windward lets you concentrate on deftly threading your ship through a tiny gap in the procedurally generated island chain, or weaving about scooping up bits of flotsam and jetsam as loot. Simply moving around is fun, or certainly vastly more tolerable than the majority of games at the worst.
Fighting is where the game really throws down it's arcade leanings, with guns automatically firing from both sides of your ships at the closest enemies, while you try to maneuver yourself into optimal position. And then you use an ability that hurls a flaming barrel at a cartoonish angle into your foes, setting them all alight. With one tongue firmly in your cheek, you can expect combat against entrenched pirates to rapidly descend into an all-out brawl between half a dozen ships, hopefully some of them on your side, pretty much constantly.
It's great fun, and thrives on simplicity at it's heart. You lose hours without even realising that you've just been going back and forth across a map, performing missions to move cargo and passengers around, maybe blowing up a pirate now and then. It gets worse when you discover the button that sets up an instanced combat map, allowing you to fight a war of conquest to clear a map of pirates, before returning to your main game world.
The best part is that Windward is currently a perfect foundation. For people who like indie games with potential, Windward is worth keeping an eye on, as its current pleasing focus on getting the real basics right means there's a sturdy framework to expand in Terraria-esque fashion.

I didn't have high expectations for this game. The ending of Life is Strange left me underwhelmed. It's just a prequel. With a different studio, and differing voice actors. I was so wrong.
Character creation is downright outstanding. I can't think of any other game that would make me so emotional about characters, or, even more, change my feelings about them so rapidly and so strongly. David may be a prick, but I did get to see through that to see what is behind that harsh side. I loved seeing Joyce so genuinely happy. Even Drew, the bully, made me doubt my initial judgment. LiS never managed to go that far. Hell, barely any game managed that on this big a scale.
Story writing, too, deserves praise. No super powers. No over-the-top drama. No overly extended moments. Everything felt genuine, relatable, enjoyable. Once more, Before the Storm managed to beat LiS, by far. The golden standard of storyline heavy games.
Choices. While they still could do more, I finally felt that my decisions make some impact as the story unfolds. And it's not an impact of 'the bird eggs fell because I moved a plank' type. I do hope LiS2 will continue to improve that.
Lastly, graphics. I always loved the LiS graphic style, but the original irked me in some places, hair especially. Before the Storm nailed it. It's a game that won't age as horrible as all the hyper-realistic games, and will be enjoyable even when 8K becomes the new standard.
The only part that left me salty was the special episode in Deluxe. Sure, a bonus episode is nice and all, but it's not nice to the people with a season pass, who expect all episodes. So at least, please, make it worth the upgrade.

This game...
I am going to be writing a very biased review. I don't know what the critics are saying about this game, and frankly I don't care. I don't care what the gaming community in general thinks of this game. I absolutely love this game. I bought the deluxe version and prayed it didn't suffer from the weight of expectations. Deck Nine, thanks a ton. (No spoilers, in case you were wondering)
So, what's so good about it? Let's start with the UI improvements for the keyboard and mouse. The previous title suffered a bit from being a little clunky. Often I would have to redo parts of the game just to make sure my choices were accurate. This version fixes a bunch of things I found annoying about the first game. For example, having to play the entire episode all over again in order to get the achievements was really annoying in the first game. It is part of the reason I didn't complete it. Now you can replay bits of the episode just to get a feel for the other options after you have played the game without messing your original playthrough. Even making choices is much less clunky and fun.
Daughter. Need I say more? They just nailed the soundtrack. I don't think there is an out of place song. I spent several minutes just zoning out in the game to listen to the music, and it is not like the music is unnecessarily there either. The music direction is just really well done, in that it highlights powerful moments in the game and knows when to fade out. I bought the deluxe edition for the Mix Tape Mode and I have loved it so far. The UI for that is a little annoying, but it's an additional feature, so no complaints here. I really would throw all the money I possibly can for such good quality.
The plot is really good. It hit all the right notes and focused on a few plot points exploring them to the depth they deserve.The writing is especially spot on with the characters reacting and saying things I would if I were in that situation. I think Ashly Burch's influence is apparent in the portrayal of Chloe, but to take anything away from the other writers is a crime. The game made me love each of the characters so much that I don't feel like sharing them with the world. And yet, I want the world to know that such beauty exists. How...?
I'm sure you will be critical of this game when you play it, and perhaps your opinions will be different, but I urge you to look at all that was expected from this game and treat it with the respect it deserves. Because the truth is, this game is the best thing that has happened to me in some time, and it has earned more than my respect and adulation.

Spec Ops: The Line is a hidden jem in my opinion. From the steam page, not much is known about the true nature of the game, although, I believe anyone who does play the game will be in for a beautiful but tragic ride. At first the game seems like a normal 3rd person shooter, a decent combat system and beautiful environment makes it almost seem like a battlefield game. But things quickly take a turn when your squad transitions from soldiers to survivors. You slowly realize this isn't just another army game, the things you and your men have to do to stay alive are terrible, and both you and the characters will question the meaning of their lives and choices. The walk to insanity is a slow one, and you and your men will suffer through it.The game is tragic, dark, saddening, and lonely. Mix that in with beautiful environment, graphics, and excellent voice acting, and you have a gripping, adrenaline pumping, and tear jerking experience. It defies the rules laid out by most games. There are no right choices, there is no redemption, and you will feel the regret and pain from the repercussions. Final summary: 8.5/10, a great experience for someone who wants a psychological and deeply emotional game.

I'm surprised how little attention this game has received and how few reviews it has because, honestly, it's a really fun solid game. And while it's Early Access, it feels very complete.
I bought the game on a whim because it reminded me of Sid Meier's Pirates. And in a way it's similar - it's a pirating game with some questing and trading mechanics, but it really isn't Sid Meier's Pirates either.
The game has very solid combat mechanics and RPG-like elements to it. Ships can be upgraded through switching out different materials (your crew, your cannons, your sails etc) and because they're not permanent, you can switch it out depending on your whims.
Naval combat is somewhat automated - cannons fire automatically within range - but you have custom attacks that you can trigger manually. So far I've only unlocked volley shots and chain shots but the videos show that there are significantly more.
Trading is simpler but still rewarding. If you've explored the towns, they'll tell you which area provides the cargo they would want to buy. There's less planning involved and it feels more like a fetch quest but it's still satisfying to sail across the virtual seas.
There are pirates that roam the seas and other factions as well. You can bribe the pirates and you can capture the cities/towns that the pirates have control of too.
You can level up and unlock skills as well, and I believe your crew and captain rank and level up too - albeit at a different rate. But at any time you'd like you can switch to a different captain or crew (they essentially act as passive items) too.
I'll admit I wasn't entirely convinced of the graphics on the screenshots - they looked a tad jagged and oversaturated and the waters looked dull. But rest be assured, it looks much better animated. It's a beautiful indiegame.
For $14.99, it's a wonderful game.
Pros
- Beautiful graphics
- Solid trading, questing and combat mechanics
- Lightweight game
- Solo or co-op gameplay
Cons
- I hope the trading and questing mechanics is developed upon a little more
- The difficulty from "Challenge 3" to "Challenge 4" is akin to the leap from racing a car in Need For Speed Underground to racing a car in Grand Turismo 5, there's a sudden difficulty climb that can feel overwhelming.

What can I say about this game? It's really fun. Sure it's kind of samey, but this is true of any games. I mean it's a game where you bring stuff from point A to Point B. Be it passengers, cargo, pirate ships, and other things. It isn't limited to that. Sometimes you are tasked with building a lighthouse or guard tower. Sometimes you are tasked with capturing pirate ships and others establish new colonies or cities. There are random pirates that come and claim lands and you have to fight them off. Sometimes they are tenacious especially when their ships outnumber yours. So there is a bit of back and forth when trying to claim a new region. Which is fun. You can upgrade your ship or use other ships that you've previously purchased.
Initially you start off in a tiny ship with 2 cargo spaces and you are severely outgunned. However, thanks to some good loot drops, you can quickly come into action. Each new region is progressively more difficult, so the game never feels like you're just rolling over them.
The regions are randomly generated with various reefs and other hazards that you should sail around. There are some small exploits you can manage though which fortunately aren't very common in number. I did get stuck one time on some rocks in a fight, and died. Fortunately, as it is there is no penalty to this, in the normal difficulty setting. I am sure someone will no doubt ask for a hardcore difficulty mode. There is banter in the form of text bubbles over the ships as they pass, generally either asking you about coffee or telling you rumours about the value of cargo in certain towns. You also can receive sealed letters and open them. Sometimes, you're on a treasure hunt and end up going in circles. I think the game makes light of this fact in some of the descriptive texts.
There are a few things I would like to see in the game. The first thing I would like to see would be actual wind pushing the ships along because as it is, I believe the ships speed is constant and not affected by wind direction. Second the controls could use an actual key mapping option in the menu. Sometimes I think that ferrying passengers ought to be timed as I have sometimes gone around the map to various other ports and then finally delivered the people to the place they wanted to go. However, this is by no means mandatory. If this is a feature that exists in higher difficulties, then I apologise.  How else could the game be improved? Perhaps an auto-navigation feature Where you click on the town on the map and choose "auto navigate to" or something. Maybe connect the regions together, because in some regions they don't have certain resources that you are tasked with finding. Maybe a note taking feature for transporting various cargo between cities.
In general I am really enjoying this game. Indie titles like this are crafted with a passion that is severely lacking in their AAA bretheren. Thanks for making this. If anything happens, I will update this review. It can only get better from here though!

I finally decided to open this around noon the other day and, before I knew it, the sun was setting.  I'm not sure how to describe it; it feels similar to how I imagine an open-world version of Sid Meier's Pirates would play.
At the time of this review, it is scheduled to transition from early access into the first release version within the month, and I'd say the foundation of the game is solid.  It will need upkeep to reach full potential, but it's a delight even in this most basic state, well-polished and beautifully presented.
Tour a randomly-generated world, or one of your own design, forge alliances and save the world from the pirate-infested seas--or join them!  I'd love to say more here, I really would, but words fail me.  Try it and bring a friend or ten along for much more fun.  Before you know it, you'll have sailed your entire day away, too.
As I feel this description tells very little, I would like to use this space to ramble a bit on the game's atmosphere alone.  This, I believe, is the most important attraction about it and I am forced to cite examples of other games here to make my point.  Please both excuse and indulge me.
Imagine a world like Minecraft, or your first days in a Civilization game, where the peaceful tempo of the world becomes the experience.  You step into it with a desire to create and grow, to build something magnificent, but the environment gently abducts you along the way.  You continue your quest, of course, unwittingly sedated by the roll of illusionary waves and a pointed lack of urgency.  You have all the time in the world.
Like Minecraft, you will spend a great deal of time empowered to voyage on alone or with non-player escorts, but welcoming friends into your world has an allure of its own.  Even if each of you play independently, your ships passing one another breathes a sense of pleasant familiarity and kinship, knowing that if trouble strikes, you have a reliable ally at your side.  You need not travel together to build a world together and as your world accumulates that real flesh-and-blood population, it comes to life.  I use our familiar voxel friend as a baseline because it articulates the very same experience so well.
You come here to create a world and consequently, rather unexpectedly, you become simply a resident of it.  It's a glorious experience and well-executed.  It is my hope that the authors will nurture and develop their creation for years to come.
All of this and I have not even touched on the compelling combat system and the fun of instanced raids and dread pirate conquests.  That part I leave you to discover for yourself.  Go on, then.  You will not be disappointed.
