COTW has the potential to be a great hunting sim, or a mediocre game, and it is hurting from the developers pushing the mediocre to the determent of what could be great.  If you are looking for a good way to pass the time, this is as good as anything out there.  Great graphics and large maps – no microtransations to keep you from the intended play of the game (DLC’s are a plus, but they are not required) – enough weapons/gear to allow you to change up your playing style for even more enjoyment.
But if you are a hunter looking for a hunting sim to immerse yourself in, or a gamer looking for a shooting gallery game where the basic mechanics of shoot/die are working, there are plenty of bugs that would interfere with both of those approaches.  There are regular patches that always seem to create more bugs than fix, and there’s a lack of feedback.
In my opinion, the developers should approach this as a hunting sim, since there are not very many of them and the market is in dire need of a decent sim, while there are countless shooting gallery/FPS games on the market.  Until the developers decide which way they want to go, my honest suggestion is to stay away from it unless you fall into the very specific group (as I have) of hunters who are desperate for some sort of hunting action online, and are not too worried that any attempts at immersion will be quickly ended as the mountain of bugs are encountered. I would suggest those who are out for a shooting gallery game just avoid this title – it is mediocre at best, and any effort the developers put into making it better for you, detracts from the overall.  And since I've just learned my lesson about suggesting someone NOT buy the game... I'll go ahead and give it a "Yes", so as not to offend the Oligarchy.

Short version: Post Apoc GTA style open world with Arkham style combat. Visuals are great, sound & music is decent enough and car combat vs. ground combat is balanced. Worth the money but felt there was a lot of nothing in the wastes, hopeing DLC will fix this.
Long dirty version: Oh boy.. after the first preview I was super hyped for this. The game did live up to some of what I was expecting. It obviously had something going for it since I put almost 100 hours into it and got 100% achievements. The storyline is basic but done well, the combat is fun but gets repetitve after a while with very limited weapons. Huge range of cars to choose from but only can modify your special "Magnum Opus" which is fine but would have been cooler if only certain mods worked on certain cars.
Graphics: Excellent. Very nice and can easily make your machine run hot but the visuals are really decent. I love how the world changes complete when the giant storms hit, feels like the world is ending. The enemies are varied and there is a lot of little bits any pieces around the environment that makes you feel the artists/designers put in a lot of effort the problem is a lot fht environment ins't interactive which is a shame.
Sound/Audio/Music: The music is decent enough but very forgettable. The sound effects are nice and meaty in combat and the grinding of metal when you have car on car action is great but they become quite average after a while. The voice acting is excellent and the war cries of raiders/bandits and savages is haunting.
Gameplay: The combat system is right out of the Batman Arkham series. It's simple and works and gives you some nice disarm/kill options and is brutal BUT... doesn't get cooler or more interesting as you upgrade your combat skills which is sad. Barely any weapons: Shotgun & Knife with the occasional pickup of a staff/blade/bat type that you have to ditch which I think it lame. You do get a sniper rifle but only from the car which is a bit meh.
The car combat is nice but only nice. With so many different cool car gadgets from various movies they could have incorporated some more Road Warrior style anti-vehicular weapons. They do give you missiles & a grappler harpoon and side flamers but only one other car gives you land mines and that's it. More ramming accessories would have been cool, oil slicks (given oil in this post apoc seems to be everywhere esp. in GasTown), direction mounted flamer throwers, grenade launchers, machine guns... alas.
Ground combat... they could have added an Attack Dog component. That alone would have been AMAZING.
Final word. Get it. It's worth playing and is decent fun. Harpooning a raider and then driving off through the desert dragging them behind you is worth it alone... then suddenly withdrawing the winch and launching the body across the waste... very awesome.
Enjoy!

Spec Ops: The Line is a hidden jem in my opinion. From the steam page, not much is known about the true nature of the game, although, I believe anyone who does play the game will be in for a beautiful but tragic ride. At first the game seems like a normal 3rd person shooter, a decent combat system and beautiful environment makes it almost seem like a battlefield game. But things quickly take a turn when your squad transitions from soldiers to survivors. You slowly realize this isn't just another army game, the things you and your men have to do to stay alive are terrible, and both you and the characters will question the meaning of their lives and choices. The walk to insanity is a slow one, and you and your men will suffer through it.The game is tragic, dark, saddening, and lonely. Mix that in with beautiful environment, graphics, and excellent voice acting, and you have a gripping, adrenaline pumping, and tear jerking experience. It defies the rules laid out by most games. There are no right choices, there is no redemption, and you will feel the regret and pain from the repercussions. Final summary: 8.5/10, a great experience for someone who wants a psychological and deeply emotional game.

Gameplay is so-so. Cover-based shooting and not in a way you haven't seen a thousand times before. It serves its purpose and the scarcity of ammunition gives a tinge of desperation to the whole thing when you run from cover to cover salvaging the guns of your dead enemies.
But this is, first and foremost, a story game. And the story is not just good, but incredibly well told. Great voice acting and superb soundtrack sucks you into the atmosphere.
If you play for gameplay: 6/10 a decent shooter with sometimes frantic and sometimes unforgiving action.
If you play for story: 10/10 best I've seen in quite a while

I absolutely love this game. The best thing I've played in a long time.
Basically, your ship is your 'guy'. You equip items to improve your stats, and you get skill points to, of course, get skills and also improve stats. And you can upgrade to better ship types, each of which are pretty well balanced.
If you want to play casual, it's a relaxing, beautiful place to roam, with great ambiance. There are simple quests to complete for experience, money, and basic resources. Everything is just pretty and nice.
If you want action, move into another area and battle waves of pirates, or go online and play PvP.
Combat is simple, but gets deeper as you gain abilities and better items, and can get hectic with multiple units fighting in an area.
Difficulty is totally scalable.  Skills can be remaped for a price.  Factions can be changed, so you're never locked-in to a play-style.
The few bugs that have poped-up get fixed immediately by the developer.
Seriously, usually the same day they get reported.
Probably the only down-side is that the progression can be slow at the beginning. If you have A.D.D., you definitely won't have the patience to build up at the start.
Get a Schooner as soon as you can, then do quests and save up for the ship you really want.
Access to the ships depends on how big a town is, and increasing the size of the town is done by completing quests and selling them cargo that they have a shortage of. Basically you will probably have to do quests to get a town big enough to buy the ship you want. This part of the game can be a grind, so focus on one town and optimize your questing. On the way back to the town check to see if there is any cargo they need, because selling cargo at a town also counts as a quest completion.
Once you get the ship you want, things open-up and you can focus on expanding into pirate territory, collceting items from pirate bosses, or tooling around as you please.
For me, this game is already done. Any further development is just gravy. 10/10

I can't say enough good things about this game. It is a bit like crossing Sid Meier's Pirates! with an action RPG loot system. Crates and barrels float around giving you loot. They appear randomly but also when ships sink more appear. You can buy various types of loot in town - most of which add to your stats or even gives you new abilities.
The game is a time sink. It starts off a little slowly where you do some trading just to get some initial cash. Once that is done you can upgrade towns by completing quests or selling items that town needs. This will unlock better ships for you to purchase. There is also a huge randomly generated map to conquer. Plus the game has full mulitplayer! Yet even if you are in multiplayer you can create your own instance while on the server, invite friends who are also on the server to join you, and complete quests for even more loot! Reclaim an area from some pirates or make a trading/quest instance and sail to your heart's content. Suddenly it will be 6am and you won't be quite sure where the last 12 hours have gone.
In short if you like pirate games, like loot based games, enjoy single player OR multiplayer, then get this little gem! Totally worth it!

In addition the determinded makers of Euro Truck SImulator 2 Multiplayer work hard to enhance the singleplayer game to make a brilliant online experience, which is what they have done very well. So if you want to drive with friends, you can. Plus because of the effort and time the makers of the Multiplayer put in the Multiplayer is updated on a regular basis so there shouldn't be a bug or glitch left in the Mod for more than a few days.
I would recommend to anyone who is looking for a realistic driving simulator wanting either to play on singleplayer or multiplayer, Euro Truck Simulator 2 and Euro Truck Simulator 2 Multiplayer are the best truck driving simulator's by far in my opinion.
As a sidenote I would like to point out that the ETS2MP Mod is not owned by Euro Truck Simulator 2 itself, the Mod is a addition to the game which is not made by ETS2 and it also a non-profit mod, so you do not pay for it but if you wish you may donate to help out the developers to make the game better and keep the servers up and running correctly.
Hope this helps anyone interested in buying the game.

I haven't yet played this game for more than several hours or so, but I find myself deeply immersed in this spectacular landscape and motivated by an engaging hunt. Despite the few minor bugs I have already encountered, this game is well worth the price and I feel confident in its development for future updates and patches to solve any issues. This game is 100% playable and absolutely entertaining, I couldn't possibly recommend it enough for any outdoors enthusiast.
Now for something a little different in a game review -some suggestions (for what it's worth).
First, the camera view is a little distorted when you angle the camera from the focus of your player (turn away from center focus). It's almost like looking through a Coke bottle or a lens and objects like trees and buildings become elongated and distorted. I don't know if there's a particular setting to change this, or of it is vanilla (part of the game). I would definitely try to change this if possible, because after a few hours it tends to mess with your eyes.
Second, the pace of your hunter is extremely slow. I mean, it's ridiculous, really. I would like to see a trainable skill set to increase your stealth and stalking skills to provide for faster movement to remain undetected while moving faster. I look at it like this -this game attracts all sorts of people, but I would guess more adults than children. And like most responsible adults who can afford to buy a few games, they have jobs. Ain't nobody got time to tip toe at a snails pace these days. Besides, being Native American and an avid hunter myself, this would mimic real skills appropriate for a hunter who can, if he is skilled enough, move about through the woods quickly, unseen and unheard.
Third, I have some firearm suggestions for the opening of the game (since I do not know if there are bigger and better guns later on and after checking the first outpost there really wasn't anything there worth considering due to the cost). The 30-30 lever action rifle is a popular choice, and it is in the game but very expensive. The venerable .308 Winchester model 700 is perhaps the most suitable of all, but I didn't see it anywhere. And of course there's the 45/70 Gov't rifle platform which is no slacker, either, and it's a favorite for many Pacific Northwest hunters, but it is probably the most expensive and way out of reach for a long time. Again, these are only suggestions, for what it's worth.
In conclusion, I think I love this game. I purchassed all of the DLC because I feel obligated to support any and all developments with this game, and as a final measure I will say the DLC is definitely worth purchasing at the $3.99 price point. Thank you, Expansive Worlds. This game is fantastic.

Rogue Legacy...The whiskey of video games.

I think I only got a few hours into Rogue Legacy the first time before I shelved it. Platformers lean heavily on how you move and what you can do with those moves, and the mish-mashed castle of aggravating traps and meaty foes to hack through wasn't ticking the right boxes for me. I had something of a breakthrough when I returned to it, though, a new way of looking for upgrades and building my manor. Before I knew it I had beaten it, and my reward was a new perspective on what Rogue Legacy accomplishes in its tight designs.
If nothing else, Rogue Legacy gets points for having probably the best setup for a roguelike possible. You hail from a long line of adventurers delving into the ever-shifting halls of a forgotten castle, and when you die you take on the role of one of your children. This means your successor (you pick one of three offered) is fully randomized, from class to skills to quirks like flatulence and vertigo. The story fully utilizes this setup as well, which is really cool when (if) you reach the end and see how it all ties together. It would be a shame if that hook was wasted, but luckily the game is a pretty solid platformer and roguelike to boot.
Before each run, you get the option to upgrade your manor which serves as a sort of skill tree for your characters. Cash can be spent on stat boosts, new class unlocks, or a few special effects that alter the way you play. You'll also drop gold on new gear and enchantments which need to be found in the castle first and offer dramatic gameplay enhancements like lifesteal attacks, difficulty bumps, and multiple air jumps and dashes. The last option offered is locking down the castle layout for your next run, allowing you to explore the same halls as your last hero did at the cost of most of their gold. It's an interesting feature that's not common among roguelikes, adding a layer of strategy that gives you a better shot at finding specific upgrades or reaching bosses by sacrificing your other treasures.
The actual platforming inside the procedurally-generated castle is probably the weakest part of the game as I mentioned, but by no means bad. The trade-off for randomization is very simple room layouts, mostly spruced up by liberal application of breakables and traps. There are special challenge rooms, miniboss rooms, and stranger secret rooms to find as well which do help keep exploration fresh. However, the game can be pretty aggressive about murdering you with its elaborate traps and vicious enemies. Each of the four wings of the castle has a general difficulty level but it can be hard to tell where exactly you fit at the moment, especially if the place has not been kind with upgrades. My first dozen generations passed without finding a new sword, for example, which contributed to me punching out early in my original attempt at the game.
There's a certain attitude to Rogue Legacy as well, one that I can't say I appreciated much. It stems from the particularly punishing design of a lot of the trap-based rooms, many of which withhold their rewards if you get hit before reaching the end. These rooms will happily trick you into failing them with cheekily-placed monsters and spikes in what feels like some rather spiteful design. NPCs also enjoy berating you for failing at nigh-impossible tasks, and though they're not a huge part of the game they do contribute to the atmosphere. Still, this is offset by the cartoony graphics, the energetic soundtrack, and the raw fun factor of chugging through the challenges once you get the hang of them. If you stick with it, learn to synergize your gear with your class, and grab all the treasure you can, it'll end up being one of the more rewarding games to complete.

the little rogue that could leaped forward with determination sustaining a mighty roar matching that of the beast he was about to fight against.

the little rogue that could came back from the dead as if nothing ever happened to him.
now fulled with rage and thirst for vengace not only for his lost parents but because of his almost lost life, he felt more ready than ever to strike.
but that wouldn't stop him from thinking on a different strategy.
and so he did try to fight fire with fire as he had heard from the adventures long lived by his ancestors adapted into the form of books.
without hesitation the little rogue that could pulled out a fire shield out of his pocket so swiftly the ponce de leon didn't have a chance to react.

I purchased this game at ~$20 during the Christmas sale. I cannot tell how I would have felt about it if it were full price, but I honestly think I would have still been pleasantly satisfied with it considering how much time I played.
Mad Max is a pretty solid game. Hand-to-hand combat is very much like the Arkham series, which I personally enjoy. All those V6s and V8s roar to glorious effect. Vehicle combat possesses a diverse set of features that are enough to not get boring. Tons of collectibles are strewn across the large, albeit barren, map waiting to be acquired. And the world has a personality that is pretty near to consistent with the movies other than a few minor qualms.
However, Mad Max might get repetitive to some. There are only about 4 or 5 unique enemy types so fights play out the same most of the time. The same pretty much applies to vehicle combat as well. Comparing it again to other AAA titles, this actually isn't too terrible but it is something to consider before purchasing it. Even boss fights don't feel all that unique other than maybe one or two fights with the main antagonist near the end of the game. The landscape is barren, understandably, but the devs appear to add some life to it by utilizing their assets to tell a quick little story (usually skeletons or corpses positioned in one way or another). You also have historical artifacts in the form of notes and pictures that tell the story of the world before the catastrophe.
All that considered, I'd recommend the game if you like games like Just Cause 2, Assassin's Creed, or any Arkham game. It's not as over-the-top as Just Cause 2 but it's interesting enough to be fun. If you don't feel strongly about those titles, still give it a look. I was pleasantly surprised with it.
I truly enjoyed this game.

My advice: At current price, this game has a ton to offer. Only folks who should stay away are those who don't like shooters.
Genre: Third-person shooter
Writing this review is difficult, because there are two kinds of games Spec Ops: the Line can be. From one point of view, it's a generic, linear shooter, in a land filled with waist-high walls and conveniently placed guns. On the other hand, the story and choices the player is forced to endure are so investing that it forces you to think and... to some extent, even feel guilt.
You play as the captain of a small task force, entering the city of Dubai following a massive sandstorm that has all but destroyed the city. As you explore and attempt to rescue civilians, and the lost 33rd platoon who was previous sent it, you start to discover a destitute war-zone akin to Lord of the Flies. The story digs deeper as you see the kind of person who would be willing to perform these atrocities, and you start to realize you might need to become that way yourself, just to help save everyone else.
Despite the chaos and gore, the setting and environment for this game are gorgeous, and the attention to detail is fantastic for a game this price. There are a number of moments the game leads you through that are really meant to etch into your skull. I think that's really what the game has going for it, though. You're playing this almost generic shooter, and the game starts to question your motives --and even taunt your poor decisions, when they do occur. Don't expect a happy ending walking into this game, but whatever route you choose, it's a satisfying, justified one.

If you don't want to read all this, then, in summary:
Borderlands is a great game, for the first couple of playthroughs. I could not stomach a third- I only mention additional run-throughs, as the game actively encourages it with the "vault hunter" modes. This difficulty increase just seems to be a 10 or similar multiplier of enemies health and gun damage, which is rather poor, however you cannot blame the developers for this, as many games do this "one full game, unlock hard mode" scheme. Story was nice, characters moderately enjoyable, however comedy slightly lacking.
I like to try and complete games to their fullest, to their brims of their available quest content, however, Borderlands is a game where that is increasingly hard task to furfill, not due to the difficulty, not some bogus mechanic, but instead my own attention span.
The main villain is the game is original, and enjoyable. Your virtual hatred for this person usually just stems from him calling you up and being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and that's alright, I guess. It makes the character alot more communicative with the player, however it was plot devices like this that didn't make me hate hate him. You get to the end of the game,
The characters are enjoyable. Borderland is not, and did not set out to be a strong story game. I didn't fully enjoy the characters as they weren't immersive, however the game did not set out to be that way.
The comedy- Borderlands main selling  point. It isn't to be taken seriously, because the game isn't serious. That's fine, I just didn't really chuckle or do a heavy breathe-through-nose sound in approval. The comedy just wasn't great. It's not a bad thing, me and the game don't have the same sense of humor.
Running and gunning is what this game sells itself on- if you like a bit of mindless murder, sure, go for it, however, as this may seem like a brilliant idea on paper, I just don't get the same enjoyment out of killing a Ultimate Badass Goliath as I did the first time.
I enjoyed my first playthrough alot, it was great. Second time around, bought some friends the game, finished it again. I don't have the balls to try again. Killing and killing and more killing is completely fine, Borderlands just finds a way to make it boring sometimes, especially after 2-3 hours of play.
Side quests consist of:
These side quests are fine! It's just that doing them seems like a bit of a long chore for very, very low reward. Go out, kill about 100 bandits for me, and you'll get a nice blue gun and $2000, which you'll probably loose within 20 seconds when you die.
There's alot of guns. Alot. However, we have to remember these guns aren't handmade by GearBox, they're just a random generation of numbers, to pick a model and stats. Nothing really that special, it's nothing to wet yourself over.
Golden keys.
This is the part where the game felt strange in its mechanics.
If you loot an area, you'll get a metric ♥♥♥♥tonne of white little guns, and then maybe a blue if you're lucky. All of these will do about 80% less damage than you need them to, so how do you get your guns? Input codes from the Internet! It feels kind of cheaty and wrong to have a system where decent guns are very, very hard to attain if you don't use these keys. Try a playthrough without it- it's hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥ So GearBox ultimately forces your hand to open up Steam Browser, find some dodgy Facebook page and manually type in some string of letters in the hope you'll get something that you couldn't without a long time of grinding, or actually playing the game. Just thank god that Valve didn't co-develop this, or golden keys would be £1.99 and the guns marketable for £0.03. At least these codes are free.
Not much to say about the graphics. It's original, I do like the artstyle. Optional PhysX adds more random cloths and explosions (if you needed anymore from a rocket launcher that fires grenades which explode into more grenades and fire more rockets when reloaded) at the cost of 100 FPS.
Great game, if you like to grind for hours. Or, input a code for a decent weapon!
Borderlands is what actually got me to like certain FPS. Truly I didn't want this to end.

As of now I have played over 15 hours of this game, before I go onto listing the pros and cons I will say that this game had the potential of providing a VERY solid gaming expirence, but due to some questionable and shady design decissions, I would have to say that I cannot with good conscience recommend this game.  I've heard people say that we shouldn't have to worry about it because it is "Early access", but I have HUGE doupts about that.
PROS:
-Graphics:
Graphically the world is breath taking, and thanks to the dynamic weather system presents moments  that are simply awe inspiring, almost photo realistic.  Tall grass can even be pushed down to make trails by the player and animals, which can be a useful way to track animals.
-Sound and voice:
Theres only a few short orchestral songs, but they add to the overall atmosphere.  Nothing to write home about.
Voice acting is surprisingly good, people call you over your cell phone.  The writing is simple, but its pleasent to listen to.
The ambient sound is great!  Really mixes well with the enviornment to make the expirence immersive.
-Tracking, and luring:
The game has a pretty good tracking system, similar to The Witcher 3, but without quest markers guiding you.  There are more than a few ways to track an animal, tracks (Foot prints), you can see how fresh poop is, and blood stains from gun shot wounds. There are tools to lure animals in with sound instruments (Mimic animal noise), and sprays that mimic animals smells.  You can also find where and what time they rest, eat and drink.
-Gameplay:
Hunting animals is great, theres a real viseral feel when you snag an animal you've been stalking for a while!  The AI is pretty realistic too.  You have to sneak by hiding yourself while making as little noise as possible, which the game does a good job doing balancing the game.  Possitioning is key, things as minor as the direction of the wind blowing can effect whether or not an animal will detect you.
The game also features a lite RPG system you get everywhere else, haven't gotten far enough to really get into the meat of it.
Other than that it serves it's purpose, more will be explained down below.
Cons:
- Animal AI is good, but sometimes its a little TOO good at finding you, sometimes they're find you when they shouldn't, and they'll see you on the otherside of large hills.  This is particuarly frustrating early on in the game, especially during the third mission.
-Speaking of the third mission, ♥♥♥♥ THAT MISSION.  It requires you to find and hunt down a red fox WITH A BOW.  These ♥♥♥♥ers are VERY, VERY good at hearing you and are very sneaky if you are using their lure.  I tried sneaking up to them, I tried using lures, than I just ran to it and got a lucky shot on its foot, while it was running through the bushes.  This was not a good way to introduce a new player to the game.
-Running and crouching speed is VERY SLOW.  I understand if it was for sneaking and balancing purposes, but man oh man, you have a lot of traveling to do in this game.  Whats more is that this particuarly makes stalking pray very hard to do when said prey is constantly on the move.  This problem would have been midigated if only they didn't...
-Removed vehicles, they removed the only vehicles in the game as "DLC", even though its plastered on the GOD DAMN PROMOTIONAL ART.  IT IS THE NUMBER ONE REASON I SAY NOT TO BUY THIS GAME, because if you don't have this vehichle the game ends up becoming a gigantic time sink.  To me it insults the players who put out their hard earned cash to buy this game, for such a simple feature!  This wouldn't be as much of a problem if...
-Outposts are too far apart when considering how slowly your character moves.
-They also removed tents as "DLC".
-Switching between items is really slow as well, it seemed minor at first, but became annoying overtime.
-This game is also very buggy, and crashes, sometimes rage inducing.  There is a glitch where you will randomly die because of some weird collision issues with the player hitbox and the terrain, killing you instantly, which is further infuriating when you have to walk your slow♥♥♥♥♥back to where you were going.
-Ui is garbage and confusing at first
-You can't change resolution settings INGAME, I had to change them outside the game using word.
Conclusion:
There are more comments I forgot to mention, but I think you get the gist.  This game has a very solid foundation, but decisions by the developers, a LOT of minor issues, and the fact that the game is clearly not finished, forces me to NOT recommend this game in it's current state.  There are some changes that are surly needed, starting with the removal of anit-consumer choices, inclusion of "DLC" that should already be in the game, or faster player movement speed.
EDIT:
The game gets a lot better after mission 3 (Fox mission), and mission 4 (photo mission).  In a weird way the fox mission prepares you for the rest of the game, probably because you spend so many hours just trying to kill the ♥♥♥♥er.  Still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t mission.

Most of where the action is happening is over 200+ ping away. Everyone has sadly moved on.

My recommendation for anyone that reads this is unless you buy the DLCs and have your own friends that you can party up with, it's unlikely you'll join a full party of people. I still recommend the game, it's just that you'll find yourself playing solo a lot more often.

I purchased this game at ~$20 during the Christmas sale. I cannot tell how I would have felt about it if it were full price, but I honestly think I would have still been pleasantly satisfied with it considering how much time I played.
Mad Max is a pretty solid game. Hand-to-hand combat is very much like the Arkham series, which I personally enjoy. All those V6s and V8s roar to glorious effect. Vehicle combat possesses a diverse set of features that are enough to not get boring. Tons of collectibles are strewn across the large, albeit barren, map waiting to be acquired. And the world has a personality that is pretty near to consistent with the movies other than a few minor qualms.
However, Mad Max might get repetitive to some. There are only about 4 or 5 unique enemy types so fights play out the same most of the time. The same pretty much applies to vehicle combat as well. Comparing it again to other AAA titles, this actually isn't too terrible but it is something to consider before purchasing it. Even boss fights don't feel all that unique other than maybe one or two fights with the main antagonist near the end of the game. The landscape is barren, understandably, but the devs appear to add some life to it by utilizing their assets to tell a quick little story (usually skeletons or corpses positioned in one way or another). You also have historical artifacts in the form of notes and pictures that tell the story of the world before the catastrophe.
All that considered, I'd recommend the game if you like games like Just Cause 2, Assassin's Creed, or any Arkham game. It's not as over-the-top as Just Cause 2 but it's interesting enough to be fun. If you don't feel strongly about those titles, still give it a look. I was pleasantly surprised with it.

I have followed the entire Life Is Strange series since day one. Since then, I've had so many crazy memories with this game and I still remember literally shedding tears at the final episode when I finished it on its release date, a little more than one year ago. I still quote lines from the game to this day because of how unforgettable the series had become. In this past summer, Before The Storm was announced, and now that I have finished this game too, I can definitely say my expectations were met. Personally, I find some reliability with a few of the characters, but my struggles don't even come close to what goes on in LIS. I show empathy with Max, Chloe, and Rachel as they have pondered and struggled with relationships, friends, enemies, the works. I feel like I've gained closure in not only a video game perspective, but in my own lights too. I truly feel the happiness and pain of each and every character because of how stunning the voice actors are and their power to fuel the foundation of such an exceptionally remarkable universe. The final episode of Before The Storm left me in absolute tears as well and just like last time, this series has blown me away completely. Thank you Square Enix, Deck Nine, and DONTNOD, you all have not only birthed a unique everlasting fictional series, buthave pieced together such a lovable cast, a wonderfully orchestrated story, and a world that we will never forget, creating a cult following that I have been very happy to be a part of since the very start.
A masterpiece. Equal to the original Life is Strange itself.

So were back again huh? Back to the universe that is Life is Strange. I cant express how upset i was that they handed square enix handed it off to Deck Nine at first before playing. But after a full playthrough i can understand that they made the right choice. BTS is fantastic and just as good as the original. Yes its only 3 episodes with a bonus episode. But the 3 episodes are one of the most well crafted and well produced any episodic game has ever been. I will not say whether it is better than the original but it is certainly just as good. It still hurts you with every fiber in its being. Every episode is fantastic and worth every penny. My only complaint is that it shouldnt be so expensive for only 3 episodes. Will they ever make another LiS? I dont know. Without spoiling it, This might be the last time we see arcadia bay. And what an amazing journey it has been. Deck Nine you have proven yourslef worthy to take on this franchise and you made the game more amazing visually and emotionally. To whoever is reading this. Thank you for taking the time to read this. I hope you enjoy this game as much as i did.

I've received this game 2 months after it's release.. The overhype was overrall not worth it, because IT WAS JUST ok. I hestiated in writing this review before because of many people solely disliking the review because they were currently infatuated with the game. Now that the fame has died down a little, let me tell you something:
If you're expecting a very long game. DO NOT get it. There is a reason why I have only 18 hours (and the length of the game is SHORTER than what I have played.)
If you're expecting a game to replay. DO NOT get it. It can be boring to replay, but if you want to achieve "something" you can do so. But it can be SO BORING to replay.

I have no idea if that even spoils anything, but heed my words; Get this game if you are looking for a casual, fun, and specks of fantasy type of story, GET this game. The graphics aren't much to talk about, since it is a indie game, has a fun story and the graphics don't matter.
The reason this game has so many 10/10s is solely because of how many people have YET to experience a story better than this.
So in conclusion for ME.. it's a 7.5/10. It's not that AMAZING story everyone talked so great about. It's a great story, but not worth replaying.
Oh, one comment about the fanbase: It's terrible, but not the game's fault.

So when these dudes put out Primal, a spinoff about shooting dinosaurs, people hoped it'd lead to these guys doing real releases that don't nickel-and-dime you to death. But then they abandoned it and went back to the cashShop hell of theHunter. Now, at last, we have an appoximation of the original game but without the need to endlessly pay for the right to play the game. Is it good? Yeah, if you like hunting sims. Otherwise, no.
Now, when I talk about hunting games you need to realize there's different kinds. Some, like CABELAS DANGEROUS HUNTS 2013, are ridiculous call of duty games with animals. Others, like this, are very serious and attempt to replicate, at least somewhat, the experience of hunting some animals in the woods. Lots of walking, lots of hearing a fox and then never finding it, or indeed anything at all. Now it's not the most realistic I've seen; it doesn't seem to have a very detailed bullet model or whatever, but it's certainly trying to be pretty serious and is commendable in that way. It does have baffling open world stuff too, though, like collectibles and towers you climb to reveal the map like some sort of Assassin whose Creed only involves shooting deer. There are landmarks to see, perks to earn, stuff to buy, quests to fulfil (mostly just about killing animals in specific ways or taking photographs), etc. Apparently the new expansion has a sort of thriller storyline, but I don't own that yet so I can't judge it; the base game's story is pretty much just that you are a guy who like to hunt and you do it, good job.
One thing to note: there IS some DLC which is kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. You have to pay a couple bucks for the right to drive ATVs and again to unlock tents, which are portable fast travel spots. Both feel like they're cut from the game to sell to you because they are, and that sucks. But like I said, it's still a hell of a lot more fair than anything else on the market right now and it's good. Unless you don't want to shoot Bambi's father, in which case go play a Cabela's Dangerous Hunts game cause they got wizard lions and♥♥♥♥♥♥like that.

Windward is a sailing game where you choose a faction who give you different ''boost'' like firepower, speed, trade profits... trying to conquest different regions and dominate the seas, improving your conquisted towns and get better stuff and ships.
But "where is the challenge?" Arrr, All aboard! Tons of pirates everywhere, who try to get your regions and sink your ship in trade functions.
In addition other players can challenge you to get regions, so the war and fun is guaranteed!
We have a plenty of possibilities is the customization, from equipment for the ship like cannons, sails, crew... which boost our ship stats to hull paints, sails paints, sails drawings... and even flags that we can use to change of faction, disable pvp or even be pirates! We have the possibility of customize our own map when we start a world too.
Another important aspect of the game is the possibility to create and add mods, which is a very interesting possibility and can expand the gameplay a lot. At the moment few mods were released, but the community is pretty nice and in some months I think some interesting mods will start to show up.
-Pros
* Pretty nice graphics, that can be supported by mostly of economic graphic cards nowadays.
* The gameplay is easy and very fun.
* The IA of the npc's is pretty good ( Still having some cons ) but they does their job and the quotes are interesting and fun.
* The customization is just great, from the appearance of the ship to his stats.
* The skill system is a good motivation to get levels and are useful.
* Combat system is simple but fun, with some details like the sails deterioration that affects the mobility and speed.
* Quest system is useful not just for XP and resources, it upgrade your town to get better items, profits, and ships, giving a good reason to do the quest and get better towns.
* The factions are defined, having each one different features, so you can choose according with your style.
* Mods support, something awesome to not get boring of the same functions always.
* Frequently updates and active dev in forum.
* The community seems nice and help.
-Cons
* The IA is useful, but sometimes allies ships does weird things like ram you all the time or damage you in combat frequently.
* Skills are useful, but in my opinion too useful, I mean, with the whole skill tree of defense I can kill 4 ships  at the same time with my ship of line, some needs a downgrade.
* At the moments there're just 10 quest, it's a good amount of them to start, but when you have some time playing the quest are so repetitive.
All the cons will change with the time, it's just a early acess at all, but the game have a great future, congrats to the creator, it is a great and fun game, and I hope we can enjoy it much more.

Let me begin by saying that this game was truly a welcome surprise, I expected not to like it and boy did it prove me wrong...
So, what is it ? Is it really a rogue like ??? oh sure, in a sense... I mean there is no real save and you restart your adventures in a procedurally created dungeon every time... on the other hand not really because you actually do improve each time over and thats a fundamental no-no for rogue likes....
At the end of the day its a hybrid, that will appeal more to non rogue-like fanatics, rather than the true fans of that genre.
The thing is that if you look past all that, its a truly fast paced, fun-filled plat-former that will make you swear, cry and smile every-time you give it a go and believe me you will give it a go and another and another and so on... its so compelling to just try to do a bit better each time.
The main concept of the game is that each time you die you can start over with one of your descendants all of whom carry over the abilities of their ancestors (and their flaws). So you gather money with each run and but abilities and equipment and each generation is a bit stronger - mind you you cant keep your gold (or at least most of it) between runs, since you need pay death each time you enter the dungeon (except in cases where you have found a special item that you turn on instead of gold).
A similarity to rogue like games is that it starts out very hard and that will frustrate most players (but you will come back for more). However as you progress and improve it becomes easier and I must say (this is one of my grievances with it) after a point it becomes, perhaps too easy.
The bosses are somewhat easy (with the exception of the four special bosses that are insanely hard - but those are not necessary to finish the game) and each new play-through increases the difficult (ala Dark Souls New Game +1 ect).
One thing that ticked me off, which becomes apparent when you master it, is that it is actually short and it really makes you yearn for more.... perhaps with some expansion or dlc but you would like to do more much more (and this is another point where it differs dramatically with true rogue-likes).
The graphics are pix-elated but beautiful and the retro style suits it so well, the music can get a tad annoying at times but then again its very reminiscent of 8-bit era game music.
Overall I have to say I loved the game and I truly wish it had more to offer, but it doesn't. Is it worth playing in spite of that ? Hell yes - its so much fun....
But after 5 play-throughs and all achievements equipment the only thing left was the special bosses. I did spent the time to kill one of them but its for the true hardcores... perhaps I may go back and try them again for the achievements alone, but at this stage there isn't a lot of re-playability.
Again, regardless of any shortcoming I described, its so much fun and totally worth it (which is why its a bit disappointing at the end).

WARNING: A LOT OF FORESHADOWING HERE, BUT NO SPOILERS
The best works of art are created in a time where they are most needed, and found in the places no one would bother to look. In today's gaming industry, many are looking for the next great narrative to be found in a small indie game, or an expertly crafted RPG. Absolutely nobody was expecting a third-person military shooter to be the breakthrough they were desperately searching for, and that just adds to the utter brilliance of Spec Ops: The Line.
As you may have heard, the game is very much intwined in the same themes as Joseph Conrad's incredible novel, "Heart of Darkness". You are a Special Forces captain sent in with your 3-man squad to the ruins of Dubai. The way the city is presented is unlike any other world design in recent memory, as you truly feel the suffering of the survivors, from the rotting, strung-up corpses to the creepiness of the multiple murals and graffiti you will stumble upon. Even with the bright aesthetics of sand and sun, make no mistake; Dubai is a wasteland with nothing left to offer.
However, world design takes a backseat to narrative here, where the characters you encounter and the actions you take break down every preconception you might have had about military shooters. From the eerie antagonist to the journalist who could've very well been the brother of Dennis Hopper from Apocalypse Now, every character here feels needed. You will be forced to take actions that will genuinely shock you. By the third hour, I had committed what was by far, the most horrifying thing I have ever done in a video game. And make no mistake, none of this is purely for shock value, but truly necessary thematically, in order to build up to an unforgettable finale.
By the end of the game, you will wonder why you bothered to play this game at all. But really, that's just it. In this game, you are not meant to be the hero. You are not supposed to have a happy ending, you are not meant to be the great patriot fighting for his country. It is the war epic that is needed after America's decade-long conflict in Afghanistan. It is what "The Red Badge of Courage" was to the American Civil War, what "The Deer Hunter" was to Vietnam. Even the game asks you towards the end, "Do you remember why you came here?" But that's just it. You may have forgotten why you played this game, but you'll be glad you did.

This game is a big pile of awesome.
If you are looking for a fantastic prison-builder game, then you've hit the jackpot.
This game definitely makes my top 10 games of 2010-2015 list, and believe me, you should get it right now.
You can build and manage your prison with such detail, down to things like choosing the meal quality and quantity or deploying guards in certain areas (such as cell blocks), or setting them on patrols around your perimeter. Now, I know that you're probably thinking "Micromanagement SUCKS!". But, not in this game. This game is one of the very few exceptions to the whole micromanagement issues, because this game does it very well. It's not overdone to the point that it's just flat-out boring, instead being just right so that you can tune your prison to your specific wants/needs. These options are unlocked via a research system (in-game), so if you don't want the extra micro-management, then don't research it. Even then, this game is still fantastic. Updates are released every month, and they are almost always big game-changers, adding new features, fixing lots of bugs, and making things much more smooth and balanced.
Don't think it's for you? Look up videos of it on youtube.

Prison Architect is fun.  As more things are released it just gets more enjoyable.
There are two ways to play Prison Architect.  Free mode where you don't have to worry about money or failure outcomes; this is a perfect mode to test your layouts before hand.
The second is a lot more difficult as there are a lot of needs you will have to satisfy your prisoners if you want to keep them in line and behaving well.  That of course really depends on yourself though - you could have a 22 hour lockdown for all prisoner types, 1 hour for meals and 1 hour for free time with an available shower block that SOME not all prisoners will decide to use.  Your prison will get very dirty though.
It's still fun to see what will happen under different regimes and different prisoners though.
If they added multiple levels it would be absolutely fantastic as currently making room for the extra items can be difficult, and it's not an easy game to start out playing - hire at least 20 workers and turn off the prisoners until you have the very basics set up and ready to go. - reduce the worker count as you need it.
I really wish there was a way of turning the automatic light placement as well, because the AI doesn't do it properly, no matter what dimension the building is.
Very highly recommended and looking forward to each new update; generally monthly will be interesting to see what they introduce next and where to place it.
Anyway, I've got to go and finish creating the first building for low security prisoners.

tl;dr / Final Thoughts - Life is Strange: Before the Storm is an amazing game, with it's biggest downfall being that it is a prequel to an even better game, the original Life is Strange. While this game has a gripping story that gave me goosebumps time and time again, it is more dramatic than it is depressing (which is not what I expected when I made my purchase).
Before I get into each episode specifically, here are just some general things...
As someone who has played through the original Life is Strange more times than I am even going to attempt to count, my hype certainly influenced my opinion of the first episode. It was great seeing all the old characters plus some new ones. As for the story, it took so many twists and turns that I had very high hopes for the next two episodes to come. I don't know why so many people were scared over a change in voice actress for Chloe, because she sounded just fine. David, however, sounded more nasally than I was used to. The puzzles were not too time consuming, but were present. Overall I really enjoyed this episode.
Holy guac-on-my-mole, this episode is so long. That is definitly not a bad thing, as it means there is more game to play, but I expected to be able to finish it in one sitting...I did, but it was long. The puzzles were longer, occasionally more difficult
but overall added a game element to a walking simulator. The story continued to amaze up until the very end, where the voice acting of
just completely ruined it for me. Unfortunatly, that character's voice acting doesn't get much better throughout the rest of the game, but it isn't a deal breaker by any means. Overall an enjoyable, long, and plot twist full episode.
The final episode is really the only one that matters, if you think about it; it's the one people will recall when looking back at a game. The choices you made in the first and second episode come back to haunt you the most in this episode, which is what I was waiting for all along. They wrap up the story very nicely, and (if the global choices that people made are anything to go off of) there seems to be several endings to some character's stories. The final decision is one that seems to have an obvious answer if you just pay attention to what people are saying, but that's just my opinoin on it. The puzzles are the longest and most pointless in this episode, but aren't terrible. There's also a tie in after the credits to the orginal Life is Strange, which is very off putting. This is probably my favorite episode of this game.

She then asked me to turn it down to which I responded "I'm disinclined to acquiesce to your request. Means "no"."

***This review was written using a key provided by the Developers for review purposes***
Windward is a top-down sandbox sailing game which is currently available in Early Access. In Windward you take to the seas in a boat from one of four factions each with their speciality ranging from combat prowess to diplomatic success. Whether you choose to focus on combat, trading or diplomacy you will always come across ways to make money as well as danger in a giant procedurally-generated world. As you travel through the world you will come across many enemies to kill, towns to set free from pirate occupation, quests to take and all the loot you could ever dream of!
+Nice graphics and everything is well designed especially the ships
+Simple but very effective UI which stays out of your way while still being easy to navigate and use including a handy little mini-map
+The map is fully customisable but if you don't edit it the map is procedurally generated anyway so you'll never play the same game twice
+Completing quests for towns helps them to grow which in turn means you get higher rewards for future quests but also visibly changes the town by making it bigger
+Combat is again, simple but fun, think top-down ACIV naval combat
+A large skill tree where each skill really does make a big difference
+The four different playable factions have different pros and cons and they really are noticeable, having played as the Consulate (democratic) and the Valiant (militaristic) it was clear to see that Valiant ships are considerably better in combat and Consulate captains are much better at negotiation
+Good trading system where different towns have different needs and are willing to pay much higher prices for resources that are in high demand
+An excellent reputation system where as you sink more AI the AI gradually become more afraid to you until a point where they will try to avoid you all together unless they're a high level enemy
+When playing on a default map the difficulty increases at a speed which really eases you in to the more difficult areas
+The game features something called Instances which are small missions you can trigger at any time which earn you loot and EXP
+Occasionally you will find things after destroying enemy ships such as new cannons or a different hull material which you can use to upgrade your ship
+Dynamic weather which effects your ship's speed, in stormy weather you travel slower than you do in clear weather
+Both fun and relaxing to play, the game focuses on being a fun experience for all rather than focusing on providing a realistic sailing simulator
+Reasonably frequent updates
+The dev is very active on the forums and clearly adores this game (I mean he has over 750 hours in it) which is really good to see
-The music is good but there is very little variety and often there is no music playing at all
-Early ships have tiny cargo holds which makes it hard to earn money through trading early in the game
Worth a mention:
-The game has no story whatsoever, it is purely a sandbox experience which personally I quite like but others may not.
Verdict:
9
An excellent sea-based sandbox game with a great AI system and procedurally generated maps that still has a lot of potential for expansion.

An addictive action/adventure game with frustrating balance issues.
Rogue Legacy is best described as a clone of Castlevania: Symphony of the Night or any one of its many successors on the Game Boy Advance and DS. It's a 2D sidescrolling adventure game where you fight your way through the many rooms of a fully interconnected, nonlinear castle, finding gold, runes and other equipment to power yourself up. But oddly, the game really gets interesting when you die: your character is killed off permanently and you have to pick their successor from one of three random choices, and can use the gold collected by the previous character to buy new stat upgrades and equipment for your subsequent characters. However, once you re-enter the castle, the castle's layout is randomized and you'll lose all your gold, so it becomes an interesting challenge to see how much gold you can amass in this new castle to improve your next character before the baddies take you down again.
When you buy enough upgrades from the manor, you'll eventually unlock new classes with new abilities. This is where the game runs into problems. Firstly, the classes aren't all that different from each other. They all use the same equipment. They all tote around that same comically-huge sword. Only their stats really change.
The second problem is that most of these classes trade health for other abilities: hokages can do a lot of damage with each strike, but they die easily; mages can have a lot of magic power and use their (not terribly useful) spells often, but they die easily; miners can collect larger amounts of gold, but... You get the idea.
This wouldn't be such a big problem except for the fact that the game repeatedly swarms you with enemies and projectiles. There are times where you're being attacked from all directions at once while being bombarded from off-screen by dozens of fireballs, missiles and bouncing spiked balls that you can't destroy. Bosses similarly crowd the screen with bullets and smaller enemies, meaning all your added attack power is rendered largely moot unless you've got completely insane dodging abilities with which to preserve your measly health bar. This severely limits the use of any class beyond the ones with high HP.
Beyond that (and the fact that the opening hour or so of the game is pretty boring, at least until you can unlock new stuff. And that the game needs more music variety because that Castle Hamson theme just gets ANNOYING after the 20th-or-so respawn), it really is a very fun and highly addictive game. The controls are pretty much spot-on, the graphics sport good animation, vibrant color and cute designs, and it's compelling to see how much further you can get into the randomized castle and how much gold you can collect THIS time. I just wish so many of the character classes didn't feel so impotent.

My God... this game. Why is everyone not still talking about this game?!
I picked this up based on Yahtzee's
recommendation, and it was everything he said it would be. Incredibly well written and thought-provoking, this is the first game I've ever played that actually
hold a mirror up to the medium, the genre, society, players, even the developers themselves. I have never been so morally challenged by a game, and I didn't think I could be more shocked or emotionally distraught over the events in a game than the first time I saw the sword erupt from Aerith's chest. But when you get to
, you'll understand why I put this game down for nine months before charging back through it.
When you finish the game (and you really should attempt to get at least two of the endings), I suggest you also read up about
as well. It's unfortunate that the necessary evil of the video game distribution model forced Yager to acquiesce to 2K's demands and dilute
the themes of the single-player campaign through the inclusion of a multiplayer mode. In the current climate of cynical knockoffs and safe, bland sequels, the ambition shown by the developers at Yager is amazing. Their willingness to explore unpleasant topics and themes in the pursuit of their message is worthy of high praise.
The only caveat I would offer is that the game play can feel unbalanced in a handful of places. There are a few sections that are punishingly difficult to get through, where your squad mates are more a curse than a blessing. While I'd like to think this was also intentional by Yager, it felt more like the product of unfortunate choices in event and checkpoint scripting.
This game is impressive, important even. Everyone who enjoys the FPS genre (even though this is technically a third-person shooter) should play this. It will make you level up as a gamer... and as a human being.

Spec Ops: The Line seems like any other shooter at its beginning, but it turns out to be much more.  Set in post-apocalyptic Dubai, the brown, lifeless landscapes that are present in many other shooters are replaced by colorful citiscapes and opulent urban backdrops.  Bullets are scarce, so the game encourages intelligent approaches to conflicts through environmental destruction as well as your standard conveniently placed explosive barrels.
Most of all, the game succeeds in being fun to play while also possessing uncommon emotional weight.  As your character is affected by his actions, so, too, is the player.  Intelligence pickups function similarly to Bioshock's audiologs, providing additional information to flesh out the narrative and provide deeper looks into the player character's perceptions.
It's a relatively short game (~6 hours per playthrough), but it accomplishes more over its short duration than most games do over any length.  If you're a fan of exposition and don't mind breaking a few heads along the way, Spec Ops: The Line is very worthy of your consideration.  It's an experience I won't soon forget.

I didn't like the game too much. I got to chapter 7 (of 15) and uninstalled because I needed disk space for other games.
First of all, controls are very unintuitive for PC players, and your muscle memory will keep you tripping over defaults. While you can redefine the keyboard bindings, they are *grouped* awkwardly (for example same key must be used for run and cover so when running or trying to find better cover your character "sticks" to all kinds of wrong cover constantly). Additionally if you have a controller plugged in (but not using it) game will keep displaying controller keys in all context popups which is very confusing.
Gameplay itself is okay, nothing especially good, it plays and feels like a generic "on rails" linear-levels console port with added inconvenience of terrible controls on which you'll either have to get used to or suffer. Also notable thing is that it is very easy to die and get in inescapable situations. Gameplay protip: default pistol is fantastic for whatever-range headshots - which you'll need because ammo is not plentiful (unlike deadly enemies).
Level design is absolutely linear and you can only go and do what the script says. Enemies spawn at predefined time, position and distance as you pass trigger points. For such "on-rails" linear game as is Spec Ops: The Line, scarcity of ammo really hinders game flow.
I won't comment on the story too much because I only endured until chapter 7 until I gave up due to unrewarding gameplay and awkward controls, but so far the story was basically a proverbial "junk food", and I'm not saying this as a bad thing.
*** CONCLUSION ***
I don't recommend the game at full price, even if you are just interested in the story.
Because I got it on sale for €4.99 I don't feel I wasted my money for what I played + I avoided wasting my time when game got sufficiently unrewarding to play.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a great game for those who enjoy relaxed, slow-paced games, which can be explorative and interesting. The game is first and foremost a simulator, meaing you have to use your signal lights, use your windshield wipers when it rains, turn on your lights in the dark, etc, etc. All of this leads to a very immersive experience wherein you can drive across the entirety of Europe without leaving your home. You can haul all types of cargo, you can start a trucking business and become a trucking empire!
I do have a few issues with this game, but the overall quality greatly outweighs the negative aspects. The speed limit in the U.K. lowers at certain points, and then a speed camera snaps you for going over the speed limit! Another issue is the optimization; for me, the game can lag and become choppy at seemingly random points, although my overall framerate sticks above 60 FPS.
In the end, it's a great relaxation game with great simulator elements, I reccommend it, but if you're into fast-paced games, stay away.

Borderlands 2, the sequel to the surprise hit first person shooter with RPG elements and Diablo loot system, is back with a vengeance. 4 new Vault Hunters take on the magnificently evil Handsome Jack on a quest to obtain as much loot as possible and, on a side note, save Pandora from total destruction.
+It should be a given for a good game, but Borderlands 2 is so fun to play... all available characters have vastly different skill trees that tend towards specific playstyles which are all good, challenging and rewarding in their own right, and the base gameplay itself is satisfying enough to make millions of people forgive, if not enjoy, the fact this game is 95% shooting the hell out of everything that moves.
+Depending on how much you like it, this game can last you forever. The base content alone has a main storyline and a ton of side missions and quests worth a good 70-85 hours of gameplay. Then there are the DLCs, which vary greatly in duration and cost but offer new characters, longer new campaigns in brand new areas with a generally high quality (Tiny Tina's D&D spoof is particularly great) and smaller content still quite good. All in all it may take around 130 hours, maybe more, to completely clear the game. And then there's new game +, which can be repeated basically forever. And let's not forget you may want to try out a different character than the one you started with... you get the point. If you can't get enough of this game, it is a long term investment.
+Borderlands 2 takes the unique cel shading that gave the first game a distinctive graphical personality, if a rough one, and gives it a bigger budget. The result is an absolutely gorgeous looking game that offers a ton of eye candy without giving up its style.
+Depending on your taste, you may find this game's crude black humor tasteless and forced. However, for most players it's just the icing on the cake, and it's rare to find a shooter that manages to make you smile every time you read a mission briefing or hear someone blab in your comms.
+The audio department, especially the soundtrack and voice acting, is quite great, which is a welcome bonus.
+The PC port is almost as good as they get nowadays. Nuff said.
+This game is quite fun and entertaining for me in single player. The co-op, however, is a different thing entirely: taking on the hordes of empowered enemies with up to three friends (playing with randoms isn't recommended) is exhilarating, and the ferocious arguments over loot are... well, sadomasochistically fun.
+Did i mention this thing even has a respectably good plot? Unlike the first game, twists and great moments abound, and the characters' personalities are all fairly fleshed out. Handsome Jack, then again, is a memorable villain in general, not only within the series.
-If continous slaughterdome fueled by repetitive objectives (that nearly always include "go there, kill everything, retrieve that, get back here" or something like this) doesn't sound particularly thrilling to your ears, this game will inevitably bore you, since it's literally all it's about.
-The quality of this game's myriad of DLCs goes from passable to excellent, but the amount and pricing of additional content are both quite high, which means if you bought the game at launch you may spend an insane amount of money to acquire all the new campaigns and characters, not to mention the paid clothing for each character. Not even the GOTY edition is comprehensive of everything available for the game, which is quite shameful.
-Enemy respawns are on Far Cry 2 levels (imagine clearing a tough dungeon and backtracking to get the hell out of there only to realize the enemies at the start have respawned), which can get quite annoying when you're simply trying to go from A to B.
-Some classes are clearly better than others when playing solo. In particular, every class that can give the enemies someone or something other than you to shoot at for more than a handful of seconds (Axton, the Mechromancer...) will be more easily capable of catching its breath, while classes that have short (Zero) or no distractions available will struggle more.
It's not a common occurrence that a sequel is so much better than its predecessor that it completely obscures it and goes from good success to massive blockbusting phenomenon. However, games like this prove that "bigger and better" sequels exist, and they're amazing. If you liked Borderlands, you will love this game. Everybody else: give it a shot. It's fun as hell and not too convoluted, while still maintaining enough depth to distance it from generic first person shooters.

LiS lost me near the end, exactly for that reason. And BtS came pretty close to doing the same.
Or in other words:
That kiss on the streets, that train ride, fixing up the car and stuff like that will stay in my memory. That climax (in both games) won't. Plain and simple.
I just think that deciding whether to lie or tell the truth to a person you love is a far more impactful choice than attacking the token baddy with a knife or not.

Life is Strange: Before the Storm is the prequel to Life is Strange and focuses on Chloe Price, one of the main characters from the first game. Even though this game is two episodes shorter than the first one, it lacks absolutely nothing in terms of quality.
The characters and their complex and often ambivalent, but also often fun relationships are portrayed very well, the story is interesting with a few twists and the choices, while not all of them have major effects, are very interesting to think about, especially in the third episode.
As with the first game, the soundtrack is absolutely amazing and atmospheric and the artstyle is beautiful as well. Also, the character animations have improved drastically compared to the first game and convey much more emotion.
The only flaws I can really think of are minor technical issues like some delayed or cut-off sound effects. But these could also be related to my system.
Overall a very great story- and character-driven game that will make you feel almost every emotion imaginable.

So I just finised this game today and after playing, decided to write a review.
A modern military 3rd person shooter, putting the player in the middle of unspeakable situations.
Yes, I can agree with that.
My take on the game is this: Its a modern version of Apocalypse Now. I see so many things in common with that film. The background is that the large city of Dubai was destroyed by a sandstorm and then a large amount of troops were sent in to rescue them. Nobody escapes and all contact with the city has been lost. It has been left to rot.
Enter a 3 man elite Delta Force squad searching for answers. Once entering the city and being attacked, they decide to find the rouge Colonel (ala Apocalypse Now) and find out what exactly happend.
Not going to ruin the game by what entails, but it is sick and horrifying. Choices are presented to you, but it feels like it makes little difference because the choices are so horrible.
The game is short. I tend to play my games on easier difficutly and I completed the game in about 5 hours.
A good selection of weapons. You can only carry 2 weapons at a time, and some ammo is scarce for certain weapons, so I found that I swapped weapons quite a bit.
Pretty straightforward game. No puzzles or backtracking. Kill the guys, move into the next area, cutscene, repeat. I did enjoy some parts that allow you to cover your other 2 guys when you get separated or shooting the minigun on the helicopter. No vehicles for you to drive, this game is all on foot. You are able to issue some limited commands to your members as well.
The AI for the squad members, I must admit is great. Instead of some games that AI units just follow you around and take some cover, firing every now and then at an enemy. In this game, my AI squad took cover, and KILLED units. They covered me when I moved. They moved ahead of me on the map and engaged and killed units.
The audio is ok. I actually got a little tired of some of the phrases they shout. I wish they couldve included a few different lines because every firefight I got into, it always sounded the same. But whats there is good and sets the mood. Music is ok, nothing really major to speak about. Gun sounds are decent as well.
Graphics are pretty decent as well. The unreal engine 3 is starting to show its age a little, and even though I had the graphics at max, some textures were blurry, but still decent. Large landscapes and sprawling desolate city was nice. I really enjoyed the sandstorms. Every once in a while during the game, a sandstorm would come through. Wind, low visibility and all was pretty decent and felt intense when one hit in the middle of a gun fight.
I think my biggest gripe with this game is the controls. For me being almost strictly a PC gamer and have played other 3rd person shooters, the controls felt a little wonky. You hit space to run, and once you start running, do not have to hold down space. You also use space to take cover behind anything you can, be it a wall, destroyed vehicle or side of a building. The control key is used to duck/croutch. However, since the spacebar is used to take cover behind something, I felt this wasnt needed at all in game since when your being shot at, will use the spacebar to take cover, not croutch behind something. I kept mixing them in game and died a few times because of it.
So over all, I give the game a 7.5/10. A good, if some what short game that will make you think about the morality of being a soldier.

Right up front I will say this: If you enjoy tycoon, management, and building sims then you will most likely enjoy this game. It is definitely worth purchasing, especially if you manage to catch it on sale. I highly recommend it.
Prison Architect is a prison building and management sim wherein you manage a prison from on high as a sort of prison god. You are given planning tools to plan the layout of your prison. You have access to building tools that allow you to directly place walls, floors, doors, ligths, and equipment. You can hire staff. You can set patrols for your guards. You can order searches and shakedowns. You can set schedules for your prisoners to follow. You can institute educational and work programs. And you can have your guards run phone taps to discover when a prisoner may be expecting some illicit goods to be thrown in over an exterior wall. There are of course the expected shower shankings and prison riots as well.
There is a ton to do and a lot to like about Prison Architect. Planning and managing successful prison is a rewarding experience that comes with a fair number of challenges. Those interested in a more easy-going experience might run a lightly secured prison for minimum security (white-collar crime) prisoners. If you're interested in a real challenge you can turn on "continuous intake" and load up on maximum, or super-max security prisoners until your prison is consumed by a full on riotous bloodbath that must be quelled by the military.
Honestly the game is one of those that you can tweak to suit your playstyle, which is one reason why I find it so appealing. Heck, if you're into logic puzzles or programming you can even combine timers and logic gates to control your doors and make your prisons even more secure through automation.
If I have any complaints at this point they are these:
First, with the game still in development there really is no tutorial to speak of. If you're new, you'll have to spend some time learning what it takes to make a good prison. The grants do a good job of giving you goals to work towards to set up your first prisons, and they are helpful. But the logic circuits and pressure plates controlling your doors, the confidential informants, and some rooms like the library and the chapel are all examples of new(ish) additions that do not yet have in-game tutorials. I'm certain this will be fixed in time, but for now if you want to learn about these things checking let's plays on YouTube or exploring the wiki are your only options.
And second, there are some performance issues. This is Alpha, and I admit my computer is behind the times, but in the utilities screen especially I experience significant slowdown in comparison to the rest of the game. It's still completely playable, but something to note. Certainly not extreme enough to be a deal breaker.
Those are my only gripes. And I can easily overlook them because A) This is an Early Access title, and B) The developers are very communicative, provide regular updates, and are clearly putting every effort they can into making this game excellent.
I can easily, unabashedly, recommend Prison Architect. It's incredibly fun already and continues to improve. Even if for some reason the developers suddenly vanished from the face of the earth Prison Architect would still be worth purchasing and playing in its current state.
