An addictive action/adventure game with frustrating balance issues.
Rogue Legacy is best described as a clone of Castlevania: Symphony of the Night or any one of its many successors on the Game Boy Advance and DS. It's a 2D sidescrolling adventure game where you fight your way through the many rooms of a fully interconnected, nonlinear castle, finding gold, runes and other equipment to power yourself up. But oddly, the game really gets interesting when you die: your character is killed off permanently and you have to pick their successor from one of three random choices, and can use the gold collected by the previous character to buy new stat upgrades and equipment for your subsequent characters. However, once you re-enter the castle, the castle's layout is randomized and you'll lose all your gold, so it becomes an interesting challenge to see how much gold you can amass in this new castle to improve your next character before the baddies take you down again.
When you buy enough upgrades from the manor, you'll eventually unlock new classes with new abilities. This is where the game runs into problems. Firstly, the classes aren't all that different from each other. They all use the same equipment. They all tote around that same comically-huge sword. Only their stats really change.
The second problem is that most of these classes trade health for other abilities: hokages can do a lot of damage with each strike, but they die easily; mages can have a lot of magic power and use their (not terribly useful) spells often, but they die easily; miners can collect larger amounts of gold, but... You get the idea.
This wouldn't be such a big problem except for the fact that the game repeatedly swarms you with enemies and projectiles. There are times where you're being attacked from all directions at once while being bombarded from off-screen by dozens of fireballs, missiles and bouncing spiked balls that you can't destroy. Bosses similarly crowd the screen with bullets and smaller enemies, meaning all your added attack power is rendered largely moot unless you've got completely insane dodging abilities with which to preserve your measly health bar. This severely limits the use of any class beyond the ones with high HP.
Beyond that (and the fact that the opening hour or so of the game is pretty boring, at least until you can unlock new stuff. And that the game needs more music variety because that Castle Hamson theme just gets ANNOYING after the 20th-or-so respawn), it really is a very fun and highly addictive game. The controls are pretty much spot-on, the graphics sport good animation, vibrant color and cute designs, and it's compelling to see how much further you can get into the randomized castle and how much gold you can collect THIS time. I just wish so many of the character classes didn't feel so impotent.

Axton the Commando: Sabre Turret Action Skill, reliable damage output

With Windward now out of Early Access, this review deserved an overhaul.
Windward is an incredibly awesome ship sailing, questing and trading RPG game, this has been compared very favourably with games like Sid Meier's Pirates. There's so much to do - sail across the seas to towns, claim said towns in your name (claim a majority of the towns in order to claim the region for your faction), fight pirates (and on occasion other faction ships), do quests for the town to help them grow...and as you progress you can upgrade your ship and skills to make you even more powerful in combat. Or whatever it is that you choose to specialise in, anyway (you can change it if you want, though).
While it was in Early Access, I felt the game was way too good for Early Access. Thankfully, other players and the developer could see through the game's shortcomings, and a boatload of new features were shipped out to the game between the start of Early Access and the official game launch in May. The current version of Windward at release feels a lot better than when I played it a few months back. (Incidentally, I apologise for the ship puns. It's arrrrr rather infectious trend.)
In-between Early Access and game release, there have been a few (that's a gross understatement) interface changes and game mechanic tweaks so the game is much easier to follow. Instances, one of the most recent additions, creates a region appropriate to your ship level - a fun and challenging distraction that, when farmed properly, can be incredibly profitable. Of course, it is even better with friends/on a multiplayer server - high level Heroic instances make the pirate enemies drop VERY good loot. This is where Windward REALLY shines - it is all about the player interaction and cooperation on these online servers.
What was already good about the game though is the combat, the quests, and the music (which dynamically changes depending on whether you are in combat or not).
I only really have 2 gripes regarding the game. The physics occasionally feels wonky and sometimes my ship gets stuck in an odd situation...then explodes in a raging fireball. I understand though this is due to the quirkiness of Unity, so not much that can be done. However, Unity should not be knocked (so much, anyway) - this really looks stunningly beautiful.
My other gripe is something that can easily be fixed with high-level friends - if you're trying to do it solo, you're going to have a hard time. One of the achievements requires you to drive pirates out of a level 13 (39 talent points) region - chances are you likely won't have strong enough equipment if you were playing it solo. Leveling it up in order to better combat them may at times feel too grindy (however, the satisfaction of sinking the pirates overshadows that for me).This is where Heroic or high-level instances and a couple of powerful friends saves the day - farm these instances for the high-level equipment then return to the level 13 region and decimate the pirates.
Developer ArenMook is one of the friendliest, most helpful and hardworking devs around. He actually comes into the servers to play with us mere mortals, ahem, sailors - and regularly pushes out bugfixes, game updates, all kinds of updates. You can't get any better customer service than that!
As far as I'm concerned, this game is the closest I can get to living out my Somalian Pirate Fantasies™, for those who know me. Download size is surprisingly (and pleasantly) small, and it runs great even on low-spec computers. Highly recommended.
Buy a four-pack and play the game with 3 like-minded friends. You'll probably end up sinking a lot of time (and pirates...okay, enough ship puns. I'm sorry.) into it for it to be worth the cost - it's just that fun.

Of course procedurally generated with very nice result. For me, one of the greatest strength of this game is fact you can choose pace of your game, you can always tailor your playstyle. You aren`t forced into doing anything and you got this feel that if you want to play 'slow' today game adjust to you, not other way around. And it transfers to multiplayer! Having big number of regions is greatest strength - if you want to play today with friends/strangers, just go to some server and be in same region and do stuff together. Want to be on multiplayer server, but do some stuff alone? Cool, just go to other region, or just ignore them.
If you like those type of games and/or always liked this type of world setting (like me) you are going to love this game.
And don`t get stopped by being in early access, this game have the best developer I ever encountered. He reads *every* post on the forum, always respond and give advices or help if needed, even proposes himself if there is a need.
If you have ideas, post them on the forum. While Dev have strong vision of the game he is building (which is good actually), if you have concept that is agreedable with his vision you will have that idea implemented into the game. Probably tommorow - if it is a small one, as dev is throwing updates almost every day.
This is a genuinely enjoyable idea. Variety, replayability and a really nice merging of concepts from many different games that provides a depth of gameplay I was not expecting.

OMG... BUY THIS GAME.
I've never seen a transformation like this before. Did you play the "free" version of theHunter?
Yeah, forget that micro-transaction fest of a game.
Pros:
Incredibly well optomized (can practically run on a potato and still look amazing),
Solid character progression,
Solid gameplay mechanics,
Huge variety of wildlife of varying difficulty to hunt over many regions and reserves,
Great animal AI,
Incredibly immersive audio experience,
Excellent tracking system,
Great ballistics models,
Excellent optional multiplayer (competitive co-op),
Singleplayer and multiplayer share the same character and global unlockables,
Mission objectives to gently guide your experience, but without restricting you,
Great selection of real world weapons, ammo, and gear,
Collectables,
Discoverable locations with lore,
Lookout towers and observation points reveal nearby undiscovered locations marked with questionmarks on the map,
Optional vehicles (DLC) that are fun, but not neccessary due to fast travel,
More stuff that I won't go into for now.
Cons:
Player models are ugly,
3rd person animations are bad (ask your buddy to aim, and see where the buttstock rests, or have him crouch walk while using the bleat call),
Menu navigation needs work to be more obvious and seamless,
Janky bugs when using a controller (can't interact with map elements, janky crouching, character stands up before going prone, which can tack on another couple of hours of stalking),
Hints on the left of the screen are in a very tiny font, not worded particularly well, and disappear faster than you can read some of them (I'd like to think I'm a decent reader, as my Reading Comprehension score on the ACT was 35/36),
Singleplayer objectives can't be accomplished in multiplayer,
Leveling up is a bit grindy (but not too grindy... grindy enough to put in the cons section),
Can't go in the WWI German bunkers (how cool would it be to use them as a deer blind, am I right?).
On to the TL:DR part of the review!
tH:CotW is so polished an optimized that even id (Doom) would tip their hats. At maxed settings, I'm rocking near-photorealism at a solid 80fps. Even my friend's potato of a gaming PC is rocking this game on a mix of high and ultra settings.
As for the important part, gameplay, I have to give this game my rarely doled-out 9.5/10.
Seriously, they've almost nailed it. it loses 0.5 points because you are forced to use a mouse to make use of waypoints and fast travel on the map. If you're like me in that you prefer an analogue axis for movement in a stealth game, this can be a bit annoying.
As for HUD, bravo on a decent degree of customization, including colors of key HUD elements for tracking, as well as the option to go hardcore and completely eliminate the HUD (while insanely difficult, it is possible to track without the HUD), great for end-game hunters who want the best hunting challenge they can get in the livingroom. Another great HUD feature is the camera comes stock with a rule of thirds (Golden Ratio) guide, extensive zoom, and best of all for my fellow screenshot junkies, taking a picture with the camera takes a HUD-less Steam screenshot simultaneously!!!
The user interface needs a bit of work. As it stands, everytime you press start, or back, it always takes you to the map, and then you have to back up once to get to your actual menu. Same deal when accessing the store/locker; it always sticks you in the store menu, and to get to storage, you have to back out one level. Not too big of a deal, but annoying nonetheless. If you change your quick access bindings, be aware any item bound to them will be cleared. If your rifle suddenly dissappears, you can re-equip it, the ammo, and the scope from your rather unintuitively accessed inventory (open map, back out one step, then select the really old-school bag on the left side of the screen. Remember to put the ammo and any sights on the weapon.
Audio in this game is king. Gorgeous music plays in the title menu, and whenever you enter a new region, but the music DOESN'T play during most gameplay so that you can hear every little leaf rustle, twig snap, or faint distant animal call. Full 3D audio, too. This game is amazing with quality surround sound headphones with adjustabe bass. You completely loose yourself in the game. I've gotten so immersed that I forgot I was in my livingroom!
Ballistics are really well implemented in this game, too. There's a bit of that Sniper Elite feel to it when you claim a trophy and that interactive 3D x-ray shows on screen. The pose of the animal's x-ray is the pose they were in when the bullet hit. Did you nail a Roe deer's heart in a dead sprint at 200yds? Take a screenshot, because all the proof you need is on screen! If you or another player landed multiple hits, you can even cycle through each individual hit to see the pose, projectile trajectory, organ/flesh/bone hits, as well as who made the shot, with what weapon/ammo, and how much of the total damage was due to said shot. The hunter with the best damage gets the trophy score and cash, but you still get your due weapon experience.
I could go on with this review, but I hear the Call of the Wild, so I bid you farewell, and good hunting!

So I just finised this game today and after playing, decided to write a review.
A modern military 3rd person shooter, putting the player in the middle of unspeakable situations.
Yes, I can agree with that.
My take on the game is this: Its a modern version of Apocalypse Now. I see so many things in common with that film. The background is that the large city of Dubai was destroyed by a sandstorm and then a large amount of troops were sent in to rescue them. Nobody escapes and all contact with the city has been lost. It has been left to rot.
Enter a 3 man elite Delta Force squad searching for answers. Once entering the city and being attacked, they decide to find the rouge Colonel (ala Apocalypse Now) and find out what exactly happend.
Not going to ruin the game by what entails, but it is sick and horrifying. Choices are presented to you, but it feels like it makes little difference because the choices are so horrible.
The game is short. I tend to play my games on easier difficutly and I completed the game in about 5 hours.
A good selection of weapons. You can only carry 2 weapons at a time, and some ammo is scarce for certain weapons, so I found that I swapped weapons quite a bit.
Pretty straightforward game. No puzzles or backtracking. Kill the guys, move into the next area, cutscene, repeat. I did enjoy some parts that allow you to cover your other 2 guys when you get separated or shooting the minigun on the helicopter. No vehicles for you to drive, this game is all on foot. You are able to issue some limited commands to your members as well.
The AI for the squad members, I must admit is great. Instead of some games that AI units just follow you around and take some cover, firing every now and then at an enemy. In this game, my AI squad took cover, and KILLED units. They covered me when I moved. They moved ahead of me on the map and engaged and killed units.
The audio is ok. I actually got a little tired of some of the phrases they shout. I wish they couldve included a few different lines because every firefight I got into, it always sounded the same. But whats there is good and sets the mood. Music is ok, nothing really major to speak about. Gun sounds are decent as well.
Graphics are pretty decent as well. The unreal engine 3 is starting to show its age a little, and even though I had the graphics at max, some textures were blurry, but still decent. Large landscapes and sprawling desolate city was nice. I really enjoyed the sandstorms. Every once in a while during the game, a sandstorm would come through. Wind, low visibility and all was pretty decent and felt intense when one hit in the middle of a gun fight.
I think my biggest gripe with this game is the controls. For me being almost strictly a PC gamer and have played other 3rd person shooters, the controls felt a little wonky. You hit space to run, and once you start running, do not have to hold down space. You also use space to take cover behind anything you can, be it a wall, destroyed vehicle or side of a building. The control key is used to duck/croutch. However, since the spacebar is used to take cover behind something, I felt this wasnt needed at all in game since when your being shot at, will use the spacebar to take cover, not croutch behind something. I kept mixing them in game and died a few times because of it.
So over all, I give the game a 7.5/10. A good, if some what short game that will make you think about the morality of being a soldier.

While the gameplay is decent, it's nothing very innovative or fun. Either one is fine on its own, but when you have a twist, you need to explain it clearly. Finally the game's message of "You always have a choice" is rendered moot in a game where no real choices are given that will change the course of the game. This might have worked with a movie, but it feels strange to have choice be one of the central themes, while giving the player no choices.

Originally, I picked this up because I hadn't played a third person shooter in a while. I didn't expect much, but I heard good things about this game. So I played for an hour or so, dropped it for a bit thinking it'd be the typical shooter that I can finish whenever, then I picked it up again one day and continued. Two words:
HOLY. CRUD.
This game makes a beautifully horrific (those who've played know what I mean) transformation from seemingly generic shooter to a highly psychological shooter. You kill and kill and kill in most shooters, but in this game...in this game...after playing for a while longer, by the time I finished it...I was just thinking, "THAT was heavy. Hit me right in my morals."
The writing is brilliant and the story hooks you deep. The gameplay is shallow, but it's a good shallow in my opinion since the game is supposed to project an overall point in its story so I can forgive shallow gameplay in exchange for focusing on story.
Overall, I give this game a straight up: 10/10. For those who want a game that plays with your head (I won't spoil anything), GET THIS GAME (it goes on sale pretty often on Steam).

Great Simulator. It`s simple you get truck and you are driving this truck. Singleplayer mode is quite boring but also you can download Multiplayer version and play in this game with your friends what is amazing :)

What is it with this game?
It seems pretty straightforward: you drive trucks. In Europe.
Yet, once you get on the road for your first transport, you're kinda hooked. It's always "just one more job". And it's 4 am. And you have to get up in three hours.
"Just one more job".
There's something mesmerizing about driving a truck, loaded with cargo, from one city to another. You turn on the radio, go into cruise control and keep an eye on the road. Time flies,
Getting jobs done is rewarding, you get cash that you can invest in a new truck or building your empire, which means hiring drivers and getting trucks for them. Your AI drivers will look for jobs and level up, developing their skills in the process.
Starting your career is a slow process, so this game surely isn't something for the impatient among you. Also, there's not much happening. You just drive. Sometimes you need to brake or turn, but aside from that, there's not much stress.
But you keep spending countless hours playing it, I just don't understand this phaenomenon.
Oh, and the user interface is superb. Self explanatory and logical, very well done.
The graphics are nice, but you won't have much time to admire the views. They don't put much of a strain on your graphics card, so the game should run well on older computers.
So, do I recommend ETS2?
Yes, definitely. It's a solid product, and if you like a game in which you can actually relax, listen to some music and have fun without shooting people.

As of today the game still has breaking bad bugs. For instance, my prison currently has a wing that does not get any food delivered even though it has its own dedicated kitchen that kinda worked an update ago.
My prison has remote controlled doors, and sometimes during shift changes the guard that get assigned its remote control job is far from the security outpost, causing all doors to remain permanently closed because the guard's path is blocked by remote doors. Yes I consider that a bug, since the security outpost has a lot of idle guards. Or at least the guard ending his shift should remain in their seat until the replacement guard comes.
Other than that, the difficulty level of the game is difficult to gauge, due to these bugs. The pirates of Windward are a scurvy and loose-moraled bunch, stealing port and cargo, along with your free time.
Tasharen' Entertainments procedural pirate project is near its 1.0 launch, and the quality of the game shows it.
Windward casts players as salty seadogs wrangling waves for 1 of 4 factions in a bid to dominate the known world via commerce and cannons.  Players begin in a simple sloop, in a region controlled (mostly) by your faction, in a small port.  Your approach from here depends largely on your play style; do you load up on cargo, and make your life as a trader?  Do you take on the requests of the locals and complete quests? Or perhaps you are a fierce pirate hunter or privateer, laying powder and shot to any ship within your sight.  Any of these are viable options, and you'll likely find yourself doing a mix of these things, as well as others.
As you make sail around your particular set of procedurally generated islands (across a span of biome types), you will harvest resources and develop towns for your faction, while making money and advancing a perk system in the process.  Your general goal is to explore and control as many regions as possible within your world.  You accomplish this by driving pirates out of region after region, whilst taking ownership of towns in the region, as well as potentially making your own.
The game is present in a birds eye perspective from above your ship.  Mouse or keyboard (wasd) controls will ferry you about the map.  Combat is handled in an appropriate manner, with the broadsides of ships used to fire devastating volleys of cannonfire.  This opens up some unique experiences and victories, as a smaller, quicker ship can occasionally sink a much larger foe by superior maneuvering and speed.  The oceans of Windward are also rife with detritus, that can be collected to build resources, gold, provide highly rewarding quest and trade incentives, as well as containing loot.  Player loot, not pirate booty (well, that too, but you know.)  I mean gear.  Your ship has 10 equippable slots, that you will fill with sails, cannon, shots, hulls, captains, and crew, to name a few.  These items have honest-to-goodness meaningful stats, allowing you to build a decent variety of different ship concepts.  Add to this a multitude of different ships and purely cosmetic items, and you have a challenging and entertaining time-sink of a semi-grindy nature.
Your grind will likely be fun with friends and atmosphere, at least in this writers opinion.  The scenary is easy on the eye, and tactical to boot.  Coupled with a fairly soothing sound track and a few friends, you can easily lose an afternoon to this one.  The game offers server software standard, and running a server is fairly straightforward.  Public servers were available and populated at all hours, including a development server hosted by ArenMook, the games chief architect.  The game also sports mod support.
Windward surprised me.  Honestly, I had high hopes.  Those hopes were not misplaced, it seems.  After basically absconding with an entire weekend, this polished pirate darling certainly has my attention.  I'm looking forward to several weekends spent buckling swash into the wee hours of the night.

Everytime that you're looking for a game with tall sailing ships and pirates, you rarely find one that does it just right - or at least, just right for me. You're not getting a ship simulator. You don't have to steer with the wind or learn to sail a ship. There is no swordplay. There is no dancing with the Governor's daughter (thank god). You don't need twelve of your friends just to hoist the sails.
This is not a simulator. What it is, is the best parts of a trading game, naval game and RPG game combined for fun. My kind of fun. The ships move like ships, they take its time to accelerate, they don't stop on a dime, they turn and bow to the side to emulate how ships look. That also means when you shoot, the cannons fire from the side. So you have to learn to show that side to your opponent while... ok you get it. But there's a simplification of every element to just the amusement. You can sail across the entire region and you will have to. There's no teleportation. You can run aground and damage your ship. The captain, the crew, the sails you use, the cannons, the ammo, they all add to your stats. You can get a better ship. You can hire additional ships to fight for your side or bribe them if they don't belong to your faction. And your cargo hold can be use for quests such as ferrying passengers, buying resources low and selling them high and different other missions you can pick up.
Towns around the islands grow in size, sometimes you even get to settle new towns and provide them with lighthouses and guard towers - although this is not a city builder, it just has very light elements from that genre. The needs of the town to you are just a way to make more cash by buying from another town that has more. In the beginning, you start on areas that are controlled by your faction, to eventually struggle on regions were you have little support.
I'm barely into this game, but after 7 hours I think it has me. After venturing into a second region and getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked, I went back to the starting region, build up some cash, got a bigger ship and went back. After hiring two allies and bribing a pirate, I went full conquest and won. Of course, if you don't want to start with Exchange (trading is what they're better at) then you can go full pirate as well. Me, I like me gold.
Just so you know, there are no animated characters SimCity-style coming up on your screen to stop the flow of the action. It doesn't feel like a cartoon and I really hope they keep it that way. There's really never any need to put text on the screen alongside some goofy looking comic relief muppet because this is not a pop-up book! You don't need a mission to move. You don't have to move because of a mission. There are no rails except the limits of the region you are in. And there are a lot of regions in just one game.
I will recommend it if you were a fan of the ships of 1701 AD and/or Age of Empires. Or if you wanted to play a less serious version of Port Royale. Or a more serious version of the original Tradewinds. Not that they look alike. Windward is to Tradewinds what the latest version of GTA is to the first version of GTA. This is a fully gorgeous 3D modeled world from the top down isometric perspective. The water does look like water, it shines with the sun, fish swim, seagulls fly overhead, sails puff up. I would add a little waves on the shore but it's really not necessary. It's flawless as it is.
That will do for now.

A great prequel that makes the punch to the gut in the next game that much harder and leaves you with a constant feeling of dread for what you know is to come.
Pros:
- Great story telling & Dialogue that makes you care about the characters
- Choices almost always feel like they matter
- Adds a lot to the previous game, it would be cool to play the games in the correct order.
- Episodes didn't out stay their welcome or feel longer than they should have been.
- Lots of journals, optional dialogue and things to interact with if you like to delve into the world head first
- Aristic style is just as good as the previous game
- Fantastic music (just like the last game) that adds to the impact of scenes.
Cons:
- Choices felt like they mattered, except in the last episode where I felt a lot more powerless. There was a serious decision that I never even knew I could make until I finished the episode.
- A bit of filler ocasionally. I ocasionally found myself moaning with boredom while I ran around a junkyard finding a tarp, but it wasn't too much.
- Will make you uterrly miserable...I'm joking...kinda. Knowing what happens in the last game leaves you with a constant reminder of the utter missery to come any time there is a happy moment in the game and the final scene of the final episode hits you like a ton of bricks.
I'd definitely recommend this to anybody who was a fan of the previous game (which is set after the events of this game), this prequel didn't feel out of place or forced. A welcome addition to say the least, just make sure you have a few hours to feel like sh*t when the game is over.

What otherwise would have been a solid game is completely undone by a few design decisions that ultimately ruin the experience.
I know, I know, 47 hours on record right?  How can I not like the game if I sunk 47 hours into it?  Long story short the game held my attention just barely enough to keep me playing and then after 47 hours the game put a boss fight in front of me that was so frustrating I uninstalled the game.
To distill it down to it's essence:
Pro:
- amazing sound
- solid voice acting
- grim wasteland is nicely realized
So so:
- graphics are decent but not groundbreaking.  They get the job done.
Con:
- intentionally confusing base design leads to mind numbingly boring "hunt the objective" gameplay.
- repetetive combat, only change to difficulty is just more enemies but there's nothing original or interesting about any of it.
- game breakingly horrible boss fight at the end after you've wasted hours of your life to get to that point.  Literally like, uninstall the game bad.
- repetetive combat
- all melee bosses use the exact same tactics and are defeated in the exact same fashion, after you master it they are mind numbingly easy to defeat.
- car combat is horrible - brush up against anything and your car spins out.  Like seriously, this is Mad Max.  Car combat should be this game's heart and soul.  you had one job, game designers, get car combat right, and you utterly failed...
- Do I really need to watch max fill up his canteen every single time?  Or eat a can of dog food?  Those animations were cool the first 400 times but they get so boring, so fast.
- Did I mention repetetive combat?
tl:dr: don't buy this game unless you like mind numbingly boring "hunt the objective" nonsense, repetetive combat, and a game breakingly horrible boss fight dozens of hours deep into the game.

"TL;DR" Version:
Undertale is a wonderful game and experience that tells a great story, posesses very well-written music, and has a unique style of gameplay. If you're struggling with your decision of buying this game, I'll help you out; scroll up, click the "Add To Cart" button, click "Purchase for myself", then choose a payment option and click "Continue". Now, go collect as many friendliness pellets as you can.
True Review:
This is more than a "game"; this is a lovely, beautiful, and bitter-sweet experience that can really change your perspective of games, and even life itself. You will encounter characters that are silly, nervous, bold, caring, and many other traits. You will laugh, you will cry, and you might even see a dog or two. The gameplay is very simplistic and straightforward with a "bullet-dodge" style of combat, and you can either fight or negotiate with "enemies" to overcome your challenges. Oh, and the soundtrack? Simply phenomenal. I am a musician—I play the saxophone—and I have taught myself practically the entire soundtrack just because of how much I love it. The music blends really well with the gameplay and the story. This brings me to one of the strongest aspects of Undertale: its dynamic story-telling. Whether you're a good guy, a bad guy, or maybe a little bit of both, you will receive a powerful message or moral which is determined by what you do. Oh, and yes, your actions have consequences; whether they be good or bad is up to you. With that being said, it's best to go in blind for your first playthrough. If you run across a few spoilers, that's alright, but keep in mind that one of the best parts of this game is the story that it tells. Perhaps this game isn't for everyone, but if you're reading this review, I would say you should at least give it a try.
P.S.
The "fandom" of Undertale is comparable to a typhoon or twister: if you get sucked in, it's unlikely that you will get out, and fatality rates will be high.
Stay determined, dear friends.

Windward is a game that falls into the "get a ship, now do whatever you like!" category of games; similar to Space Rangers or for those old enough to remember Uncharted Waters on SNES.
Windward has a fairly engaging set of mechanics that keep you playing for hours, cities offer quests which range from trading-like activity (deliver stuff), exploration, or combat missions. There is also the standard merchant style of play where you buy low and sell high. Finally you have the more combative gameplay where you can hunt down pirates and liberate cities and defend your waters.
The only negative thing I have to say about Windward is a severe lack of explaining how useful the right click button on your mouse is when playing. A common item in the game is something called a "Sealed Letter" better known as "This item begins a quest!" which are found as flotsom in the ocean or from the sinking hulls of your enemies from time to time. One such example where a merchant requests a shipment of goods for no gold but will trade you a (good) item in return. Think a blue or purple type item (legendary in one case for a buddy of mine) by completing these quests. However the Sealed Letter adds a quest item to your cargo area then you go buy the relevant cargo as well (spices, tobacco, fur, etc.) but when you arrive at the appropriate town nothing happens (most town based quests hand in automatically when you approach the right port). You have to open your inventory and right click the "Opened Letter" quest item (it's not so sealed now) and select "Advance Quest."
There are also several tools in the game: diving gear, a spyglass (telescope), and grapping hook that can be equipped in your tool slot. However right clicking it and selecting "Add to Captains Tools" creates a new item that incorporates all three items into one swiss army knife type item that can be equipped. No more picking and choosing.
All in all a great game, look forward to more!

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a great game for those who enjoy relaxed, slow-paced games, which can be explorative and interesting. The game is first and foremost a simulator, meaing you have to use your signal lights, use your windshield wipers when it rains, turn on your lights in the dark, etc, etc. All of this leads to a very immersive experience wherein you can drive across the entirety of Europe without leaving your home. You can haul all types of cargo, you can start a trucking business and become a trucking empire!
I do have a few issues with this game, but the overall quality greatly outweighs the negative aspects. The speed limit in the U.K. lowers at certain points, and then a speed camera snaps you for going over the speed limit! Another issue is the optimization; for me, the game can lag and become choppy at seemingly random points, although my overall framerate sticks above 60 FPS.
In the end, it's a great relaxation game with great simulator elements, I reccommend it, but if you're into fast-paced games, stay away.

All I ever heard about this game was how amazing it was and how it had a great story for a shooter. Well, I am was impressed. The controls are not great. I died quite a few times to grenades because my character would not run when breaking from cover. I didn't like the over-the-shoulder shooter style. This style may work in games like Mass Effect, but here it made me feel lopsided disconnected from my character. The scenery/environments were interesting, and I thought the game looked pretty good for when it came out.
However, the biggest drawback for this game was the story. Let me say first that I love surreal, complex, and philosophical stories. Although the game's story does pull you in on some amazing levels by getting you to hate your enemies so much that you make choices that you wouldn't have at the beginning of the game (mirroring your character's moral descent), I ultimately felt that the ending was hollow and made the entire game seem pointless.
An example of where this game succeeds spectacularly is a case where I was forced to make a split-second decision and made a choice that left me shocked and disturbed. I reloaded, determined not repeat this incident, only to make the same disturbing decision in the situation. The story's ability to coax you into letting go of your morals/ethics in very short amount of time was astonishing.
However, any emotional capital that was built up throughout the game's ethics shredder was evaporated by an ambiguous ending that left me feeling like I needed to play the game several more times to understand what really happened (if there even is anything to understand). This is not something you want to hear after firing on civilians and executing wounded soldiers for 6 hours. Only the worst kind of psycho bred in Dubai's moral ruins would want to start down that path again.
If you want a game that will make you question your very sanity and question every decision you make, then this is the game for you. Plus you will feel bad for everything you do in this game.

So now that all the episodes for this are out, I'm finding myself in a spot where I need to rant and review a bit about things. Now, don't take any negatives as a reason to not buy this. It's a DAMN good story, and if you played the original Life is Strange, you know what to expect. But it began to fall off a little bit towards the end. Might make this review a bit spoiler heavy towards the end, but I'll do what I can before that.
Episode 2 > Episode 1 > Episode 3
Episode 1: Amazing opening to Chloe as a character and the new argument/roast session system. The choices it gives you alongside of that shows exactly the kind of rebel teenager that she is as a person. I fell in love with it almost immedietly, and once you meet Rachel the drama and their relationship as people just get better and better. Though some of the puzzles and zones in the middle of the episode seemed a bit boring and lacking, the parts that were there for the story was great, and consistently hit you with feels as the episode ended.
Episode 2: I honestly didn't see anything wrong at all with this one. It had perfect pacing, separation of different emotion it was trying to hit you with, and that play you end up acting in was probably one of the best moments I've ever seen in any point and click/story based game. You see Chloe get into a lot of trouble, but still manage to hang on to herself as a person and keep her sense of badassery, punk, and rebel personality. Her and Rachel just end up getting cuter as the episode progresses as well. Easily the best of the three.
Episode 3: This one was a bit off to me. I'm not going to say it was horrible, there were always jaw dropping or heartfelt moments like there are in any games like this, but there were very few of them. Moments that could've easily been the same way were ruined in my opinion by weird settings, characters that weren't entirely a part of what was going on, and leaving you with a lot of scenes that just didn't have any actual voicing to them. A lot of scenes tried to be atmospheric and immersive by not playing any music and just letting sounds play, but Life is Strange was always kind of known for bringing music up at perfect times to make you *feel* something. Not only that, but when songs did play, a lot of it was just a 7 second clip of a song as scenes switched with a really quick fade out. It never really let any emotion stick before changing the entire mood of the situation or just changing the situation entirely. The good in this episode however was just a lot more character development as things started to wrap up. I sat around figuring out who to be scared of, exploiting people based off of what I learned in the first game as well as previous episodes, and just continuing to play Chloe like she's supposed to be. Learning more and wrapping up the main conflict of the last two episodes was a little satisfying as well.
Overall: This game is still a solid 8/10 for me. May be a little bit bias towards that rating but, I really did love the majority of it. The music was god tier as well, if you're into stories and don't mind a little bit of point and click with minimal gameplay and you haven't picked this game up yet, you're really missing out.

Life is Strange is my favourite game of all time. I played it two times, I cried a lot. It was inspiring, nostalgic, interesting, deep. When the prequel was announced I was VERY sceptical, but the trailer made me more hopeful. Unfortunately, this game...is definitely not good if you ask me...
The whole game was BORING. I felt like I was looking for bottles like in the first game all the time. The story was so dull and unemotional. I didn't care about what is happening at all. It wasn't that bad when it was about Chloe, but Rachel? Why the heck should I care about her? In the first game characters were dying or had VERY serious problems that I don't want to spoil. There was a big mystery! There was manipulating time! There was a tornado coming! There were matters of life and death! I'm not saying that Rachel's problems aren't real problems because she's not dying but it's hard to care when she has a perfect life. Why isn't game focused on Chloe more??? I don't know, maybe I feel like there was not enough of her because I'm so annoyed with Rachel's part of story. When there was a scene that was supposed to move me I cringed or started laughing. The game was like some cheap teenage drama.
And the characters...My god, the characters...So uninteresting and out of character. Chloe didn't feel like Chloe at all. She is generally not easy to identify with, that's why the writing of the game should make us think more like a teenage punk girl. But intead of it, she is just more neutral person. And it doesn't have sense. Game makes us want to be kind to David but it doesn't have sense! We know that Chloe hates him and will hate him even more and not much can't change that. It's hard to feel Chloe's hatred. I would prefer to understand it more and then make a choice whether I should be polite or not. I just can't imagine this girl to be Chloe from the first game in the future. And that's bad, as a prequel it should make us understand her better.
Rachel's parents were indescribably boring, I was annoyed whenever they had a line. Elliot didn't have a personality in comparison to Warren from the first game. Drew, Mikey and, ehh, that girl weren't really interesting to me. That game you could play with them was annoying and didn't have any purpose.
Hm, what can I say more. I guess a lot of people like this game so I'm the weird one here. Personally, I was incredibly disappointed. Maybe I expected too much. Anyway, if you're looking for the same emotions you felt when you played Life is Strange, I can not recommend this. I wasn't moved at all. Life is Strange was such an inspiration for me, I still listen to the soundtrack, I'm still mesmerised by the story. Please don't hate me for such an opinion, I tried very hard to like this game.

Great platformer for casual gamers. There is a game mechanic to prevent steady grinding away at it for gradual increase in resources, equipment, etc. where Charon requires you give up all (or, later on, a majority) of your currency to get back into the dungeon for each generation.
This is the type of game where the player must primarily level up their real-life skills with the controller (or keyboard) for more success in the game, only mildly supplemented by in-game powerups that can be earned.
While definitely geared toward a casual game here and there as time permits, the powerups are very diverse with a skill tree, collectible artifacts that unlock purchasable armor or abilities, and boss characters that are near impossible to beat without a very distinct strategy and some luck make this appealing for more hardcore retro-style players.
One thing I would prefer is to have Steam Cloud enabled on here. I've already reinstalled my operating system twice since I started playing this and kicked myself for not making a backup of my save file.

If you've played Banished, you're at least mildly familiar with being thrown in to a beautiful 3D top-down world with limited information and carving a path of resources, wealth, and survival. Windward takes the joy and addiction of a game like Banished, gives you simple controls, a ship, and a procedurally generated world and with just the sound of your sails in the wind drops you in to your first map.
Normally what would follow in a review is something about how I invested X amount of hours and did A, B, C, and saw J and almost crapped my pants. I'm not going to bore you with minutiae, as more importantly that will give you information that you should learn by playing the game.
What I am going to tell you, is that I jumped the gun and paid the 15 dollars for Windward, started the game, and didn't log off for 13 hours. I played 9 of those hours co-op with my partner, and I have to say this is by far the best unit of entertainment per dollar game I have bought in YEARS.
If you look at the discussion threads, you can see the developer actively speaking with players and even including community suggestions in to the game (Diving Suit!) which means if you play Windward and want to see something or change something, your voice is likely to be heard.
TL;DR Spend the 15 bucks. You spend at least 15 dollars to go to the movies with your friends, and this investment will give you an incredible return that lasts much longer than 2 or 2 and a half hours. DO IT!
Also, Michael Lyashenko, thank you for creating such a wonderful and beautiful game.

After letting the heavy-handed ending set in, I had to really think about how to end this review. Should I recomend it, or not? As I'm sure you're picking up on, Spec ops has some really nice touches and some pretty glaring flaws. Well not necessarily flaws, but just some mechanics that aren't spectacular or polished.
Let me start with the mehs of the game. First of all, Spec ops is a third person shooter that operates as a TPS should - it has a functional cover system that is fluid in that it allows your character to vault over walls, swap between pillars, and slide into cover, but it isn't really deeper than that. Furthermore, your character is far from bullet proof, meaning you'll be stuck in the gride of HOP OUT OF COVER, SHOOT UNTIL SCREEN IS RED, DUCK DOWN AGAIN AND WAIT FOR HEALTH REGEN, etc. You really can't rush or try any strategtic manuevers, you just shoot until dead. The game also rarely includes objectives outside of go here, there are some moments that involve you protecting a water truck or shooting from a helicopter, but they have all been done before. As far as gameplay goes, Spec ops gets the job done, and doesn't bother working overtime.
If I were to leave it at that, Spec ops would probably get a thumbs down just because the gameplay isn't particularly innovative, and is a little boring if you aren't new to cover-based shooters. However, Spec ops REALLY excels at its story and enviroments, and the depth in how it explores a soldier with PTSD. Yeah, try naming the games that actually make you re-consider mowing down legions of troops. As a trooper, you are sent in with a 3 man squad to "evacuate" dubai, which was ravaged by sandstorms and is currently under martial law. The downside? The 33rd division has different plans. Without giving too much away about this fantastic setup, the story will make you question the morality of your decisions (and you can make a few as the game goes on), and you never really know who the bad guy is. I mean, sure, you have opponets, but are their motives THAT BAD? It is truly thought-provoking, and the ending is so heavy handed, I had to sit there and ponder it for about half an hour before I could even formulate an opinion on it.
Buuuuut, to go back to the cons, the game is short, clocking in at about 8 hours. This isn't bad, but for a single player focused game with virtually no one playing its multiplayer or co op modes (shocker), it can be jarring to have the game lose all value so quickly. But, at the same time, if you are a sucker for good story and convincing atmosphere, this game actually can be pretty fun, and does make you think. But if you buy it for the gameplay... you might wanna look somewhere a little more non-routine.

HIGHLY recommended. This is a game that will fool you at first into thinking it's simpler than it is. It's easy to pick up and play without any instruction, although you may not understand the significance of your choices for the initial map and options at first. I played for HOURS, thinking "I like this game" before I realized that "the map" was still just the *first* square on the larger map.
After 19 hours, I'm only on the fourth square, still in my first game, and discovering this game has great depth. I'm already looking forward to learning more detail about the specifics about the game AI. I have yet to encounter any of the other factions yet, and would probably play this first game for 50 hours or so before I start to encounter them.  I've changed the options to slow the gameplay a little (80 or 90% speed) so that I can be more strategic, but I love the fact that it is up to the user to decide whether to slow that down (or speed it up).  This is a game where you can easily spend a couple of hours a night for a *month*, building your faction, before you finally finish it. If you do. I dunno, I'm still on my first game.
The graphics are great (even at lower settings!), the ship movements and finishing touches are wonderful.  Night and seasonal effects: the snow drives me crazy with a feeling of movement (just as it would in RL). ;)  And as I am learning of what is typical of anything from Tasharen games (StarLink and now Windward), I have yet to encounter anything that faintly resembles a bug. And this one isn't even officially released yet.  As a veteran of 30+ years of software development, this developer has earned my total respect for what he's doing here. And the developer of NGUI for Unity too.
Folks, I never heard of Tasharen before StarLink (which is one of my fave games on my tablet), and I have no connection other than I appreciate great software when I see it. I don't normally take the time to review things, but I have 3 important words to say, to anyone looking at the pics and video and thinking they *might* like it: BUY THIS GAME.
If you *think* you might like this one, you will. It's not for everyone, but anyone who likes this kind of thing will be shocked at how much depth this has, once they start to get into it.

This game is a fantastic story inside of a god awful game. If you've read a review of this game, it probably praises the story more than anything else, and rightfully so. Nolan North is his usual fantastic self, and the voice work of Bruce Boxleitner is always top notch. This game explores the psychology of the average military shooter protagonist and flips it on its ear and shows us how truly psychotic these people actually would be. It starts off fairly generic, but becomes something unique and special.
Unfortunately, poorly designed gameplay mars the experience. There are bugs that will cause progression events to not trigger. The cover system sometimes doesn't work. Moving out of cover is dangerous because it puts you in to a sprint. Vaulting over cover requires pressing the same button that you use to melee, so you'll occassionally punch at the air above a chest high wall instead of going over it. On and on, I would run in to situations where the basic mechanics wouldn't work. I could forgive all of that if the actual shooting weren't so monotonous and boring.  The most intense fire fights become are pace killing once you realize that your best strategy is to move at a snails pace. Pop out, shoot, wait for health to regen. It's basically modern whackamole. This is a problem that these cover shooters have had for a while now, but the best games find a way to circumvent that inherent flaw. Not in this game.
In some cases it takes one second to almost die, and nearly 15 seconds to get all of your health back. So slow progression and unspired game play put together means that the actual game is boring. I honestly just wanted it to end.
If you do buy this, it is the story that will get you to finish it. However, I don't believe story is enough to save a game. Novels exist. I'm judging this purely as a game, and as a game I don't recommend it.

Pros:
Beautiful graphics. Incredibly immersive world. The motion blur is a small issue but at least you can disable it.
Somewhere deep within the boring wandering around at a snail's pace, terrible aim system and annoying crap, there's a fun game buried inside. Cons:
Slow as balls, even though hunting in real life requires a lot of patience as well, at least you can move around quickly in between tracking. In this game "running" is walking and "walking" is limping forward. "crawling" is so slow I can't even explain it and you HAVE to crawl if you want to kill anything.
What the ♥♥♥♥ is this aiming. When you scope in at a deer, you shake around like you have parkinson's and you're having a seizure. If you hold your breath you think "oh maybe it won't shake anymore" but it does. The aiming system is so trash that the game is almost unplayable.
Deers hear you from miles away, and I mean miles. I could be crawling on the ground with no underbrush anywhere from a hundred metres away and a message will pop up "An animal has heard you!" and I just ♥♥♥♥ing give up while the entire deer family just hops away. ♥♥♥♥in hell.
Walking backwards while looking at the ground is somehow about 5x faster than if you walk forwards. ???

First off, let me reinforce the fact that this is an EARLY ACCESS REVIEW.
Alright. So. I'm not sure what I expected when I bought this game. I'm always on the prowl for new nautical-themed games, and I like adventure, so this seemed to fit the bill. The graphics are beautiful, the music is nice, but while playing it I can't shake the feeling that there is no drive in the game. Sure, you can trade to earn coin to get a bigger ship to fight pirates to get new cities to trade with... but then what?
There's no story to really encourage you to progress. You can just stick to your faction's corner of the map and trade to your heart's delight if that so pleases you.
The reason I'm giving this a 'recommended' rather than a 'not recommended' is because it is a well-crafted game. There's no sign of shoddiness, updates come regularly, and the community (well, what there is of it anyway) is benign and helpful. However, I personally have no real attachment to this game, and there's not much to make me come back to play it other than 'i've already exhausted the rest of my Steam library and this is what's left.'
So... enjoy Windward if it's what you're into, because otherwise you won't.

I remember when this game first came out, and I completely over looked it. Looking back on it now, I find myself wanting to go back, and buy it upon it's release date. Spec Ops: The Line is easily one of the darkest, and most harrowing games that I have ever played.
The choices you make in the game are extremely important, and with almost every choice you need to choose between two negatives. That being said; some of the options are just downright disturbing, and make you feel like a bad person afterwards. This game makes other war games look like a joke. While games like Call of Duty and Battlefield make you feel like some extremely overpowered bad♥♥♥♥♥soldier, this game does the opposite; it makes you feel like a monster, and not in a good way. This game shows that real war isn't so simple.
The only negative thing I can say about this game, is that it is very, very short. Only taking about 8 hours to beat, Spec Ops is still one of the best stories I've ever experienced while playing a game. While the gameplay, and arsenal of guns are nothing too special from a standard 3rd person shooter, you'll find yourself wanting more, and more to know what exactly is happening in Dubai.
If you like dark, and twisted stories, then this game is definitely for you. Do yourself a favor, and just buy this game. It's a great story, and it only takes about 8 hours of your time.

Rogue Legacy is a game I'd heard about for a while, but never felt compelled to pay full-price for. When a recent deal offered the game at around $2, I scooped it up. While very glad I now own it, I'm also very glad I waited for a deal, as I do not think the game is worth the full price.
Rogue Legacy is a rogue lite (as implied by the name) and will suit fans of one-off dungeon crawlers (such as Binding of Isaac, Dark Dungeons of Doom, etc). You begin the game as the patriarch of a family of rogues. Tasked with entering a forbidden castle, you explore an ever-changing map full of all sorts of monsters, bosses, pickups, powerups, and gold.
If you die, your story ends, and here's where the game's most interesting mechanic comes to light. Your main character may be dead, but he left offspring who share his goals. When one character dies, you get the option to play as one of his three descendents. Each descendent has a various special ability, and several different attributes. One may be gigantic (or miniature), have a sword (or an axe), shoot daggers (or shoot magic orbs). The constant shifting of the characters provides endless playability, and it's a lot of fun to see what different strategies will suit you best as you navigate through this endless castle.
If you like games like Binding of Isaac, I'd pick this up as soon as possible. I absolutely love one-off games that I can play for thirty minutes and then put down again, and this is a shining example in the category.

For those who are getting this game, I will try to give you a piece of advice as this sale seems to be also luring those who also were on the fence for this game.

Normally I'm not a fan of straight-up open world games with low emphasis on story, but Mad Max is very fun.  Driving mechanics are enjoyable, and the car customization is awesome.  The graphics are gorgeous, and despite is being in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, they do a great job of creating a lot of different areas to explore, whether its the dry seabed you start in, filled with old ships, or a huge expanse of dunes, theres even a place that looks like the Shadowlands from the lion king, it all looks incredible, and just looking at the scenery is fun sometimes.
My biggest two problems were the ground combat, which is basically a less responsive and more frustrating version of Batman: Arkham, but with way fewer enemies (once you leave the first area, you've basically seen them all), and the story, which takes place before the events of Fury Road.  It not that the story is bad, its just that there was never a time I felt any sort of connection to any of the characters, so when things get serious, I have a hard time caring about the outcome.  Actually, the strongest emotional connection I had was to the Magnum Opus itself.
Oh, and you can't get Max's signature outfut until you finish the story, which is sad.

The development pace for this game is also a pleasant surprise. This is a very well polished game for an early access title. It has the classic "just ten more minutes" that i had with sid meier's pirates! It appeals to a larger audience however, as the game does not have a time limit imposed on you, thus allowing you to play to your preferences whether becoming a trade magnate or pirate hunter extrordinare. The varied environment brought on by the differing climate regions is refreshing instead of the sub-tropic carribbean often seen in games of this genre. I would argue that the idea of it being an RPG is more a loose term in that you change captains and aspects of the ship to increase stats. I would like to keep the change ship items to improve the ship to be kept as is and the captains tool chest is a fantastic idea. However, if I make a captain i would like to see a leveling system where by doing certain actions improves certain stats, so for instance sailing around improves speed and maneouverability, combat improves accuracy. certain stats would need to be allocated to physical items so cannons & shot improve damage and accuaracy, where as combat only improves accuracy and reload time as a crew matures and gains stats along with their salty captain. If the idea of changing captain or crew is to be kept then maybe a "familiarity" penalty could be implimented to offset the immediate bonus obviously as a crew and captain become familiar with each other then they work better together eventually becoming a well oiled machine. finially I would say maybe improving on faction identity where each faction has unique ships of the period. so maybe exchange being latin origin, valiant being anglo-frank, consulate asian and sojourn aribic/eastern med; this would mean that to access the best ships of other factions then you must conquer/trade at high end levels with other factions. I digress from a proper review. essentially the developer has created a gem of a title with few negative points, i thoroghly recommend for anyone who played Pirates! and anyone who is new to the genre.

*SPOILER FREE*
I loved this game, rich story, fun gameplay, and the first time a videogame made me cry. I recommend this to anyone that likes nice pixelated graphics, and 4th wall breaking. There are 3 paths, Neutral (Killing and Sparing), Pacifist (Sparing Everyone), and Genocide (Killing everyone). If I were to rate the endings for children and family, I would probably say this:
Pacifist: Ages +7
Genocide: Ages +9
Neutral: Ages: +8
Do not take these ratings strongly, if your child understands death and killing, then they can handle all three paths.
The game has great character development, AMAZING OST (Original SoundTrack), as well as much more, this game may be frusterating at times, but stay determined, that's what I had to do. Also, there IS a seizure warning, the final boss in the neutral route has many shakey objects, as well as quick things that happen, but not too bad, the Genocide ending has a flashing black and red screen with a jumpscare (not too bad). and a transition of a black background to a collision of rainbow-like colors heres a clip of it:
, (start the clip about 9 minutes in) it isn't too bad. I will leave you to decide wether you want to buy this or not.

To be honest when i started to play Undertale i had zero expectations, and was sceptical for its hype. Friends whom played the game were like ''Zomg when you're gonna play Undertale? You MUST DO IT!!!!!!1!!!11!'' and when i replied ''Dunno if i even want to..'' oh man, that was almost cardinal crime in their eyes.
However i never judging games before playing them hence adventure started. And after beating (probably) all endings....daaaamn...i haven't been so impressed for ages.
But first things first. Let's analyze the game.
Undertale is Indie RPG (more or less) made just by one guy, which is really impressive. Story isn't linear, it changes by your playing. Decisions you made ACTUALLY MATTERS. For every action there's consequences and that's why i love it.
Battles are interesting. Basically it's bullet hell where you try to survive. But worry not, it's not so hard as it sounds...well.. there are few exceptions but after learning pattern and with dose of determination you can do it.
The characters are so well written and have strong, unique personalities. Makes you questioning moral principes not just in the game but in real life as well.
The best thing (atleast in my opinion) is soundtrack. It's perfect for every situation which you encounter.
My final verdict is 10/10! Legendary game! (Explenation: There's no thing such as 'perfect' game. However this is closest thing what i found. The story worthy of replaying it,brutally changing by your action so you feel like you're playing totally different game and i love this concept.)
So yea....i finally understand why my friends were so obsessed.
Thanks for checking the review. Stay determinated.

Negative:

Positive:

Rogue Legacy is a game I'd heard about for a while, but never felt compelled to pay full-price for. When a recent deal offered the game at around $2, I scooped it up. While very glad I now own it, I'm also very glad I waited for a deal, as I do not think the game is worth the full price.
Rogue Legacy is a rogue lite (as implied by the name) and will suit fans of one-off dungeon crawlers (such as Binding of Isaac, Dark Dungeons of Doom, etc). You begin the game as the patriarch of a family of rogues. Tasked with entering a forbidden castle, you explore an ever-changing map full of all sorts of monsters, bosses, pickups, powerups, and gold.
If you die, your story ends, and here's where the game's most interesting mechanic comes to light. Your main character may be dead, but he left offspring who share his goals. When one character dies, you get the option to play as one of his three descendents. Each descendent has a various special ability, and several different attributes. One may be gigantic (or miniature), have a sword (or an axe), shoot daggers (or shoot magic orbs). The constant shifting of the characters provides endless playability, and it's a lot of fun to see what different strategies will suit you best as you navigate through this endless castle.
If you like games like Binding of Isaac, I'd pick this up as soon as possible. I absolutely love one-off games that I can play for thirty minutes and then put down again, and this is a shining example in the category.

PRISON ARCHITECT is basically a top-down prison design game which borrows heavily from the concepts of SimCity (IE: distributing water pipes, electricity cables, etc.) and The Sims' architecture mode.  Though the concept of this game is excellent, and the ideas are presented well, the bugs in this game make it impossible to play for long periods of time.  This will cause you to spend hours going between the game and Google to work around said bugs.  Two glaring ones which broke the game for me in the short time I played it:
- TERRIBLE AI (guards stuck in a room not doing anything, prisoners not being escorted to holding cell, standing outside not doing anything, therefore, game not progressing)
- "Failed: no route" (distributing your electricity grid + water pipes + building walls not working due to the "failed: no route" bug, so buildings not being built, thus, game not progressing)
The developers were cute enough to make fun of the bugs in the trailer, but considering this game has been in "alpha" for three years, I was hoping that a lot of these bugs would be corrected nearing its 2015 stable release date.  Nonetheless, I have a lot of empathy for independent gamemakers, and the ideas in this game are excellent.  There just needs to be a lot more work done before this game is stable enough to be played seriously.

First off, I have to say that I was not expecting to play this game all in one sitting. The story may be short, but what I mean by this is that this game captured my attention throughout the entire ride. I will provide an in-depth review of each aspect from a critical point of view, and a tl;dr of each aspect at the end with personal opinions.
STORY (no spoilers): After I fired up this game, through the first 10 minutes of playing I expected a low(ish) budget military shooter with a simple and forgettable storyline... boy was I wrong. Spec Ops: The Line doesn't do a fairly good job at capturing the players attention right away -- no, it's real strength is progressing the player through an increasingly maturing storyline focused on 3 soldiers who end up in the wrong place, at the wrong time. Surprisingly, I found the characters to be highly relatable and believable (personality-wise, not the fact that they can take 20 bullets without a hitch). You feel connected to them the entire way through, seeing as you will never play through the campaign without them (besides some small exceptions). There were many, many moments throughout the story that really made me think, or put me in awe; one part in-particular was so heavy, I literally had to pause the game and walk around for a minute to regain my composure. Spec Ops: The Line provides a seriously twisted, mature story that suggests consideration for every action you take (there are some sick  choices that must be made, and even when the game forces you into some situations you may hesitate before doing so). Overall, the story is the strongest aspect of this game and is completely worth $30, though to some of you more critical gamers i'd suggest you pick it up on sale. And when I say the story is mature, I really mean mature. If you're a younger gamer then I really stress the fact that you will be faced with some scenes that are very hard to take in.
GUNPLAY/FIGHTING: Not much to say here. If you're playing with keyboard/mouse it will feel plastic-y, but you will hit targets much easier and end the fightings scenes much quicker (which can be a good thing since you'll mostly find yourself sticking around for the story); with a gamepad and vibration it will feel a bit more authentic, and obviously you'll want to have auto-aim on since the enemies are a bit hard to hit, even with K/M. There isn't much depth to the gunplay. There is a reasonable amount of different weapons to change things up a bit as the game progresses, but it lacks any unique or interesting mechanics. The one thing supporting the gunplay, doing so very well I might add, is the cover system and locations - the perspective is 3rd person the whole game and somewhat resembles a cross between the Gears of War gunplay and the Splinter Cell: Conviction cover system. Though the gunplay may feel repetetive after a while, you'll still be engaged with the environments -- which leads to my next point.
GRAPHICS/ENVIRONMENTS: Graphics are okay, no anti-ailiasing so you'll have to put up with jaggies. While it isn't the best looking game, boy-oh-boy does it have an interesting style. The amount of detail and variety that is put into the environment, the amount of color and contrast is quite amazing -- really, the lead visual designer for this game needs a raise. If you're expecting "next-gen" from this game, you'll be disappointed. BUT, you will without a doubt get lost in the stunning detail and visuals of weather-torn Dubai.
OVERALL/ TL;DR: If you're thinking about getting this game for the story, you will be in for a real, grotesque, gritty, shocking, heart-wrenching, plot-twisting treat. I should mention, I did NOT see that plot-twist coming. If you say you did you're lying and I'll throw sand in your face. Seriously I can't stress that enough, the story was easily this game's strongest factor and it is well worth full price imo (coming from someone who is very picky about good sorytelling, trust me on this). Gunplay will leave you wishing for more depth, but overall it keeps you well enough entertained in-between the major story-based bits and supporting cutscenes. Graphics aren't spectacular, but the visuals are really quite astounding and the detail of weather-torn Dubai is quite a sight to behold. Also, excellent color contrast, very pretty game.
Critical Rating: 7.5/10
Personal Rating: 9/10
Other thoughts: This is the first really in-depth review i've ever done on a game. I really think it was worth it, since I wasn't expecting much but came out of it smiling like an idiot. Although it is worth full price in my eyes, if you're questioning the game at all wait for a sale to buy it, but I can tell you if you can sit through the first mission, it only picks up from there... and I mean REALLY picks up throughout the whole thing and doesn't stop.

Unity vs. Unreal Engine
Unlike the first game, which was made with the latter, the team behind this sequel chose to make this game in Unity, which I have to say was a horrible decision. Though first, let me bring up that I currently have 26 hours clocked in with the original, and that I absolutely love Life is Strange. This kind of school environment just reminds me of Rockstar’s Bully, but handled in a more obvious storytelling role, than focusing on actual mechanics where you earn grades.
With this sequel, it was absolutely great to see a glimpse of what Rachel was like. I can totally understand why Chloe was so into her, knowing the kind of spontaneous person she was. But it only made me wish that this prequel could have been longer, seeing as how I doubt it can really cover how she met Jefferson and being around Frank in the one episode that this series has left.
Kylie did an excellent job with playing Rachel, and I thought Rhianna did an awesome job playing a young Chloe. The more I listened to the latter’s voice, the more it had just seemed to really fit that Chloe. However, as much as I enjoyed seeing a glimpse of Rachel, and look forward to the dlc, it doesn’t make up for the prequel’s massive flaws.
The storytelling of this one could be absolutely excused, as there is so much that could be fit into one game, but playing through it was just awful. Deciding to use unreal engine, while not exactly noticeable in looks when it comes to the models, is pretty obvious when it comes to how it runs.
There is absolute lag everywhere for low end Pcs, and I’m confident that Unity is to blame for it. I can run the original pretty smoothly, since it’s made in Unreal Engine instead, and the prequel runs so obviously different. The dialogue keeps getting cut off, music isn’t played in certain moments, and the interface for a controller keeps popping up, despite not using one. It’s horrendous having these kind of problems, which still aren’t fixed.
Especially when high end PCs seemed to also face this problem. Before buying this game a couple of days ago, even the Let’s Player I had watched, had some slight stuttering issues. The quality between the two engines really shows a lot, and I have to say that Unity and its lack of v-sync are a downgrade.
Buy the game to support the series, but I wouldn’t recommend giving it multiple playthroughs, unless you’re willing to face serious lag and stuttering.

At this point, the game probably has most of its core mechanics implemented, and personally I find it very enjoyable to fire up a new prison every time a new update comes out. The early game is where Prison Architect really shines: you have to juggle a half-dozen different things while expanding your prison to a big enough capacity where you can become profitable. Meanwhile you don't have a protective custody wing yet, the new inmates have high 'freedom' needs and things could blow up at any moment. Things are generally hectic in a way that will be familiar to anyone who ever played Theme Hospital.
After awhile, though, your prison gets big enough to stay profitable, you've built one of everything and the inclination is just to hunker down and let the prison run itself. I find that after you finish expanding, prisoners get very content and there are very few incidents at all. You could be playing 'Nursing Home Architect.' There's just not a lot for the player to do besides planning and building. Remember how you could slap a minion in Dungeon Keeper to get him to work faster? Nothing like that. Even trying to get a prison guard to respond to an incident manually is quite clumsy. Introversion has yet to implement a campaign mode, and in my opinion the game would benefit from some random events, gang warfare, quotas or just a little more volatility from the inmates.
Also, don't expect any of the dark humour you would get from a Bullfrog title. Introversion is playing it a little more straight and sensitive than that. Honestly, that's probably the right call. Making incarceration funny would require too many compromises, and riots wouldn't be as terrifying as they are now. There's a great juxtaposition of cartoony visuals and realistic sound. It's just too bad that you don't feel like you're sitting on a powderkeg of anger and violence all that often, because that's when the game really shines.
Introversion has done a great job so far, and I have no doubt that more features are on the way. At the moment, though, you still have a very fun management game that's one part Theme Hospital and three parts RollerCoaster Tycoon (without the rollercoaster designer). It's just that those parts haven't gelled yet.

In the early stages of our program, Mr Alex Alexander was the quiet sort that you would expect to either never get into trouble, or to create a huge amount of trouble when you least expect it. He never got into fights. When we started up a cookery course, he immediately jumped at the chance.
Unfortunately, he wasn't the best student. He attended all the lessons, but he could never seem to concentrate for very long. It took him four attempts to pass his cookery exam.
When half of his sentence was served, we granted him parole, and he proceeded to work in some sort of fast food outlet. He has never been arrested since and has an impeccable track record.
He still sends us Christmas cards.
