I am a huge fan of Sid Meier's Pirates and comparisons are inevitable but I'm not going to get into that as I believe each game stands on its own.
I have 5 hours in thus far and I love this game. The controls are intuitive and the game world, while not terribly fancy, serves its purpose. That's not to say it lacks eye candy. You'll see pods of dolphins, seagulls, and a nice sense of water depth. The ship models are very nicely done and it seems clear that these developers have studied these graceful pre-Monitor and Merrimac vessels.
Some have complained that you can't "fire" your Murderin' Billys like you can in Pirates. The mechanic is this game is all about positioning and frankly, the battles are tense enough without having to push the mouse button. Now, that said, you CAN activate barrages and such which increase crits but at the cost of reducing your defense. This game lulls you into sort of a Zen-like state, that is, until you get jumped by a few pirates. wat was a peaceful sail around a horn has become a fight for your life.
The AI is smart and will assist you but never think that gurantees success. You really have to know your surroundings as well as getting into prime firing position. Remember, these old sea birds only fired broadsides! :)
I am playing the Valiant faction. This faction kills pirates. When you go into new territory, you and your faction members must clear out the pirate scum and that in itself is a blast. You must defeat ships, plunder towns, and later build guard towers and lighthouses. You can go on quests and trade which buold your towns into cities.
There is a LOT to do in this brilliant early access game. The developers clearly love their baby and it shows.
I highly recommend this gem and, even though you aren't officially a pirate, there is no rule that states you can't scream at the screen in your best Blackbeard voice.

Borderlands 2, the sequel to the surprise hit first person shooter with RPG elements and Diablo loot system, is back with a vengeance. 4 new Vault Hunters take on the magnificently evil Handsome Jack on a quest to obtain as much loot as possible and, on a side note, save Pandora from total destruction.
+It should be a given for a good game, but Borderlands 2 is so fun to play... all available characters have vastly different skill trees that tend towards specific playstyles which are all good, challenging and rewarding in their own right, and the base gameplay itself is satisfying enough to make millions of people forgive, if not enjoy, the fact this game is 95% shooting the hell out of everything that moves.
+Depending on how much you like it, this game can last you forever. The base content alone has a main storyline and a ton of side missions and quests worth a good 70-85 hours of gameplay. Then there are the DLCs, which vary greatly in duration and cost but offer new characters, longer new campaigns in brand new areas with a generally high quality (Tiny Tina's D&D spoof is particularly great) and smaller content still quite good. All in all it may take around 130 hours, maybe more, to completely clear the game. And then there's new game +, which can be repeated basically forever. And let's not forget you may want to try out a different character than the one you started with... you get the point. If you can't get enough of this game, it is a long term investment.
+Borderlands 2 takes the unique cel shading that gave the first game a distinctive graphical personality, if a rough one, and gives it a bigger budget. The result is an absolutely gorgeous looking game that offers a ton of eye candy without giving up its style.
+Depending on your taste, you may find this game's crude black humor tasteless and forced. However, for most players it's just the icing on the cake, and it's rare to find a shooter that manages to make you smile every time you read a mission briefing or hear someone blab in your comms.
+The audio department, especially the soundtrack and voice acting, is quite great, which is a welcome bonus.
+The PC port is almost as good as they get nowadays. Nuff said.
+This game is quite fun and entertaining for me in single player. The co-op, however, is a different thing entirely: taking on the hordes of empowered enemies with up to three friends (playing with randoms isn't recommended) is exhilarating, and the ferocious arguments over loot are... well, sadomasochistically fun.
+Did i mention this thing even has a respectably good plot? Unlike the first game, twists and great moments abound, and the characters' personalities are all fairly fleshed out. Handsome Jack, then again, is a memorable villain in general, not only within the series.
-If continous slaughterdome fueled by repetitive objectives (that nearly always include "go there, kill everything, retrieve that, get back here" or something like this) doesn't sound particularly thrilling to your ears, this game will inevitably bore you, since it's literally all it's about.
-The quality of this game's myriad of DLCs goes from passable to excellent, but the amount and pricing of additional content are both quite high, which means if you bought the game at launch you may spend an insane amount of money to acquire all the new campaigns and characters, not to mention the paid clothing for each character. Not even the GOTY edition is comprehensive of everything available for the game, which is quite shameful.
-Enemy respawns are on Far Cry 2 levels (imagine clearing a tough dungeon and backtracking to get the hell out of there only to realize the enemies at the start have respawned), which can get quite annoying when you're simply trying to go from A to B.
-Some classes are clearly better than others when playing solo. In particular, every class that can give the enemies someone or something other than you to shoot at for more than a handful of seconds (Axton, the Mechromancer...) will be more easily capable of catching its breath, while classes that have short (Zero) or no distractions available will struggle more.
It's not a common occurrence that a sequel is so much better than its predecessor that it completely obscures it and goes from good success to massive blockbusting phenomenon. However, games like this prove that "bigger and better" sequels exist, and they're amazing. If you liked Borderlands, you will love this game. Everybody else: give it a shot. It's fun as hell and not too convoluted, while still maintaining enough depth to distance it from generic first person shooters.

The characters are flawed people, the story is moving and it does all the without being edgy. Spec Ops is a mature game! Unlike so many other games that try and shock players into feeling something rather than eliciting a genuine emotional response, *cough cough* Call of Duty. I hope that more games like this are released in the future because while it’s not “fun” Spec Ops is very enjoyable.

More than a game, this is a human and overwhelming experience. As in the first game, deep themes are explored, such as drugs and addictions, love and friendship, difficulties during adolescence and school dropping, dealing with loss and blended families, bullying or even life in general. It changes how you see the world and judge people ; I would never think of talking to someone like Chloe IRL, yet I love her character. Feelings, feelings and more feelings - Life is Strange : Before the Storm is one of those games that touches your soul and leaves you wondering about life and feeling empty when the game comes to an end.
The game takes place 2 years after William's accident. There's no Max Caulfield and any power over time : you get to play as Chloe Price as her life falls appart at school and at home with her stepdouche. With her father gone and Max not really making efforts to keep in touch, Chloe goes through a rough time - graffitis, provocation, trash talk ; experience her life as she meets Rachel Amber, gets to know her and the evolution of their relationship. Great characters are back, but there are new and interesting ones to discover as well. We finally get the chance to discover more about the enigmatic Rachel Amber who was such a myth in the first game ; bittersweet experience, as you get attached to her knowing what will happen to her in 3 years.
The gameplay is practically identical to the predecessor, except that you can't rewind and change time. Same goes with the great visual and the beautiful soundtrack that perfectly fits with the spirit of the game. On this matter, you can at any moment enjoy the musics on the "Mixtape mode" - choose the songs you want to listen to, lie down and take a break from reallity. Let your inner punk emerge : you also have the possibility of changing Chloe's outfits.
I can tell Before the Storm is as good as its predecessor (except for chapter 3); the driven story telling, the characters that you love or hate, the emotions, the choices and their consequences, the lovely art, etc. I loved playing as Max, now I love playing as Chloe (even if I'm not a big fan of her inner voice in chapters 1 and 2, it gets better in chapter 3). The first chapter sets the tone ; the second chapter reaches its peak ; the third chapter is a bit disappointing however : it seems shorter and rushed, especially since the fact that there are only 3 chapters was a big letdown in the first place. I was expecting more from it, another kind of ending probably too. Now I'm just waiting for the bonus episode, Farewell, which will reunite Max and Chloe one last time. There's still so much to tell, so many questions left unanswered...

Storming the Castle is Fun for the Whole Family.
My first experience with Rogue Legacy was watching my friend Jean-Luc struggle against this giant skull demon thing named Alexander. I sat for several hours and watched him die and die and die again out of the corner of my eye while working on homework. After a half hour or so, he gave up and charged out into the greater castle, killed a whole slew of demons, died a dozen more times, found the door to Alexander’s area again, and spent another half hour beating his head against a wall until finally the dread cranium was defeated. It looked like one of the most challenging and frustrating rpgs I’d ever seen. Naturally, I had to try it.
I start the game up and run through the sepia opening cutscene. Not 100% sure what’s going on, but it seems like I’m a hero who has to enter a Castle and find some kind of treasure to cure the ailing King. Time flashes forward a bit and I choose a new hero. Walk into the castle. Use what feel like pretty standard metroid-vania controls to navigate a treacherous, spiky, platform environment, defeating demons with my trusty sword and a slew of magicks.
And then die. Sir Hero is hit by one too many fireballs, and he passes away, leaving nought but a paltry handful of gold and a painting in his memory. No checkpoint, no restoring last save. But before Sir Hero entered the Castle, he had three children: these children are randomly assigned a gender, a class, a spell, and between 0 and 2 randomized ‘traits’. Leaving Sir Hero behind, I select a Knave named Sir Taco, and he’s dyslexic. Taco navigates the castle with startling precision, but when he tries to read a sign, the letters are scrambled.
After Taco meets with his brutal end comes Lady Shanoa the Barbarian, who is near-sighted, making the outer edges of the screen blurry. Taco amassed a few hundred gold in his abbreviated rampage, and before Shanoa enters the castle she may spend his coin on permanent upgrades that are applied to every character you play, forever. Upgrades slowly become more and more expensive, but you’ll be getting plenty of gold. You can increase most of your base stats, and also buy new classes to be randomly assigned to your descendents. Each class has different health, mana, and damage ratios, and unique abilities.
A score of unfortunate children in, you’ll find the doorway to Khidr, first guardian of the castle. Each zone has a guardian, and the goal of the game is to kill all four guardians to unlock the big golden door at the beginning of the castle. After another score of unfortunate children, Khidr will lie in ruins and you may continue on your merry way.
The volume of character variations and ability combinations you can collect in this game means no two runs are ever even remotely the same, and there’s an entire castle to pillage and explore, with dozens of cool collectibles to find. For the price of an Indie game, Rogue Legacy feels like a very strong rpg-platformer, hearkening back to the good old days of the game boy advance, reminding me of good times had in games like Aria of Sorrow. For the quirky humor, nostalgic yet invigorating gameplay, and days worth of fun, I would recommend Rogue Legacy as a welcome light-hearted distraction to anyone, and a fairly intense challenge for the die-hard fans. (Next I have to figure out how to beat Volgarr the Viking, which makes this game look like a picnic)

PA is a deep strategy builder. Build a well oiled prison where everyone is happy, slap all your prisoners into a tiny holding cell and wait for the riots, have armed guards and dogs everywhere with days in solitary for contraband, or have a gigantic sprawling prison of multiple security zones with complicated eating rotations assisted by automatic doors... the freedom to build how you want and not just 'the best way' makes this game very interesting to play.
The only con I can think of, is that over the course of it's early access, so much has been added, that it is a completely different game than when I started playing. Having to worry about all the added content AND build a working prison for a new player would be daunting to me at this point; it took me a good long while to figure out how to make a well run prison when I didn't have to worry about legendary prisoners, tunnels, parole hearings, and more that have been added over time.
Still, even with the ramped up difficulty, I have no reservations in recommending this game.

This has got to be the biggest disappointment ever. I come from four playthroughs and countless recommendations of the core game (Life is Strange). I preordered this because of the trust I placed in the company that made the original - here's the twist: Before the Storm wasn't made by DontNod (the Paris-based devs who brought us the original) but shuttled out by the publisher, Square Enix, to Deck Nine - an obscure company that brought us such blockbuster hits as "Neopets: The Darkest Faerie" and "Ratchet: Deadlocked", both flops on the PS2. In fact, when they got Before the Storm handed to them they hadn't developed anything since 2013.
Even so, the name "Life is Strange" carries a lot of weight - it's a brand of quality I expected to carry over no matter who the developer is. Characters with depth, surreal and immersive storylines, heart-wrenching plot twists, and cringey-at-times but emotive voice acting are all elements of Life is Strange fans came to know and love.
Before the Storm has none of that. We follow Chloe with (spoiler alert) no time travel powers like Max had in the first game - which leaves the game feeling void of any gameplay elements to set it apart from other choose-your-own-point-and-click story games. Instead there's a confusing and rarely used "backtalk" element that's as poorly introduced and explained as it is boring to use. The mechanic holds no weight and adds nothing to Chloe's character.
Otherwise, the game's game mechanics are practically identical to its predecessor, with a few more technical issues probably due to the jump from Unreal Engine to Unity. Graphics look a lot worse - might as well be a PS2 game (and judging by the developer's portfolio, it's no surprise that PS2 graphics were the standard they held themselves to).
All this could be excused if the story and characters mattered. I spent most of my time in the first couple episodes waiting for something to happen. The most interesting things in this game are tie-ins to the original like meeting characters or visiting locations from the first game, but there's very little point beyond "hey, remember this?" Locations and characters have very little purpose and value to the story.
What story? Who knows. The plot meanders around aimlessly. Chloe gets in arguments with her parents, spends time at school, meets Rachel Amber who she has a crush on? I guess? It's unclear and heavy handed at the same time. Stilted voice acting doesn't help the process, and while I know some people criticized voice acting in the first game I tend to disagree - the voices and mannerisms felt right at home in Arcadia Bay when DontNod did it. Here, however every time a mouth opens on screen what comes out sounds like it was recorded phoenetically by non-nativespeakers. By the end of the second episode I found myself not caring whether the main character and her squeeze lived or died.
This game made me feel bad for not killing Chloe at the end of the first one.

A prequel to Life is Strange is something I never thought I'd be interested in, but I was hooked before I was even done with episode one. Deck Nine has taken the reins from Dontnod in spectacular fashion; Before the Storm fits in perfectly with the existing Life is Strange narrative and explores Chloe's life before she reunited with Max, showing how she met Rachel Amber and how their relationship grew. This doesn't retcon Chloe's story; it enhances it. I don't want to say /anything/ else about the story, because it absolutely deserves to be experienced by any Life is Strange fan rather than being read about. And if you're worried about gameplay, don't: the game plays almost identically to the original, though instead of being able to rewind time, Chloe can "talk back" to certain individuals in an attempt to sway their decisions in favor of her. It's a fun twist.
Again, when Before the Storm was first announced, I wasn't very interested. But Deck Nine pulled it off, and they pulled it off very well. If you liked the first game, you'll like this. If you loved the first game, you'll love this. It's as simple as that.

I've been playing Black Ops II multiplayer now since January 2013, so I'd like to say I've got a bit of experience under my belt. Most people purchase CoD for the Multiplayer so that is what I shall be reviewing here.
First the good stuff. Everything works. No one thing is more broken than another and most everything functions as you'd expect it to; which is flawlessly. The weapons feel solid, they're balanced and have their own unique traits but there is no real reason to use one weapon over another unless you're building classes for specific engagements/engagement ranges.
All the FPS mechanics you've come to expect from CoD are there and again, function flawlessly.
Now for the not so good stuff. Hit-reg can be a little hit and miss at times depending on your network quality and how bad your packet loss is; if I can make one suggestion it would be that you play on a good quality wired internet connection with large bandwidth. Wireless low speed connections are a big no-no in this game, more so than others, but less so than other FPS franchises such as Battlefield.
Now while CoD games are said to cater to the 'lone wolf' play style, there is one thing of note. You cannot and will not consistently win games if you do not have a party to play with (unless you are playing TDM and get your backpack on). Best played with friends but playable without.
Other things of note include:
Remington 870MCS=OP
Low playlist population
Matchmaking
No server browser
'Toxic' community (Not really, I've made a few friends on BO 2 so far)
To summarise; Black Ops 2 is a great game to play casually. Competitive isn't really a thing in CoD, if you want that go and play CoD 4 Promod or any of the Counter Strike games; you'll thank me later. But if you are looking for something to kill time (which it has done for me) and have been turned off by Infinity Ward's CoD Ghost; pick up Black Ops 2 when it's on sale.
Not quite worth the retail but still a good game.

Mad Max is an open-world sandbox game in a similar vein as GTA and other open world RPGs.
The graphics are lovely and detailed, and the look and feel of the game is almost straight out of the latest Mad Max movie. Additionally the sound is used very well - from the whooshing as the car picks up speed, to the screaming of the wasteland hordes attacking you. The voice acting isn't too bad either - and it's good to see that the fans were listened to, and Australian accents were used.
Most of the action centres around Max's driving his new car and fending off the hordes attacking him. The game does this very well, and even includes a first-person view from inside the car which allows you to feel as if you are right in the action. I would have been disappointed if they left this feature out.
Easily, the vehicular combat is the star of the show, and especially the convoy raids. You can shotgun drivers and fuel tanks, grind car tyres up with wheel spikes, blast fire at them, blow tyres out with harpoons, and later on - launch bombs. With so many options, depending on your situation, it can get quite intense and enjoyable. There are many convoys scattered around the map for Max to bring down - so you can get to relive the staple action scene of the movie many times over. Certain areas require a tougher car to face off against the more heavily armoured vehicles, and you can only get the parts if you wipe out the threats in areas of the wasteland.
Outside the car, Max can loot and investigate camps - in which are many enemies to fight. The fighting isn't too difficult or complicated (the game helps you a lot here), but is challenging up in the tougher levels. It feels a lot like "The WItcher 3" fighting system, and it works quite well. Full completion of the game means that you will need to find all of the loot and historical artefacts, so it's fortunate that the game hasn't hidden things impossibly on you. Some of the loot is challenging to find, but I was never stumped looking for it for too long.
There are lots of things to clear out of the wasteland too, like "scarecrows", snipers, and minefields. It's fortunate that given the large number of them, they are fairly easy to clear off the map when you pass them. The land mine sections were a bit annoying because there's little challenge in doing them and you have to change cars in order to bring the dog with you. These requirements make them a bit of a chore.
Between bursts of action, you are able to upgrade your car, upgrade strongholds you park in, and even upgrade Max himself with better shotgun, knuckedusters, fighting skills, and his road warrior jacket. You do this by spending scrap you find. Additionally there are storms which tempt you to either return to base, or risk getting killed by flying sheets of metal to recover "muthaloot" flying around with a harpoon.
The game story and dialogue feels true to the spirit of the movie. Your companion, Chumbucket, does an adequate task of being a comic foil and subtle tutorial giver within the game. The best dialogue I believe, belongs to the mysterious character Griffa and his somewhat intelligent conversations with Max. Unlike RPGs, however, the game is not dialogue heavy and it will get out of your way soon enough to let you get on with the action.
There's a lot to do on the map, including car races, stunt jumps, and looitng areas, and I estimate there's at least 60 hours of gaming here if you intend to complete everything.
There are only two main gripes. One is that clearing the map of things to do can feel somewhat repetitive. The game starts outstaying it's welcome some time in around the third act when you have most upgrades already and there's no more motivation to go scavenging for scrap. At this point, you'll probably lack desire to put much more effort into the game. Mad Max also suffers from the "ubi-tower" syndrome in the form of hot-air balloons.
The other gripe is a lack of multiplayer features, or endless survivial mode games. It would have made the game a lot more replayable. Imagine a team of on-line players defending a convoy, enjoying a road race, engaging in a demolition derby, or a fistfighting and endless stream of warboys? .... anyone?
All in all, the game is enjoyable without being too taxing or frustrating - which makes it a good game.... although nothing particularly groundbreaking.
If you liked the movie, you will like this game.

PA is a deep strategy builder. Build a well oiled prison where everyone is happy, slap all your prisoners into a tiny holding cell and wait for the riots, have armed guards and dogs everywhere with days in solitary for contraband, or have a gigantic sprawling prison of multiple security zones with complicated eating rotations assisted by automatic doors... the freedom to build how you want and not just 'the best way' makes this game very interesting to play.
The only con I can think of, is that over the course of it's early access, so much has been added, that it is a completely different game than when I started playing. Having to worry about all the added content AND build a working prison for a new player would be daunting to me at this point; it took me a good long while to figure out how to make a well run prison when I didn't have to worry about legendary prisoners, tunnels, parole hearings, and more that have been added over time.
Still, even with the ramped up difficulty, I have no reservations in recommending this game.

I love this game. It is so awesome to improve as a person, rather than have just your in-game character improve. Seeing my rank slowly crawl up was perhaps the most enjoyable thing I've ever done in a game. This crispness of getting a perfect juan deag or one tap or collat or spray done or ace or wallbang is so awesome to experience. Learning new skills like weapon spray patterns or how to bunny hop really do alot to create a sense of self-improvement. The game's economy being soley focused on cosmetic items was also a massive boon, preventing people from just spending a little cash to become in-game gods (hackers aside). Though Valve isn't always the best at community outreach on the game, they do push decently consistent updates that are
on target to the community's needs/wants.
I also hate this game with a burning passion. It is nearly impossible for lower level players to auctually get a rank that accurately describes their skill level because of the ungodly number of smurfs and hackers, especially in non-prime matchmaking. It's absurd that the only way to get a decent competitive game is to pay money for a third party service that mines bitcoins off your PC. I will concede that services like CEVO (rip), or FACEIT do exist and can be used for free, they are far from perfect (being dead, still having smurfs and hackers, etc.) and that there are some smaller communities that are decent for newer/more casual players. However, not having a functional built-in matchmaking system for such a competive game is aboslutely horrid. This is not even mentioning the massive bulk of griefers that make games impossible to play at times and even cause deraking and game cooldowns at other times.
I love playing this game for all its beauties, if you can spare $15 I would greatly recommend it, but you need to be prepared to work hard. You need to be prepared to spend time looking for a chunk of community you want to participate in. You need to be ready to get scream at by a 6 year-old from the motherland. You need to be ready to get called a braindead ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥♥ by some 30 something guy living in his mom's basement. If you can take that, do it.
tl;dr
Fantastic game with possibly the worst community. Spend the $15 bucks if you can spare it.

Later and most recently I tried the multiplayer again.  Same sort of luck on the usual game modes, but I chanced a try of the Party Mode (Party Mix).  THAT is a game mode I can get on board with!  Actually it's a mix of different special party style modes that keep it interesting and it helps level the playing field.  Everybody pretty much ends up with the same loadouts.  So that part I like. I might have to read up on the best loadouts before I do at least.  Loadouts are crazy in this game.  Too much to think about, but I'm sure it's fun for some people.
What I really wish - is that loadouts could be changed on the fly within a round. I understand the reasoning why it's set up the way it is, but come on...this is the modern age.  We need to relax.  We need to see beyond the boundaries of yesteryear.  Let's open it up and make it more playable for everyone...not just the elite gamers.

I give this game 4 stars, but not 5. I put below why, but not all of these things are important. Some of them are just things I wish the game would have, but I would except if it didn't.
Execution rooms
I want to use execution rooms soon though. Maybe as a punishment. If you don't know what I mean, then I'll explain. I think that if a prisoner commits a murder in your prison that you should be able to click the prisoner, then click punish. After that you'll see the list. Solitary, Lockdown, and then execute. Maybe you can add a consequence for executing them as well. Like a natural consequence, for example, all the other prisoners will get angry if he is a legendary prisoner. But if he is an ex cop or something like that then his friends outside of the prison will try and sue you. Just a few ideas I'm throwing out there.
Material
This is less important, but I would like this game a lot more if we had more materials in it. Things like different colored doors, different colored pavement, and maybe pavement numbers. I know there are mods for this... but mods are a little less reliable.
Security
When prisoners are escaping or rioting then often break out of their cells and run through out the entire prison. I wish there was a door similar to a solitary door that I could place to stop them until reinforcements arrive. There was a mod called blast door, but it had problems. Maybe make a large door that requires a servo to open. In addition to that, I have another wish that would be great... but might be difficult to pull off. Sniper towers, or watch towers. As a final problem that I have, sometimes when I have free fire on and a prisoner tries to run he gets shot, even if my other gaurds would of stopped him. Well, that makes sense, but some times if a prisoner is running away and free fire is not on he can get away clean if he gets too far. I want to have some sort of fire zone... A completely restricted area where prisoners will be shot. If the get in the warden's office, they will be shot. Also, I would like a no tollerence zone. If prisoners are in the parole room and they assault the warden, they should be shot on site. If they are in the lunch room and they attack a staff member, they should just be tazed. Maybe you can add that into your policy? I imagine it like this:
If prisoner attacks office staff: Shoot on site... And if he Kills them: Shoot on site
If prisoner attacks worker: Hold fire................. And if he kills them: Shoot on site
If prisoner attacks gaurd:  Shoot on site........... And if he kills them: Shoot on site
If prisoner attacks another prisoner: Hold fire... And if he kills them: Hold fire
I hope you understood that. Basically, you get to decide how to handle a prisoner based on the acts he has commited. This can apply to rioting and escaping as well. To sum up this secetion, I would like strong doors (that come with some hassles just to be realistic), Shoot on site zones, and for a shoot on site option for prisoners killing, but not the ones running.
Special Prisoners (A fancy idea, take it if you like it)
I think there should be special prisoners.... Two kinds. execution types, and Super Super max types. You don't decide when these prisoners come. At the beginning of the day your CEO calls. He tells you that they have an execution that needs to be done. They'll pay you 1000 dollars, but if the prisoner gets away then he'll charge you 10,000... Now execution prisoners can sometimes be accepting of their deaths... but can other times be willing to make the craziest moves to get away. If an execution prisoner gets away, it is 10,000 dollar fine. If he dies in any ways besides the electric chair, it is 5,000 dollar fine. Now for Super Super max types... These are gang leaders, terrorists, and the baddest of the bad. When ever you get one, you get a new Category of prisoners. You have minumum, medium, Maximum, protective, Supermax, and the A... You get paid a lot more for Prisoner "A". How ever a lot of people might want to kill A. secret hitman might get arrested... Go to your jail... then attempt to murder A. A lot of the time, A won't even be all that tough. You're not locking him up in a strong and secure area to keep him there... You're keeping others out. Sometimes he is a good fighter though. Sometimes he might be a crazy arson and you have to keep him away from the others... You never know untill you click accept and your CEO briefs you. Be careful, because if he dies or escapes you're fined 10,000 dollars.
Jail Breaks
I wish that there were different types of jail break attempts... Like a truck drives up with 6 armed dudes and tries to free their buddy. This would usually be for the prisoner "A" I refered to last paragraph. Maybe some would sneak up to a wall and put explosives on it. In all honesty, you've done so well with the game so far that I'm sure you have a good plan for it, but if any of these ideas tempt you... Then go for it!

On a more serious note,
Despite it being in early access, this game feels completed. The little blob-men run around the prison you create. Hardly any bugs so far that I've found after 18 hours. Updates are still coming out. Very addictive game, it's basically a tycoon game with a few differences. The differences being that there can be fighting and you must stop the fighting through a riot squad or some guards.
Your prisoners can overdose, they can attempt to escape through the sewer, they will be rowdy and get into fights for seemingly little reasons. Takes a while to get a hang of things. The graphics are nice, fitting for the theme, could be better when you zoom in. Soundtrack is yet to be released, I assume when the game exits early acess.
Pros:
+Nice graphics and overall theme feeling
+Sound effects are good and follow what is happening. E.G if there's a fight you can hear it, if building you'll hear jack hammers and drills. Mixes together well.
+Extremely addictive
+Feels finished
+Things work smoothly, most things are automated and the AI is pretty good
Cons:
-Very minor bugs
-No soundtrack yet
-Somewhat poor pathfinding at times
Highly recommend for those that enjoy tycoon/sims/micromanaging games. Or those that just like to burn things or see bloody fights.
If I could give suggestions to the devs, I'd ask for more micromanagement, meaning that you can assign prisoners to certain work areas, showers, and yards.
Anyways, overall great game. I have yet to find any gamebreaking bugs. Great job so far to the devs!

This game is annoyance and tediousness done right. The first few runs through the dungeon will be miserable: you will die quickly and make little progress. But as you start acquiring upgrades and understanding the castle, you will become more cautious in your quest to earn even more money to power your progeny. And before you know it, you are making even further progress, testing new classes, and finding yourself wanting to play just one more game. There may be a few setbacks here and there as you may have no good children or find yourself playing as an offspring with a game crippling genetic disorder but you will still feel yourself getting closer to beating the game - unlike in some other roguelikes where death can set you so far back that you give up in frustration.
If you like platformers, I wholeheartedly recommend this game with all my heart.
Easy to jump right into and hard to quit playing.  Whether you have 5 minutes or 8 hours, this game will scratch that platformer action itch.

Rogue Legacy has an interesting premise, whenever you die, your offspring take over, the only problem is you children might have something wrong with them, making it a challenge when you die. Obviously based on the title the game is Rogue-lite, the animation is retro, and the gameplay is 2D, though it isn't badly made. I like the concept and having the dungeon completely change every time you die and your child takes over, makes the game a fun and unique challenge. Really good concept, and fun to play.

Absolutely horrid for keyboard controls. The game just dumps you in a tutorial with X-Box controls highlighted by default. It took me a solid minute to memorize the controls long enough to press through it, and I couldn't figure out the "(Y) options" button (it was tab) for even longer to change it. Then when I can finally navigate to it, I find you can't even rebind the entire keyset!
The entire options menu is horrifically designed. Selecting an option doesn't actually change it, but highlights what the option is, which you then need to move left/right to actually change. This is terrible, especially for binary options like fullscreen.
I heard good things about this game, but I could already see it would be a technical struggle to play it on keyboard, so out it goes.

*** Early Access Review, will reexamine once launched ***
(Because this is an early access game, I'm specifically not rating this game based on what I consider missing features like being able to list/manage your profiles/worlds)
As the game stands right now I can't recommend it.  I played for 2 hours and found the game's pace to be either painfully slow or crazy hectic.  Either I was sailing along from town to town and being bored out of my skull because nothing was happening, or I was constantly being engaged by pirates and having to resort to hit'n'run tactics to stay alive.
The graphics are beautiful and pleasing, but in my opinion a game needs more than a pretty skin to be enjoyable; in its present state, Windward is lacking in gameplay.  It presents itself as a free form sandbox game, but there just isn't enough different things to do in the game to make up for the missing plot.  Maybe it gets more fun as you rank up and unlock abilities; certainly from the trailer it looks like there's plenty more in the game than I discovered.  I was just too bored to grind more hours into this game to find out.  My advice to the devs would be to dramatically speed up player progression.
I am sure multi-player adds that extra dimension which will make the grind seem less obvious and thus make the overall experience more enjoyable.  However, the current price tag prevents me from recommending the game to my mates, so I probably will never find out.
As it stands right now, if you are really aching for some good clean pirate action, there are better (and cheaper) alternatives to get on Steam.  Sorry, Windward.

This is just a better looking version of the old counter-strikes. It doesn't offer much of anything new except a few more gun types and skins(which cost a lot of $$$ for good ones).
I would have been happy with a solid player base and similarities of the older Counter-Strike games, which this game offers but there is a huge issue with how servers are run.
Everything is community based, there are a few but essentially no player operated servers worth frequenting. Because of this there is limited moderation. Hackers come on servers and the only way to get rid of them is if their own team votes them off; which even if the hacker is blatently wallhacking, spinbotting, and shooting through walls it just doesn't happen. Players would rather win than play honestly, and that includes letting hackers remain on their team.
Secondly, the hit registration is horrific! I'd say close to half my shots do not register. Admittedly I thought I was just bad but after watching replays I could see that my shots were infact lined up perfectly and simply did not register an impact on the server. In addition when I play LAN matches with friends enemies actually drop in 1-3 shots, not half a clip into their face and body later.
Third, the weapon recoil and damage scaling is just plain awful. The recoil is extremely high even at close quarters. There are automatic weapons (such as the P90) which can take up to four direct headshots to kill an enemy depending on range. I understand players might be wearing a helmet but that's still insane, especially if you're shooting them in the face which is exposed.
Overall it's worth getting cheap to kill some time on but it's not a balanced game in the least.

I've spent WAY too many hours on this game. No regrets, though.
Overall, the game play is tricky, but fair. Each character has a class and 0-2 individual traits. Each class has advantages and disadvantages, which makes for balanced play. Some traits are wonderful (PAD, OCD, ADHD) in that they give small advantages to the player, some traits make virtually no difference (IBS, Hypochondriac), and some traits are awful (Vertigo, any of the vision limiting traits) in that they hinder the gameplay. Collecting gold throughout the dungeoun can buy upgrades to armor, abilities, and runes which will make the game more manageable. As a rogue-like, the dungeon changes every time you enter, so each runthrough is unique. This differs from traditional platformers, so if you are used to 2D platformers like Mario, Castlevania, Mega Man, etc., this is a slight adjustment. If you play enough, you learn the layouts of the individual rooms, and can plan accordingly. The bosses are somewhat lacklustre.
There is an immense replay value to this game. You can level up your upgrade tree as much or as little, switch around different armor with different traits, use different classes, etc. Plus, with New Game Plus modes, the game can get much more challenging. In the newest version, there are (optional) extremely difficult versions of all the bosses with a weak character, for those that are looking for additional challenge.
Unless you are a pro with using a keyboard, make sure to have a controller handy.

A lot of people compare this to The Binding of Isaac because they're both randomly generated and sorta kinda have similar elements I guess??? I already think this comparison is odd because this is a platformer and Isaac is a twin stick shooter (I guess people compare them because of the roguelike elements?), but there is one major difference that I think makes this game infinitely less enjoyable.
The first time I picked up The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, I beat it. I unlocked a bunch of new items, bosses, and levels and there was so much more game to play, even though I had already accomplished so much. You beat the game to get more game.
In Rogue Legacy, the game is already there. You get permanent upgrades periodically, but a new player would NEVER be able to beat the game on their first try. You HAVE to grind, unless you've already played and practiced enough that you can play through this entire randomly generated game without getting hit. You beat the game and you're finished. No crazy new items and abilities, no new unique bosses.
So if you like grinding and don't mind that the only thing you're working towards is seeing "The End!" since there's no story and the game itself never evolves, I recommend it. It controls well, the random levels are fair. The sense of humor is refreshing.
If that doesn't sound fun to you, it probably won't be fun for you.

It's incredibly anti-war and very messed-up, so obviously not everyone's cup of tea, but I have to give it huge props for having the cojones to do what it does with (or rather, to) the characters and story, turning the feel-good heroics of the usual military shooter on their head and making you feel BAD.

First Impressions:
For an Early Access game, it has potential.  It could stand to be improved in some areas...the player/world selection style, for one.  Currently, you have to remember the name of your player and/or campaign name you've created in order to continue where you left off...a selection menu showing you a list of all of your saved players/campaign names would have been nice.  A way to delete campaigns/worlds you no longer want in-game would also be helpful.
"Windward" is a little different from the build I played in 2012 on Desura.  That older build featured quick 5-10 minute skirmishes that allowed you to earn XP and loot.  You could equip your ship with new items and assign points to a talent tree.  For the most part, those mechanics are still present...though instead of quick skirmishes, you'll generate procedurally generated worlds that span multiple "map blocks".  In essence, it became more like "Sid Meier's Pirates" as opposed to a quick multiplayer shoot-em-up.  I admit, I do miss the old build and hope the dev plans to include these quick skirmish matches as another game mode of sorts.
In this campaign, most of your time will be spent doing quests (go here, build a new settlement there, defend this settlement, etc.) and trading via a supply/demand system.  It's all very basic right now but has the potential to be a lot more.  I'll be interested to see where this goes in the near future.

Deck Nine had some huge shoes to fill when developing this game, and holy sh*t, they did a superb job.  Having just finished the original LiS (for the 2nd time) prior to starting Before the Storm, I actually think BtS might be better, but I am also seeing that BtS is much more focused on the narrative and less focused on discovery.  I think this is a byproduct of the narrative structure being different than the original--you aren't solving a mystery or trying to come to grips with your powers, you are trying to cope with the death of your dad and just get by as a teenager.
So pros:
-Roleplay as Chloe the dbag instead of nice girl Max.  It's a good change of pace.
-Absolutely hilarious, I was buckled over laughing several times during the first episode.
-The writing is solid, the feels are strong.  Doesn't seem to be as many pop culture references as the original...maybe because the references would have to be from 2010 and only older people might get it?
-All the music they licensed fits the game really well.  Sometimes it seems like there are too many songs, but the songs are great.  Being a sucker for reverb/delay guitars, the ingame music is solid for me too.
Cons:
-Not as much exploration as first game, areas feel a little more straightforward, maybe they are just smaller.
-Some screen tearing for me, this is probs cause I have an AMD graphics card (EDIT:  After just getting an NVIDIA GPU, it is still an issue on all framerate settings.  Having a dedicated Vsync option would be REALLY nice, but you can manually fix it from the Nvidia Control Panel)
-Only a few voice actors returned from LiS.
-Around the third episode it seems like almost everyone starts. saying. things. so. slow.

This was on my list for a while. The gameplay is just okay - everybody's played this kind of shooter before. But the writing/presentation/visual design is just brilliant. It's incredibly anti-war and very messed-up, so obviously not everyone's cup of tea, but I have to give it huge props for having the cojones to do what it does with (or rather, to) the characters and story, turning the feel-good heroics of the usual military shooter on their head and making you feel BAD.
Like awfully, inexcusably, monstrously bad for what you do in the game. It's a game that will make you hate, if not yourself, then at least the protagonist Capt. Walker. The campaign's pretty short, but presented well enough so, more than anything, it ends up being a sort of interactive movie with some shooting in between. But it left an incredibly strong, disturbing and lasting impression on me, and for that it definitely deserves a play.

In other words, the plot reads perfectly coherently even to one not interested in shooter games. The combat is a little rote, which actually feeds the point, kind of: military shooters are a way for someone to build themselves up as a hero without ever touching on realities like sacrifice and heartless atrocity.
The world of the game is created really well - you only encounter a few characters who aren't hostiles, but you still get a feeling of this city dying around you based on just the levels you walk around in. The grafitti is some of the best art in a game I've ever seen. The music is also pretty good, and the ending is really emotional.

First Impressions:
For an Early Access game, it has potential.  It could stand to be improved in some areas...the player/world selection style, for one.  Currently, you have to remember the name of your player and/or campaign name you've created in order to continue where you left off...a selection menu showing you a list of all of your saved players/campaign names would have been nice.  A way to delete campaigns/worlds you no longer want in-game would also be helpful.
"Windward" is a little different from the build I played in 2012 on Desura.  That older build featured quick 5-10 minute skirmishes that allowed you to earn XP and loot.  You could equip your ship with new items and assign points to a talent tree.  For the most part, those mechanics are still present...though instead of quick skirmishes, you'll generate procedurally generated worlds that span multiple "map blocks".  In essence, it became more like "Sid Meier's Pirates" as opposed to a quick multiplayer shoot-em-up.  I admit, I do miss the old build and hope the dev plans to include these quick skirmish matches as another game mode of sorts.
In this campaign, most of your time will be spent doing quests (go here, build a new settlement there, defend this settlement, etc.) and trading via a supply/demand system.  It's all very basic right now but has the potential to be a lot more.  I'll be interested to see where this goes in the near future.

My honest opinion of theHunter: Call of the Wild.
First off, it is the best hunting game out there. This is primarily due to it being one of the very few out there, but none the less, it's a good game. I've seen alot of people complaining about game issues and what not. I personally haven't experienced many issues at all.  NOTE: I'm not gonna deal with the whole DLC ordeal. Nothing I say will change that.
Here's a list of issues I deal with.
1) Holloween update messed with alot of stuff, got it. But there are a few issues that remained after it was removed. The big issue is Bears. Their stand on their hind legs and get back down to walk animation is wrecked. I've lost 4 great bears due to them standing up to look after I made a call, I pull out my bow and draw it back and shoot for the heart. Instead of the animal lowering itself back down, it just automatically goes back into the walk position. Like magic, one second hes on his hind legs then next thing you know hes on all 4's. You don't see them go back down.
2) Archery - Compound bows are very amazing tools. I've shot many different brands over the years and still activley hunt compound to this day. The Pins don't consistently reflect range as they would IRL. Now I understand different draw weights, and Arrow Grains affect the flight path. But it isn't realistically shown here. 30+yard shots are pretty impossible in the game. Add a slight breeze and you can kiss that arrow goodbye. The amout of FPS these arrows are moving shouldn't be affected as much as they are here.
3) Ground Blinds and Tents - In MP, there are issues when you set a blind or tent to where it's now placed right infront of you but you cannot access it due to "Not Being the Owner" when you just put the damn thing down. Also, you can't pick the damn thing back up because, "You are not the Owner". So now, your blind belongs to nobody and its not moving until you log back into SP to hike your tail all the way back to where it's at and pick it back up.
4) Weather - I do enjoy the dynamic weather, but holy mess you dont see 65+ rain storms with GALE FORCE WINDS in Montana every 25 minutes. Can this be altered? Maybe a storm here and there... Maybe set an entire day to inclement weather and should the hunter wish to hunt in it, they can, or they can "Rest" back at camp and wait for better weather to scout and hunt.
These are the big issues I get agitated with. There are smaller issues that I can see around and not worry about. Lets talk about some positives and things I would like to see added.
The Game has a decent variety of animals, and with the new map came some new animals and thats freaking awesome. I love seeing different things wherever I'm at. Hunting moose and next thing you now I see a herd of elk move through. Thats super cool. Also, for Bucks/ Bulls I like to see smaller antlers on the younger males and bigger antlers on the older males. Thats some good details. I would also like to see, if possible, some rare antler types. Non-typical racks w/ droptines, maybe even some in velvet. (That being a early season still growing type thing but still cool)
The Weapons choices are decent, not amazing but decent. With Bows, you have 3 to choose from with 4 different sights and 3 different Arrows. (Ammunition types) Only better thing would be to be able to customize the patters on it and add better stabalizers. Shotguns are here, but I feel pointless. Yeah, you got buckshot. But lets put that birdshot to use with some WATER FOUL!!!! (Ducks, Geese, Phesant, Quail, Etc) Rifles are all decent, but maybe get a .300 bolt action in there.
Blinds are decent, but I wish we also had tree Stands you can carry around, or maybe set up a ladder stand in your favorite spots. Possibly a Tripod Stant in the middle of an open field?
Cammo, theres some decent cammo you can buy in the game, but its litereally just for looks. I wish there was a actual drive to purchase these things. Better concealment from animals. Better Scent conrtol.. Do something... cause its 12,000 for a fashion show it seems.
Anyways, if anyone see's this and want's to talk more about it. I've got plenty of Ideas in ways to improve I'd love to share.

This is, hands down, the best game I've played in a long time. The story is engaging and honestly took me by surprise a few times. The dialogue never feels hammy and the voice acting is spot on, which really helps you to connect with the characters and actually care about them. The controls are solid and intuitive once you learn them, though occasionally you'll find yourself sprinting past cover you meant to enter, or running into a low wall. This is a rare occurrence however and overall, I can find no other faults. Visually, Spec Ops is gorgeous, filled with brilliant camera work and great level design. I found myself stopping to gawp at the scenery numerous times. Later in the game, there are a few moments that really stand out visually and add to the narrative perfectly. Death never felt like a chore in this game, either. In some games death can put you off playing but with Spec Ops, this isn't the case. Instead I felt myself compelled to learn from my mistakes and try again and again to storm that machine gun nest or fight down another bloodsoaked patch of sand in search of the mysterious Colonel Konrad. This game is well worth the money, the action is intense, the gameplay is well balanced and the difficulty curve is just steep enough to keep you feeling engaged all the way through.

However, if you play with friends, you will improve the chances of finding good loot and will most likely have more fun as you interact with one another. In Rust, every player starts naked on a beach with nothing but a rock and a flaming torch. they must gather resources to craft tools, weapons and armour, with the ultimate goal being to build the biggest base, which is made easy by its simple yet complex basebuilding system, kill lots of players and raid their bases for loot until you're sitting on a gilded throne of weapons and resources. This crafting based gameplay is typical of most survival shooter/pvp games and those who have played any similar games before will find Rust's systems intuitive and easy to pick up.
Rust uses procedurally generated maps which change every time a server "wipes" (meaning it changes the map and all progress and constructions are erased). While this may seem like a bad thing, it's not. It keeps the game fresh and stops a powerful clan of players from permanently dominating a server. Servers can choose how often they wipe, with official servers wiping Monthly on the first Thursday of every month. The most popular servers are weekly wiped servers, while some even wipe as frequently as every 2 days!
Rust's settings are very customizable, especially the graphical settings which can be tweaked so the game runs on even the most basic Asus laptop. On the flip side, the graphics can be ramped up to create some of the most stunning visuals in an open world game as big as Rust is.
In Conclusion, Rust is a great game. If adreneline fuelled gunfights and incredible visuals backed by a deep and suitably complex crafting and basebuilding system sound like your thing, then Rust is the game for you!

Before it came out, I really did think that this game would be no where near as good as the original, but so far, it's just as good. The story is interesting and engaging, and as can be expected from the prequel to Life is Strange, it has an excellent and fitting soundtrack. The characters are great, the voice acting is just as good (the replacement voice actor for Chloe is a perfect fit for the younger and slightly different incarnation presented in this game), and much of the gameplay is genuinely fun, including the new "backtalk" mechanic. There's also a lot of flavour: as with the first game, there are character profiles and texts, and the optional photos return as optional graffiti, but this time Max's journal is replaced with Chloe's unsent letters to Max, which provides interesting character development.
The game, like its predecessor, does have its flaws. The dialogue can be rough at times, and there are some puzzles that are more annoying than anything (it even has a section where you walk around the junkyard looking for various items, which is only a little less annoying than the very similar bit in the first game.)
Overall, the first two episodes of Life is Strange: Before the Storm have far exceeded my expectations, and it has certainly lived up to the original. If you liked Life is Strange, Before the Storm is an absolute must.
If you haven't played either this or the original, you should go play Life is Strange and then Before the Storm. Immediately.

Spec Ops: The Line is not an open world game in the vein of GTA, nor does it follow the path of Alpha Protocol or Mass Effect in offering a more linear experience that nevertheless changes based on your decisions as a player character.  Spec Ops offers you some options over the course of playing it, but the game rarely signposts the choices, or tells you straight out what it will mean, or if there was a decision you could have made differently to change a later circumstance.  The game setting is brilliant, even the loading screens have meaning, and the level of detail put into the way your character looks and moves and speaks contributes further to one of the most powerful and best integrated narratives in gaming.  Many games *have* a story, something that happens in between you shooting people.  In Spec Ops, as the game nears its end, the fact that you're continuing to play it becomes a part of the narrative it creates.

This is the only CoD i have ever played and after 400+ hours i can't really tell you it's a bad game now can i? the single player is terrible and probably the most boring compaign i've ever experienced in a AAA title FPS but the multiplayer is fast-paced and fun and there's really no need to grind unless you want prestige which only gives you a fancy emblem. You can be level 55 in a day or two if you're smart. One of the main gripes i hear is that the game takes no skill or SMG's are OP, etc etc and i can honestly say that none of this is true and you allways hear this from people at the bottom of the leader boards. The more you look at the game's effective range mechanics for the various guns you'll see that all guns are equally effective for different play styles or situations.
The weapons i believe are very well balanced and offer enough versatility within each gun class without making any particular weapon OP, at the end of the day it comes down to personal preference, for example with SMG's i enjoy using the Vector, Skorpion and MP7 while the general opinion is that the PDW and MSMC are the best SMG's. The most interesting thing to note about this game is that everyone i've met whines about different weapons and it's normally the weapon that is most efective at countering their play-style. An SMG's user blows away a guy with an AR in a midrange fire-fight, a shotgun user blows away a run and gun SMG user, an LMG user wallbangs a guy with an AR /sniper camping on the other side of the map. These are the kinds of situations when the tears start flowing, not because any of the above is OP but because their play-style was predicable and those that take the time to learn the maps and think about what the enemy is doing will butcher the unsuspecting run and gunner who runs around corners into the open while UAV's are in the air.
You could present a compelling argument that some AR's are just better than others, but at the same time the devs did a good job of making sure that anyone who picks up this game will have everything they need to start killing people straight away, the MP7 is available at level 4, the R870 also at level 4 and both are top-tier weapons. AR's are a different story but the MTAR and type 25 are both solid weapons and available early. In terms of tactical grenades you get concussions straight away and that imo is the best tool for an easy kill.
(which for the most part is still subjective)
- most of the maps are small- medium sized making SMG's the preferred choice for most players
- the match-making system is shithouse, enter a lobby for your preferred gamemode and everything else is random
- no mod tools
- no dedicated servers. (you cant sell DLC's with people running their own modded deddies)
- DLC's are a ripoff ($20 for a few maps is just stupid) and serve only to seperate those who dont have DLC from those who do
- Even if you do buy DLC if there aren't any people who also purchased them in your region then they'll never show up in the lobby and you'll never be able to play them, hence you payed 20 bucks for nothing (You cannot queue for them either).
- No custom game rules, no map selection and none of the other cool stuff you would expect from a game released 10 years ago let alone in 2012.
- ♥♥♥♥♥♥ console port, the lag compensation is BAD, REALLY BAD any lobby with players over 100ms and the game becomes terrible, people start warping and you start dying before the server registers you took a shot. Otherwise its fine, some lag is expected but this game i feel could have handled it better than it did, i never had these issues with games like Quake and UT.
- It is over-priced, this game should be $20-30 at full price with $5 map packs not $90 after a year with 4 $20 map packs.
It's fast and fun with plenty of weapons, perks, tacs and scorestreaks to try out and plenty of viable play-styles, albeit some more effective than others due to the small maps. Despite the dated engine and activision being greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s i still think the game is worth playing especially if you have a good rig, good connection and dont mind being ripped off. Just bear in mind that most of the people still playing are the die-hard cod fans with hundreds sometimes thousands of hours played and you will frequently be bent over and anally destroyed if you don't play smart.

However, if you play with friends, you will improve the chances of finding good loot and will most likely have more fun as you interact with one another. I recommend this game to people who want a game that will make you relax a bit but can also keep you on your toes at times.

This review is coming from the perspective of someone who waited a year and a half to finally play Undertale. I'd known about the massive popularity and praise for the game (though managed to stay spoiler-free), so I was curious if it lived up to the hype.
Long story short, I'd say it did.
The writing is phenominal. Every joke, character, and scene are delivered on point, and the attention to detail is simply mind-boggling. You rarely get a game that actually reacts to good, bad, and weird things you do. Because of that, the game is highly replayable. You'll do multiple playthroughs just to see how the game adapts to your different choices.
Speaking of which, the three main playthrough styles are all worth doing.
Neutral runs (killed at least one person, but not everyone) are the simplest, but have some of the most interesting endings.
Pacifist is easily the funnest and longest, and most of the great gags and character development happen here. Experiencing the ending for the first time is worth the game's price on its own.
Lastly, genocide is amazing in a different way. I can't think of another game where you can truly be an awful, horrible monster and feel the consequences for it. The atmosphere the game takes on, especially compared to a pacifist run (which I recommend doing first), is beautifully dark and ominous.
Also worth mentioning is the music. I've loved Toby Fox's work in Homestuck, and his work here does not dissappoint. Each theme fits the setting, whether it's in a tranquil home, a thrilling battle, or a haunting lab. The themes for each character will be stuck in your head for hours, not that you'll complain. If you enjoy listening to music, buy the soundtrack along with the game.
The game is easily worth the $10. It's definitely a future classic.

Already there are a few things I'm seeing that I'm disappointed in. Keep in mind, I have very little hours in this game. Now let me get this straight. I enjoy playing the game. The reason why my review is negative is because of these main reasons:
1. Already they are creating the same type of "BUY EVERY SINGLE ITEM WITH REAL MONEY" feel from theHunter classic, which is the biggest reason why I stopped playing theHunter classic. These tiny little new DLCs, already several of them for a game that hasn't even been out for a year. Want ATVs? well there goes $4. Want tents? theres another $4. New map? there goes $8. This is just the beginning. I hope the devs see this:
Instead of making all these tiny useless annoying DLCs, just put them in the base game, and focus on making larger DLCs that people might actually consider a good buy, like a whole new series of maps and animals we can buy (
, now that would actually be a smart choice for a DLC).
2. The variety of equipment is very underwhelming. Why not just bring all of the weapons, equipment, blinds, treestands, etc. from theHunter classic into this game? Like I said earlier, the main reason I bought this game is because I wanted a non-subscription based payment method for a good hunting game, and where we dont have to buy literally everything with real money. I mean, jeez, if I'm gonna pay like $100 on equipment, I can just go hunting IRL. That was the big problem with theHunter classic. I like the feeling of having the possibility of being able to unlock everything in a game, a sense of completeness. In theHunter classic, the only way that was possible was with your wallet, not with your game progression. I wanted this game to change that, and while it does offer us in-game currency that can be earned through playing, theres not a good variety. Very few weapons, very few equipment items, very few structures we can place.
3. While this one is not much of a concern to me, I'm used to early access games, it is still there. This game is very buggy, and instead of the devs putting their time into optimization and bug-squashing, they put it into these useless DLCs that just annoy the players when we have to buy them to unlock the full game content. Focus on new game content, bug fixes and optimization, not on these little DLCs, please.
If they were to just give us a better variety of equipment, stop these stupid little DLCs and make some REAL ones, and focus on bug fixes, I'd definately give this game a thumbs up. Overall the game is beautiful, and has great potential, but potential must be captured and executed properly by the developers before that potential is converted into a good game.

I got this game not long after it came out, and at that time i felt it was a waste of money, and time. There were bugs evrywhere, the sound was off or gone, animals got stuck and never moved from a spot, it felt like the animals heard you miles away, even if you crouched, and you could never kill an animal with one shot, always needed two, and there were many more. This made evrything about a realistic hunting experience vanish and I forgot about the game entirely.
Now, a few days ago I tried it again, and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥this game has been improved. I don't know if everything i mentioned above was a bug, or maybe I were just bad at the game, but now i feel like everything works. Animals doesn't get stuck the way they did, now they would mostly get stuck by running on a fallen log or something, but they get out of it fast. I can shoot an animal and kill it with one shot now. The sounds are always synced, only thing is that when an animal calls you don't always get the notification of where it's at, but thats a minor bug that everyone can live with.
As of now, in the games current state, I onlt notice bugs maybe once or twice every 3 hour. Those bugs usually are minor and doesn't make a big impact on the gameplay and is not annoying at all.
I think the game is a lot of fun and you can play for hours without getting bored, and when I get bored or I don't really wanna play it, i take a 30min to 1 hour break, and then im good to play a few more hours.
There is still something that makes the game less fun than it could be, but I think the devs are working on it, so here are my "complaints" as you could call it.
I feel like there is not enought animals. There are different types of deer, but at the end of the day, they are all the same I feel like. The different reserves got about 6 animals or something, this is counting the deer. i do think 6 are a good number, but this would be without counting the deer. You have whitetail and blacktail at same reserve, you have doe deer, fallow deer, red deer and musk deer. Raindeer is also in the game, but i dont feel like thats really a typical "deer".
In the game there are 18 animals spread around 3 different reserves, and 6 of these are deers. 2 at one reserve, 3 at another and then 1 at the last. the last one is a paid DLC. This makes the entire game consist of about 33% deer. And the different deer doesnt really have any different traits, or difficulty. I feel like they are the excact same to hunt, except different name and a slightly different look. This isn't a major thing, but adding more to the already consisting reserves will get the game in a better and more fun state in my opinion.
the same goes for weapons. There are not that many rifles, 8 I think? 3 handguns, 3 bows and i havent really bothered checking the shotguns since there are no particular small game. I think you can kill the bunnies and squirrels that pops out from bushes from time to time, but they are counted as critters and iv never been able to kill any of them so idk.
I think the devs are working on this too, or at least they should because adding new weaponry is key to make this game live longer and make people coming back to it.
I really like how yoiu can choose wich ammo you want to use for the guns, even tho it's only 2 different types at the moment, it's cool. With bows there are 3 and handguns and shotguns I don't really know.
The skill tree is alright, its a good portion of skills to unlock, but the grind is real. You don't get a skillpoint for every level like in most games, but you get a skill point ever 3 or 4 or something. Idk if i like that because i have to spend so mutch time grinding XP to get a skill i want, not a big deal, but is a tiny bit frustrating and a few times boring.
The last thing i wanna talk about when it comes to content is the unlocking. To unlock anything escept guns and ammo, you have to lvl up you character. This is a also a bit annoying because it's the same as the skill points, you have to grind even more to unlock stuff. The hours iv been playing I have barely unlocked anything, maybe 3 callers and 1 scent, and a 2 or 3 other stuff I don't know about. Im in lvl 12 at the moment, with 25,4 hours of gameplay. And to unlock callers for anything other than deers you have to be around 20 and up. I have been very lucky to find packs of deer with 8 deers or more, and I were able to kill them all and farm like crazy, but i don't think this is the case for everyone and i can't imagine the time others might have spent to get this far.
Now to a bug that does not accour often, but when it does, it's soooo annoying. Don't know  how many others got it, but if my frames go to 29, 30 or 31 the sound starts to stutter a LOT. This cause the game to literarly ear♥♥♥♥♥♥the♥♥♥♥♥♥outa you if there is a strong wind. I usually have my fps at 40-50, but if it rains alot/snows, my frames tend to drop to around 35-40. If it goes to 31, 30 or 29 the sound lags, not the game, but the sound lags like crazy. This is soo frustrating and only happens with this game. Idk how, why or anything, it just happens. Don't know if it's fixeble but i really hope so, for my ears' sake.
I know i have been a bit negative in the review, but this is still worth the money, and im really happy with the game, it is worth checking out and in my opinion it's better than the classic, just because you can unlock "everything" for free. Except the ATVs and the tents which are DLCs. The DLCs aren't overprized at all like all the stuff was in the classic game, so everyone that can afford the game, can afford the DLCs.
I love the game and will recommend it to everyone that likes stealth, hunting, shooting, assassination?, realism, tracking, realaxing yet exiting and challenging.

This game is like cocaine.
I always tell myself just one more, then im done. I'll do homework. I'll sleep. I'll eat something.
But you know what? That last death was cheap, I'll do one more to make up for it. I just need 1000 gold for that upgrade, I'll just do one more to get it. Always just one more.
Things I like:
+The RPG elements are well done. -- As you gain gold you can purchase upgrades, which also build a castle. As you build it further, you unlock more upgrades. It is a very satisfying spin on upgrades. Additionally there is a good variety of gear and runes which allow for some really interesting build options
+The game is witty and has flavor. -- there are various conditions your new characters can have such as being blind, gay or having a fear of chickens, amongst many, many others. Dying is in this sense, pretty fun. On top of that there are many elements of the game that just give it a certain charm.
+The controls are very tight -- this game has good controls. It's easy to do what you want, which is good because it's very tough and you will die a lot.
What I didn't like:
- The bosses in new game plus don't get harder -- As you progress into new game + or ++ or +++ and beyond, the bosses don't scale well, despite the general enemies leveling up to basically become bosses themselves. Not a huge deal, but it's the only negative I have.
Then at some point you realize you've beaten the game, Thankfully there is a new game plus.
Maybe just one more playthrough...

The only problem I find with the game (besides expected bugs due to alpha) is the players. There are far too many who simply shoot on sight, without considering that not everyone is hostile, nor able to even see the world pass by at more than 15 fps in a relatively untextured, blocky state (so that guy running across the ridge you are in a panic over, might not even be able to distinguish you from a bush at more than 10m without risking a drop to 5 fps).
DO NOT go by the minimum system requirements, these specs may load the menu and might be semi-playable on a private hive PvE server (not many of those you can access unless you already know someone to get you whitelisted, don't even get me started on the monopoly on hosting with the ridiculous prices simply to have a local database instead of hooking into a remote one, dedicated server hosting is rarely as expensive), but for any chance to play against other players, you will need to sink a couple thousand dollars into a decent system.

So far so good after episode 2. I'm a fan of Life Is Strange, and I was looking forward to this expansion of the story. I think that I relate much more to Max than I do to Chloe, so that colors my impression of this game. I want to make the ethical "Max" decisions, but I keep coming back to what would Chloe do. It means that my choices are probably rather scattered and confused, and don't follow a cohesive pattern like they did when I played the original. That's probably appropriate, given that we're talking about Chloe.
I'll update my review after finishing the game, but here are my thoughts so-far:
The good:
-The game captures the general feel of the original LIS.
-Still, it has enough different things that you can tell that you're inside a different character.
-The Visuals are quite good.
-The music, while not quite as good as the original, is still very good.
-I've got mixed feelings about the loss of the rewind power. But on the positive side, it makes the important decisions feel much more weighty, knowing that I can't just go back and change my mind right away. I'm sure I'll play through the game once or twice more after finishing the first time so I can explore the other choices.
The not as good:
-The story lacks the same gut-punch that you got with LIS. Probably due to it being more on the rails as a game without the time-travel, chaos theory, prophetic dream element of the original. It feels much smaller and less epic than the original. The story is good in general, but it feels a little flat.
-I wish the devs had settled the dispute with the voice actors union. The voice actors are not as good as the ones who worked on Life Is Strange. I think I would have related better to Chloe if the acting had felt more naturally an extension of the original Chloe. The minor characters were fine, but it was noticeable that some of the actors were different, which was just distracting enough for a fan of the original LIS.
-Something about Rachel makes me uncomfortable. I'm not sure if it's just a subliminal sense of knowing what happens to her, or if it's something substantive about her character.

I feel like I'm in love with Rachel Amber.
In all seriousness though, great game, great storyline. Definitely pulls you in.
