Spec Ops: The Line is a great story crippled by bad gameplay.
Clocking in at just over 4 hours (with very little replay value), it focuses on a solid storyline filled with twists, turns, and a lot to think about - it was absolutely one of my favorite video game stories in a long time. Unfortunately, the story was often broken up by its gameplay, which had two modes: Satisfying difficulty & insanely hard.
The number of deaths I've had throughout the game were 0 - until two or three specific "climactic" areas, where I died anywhere from 4-8 times per fight. These usually came up in sections where I was in the middle of a plot point - the weird shift in difficulty only really distracted from the story, which was this game's redeeming feature.
Gameplay on its own is interesting - not groundbreaking, but the cover system and "wild firing" made for some fun times. You mow down squad after squad, so it's not quite as realistic as I prefer, but ultimately it was a very good game and an enjoyable (though short) ride.
For a Steam Sale? Absolutely pick this up. Anything over $10? Wait and see.

A cool driving simulator, with trucks.

RELAX
You know the feeling when you get in a car for a long road trip? Just you, the car, the road and the nice music that fits perfectly in your traveling mood.
That is what this game/simulator is all about. Just you, the truck, the cargo, the (incredibly stupid) AI and the ingame radio.
The amount of relaxation you get from this game is beyond me.
After a hard day at work or school you just go to you pc boot up ets2 and it's practically the same is getting a massage from your crush or drinking a moghitto on the beach with bellydancers all around.
STEERING WHEELS
The greatest thing about this game is the immersion. When you have a steering wheel (the G27 for example), you will see that this driving sim has one of the best configurated Force Feedback systems. You can basically feel the road in the palm of your hand. When you take a turn you can feel the wheels turning in the right direction and the road resisting it.
The FFB goes crazy when you hit a wall, drive on dirt or cobblestone and even when your revs are rising. It is that amazing.
ENVIRONMENT
Have you ever been to the mountains in Austria? Ever seen the clifsides in the east of europe? Been on a citytrip in Brussels? Well if you have don't go away just yet, you can do it again, in a bloody truck!
This sim has an amazing environment. Especially when you are in the mountains where a cliff of doom and death is waiting right next to you and where little peace of heaven and beauty is welcomming you in the distance.
In the countryside, cows and horses will be greeting you as you pass by, on the highway you can have a look at nicely rendered trees and other vegetations.
AI
You might have seen how I praise this game to be declared holy by the pope of videogames. Well, hold on because♥♥♥♥♥♥is about to go down.
Nobody has experienced a vast majority of stupidity in AI.
As you blink they never get out of the way.
Beacons to show them to stay clear of this truck don't seem to help.
Right of way... no right of way.
When they stop to let me pass by, they start accellarating as I move past.
Sigh... sorry... moving on.
GRAPHICS
In the last couple of updates there has been major changes on the graphical side of things. And oh boy were they amazing. As you sit within you cabin you can see the dawn come to greet you as the sunbeams flow all the way through the windows and reflect on your sidemirrors. When you are parked you can see every little detail on the road. Thi sim has beautifully rendered textures and an amazing light engine.
MODS
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is very mod friendly. They even made an interface were you can enable your mods and prioritize them in the last update. And there are many mods out there. From cabininteriors, truck skins, cargo types to even complete map extentions.
Overall this game/sim is completely breathtaking while receiving 97/100.

I completed the vast majority of the game and it's very good. It has a lot of good things going for it and few cons.
The atmosphere and characters are great. I think they really drive the game forward in a meaningful way. All the camps you clear are sufficiently different that they don't feel repetitive. Upgrading the magnum opus and Max paces nicely and the game world is a good size. I was worried after I played Just Cause 2 that the developer (Avalanche Studios) would try to make a game with that oversized map again. That didn't happen. It doesn't feel overwhelming like you'll never clear all the main locations. It's doable and doesn't get repetitive as they differentiated the camps very well. Also, the game runs well on low end systems. Even though mid-range cards are suggested to play it. I played it smoothly at low settings at 720p on an AMD A10-7870k integrated graphics setup.
The cons of this game that aren't too subjective would be the boss fights and visual styling. The boss fights exciting at first, but they're pretty static throughout and they actually get repetitive as you do the last few. Each boss has weaknesses, but they don't matter that much because the bonus damage from exploiting the weakness is negligible. The visuals of the game are bland. I know that it's set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, but it's like Fallout 3 in the visuals area. There is just this sand-colored filter that seems to follow every scene and the rust gets old. I understand that it's supposed to look like that, but it's underwhelming to watch.
My only other con is a personal preference and that's for the game's ending. I know it's great at following Mad Max themes and such, but it's still not my cup of tea.
Those cons aren't serious issues though. It's a very good game and I highly recommend it.

What, a movie tie-in game that's actually really good at being Mad Max-y, and good at being a game?
The good:
-Manages to faithfully capture the atmosphere (and weirdness) of the Mad Max movies down to fine details while also being a fun game. It's like they watched the films and thought "oh wow, that bit would be really fun to do, let's figure out a way to work that into our game" - I imagine the convoy bits are one of those, as when I saw the films I always wanted to play something like that... chasing after a big dust cloud in the distance, closing in on it, taking out each car one by one as the situation allows (some of their cars are weak enough that you can yank off their tyres, or take out their doors then charge up and shotgun them in the face, or just ram them off the road at oppurtune moments) or just dashing up to the lead car to take it out while being bashed and honked at while guys with bizarre face paint leap onto your car, with the roar of about 10 V8s in the background. Glorious!
-Oh, and the several other parts of the game which are basically all the bits of the film you'd want to do (hint: TWO MEN ENTER, ONE MAN LEAVES!). Half of the car upgrades are tied into side quests or challenges too, of which there are many, so there's plenty to do (though little variation, but i'll get to that).
-The environments are surprisingly mixed for what's basically one big desert so it doesn't look samey after an hour or anything.
-Car customisation is very good, and fun, with thousands of possible combinations. Mods for armour/defence add weight (so hurt speed, grip and handling) so it doesn't always make sense to just max out everything unless you're happy with a middling all-rounder (which looks badass though, so there's that).
-As others say, it runs really well for a console port (sad that this has became something of an exception), my computer's showing its age but runs this on medium settings with no problem (apart from very rare 4-5 second freezes, oddly).
The bad:
-The story kiiind of meanders a bit and isn't much, but then none of the Mad Max films had deep stories, more of a... I don't know, a backstory that told itself (from the freakshows that are the characters, hints in dialogue, and the general scenery) while the events on screen played out? That's not to say they're shallow, all-action films (i'm sure it's about 30 minutes into Mad Max 1 before there's even any dialogue), just that if you're looking for a story to follow, you won't find much of one. It's not noticeably *bad* at all, just meanders a bit, but that's Mad Max (as a series, or "franchise" to use that dreaded word) for you.
-Combat (hand to hand) is a bit... samey. Even if you're surrounded by bad guys it's easy as you just have to parry when you see the symbol and you can almost avoid getting hit entirely (unless there's tons of them, in which case it's hard work keeping up as 2-3 of those can be trying to hit you at once) - despite several enemy types with different strategies, it still mostly comes down to 'parry when you see the symbol, a couple light hits then a strong hit to finish'. You're invulnerable during finishing moves too. So yeah, fights are mostly an obstacle rather than a challenge, but not unenjoyable.
-The missions are pretty repetitive - pretty much all you'll be doing is drive somewhere, blow something up, beat up some bad guys, job done. Sometimes there'll be a boss. Otherwise you'll just be pulling down sniper towers or scarecrows with a harpoon. (That aside, it's strangely addictive, "i'll just clear out this enemy camp then go to bed..." [5 hours later] "...oops")
-Possibly a nitpick, but slightly awkward menu system that was clearly designed for consoles, PC-ised as an afterthought. The controls ingame reflect that too, so take a little getting used to, but not really a problem after you're familiar with them. Funnily enough there's controller support but you can't use both without third party software.
-Oh, one last thing, really minor, but don't waste points upgrading fuel efficiency. You're blasting a V8 around full pelt in a heavy armoured car, yet a full tank lasts over an hour of abuse. And fuel is fairly plentiful despite the films making a point of it being a sought after commodity.
That's about it really. I should stop since I've already written too much. Had to try hard to come up with bad points (they're mostly bit nitpicky, as admitted) so on balance, I really enjoy this game and have been recommending it to a few people. Have 31 hours in it currently and can see myself happily putting in another hundred, or however long, to 100% it.
TL;DR - Yes.

Spec Ops: The Line is a great story crippled by bad gameplay.
Clocking in at just over 4 hours (with very little replay value), it focuses on a solid storyline filled with twists, turns, and a lot to think about - it was absolutely one of my favorite video game stories in a long time. Unfortunately, the story was often broken up by its gameplay, which had two modes: Satisfying difficulty & insanely hard.
The number of deaths I've had throughout the game were 0 - until two or three specific "climactic" areas, where I died anywhere from 4-8 times per fight. These usually came up in sections where I was in the middle of a plot point - the weird shift in difficulty only really distracted from the story, which was this game's redeeming feature.
Gameplay on its own is interesting - not groundbreaking, but the cover system and "wild firing" made for some fun times. You mow down squad after squad, so it's not quite as realistic as I prefer, but ultimately it was a very good game and an enjoyable (though short) ride.
For a Steam Sale? Absolutely pick this up. Anything over $10? Wait and see.

What starts off as a rugid, lifeless, military sandstorm develops into a gut-wrenching, well paced, colourful storyline. It is a morality-based third-person shooter that isn't about war, protection, rescue or defeating a threat, it is about you. It has a classic feel while having great controls and randomly generated levels that aren't absurd. When they do produce something weird, it's actually kind of fun, like walking into a room that just has spikes at the bottom. There are a wide variety of enemies and "minibosses" and a chance to play a tripped out version of the bosses once you beat the original The different classes of warriors are interesting, and some of the miscellaneous attributes are hilarious (for instance, being flatulent, balding, gay or nostalgic). You don't grind in the game per se, but you definitely need to get all the gold you can to buy runes (powers), gear and skills. When you first start playing it'll seem like you can't stay alive at all but as you get more used to the enemies and buy powers you will get a feel for it (I never imagined I would be able to go through the entire castle in one life, I did that a couple times though, feels crazy). You also get the interesting choice of having the "architect" preserve the castle as it was for a fee, if you think you found something or have the chance to get further.
All of these little things contribute to the game having the highest replay value of almost any game.
The music is good (although if you play the game long enough, you hear the song at the first section of the castle a milion times, which would be a minor complaint). I think had other small complaints but they really don't matter that much.
This is one of those rare games that has a classic feel but is completely fresh. Super highly recommended.

I completed the vast majority of the game and it's very good. It has a lot of good things going for it and few cons.
The atmosphere and characters are great. I think they really drive the game forward in a meaningful way. All the camps you clear are sufficiently different that they don't feel repetitive. Upgrading the magnum opus and Max paces nicely and the game world is a good size. I was worried after I played Just Cause 2 that the developer (Avalanche Studios) would try to make a game with that oversized map again. That didn't happen. It doesn't feel overwhelming like you'll never clear all the main locations. It's doable and doesn't get repetitive as they differentiated the camps very well. Also, the game runs well on low end systems. Even though mid-range cards are suggested to play it. I played it smoothly at low settings at 720p on an AMD A10-7870k integrated graphics setup.
The cons of this game that aren't too subjective would be the boss fights and visual styling. The boss fights exciting at first, but they're pretty static throughout and they actually get repetitive as you do the last few. Each boss has weaknesses, but they don't matter that much because the bonus damage from exploiting the weakness is negligible. The visuals of the game are bland. I know that it's set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, but it's like Fallout 3 in the visuals area. There is just this sand-colored filter that seems to follow every scene and the rust gets old. I understand that it's supposed to look like that, but it's underwhelming to watch.
My only other con is a personal preference and that's for the game's ending. I know it's great at following Mad Max themes and such, but it's still not my cup of tea.
Those cons aren't serious issues though. It's a very good game and I highly recommend it.

What, a movie tie-in game that's actually really good at being Mad Max-y, and good at being a game?
The good:
-Manages to faithfully capture the atmosphere (and weirdness) of the Mad Max movies down to fine details while also being a fun game. It's like they watched the films and thought "oh wow, that bit would be really fun to do, let's figure out a way to work that into our game" - I imagine the convoy bits are one of those, as when I saw the films I always wanted to play something like that... chasing after a big dust cloud in the distance, closing in on it, taking out each car one by one as the situation allows (some of their cars are weak enough that you can yank off their tyres, or take out their doors then charge up and shotgun them in the face, or just ram them off the road at oppurtune moments) or just dashing up to the lead car to take it out while being bashed and honked at while guys with bizarre face paint leap onto your car, with the roar of about 10 V8s in the background. Glorious!
-Oh, and the several other parts of the game which are basically all the bits of the film you'd want to do (hint: TWO MEN ENTER, ONE MAN LEAVES!). Half of the car upgrades are tied into side quests or challenges too, of which there are many, so there's plenty to do (though little variation, but i'll get to that).
-The environments are surprisingly mixed for what's basically one big desert so it doesn't look samey after an hour or anything.
-Car customisation is very good, and fun, with thousands of possible combinations. Mods for armour/defence add weight (so hurt speed, grip and handling) so it doesn't always make sense to just max out everything unless you're happy with a middling all-rounder (which looks badass though, so there's that).
-As others say, it runs really well for a console port (sad that this has became something of an exception), my computer's showing its age but runs this on medium settings with no problem (apart from very rare 4-5 second freezes, oddly).
The bad:
-The story kiiind of meanders a bit and isn't much, but then none of the Mad Max films had deep stories, more of a... I don't know, a backstory that told itself (from the freakshows that are the characters, hints in dialogue, and the general scenery) while the events on screen played out? That's not to say they're shallow, all-action films (i'm sure it's about 30 minutes into Mad Max 1 before there's even any dialogue), just that if you're looking for a story to follow, you won't find much of one. It's not noticeably *bad* at all, just meanders a bit, but that's Mad Max (as a series, or "franchise" to use that dreaded word) for you.
-Combat (hand to hand) is a bit... samey. Even if you're surrounded by bad guys it's easy as you just have to parry when you see the symbol and you can almost avoid getting hit entirely (unless there's tons of them, in which case it's hard work keeping up as 2-3 of those can be trying to hit you at once) - despite several enemy types with different strategies, it still mostly comes down to 'parry when you see the symbol, a couple light hits then a strong hit to finish'. You're invulnerable during finishing moves too. So yeah, fights are mostly an obstacle rather than a challenge, but not unenjoyable.
-The missions are pretty repetitive - pretty much all you'll be doing is drive somewhere, blow something up, beat up some bad guys, job done. Sometimes there'll be a boss. Otherwise you'll just be pulling down sniper towers or scarecrows with a harpoon. (That aside, it's strangely addictive, "i'll just clear out this enemy camp then go to bed..." [5 hours later] "...oops")
-Possibly a nitpick, but slightly awkward menu system that was clearly designed for consoles, PC-ised as an afterthought. The controls ingame reflect that too, so take a little getting used to, but not really a problem after you're familiar with them. Funnily enough there's controller support but you can't use both without third party software.
-Oh, one last thing, really minor, but don't waste points upgrading fuel efficiency. You're blasting a V8 around full pelt in a heavy armoured car, yet a full tank lasts over an hour of abuse. And fuel is fairly plentiful despite the films making a point of it being a sought after commodity.
That's about it really. I should stop since I've already written too much. Had to try hard to come up with bad points (they're mostly bit nitpicky, as admitted) so on balance, I really enjoy this game and have been recommending it to a few people. Have 31 hours in it currently and can see myself happily putting in another hundred, or however long, to 100% it.
TL;DR - Yes.

I will admittedly say that because this game was inspired by a movie, I was half expecting it to be a flop... I was pleasantly proven wrong.
This game provides a nice open-world experience with plenty to do and a fun combat system that makes running around doing things that seem tedious actually quite fun.
The story is relatively minimal, and the way the game lays out your "objectives" leaves a lot of interpretation up to the player as to how you go about completing your missions. Many missions will have criteria that must be met for you to start (such as previous objectives, certain upgrades, etc.) that will force you to go out and complete tasks in order to earn those upgrades and progress further into the story.
The game is based very heavily on driving, specifically, your very own car that you upgrade with you like a man and his dog. The car will become your primary source of combat, means of travel, as well as the ability to reach new areas. One aspect that I thought was pretty intuitive was the introduction of the fuel gauge-- that's right, your car has to run on actual fuel. At first, it seems like the fuel supply is low, restricting your ability to go anywhere and do anything, but there are numerous ways to increase the efficiency as well as find spare fuel all over the place (you can also get special projects in each stronghold that will give you an instant full tank), so I never actually had an issue keeping the tank full.
The gameplay and the controls are pretty well implemented, following gameplay style like the Arkham series and Shadow of Mordor (both WB productions), and with the detail of Just Cause 3 (same dev). The only complaint that I'd have about the gameplay, is the jumping... your character can jump, but not more than a foot of the ground. You rarely have to use it, that it just seems like it's there to keep some semblance of realism. It's more of a gripe in that it somewhat restricts your ability to go "anywhere".
The music is also very well set to the game, it provides an ambience that puts you right in to a savage wasteland with some creepy inhabitants, and never feels like it gets in the way.
The menu system is pretty comprehensive but I will give a summary of my pros/cons that will address a few quirks I noticed.
tl;dr
Pros:
+ Fluid gameplay mechanics
+ Interesting combat system (both on foot and in car)
+ There's lots of content that can be accessed before completing major missions
+ Upgrading your car and customizing the builds are satisfying to your type of play (speed, attack, weaponry, etc.)
+ Fuel is plentiful (you just have to be observant)
+ Map and fast-travel system is very useful
+ Engaging story and fun missions
+ You can cheat in death runs (races)
Cons:
- The main side content is just different takes on the same few concepts (which can get repetitive quickly)
- Finding large quantities of scrap is annoying
- The game can "hold your hand" in places (look for yellow everywhere to indicate where you can go)
- The menu interface can be annoying when you find a new part and you have to switch back and forth to effectively compare two parts (hood ornaments mostly)
- The jumping mechanic is just filler
Overall, I had a good time with this game. Give it a chance if you like open world, combat focused entertainment.

When I originally purchased this game during the summer sale I had no idea what I was getting myself into. A game about driving across europe in a truck roving from country to country and delivery to delivery? How good can it be? Turns out it can be damn good. Don't knock it until you try it.
The core of the game involves, you guessed it, driving around in a euro style big rig making pick ups and drop offs at various locations around much of Europe. You start off simply enough by taking jobs where a truck is provided to you and you can get your feet wet without having to use a lot of the games systems, but soon enough you will earn enough to buy your own truck from one of the many real world manufacturers licensed in the game from the popular Scania to the recently added Mercedes Benz line. This is when the real fun begins.
Once you have your own truck, an element of strategy kicks in as you can now make a delivery to one place and then choose the best job nearby and it becomes a hunt to find efficient routes and maximize profits but now you have to balance the need for sleep, keeping an eye on your fuel gauge and avoiding accidents that lead to the need for expensive repairs. Eventually you can even by garages and hire additional drivers and develop an international trucking empire of your own.
As you drive and make deliveries you will gain experience which will allow you to unlock various certifications and boosts that will allow you to make more money off of jobs, take newer and more challenging delivery types, or simply make driving more efficient.
SCS put a lot of effort into capturing real truck sounds and it makes for a more immersive experience. As for music, you can import your own or you can stream internet radio from across Europe in multiple languages.
This isn't a AAA title but the graphics are pretty easy on the eyes. There is a lot of detail in the various interiors of the trucks and driving through the countryside or one of the many cities included in the game there is always somethig new to see, from quaint villages and fields, to larger cities with towering skylines.
There is a bunch of DLC for this game. A lot of it is purely cosmetic in the form of new paint jobs that you can purchase for your trucks. There are also a couple of dlc's that you will want to pick up at some point, specifically the Going East and Scandinavia dlc's, which add new countries, jobs, roads and sights to see.
Even if you don't buy any of the DLC there is new content regularly added with each new patch including new places to visit, new vehicle upgrades, new truck lines such as the above mentioned Mercedes trucks and more. SCS has shown a lot of support for this game and loyalty to their customer base who have already purchased the game by adding regular updates and additional content for free with no signs of stopping.
ETS2 isn't a game that looks like much at first glance, but give it a chance and you may soon find yourself cruising around the highways of virtual Europe making deliveries and developing a logistics empire of your own. Give it a chance, you won't be disappointed.

I've seen strange games came out of Early Access, but Gang Beasts is definitely one of the strangest. That isn't actually a bad thing, though, as it uses this to its advantage to create one of the most hilarious, addicting, and creative fighting games I've ever played.
Gang Beasts' strongest factor is its hilarity. Your silly, gelatinous characters are so fun to beat around that it's so fun to put them in an arena and watch them fight to the death, punch each other unconscious, and throw each other off buildings, window washers, elevators, ferris wheels, storage containers, and into fan blades, onto train tracks, and even into garbage incinerators. It's even more fun when it's your friends falling/burning to their death. The online mutliplayer is suprisingly reliable because most of the time I was able to get into a game without many problems. The customization system is also strong, with plently of options to make your own character.
The only things that hold the game down are mainly technical issues that include characters glitching out of the map, certain stages lagging to the point of the game crashing, and the score never changing no matter how many times I won a round. Aside from the stage lagging, these problems can be easily fixed by restarting the game. It would be nice if the devs could fix this stage issue. Also, $20 is a lot to ask for the game in its current state. I'll tell you, it's worth it, but I feel like lots of people will be put off by the price, when more players would only help the game. It's an investment, but one that I feel is really worth it.
Final Verdict:
Gang Beasts is great fun, espically if you play with friends, but it has a long way to go before it can be the game you host a tournament for your friends with. It's a steep price, but it's totally worth it if you're looking for a great, silly party game.

I may have unknowingly snuck in a few subtle spoilers while spontaneously writing this, so heads up.
This is the 3 episodic prequel to the award-winning title Life is Strange™. Since I pre-ordered the standard edition several months back, I still need to wait for Episode 3 as of this review. Nevertheless, the first two episodes were enough to get me started.
The voice change didn't really bother me as much further into the game (you get used to it) but I still felt it didn't give the same personality to these characters. At times, it somewhat made the dialogue kind of awkward (or maybe it's just Chloe's weird sense of humour). I like how they changed the way you select options in-game like - Look, Select, Graffiti with the WASD keys instead of dragging your mouse. I found the "dragging" in the first game confusing and quite a hassle in the beginning. There are technical difficulties in this game where in some instances - subtitles were left to repeat, glitches in sound and the occassional bugs. Hopefully future patches will fix all of this.
Nevertheless, I am glad this prequel was made. One of my biggest curiosities (as well as many others) in the first game was the history between Rachel and Chloe. We really dive into their relationship in this game and here we can see first-hand why the loss of Rachel in the first game was a devastating one to Chloe. Apart from this, it really is wonderful to see the other characters in their younger years too. An insight to the Blackwell before Max came back.
The biggest change (in my opinion) was the removal of the time-travel element. In the first game, this was a luxury given to us in the role of Max. Whenever we come face to face with a choice (important or not), we can simply rewind if we didn't like the choice we've made. In this game, Chloe (obviously) doesn't have that power. This means every choice you make is a more permanent one. This isn't necessarily a bad thing either. It makes us more wary of the choices we make and the consequences our choices hold. Which I feel ultimately makes the game more exciting.
It is not a 'Life is Strange' game without the constant ride of emotions. This game so far, reminds us what makes the first game great. Here, we are Chloe. We see first-hand how her problems affect her. Sometimes from the choices we are given, non of it are good ones. We can see step-by-step how she changed to the Chloe we know in the first game. Even her main ability is non-other than 'back talking' (which I find hilarious).
Even though Episode 3 hasn't come out yet, I am confident enough to say that this is a game worth playing.

Rogue Legacy is awesome. A short description if you somehow don't know. It's an action platformer game in a castle whose layout is randomly generated. You run around swording dudes getting gold and loot. The cool bit is when you die you pick a new character from three choices, each of whom are given a random class, spell, and traits that could be benefits or drawback. Each character requires you to adjust your playstyle to match. You then have the opportunity to spend the gold you earned on character upgrades (these apply to every future character you get), new and better gear, and runes (these confer abilities like adding up to 6 air jumps) which can be swapped out for each character. Spend what you've got since the reaper will take all your gold (this can be reduced to half through upgrasdes) on your way into the castle, which is given a totally new layout.
I've spent about sixty hours in the game now. The thing that hooks me the most is that Rogue Legacy is one of the best playing games I've ever played. The controls are as responsive as they come, on par with a Super Meatboy (without the momentum model), but the way it controls includes a lot of gameplay nicities. You can move while swinging your sword, but damage is done when an enemy collides with your sword, not when you push the button. So for faster classes you can play fighting game style footsies with enemies by swinging, running forward to poke a dude then dashing back before he hits you. This can be further enhanced by character traits like flexible, which allows you to change directions while swinging. You can even dash in a direction your not facing giving you complete control over your mobility.
When you combine runes, classes, traits, and gear (some of which might favor spellcaster, or have added effects like +2 air jumps), every time you go into the castle you're going in with a different playstyle. The game then has massive difficulty scaling through its new game plus features and remix bosses. I've never beat a remix boss (they are so hard), but have beaten the game on NG+++++. I will unquestionably recommend this game. You'll get an amazing game with tons of replay value, its definitely worth the fifteen dollar ask.

I never thought in my wildest dreams of 20+ in years gaming that we would reach the point where this exists. This is the absolutely most gorgeous game I've ever had the pleasure of playing. Not just wonderfully rendered and optimized, but the level of detail is staggering. I sincerely hope the content directors of this game were paid a hefty sum, because they certainly deserve all credit due. From random debris drifting along the dunes, to the licks of burning fuel dripping out of the exhaust, and sandstorms from the depths of Hades. Sand, grime, blood, oil, unholy amounts of rust befitting the utter collapse of civilization.
Gameplay itself is quite straightforward and rewarding, yet punishing enough for an enjoyable challenge. Max's personal equipment and fighting skills are easy to level up. The somewhat grind comes in finding parts for your various vehicle outfittings. Though tearing through structures, war boys, and cars with the "Magnum Opus" will sate your urge for downtown road rage to be sure!

You'll notice Max has an odd gait and brace on his leg. Combine that with the armor and equipment he has straped to him at all time, and the naysayers who complain about the platforming are just silly. Even if not permanent I really appreciate the effort taken to show persistent wounds and bruises as well.
The storyline is great. Combine dehydration, malnutrition, lack of medicine, constant fear of being raided, with some good old exposure to the elements, and you can understand why most of the people you interact with don't have all their cylinders firing... if you catch my drift there.
This is a faithful companion to the new Fury Road. The reboot seems to have a vastly more aloof and gritty personality for Max. As well as perhaps giving a nod to the realities of everything going to absolute hell: PTSD, survival of the fittest, empaty not having much signifigance because it's a luxury. This felt less like a game and more as an experience. You have to keep in mind George Miller created this story as a way of sharing what he lived through when treating victims of vehicular carnage while he was an emergency room doctor.
A few points of minor complaint I had:
-The dog and associated uses for it were nearly useless. Not sure if an afterthought or someone's "pet" project that never got the attention it deserved. Could have really made things interesting like a helpful attack dog, and/or sniffing out supplies. Not even once did mines ever pose a problem for me.
-No deadly desert critters, or tasty lizards to roast? Missing out on the best parts of Australian outback there mates.
-No ability to make my own war-boy possee complete with flamethrowing guitars of the metal gods? What gives Avalanche... what gives?
9.8/10

I've done one playthrough in the no kill section and I didn't find it all too enjoyable. Perhaps it was the absolute joke of a community this game has following it that first soured my experience as I was rather late to the party playing this game. I will list off all of my issues in as much detail as possible.
The first issue I found were the graphics. No I don't mean I need great visuals to get me through the game being that my favorite game is Dwarf Fortress (No texture pack), but the graphics for the most part just feel cheap. There aren't any nice contrasts or color creativity at all throughout the game. Every enemy while some nicely designed felt bland and soulless.
The characters looking unappealing leads into my next issue, the characters. They feel as if they're just made of one "quirky" emotion. Every character is misunderstood. Every character is made to be a cringy tumblr meme. Every character has a secret soft side. Flowey is the only character that I felt had more than one emotion which is why it's by far the best character. Flowey could not carry the game because the piles of "querky" characters you meet feel uninspired and one dimensional. I don't need a deep story to carry me through a game though. It's just that the story isn't a very good one. Not a bad one, just not very good. Starting the genocide as suggested by a commentor hasn't changed my mind about the characters, if anything it's only made me loathe them more. Their blissful ignorance in this supposedly horrible world makes me feel that they deserve the fate of being underground for being so bland. Playing through in genocide is much more satisfying because I don't have to sit through the same three lines of dialogue at nausium as I try to figure out how to make the stupid♥♥♥♥♥monster go away for three steps until another comes. It makes Pokemon feel like it's not grind heavy.
The game's system of either not killing the enemies or murdering all of them may seem creative at first. I thought this was the main selling point but the bullet hell gameplay is exactly that, hell. It wasn't that it was too hard for me, for the most part it was easy street. There were random points though that would just spike in difficulty for seemingly no reason. Certain fights would go to silly difficulty levels and then plummet back to the easy gameplay. Another problem is that the gameplay is so repetetive. You either talk a creature into not killing you over and over in the same way with no variation or you kill them in the same way over and over again. It's like playing through an jrpg with no party: you get one basic attack and tired visuals.
Next topic is the fandom. I don't think any fandom is beneficial to anything besides mob mentality. Everywhere I go people making Undertale references is just about as common as Youtube commenters having weeb profile pictures. They've turned into a more annoying fandom that the bronies and the FNAF people combined. That is genuinly a feat. Some of the "edgy" kids even at my school who have never touched a game in their lives consider this game a gift from God because their favourite cookie cutter youtube idol played it and had a forced reaction. Until you actually play this game you can't boast about its virtues because playing it is a pain. I wish I had just skipped to the "good" bits of a lets play than play this. That is how bitter and toxic this fanbase is. Without them I would have found this game painfully mediocre, maybe even good on some levels but never something that I'd consider spending more than five dollars on for an afternoon.
I guess I'll move on to a more subjective point: the humor. For people who like "meme humor" will like this game. People who like any other kind of joke will not be able to stand this game. The humor reminds me a lot of what a Jeff Dunham joke is. The jokes are built off of either shock or the one character trait of one of his characters. It works the same way here. Aw Papyrus is a very bad villian and he's not very good at being one because he's got a heart of gold. Let's dedicate a significant portion of this game showing you this same "quirky" joke over and over until we move on to the next "quirky" and "cute: villians. The comedy hurt at times. Not in a my sides hurt kind of pain, the second hand embarrassment kind of pain. The kind you get when you do something stupid and then watch the movie Elf.
This game just isn't for me and I can't really see how it's for very many other people either. The game it's inspired by (Earthbound) is still a more enjoyable exprerience with well thought out jokes and characters. The game also has a more consistent and eye apealing art style despite coming out, what, 30 years ago? I just can't recommend this game because there is so many better things out there for your money.

Rogue Legacy is a 2D action RPG rogue-like beat em up. You basically try to clear a castlevania-esque castle full of monsters, treasure, weapons. and bosses.
Each time you die you lose your progress through the castle but keep all upgrades/weapons/money/boss kills. Your ancestor then gets his/her own castle and all the money from the previous run. You spend money on a giant branching skill tree, purchasing weapons, or buying skills (like double jump or dodge) before each castle run. Entering the castle will remove all money and reset all monsters and treasure.  There can be a bit of grinding going on if you are stuck and need upgrades but overall its a lot of fun.
The game also has a class system. Each time someone dies you are presented with several ancestors with randomized classes and abilities (some see in black & white, some are large/tiny). The differences between the classes boil down to different multipliers on your Strength, Mana, and HP stats and different active skills.
Melee combat is very fast, very responsive, and great fun. The controls are very snappy as you would expect for this sort of game. You only have two speeds go and don't go. This makes controlling the character feel very intuitive, allowing you to jump up to people get a swing in then change direction and safely fall out of their attack range. You also get an item and a spell. The spell is class dependent and the items are random but some classes seem to get one type of item more often than others so im not sure its entirely random. Cant speak for magic using classes, I just really never got into the magics in this game. I'm sure its equally deep and fun but I much prefer melee in this sort of game.
Overall gameplay feels and plays solid. I never felt cheated when I died. Due to the game's random generated castles, you will come across room layouts (mostly challenge rooms containing blueprints for weapons/armor or runes for skills) that are totally impossible on your current character. Minor gripe, but it is slightly annoying knowing Ill need to do another run to get w/e was going to be in that chest.
Overall I would highly suggest this game to anybody who enjoys these types of 2D platformer hack and slash games with RPG elements and a forgiving perma-death system. There are alot of games out there like this, but much like how binding of issac is the king of isometric bullet hell rogue-like RPGs. Rogue legacy is the head of its genre.

Excellent game. Platformers usually don't appeal to me, but the humor and roguelike/lite elements in this game made it interesting enough to try and even though I was initially terrible at it, I was really enjoying it and kept wanting to try again and again. Maybe each run doesn't have as much variation as something like Isaac, but they're just different enough and the progression system compelling enough that 19 hours in I'm still wanting that one more run.
My only real complaints would be that the upgrade system can sometimes stall you out if you're not very good at the game, and that perhaps the items, on the rare occasion you find them, are not all that varied or interesting.
The items just seem lack-luster. The blacksmith items are usually just linear upgrades: more damage, more health, more armor. There do seem to be a couple more interesting ones but they are random drops from randomly spawning chests so you may or may not see much of them. So far I have not. The random items you find in the castle don't seem all that remarkable either. Whenever I happen to find one it's usually either the death defy ring (which is nice) or the compass or maybe Herme's  shoes. Not sure how many items there actually are, but it doesn't seem to be a very large pool at all and their effects are usually not very sweeping.
As for the upgrades, they are also usually linear upgrades but the class unlocks keeps things interesting. My problem with these is that it feels like getting some "bad" (weak) upgrades can actually hurt you since each time you buy an upgrade all future upgrades become just a little more expensive, and it's happened to me on more than one occasion that I can't buy an upgrade by like just 10 or 20 coins.
(Minor spoilers ahead, related to stats)
Thus it really feels like spending on some upgrades can do more harm than good and there is a "wrong" and a "right" upgrade path.
The events are also somewhere they could have added more content. The carnivals are a nice touch but would be awesome if there were more variations on them or other such active events. The guy with the three chests has become something I just dont bother with most of the time now. And other than that it's pretty much just a random item, a journal entry, some info on the developer's other games, or a healing fountain. And I feel this is an area the game could have been improved upon.
The aesthetics are charming in my opinon and I feel the overall art style of this game works pretty nicely. The combat is very simplistic but I feel all the dodging and platforming you constantly have to do keeps things lively enough. Though I do find it annoying that you can't really turn around without moving a bit in the other direction, so I sometimes take damage trying to turn around to hit something coming up behind me. It is entirely possible to just maneuver around to avoid damage, and your sword swing has a bit of an arc above and behind you, it's just something you have to learn and get used to.
All in all I would highly recommend it. If you're into roguelike/lites or action platformers at all, you'll probably find some enjoyment here.

This game very much disagrees with what it's trying to be, in a good way. It's trying to be a standard fun shooter, but every action you do makes you feel more and more horrible inside. It is the only game I know that properly depicts the horror of war. Or, at least how horrible I'd imagine it to be. The strong point in this game is the storytelling. I personally don't value that aspect of games that much, so me saying that means that there is something remarkable here. The gameplay is average, and I don't think praising games for what they don't have is appropriate. That said, I'm just going to mention the total absence of QTEs, and the lack of near-infinite ammo that modern shooters have. Those problems don't exist. Cutscenes are cutscenes, and resource management is a real thing.
There are some objective problems though. Even though the vast majority of PC players play with their eyes close to a desktop display, the game runs in a console-like couch distance FOV of 72°, when it should be 90°, to keep central visual feedback from falling in the human peripheral vision. And that setting can't be changed. Secondly, some completely unrelated actions such as sprinting and jumping down from ledges, and melee and vaulting obstacles, are filed under the same contextual key. The PC keyboard has 105 buttons, so why do we need to have the same button for unrelated actions? Thirdly, the game has built-in mouse acceleration that can't be toggled off, so basically someone spent real, paid work hours to make the mouse control worse than it could have been if someone just left it in raw input.
But while those objective faults made me stop playing Mass Effect 2, for some reason they didn't stop me from finishing Spec-Ops. I guess every moment I spent in the average gunplay was properly decorated with the sheer disgusting horror that I couldn't get enough of. The gameplay mechanics are simple, with some competently streamlined special mechanics such as giving orders to your squad mates with the press of a single button. Enemies are very good at keeping you pinned down, and you do need your buddies to survive. There are some environmental hazards that you can use against your enemies, but they are too few and far between, so you might not even realize they're there. The underuse of the setting in this way makes it a failed gimmick.
So it's a decent game with a few minor problems, that isn't as good on PC as it could have been with better PC-specific features, lacking in many modern negative game tropes, and finally, the story is hauntingly amazing. It isn't a game that you want to keep playing. It is a game you will want to finish, and then throw up afterwards, while crying conflicted tears of agony and joy. Nobody is perfect, but Spec-Ops: The Line is a one of a kind masterpiece of horrific beauty.

The Most Honest Review Yet
The Pros:
Graphics - The graphics is sunning and the scenery is beyond par. Even on the lowest settings, the graphics is beautiful. The world is massive, like GTAx10 massive imo. 50+ hours and i have yet to fully explore 1 region. The focus in this game is so good that the details you didnt expect to see when using a scope, appears vividly before your eyes.
Game Mechanics - The guns in here is a very accurate portrayal of the real things. There is bullet drop so praticing ur shots for targets 200m is a must. Animals in here act and react the way they are supposed to. The path they run and walk is completely random if they get scared. Certain hot spots like feeding zones will increase your chances at an easier kill. Animals tracking and attacking other animals when they are bleeding is very interesting.
Price - for $30 its not bad. infact its pretty good compared to the $60 price point most AAA titles that come out now days will have a hard time competing with this game.
The Cons:
Bugs & Glitches - I though this game was buggy because of my mid range computer set up. However, I'm glad I not alone. Playing with friends with GTX960's and 1080Ti's they all experience their own glitches and bugs. For me it was flickering images and player ghosting. Sometimes my character head angles when falling off a cliff or taking damage forcing me to restart my game. For my friends.they experience blacked screens in random areas and spawning in the middle of the ocean or in space. Some animals get stuck between trees, rocks, and mountain sides. The ATV (bought DLC) is extremely buggy. If you hit your friend or jump off the bike, it sometimes sends the atvs flying to outter space. You occasionally spin out because of imaginary rocks or cracks. The ATV is non repairable, making your ATV really, a one time use. After that, you have to go back to an outpost and recall it (for no charge).
Price: I know there is a pro about the price but this one also has a negative. The bad thing about this game is that with the low price point for the base game, they charge for everything that should already be included in the base game. This game plots you in a map, and you have to walk and run everywhere. $4 DLC isnt much to complain about, but once you start experiencing all the random bugs and glitches this game has with the atv, you start to question why your $4 was justifiable. Me personally, I am deeply discouraged to buy any other DLC after the ATV experience. As they release more and more additions, this game will start to cost more and more than an AAA title.
I actually do recommend this game only if you like the challenge. If you are a RNG kind of person, dont even bother. The reason why I do not recommend it right now, is because of how buggy this game is. The random frame glitches of the animals through the wood, water, rocks, and tracking under the world map, are all examples.

Never left a review on Steam before, but I was absolutely compelled to do so after playing this game.
It completely took me by surprise - so much better and more involved than I ever expected. The visuals are beyond incredible. Never seen an environment look so convincing and beautiful before this in my 30 years of PC gaming. The realistically balanced audio just topped it off for me. And I was happy with just these features. But then I realised just how deep the game went in it's gameplay.
Animal tracking mechanics are incorporated brilliantly. Being able to sit and wait for animals in areas likely to for them to pass through, but may not necessarily do so, is excellent. The need for absolute quiteness and patience when sneaking up on your prey is priceless. The tracks left by both you and your prey, and even your online hunting friends, is mind-blowing. I'm running out of adjectives to describe how great this title is. It's an experience that so few games offer and it's so refreshing to play that I'm totally hooked and can't put it down. Even the animal population dynamically varies itself depenindg on how much 'hunting pressure' there is in a given area. Absolutely incredible!
Honestly, I never really considered the idea of a hunting game. Hunting for animals in games like Far Cry never really took my fancy, and I really only picked this up for the co-operative component. But I am so glad I did end up buying it, because it's introduced me to a totally new type of sand-box environement with a different focus - one that's quite hard to explain, and really, you need to experience it for yourself to understand. It's not going to be for everyone. If you fall into the former category, you owe it to yourself to pick this one up.
This is proper, classic PC gaming at it's best. Don't miss out on this. We need more games like it. Buy it now!

I really don't understand the mind set of those aggrieved by this, especially considering how monstrously big the new DLC hunting reserve is. The developers deserve the money and I have no problem handing it over. It's a matter of value, and this game offers a staggering amount of it compared to almost any other title I've bought before this. You should all be thanking these developers for not succumbing to the watered-down, mass-appeal attitude that 'big business' gaming subjects us all to on a daily basis. I certainly do!

You know the feeling when you get in a car for a long road trip? Just you, the car, the road and the nice music that fits perfectly in your traveling mood.
That is what this game/simulator is all about. Just you, the truck, the cargo, the (incredibly stupid) AI and the ingame radio.
The amount of relaxation you get from this game is beyond me.
After a hard day at work or school you just go to you pc boot up ets2 and it's practically the same is getting a massage from your crush or drinking a moghitto on the beach with bellydancers all around.
STEERING WHEELS
The greatest thing about this game is the immersion. When you have a steering wheel (the G27 for example), you will see that this driving sim has one of the best configurated Force Feedback systems. You can basically feel the road in the palm of your hand. When you take a turn you can feel the wheels turning in the right direction and the road resisting it.
The FFB goes crazy when you hit a wall, drive on dirt or cobblestone and even when your revs are rising. It is that amazing.
ENVIRONMENT
Have you ever been to the mountains in Austria? Ever seen the clifsides in the east of europe? Been on a citytrip in Brussels? Well if you have don't go away just yet, you can do it again, in a bloody truck!
This sim has an amazing environment. Especially when you are in the mountains where a cliff of doom and death is waiting right next to you and where little peace of heaven and beauty is welcomming you in the distance.
In the countryside, cows and horses will be greeting you as you pass by, on the highway you can have a look at nicely rendered trees and other vegetations.
AI
You might have seen how I praise this game to be declared holy by the pope of videogames. Well, hold on because♥♥♥♥♥♥is about to go down.
Nobody has experienced a vast majority of stupidity in AI.
As you blink they never get out of the way.
Beacons to show them to stay clear of this truck don't seem to help.
Right of way... no right of way.
When they stop to let me pass by, they start accellarating as I move past.
Sigh... sorry... moving on.
GRAPHICS
In the last couple of updates there has been major changes on the graphical side of things. And oh boy were they amazing. As you sit within you cabin you can see the dawn come to greet you as the sunbeams flow all the way through the windows and reflect on your sidemirrors. When you are parked you can see every little detail on the road. Thi sim has beautifully rendered textures and an amazing light engine.
MODS
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is very mod friendly. They even made an interface were you can enable your mods and prioritize them in the last update. And there are many mods out there. From cabininteriors, truck skins, cargo types to even complete map extentions.
Overall this game/sim is completely breathtaking while receiving 97/100.

one of the most creative, clever, fun, crazy, funny and chaotic games I’ve ever played, but the recent updates have ruined it to the point that the game isn’t even playable anymore.
Here is an in-depth talk about Gang Beasts, before and after the beta release:
MAPS:
Gang Beasts has got some amazing and fun maps. Such a shame they remade all of them and now they suck. Well, to be honest, some of the remakes are actuary quite nice, but most of them are horrible. Subway, Fans and Containers are the only good remakes, every other one sucks. For example: Gondola’s remake added a large, annoying framework above the gondola, Tower’s remake made the tower and its surroundings look uglier, Grind’s remake made the railing indestructible. Sure, the remakes may have added in some nice things, but they still took out the best parts of the maps.
MULTIPLAYER:
As I’m sure you know, the game’s multiplayer is the worst multiplayer you will ever find in a game. Connection problems happen once every couple of rounds, and it's SUPER rare to even do one full cycle through the all maps without crashing, timing out or disconnecting. It’s insane. Playing with friends is also pointless because even if you do get into a stable game (which is unlikely) there is a VERY small chance that all of your friends will be able to get into the server. (EDIT: As of recently, this has been improved, but not fixed.)
SINGLEPLAYER:
Jon the Gang Beasts Dev: Alright guys, singleplayer is working now and has plenty of features! I think it’s time to port the game from Alpha to Beta and start working on online multiplayer!
Bob the Gang Beasts Dev: I have an idea!
Jon the Gang Beasts Dev: What is it, Bob?
Bob the Gang Beasts Dev: I think we should remove literally every feature for the singleplayer mode.
Jon the Gang Beasts Dev: But why Bob?
Bob the Gang Beasts Dev: *Inhuman Screeching*
Seriously though, they removed the ability turn off cycling through maps, so now the map just changes whenever you die. This can’t EVER be turned off and is super annoying. They also RUINED the bots…
SINGLEPLAYER BOTS:
I was originally going to talk about the bots in the ‘Singleplayer’ section, but so many great features the bots had were, for no reason removed from the game. Now the bots suck. Not only do the bots have horrible AI and will just follow you around, if you kill even just ONE bot, the whole round will end. It doesn’t matter how many other players or bots you have, killing one bot WILL end the whole round, no matter what. This can’t be turned off, either. In Alpha, the bots had better AI and didn’t end the round if they died. Speaking of Alpha, the Alpha bots would spawn with a random combination of clothes. In the current version, the bots are always grey. No exceptions. Also, in the Alpha versions, you could spawn in big buff bots, this was removed from the game for no reason.
GREAT FEATURES THAT WERE REMOVED:
1: Sandbox mode
2: The actually interesting Alpha/Legacy menu. (I’m talking about the one with the characters fighting in the street.)
3: The rooftop map from waves mode.
4: The street map.
5: The surprisingly fun tutorial.
Thanks for reading!

Every month or two for the past three years (count 'em) I come back to play DayZ for a while, with the same result: completely unchallenging zombie play, token survival that only requires you understand a few tricks, and enraging PvP with clunky movement and lag.
Zombie play was never very challenging to begin with years ago, when all you had to do was know how to side strafe and punch them in the head; the three zombies that show up that you do not get away from by going into buildings or through the trees, that is. For the longest time zombies that could glitch through floors and doors provided some challange, and every so often you would get an invisible zombie, but now alas that and these gliches are gone. So you will find yourself seeing zombies as a nuisance like they are in the latest Walking Dead seasons. Zombies are there for casual inturruptions in your inventory management and walking immersion gameplay.
Survival's little enjoyments--figuring out how to build a fire so you don't freeze to death, and cook food on it, or how to piece together a bow and arrow and make clothing--these constitute a few hours of gameplay, and are much better found in other survival games that have playability after that with some real impact on the larger world. Wolves getting added to the game, like almost everything else, just takes you knowing a trick or two for the threat to become pointless.
PvP late game consists of you running for half an hour from the coast to a military loot spawn point, where you hopefully time the loot spawns right, get geared, and then meet up with friends. After an hour or so of prep, you can find a lot of heart bracing moments stalking other player teams. When the gunfire starts, though, you will be rolling the dice on network issues and glitchy movement, as much as you will be trying to out think or out shoot your opponents. To be fair: if you are into hours of walking and inventory management for a few minutes of gunplay with unpredictable results that inspire vast swings in emotion which destroy friendships, this is the PvP experience for you.
After all these years and money and hype, DayZ still has less content and is less enjoyable than the mod that inspired it. The lasting impact of this game will not be for its devs and players that have invested so much time and money into it, but the ideas it once hoped to achieve which have spawned so many other games.

This game very much disagrees with what it's trying to be, in a good way. It's trying to be a standard fun shooter, but every action you do makes you feel more and more horrible inside. It is the only game I know that properly depicts the horror of war. Or, at least how horrible I'd imagine it to be. The strong point in this game is the storytelling. I personally don't value that aspect of games that much, so me saying that means that there is something remarkable here. The gameplay is average, and I don't think praising games for what they don't have is appropriate. That said, I'm just going to mention the total absence of QTEs, and the lack of near-infinite ammo that modern shooters have. Those problems don't exist. Cutscenes are cutscenes, and resource management is a real thing.
There are some objective problems though. Even though the vast majority of PC players play with their eyes close to a desktop display, the game runs in a console-like couch distance FOV of 72°, when it should be 90°, to keep central visual feedback from falling in the human peripheral vision. And that setting can't be changed. Secondly, some completely unrelated actions such as sprinting and jumping down from ledges, and melee and vaulting obstacles, are filed under the same contextual key. The PC keyboard has 105 buttons, so why do we need to have the same button for unrelated actions? Thirdly, the game has built-in mouse acceleration that can't be toggled off, so basically someone spent real, paid work hours to make the mouse control worse than it could have been if someone just left it in raw input.
But while those objective faults made me stop playing Mass Effect 2, for some reason they didn't stop me from finishing Spec-Ops. I guess every moment I spent in the average gunplay was properly decorated with the sheer disgusting horror that I couldn't get enough of. The gameplay mechanics are simple, with some competently streamlined special mechanics such as giving orders to your squad mates with the press of a single button. Enemies are very good at keeping you pinned down, and you do need your buddies to survive. There are some environmental hazards that you can use against your enemies, but they are too few and far between, so you might not even realize they're there. The underuse of the setting in this way makes it a failed gimmick.
So it's a decent game with a few minor problems, that isn't as good on PC as it could have been with better PC-specific features, lacking in many modern negative game tropes, and finally, the story is hauntingly amazing. It isn't a game that you want to keep playing. It is a game you will want to finish, and then throw up afterwards, while crying conflicted tears of agony and joy. Nobody is perfect, but Spec-Ops: The Line is a one of a kind masterpiece of horrific beauty.

Having played this game for a while (about one day of time as I write this), I can tell you this is a game that is most definetely worth getting. I bought this game and the "Going East" expansion for $7 during the Steam Summer Sale, but I would still pay the twenty or so dollars for this game. The simulation is extremely realistic, and there a several features that make this simulator realistic and similar to real world driving.
In the game, you start by working as a driver for hire, doing jobs wherever they are available (and believe me when I say they are always available, and tons of jobs to choose from). Afterwards, you can save up to buy your first truck, or take out a loan to buy a truck of your own. The benefit to owning a truck is that you can be payed more for jobs. After doing this, you can continue to make more money, pay off your loan (if you took one), and buy more trucks. Note that you will need to get a garage or upgrade the garage you're given in the beginning if you want more than one truck. Then, with new trucks, you can hire drivers to do jobs for you, and make more money after this.
So, if you're looking for a great way to spend some time, try this out. Though the game may look boring, I can say from personal experience that this is a game worth checking out. Additionally, last time I checked there is a free Euro Truck Simulator Two demo version you can download off the internet (I believe it is on the Euro Truck Simulator website). You can try it out, and can experience about four hours of gameplay.

So when I first opened the game, I had never heard of the movies. I admit, I might have been living inside the barrel for a while, but I played the game 20 hours until I watched "Mad Max: Fury Road". And guess what? I definitely enjoyed it.
Mad Max is a game about a man who has lost everything, in the beginning his car, and then starts his hunt to get the car back only to meet Chumbucket, a hunchback who will build him a new car called "The Opus Magnum". So in a nutshell, Mad Max is a game about a man who looses his car, meets a hunchback that builds him a new car and now is searching for a V8 motor for the "Magnum Opus" in a desert wasteland.
As I said, the game itself is open-world, post-apocalyptic and on times challenging: not too hard, it's repeating a lot of tasks. There's no hard ending due to repeating tasks. Surely, it's not like some other games, but it's still great. It's filled with places to loot to with enemy camps and easter eggs which are easy to miss if you haven't watched the movies or played other games from this studio. I mean, there's a lot of references are straight to the movies, like eating the "Dinki Di" food to restore health. So I'd recommend watching the movie(s) and then play the game.
I currently play with a EVGA GTX 980 Superclocked (4GB) and I minor problems with the game. Some minor crashes in certain locations, but overall the FPS was solid 60. Definitely a huge plus. Even in the most intensive sandstorms the FPS stayed as a solid 60 with no drops at all. The game is amazingly good optimized, looks pretty, even runs pretty.
If you don't like to drive from one location to another or hates driving, the game isn't for you.
Otherwise, I truly recommend the game. Great game and it even has replay potential, 10/10.

So my original review I had it as "not recommended"--after playing the second and third episodes, I retract that review.
I reviewed and judged the entire game on the basis of just one episode. That was wrong of me to do so.
Alright, story-wise, Square Enix nailed it. I'm eager to wait for the fourth episode that will be released in early 2018 for Deluxe version users.
Now, I said that there are longer cutscenes in this sequel. I started to no longer mind it too much after episode one due to the story getting more interesting. The cut scenes told me crucial parts of the story in which I enjoyed to watch.
While the key element of Life is Strange: Before the Storm is missing such as the rewind of time, I believe this is still a great game, as its amazing story carries the weight of the game. I've always loved the graphics and visuals of this game since the original series. Square Enix wanted to do something different with this game visually.
Instead of having realistic graphics like what every other game tries to do, the developers went in a different approach for the LiS series and I applaud them for that.
I also have been lovin' (since the original Life is Strange) the choices you make and how deeply they affect the entire game. In literally NO OTHER game has choices that affect the future so deeply as much as this one. Take Mass Effect Andromeda for example. You can have choices of words, but it doesn't affect the future or have any affect at all.
With the choices you make in Life is Strange, you have the choice and how you end the game. Each choice can lead you to play a different experience than another person that also bought Life is Strange with a different ending and modified storyline.

REVIEW BEFORE THE EDIT (DEC 01 2017):
I've been a huge Life is Strange (LiS) fan since the original series; I've played every episode on the original Life is Strange series.
However, after buying and playing LiS: Before the Storm (Deluxe Edition), I'm disappointed. I didn't know what I was expecting, but this is not a game. It's a "interactive movie" at best. There is about 30 seconds of gameplay before you come across a 5-minute cutscene. The original Life is Strange game was not like that, it had a nice balance between cutscenes and gameplay.
I really wanted to give this a positive rating, but I honestly can't. I'm not giving this a negative-rating game because it's "bad" or anything; I'm giving this a negative rating because of its lack of balance between cutscenes and gameplay. It fails to keep the audience engaged.
Square Enix disappointed me deeply for this sequel.

Rogue Legacy is a great game and with the unending possibilities, there is an unending amount of playtime.

This game is very fun and original. At first glance, it might seem like a generic RPG, but it's completely different. Every time you play, it's going to be different, so you have to adapt and create a new strategy.

An unconventional Metroidvania/Rogue-Like, Rogue Legacy hits all the right notes.  The way characters are generated is a wonderful change of pace from the usual conventions used in perma-death games.  Increasing your stats and abilities are done through an also unconventional system, where you buy stat increases between deaths.  The weapons, items and armor have several great effects and interactions.
Anybody who  says Rogue Legacy is lacking in 'RPG conventions' is dead wrong.  They're looking for a single skill tree packed with nonsense, and tons of randomly generated equipment, most of which you sell to a vendor for coppers any way.  Instead you have to be creative in selecting enhancements and gear, making decisions that fit your needs or compensate for the... inadequacies that some Heroes will be born with.
Combat is fluid and fun, enemies are varied and dangerous.  Feature-rich, very re-playable (to a point), and well made; Rogue Legacy is a different take on the Rogue-Like genre that succeeds at almost everything it takes on.  One of my top five Rogue-Likes available on any platform.  And, unlike many independent forays in to these genres, the game does not feel incomplete or lacking in content.

Mad Max is the game you can play after watching Mad Max: Fury Road.  This game proved to be one hell of a ride (pun intended.) The game has great graphics and is very nicely optimized. The character and car models clearly have a lot of time dedicated to them, they are all fantastic. The menu for me was a bit difficult to adjust to. The melee combat can become a bit dismal after you have unlocked almost everything there is to unlock in the game, but that doesn’t just mean you can sit back and take a beating. The combat consists of both car and on foot combat, both are really well done. There are plenty of ways to take down enemies both in the car and on foot. The game seems to bring forth ideas from the Assassin’s Creed franchise pertaining to a vast quantity of collectables, instead of climbing towers you are raising yourself up in hot air balloons. The story isn’t really stellar at all, it’s quite mediocre.  There are plenty of side quests that you can partake in and they will reward you in some form or another, there may occasionally be sandstorms which bring out great scrap crates if you can stay alive long enough to collect the scrap. There are upgrades that are unlocked for the car, the Magnum Opus can be unlocked by lowering the threat level in certain areas centered around forts of the wastelands. Some things that lower the threat level in an area are liberating camps in the area, disarming mind fields, destroying convoys, and killing snipers. There are several projects that can be completed in the forts to add things on like refilling Max’s health and canine, refilling the car’s fuel and even collecting scrap while the player isn’t playing the game. Overall there are certainly aspects of the game that could be improved upon and that is why I would rate this game an 8/10, if a friend was thinking of buying it I would probably encourage them to do so but I wouldn’t say this is a must own.

One common gripe I have heard is that this game feels empty.  That it is just another open world sandbox game.  This is partially true.  The game is really fun, and keeps you engaged.  The problem is that it has a slow start.  It starts you off with baby steps to acclimate to it's world and mechanics.  And I fear most players got bored with the game before it starts firing on all cylinders (pun intended).  Once this game heats up, it is GRAND.  It is MAD.  MAD MAX!  This game is very Mad Max.  They nailed it.
GRAPHICS: Holy baby Jesus this game is -=BEAUTIFUL=-!  It is also highly optimized.  If you have a nice graphics card this is a showcase game.  The best looking desert vistas games I have seen.
AUDIO:  Dynamic.  Max's shotgun has tremendous oomph.  Max's voice actor is perfectly cast.  Chum's performance is very good and he gets to be quite lovable.  I just wish he didn't have an american accent.  Many of the baddies also sound american.
MUSIC: The music perfect for a Mad Max adventure.  When things are quiet, the haunting, desolate beauty of the desert wasteland is gently underscored.  When you find yourself chasing down a convoy, the music is fierce enough to make you shout, "What a lovely day!"
ON-FOOT GAMEPLAY:  Combat is very much like the Batman Arkham games.  There is only one button for strikes.  The enemies do not take turns attacking you.  There is also a parry button and dodge button.  Perfectly timed parrys will grant you devastating counters.  You can also use (and in some cases throw) weapons.  My favorite is the spear with an explosive head.  So wonderfully gory!  The game has a bit of platforming.  This is one of the game's clumsier areas.  You can run and jump, but when Max tries to negotiate his way up something higher than his shins things get derpy.  Climbing or pulling yourself up is not allowed except only in designated (and marked) areas.  Fortunately the game's weak platforming is not a large part of the game.
VEHICLE GAMEPLAY: This game has a sort of "vehicular Metroid-Vania" quality to it.  After various upgrades you will be able to reach new places.  Tubo boosting can thrust you up to a level that would have been impossible before.  Vehicle combat is where the game shines brightly.  Smashing vehicles into oblivion is very satisfying, seasoned with just the right amount of slow-motion.  Chumbucket's harpoon gun is great for ripping the doors off of enemy vehicles, which then exposes the drivers which you can also yoink out of their seats with a well-placed harpoon shot.
EXPLORATION: Exploration is simple... Maybe even a bit too simple.  Everything is marked.  When you get to a marked location it tells you how many scrap locations, insignias and other collectables remain.  Then you wander around the zone until you find them all (or decide not to).  As you get deeper into the game some items on your to-do list get more hidden and almost puzzle-like.  Collecting them all grants you upgrade chips.  I think if everything was not marked and itemized ahead of time it might have made the game a bit more Fallout-like and more fun.  Just my opinion.
+ GRAPHICS (Holy balls this game is beautiful!)
+ SOUND
+ COMBAT
- Platforming (Sparingly used fortunately)
- Exploration (Minor negative)
