1. Stop reading reviews, look at some screenshots and if you think you'd like to play an RPG that looks like
does, you will like
. It's a great game but discussing why it's great is a always going to involve spoilers to some extent. That is just the nature of the game. Not my fault.
2. The thing is
is all about playing w/ what you expect from the genre.
3. The artsyle here is lovely. It's retro but it's not mired in any one particular era. It looks like a bit-era RPG mostly but there are touches outside of that realm all over the place that lend a unique charm. Combat looks like some CGA PCRPG. In outdoor areas, there is often many layered parralax scrolling well beyond the capabilities of old consoles. One section pretty much looks like an old Flash game or something. These are the sort of little surprises
doles out over and over.
4. The music and sound design take a similar approach. Something about it feels classic but the sound palate used mixes chip-based synth sounds w/ more modern patches and samples. Sound effects are of the same stripe and I have a particular affinity for the vowel-y sounding staccato notes they use in lieu of voiced dialog.
5. Gameplay... Well, it's okay. You can walk around just fine and the menus are only a little annoying. Combat has some unique twists, which I may or may not discuss in an upcoming point. Stay tuned to find out!
6. Combat is the first place you get the notion there is something really unusual going on. Initial enemies grant no experience or gold and right away there are options to spare enemies rather than kill them either by beating them half to death and leaving them or performing various enemy dependent actions in the right order. Doing this costs you experience points which causes you to level up slower and really grants you no advantage at all.
7. You are given a reason why you might do this though. Very soon into the beginning of the game, it is made apparent that you are living in a world that is basically the point in the RPG timeline after the player has defeated the final boss and sealed away all monsters for eternity. The thing is, the monsters don't seem to be all bad. Many of them are quite cordial. The rest seem to either just misunderstand who you are or maybe just be in a tight spot themselves.
8. One fellow you run into early on is named Sans and I reckon he's one of the most likeable NPCs of all time in any game of any genre.
9. This is a serious game but it doesn't take itself too seriously.  Suffice to say, the dad jokes are strong w/ this one. This sense of humor is a maybe not-so-subtle nod to the dumb jokes which are a staple of old RPGs but
openly admits that these are cringeworthy. The character, Sans, I mentioned above even gets rim-shots for some of his efforts.
10. Storytelling is done through a lot of means. There is your standard gameplay and interactions w/ NPCs but then there is also lots of little plaques all over the place which, along w/ everything else, flesh out the world you're in and what its inhabitants have gone through.
11. Getting into the later portions of the game, the story feels less and less about your character and more like a final chapter about the game world itself.
12. If you've read this far despite my earlier spoiler warnings, I might as well tell you it's a good idea to play this game through once w/o looking at any sort of playthrough. Nothing will go wrong. And, yeah, if you liked playing through once, this gives you ample reasons to play through again. It really plays w/ the notion of when a game begins and when it ends and this is a primary element of its storytelling and gameplay.
13.

The mechanics of Rogue Legacy are simple. You have a sword to slash, magic spells to use, and the occasional class ability.  You travel through 4 areas of a pseudo-randomly generated castle fighting the many enemies and the occational mini and full bosses. Though the game may sound like a grind, and may even feel like it for the first few lives, you soon will become addicted to its rewarding and fun gameplay. The mechanics are greatly executed and the gameplay keeps interest over several playthroughs. Controls are spot on, but I would recommend using a gamepad if you have one. One more thing, if the normal game is not enough of a challenge for you, the remix bosses will make you cry.

Rogue Legacy is a fun, light-hearted take on the rogue-like RPG genre. The game's simplistic gameplay, humorous characters and flexible upgrade system make it a very enjoyable experience.
The gameplay is nearly perfect, in my opinion. It's a very simple game, using just directional buttons and three other buttons: jump, attack, and cast spell. After buying a few upgrades, you can unlock a couple of other buttons, but those three are the main ones you'll be using. This makes the game very easy to learn, since there isn't a huge complex control scheme to figure out, but it's very difficult to master.
At the beginning of the game, you're introduced to an unnamed rogue. That rogue is the ancestor of all the characters you will play as in the future, which will likely be quite a large number. Every time you die, you are taken back to the title screen and then you begin the quest anew with a rogue descended from the previous character. You get to choose one of three descendants for each restart, and the variety comes from a range of traits each character may have. These range from silly to serious, and all affect gameplay in various ways. For example, if your character has ADHD, you'll move 30% faster, or if your character has vertigo, the entire game will be flipped upside-down. Each character also comes from a particular class, which affects your base stats. A knight is the standard character, whereas a barbarian has 150% HP and 50% MP. These combinations make each character unique, although by choosing which one you prefer, you can try to develop your playstyle in one category. It all sound very complicated, but it's much easier in practice since it tells you right there what each trait or class does.
There's also an upgrade system that allows you to add rooms to your manor, which will let you purchase upgrades from NPCs, as well as upgrade your base stats like HP and attack. All of this costs gold, which is earned in-game as you fight your way through the dungeon. Unfortunately, you lose all your unused gold when you enter the dungeon, so be sure to use as much of it as possible before progressing.
I really enjoy this game. The platforming and action is top-notch, and the enemies are well-balanced to present a challenge while not being impossibly strong. Early in the game, you'll die a lot, and I really mean A WHOLE LOT, but as you upgrade your manor and buy new armor and weapons and spells, you'll find yourself getting further and further in the dungeon. This is one game where I find myself saying "just one more run!" ten times in a row as I try to get better upgrades for my characters.
Overall, I think Rogue Legacy is a must-play for any fans of the 2D RPG genre. The platforming is great, the randomly generated levels are fun and challenging, and the method of playing as your previous characters' descendant adds a novelty to the game that doesn't wear off quickly thanks to the unique traits and the manor upgrades. If you like 2D side-scrollers, do yourself a favor and try this one out.

Undertale is amazing; let's just get that out of the way. Unfortunately, it's also the kind of game that works best when you go into it with no prior knowledge, and it's also very difficult to pin down genre-wise (though my best attempt would be a bullet hell RPG), so it's very hard to explain exactly
it's good. But I'll give it my best shot.
: Undertale is primarily a story-driven game, and every aspect of the story is polished to perfection. All the people you meet in the game, from plot-important characters to random enemy spawns, are beautifully chracterised, with complex and believable personalities. The overall plot of the game is solid. World-building is done efficiently and effectively through your various interactions. And the meta-narrative is actually meaningful and thought-provoking, rather than the more common "oh look I'm breaking the fourth wall isn't that smart of me" kind of thing you see in other games. And yet, nothing ever feels pretentious, and the depth and heart of the story are balanced equally by genuinely funny humour.
: Rather surprisingly for such a story-heavy game, the actual gameplay mechanics are actually solid and can stand up on their own. Combat works like a mix between turn-based RPG and bullet hell, where you select commands to interact with the enemy and dodge their incoming bullet hell attacks. Difficulty increases organically as multiple enemies fire their unique bullet spread patterns simultaneously.
: This game pushes chiptune to its absolute limit. The music in this game is amazing, and it's not just that the developer crammed a bunch of good songs into the game. The songs are not just good on their own, but work brilliantly together to elevate every moment of the game.
Of course, no game is perfect, and Undertale is no exception. The graphics are overall serviceable for the purposes of the game, but it's not exactly pushing the boundaries of visuals. And of course, even counting the multiple playthroughs needed to get the full plot, the game is still heartbreakingly short, though that perhaps points to the density of good content in this game.
In conclusion, Undertale is a good game, and I'd even go so far as to say that it is a landmark of gaming culture. Years down the road, gamers will talk about Undertale the same way they talk about Super Mario or Half-Life 2 today. When that happens, don't be the one who never bothered trying it out because of the bad graphics or annoying fans.

I played theHunter years ago and absolutely despised it. You can read my review of that game - the funny poem I wrote about it. So when I heard about theHunter: Call of the Wild, I was hesitant. I waited months and months before actually wanting to show interest in it, because the last installment was just more miss than hit for me. I eventually watched a few videos on YouTube, and started to gain a lot of interest for the game. With only just over 5 hours of gametime put into it, there is so much I love about this game. So read further, if you please.
in theHunter: CotW, you're exactly as the title says; a hunter, in the wild. The base game has two huge hunting reserves for you to choose from: Hirschfelden, a European reserve; and Layton Lake District, a reserve that takes place in the Pacific Northwest. There's a third hunting reserve via DLC, Medved-Taiga, which takes place in Siberia. The two reserves you start out with in the base game are gigantic, and it can seem a bit daunting at first when you realize that you're on foot and there's so much terrain to traverse. That's one of the amazing things I love about this game, the sheer scale of things. And you're probably thinking, well the reserves are huge but that just means animals are far, few, and between.
. You will encounter animals the very moment you jump into the game, and as the tutorial begins, you will most likely have spotted your first target.
There are some free DLC for the game, which add backpacks, more outfits, a bow, and a hunting range in Hirschfelden; then there are paid DLC that will unlock more blinds and tents, and the ability to use an ATV to get around. The best part of all, these paid DLC are fairly cheap: ATV DLC for example is $3.99 at the time of this review, and the Medved-Taiga DLC is $7.99. All of these are well worth grabbing, or you could even wait for a sale to see if the price lowers. Personally, I haven't grabbed any of the paid ones, including the ATV DLC, but plan on doing so in the near future.
As you venture through each reserve, missions will pop up for you to tackle if you wish to do so. I have finished a few here and there, as they do tend to give you some decent XP and cash, which helps you unlock better gear later on. Don't let the missions side track you from the game, though, as in my experience I have found that havng a side mission up while hunting in an area near the mission itself can lead to you bagging a kill that gives you a lot of cash and XP depending on the tropthy value of the animal you bagged.
Then there's multiplayer. You can have up to 8 people in a session, and there's something about having a few buddies or complete strangers join up and go out hunting. This is especially crucial on kills that it may take a few set of eyes to spot, and a few guns to take down - like Bison. Seriously, those things will charge at you after the first shot.
So now that you've read a good chunk about the game, I will dive right into what I love and wish were different in the game.
I know it's hard for me to come up with something negative about the game after going on about how much I love it, but there are a few things that do bug me. Even though I love the walking, and the huge map, so far you can only fast travel to an outpost you have unlocked. And those things are so spread out across the reserve, that if you are out and about, away from an outpost, then exit the game...you start off at the last outpost you were at, rather than where you exited. While this doesn't take away from the overall fun factor, I wish they'd implement the ability to fast travel to lookouts, too. Especially since I haven't purchased the ATV DLC, walking for an hour or so in real-time, only to exit to take a break and have to come back to the last outpost I was at, which is miles upon miles away from where I left off can be a bit frustrating. Really, that's all I can think of. It would be nice if they added fishing to the game, since there are an abundance of lakes in the game, but that is just a wish and not even a con.

I had a hard time deciding wether to give this a thumbs up or thumbs down. It's a 6.5/10 game. The biggest issue with Mad Max is that it is AWFULLY repetetive. I've spent 30 hours playing this but most of the time the activities felt like a chore. The whole gameplay looks like this:
1. Open map and set waypoint on a stronghold icon to liberate.
2. Kill all the bad guys at stronghold and blow up all fuel tanks.
3. Repeat step 1 and 2 several times until you lower the threat level of the area by 1.
4. Open map and set waypoint on a 'Sniper' icon.
5. Ride around the area from one sniper to another, killing them one by one.
6. Repeat steps 4 and 5 until you lower the threat level by 1.
...and so on and so forth. You basically ride around the map doing chores to lower thrat levels. And you need to lower threat levels to upgrade your car. It is boring. Don't get me wrong, the is fun but for like 10 hours, not more. After that, the fun is gone and repetetivness takes over. There is also not much of a story here to keep you interested to get over all of those rinse-and-repeat tasks.
With all that being said, the game is worth buying if you get it cheaply and don't expect it to be anything grand. Shadow of Mordor is very similar in concept but is a better game overall, if you have not played it, I recommend it over Mad Max. If you have Played Shaodw of Mordor, Mad Max will feel familiar but its just more boring, especially hand-to-hand combat is far worse.

Euro Truck Simulator 2, bring trucking of the real world to your home. A great game for you to play on your own (if the AI dont knock you off the road). Or even better playing with your friends in the multiplayer Mod.

Need to choose between American or Euro Truck Simulator? Here's my guide:
- ATC has masculin trucks, ETS2 does not - only the Scania burble gets the idea
- ATC has a glacial DLC development pace
- ATC has a very slow economic progression due to its new map scaling
- ETS2 has more and better gameplay; about all changed elements in ATC are less fun
- ETS2 has more variation: right and left wheel drive, ferries, train crossing, different toll gates, ...
- ETS2 has the awesome Pro Mod which outshines even the best DLCs (Scandinavia and France) and adds insanely stunning routes such as Iceland and Estonia while replacing a lot of monotenous routes in central Europe.
- Both have a ridiculous damage model and stuff like industructible boom gates and invisible walls.
- In both, you don't encounter trucks from your company on the road.. :-/
Both are a I'll-do-one-more-freigth low intensity and very decent driving sim plus a lightweight economic sim; ETS2 is strangely addictive. Popularity's a scary thing.
I'm a big fan of this game.  Who isn't?  My thoughts here aren't really what you're here for, and I know this is because this is Undertale and its praises have been sung to the high heavens.  There's no real reason for me to go on about how I loved that the overall themes of the game are tightly woven into both the game's gameplay and story in ways that most games wouldn't even dream of.  There's no reason for me to go about how I loved the characters and how fantastic the music was.  There's no reason for me to go over any of this because all of the praise is already out there and I don't have all that much to contribute on that front.  Except for one thing.
Let's talk about choice.  See, choice, as far as extrinsic rewards are concerned, is fairly straightforward.  You're given options and, for the most part, you have some understanding of exactly what it is you're getting.  Choice as far as intrinsic rewards, though, is largely affected by how well you know the outcome.  If you know what the outcome of your choice will be, generally it will be the same as going through paces.  While the outcome may still have an effect on you based on how it's executed, it's pretty rare that it will have the same effect had you not known about the outcome nor the execution at all.  And in the case of Undertale, to most of the fanbase, the choice was not so much about "what would I do" so much as "when would I do what".
I think it's obvious enough that there's a certain opinion of the game's fanbase that either turns people off from the game entirely or does just the opposite, but regardless of what effect it has the problem persists that for those other than early adopters (basically those who played it within a few months of release), the game didn't really feature all that much choice at all.  I was lucky enough that the only thing that was really presented to me was
, though without context.  So for me, it made sense that I would play the game as I wanted and make choices because the game always seemed to react to the things I did.  And it was for that reason that I had so much fun.  Nothing in the game existed for me until I experienced it, and it was upon that experience that, that discovery, that I fell in love with the game.  After all, it was pretty clear from just the first few minutes of the game that Toby didn't want people knowing exactly what the game would be until they got their hands on it themselves (and he later openly said this).
And then the game blew up.  Characters in the game appeared everywhere in the forms of figures, animations, cosplays, and art; lines and scenarios from the games became viral memes that were uttered in every corner of the internet; the praise sung to the game was eerily loud.  That this little game with so little advertisement and a pretty small following became so large is mindboggling, and fantastic, since it's one of the few times where I can say that subverted gameplay mechanics or ideas are imployed in a game without feeling particularly biting or half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  It deserved what it got, but this also created a divide.
The early adopters, we got to experience this new journey full of surprises.  People playing around and after the date that this review is going up probably will, too, as the hype has gone down considerably.  But in the time between, what Undertale was to prospective buyers was very clear.  They knew how they were going to play, knew who characters were, knew what was going to happen in a lot of cases- and it's hard to blame them considering they didn't really...have a choice.
That's not funny.
The reason that I even mention all of this in a review is because I feel that that divide definitely comes with a difference in enjoyment.  Because while I don't think every experience is necessarily better going when you go in knowing nothing, Undertale was built on the idea of surprise and discovery.  Experiencing these things for the first time, and having first-hand experienced the difference between a player who bought into the hype and got the game versus one who went in knowing mostly nothing...well, that's the difference between a suggestion to wait until you can go in fresh and a recommendation.
Yes, I do recommend Undertale if you just don't really know what it is or just happen to know about its reputation and not much else, because that's how I feel it will be best experienced.  But if you were subjected to the the hype machine known as 2016, I'd give it a little while, as otherwise those who are skeptical will merely be falling into a self-fulfilling prophecy and others might find themselves wondering what the hype was about to begin with.

An absolutely fantastic Rogue-Lite game that takes elements of Castlevania and Monster World with a small blend of RPG elements to create a rather fun indie experience that is absolutely worth a look at. The game will take about 9-12 hours to complete for most core gamers, but more casual gamers will probably take longer than this (though there are special items to help reduce difficulty if you're struggling) and the difficulty, while can suddenly spike into crazy hard territory, rarely feels unfair. The story is pretty standard fantasy fare and I saw the plot twist coming a mile away (I remember calling BS on the "cure" the castle is said to contain, which is mentioned in the first Diary entry, the game's way of telling the story) but it was still pretty fun to watch it unfold and the execution made for a pretty fun finale.
Imagine playing a Metroidvania game (not a fan of the term but it's commonplace these days so whatever) where the goal is to simply find four bosses and kill them in order to open up one last door to the final boss. Sounds simple right? Well, there's an army of knights, skeletons, zombies and other monsters that are going to make your job harder, plus plenty of traps that will spell the end for any hero who isn't agile enough to outwit them. Now add on another layer to the game, when you die, that character is dead, for good. Every time you die you get to select from one of 3 new heroes (you can reroll them once a run later on) of various classes, many more can also be unlocked and upgraded and they all have different playstyles that can cater to any player's playstyle and what the game might favour at the time. After selecting your hero, the castle doesn't remain the same, introducing the Rogue-Lite element. Every time you enter (unless you ask a special NPC, which means you make less money) the castle will rebuild itself differently, though some basic rules DO apply, so it's easy to get to an area you want to when needs be. Another feature that makes this game fantastic is each hero has up to 2 different traits as well as a class. Some are positive, such as not setting off spike traps and being able to see every enemy on the map, some are negative, such as not being able to knock back enemies and having to play with the screen flipped UPSIDE DOWN, and some are neutral with effects that may or may not help or hinder you, such as being colour blind and farting when you jump. This adds and extra layer of strategy to your choices, a Paladin who can throw a knife backwards vs a Paladin who is a Dwarf could make a huge difference to how you play and how far you may get on your run.
Controls are some of the tightest I've ever seen in a game EVER. The game's very responsive and although your basic attack has a small delay before it strikes, it's very easy to get used to and being able to use the game's mechanic of not turning while swinging your sword can be used effectively to kite enemies once you're good enough. Graphics are also great, the pixel artstyle calls back to the SNES and Mega Drive days as well as some Playstation titles, and the game doesn't feel like it's screaming "LOOK AT ME I'M RETRO GUYS" overall, looks very colourful which helps you to see things, but it's also easy on the eyes. The soundtrack is also incredible (special mentions go to the main theme tune and the 3rd Boss Battle theme) managing to mix 8-bit chiptune with a variety of musical styles, but again, the soundtrack doesn't feel like it's screaming "LOOK AT ME I'M RETRO GUYS"
After you've beaten it there's also a New Game + mode which allows you to carry on your legacy (starting with the hero who beat the final boss) but the castle becomes MUCH harder, so if you think it's a bit "too easy" then wait until that comes around and you'll be sure to have a good challenge. Also the challenge bosses should test the wits and skills of any gamer. I haven't even managed to beat one yet but I found all but one boss fairly straightforward on the first run once you knew what to do. Though one problem is some gamers may tire of how repetitive the game can feel at times, as even though the levels are randomized the enemy variety isn't huge and the castle's zones are always positioned in the same areas (well, without one trait that also prevents the player from reading almost any of the game's text)
Pros
Fantastic Controls
Beautiful artstyle and soundtrack
Procedurally generated level to play in
Very challenging, especially on new game + and onwards
Lots of fun traits to mess around with
A good variety of classes to fit any player's style
Cons
Enemy variety feels lacking at times
A predictable story, but the plot twist was pretty well executed
Final Verdict - A fantastic Rogue-Lite Hack and Slash game that will bring plenty of hours of entertainment, if you're looking for something new to try give it a go. If it's on sale or in a bundle and you're curious I'd say just go for it, you won't be sorry

Having played this game for a while (about one day of time as I write this), I can tell you this is a game that is most definetely worth getting. I bought this game and the "Going East" expansion for $7 during the Steam Summer Sale, but I would still pay the twenty or so dollars for this game. The simulation is extremely realistic, and there a several features that make this simulator realistic and similar to real world driving.
In the game, you start by working as a driver for hire, doing jobs wherever they are available (and believe me when I say they are always available, and tons of jobs to choose from). Afterwards, you can save up to buy your first truck, or take out a loan to buy a truck of your own. The benefit to owning a truck is that you can be payed more for jobs. After doing this, you can continue to make more money, pay off your loan (if you took one), and buy more trucks. Note that you will need to get a garage or upgrade the garage you're given in the beginning if you want more than one truck. Then, with new trucks, you can hire drivers to do jobs for you, and make more money after this.
So, if you're looking for a great way to spend some time, try this out. Though the game may look boring, I can say from personal experience that this is a game worth checking out. Additionally, last time I checked there is a free Euro Truck Simulator Two demo version you can download off the internet (I believe it is on the Euro Truck Simulator website). You can try it out, and can experience about four hours of gameplay.

The game feels old. The graphics haven't matured at all in this series. Things look very similar to modern warfare 2 (partly because this is running on a modified version of COD4's engine) and end up being distracting. The lens flares and neon accents look nice, but the low polygon models and low res textures make it all too apparent that you're playing a game.
Multiplayer feels less sophisticated than previous titles in the series. This game seems to focus further on the one man army approach to multiplayer. If you want a game with small levels and small teams where you kill quickly, die quickly, and operate alone, this is for you.
The single player is pretty bad too. Not as bad as some others, but it's pretty much a repeat of established cliches. The bad guy wants to get captured as part of his plan(skyfall, the avengers, etc), the boss is beaten while in slow motion (COD mw1, mw2, etc?, MOH), and the entire story is told through the flash backs of some old dude (black ops1). The originality of the series is completely gone.

An absolutely fantastic Rogue-Lite game that takes elements of Castlevania and Monster World with a small blend of RPG elements to create a rather fun indie experience that is absolutely worth a look at. The game will take about 9-12 hours to complete for most core gamers, but more casual gamers will probably take longer than this (though there are special items to help reduce difficulty if you're struggling) and the difficulty, while can suddenly spike into crazy hard territory, rarely feels unfair. The story is pretty standard fantasy fare and I saw the plot twist coming a mile away (I remember calling BS on the "cure" the castle is said to contain, which is mentioned in the first Diary entry, the game's way of telling the story) but it was still pretty fun to watch it unfold and the execution made for a pretty fun finale.
Imagine playing a Metroidvania game (not a fan of the term but it's commonplace these days so whatever) where the goal is to simply find four bosses and kill them in order to open up one last door to the final boss. Sounds simple right? Well, there's an army of knights, skeletons, zombies and other monsters that are going to make your job harder, plus plenty of traps that will spell the end for any hero who isn't agile enough to outwit them. Now add on another layer to the game, when you die, that character is dead, for good. Every time you die you get to select from one of 3 new heroes (you can reroll them once a run later on) of various classes, many more can also be unlocked and upgraded and they all have different playstyles that can cater to any player's playstyle and what the game might favour at the time. After selecting your hero, the castle doesn't remain the same, introducing the Rogue-Lite element. Every time you enter (unless you ask a special NPC, which means you make less money) the castle will rebuild itself differently, though some basic rules DO apply, so it's easy to get to an area you want to when needs be. Another feature that makes this game fantastic is each hero has up to 2 different traits as well as a class. Some are positive, such as not setting off spike traps and being able to see every enemy on the map, some are negative, such as not being able to knock back enemies and having to play with the screen flipped UPSIDE DOWN, and some are neutral with effects that may or may not help or hinder you, such as being colour blind and farting when you jump. This adds and extra layer of strategy to your choices, a Paladin who can throw a knife backwards vs a Paladin who is a Dwarf could make a huge difference to how you play and how far you may get on your run.
Controls are some of the tightest I've ever seen in a game EVER. The game's very responsive and although your basic attack has a small delay before it strikes, it's very easy to get used to and being able to use the game's mechanic of not turning while swinging your sword can be used effectively to kite enemies once you're good enough. Graphics are also great, the pixel artstyle calls back to the SNES and Mega Drive days as well as some Playstation titles, and the game doesn't feel like it's screaming "LOOK AT ME I'M RETRO GUYS" overall, looks very colourful which helps you to see things, but it's also easy on the eyes. The soundtrack is also incredible (special mentions go to the main theme tune and the 3rd Boss Battle theme) managing to mix 8-bit chiptune with a variety of musical styles, but again, the soundtrack doesn't feel like it's screaming "LOOK AT ME I'M RETRO GUYS"
After you've beaten it there's also a New Game + mode which allows you to carry on your legacy (starting with the hero who beat the final boss) but the castle becomes MUCH harder, so if you think it's a bit "too easy" then wait until that comes around and you'll be sure to have a good challenge. Also the challenge bosses should test the wits and skills of any gamer. I haven't even managed to beat one yet but I found all but one boss fairly straightforward on the first run once you knew what to do. Though one problem is some gamers may tire of how repetitive the game can feel at times, as even though the levels are randomized the enemy variety isn't huge and the castle's zones are always positioned in the same areas (well, without one trait that also prevents the player from reading almost any of the game's text)
Pros
Fantastic Controls
Beautiful artstyle and soundtrack
Procedurally generated level to play in
Very challenging, especially on new game + and onwards
Lots of fun traits to mess around with
A good variety of classes to fit any player's style
Cons
Enemy variety feels lacking at times
A predictable story, but the plot twist was pretty well executed
Final Verdict - A fantastic Rogue-Lite Hack and Slash game that will bring plenty of hours of entertainment, if you're looking for something new to try give it a go. If it's on sale or in a bundle and you're curious I'd say just go for it, you won't be sorry

(Note: I have between 20-30 hours played on the Playstation version of this game.  I got it on Steam in a bundle and I replayed it for a few hours just to make sure I my opinion hadn't changed.)
I love platformers, especially retro-inspired ones or ones with roglue-like elements.  Most of my Steam library is made up of these types of games.  They are my favorite genre.  This game seems really great when you first start, it appears that there is so much to unlock and so much to explore, but the reality is that it never begins to fill one tenth of the potential it appears to have at the start of the game.  Despite a couple novel ideas, the game quickly reveals itself to be a mediocre Metroidvania clone.
This game tries but fails to create a memorable new retro platformer.  The controls are okay, though they don't feel as tight they should.  Random level design can be great, just look at Spelunky, but the random designs in Rogue Legacy too often result in just plain bad layouts, platform and enemy layouts that seem unfair and are impossible to traverse without being hit, regardless of player skill.  The other big problem with this game is that leveling up your character seems to have very little effect on his effectiveness in the dungeon.  Even after 20+ hours, it's still very easy to die without progressing far at all.  On top of this, the game punishes you for dying by making all your skills most expensive to purchase every time you enter the dungeon, whether your trip is successful or not.  You grind and grind but your hard work never seems to pay off and this ultimately leads to a general feeling disappointment when you realize how shallow the game really is.
So what do you get when you put it all together?  A platformer with bad level design, lots of really annoying enemies, and a character that's continuously weak and prone to dying.  This game is hard for all the wrong reasons and none of the right ones.  If you want some great Metroidvania action, skip this game and pick up Castle in the Darkness, it's less than half the price and more than ten times the game.

Having played this game for a while (about one day of time as I write this), I can tell you this is a game that is most definetely worth getting. I bought this game and the "Going East" expansion for $7 during the Steam Summer Sale, but I would still pay the twenty or so dollars for this game. The simulation is extremely realistic, and there a several features that make this simulator realistic and similar to real world driving.
In the game, you start by working as a driver for hire, doing jobs wherever they are available (and believe me when I say they are always available, and tons of jobs to choose from). Afterwards, you can save up to buy your first truck, or take out a loan to buy a truck of your own. The benefit to owning a truck is that you can be payed more for jobs. After doing this, you can continue to make more money, pay off your loan (if you took one), and buy more trucks. Note that you will need to get a garage or upgrade the garage you're given in the beginning if you want more than one truck. Then, with new trucks, you can hire drivers to do jobs for you, and make more money after this.
So, if you're looking for a great way to spend some time, try this out. Though the game may look boring, I can say from personal experience that this is a game worth checking out. Additionally, last time I checked there is a free Euro Truck Simulator Two demo version you can download off the internet (I believe it is on the Euro Truck Simulator website). You can try it out, and can experience about four hours of gameplay.

I didn't know computer games could be impactful to the point of life changing until I started playing the LIS series and the prequel is no different. I'm 25 and weep like I'm 16 again when I play. these games haunt me in the most overwhelmingly beautiful way.

What I personally like about this game:
- The basic and obvious fact that it is a "Life is Strange" game that brings you back to Arcadia Bay under Chloe's perspective, etc. I personally adored Chloe in LiS, so when I learned that Before the Storm was going to be based on her story with Rachel, I geeked out.
- Selecting your choices using WASD instead of drag and click.
I just think it's more practical and easier.
- The soundtrack. Holy crap, the soundtrack.
Daughter composed pieces for this game that are beyond wicked (or hella) amazing; caputring scenes with music that can be so haunting and beautiful at the same time. Of course, a select few peices by other artists were brought into the mix, and I'm happy that they stuck with mainly indie groups.
- Achievement style.
I'm kinda digging the graffiti just as I did with the polaroids! I'd never say no to tagging David's tools as "Box of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥"
What I'm personally not a fan of:
- Can't replay single episodes like in LiS.
You can play specific scenes under collector's mode, but it won't effect your game if you accidently selected the wrong choice in mind and didn't want to play out the rest of the game with it on your conscience, or if you're a derp like me and forgot to grab the dang beanie from the glove compartment in Ep. 2 in order to unlock an outfit that you restarted the game just to achieve and only realize it when you're in the following scene/dream sequence, (I'm not bitter or anything~). You have to start at the VERY beginning of the game. We're talking Firewalk concert at the mill, beginning.
I did it anyway, shakah brah.
- Only 3 episodes. With a topic such as Rachel, who was one of the prime mysteries that drove LiS, you would think that it may need a tad more content than just 3 episodes to learn why she became so important to Chloe's life. I'm aware that the main idea of "leaving Arcadia Bay" was already brought up, then there was the obvious Tempest scene, the kiss, and that there is a 2 year gap for anything else to happen.. But dang! We just want a little more! Maybe I shouldn't judge before Ep. 3 comes out, because who knows if it'll have a little more umph to it so we can all feel like there is a conclusion that we can cope with!
- Voice acting for Chloe: I'm not saying it was terrible and that I had a complete and absolute negative experience with it, nor am I outraged that they didn't use the same actress from LiS. I think the voice choice was great for Chloe under the circumstances. But there are some moments when the voice acting just wasn't convincing, and sometimes sounded rather awkward.
Overall, I'm really enjoying this game and I'll be sad when it ends!

An unbalanced game with dialogue that Friedberg and Seltzer would admire. The port is significantly better than the first game's, which is to say it works decently well although I still have about 10 crash-to-desktops per character to this day, and I haven't even beaten the game. On that topic, Gearbox rewards anyone who was foolish enough to buy the first game with exclusive content; on THAT topic, there's over $150 of DLC for this game and I assure you that it is not 2.5 times the content of the base game.
Borderlands 2's story picks up where the first Borderlands left off. Actually, I just wish I could say this; there was really diddly squat for a story in the first one and this is practically a reboot. The vast majority of the story is told through people trying to do Archer voices over your intercom like System Shock, but two decades later. The dialogue, despite coming several years after BL1's redesign from a more seriously-toned shooter a la RAGE, still reflects some of the most tasteless and puerile humor you could possibly conceive of in a video game. In some cases gross-out humor is attempted, but it falls short of Oddworld or a Leisure Suit Larry game. In some cases Sandleresque shouting is evoked, but that also doesn't work because pretty much everyone in the game shouts. Throughout the game, the main antagonist whom every 12-year-old fan of BL loves, Handsome Jack, calls you up and makes statements that are less than passive-aggressive but are intended to be - what? Comedic? Conversational? Despite never receiving any apparent response, Jack continues to spout dialogue written by your slightly unsavory middle school friend throughout the entire game.
At one point, I set dialogue volume to 0 and turned subtitles off and the game became almost silent, even in combat. It also became much less annoying.
Of course, this is not surprising given the attitude of xtreme individual Randy Pitchford who is basically the John Romero of the 21st century, but now people don't know that there are better games than Daikatana.

It's just not fun, or funny, or worth it. I would recommend that Gearbox stick to expansion packs and ports, but making kids' games is probably better business than making Halo ports without co-op or completing projects that everyone knows will be terrible, like DNF.

Story: There is a break point in the game, where Max stop to be just an observer and really became a main character of the game. Of course it is because of someone else and you can even feel a glimpse of hope for some time, but this is Mad Max and of course everything turn to♥♥♥♥♥♥

Last one thing I´d like to say. This game never crash on me. 60 hours of play and no CTD! This is one of the best port of console game to PC. Please, do more conversions like this. I thank you for this a lot.

Spec Ops: The Line is undeniably and enjoyable game. But it is not without its problems. There's a few bits that just kinda don't work, some seem to be made for some sort of tension, or maybe to kind of give some hint of insanity to the whole thing. But really, whenever you walk into a room and you pretty much literally can't see because the screen is flashing to "add tension," there's a problem. Luckily, that less than five minute sequence did not ruin the game for me. The game was still enjoyable but there was possibly a lack of immersion for that scene, and at the very very least, it annoys you. But one horrible scene does not ruin an excellent game.
The end kind of has an M. Night Shamalayan feel to it if that doesn't spoil it too much for you. It's kinda silly, but it really is quite a good ending anyways.
The gameplay is pretty standard third-person-shooter fare, it isn't bad, perfectly functional, and I've certainly played third-person-shooters that didn't have the amazing story and had worse shooting. There's a bit of a squad-command function that you can use but don't think that your squad will really be able to do way too much. They help in a pinch but there's no doubt you're carrying them both the whole way.
Overall, many of the things I've said have a kind of negative sounding feel. But really I have quite a positive opinion of this game. I think it really exemplifies [POSSIBLE SPOILER] the choice and responsibility of the player of a game. Something that I don't think I'll really forget, the way the game presents that final moral is a real mind♥♥♥♥.
So, pick up this game if you enjoy third-person-shooter mechanics and particularly if you enjoy a very nice story, no matter your opinion on third-person-shooters at that point.

I just finished a lenghty Spec Ops achievement marathon. Played this game a lot in my freetime and now I finally can put it to rest. While I don't want to consider myself an achievement ♥♥♥♥♥, I like to pay games I really enjoy a tribute by completing them 100%.
Now, this introduction perfectly fits (more or less) into the message of the game. Are violent games really just games, you play and get an achievement for your 50th headshot? Is it okay to sit back and enjoy war, while you are the hero, kicking the♥♥♥♥♥of all the terrorist scum that threatens to destroy the world? I can't really compare Spec Ops: The Line to Battlefield, Call of Duty setting-wise or Gears of War and Mass Effect gameplay-wise, as I've never played them. But what I can say is, that, in my humble opinion, Spec Ops: The Line is a masterpiece. Not without its flaws, but a masterpiece nonetheless.
Gameplaywise, you get the typical brown modern war 3rd person shooter thingy. What do you expect? You play a badass dude to murder tons of evil dudes. Simple as that. But storywise, you are encountered by some moral questions, you might not have asked you yet. And suddenly, all the dull gameplay makes sense in a more complex way.
I don't want to spoil too much here, so I'll keep it short: If you are expecting a breakthrough in modern warfare gameplay and gunfights, this game is nothing for you. If you are interested in a good and gripping story, with one ore the other twist and an underlying message, you must play this game, even if you don't care about war shooters, like me. Highly recommended!

About 4 hours into this game I was really starting to get frustrated to be honest. I just felt as though I was getting pretty much nowhere. However every time I quit out thinking "To hell with this, too hard" I found myself, within hours, wanting to jump back on. There's something about pitch perfect controls in a 2D platformer that will do that to you.
Eventually I started getting further and further into the game, little by little, whilst meanwhile powering up at every available opportunity. I would reach a point where I had just about gotten to grips with an area before hitting up the boss or the next area and immediately getting ruined. But each time I'd jump right back in and carry on regardless. The difficulty curve really is sublime once you start powering up effectively.
Jump forward over 50 hours, I've reached NG+ 5, unlocked and maxed out every available power up, rune and blueprint, powered through every remix boss battle and grabbed every single achievement on the board. From someone who actually hunts yearly in South Texas (since I was 6 now 28) this game is amazing.  The visuals, the gameplay depth and the expansive environments all make for a experience you can easily get lost into.
If your looking for a chill game to get your hunting fix. Or want to experience a close as possible hunting trip for the first time this game is for you.
The rest of this is just my opinion on some complaints I’ve read and extras.
For those who have never hunted or rage when that headshot didn’t kill that deer I have a very important tip for you (!!This is not a FPS it is a HUNTING simulator!!)
Shot placement is VERY important.
And just like in real life a bullet entering your head in general doesn’t mean insta death it HAS to enter or splinter bone or bullet fragments into the brain, brain cord or hit the spine at the base for that. In real life hydrostatic shock could kill you as well so there is some feasible thought there. But that’s not so applicable here for reliability purposes.
For reference a deer, rabbit and squirrels brains are located to the rear of the skull usually in between the ears, the front elongated part of a deers head is for its nasal cavity and jaw structure.
In reality you should always be aiming for that broadside lung or frontal heart shot. I’ve never met a serious hunter in Texas who shoots deer in the head, not only is it unsportsmanlike but the game warden would have some choice words for you when inspecting your tagged heads.
But seeing as this is a game we are free to shoot whatever however we want I just wanted to point that out. If you want that headshot you need to calculate depending on his angle to you where his brain actually is within his head. Or aim in the VERY center of his neck for that spine.
For Boars I’d aim for the head or like in real life right behind the ear to liquify that brain pan tho.
Also please note your caliber and bullet penetration make a difference. If you shoot a bear with a 357 soft point EVEN in the head YOUR GONNA HAVE A BAD TIME lol

Undertale is a game about a child who fell down a mountian and comes across an underground civilization.
I like this game because it has a unique story to it, and alot of details here and there.
The game uses alot of great personalities for each character, too.
For an example, Undyne is a fish that has abs and is in love with a Lizard, Alphys.
Mettaton is a entertainment robot that the royal scientist made for the underground.
Sans is a magical skeleton that can summon bones with a magic blue glowing eye.
Those 3 examples sure are very odd, arent they?
There are 3 ways to play this game, too.
You can go pacafist, and decide to spare and care for each monster you encounter.
You could go genocide, and kill literally every single monster in the entire underground.
Or, you could do a mix of both runs, and go neutral and kill some and spare some.
This isnt a game about graphics, and I hate when people give this a thumbs down just because of that.
As I said, the game has a long and interesting, juicy story, that actually can be sad at some points.
((Please notice that the boss monsters in this game on the genocide route are stronger because they think you played the pacafist route before))

I loved the first game, and was pretty damn hyped when Before The Storm was announced. I didn't even realize that I wanted to know what'd happened to Rachel until Chloe got to know her better.
And while I do love the game, so far I haven't enjoyed it as much as the first one. Maybe because I just really liked Max's innocence.
At the time of writing I've finished the 2nd episode, and thus played over half the game. Yet, I feel like the story isn't unfolding as much as in the first game. Yes, you find out some small things, but in my opinion they don't contribute that much to the story. Of course that's partially because of this game only having 3 episodes, whereas the first game had 5. There's just not that much time to get a really big story going, which I think is a real shame since I'm a sucker for a good story.
Then, the characters. At first I didnt't like playing as Chloe, but after a while she started to grow on me. I feel like I can relate to her more than I could to Max. You just see more of Chloe's family life, which I think plays a big role in relating to a character and understanding how they see the world. For me, this is a big part of Life Is Strange's gameplay, because I try to make the choices the characters would make, not the ones I would make. Max just... didn't feel relatable the way Chloe did for me.
All in all, I did really like the game, but not as much as the first one. Guess I'll have to wait and see what episode 3 brings.

I dont write reviews on games that often but I just had to make one for theHunter: Call of the Wild.
First of, this game is absolutely amazing, the nature, the ambience, the game, Everything makes it feel like you really are walking in an actual forest or across open fields, plains and mountains. I got my graphics set on low due to possessing a potato computer but even with those settings, the game looks absolutely stunning.
As for hunting, Which the game is about, duh. I find it very realistic and the animals react accordingly to their surroundings. They can smell your presence if the wind is against you, They will hear you depending on how loudly you move and how close. (Run, Walk, Vehicle). I like the challenge of getting really close-up to them and just surprise ambush them from behind a tree. Skillpoints and Perks allows you to improve various abilities such as Stalking, Ambushing, Rifle, Bow and much more. There is a Level up system which allows you to unlock these Skillpoints and Perks aswell as new gear and items.
This game has alot more opportunities than just hunting, Lets say you are one of those tree hugging forest hippies who refuse to hurt a virtual animal. You can still just go for a walk in the massive maps, enjoy the scenery and take pictures of the animals instead of killing them. Explore and unlock different Lore points, Outposts and Outlooks, Find hidden objects like antlers and badges. Drive your ATV off a cliff while singing "I believe I can fly". You name it.
Pros & Cons:
+ Very realistic and absolutely stunning scenery/enviroment.
+ Skills and Perks
+ Fast Travel and Tents that allows you to quickly access the Storage.
+ Leveling various weapon skills.
+ Multiplayer
+ Massive Maps
+ Vehicles for faster movement.
+ 1v1 Agressive animals like Bears and Bisons
+ Your progress on Multiplayer and Single player is shared.
- You cant complete missions on Multiplayer
- Not alot of options other than kicking hackers on Multiplayer (They can join again sadly)
- A few rare glitches here and there like Animals getting stuck and cant be killed.
Things I would like to see in future updates:
Dog Pound
Access a hunting dog from the pound in the menu under Garage
Hunting Dogs that tracks animal and warns/barks when they are close. Searches for animals and stands on point to inform the hunter where they are located. They could have their own leveling system where the dog becomes more trained the more time you´ve spent hunting with it aswell as perks such as more accurate tracking and similar. Different Breeds depending on their job. Example, Tracking: Blood Hound, Beagle. Driving Dog: Harrier. Standing Dog: Swedish Elkhound. Fetching Dog: Retrievers (Fetching smaller prey such as fox, lynx, cayote and musk deer)
More silent vehicle/mount options
The ATVs are great but very loud which means most animals have been scared far away by the time you arrive.
Option to change their engines to more silent ones or a new perk system for vehicles that allows you to adjust their speed and volume. Other more silent vehicles or mounts such as Horses or Dog sleds (Altough dog sleds would probably only work in the Siberian map)
Mushrooms/Gathering
Yes you heard it right, Mushroom picking. There you are, following a moose through the forest and suddenly something yellow is glowing behind a tree. It is a chantarelle that gives experience! Could work with other things aswell such as berries.
Fishing:
There are too many lakes and waters in the game to keep this option out of the suggestion table, another way of gaining experience and fishing skill. Perks and Skills to improve the Fishing / how large fish you are able to catch. Different fishing poles and baits available depending on the skill.
Happy Hunting!

This creates a connection with them and yourself which later on into the game, plays a large part in conveying it's ideas of glory and righteousness. it also dives into the world of ethics, giving it's views on what should or shouldnt be allowed in war, or in the case of this game, a rebelion of sorts. Gang Beasts is a total cluster♥♥♥♥ of physics and destruction, where you play as a blobby cartoon man with hyper realistic fists. You gotta understand me, I've been around since the first ever alphas, and since then, the game has evolved, and moulded into one of the funniest, pick up and play fighting games ever.
The original alphas we're never glitchy. These are some of the most polished beta's ever, other than a few minor clips through platforms, that made no hinderence to gameplay. The gameplay and graphics we're as simplistic as it gets, so much so, that it ends up running perfectly on my cheapo toaster PC.
Since then the gameplay and the graphics have become alot sharper. The fighting is so smooth, and the knockouts are extremely satisfying, but also dangerous, because the chances of not getting up quick enough are increased tremendously, with the added betas, to stress you out, and add tension to the gameplay. It's a balance of tension, and technique. Also, climbing is much easier which is a solid plus in my book.
Gang Beasts now has a points system between rounds. You could say this is repetitive and redundant, I say this brings a moment of peace between players. A moment to reflect on the round you just played. It's long, and stupid, I suppose, but a neat little addition to the game.
The only complaint is the price. $20? it's maybe $10-$15 too high, for a game that has as much playtime (so far) as gone home. (2 hour walking simulator for the same price.) Those who are interested should wait for the next sale before buying the game, but the wait is simply worth it. I found the old floaty physics to be slow, and beating up people felt unsatisfying, until the latest uptate arrived.
When the finished game comes out, It should be worth the $20. I remember when playing the alpha, there was A tutorial, a sandbox mode, the biggest map in the game, with all sorts of playful things to do in the game, and a street level, which was co-operative. You would verse the AI gang beasts, walking up a street. If, for the final game, bone loaf we're to keep the moon-jumping, satisfying combat, polished graphics, bring back the three stages that don't exist anymore, as bonus features, or something, like a singleplayer mode, revert jumping to it's moon-gravity state, and shorten the intermissions between rounds, then by-god, the game would be simply perfect, and well worth the $20 the game is for sale.
As the game stands on it's own, It is built up to so much potential. I find the game now to be excellent, while others disagree. Gameplay has evolved, and combat is satisfying. Graphics are satisfying and the re-vamped stages are great. (trucks could be better though, I found the spinning camera to be fantastic, and signs were unpredictable.) With all these great things, the price, jumping, trucks stage, and  the repetitive overdone intermissions only just bring this game down, to a 4/5, but if the final product has anything to do with fixing the issues, and adding the deleted stages, Gang Beasts could easily become a 5/5.

Mad Max is an open world GTA-esque “game-sequel” to the movie Fury Road. You play Max of course, and start out looking for gasoline in order to be able to cross the Plains of Silence. You are rudely interrupted by the son of Immortan Joe (Scrotus) who destroys your car and your hopes of reaching your goal, at least until you happen upon a strange hermit mechanic with dreams of building a super-car called the Magnum Opus…
Like I mentioned before, the game is open world which means you will be given an almost overwhelming number of optional objectives to distract you from the main plotline. These range from removing wasteland hazards (snipers, minefields, scarecrows, camps) to reduce “threat” which is an arbitrary score for determining if you are eligible for receiving certain upgrades for the Opus. There are also four strongholds full of desperate people whom you can help by finding materials to build objectives that benefit both the people of the stronghold as well as providing free ammo, water, gasoline, and other perks for Max.
A lot of the game will be spent running around on errands and fighting rival factions, which will be pretty fun at first but eventually gets kind of tedious. Around the 60% mark you’ll notice that the level design starts to fall apart for most of the remaining optional areas (camps in Pink Eye’s region, the entire Deep Friah region) and it’s pretty obvious that the devs put their remaining effort into the main quest-line. The racing sections aren’t particularly gratifying because even with all the handling-boosting equipment, your car still steers like a bathtub and you’ll find yourself winning races the more “traditional” Mad Max way (e.g. killing every other racer, which is still pretty fun). Additionally, searching every inch of a camp to find that last bit of scrap or an insignia gets old after the 10th time.
Mad Max’s one saving grace is that the majority of the boring parts are optional, so it’s really up to you whether you want to tough it out for ~40 hours or go full-on story mode and plow through the game in 12 hours. The story is acceptable for what it is, but the gameplay reminds me of that one scene from Fury Road with Immortan Joe blessing a war boy trying to take down Furiosa. Lots of fun and hype for the first half, followed by a resounding “MEDIOCRE!” It’s still worth picking up on a sale though, if only for all the wacky wasteland antics.

Everyone's already probably heard that Mad Max combines elements from Far Cry 2 & Batman Arkham, while being the spiritual parent to Borderlands. I liked all of these games, but the combat and cars reminds me the most of the excellent Sleeping Dogs. Gameplay is solid. On the ground you can hold your own but you're no superhero. Even the weakest enemies can overpower you if they are too numerous or your reactions are too slow. The best part is the cars. Three of the initial 5 car bodies are reminiscent of the classic Interceptor, so you can play the campaign in a heavily customized ride that "feels" right. Max's legendary set of wheels are automatically unlocked after completion of the campaign. Depending on your level of devotion to this world you can take your time with the story or just putter around exploring the barren landscape to hunt for treasure and fight bandits. If you are a completionist Mad Max could be a grind, particularly the vehicle combat. To accomplish all challenges, it is recommmended to avoid clearing areas totally to keep enemies spawning. Movie adaptation games are usually in the "miss" category of hit or miss, so I'm very happy how Mad Max turned out. Being fond of the original film & the excellent Fury Road made this experience all the more enjoyable.

Much to say about this game but Ill stick to the important aspects. Also this is only about the single player and the multiplayer doesnt interest me.
First the good. Its a solid shooter, with good graphics and the expected (linear) so-so storyline. Theres a fair amount of overacting from certain characters but it was fun to see some familiar actors in the game. The controls are solid and the weapons/kit customization options add some interesting variation.
Now to the meh... The game makes an attempt to have your in-game actions influence the outcome with a limited degree of success. There are two very different endings depending on how you play. Ultimately Im not sure its worth a replay just to see the alternate ending when you could just Youtube it as the other "changes" (if you can call them that) to the story/cutscenes are minimal or non-existant.
As to the bad. There is no possibility to reload from the last checkpoint, which can get really annoying when trying to get that last piece of intel, finish a challenge or do some achievement hunting. If you mess something up you get to redo the entire level. The fact that you cannot skip/fast forward through roughly 80% of the in-game/major cutscenes also rubs the wrong way. This in particular becomes and issue when trying to complete the game on the highest difficulty level and the fair amount of terrain/geometric glitches causes you to buy the farm time and time again.
Overall I would give the game 7/10 and is a fun diversion but would recommend waiting for it to come on sale before buying it.

I honestly don't know how I feel about Undertale. I often find it difficult to like extremely popular things, or I at least resent them when I don't understand why exactly they're popular. Is Undertale just the fidget spinner of the video game world? I generally wait a while until the hype settles down, and then I give it a whirl. It seems like the excitment surrounding Undertale never really did die down. There are 1000+ people playing as I write this.
I got a neutral ending, wrapping my game up about 15 minutes ago. I started playing about 3 weeks ago, played half an hour here and there, but then sat down yesterday with the goal of finishing. I REALLY enjoy some of the music (Nyeh Heh Heh! fading into Bonetrousle had my head nodding hard AF). The story is fun to follow at times, but certain characters are absolutely awful (Sans and Alphys). I like the little "hur hur" effect when Sans speaks, but his dialogue is cringy. Alphys on the other hand, I can't think of a character I've ever loathed more. Not only is the actual character a piece of crap, but she constantly interrupts progress with text bubbles. I was furious. I couldn't even have the payoff of a good thwack on her huge dinosaur♥♥♥♥♥head? Thanks. I thought Papyrus, Undyne, Mettaton and Asgore were all pretty endearing with good stories. I accidentally killed Toriel, so I have no idea what she had to offer.
The battles though? I avoided looking up content or spoilers, so I assumed I had to fight. The ACT prompt was often misleading, or served a variety of purposes that weren't apparent or clear. I gave up on that pretty quick. I battled every opponent. Most were simple, some were frustrating. I think the issue herein for me is that I had to learn through Undertale that I hate "Bullet Hell". Bullet Hell is the majority of the game. Argue whatever you want about how I chose to play, but I played what I played. Fights against Undyne, Mettaton, Asgar, and Flowey were just not fun for me. I almost quit on Flowey before doing a quick search and discovering that it has some quirks. Undertale doesn't do a very good job of informing the player of some of these things.
I find it hard to recommend because I personally hated the Bullet Hell stuff, but there is a certain charm that makes me question if my hate was justified. It was a worthwhile experience, if only for the character development and some pretty good tunes.

You want to know what it is like to play this game, let me give you a perspective.
Friends says he found this great game, still in early access but going strong. I jump on steam and find it. As it was early access the price was great. On top of that  DayZ strongly appealed to my love for rpgs, survival and zombie games; and the future they had planned for the game got me pumped. I whipped out my wallet and bought it. A half hour later it was downloaded and ready to play.
Started my first game....
Load in with only a barn and a house near me. I run over to the barn and search it. Nothing there...well try the house. I sneak over to the house looking and listening for any zombies that may try and get me. I sneak into the house and search everything. "Oh look a shirt....".
Undeterred I press on. No clue where I am I pick a random direction and start running watching for zombies along the way. Then I ran, and ran, and ran some more. "S*&^ a zombie...., I'm going to die....." Umm well maybe not, if I walk at a brisk pace they will never catch me. Must of been a slow zombie so I press on some more. Running, running, running...... Finally, a town. Eagerly I jumped into search mode checking every nook and cranny of a dozen buildings; ever vigilant of an unknow horde of zombies that may be lurking around the corner.....or not.
So, Finished ransacked the town let me look at my haul of supplies.
Soda - Check
Pair of pants - Check
Really?!?!? There are buried Egyptian cities that have been abandoned for thousands of years with more stuff then this.
Message my friend to ask what I am doing wrong?
He tells me I have to head to a Military base to get anything good.
With my new pants with 2 extra storage slots and my soda in hand I was off to find a Military base.
Running, Running, Running, Running, Running, Running, Running
Finally found the coast, at least I have a landmark now. I pull up Firefox and google a map. Using the map and my godly sense of direction I determine that to get to the big military base I just have to keep the coast on my right and that will take me to the North-West of the map close to the military base.
With my plan in hand, I drink my soda, and take off to the military base.
Being that it's the coast I hit up a couple of more towns on my way and get some amazing loot.
Backpack - check
Can of dog food - check
Box of .22 ammo - check
Now we are getting somewhere. If only I could find a gun to use my ammo.
Wait wasn't this supposed to be a zombie game? Where are all the zombies?
No time to think of that now, I got a military base to plunder. Armed with my backpack to put my haul into I finally see over the horizon the goal of all my running.
I sneak over to the base, my friend had already warned me about the player ganking that happened on the bases. I busted open my dog food and slurped it down. I know I am going to need the calories if SHTF. I slowly move from cover to cover, checking my surroundings. I get to the first building. It's a barracks. I go in, check my corners and proceed to loot, keeping an eye on the door.
Military cargo pants - check
Axe - check
Well got a usable weapon and more storage. Off to the next building.
Next building is a control tower. I sneak in the back door and begin to check every square inch. There must be a gun around here somewhere. Eureka I found a gun. A rifle that uses .308 ammo. If only I had ammo for it. Continuing to look around I find a box of ammo. 5.56....well that’s not going to work.
I hear footsteps....
I look down the stair well and see another player coming in. Player is decked out in head to toe fatigues with body armor and a rifle. He sees me and shoots right away. I attempt to hide. No use...he is coming right for the room I am in. I got no choice. I equip my axe. As he comes around the corner I start swinging like a madman, I aim for the head thinking that will be the best option. The other player looks at me with a smirk on his face as he turns. His gun is now pointed at me. I feel my heart skip as I hear the sound of the gunshot. I'm dead.
My heart sinks as I look at the clock. I just spent over 3 hours attempting to get some meager supplies to only get shot by another player.
Undeterred I tried again.....same story, and a third time....same story

I picked this game up from a Steam sale because, hey, 2$ for a game is great, right? Well, this game is riddled with issues. Its main gimmick of giving you a new character to go with wears off after you start unlocking more classes (because you need to unlock stuff in order to be able to unlock some of the really good skills) and you find out just how weak many of the classes are. Mages aren't very useful when magic is such a tight resource and get vastly outclassed by spellswords, Liches aren't very useful, and assassins are outclassed pretty much completely by ninjas. Even the "best" class (which is really just the hardest one to unlock), the Dragon, is pretty much useful for one thing, killing the 4th boss, which the right spellsword just does better. Basically any time I didn't have a Barbarian, Paladin or Ninja I just felt like I could be doing so much better. And some of the quirks are just awful, such as Vertigo or MP/HP swap.
The game restricts your ability to play it with its various character classes and quirks, which you only have a very small amount of control over. While this leaves a lot of variety, it leaves the entire experience inconsistent and pads the game length.
And then the bosses just weren't very fun, outside of the final boss. A giant floating eyeball, a floating fire head, a giant slime, is that really the best they could come up with?
All around the game is fun when you actually have what you want, but that is so sporadic that the entire game just feels out of your control and much of the game you spend playing inferior characters in the vain hopes of getting enough cash to buy something better.

At it's core, Before the Storm is the same narrative driven character drama from the orignal, without the superpower elements that ultimately hampered the otherwise great original Life is Strange. And that is a very good thing. While the gameplay itself is similar and simplistic, it is also oddly compelling (I love wandering around each environment and interacting with everything, there is so much believable detail in this world, reveling in its gorgeous artstyle), but it is the writing that stands out. While there are a number of returning characters from the original, the game focuses primarily on the developing friendship of two key characters, a relationship that served as the catalyst for the events of the original. Obviously I won't be spoiling anything here, but it is safe to say that developer Deck Nine nailed this. There is obvious, very real chemistry between these two characters, and though the exact nature of their relationship is based on player choice and interpretation, their friendship is both endering and heartwrenching, and their personal struggles will elicit feelings of empathy, joy and sadness. And all of this backed up by an excellent indie soundtrack. Each song manages to perfectly capture the emotion of each scene, and the music that plays over the main menu haunts me for hours each time I play the game; achingly beautiful, it brings me to tears everytime I hear it.
Like the orignal, Before the Storm stands as a rare thing in this industry: it is a game that finds beauty in the mundane. There are no quests to save the world, no villians to defeat. Only people, and the trials, quirks and personalities that make life so strange and yet so interesting; and how important the bond of friendship really is. Because sometimes that's all any of us have in a world that can be unnecessarily cruel.
Bottom line, should you buy this game? Well, do you enjoy strong, engaging characters? Do you like a bit of melodrama? Do you like stories that engage your emotions, not just your reflexes? Did you play and enjoy the original Life is Strange? If you answered yes to one or more of those questions, then by all means buy this game. It is a game that will make you laugh (I wasn't prepared for how funny the game actually is), it will make you cry, and you will grow oh so attached to this flawed and eccentric cast of characters. As much as I enjoy action/shooters like Tomb Raider and Mass Effect, I don't think a series has affected and moved me quite as much this. Sharing a pair of headphones a train; playing a quick match of D&D; having an awkward family dinner. Life is Strange and Life is Strange: Before the Storm are heartwarming, gutwrenching, soothing, even cathartic.
And I am so hella glad that they exist.
