Spec Ops: The Line, is a great game. It combines one of the best stories I have ever seen in a game with some excellent gameplay moments. It is a nice change from the almost boring, modern military shooters. It is a great third person shooter and well worth the money.

Spec Ops is a game that tries to move itself away of the tradition of linear military shooters by using a more dark/grim (not gonna use "mature", sorry) story to talk about the horrors of war, and how ludicrous other military shooter's stories are.
But there is a stroong feeling that the developers were too focused on the history to realize that they were doing a videogame, and not a movie.
First, gameplay wise the game is as average as any other linear cover-based shooter can be: Scripted scenes, only one, defined, path, you can "blind fire" while in cover with such good accuracy is a joke, regenerative health, useless squad commands (Well, useless until you start to find the heavy weapons soldiers, then you use 'em to order "attack that guy". And that's all), machine guns that in the moment you man them a stream of enemies appear... the covers have that "magnetic surface" syndrome, meaning that you can't run near a cover without getting automatically attached to it. Really fun in a cover-based shooter in which ALL the maps are casually covered in makeshift parapets.
There's only one original mechanic: The sand deposits you can shoot to bury alive your enemies but there are only over 5 deposits on the whole game.
Don't get me wrong: Average does not really means "bad": The shooting is as fun as it can get, there are plenty of different weapons, and very remarkable moments (Like when defending your teammates through a mall with a machinegun). But still there's nothing specially interesting, nor a really good challenge even in the hard difficulty.
But, second, and more important: The story.
All Spec Ops is about the story. An interesting story about Dubai being blocked by, eh, ok, let's believe that, sandstorms, and about a delta force squad going in to see what the hell's going on.
Spec Ops has a movie story. Is a really good one, but is not a good story for a videogame. Or at least is not told as it should have in a videogame.
Starting with plot holes and unexplained details that are shielded in the "we don't know what's going on, we will understand later" excuse, the game makes the player go through several "war is hell" moments which can be summarized with "civilians being slaughtered, soldiers being slaughtered" all in an intent to make the player feel bad about what's going on around him and what is he doing, as a soldier, in Dubai.
But the concept failure, the main problem, is that you can't make me feel bad about kill people (Civilians or "good" soldiers) in an action game whose main point is, well, kill people. It's all about contradiction, as the main message the game seems to be sending is "You should feel bad for what the script and the core gameplay mechanic is telling you you have to do."
And that's a big "no ♥♥♥♥ing way". I can't feel empathy for the main character (As I would in a more open game) or feel that "I'm" the Main Character because the story is telling HIS story and making me just move him around from one cutscene to the next one. The game is so linear that even the "moral choices" only affect in which achievement you get. There is no way to try to avoid the more conflicting moments of the plot, even though you are seeing what its leading to ("Hey, let's kill all those orphanages." "Ok, but we are going with you because you didn't shoot us"). Some people say that not having choice is "part of the message", and I call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on this: You can give different choices to the player which will end in bad/worst results, and they will feel much better than forcing the player into a bad designed bombing scene (Floating parachute, if you play the game maybe you'll get it) so the plot can trigger its main element.
Spec Ops tried to move forward the military/cinematic shooter. It tried to make a more crude story, but it forgot that it is still a cinematic military shooter with nothing new to show. It forgot that what it is and what it tries to tell are oppossite things. If Spec Ops were a survival horror (With few killing and more puzzling), or a Fallout-esque RPG, allowing you to join any of the factions, the result could have been better and everything would have made much more sense.

Rogue Legacy is a roguelike hack-n-slash platformer with very challenging gameplay, that rewards mastery of movement controls above all else. However, every run through the shifting castle dungeon gets you a little further- any gold you earn can be used by your next character to purchase upgrades and gear. The game has a sort of heritage system, in each run you choose a child of your previous character, who can be one of several classes and may have any number of beneficial, harmful or completely benign medical conditions, another element of randomization atop the expected ones: randomized dungeon layout and loot. Character customization is extensive, with various gear setups of weapons and armor, and skill runes that add things like extra jumps or air dashes. I died many, many times over the course of my playthrough, especially during the very difficult (perhaps even cheap) boss fights, but unlike some roguelikes the game never really punishes you for that. You're even able to "lock" the castle and reenter the same layout as your next character, expiditing your progress to say, a boss room. I found myself addicted to the game, wanting to go on "just one more run" to get another upgrade before moving on to something else. The game has decent music and a charming art style as well, which clashes nicely with its rather grim lore. The game delivered strongly on that "what's in the next room?!" factor that I love about these sorts of games, including action roguelikes like Diablo and its derivities. Rogue Legacy was persistently entertaining throughout and I can recommend it to most, even those who would normally shy away from a roguelike.

Having played this game for a while (about one day of time as I write this), I can tell you this is a game that is most definetely worth getting. I bought this game and the "Going East" expansion for $7 during the Steam Summer Sale, but I would still pay the twenty or so dollars for this game. The simulation is extremely realistic, and there a several features that make this simulator realistic and similar to real world driving.
In the game, you start by working as a driver for hire, doing jobs wherever they are available (and believe me when I say they are always available, and tons of jobs to choose from). Afterwards, you can save up to buy your first truck, or take out a loan to buy a truck of your own. The benefit to owning a truck is that you can be payed more for jobs. After doing this, you can continue to make more money, pay off your loan (if you took one), and buy more trucks. Note that you will need to get a garage or upgrade the garage you're given in the beginning if you want more than one truck. Then, with new trucks, you can hire drivers to do jobs for you, and make more money after this.
So, if you're looking for a great way to spend some time, try this out. Though the game may look boring, I can say from personal experience that this is a game worth checking out. Additionally, last time I checked there is a free Euro Truck Simulator Two demo version you can download off the internet (I believe it is on the Euro Truck Simulator website). You can try it out, and can experience about four hours of gameplay.

The campaign is salvageable, it offers a few fun missions to play and even replay to see a different outcome like the endings (or get more achievements if you care about those) which was a really good addition to CoD. But, the campaign isn't as epic as Modern Warfare 1. The Strike Force missions were a cool new addition but poorly executed and very frustrating, the unit AI wasn't on the top, I almost lost them on most occasions. With Zombie mode, the same can be expected as previous Treyarch CoD that offered that mode although, I'd still say Left 4 Dead offers a more satisfying experience.
PROS:
+Campaign is interesting and offer decent playtime.
+Story choices are often tough and encourage replay.
+Amazing soundtrack and theme by Trent Reznor, Nine Inch Nails' frontman.
+Strike Force missions are an innovative play (even if I didn't like them).
CONS:
-Unstable and very buggy at release (a year later, game is finally playable).
-Extremely linear experience.
-Lots of invisble walls, forcing you to head towards the developers chosen direction or do a specific action to trigger a pre-rendered lame animation.
-Vague objectives at times.
-Enemy A.I's. always focus their fire on you instead of easier friendly A.I. targets nearby.
-Strike Force missions were beyond annoying on Veteran difficulty setting. Limited replay from the points system. Poor friendly A.I. makes it close to impossible to beat it which made me skip those missions entirely.
-NO DEDICATED SERVERS FOR THE MULTIPLAYER... meaning, don't play this game online as it is pointless. Get Battlefield 3 instead for online play.
-Zombies mode is stagnant (doesn't offer anything new but you can expect the same thing from previous Treyarch Zombie modes).
OVERALL:
I played this game for like, 3 hours at the game's release and lost interest at the campaign's Strike Force missions. The SF missions really annoyed the hell out of me especially if you failed a SF mission, you had limited replay points to change the outcome. So now, a year later and after having played CoD Ghosts, I can honestly say that I preferred Ghosts than Black Ops 2... in fact, I'd say Black Ops 1 was better than its sequel. Ghosts was more forgiving and the hit detection system seemed more refined too.
RECOMMENDATION:
I would say that BLOPS 2 would be an acceptable addition to the series but please, buy it at a reduced price! Ain't worth spending the big bucks for the campaign alone!

Borderlands was a game from 2010 about a prolonged second-hand gun bring-and-buy sale which some people liked and I didn't very much. There's a longer version of this story obviously, but basically while shooting Jason Vorhees in a scrapyard might sound like a stimulating escape from the workaday world, it loses something when it's all you're supposed to do for about twelve hours. Borderlands? More like Bored...rlands!
*pause*
But now it's time for the sequel and just to remind you of my personal formula for sequels, a good sequel leaps off from the original spreading silvery wings to explore uncharted skies while a bad sequel spends most of its runtime motorboating the original's ♥♥♥♥♥♥s and rubbing its head in the gravel. So in what category sits Borderlands 2? Well, from the comfortable territory of shooting Jason Vorhees in a scrapyard, Borderlands 2 has shyly thrown aside its dressing gown and taken its first nervous tentative step into the unexplored realms of shooting Jason Vorhees in a scrapyard and also it's been snowing a bit. Borderlands? More like Snore-derlands... 2!
*pause*
Anyway, we return to the planet Pandora (or to give it its full name, the planet Pandora-No-Not that one) with four Vault hunters of varying skill sets, different superficially from the four Vault hunters from the previous game but not in any practical sense, and after the Vault that drove the first game's plot was revealed to be short on treasure and long on tentacles, it turns out there's actually more than one treasure Vault on Pandora-No-Not that one, some of which actually do have treasure in. So that means that everyone in the game gets to keep calling you Vault hunter. Phew, thought we'd have to change our stationery!
But now your quest is to end the tyrannical regime of one Handsome Jack who lures you out to Pandora-No-Not that one and then try to kill you because he hates Vault hunters! Oh no, wait, actually he wants to manipulate Vault hunters, but then why would he try to kill you? Oh stop thinking about it and kill some more Jasons, Mr. Picky-Pants! After Rage demonstrated that you can't ask someone to hate a villain who spends most of the game quietly minding their own business behind a big wall, Handsome Jack's job is to call you up every five minutes and be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at you, although come to think about it, that might describe the behaviour of every character in the game.
The hilarious thing about Borderlands 2 is that its main strategy for ramping up the stakes is to tell you the stakes are ramped up and that's about it. The player characters from the last game show up as NPCs just to confuse matters, let's call them Team Widdlebiscuit, and when a big robot boss shows up some way into Borderlands 2, they make a point of going, "Oh no, not that guy! He defeated all of Team Widdlebiscuit off-screen, no really!" And then I took him down inside five minutes! Now bearing in mind Team Widdlebiscuit basically defeated Shub Niggurath last time around, either we take from this that the new characters are all super-powered in the least apparent way possible or maybe Team Widdlebiscuit have spent the last two years sitting around drinking pints of cream with ring doughnuts hooked over the rims.
Or alternatively, Gearbox is trying to dress up the sequel as bigger and better despite it being neither of those things and not having significantly evolved in the slightest degree, and if that's the case, then the really insulting part is the halfheartedness in the disguise. It's like a small boy sitting half-in and half-out of a bear's mouth and trying to get into a nightclub by claiming to be Robin Williams.
So like its predecessor, Borderlands 2 is a game that's all wallpaper and keeps introducing new quirky characters with graphical freeze-frame effects like how a character called Jimmy Nine♥♥♥♥♥ would be introduced in a Guy Ritchie film, and then every single one proceeds to stand around doing bugger-all except explain that you're going to have to raid another bandit camp. Usually it's because the bandits nicked some component you need for the story mission. Yes, bandits snuck into someone's house while the occupant was presumably off doing something wacky and hilarious, and made off with a single dubiously resellable piece of highly technical equipment rather than any, say, money.
Perhaps everyone should rethink the standard home security policy of letting every random thug wander in and ransack every box with a green light on the front. It's like bandits are the local equivalent of Oompah-Loompahs whose job is to contrivedly pad out the gameplay before too many interesting things happen in quick enough succession to actually start engaging me. Strip off that quirky wallpaper and we're left with dull repetitive shooting where every gun somehow manages to be slightly worse than the previous one.
Borderlands is a game in which the central mechanic is the maniacal gathering of random objects, like a fat ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who suspects he's about to be thrown out of the buffet, and proudly self-identifies as a shoot-and-loot game. Personally though, I call it stop-and-start. It's like riding a rollercoaster that just won't build up a decent speed because it comes to a lurching halt every ten feet so you can pick some flowers. You clear an area of baddies (perhaps you might even enjoy doing so, you monster), but then you have to rummage around opening the empty boxes and lockers, holding down X to pick up the ammo and money, checking every weapon against all your current weapons to make sure they wouldn't make things 0.1% more dead. Why make us open five ajoining lockers one by one when we could have dumped all their contents into one convenient trough? It's like the game takes perverse pride in flowing like a string of three-inch beads into a virgin ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
And why can't I track more than one quest at a time? Is it so maddening that I might want to take care of a few issues in the same general area at once rather than adhere rigidly to the to-do list like a passive-aggressive beaurocrat? Believe me, Borderlands, it would work in your favour to let me spend as little time as possible in the company of your user interface. Me and that guy, we don't get along too well. He got drunk at a party once and started asking women to sort his tabs. I can't remember, did I mention that the vehicles in Borderlands handle like♥♥♥♥♥ Well, they do, as in they literally handle like someone stuck a steering column into a giant pair of twitching buttocks that slide along the ground leaving a trail of ball sweat.
The best way to review a game I find is to start with the broad overall gut opinion about it and then work backwards to explain those feelings, and in the case of Borderlands, my broad analysis is that it bores me to ♥♥♥♥ing tears, and in fine analysis, there are lots of little reasons for that: the quest system, the item grind, the fact that I spent several hours stuck using an assault rifle with a ten bullet clip and a four second reload time. But at the end of the day, all you need to take is that after a while, I was greeting each new swarm of baddies as a data entry clerc would treat a fresh stack of forms plopping into their in-tray at four in the afternoon.
I don't even have the enthusiasm to hate it that much. Well, I used to, but then some bandits nicked it! - Yahtzee

I hunt and this game is fun. Obviously they cut out many aspects of hunting IRL, like waiting hours in a tree stand for a buck you saw on your trail camera, or making deer calls that have no statistical chance of actually attracting a deer to your location. Not to mention field dressing and having to hiking it back to your camp/vehicle. This game does let you practice your terrain scanning, playing the wind, and probably stalking if you're out west and you do that (I don't).
The other thing I like about COTW that some negative reviews don't realize, is that you can bump your deer if you're impatient after a slow-bleeding shot. Yes, if you didn't have a good shot, you'll be tracking that animal for quite a while, just be happy its not like real life when the blood trail goes away because the fat or coagulation from your poor gut shot plugs the wound. The fast-paced nature of the game (when compared to hunting) comes to a screeching halt once you take a shot that isn't the best. You need to wait, let the deer bleed out and you'll have a much easier time finding it. To give some perspective, I've sat in a treestand for about 40 hours so far in the past 30 days and harvested 1 deer. This game I believe I'm on #50 for 19 hours on record. So, try and remember COTW....is a game. You won't see that many wildlife when you're out in the woods and hours of boredom will be reconciled by moments of pure adrenaline. Have fun, this game is great, I'll continue to play it for as long as they update it and its fun to come home from a day out in the woods and check out a bear, stalk a coyote, or just wait until you get a warning call and stalk a blacktail deer.

Spec Ops: The Line, is a great game. It combines one of the best stories I have ever seen in a game with some excellent gameplay moments. It is a nice change from the almost boring, modern military shooters. It is a great third person shooter and well worth the money.

Spec Ops is a game that tries to move itself away of the tradition of linear military shooters by using a more dark/grim (not gonna use "mature", sorry) story to talk about the horrors of war, and how ludicrous other military shooter's stories are.
But there is a stroong feeling that the developers were too focused on the history to realize that they were doing a videogame, and not a movie.
First, gameplay wise the game is as average as any other linear cover-based shooter can be: Scripted scenes, only one, defined, path, you can "blind fire" while in cover with such good accuracy is a joke, regenerative health, useless squad commands (Well, useless until you start to find the heavy weapons soldiers, then you use 'em to order "attack that guy". And that's all), machine guns that in the moment you man them a stream of enemies appear... the covers have that "magnetic surface" syndrome, meaning that you can't run near a cover without getting automatically attached to it. Really fun in a cover-based shooter in which ALL the maps are casually covered in makeshift parapets.
There's only one original mechanic: The sand deposits you can shoot to bury alive your enemies but there are only over 5 deposits on the whole game.
Don't get me wrong: Average does not really means "bad": The shooting is as fun as it can get, there are plenty of different weapons, and very remarkable moments (Like when defending your teammates through a mall with a machinegun). But still there's nothing specially interesting, nor a really good challenge even in the hard difficulty.
But, second, and more important: The story.
All Spec Ops is about the story. An interesting story about Dubai being blocked by, eh, ok, let's believe that, sandstorms, and about a delta force squad going in to see what the hell's going on.
Spec Ops has a movie story. Is a really good one, but is not a good story for a videogame. Or at least is not told as it should have in a videogame.
Starting with plot holes and unexplained details that are shielded in the "we don't know what's going on, we will understand later" excuse, the game makes the player go through several "war is hell" moments which can be summarized with "civilians being slaughtered, soldiers being slaughtered" all in an intent to make the player feel bad about what's going on around him and what is he doing, as a soldier, in Dubai.
But the concept failure, the main problem, is that you can't make me feel bad about kill people (Civilians or "good" soldiers) in an action game whose main point is, well, kill people. It's all about contradiction, as the main message the game seems to be sending is "You should feel bad for what the script and the core gameplay mechanic is telling you you have to do."
And that's a big "no ♥♥♥♥ing way". I can't feel empathy for the main character (As I would in a more open game) or feel that "I'm" the Main Character because the story is telling HIS story and making me just move him around from one cutscene to the next one. The game is so linear that even the "moral choices" only affect in which achievement you get. There is no way to try to avoid the more conflicting moments of the plot, even though you are seeing what its leading to ("Hey, let's kill all those orphanages." "Ok, but we are going with you because you didn't shoot us"). Some people say that not having choice is "part of the message", and I call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on this: You can give different choices to the player which will end in bad/worst results, and they will feel much better than forcing the player into a bad designed bombing scene (Floating parachute, if you play the game maybe you'll get it) so the plot can trigger its main element.
Spec Ops tried to move forward the military/cinematic shooter. It tried to make a more crude story, but it forgot that it is still a cinematic military shooter with nothing new to show. It forgot that what it is and what it tries to tell are oppossite things. If Spec Ops were a survival horror (With few killing and more puzzling), or a Fallout-esque RPG, allowing you to join any of the factions, the result could have been better and everything would have made much more sense.

I honestly don't know how I feel about Undertale. I often find it difficult to like extremely popular things, or I at least resent them when I don't understand why exactly they're popular. Is Undertale just the fidget spinner of the video game world? I generally wait a while until the hype settles down, and then I give it a whirl. It seems like the excitment surrounding Undertale never really did die down. There are 1000+ people playing as I write this.
I got a neutral ending, wrapping my game up about 15 minutes ago. I started playing about 3 weeks ago, played half an hour here and there, but then sat down yesterday with the goal of finishing. I REALLY enjoy some of the music (Nyeh Heh Heh! fading into Bonetrousle had my head nodding hard AF). The story is fun to follow at times, but certain characters are absolutely awful (Sans and Alphys). I like the little "hur hur" effect when Sans speaks, but his dialogue is cringy. Alphys on the other hand, I can't think of a character I've ever loathed more. Not only is the actual character a piece of crap, but she constantly interrupts progress with text bubbles. I was furious. I couldn't even have the payoff of a good thwack on her huge dinosaur♥♥♥♥♥head? Thanks. I thought Papyrus, Undyne, Mettaton and Asgore were all pretty endearing with good stories. I accidentally killed Toriel, so I have no idea what she had to offer.
The battles though? I avoided looking up content or spoilers, so I assumed I had to fight. The ACT prompt was often misleading, or served a variety of purposes that weren't apparent or clear. I gave up on that pretty quick. I battled every opponent. Most were simple, some were frustrating. I think the issue herein for me is that I had to learn through Undertale that I hate "Bullet Hell". Bullet Hell is the majority of the game. Argue whatever you want about how I chose to play, but I played what I played. Fights against Undyne, Mettaton, Asgar, and Flowey were just not fun for me. I almost quit on Flowey before doing a quick search and discovering that it has some quirks. Undertale doesn't do a very good job of informing the player of some of these things.
I find it hard to recommend because I personally hated the Bullet Hell stuff, but there is a certain charm that makes me question if my hate was justified. It was a worthwhile experience, if only for the character development and some pretty good tunes.

Mad Max 2015.. what a fun game!
See below for pros and cons.
I originally thought of this game as a Shadow of Mordor clone, but with cars and desert, and it kind of is but the immersion was more on point than it was with Shadow of Mordor, at least for me it was. It nails the wasteland feel perfectly and manages to pull you in the world of Mad Max and all it's craziness without falling flat. And I must say this game has been optimized beautifuly
You play as Mad Max(as if that wasn't obvious) and take on your fellow companion,
Chumbucket who has devoted his life to serve you as his blackfinger, and your car, the Magnum Opus as your angel. You will be doing wasteland missions for a ton of interesting characters
and help them thrive as the new leaders in their own regional territory. But Max mostly wants to get his car rebuild after it being wrecked by Scrotus at the beginning of the game, needing to build a car faster, stronger and more badass than his original car, the Black on Black.
It follows the simple Batman Arkham games combat, and makes it more brutal, every punch feels powerful and painful to look at, and if you can get behind the combat on foot, you'll be very happy with this game. You'll be equipped with a shotgun for long range, shivs for combat finishers and the brutal yet satisfying Fury Mode which your punches are harder and looks like Max is putting his whole body in them. Now we have the car combat which is very hit or miss, as the car controls are heavy and delayed, almost like a real car. You can add on extra stuff on your car such as grinders, rams and armors which will affect your cars performance. Your car will be equipped with a harpoon, sniper and thuderpoons and other stuff I never used such as burners(side flamethrowers). Max can gain upgrades as well but they are very direct and are just direct upgrades from what you already have, such as shotgun, knuckles, armor, ammo capacity etc.
I will be adding replayability because the whole game is your replaying missions all over again, in order to unlock story missions you need to attack strongholds, that have the same objective(Find oil rig and blow it up) or anything that will lower threat in a territory. Some story missions include doing these same repetitive tasks in 5 regions of the map, if you are ok with this then the game won't be a problem for you, but the game requires you can tollerate the combat and everything else the game offers you, otherwise the game will fall flat near the end.
All in all, great game, immersive and great atmosphere. A bit repetitive and meh car controls.
I'd give this game a 8/10

A fine consolidation of "open-world" (think Far Cry 3) game elements, and some other things:
* arkham combat
* gta driving
* shallow but significant crafting/base-building
* decent (in some cases, great) npc characterization via writing and voice acting
My main complaint about this game is the design decision to use the same button do six things when it is sometimes possible to do two or more simultaneously--the logic sorting isn't always good so one may find oneself frequently picking up or dropping held things while attempting to loot.  This problem is not unique to Mad Max, but it stood out in a user experience that largely includes pleasant, even familiar things.  Also, making deeper characters of the friendly/enemy warlords and their bands would have made building up friendly bases and crushing enemy lairs even more satisfying.
Over all, however, a very fun experience.  I would love to see more content regarding:
* intense melee combat
* more encounters with ever-weirder freaks underneath the surface of the desert
* more interaction with/plot elements with the NPC "Griffa"

Really enjoyable game!
First the bad, because there is not much:
- Apparently not one for keyboard plus mouse (according to others), but with a 360 controller I've been loving it.
- The downthrust mechanics could be better, but it's not a huge deal to me.
- There is a thing where enemies shoot through walls and you may be  a bit confused why it sometimes works and sometimes doesn't -- but if you watch closely, you'll see that it depends on the positioning of the spell emitter.  Some people think this is a bug, but I think it's just a case of them not watching carefully.  The mechanic seems valid to me.
- Some of the various attributes of children, relating particularly to vision being blurry or dark or sepia-toned or whatever are pretty annoying.  It's not a huge deal at all, but I try to avoid those.  It feels like they are mostly there for novelty and not actually making interesting gameplay.  All the rest are great, though.
Then the good (which is basically everything else. although I'll try to hit the high points:
+ Movement and jumping is fluid and old-school.
+ You will die a lot, but the mixture of stakes versus things that you get to keep makes things feel fair and fun -- while still appropriately tense.  Very good mix there.
+ Your runes, equipment, perks, and so on all remain after you die.  Yay!  But your character is gone, and so you wind up with a different class and different traits on that child, etc.  Very nice.
+ You can only choose between three randomly-rolled children.  This means that you don't get exactly what you want every time, and so you have to play more broadly.  Since all the classes are pretty enjoyable, this is actually really nice.  You can't just minmax the kids, and it creates a different feel for each run, which is really nice.
+ You lose all of your money when you ENTER the castle the next time, giving you a chance to spend it between runs.  This really makes a lot of sense and keeps the stakes feeling meaningful without being overly penalizing.  You can upgrade your character so that you lose only 90% or as little as 50% of your money between runs.  I'm not sure that more than 70% is actually worth the cost, though.
+ Exploration feels fun, and the enemies scale well.  You can also make them scale harder or easier with runes.
+ Beating bosses is suitably hard, and then an even harder version of the boss pops up as an option some time after that (completely side-quest so far as I can tell).
+ Good mix of rooms styles and traps and enemies.
TLDR: It's worth full asking price if you like this sort of game.  It isn't without some flaws, but they are minor in the grand scheme.

Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a prequel to the original game Life is Strange. Set 3 years before the events of the first game, Before the Storm focuses it's attention on the relationship between two iconic characters of the series; Rachel Amber and Chloe Price. With 3 main episodes and one extra episode where the player can play as Max Caulfield for one last time within Seattle, the game contains plenty of content leading very quickly to hours of exploration and enjoyment!
Like the first game, the events which unfold within the story are heavily player based, however this is not necessarily a bad thing as the freedom of choosing what actions and things are said within the game are what make the Life is Strange experience and Before the Storm certainly doesn't disappoint!
In terms of performance at first I encountered a couple of game crashes when the first episode first got released, however updates from Deck Nine have since fixed the issue it seems, the game is very well optimised and will run well on a number of systems with different hardware specifications. For reference I am running the game on an i5-4690K, 8GB of RAM and a GTX 960 GPU.
In conclusion Life is Strange: Before the Storm is one hell of a game and an amazing experience for those who wish to return to Arcadia Bay in order to explore the story behind the relationship involved between Chloe Price and Rachel Amber!
Singlehandedly the best story driven game of all time! Aside from the first Life is Strange heh.

A few years ago in the town of Middlebury Oregon, there was a man named Joseph Woodstock. He liked to be called Joey. He was a nice fellow, with a few close friends. The local ladies who saw him sometimes bowling at the local Bowl-o-Rama Bowling Alley said he was pleasant on the eyes. He was a nice guy to be around, and a very pleasant conversationalist. He knew all the right things to say, and never seemed to be on anyone's bad side. He never had a run in the with local police, and was very straight and narrow. He owned an auto parts store in town. the shop being one of only 2 auto places in town was profitable, leaving Joey to skip the 9 to 5 grind, and have plenty of free time to pursue more leisurly activities. Joey was American as apple pie, and loving life to the fullest. He did have a girlfriend, whom he had even asked to marry him recently. She gladly accepted. Joey's life seemed set.
Joey was a good wholesome average man, with lots to live for. Which is why none of the rest of this makes sense...
On the night of September 14th, 2012, Joey was last seen sitting outside of his 2 story home, on his steps. A neighbor recalls seeing Joey through her window across the street. Joey appeared to be shaking, wearing only what appeared to be a towel, shorts (possibly boxers), and no shoes on. He looked a mess. The neighbor went downstairs, and when she went out of her door to see if Joey was okay, he was gone. She went to his front door and rang the doorbell, but there was no answer.
2 days later, Joey's body was found outside of town washed up in a riverbed.
Police say there was no signs of foul play, and it appeared that he had commited suicide by jumping off a bridge located further upstream, breaking his neck on impact. None of this made sense. This man, whom was recently engaged and not in any trouble financially or otherwise, took his own life? This made no sense at all.
Police searched his home and found no evidence of foul play. When they searched his den, the lights were flickering off and on, with a faint humming coming from a computer fan. The computer had been left on. Maybe there were clues here? One officer walked up to the computer desk, and touched the mouse enough to get the computer out of sleep mode. what he saw haunted him. A few seconds later, the computer monitor sparked, and then it shut off. It had died. As well as the computer with it.
Haunted by what he had seen, officer Henry King mentioned none of this to other officers, and left what he had seen on the screen out of his report.
4 days later, Henry King was found dead in his apartment. He had hung himself the night before.
On his computer monitor it flickered off and on. Call of Duty®: Black Ops II. Scribbled on a notepad also on his desk, in almost illegible hand writing was a small message: "Abandon all hope ye who enter here"

-Satisfying when you finally get a 1-hit kill.
-Well crafted, lively animated worlds with impressive weather systems and time of day.
Cons :
-Animal interactions are limited.
-Often question how the game spawns animals, sometimes you'll see nothing for miles, then you see 20-30 different animals in a dense crowd somwhere.
-No animation blending.
-Limited content, and what is there is level locked for seemingly arbitrary pacing.
-Animals bug out hard in multiplayer.
Summary :
It's a game that feels like they could do so much with it, and I hope they do. But their current track record is that every new thing will be DLC... So, that's something to consider.

Heard about this game a couple years ago, picked it up when it went on sale.... And have been hooked!
The game really goes back to the roots of hard NES games where once you die, you have to start over again. BUT there are permanent upgrades you can buy to beef up your heros for the next play through. The levels are randomly generated and each new area you go to goes up in difficulty which makes the game have unlimited replay value. There are secret rooms, and puzzle chests placed randomly in each stage. They which grant either items or magic runes you can equip before setting foot in the starting level(once you enter the castle you can't go back so choose your loadout wisely).
Every time you die it shows what you killed(how many as well) and what you died by, then you must choose your heir. Each heir has either pros or cons or neither which affect gameplay slightly but can be balanced with items. This makes every playthrough different, humorous and challenging.
The only gripe I had with the game was the constant grind to get gold for new weapons, runes or hero upgrades. But it is all apart of the game and it grows on you.
I would highly recommend this game if you are into rougelike rpgs and are up for a challenge!

I really want to like this game. Rogue-likes are one of my favorite things out there. But this game just fails at it.
Not even looking at the extremely similar recolored enemies, boring level design, and overly frustrating small resolution, there are a lot of problems. The game emphasizes heavy grinding and global persistence. That works when the persistence doesn't give you sheer number advantages (such as new class unlocks or different options to play), but when you play just to farm gold to get more damage for your next run it kills everything "rogue-like" about it.
The game is extremely unforgiving, which I enjoy. I love games like The Binding of Isaac and Crypt of the NecroDancer ... but both of those games allow you to get better through quick learning and good feedback. This game has none of that. It just kills you for not being able to see a small projectile from a room away or because you're hopelessly outgunned due to never leveling up the "correct" path. Plus, upgrades get more costly whenever any of them is upgraded. I understand the design decision behind it (to encourage diversity in paths), but it just fails. Even the designers themselves said that in their GDC talk.
Ugh. I so wanted to love this game and it is decent for $3 or so that I paid, but I couldn't imagine spending $10 or even $15 for it. So many problems that just adds up to making it a meh title.

First of all, I hate Rogue-like games. I hate them so much that it's taken me two whole years to even try this game, and I honestly wasn't expecting much. Rogue-like games are so... stupid. You die. A lot. You explore a new, randomly generated cave/castle/ruin/whatever every time, but they all look the same, so what's the point? And did I mention you die a lot? So one mistake, and all your progress is wiped. Bye bye, last hour or so of my life. It was nice knowing you. Too bad I have nothing to show for it.
At least, that's how I see Rogue-like games. So with that in mind, I gave Rogue Legacy a chance. How did it end up? Wel... pretty darn sweet, actually. To address my initial concerns about this genre: Yes, it's difficult. Yes, you will die a lot. And no, it's actually not pointless at all. Far from it. Here's the thing: When you play, you gather money, blueprints, runes etc, but you have absolutely no use for it in the castle itself. Instead, when you die, your character remains dead, but you get to play his or her child. This child will inherit everything the parent found in the castle, meaning you can spend the money your dad got to buy a new sword, new armor, upgrade the castle or whatever.
Dying was always my biggest issue in games like this, as I hate perma-death. But in Rogue Legacy, dying simply means you can finally claim the rewards you got in the castle. True, the whole "inherit the loot" is just a gimmick, but it's interesting. Plus, you can also choose to keep the old castle, though it means you'll only get to keep 60% of the gold you find. Still, when you find that sweet castle with tons of loot in the beginning, it can be worth sticking around to loot it over and over to get better gear and upgrades.
Anyway, the point is Rogue Legacy removed the death-penalty by making death rewarding, and just like that, the game ends up very, very addicting. Difficult, yes, but you get better and better as you play, you can keep upgrading your characters, and pretty much just enjoy yourself. Even I enjoy the hell out of this game, and as I said, I hate the genre with a passion.
Rogue Legacy: The Rogue-game for Rogue-haters. :-D

I found, however, that there are a ♥♥♥♥ ton of unofficial servers that have high activity, each with their own adapted mechanics such as INCREASED LOOT SPAWNS, HASTENED (sped-up) DAY TIMES (and others such as +/- zombies, PVE only, etc.), which immediately negate my previous worries about the game. I actually don't hate playing this game because the things they did right (environment and graphics) they did REALLY well. So it's a joy to walk around in this game and take it in. Same with the sound. I even bought the new map because I like cold snowy environments and immediately wanted that experience.
Unfortunately, I can't really endorse a buy on the game right now. The animal AI is pretty brutal. It'll go from animals scaring too easily, to not scaring easily enough, to running in circles then standing 3 feet in front of you for no apparent reason. That is the most obvious need of fixing. I'm not sure about the ballistics, but sometimes I wonder about them being all that good based on some of the shots.
I definitely dislike the inventory/store system they have in place. Locking most the stuff just seems silly and arbitrary. In general the equipment leaves a lot to be desired. In a game where you could probably make a pretty penny for customizing rifles, clothing, etc. it feels like they didn't put much effort into these cosmetic items. Overall I think this part of the game could do with a total overhaul. They items and the store system make me less engaged in the game, not more.
Finally, while they said they won't be adding any survival elements, I feel like managing survival would be much more fun than the story and side quest missions they throw around. Not saying they should toss those completely, but the missions don't do much for me. A survival aspect though can't introduce a lot of fun. Managing food, buying clothing for the appropriate setting, little things like that give much more a sense of purpose than random missions. It also introduces more urgency in a game that does really feel like there is any sort of real threat.
Also, would be cool to have a little more severe weather implemented. Not that it would matter much given no survival aspect, but a really heavy snow storm would still be fun to trek through.
Overall, especially given the price, I can't recommend buying. If it's goes cheap (by your standards) or you get it for free, sure. It has some redeeming qualities. But I get no sense the bugs are going to be fixed, and the thrill of the hunt quickly disappears when you don't feel much sense of purpose beyond that shot (and the main/side missions do zero tho change that).

Despite some wonky audio during my playthrough (certain sound effects not always playing when they should) this is a very well made and optimized game.  Looks outstanding, sounds good (for the most part), plays great.
If you know Mad Max, the story isn't anything new and is mostly predictable but it is still satisfying and has a few seriously cool gameplay moments and cutscenes that really make you feel what Max is going through.
The on-foot combat is mostly inspired by the recent Rocksteady Batman games and it works really well.  As fun as that is, I think I liked the car combat even more.
If you're a completionist junkie like I am, you'll also have lots of stuff to search for and collect.
Most all of the upgrades for Max and the Magnum Opus feel worthwhile and give noticable increases to power, while usually looking badass in the process.
My primary annoyance/con was the camera sometimes taking a cinematic angle while engaged in vehicle combat or racing around.  You can adjust it on the fly but I would've prefered it just remain directly behind the Magnum Opus so I could focus entirely on not crashing into things.
Overall, Mad Max is a great game that I feel deserves more attention.

Alright so after a little while in game and getting used to how the game plays, I decided I needed to update my review. While I still absolutely love this game, I love it knowing that it feels very much like an incomplete game that has some (But not many) glaring issues that I feel are desperately in need of fixing. I will list them below in order of significance (in my opinion).
1) Firstly.... The game needs more caliber weapons. NEEDS more caliber weapons, if not more weapons as a whole. I have yet to come across a situation where I actually used a shotgun or revolver, so. Those feel a little wasted. I'd like to see a few more weapons in the game such as rifles chambered in .308, .30-06 and maybe .300 Win Mag as the end all be all. Or if they're feeling really crazy, .408 Cheytac.
2) Secondly, I think the game's AI system for animals really needs to be improved. Part of what drove me to write this email was what happened just a few short hours ago. I sighted in a herd of 6 Fallow Deer at about 200 meters, and proceeded to shoot 5 out of 6 of the Deer without changing my position once. PLEEEEEEEEEEEASE fix this. As nice as it is raking in 5-8k in a matter of minutes, it really is immersion breaking.
3) Thirdly, the tracking system at times feels a little off. Tracks will on occasion completely vanish. Maybe I'm just not looking hard enough but when I search a 200 meter area in a grid search for a single set of tracks.... come on.
4) And finally, the environment feels out to get you. I think over the course of playing this game I've gotten killed by the environment due to glitches or bugs more than 10 times. And I only have 15 hours of playtime on record. So.... Yeah. Attention needed here.
All in all, still a great game, and I am still glad I purchased it, but it could use a little more TLC from the development team. But this does not change the fact that I will still recommend this game to any avid outdoorsman who also has a flare for PC gaming.

theHunter: Call of the Wild is one of the few hunting games that I've seen that made me want to actually buy it.  I've played a few in the past, and this one takes the cake when it comes to immersion and realism.
The game starts you off by doing 'tutorial' quests, but in the end you could do what ever you want; either of the two parks/locations are vast and have no invisible barriers (except the map barrier of course).  On that note, some very short trees/bushes have collisions and can be a bit of a problem.  Eventually you'll visually learn which ones have collisions and which ones don't.
For the most part, I have no DLC, and still enjoy the game.  I feel tents and ATVs add some versatility but in the end aren't necessary.  Exploring will take longer, but you may overlook things on an ATV.  I heard tents are glitchy and known to disappear, but I'm sure they'll iron those kinks out.
The only gripe I have for the game is aiming.  If I'm aiming through a scope, I would expect only the scoped portion of the screen to zoom, but the ENTIRE screen zooms.  This happens with EVERY scope.  I'm sure it wouldn't be too hard to fix.  I doubt it will though, considering this is such a minor thing.
Overall:  Excellent game, and I will be buying the new map.

Despite some wonky audio during my playthrough (certain sound effects not always playing when they should) this is a very well made and optimized game.  Looks outstanding, sounds good (for the most part), plays great.
If you know Mad Max, the story isn't anything new and is mostly predictable but it is still satisfying and has a few seriously cool gameplay moments and cutscenes that really make you feel what Max is going through.
The on-foot combat is mostly inspired by the recent Rocksteady Batman games and it works really well.  As fun as that is, I think I liked the car combat even more.
If you're a completionist junkie like I am, you'll also have lots of stuff to search for and collect.
Most all of the upgrades for Max and the Magnum Opus feel worthwhile and give noticable increases to power, while usually looking badass in the process.
My primary annoyance/con was the camera sometimes taking a cinematic angle while engaged in vehicle combat or racing around.  You can adjust it on the fly but I would've prefered it just remain directly behind the Magnum Opus so I could focus entirely on not crashing into things.
Overall, Mad Max is a great game that I feel deserves more attention.

I got this game as a birthday present from my friend and i immediately fell in love with it. Undertale is a RPG game filled with puns and puzzles. It's an amazing game that will mess with your emotions. This game is great as there are three paths you can go. Pacifist, Neutral and Genocide. As you go through the game you'll notice changes depending on how you play.
What i liked about the game are the characters. Some of the characters include Flowey, Toriel, Sans, Papyrus and lots more. Sans the skeleton is one of my favourite characters as he is very mysterious. People say that he is able to teleport, he is also the only know skeleton (Out of Sans and Papyrus) to have known magic powers (His gaster blasters).
The games story is incredible as you can choose what path to go down. All the routes have different endings based on the decisions you make in the game. Wether you kill everyone or spare their lives the characters will be a bit on edge and their dialogue will be slightly different if you've done genocide. That's what makes this game so unique. Undertale is so mysterious and deep yet because the game looks simple. It kind of looks like a normal RPG game at first but when you start putting the pieces together and play it for yourself it's actually more deeper then you think.
Although some players hate the fact they're left with unanswered questions; others (Including myself) love the puzzle. Toby fox Developer and Publisher of Undertale drops a few hints about what i believe to be the biggest mystery of the game and that is the former royal scientist, W.D. Gaster. Some of the fanbase love this as they get to use their imaginations and theorise for themselves. For example some people believe that Gaster was their dad. But that's the point because we haven't been given an answer (That i know of) us fans can make up theories and be creative.
In conclusion i think that Undertale is a phenominal game. With adoring characters and an amazing story. Maybe the skeleton brothers has a bone chilling backstory as they just appeared out of no where? Maybe Gaster could still be alive somewhere? It's all up to us. What do you guys think?

After 150+ hours, I decided it was time to write a review.
Is Euro Truck Simulator a good game? That is all up to personal preferance. If you like simulators, this game is something that you will most likely enjoy. I love to sit down and listen to some music while I play this game on a rainy day. I love to add on lots of hours during the summer time if its raining outside or if I just dont feel like going outside. It just an all around great game.
Another great feature of this game is that it suits every players needs. If all you want is to sit down and truck, go for it. If you want to 'tycoon it up,' you can purchase more trucks and start a buisness hiring drivers. The game also has many DLC options. Want a paintjob for the country you live in? It's most likely in the store. Do you want a bobble head dog sitting on your dashboard? You can get that too. And also enjoyable feature is the fact that the map is ever expanding. You can get the 'Going East!' expansion pack, allowing you to head on down to eastern Poland and Hungary. Do you want to test out that new heater? Get the 'Scandinavia' pack and get up in that chilly Norway! And soon to come is the all new 'Viva le France' that introduces a bigger France!
Overall, this game is perfect for me. Sometimes I just need to pass the time when Im going stir crazy. And this is a great way to do it. For some reason, I purchased American Truck Simulator about 2 days after release, but it just never really stuck with me. This game did though, and I can just never get enough!
Are there any cons to this game? No. If there isnt something you want in the game, you can download a mod for it. This game just has so much potential that is being pursued.
Do i reccomend this game? Yes. It is a great game if you enjoy simulators, and id suggest taking a look into it. There is no going wrong with this game. Enjoy!
-Dan

Mad Max  is Avalanche Studios movie tie-in for last year's Mad Max: Fury Road, being set before the events of the movie, as it follows the events in which Max Rockatansky reclaims his prized V8 Interceptor. On a technical aspect, Mad Max is a perfectly functional PC Port, as to be expected from the developer. It has good controller support, functionality for a wide range of system specs and is well-optimised in terms of performance; however, this aspect alone does not make the game worthy of praise. You can have the best port in the world, but if the gameplay is terrible, it doesn't mean anything. Mad Max's gameplay is not terrible but I'll move on:
As with many other recent big budget releases, Mad Max is an open world sandbox action game, with extra emphasis on vehicle combat and customisation this time around. As with most formulaic sandboxes, the majority of your time in the game will be spent exploring the map and performing menial tasks to unlock new upgrades, and to unlock new missions. This formula has been popularised since Ubisoft in 2007 and by this point, it takes some very interesting twists to make this style of gameplay feel at all interesting, Mad Max has some such twists, but most of the time it will feel like what I just described - an expanding checklist of menial tasks.
One of these such twists is the vehicle combat. When in vehicles, enemy mobs and convoys can chase you meaning you're supposed to either outrun them or take them down with crashing into them or using certain weapons. The main three vehicular weapons are the thunderpoon, harpoon and shotgun, there is a locational damage system for vehicles, meaning shooting different parts of vehicles produces different effects. Firing the shotgun at a fuel tank will cause the vehicle to explode, whereas tearing the door off a vehicle with a harpoon will then allow you to rip the driver out from the vehicle. Additionally, enemy foot mobs can try to climb onto your vehicle, so that vehicle combat doesn't exist in a void. These mechanics combined with the great explosion effects and good visuals in general can make it the most fun aspect of the game by far, and there is also a vehicular boss fight later on in the game which is a good challenge that makes good use of these mechanics. The big problem however is that the main car you will be driving throughout the game - the Magnum Opus, feels strangely underpowered compared to other vehicles you can bring to forts. This is a problem because the Magnum Opus is the only vehicle with your sidekick - Chumbucket, who can repair your car for free and it is the only vehicle to receive upgrades. The consequence of this is that you will often be finding yourself having to avoid vehicular conflict, which is stupidly counter-intuitive for an entry in the Mad Max franchise.
As well as fighting in vehicles, you will also be fighting enemies on foot, which is much less polished for the following reasons: FIrstly; Mad Max uses the same simplistic "FreeFlow" combat system as the Batman: Arkham series and Shadow of Mordor, although the animations can look nice and "flow" effectively, Mad Max does little to innovate on this combat system apart from the occasional use of a dodge-roll and it ends up as a repetitive exercise in spamming attacks and counters. The boss fights are also all reskins of the exact same boss you see in the starting areas, and the enemy variety in general is pretty limited. For example, Max is the only person in this world who can use a shotgun for some arcane reason.
Although the world of Mad Max does look pretty, exploration quickly starts to feel like a chore, as you cannot manually pick up currency (and since scrap drops give so little currency, prepare to hold down e on the floor a LOT) and there is little variety in the menial progression tasks, once you've taken down one scarecrow, you basically know how the rest of them will be like. The story (or more importantly, dialogue) is also nothing to write home about, I usually don't care about story in videogames but in this game the lack of an engaging plot feels like a missed opportunity as some better context could have made the exploration more compelling. The only positive I can give to the exploration is that each enemy stronghold as a different visual design, which helps the variety somewhat.
Overall, Mad Max is a perfectly functional sandbox action game, and some of the main missions and the fun vehicle combat did certainly engage me for quite a while, but functional is all it is. It's another formulaic action game made to be as "safe" for profit margins as possible, rather than being made for the sake of making a good game, for that reason I just can't recommend this game at full price, I would recommend that you spend your money on less generic games and wait for a sale instead.

I was becoming bored. The hunt became a grind. Popping between campsites, downing whatever was foolish enough to exist within 400 meters of me. I thought a 7mm would bring me joy, but it didn't. I tried bow hunting, which was a blast... for a day. I had forgotten the hunt. Not the shooting and harvesting, the HUNT. So I travelled on foot. Day, night, shooting and arching along the way, I had fun again. So much of the map had I left uncovered. I was getting that old familiar feeling. I could almost smell the rain on the grass. There was so much I was missing in my chase of an easy thrill. My travels brought me to North Lake, and in my search of a landmark I came upon a most chilling call. It shook my core, I was frozen in fear or anticipation. Awestruck is how the old man tells it to me. His words became my truth when I levelled that 7mm towards the most gracefull creature ever stood before me. A Roosevelt Elk, the biggest I'd ever seen about 100m away, and another beside him, not as big but just as majestic. I knew I could only have one, but neither gave me a clear shot. I called, He spun around and called back. I felt a click as the trigger pulled, and suddenly I was looking skyward because the magnum has her own part in every discourse. He was down. The feeling I had the first five minutes in the preserve was back. The wonder and grandeur of this magical place came flooding back into my veins. I realized I hadn't taken a breath in at least a minute as my rifle came down to survey my quarry. And there it was, the stag I earned, the stag I hunted.

Full review here:

Have you ever played a Modern Military Shooter, such as games from franchises like Call Of Duty, Medal Of Honor, and Battlefield?  Did they leave you feeling vaguely uncomfortable, for reasons you couldn't quite define?  Maybe you are tired of the constant portrayal of the western protagonists as a technologically superior force for truth and justice in the face of a ragtag army of foreign soldiers that despite being outclassed in every way by the heroes are still built up as a overwhelming and faceless threat to all that is good and right in the world?
If so, then Spec Ops: The Line is the game for you.  In purely gameplay terms, it functions as an adequate cover shooter; enemies pop up, you hide behind stuff, you shoot at each other.  Maybe you order your AI squadmates to throw a flashbang, or snipe a specific target, or shoot an environmental object to hamper your enemies.  Pretty basic stuff, but it handles well.
What makes Spec Ops: The Line special is it's scathing critique of every cliche that has been fuelling the Modern Military Shooter genre for the past ten years.  Set in Dubai, following a sandstorm that leaves the city in ruins, a team of operatives is sent in to investigate a distress signal, apparently sent by a US Infantry Battalion caught in the storm during the relief efforts.
Without being too specific and risking spoilers, the situation quickly spirals out of control, and your squad struggles to resolve it, through the application of force against foes as desperate for survival as you are .  The protagonists behave as characters in these game normally do, assessing the situation, coming up with plans, and acting accordingly, which doesn't always work out how you'd expect.  Not only that, but they also suffer from the emotional impact of their situation and the actions they are often forced to take, that often manifest in subtle an interesting ways.  This is rare in a genre dominated by the type of stoic action heroes that do whatever is necessary to complete the mission, without suffering any mental scars that any normal person would have after massacring hundreds of people.
To give you a hint, one of the characters your squad is attempting to track down is called Konrad.  This illustrates the kind of literary influences this game is drawing from.
So if you are in the the market for a competent cover shooter that features a deep and interesting plot that provides commentary on the genre it emulates, you could do worse than Spec Ops: The Line.

As a shooter, Spec Ops is solid but shallow. There is a glaring lack of stealth gameplay; weapons loadout is forced on the player, with sniper rifles conveniently leaning against the wall 10 meters before each sniping opportunity; and the combat system itself misses the opportunity to capitalise on the three-man squad setup.
This game leads you by the nose - little effort is made create the illusion of free roaming. This is forgivable, as the narrative by and large manages to stride between two cliches - the patriotic shoot 'em up, and the war is hell morality play - avoiding both (for the most part).
Spec Ops does a good job of engaging the player by presenting meaty moral decisions with real impact. Given this, the times (one in particular) when choice is removed from the player, when you are forced to make one egregious choice when others are so obviously available, are both glaring and unforgivable.
Despite all this, the game has a consistent, unique style. If played in one or two sittings, you may find yourself swept along by the narrative, and at times genuinely moved, like I did.

I've owned this game for quite a while, I've not clocked a substantial amount of hours, but there hasn't always been a great amount of content to explore. Skins and Player customization are a nice feature, but lack the charm some of the original characters had. What I'm getting around to saying is, this game has changed a great deal since the early stages. I'm not sure I agree with some of the changes that have been made Graphically, and Mechanically during development. The old climbing and Gripping had to be the most fun feature in the game, as you could climb up on top of buildings, and into places you never would be able to experience otherwise. Limited jumping may seem fine to a new player, but now that it has been removed, it feels a bit lackluster. I know it sounds like I'm blowing it out of proportion, but I really do feel that the original variants of the maps were much more interesting than the new ones, as simple as the old ones were.
After all that I've said, can I recommend this game? Yes, well... Sort of.
For 20$, the time that I've had with friends on the couch is one of the funniest, most enjoyable experiences in gaming that I've ever had the pleasure to recieve. The glitches are almost never game breaking, but add to the hilarity of the experience. There was a glitch on one of the old maps that allowed you to break off a piece of Gondola cable and fly around on it like a broomstick from Harry Potter. I really do hope that the devs take the time to understand what the community for this game is asking for, and push their game in the right direction.
If you have a bunch of friends, and a steam link or have your computer next to a couch, get this game, the local multiplayer is a blast.

It really breaks my heart to give a negative recommendation to this game. But if you have already played Life is Strange, keep it like that. This game kind of ruins the first game.
However, if you didn't, then play this game BEFORE the first game.
SPOILERS AHEAD!
What makes the first his game beautiful and unique is obviously not the graphics, but two things:
1. The way that the story is told
2. Mechanics
The ability to rewind the time, and a deep journey to the memories of a teenage girl using this very ability is fascinating. Some choices change the course of the game completely, including the achievement you can unlock.
In this game, however, the rewind ability is completely gone (obviously), and some "yapperness" and "wittiness" has come instead, which completely opposite to the philosophy of the first game.
In the first game, there was no right or wrong, there was only choices and consequences. In this game, there are some right answers during the dialogues.
Gameplay is more or less the same with the first game, but the storyline changing based on irrecoverable dialogue options is kind of lame in terms of this game.
What I liked in the first game the most was the feeling of Braid (PC Game). "What would happen if we could rewind just after we did something stupid?" was the main question that is answered in the first game. In this game, there are only questions, but not answers. You need to play it all over again to find out the answer.
To sum up, if you played the first one, don't play this. If you did not play the first one, play this one first.

For this reduced price (30€) I can certainly recommend the game. The multiplayer is solid, like pretty much every Call of Duty. There are a few innovations over Black Ops and Modern Warfare 3, like the revamped killstreaks, the class creation system, weapon unlocking mechaning, and some pretty unique weapons. The maps are alright, nothing to special there. I can recommend Nuketown 2025 and Hijacked the most since I always seemed to have the most fun on them. I don't really like the perks since some of them like "Dexterity" or "Toughness" are just pretty much no-brainers and you always end up taking them no matter what, really hurting variety in the respect. Same goes for the weapon pool in some respect, I'd have liked to see more than 4 weapons in the majority of categories. The only categories that DO have more than 4 weapons available are Assault Rifles and SMGs, everything else doesn't offer much variety. As for weapon balance, its pretty good fram what I experienced. There a some, if very few over/underpowerd guns like the "Executioner" which is a terrible shotgun-revolver-thingy, and some that are mostly stronger than everything else in its class like the "AN-94". That's another problem right there: Since the classes mostly only have 4 weapons available, its pretty common that one gun kind of trumps that class. For example, there are 4 LMGs. Two of them are Beltfed and the other two are magazine based, which leaves te first two with larger magazines and longer reload times, while the other two are the exact opposite. One of those LMGs in each category is more long-range and the other more short-range capable. Now, one of the first attribute is going to end up being better than the other one. There is just no balancing right there, it's more or less a fact. Same goes for the second attribute, which leads to one gun of the four of them being the best allrounder, even if it lacks a few skills the other guns have. And that again leads to you, and most people online just using that one gun in every class. I would like to tell you can use these guns situtaionally, for example if you play a long-ranged map like Metldown you can use the long-range HAMR, or if you play a short-ranged one like Nuketown you just use the QBB LSW. But you can't really do that unless you're willing to actually go out of your way and pay anoter 1,99€ for a slotpack DLC, because you only get 5 custom classes by default! That doesn't leave you with much flexibility when it comes to choosing situatinal weapons, because if you're anything like me you'll want to have at least one custom class for every weapon category, and not four classes just for LMGs. Also, if you're going into this thinking of quickscoping, I have to tell you that you're probably better of with anoter CoD that suits itself better to that. Don't get me wrong, its perfectly possible but due to long zoom-in times with pretty much every sight and extremely slow firerates AND bolt-action prolonging time inbetween shots, it's pretty damn challenging since you can get mowed down so very fast. If you do want to try it out though anyways, I can safely tell you that the "Ballista" with an ACOG-Scope is by far the best candidate for quickscoping.
I think that's all I wanted to say. For 30€ (Or your reginal equivalent) I can definetely recommend this game for all the fun I had, which do almost completely shadow the flaws I just mentioned for awareness purposes.

A bit like the old Castlevania, or Ghosts and Goblins, or something like that.  Side-scrolling castle exploration and treasure hunt... with a few twists thrown in to make it more challenging than just "kill the monsters and grab the loot."  Trust me, you will get frustrated with the difficulty level until you run through the castle enough times to amass a small fortune to buy upgrades for your heroes.  Traps like spike floors and fireball cannons can kill you.  Flying monsters can kill you.  Warrior monsters can kill you.  Wizard monsters can kill you.  The whole place is a death trap.  But it's fun, too.
You have a mansion of your own that you rebuild using the gold you find in the castle.  It allows you to hire a smith, an enchantress, and others.  It also provides upgrades to your health, mana, strength, and the amount of armor you can carry and wear.  Your mansion is permanent; it remains the same even after you die, though sometimes the upgrade prices change without notice.  So it is essential to making your journeys through the castle easier as you progress.
The smith sells weapons and armor.  They cost a lot of gold.  The enchantress sells upgrades like super-jump and damage boost.  For gold.  So gold makes the world go around here.
After you have finished dealing with your mansion, your hired help is on the next screen.  Then you walk up to the castle gates where the demon Charon (Grim Reaper?) is waiting for you.  He takes ALL of your current gold in order to let you into the castle, so make sure you spend it all before you talk to him!
Once in the castle, you are trapped there UNTIL YOU DIE.  Kill monsters, break furniture, open treasure chests, etc.  Basically you are looking for items to help your hirelings build better equipment for you, and you are looking for GOLD to buy more upgrades.  Eventually the traps or the monsters will kill you.
Now you get to choose one of your children, each of whom has different characteristics, to take your place in the next run.  Your new hero can spend all the gold you found on the previous run.  Just remember to spend it all because again Charon will take whatever you have left before you enter the castle again.  Some hero traits are good (like "OCD" which restores some MP when you break furniture) and some are not so good (like glaucoma which makes the world go dark so it is hard to see where you are going).
Each time you die, the castle will CHANGE so you get a whole new map to explore.  There is a hireling who can LOCK it in its last layout, but he will collect a huge portion of the gold you find in return for his service.  If you really love a certain map it might be worth it, but otherwise just enjoy the randomness of it.

The game drew me in because of the beautiful graphics, immersive audio and dynamic weather. I've put in 62 hours into the game, so at a dollar per hour, I can say that I've wrung my expected entertainment when I paid full price. It's a damn shame that when so much work has been put in to make this such a gorgeous and immersive "simulation", there are game-breaking bugs that stop me from recommending this game to anyone.
The callers have a rage-inducing bug that loops the animation as you raise the caller to your lips, and put it down again. I've lost countless kills to this bug, while animals wander towards my initial call and I'm helplessly stuck mashing keys in hopes of equipping anything else, and I watch them haul♥♥♥♥♥once they notice me with pants around my ankles.
I've googled for fixes, only seeing posts after posts of gamers helping other users with tips like "you gotta right click at the right moment, and it might stop the loop. Works for me sometimes." Since release devs are silent on any updates or bug fixes, but they're releasing a new map this month, at the low low price of 7.99. I was also suckered into purchasing the ATV, that I believe is ESSENTIAL to the gameplay because of how vast the maps are, you aren't able to reach checkpoints unless you're willing to put in hefty time to traversing the map at a snail's pace.
In short, I'm disgusted that the devs aren't interested in fixing bugs, or releasing new content unless you cough up more cash. I can't support or recommend this game because these kinds of practices set precedent for future games, and it's not something I'm willing to encourage.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 (or ETS2 as I'll be refering it as) is one of the best simulators available to date in my opinion. Most simulators are games that allow you to only achieve or do one specific set of actions then just continuously repeat them. ETS2 has so much more depth than a normal simulator would normally have by allowing the player to not only drive around freely when not completing orders, but allows the player to start their own company and slowly expand and grow an empire in the trucking industry. This simulator also allows you to drive all accross Europe (islandic and continental) just at a smaller scale with diverging routes rather than just making you stick to a single road for exceedingly long periods of time. The graphics that this game has also shatters that of most simulators by not only displaying damage done to the vehicle, but by showing the effects of rain upon the truck and road (the rain also causes the road to become more slippery if you so wish adding to the realism) as well as allowing you to customize not only your own truck with different appearance and performance changes, but allows you to do so with every single truck in your company. If I was to rate this game for specific characteristics, graphics: 9/10, gameplay: 10/10, replayability: 10/10. In the end, ETS2 is a must have for any simulator enthusiast, people who simply enjoy a nice calming drive around the city or country (such as myself), or people who like seeing their creations grow from something small to an expansive empire (aka Monopoly enthusiasts)

What can be said about Undertale?
Its characters are loveable and funny, it's clever and unique and the story is compelling, emotional and sometimes makes you wanna cry! Either a story of pacifist play or genocide on all life, this game gives you a level of choice not present in other RPGs. I guarantee you'll enjoy every moment in this game!
The story is great. You have to complete all of the endings to fully understand what's going on in this world. I honestly can't think of a bad part of story direction or plot-hole. Every part is fleshed out and enjoyable. It really fills you with determination! Get it... no... oh...
The characters feel like real people. They aren't 1-dimensional or a cliche that's been over-saturated; they all feel like somebody you would find in a real world and not in a terrible video game. There's always character down to the bone! Get it, cuz one of the characters is a skeleton... no... it seems my jokes aren't pulling your funny bone! I've got a serious problem with these puns...
The animation and visuals aren't a revolution, but they sure do feel very nostalgic.
The gameplay is like if you mixed an RPG and a bullet-hell shooter in a blender. It's enjoyable and fast-paced.
So there you have it - Undertale in a nutshell, spoiler-free. I personally think it's one of my favourite games. Do I recommend it? Whaddya think? I've drowned it in positivity! Of course I recommend it! It's one of my favourite games! Seriously, this game's great and I think you'll like it.
