For this reduced price (30€) I can certainly recommend the game. The multiplayer is solid, like pretty much every Call of Duty. There are a few innovations over Black Ops and Modern Warfare 3, like the revamped killstreaks, the class creation system, weapon unlocking mechaning, and some pretty unique weapons. The maps are alright, nothing to special there. I can recommend Nuketown 2025 and Hijacked the most since I always seemed to have the most fun on them. I don't really like the perks since some of them like "Dexterity" or "Toughness" are just pretty much no-brainers and you always end up taking them no matter what, really hurting variety in the respect. Same goes for the weapon pool in some respect, I'd have liked to see more than 4 weapons in the majority of categories. The only categories that DO have more than 4 weapons available are Assault Rifles and SMGs, everything else doesn't offer much variety. As for weapon balance, its pretty good fram what I experienced. There a some, if very few over/underpowerd guns like the "Executioner" which is a terrible shotgun-revolver-thingy, and some that are mostly stronger than everything else in its class like the "AN-94". That's another problem right there: Since the classes mostly only have 4 weapons available, its pretty common that one gun kind of trumps that class. For example, there are 4 LMGs. Two of them are Beltfed and the other two are magazine based, which leaves te first two with larger magazines and longer reload times, while the other two are the exact opposite. One of those LMGs in each category is more long-range and the other more short-range capable. Now, one of the first attribute is going to end up being better than the other one. There is just no balancing right there, it's more or less a fact. Same goes for the second attribute, which leads to one gun of the four of them being the best allrounder, even if it lacks a few skills the other guns have. And that again leads to you, and most people online just using that one gun in every class. I would like to tell you can use these guns situtaionally, for example if you play a long-ranged map like Metldown you can use the long-range HAMR, or if you play a short-ranged one like Nuketown you just use the QBB LSW. But you can't really do that unless you're willing to actually go out of your way and pay anoter 1,99€ for a slotpack DLC, because you only get 5 custom classes by default! That doesn't leave you with much flexibility when it comes to choosing situatinal weapons, because if you're anything like me you'll want to have at least one custom class for every weapon category, and not four classes just for LMGs. Also, if you're going into this thinking of quickscoping, I have to tell you that you're probably better of with anoter CoD that suits itself better to that. Don't get me wrong, its perfectly possible but due to long zoom-in times with pretty much every sight and extremely slow firerates AND bolt-action prolonging time inbetween shots, it's pretty damn challenging since you can get mowed down so very fast. If you do want to try it out though anyways, I can safely tell you that the "Ballista" with an ACOG-Scope is by far the best candidate for quickscoping.
I think that's all I wanted to say. For 30€ (Or your reginal equivalent) I can definetely recommend this game for all the fun I had, which do almost completely shadow the flaws I just mentioned for awareness purposes.

Bought this game after seeing how highly recommended it was. Loved the storyline and how your morality comes into play.
Most shooters don't make you question your choices (most don't really have any), and majority of the time, shooters are pretty simple- run and gun your way from point A to point B using the weapons you have around you and make sure you don't get yourself killed. Simple. Spec Ops: The Line, on the other hand, starts off running the same way any shooter would: you have enemies ahead, kill them and move on. Then it hits you with choices and decisions you don't expect to have any impact on your gameplay or expect to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥a few minutes later.
Without wanting to spoil too much, I highly recommend this game. While the controls are a bit clunky sometimes (run and cover are the same key and many times you end up in frustrating situations where you're crouching in full view of enemy fire) and some of the firefights can be pretty tedious, but those issues can be easily fixed and aren't really as important. It's not aesthetically graphics heavy- considering how the game is based in Dubai buffeted with giant sandstorms, but its art style does have impact, especially coupled with the story. The game is worth it immensely for its storyline and in the end, I found myself replaying certain parts just to see what difference another choice would've made.
Don't spoil it for yourself by looking for which choice is best in each situation as you play. Go into it blind (or mostly so) and experience it for yourself.

Spec Ops: The Line. I can't say enough about how good this game is, so I won't....... This game is beyond that. I haven't had a game that has made me come to tears 13 hours AFTER I completed it and I am writing a review. Right now my eyes began watering as I think about what could be the appropriate discription of such a heart-wrenching game. This game isn't about the main character. It's about you... and me. When I pressed the buttons on my gamepad and began firing a weapon, I no longer was controlling a character. I was there. I killed those people. Captain Martin Walker didn't kill those people, Colonel John Konrad didn't kill those people.... I did. And there is no reason why you or anyone, shouldn't play this game. The emotional death toll on your heart is enough to make a man question his own life.

Right off the bat, I'm gonna say 6/10. This game, while it has an amazing story, was what a cover-based third person shooter was not supposed to be. The story about the three American soldiers sent in to find out what's going on in Dubai was just fantastic, but the gameplay just doesn't do the story justice. If they made a movie about just the story mode of this game, with little to no gameplay involved, it'd be a pretty good movie; probably an 8/10. It's only benefit is that the game is so short, that the story can at least be acknowledged. At less than 5 hours long, the gameplay for the game starts off like any other cover-based shooter, but eventually turns to be ridiculous as even in normal mode, you're spending 3 clips of ammo for a heavy machine gun into the head of an enemy foot-soldier. Why? Because helmets protect them from headshots, and the enemies ALSO know how to use cover. They also use some gimmicks here and there to keep you interested, but it's not enough to get past the horrible gameplay they made. I'm still recommending it, but only due to the story. Just watch it in a video, or play easy mode. You don't want to be playing this any longer than you have to.

I could post a meme, but instead I'll post this:
When I first saw the trailer for this game, I was deeply cynical. I thought it looked really dumb. I was reminded of people whom I will not name, who participate in communities that require a lifetime of reading/participating in a very long browser-based narrative that I will also not name. Many of my friends are fond of this narrative. I respect their interests, but also do not wish to participate, for almost every color aspect of the styles used cause me extreme eye strain.
Then, I picked up this game upon release. It was on a whim. I was certain that I would dislike it, in spite of the fact that the few reviews around at the time were very excited, it didn't seem like something I would like. The one thing that sold me on it was the constant joking the playerbase was getting at. What was this "determination"? I would find it. And find it I did.
Now I stand before you, a changed person. This game is great. All of the characters quickly begin to feel like your actual friends. Also, the music is awesome and feels like a throwback to the games I played on my uncles Gameboy when I was visiting my grandmothers house. The art style is actually really nice, and as you move through the different places in the game you'll begin to realize that the simple style was completely on purpose, as the locations have some of the best pixel art I'd seen up to that point.
I would recommend this game. Especially to people who hate the game just because other people liked the game. Try to go in without expectations. Imo, it's pretty great, and has left me with a number of memories that can still make me chuckle.
Good luck out there!

Bought this game after seeing how highly recommended it was. Loved the storyline and how your morality comes into play.
Most shooters don't make you question your choices (most don't really have any), and majority of the time, shooters are pretty simple- run and gun your way from point A to point B using the weapons you have around you and make sure you don't get yourself killed. Simple. Spec Ops: The Line, on the other hand, starts off running the same way any shooter would: you have enemies ahead, kill them and move on. Then it hits you with choices and decisions you don't expect to have any impact on your gameplay or expect to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥a few minutes later.
Without wanting to spoil too much, I highly recommend this game. While the controls are a bit clunky sometimes (run and cover are the same key and many times you end up in frustrating situations where you're crouching in full view of enemy fire) and some of the firefights can be pretty tedious, but those issues can be easily fixed and aren't really as important. It's not aesthetically graphics heavy- considering how the game is based in Dubai buffeted with giant sandstorms, but its art style does have impact, especially coupled with the story. The game is worth it immensely for its storyline and in the end, I found myself replaying certain parts just to see what difference another choice would've made.
Don't spoil it for yourself by looking for which choice is best in each situation as you play. Go into it blind (or mostly so) and experience it for yourself.

Spec Ops: The Line. I can't say enough about how good this game is, so I won't....... This game is beyond that. I haven't had a game that has made me come to tears 13 hours AFTER I completed it and I am writing a review. Right now my eyes began watering as I think about what could be the appropriate discription of such a heart-wrenching game. This game isn't about the main character. It's about you... and me. When I pressed the buttons on my gamepad and began firing a weapon, I no longer was controlling a character. I was there. I killed those people. Captain Martin Walker didn't kill those people, Colonel John Konrad didn't kill those people.... I did. And there is no reason why you or anyone, shouldn't play this game. The emotional death toll on your heart is enough to make a man question his own life.

Right off the bat, I'm gonna say 6/10. This game, while it has an amazing story, was what a cover-based third person shooter was not supposed to be. The story about the three American soldiers sent in to find out what's going on in Dubai was just fantastic, but the gameplay just doesn't do the story justice. If they made a movie about just the story mode of this game, with little to no gameplay involved, it'd be a pretty good movie; probably an 8/10. It's only benefit is that the game is so short, that the story can at least be acknowledged. At less than 5 hours long, the gameplay for the game starts off like any other cover-based shooter, but eventually turns to be ridiculous as even in normal mode, you're spending 3 clips of ammo for a heavy machine gun into the head of an enemy foot-soldier. Why? Because helmets protect them from headshots, and the enemies ALSO know how to use cover. They also use some gimmicks here and there to keep you interested, but it's not enough to get past the horrible gameplay they made. I'm still recommending it, but only due to the story. Just watch it in a video, or play easy mode. You don't want to be playing this any longer than you have to.

Mad Max is a game set in a world where careless waste, political terrorism, and general public unhappiness was permitted to boil over into full out rage, leaving the world a scarred, barren wasteland.
The world of Mad Max, is completely different, from the world you and I know. The world you delve into in this game, is ruled by violence, governed by strife, fueled by crude oil, gasoline, and rig job cars built for war, and the only living one does here, is a filthy, misserable, dry-mouthed and perpually starving one, but in this world, simply being alive is a luxury few can claim to own. In this world, a car is required to be anyone or anything, including alive, and nothing but death, and dry bones await those with no car to carry them over the seemingly endless dunes of sand, which have long since covered the unfortunate would-be's who tried to survive before them. Money is worthless here, little more than tinder. The only thing people care about here, the only thing one could safely call 'money'. Is scrap metal. Piles of it, things used to create more cars, and therefore, more survival.
The game is set in an obscure area in future America, seemingly in an old refinery town long since lost to the sands of sorrow. The only thing still standing, and furiously customized to grow to a sorry, pathetic excuse for a community, is Gastown, a large refinery that still stands and pumps gasoline, natural gas, and oil from the ground below at reckless speeds to fuel the governing group of lunatics, psychopaths, and bestial, carnage worshipping madmen: The War Boys of Scrotus. Much of the game happens in the southern outskirts of this town, a small 'oasis' that, upon arrival in it, seems more like a cruel joke, this area is a small space in the middle of what seems to be an endless expense of send dunes, extending for as long and as far and as unforgivingly constant as the eye can see no matter how high into the sky you go(with airballoon included). Wastelanders and Madmen alike refer to this ocean of endless death and barren dryness that surrounds their homeland as "The Big Nothing", and is routinely referred to as the place desperate people go, not to seek a better life, no matter what they themselves think, but to die. Some rumors say that the oceans which used to fill the entire area, which receeded many many many years ago, still recide far far beyond the Big Nothing, and if one survives the trek across it, they'll be rewarded with a sight of an endless ocean, stretching as far, if not further, than the big nothing, a never ending blanket of pure blue. Many have tried to seek this, and have never been heard from again, which only spurs the rumors on.
Gameplay:
First of all, yes, this game is an open world action RPG game with a garnish of crash car derby style gameplay.
You play between driving and on-foot exploring most of the time. Long-range weaponry like handguns or rifles are a thing of the past, and extremely rare. Few rifles exist, and even few small arms. The only shotgun seemingly in existence for hundreds or thousands of miles around is Max's own.
Driving is by far the most entertaining, but also the most difficult, requiring some driving skill depending on what surface you drive on, what tire type your car has on, and how much armor you wear(Cause armor is heavy and might make you stuck in the sand!). Car combat is a fine-tuned dance between excellence, and complete failure, it is almost impossible to be 'sort of successful' or 'sort of failure'.
On foot is more straight forward. Mad Max is not just the name of the game, but also the protagonist whom you play. He is indeed mad, and is prone to bouts of uncontrolable rage towards those who attack him, sending him into a state the war-like factions call 'Kamicrazy'. He is, despite his lunacy, extremely skilled at hand to hand combat, and is capable of downing dozens of manic enemies with little effort(Assuming you're good at the game).
The game has lots of content, many side missions, and countless things to do and see in the world. From lowering the presense of the incredibly powerful and horrificly aggressive faction called 'The Warboys of Scrotus', to progressing the main story of helping Max rebuild his lost 'Black on Black' car, which he loses in the prelude to the game's beginning. A new car, which he begins to build with the help of his newly found friend and ally, Chumbucket, the hunchbacked 'black finger' super mechanic, who knows little more than twisted, gas-combustion based religion, and making engines go vroom and wheels to spin. This car is named by Chumbucket, and is named 'The Magnum Opus'. Foretold by Chum to become 'faster, stronger, and better in every way, than the black on black, filled with holy purpose.'
Graphics:
The graphics are appropriate for the game, requiring not much in the way of fauna or foliage since no plants seemingly exist in the world, anywhere. There is just dust, rock, and crude oil oceans made up of saturated sand. The graphics can be good, without being crazy, and still look amazingly detailed and more than adequate for giving a very realistic, very high caliber experience. Based on what I can tell, it appears that a lower grade rig could play this game at lower settings than highest/max, but it's always a good idea to google 'can I run it' and see what that says about your chances.
Sound:
It supports 7.1 surround sound, which is pretty flipping wonderful. I wish more games did. It gives an extremely realistic settings that makes you feel like you're standing in the middle of it. Of course you'd need 7.1 capable headphones, which mine are. Other than that, there's no desyncing between the voices and the animation of the mouthes, and the sound quality is very high, from both voice actors' skill, to the sounds taken for engines, and metal grinding against metal.
Final word:
I'm sure all of you want me to answer this question: "Do you recommend it or not!?" And yes, I absolutely do. I have little to nothing bad to say about this game. Extremely well executed, extremely well put together, an overall victory of considerable magnitude for the developpers responsible for this fine-polished diamond of a video game. If you like steampunky, violent, bitter and gorey messy games that takes unbearable living conditions, and makes them the norm for human survival and living style? Then this game will surely scratch that itch for guzzoline guzzling, oil burning, oil slicked finger licking car games that many of us have.
I, for one, have been absolutely addicted to this game for the past 4 days, and I see no end to the game yet.

What can be said about Undertale?
Its characters are loveable and funny, it's clever and unique and the story is compelling, emotional and sometimes makes you wanna cry! Either a story of pacifist play or genocide on all life, this game gives you a level of choice not present in other RPGs. I guarantee you'll enjoy every moment in this game!
The story is great. You have to complete all of the endings to fully understand what's going on in this world. I honestly can't think of a bad part of story direction or plot-hole. Every part is fleshed out and enjoyable. It really fills you with determination! Get it... no... oh...
The characters feel like real people. They aren't 1-dimensional or a cliche that's been over-saturated; they all feel like somebody you would find in a real world and not in a terrible video game. There's always character down to the bone! Get it, cuz one of the characters is a skeleton... no... it seems my jokes aren't pulling your funny bone! I've got a serious problem with these puns...
The animation and visuals aren't a revolution, but they sure do feel very nostalgic.
The gameplay is like if you mixed an RPG and a bullet-hell shooter in a blender. It's enjoyable and fast-paced.
So there you have it - Undertale in a nutshell, spoiler-free. I personally think it's one of my favourite games. Do I recommend it? Whaddya think? I've drowned it in positivity! Of course I recommend it! It's one of my favourite games! Seriously, this game's great and I think you'll like it.

The gameplay is essentially that of a fairly simple, linear, third person, cover-based shooter. However it is fun to play. There's a variety of weapons to play with which are all quite fun to use. The main reason to switch between them is the limited ammo - it is very rare in a game that I have to switch to my side-arm because I've run out. Your two mates never get in the way and really feel like a valuable part of your squad. I genuinely felt a sense of desperation when one of them was out of action and I needed to get over to him to heal him.
The main thrust of this game is the story. It actually managed to get me involved emotionally. Throughout, one has the niggling feeling that we don't really know what's going on and, without spoiling anything, it turns out there's a good reason for that. It conveys a sense of increasing confusion on the part of the characters. The dialogue is well-acted, with Bruce Boxleitner fitting well as Konrad. It's arguable that more complicated gameplay would detract from the story-telling and I find that that this can often be a difficult balance to achieve. Soldiers tend to be simple creatures though and I think the right balance has, more or less, been achieved.
The game has a few features that made me smile. For example, kicking an enemy in the face by vaulting over a barricade. The sand effects are unique in my experience and add to the game both in terms of visual spectacle and putting you into the story which is set in a place ravaged by sandstorms.
Overall, whilst this isn't a long game - it took me seven hours to complete - I would definitely recommend it. The gameplay is relatively generic but fun, and the story - which I feel is the main reason for playing - is strong.

All I remember of Mad Max was a dusty Mel Gibson, a big bad car, and feeling a connection to the desperate wanderers he came across.  In a way, it's one of the first apocalyptic worlds I'd ever seen.  It has it's appeal.  Thunderdome and Tina Turner with the crazies and bloodlust.  These days it's all post-apocalyptic hell with zombies, so seeing a wasteland in a new but familiar universe of Mad Max wasn't hard to process and a nice change for all the end-of-the-world-ness in games I see.
Well then, what's it all about?  Giant open world areas, some fun car caravan takedowns, the usual batman-eque fighting, using a  fast car to destroy stuff, and mostly enjoying the world of Mad Max in a video game.  A first I thought, "Ok, Batman-junior with a car. Not bad".  There is a fervor in the knuckle-fighting that is Max.  It's not a precise brawler, yet not a hack n slash either.  I couldn't really stop, though.  Insert coin, get video game fast food adrenaline rush.  My goal was to try and take them all down without firing a shot, that made the fights extra edgy.
The fun bit for *me*, though....the open world car takedowns.  And this varies from gamer to gamer because some folks dislike open world.  Personally, I just dive in and forget to actually play the missions.  After playing for a few hours I left the main campaign and drove around the open world leveling up for 20+ hrs.  Then I got back to the campaign all uber-leveled with a wonderfully growling car only to find I could not get to the next mission. I wasted about an hour or more trying to get it to work.  Finally, I gave up and looked online. I found I had to level *down* my car to get to the next mission.  What is up with that?  At least give me a hint, but to keep it completely out of the mission description?  Weird.  Why bother making an open world if you need a linear leveling playthrough?  So, *that* kinda stunk.
Next up was learning to attack cars, gates, and snipers with my grapple hook.  Soon to be upgraded to a THUNDERPOON.  Yep, it's called a THUNDERPOON.  Basically having a lightweight RPG gunner in the back of your car.  Sweet.  But I preferred the grapple personally.  Maybe it's more batman-ish, but I enjoyed aiming it at tires and stopping bad guys with a hook to the chest.  Pooning was a bit too easy and I only used it for aiming at gas tanks at camps.  Some of those camps had several flame inducing gas tanks, snipers in tight areas, and defense towers made of shooting fireballs. These were a great joy to attack.  That was the best part really.  Once you got past the defenses, you crack some heads until you get to a mini-boss with minions and usually giant blazing stationary flamethowers.  I ran my bosses into those as a fast way to finish.  The problem?  ALL the mini-bosses were like that.  It got old after awhile.  Even down to the last side mission, it was all the same attack, evade, attack.  Not much to it.  Makes me scratch my head how come they didn't add some variety to the bosses.  It would have added so much more to the game if *any* of them had some special abilities.
Now I loved the driving and chasing the bad guy on their supply routes.  It was sorta GTA style and even though the car was hard to maneuver I never got tired of it.  You can add more armor and stabilizers to get better handling, but I found the armor slowed me down.  Better to stay light to keep up.  Unless you skid out of control and end up in a ditch.  But, the car could take a good beating.  The death runs were okay and just required a bit of practice to remember where to slow down and speed up. Using nitro was also a good help on a straight path with it's fast speed boost, but in general made me lose total control if I made any sort of turn.  What NAILED me was the race against Stank Gum. It was there - after a bajillion attempts - that i realized i had too much armor and needed to lighten up the car to keep up. Once I did that, i was able to complete the mission with just a handful of tries.  That can be the hardest part of the game, or the easiest.  Depends how good you are at driving games and how heavy your car is when you start.
Right around that part of the game, the story *finally* gets interesting.  Before, it was mostly summer-movie-story-action filler.  But towards the last 15% of the game the story makes some good progress. Which is great because after awhile I would just get bored and chat with my buddies on steam or watch twitch while I played 10 minutes every hr.
Some nights I'd play maybe 20 minutes with the game running all night long.  I was losing my interest pretty bad.  Past the Stank Gum mission, though, you may finish the game a little faster because it's getting more varied as you go.  I will say the end mission is pretty decent and I felt like it was a good ending.  I'm not going to spoil it, but that ending was a lot better than say the ending to Shadow of Mordor.  I had to play the Bright Lord DLC to get a good ending to Mordor - which is a shame because I *loved* Mordor other than that ending.  Mad Max ends well and becomes a decent game towards the last 15%  of the campaign.
Story isn't much, but it's voice acted well and frankly I liked the storyline more than the movie.  That isn't saying much because the movie was mostly an action packed sequence with little dialogue going on ( in my opinion ).  But the game has a lot more going on.  What it *is* missing is the connection to the people surviving out there in the vast dry death of a world Max lives in.  You get some connections here and there, but mostly you bounce from camp to camp and just do missions without really talking to anyone.  Where is the love?  Max is a loner, I get it.  But, wow, there wasn't anything even close to a personal experience until the end.
Art direction is a gritty gorgeous wasteland.  A perfect Mad Max open world with quite a lot of detailed landscape and nicely working physics.  I got into it.  Maybe I'm a loner too, who knows, but it appealed to me.  At least until I finished and decided I need to move on to my backlog again.  Lemme drive all over and smash into bad guy cars.  I loved that.
One more thing towards the end - and here I will be critical - it gets more and more glitchy.   A few scenes had my car inside of another car, I drove all the way to the end of a mission only to get stuck on geometry for 15 minutes while i wiggled everything possible, and the occasional cutscene where the person's head disappeared.  But my biggest gripe was the last side quest.  Someone decided to make it only work *at night*.
I could not fast forward time!  I tried upgrading the camps with scrap metal which seems to fast forward time a bit, but it would miss the nighttime somehow.  So, i drove around for over 2 hrs until I got to a night scene in order to finish the game sidequests. That was *so* annoying.  Somebody got cut a check for that idea.  Arrgh. I'm glad I went into this game with low expectations, as movie-franchise games usually are.
I was completely, utterly wrong. This open-world-style post-apocalyptic alternate-universe Australia simulator is fantastic!
Action, artwork, cutscenes, voice acting, characters, graphics... all fantastic. And man, I could write a poem on how they managed to capture the throaty sounds of a supercharged V6 gas-engined car (soon to be extinct!) in this game. Love the little details like fire dribbling from the exhaust, the explosion detail, ripping parts off cars during road fights with your Harpoon, the ambient life, the desolation, all the fun tools at your disposal for dispatching vehicles, people and structures... I even like that I've died quite a few times already, because it means this game is NOT EASY. :) The physics engine is quite accurate, the lighting effects are fantastic/atmospheric.
The only criticism I can think of is that the entire earth must have been covered by ocean before the Apocalypse as there are dry coral reefs, dry seaweed, and dock piers jutting out into empty space EVERYWHERE. (Was that part of the story? Things got flooded and then completely dry?) Anyway it's probably something I missed, as all the OTHER attention to detail in this game is fantastic and super-immersive.
I wish I was able to carry ONE melee weapon permanently, but whatever. I got this game for $20 in a Steam sale and that was a goddamn STEAL.

Mad Max is a game set in a world where careless waste, political terrorism, and general public unhappiness was permitted to boil over into full out rage, leaving the world a scarred, barren wasteland.
The world of Mad Max, is completely different, from the world you and I know. The world you delve into in this game, is ruled by violence, governed by strife, fueled by crude oil, gasoline, and rig job cars built for war, and the only living one does here, is a filthy, misserable, dry-mouthed and perpually starving one, but in this world, simply being alive is a luxury few can claim to own. In this world, a car is required to be anyone or anything, including alive, and nothing but death, and dry bones await those with no car to carry them over the seemingly endless dunes of sand, which have long since covered the unfortunate would-be's who tried to survive before them. Money is worthless here, little more than tinder. The only thing people care about here, the only thing one could safely call 'money'. Is scrap metal. Piles of it, things used to create more cars, and therefore, more survival.
The game is set in an obscure area in future America, seemingly in an old refinery town long since lost to the sands of sorrow. The only thing still standing, and furiously customized to grow to a sorry, pathetic excuse for a community, is Gastown, a large refinery that still stands and pumps gasoline, natural gas, and oil from the ground below at reckless speeds to fuel the governing group of lunatics, psychopaths, and bestial, carnage worshipping madmen: The War Boys of Scrotus. Much of the game happens in the southern outskirts of this town, a small 'oasis' that, upon arrival in it, seems more like a cruel joke, this area is a small space in the middle of what seems to be an endless expense of send dunes, extending for as long and as far and as unforgivingly constant as the eye can see no matter how high into the sky you go(with airballoon included). Wastelanders and Madmen alike refer to this ocean of endless death and barren dryness that surrounds their homeland as "The Big Nothing", and is routinely referred to as the place desperate people go, not to seek a better life, no matter what they themselves think, but to die. Some rumors say that the oceans which used to fill the entire area, which receeded many many many years ago, still recide far far beyond the Big Nothing, and if one survives the trek across it, they'll be rewarded with a sight of an endless ocean, stretching as far, if not further, than the big nothing, a never ending blanket of pure blue. Many have tried to seek this, and have never been heard from again, which only spurs the rumors on.
Gameplay:
First of all, yes, this game is an open world action RPG game with a garnish of crash car derby style gameplay.
You play between driving and on-foot exploring most of the time. Long-range weaponry like handguns or rifles are a thing of the past, and extremely rare. Few rifles exist, and even few small arms. The only shotgun seemingly in existence for hundreds or thousands of miles around is Max's own.
Driving is by far the most entertaining, but also the most difficult, requiring some driving skill depending on what surface you drive on, what tire type your car has on, and how much armor you wear(Cause armor is heavy and might make you stuck in the sand!). Car combat is a fine-tuned dance between excellence, and complete failure, it is almost impossible to be 'sort of successful' or 'sort of failure'.
On foot is more straight forward. Mad Max is not just the name of the game, but also the protagonist whom you play. He is indeed mad, and is prone to bouts of uncontrolable rage towards those who attack him, sending him into a state the war-like factions call 'Kamicrazy'. He is, despite his lunacy, extremely skilled at hand to hand combat, and is capable of downing dozens of manic enemies with little effort(Assuming you're good at the game).
The game has lots of content, many side missions, and countless things to do and see in the world. From lowering the presense of the incredibly powerful and horrificly aggressive faction called 'The Warboys of Scrotus', to progressing the main story of helping Max rebuild his lost 'Black on Black' car, which he loses in the prelude to the game's beginning. A new car, which he begins to build with the help of his newly found friend and ally, Chumbucket, the hunchbacked 'black finger' super mechanic, who knows little more than twisted, gas-combustion based religion, and making engines go vroom and wheels to spin. This car is named by Chumbucket, and is named 'The Magnum Opus'. Foretold by Chum to become 'faster, stronger, and better in every way, than the black on black, filled with holy purpose.'
Graphics:
The graphics are appropriate for the game, requiring not much in the way of fauna or foliage since no plants seemingly exist in the world, anywhere. There is just dust, rock, and crude oil oceans made up of saturated sand. The graphics can be good, without being crazy, and still look amazingly detailed and more than adequate for giving a very realistic, very high caliber experience. Based on what I can tell, it appears that a lower grade rig could play this game at lower settings than highest/max, but it's always a good idea to google 'can I run it' and see what that says about your chances.
Sound:
It supports 7.1 surround sound, which is pretty flipping wonderful. I wish more games did. It gives an extremely realistic settings that makes you feel like you're standing in the middle of it. Of course you'd need 7.1 capable headphones, which mine are. Other than that, there's no desyncing between the voices and the animation of the mouthes, and the sound quality is very high, from both voice actors' skill, to the sounds taken for engines, and metal grinding against metal.
Final word:
I'm sure all of you want me to answer this question: "Do you recommend it or not!?" And yes, I absolutely do. I have little to nothing bad to say about this game. Extremely well executed, extremely well put together, an overall victory of considerable magnitude for the developpers responsible for this fine-polished diamond of a video game. If you like steampunky, violent, bitter and gorey messy games that takes unbearable living conditions, and makes them the norm for human survival and living style? Then this game will surely scratch that itch for guzzoline guzzling, oil burning, oil slicked finger licking car games that many of us have.
I, for one, have been absolutely addicted to this game for the past 4 days, and I see no end to the game yet.

I could post a meme, but instead I'll post this:
When I first saw the trailer for this game, I was deeply cynical. I thought it looked really dumb. I was reminded of people whom I will not name, who participate in communities that require a lifetime of reading/participating in a very long browser-based narrative that I will also not name. Many of my friends are fond of this narrative. I respect their interests, but also do not wish to participate, for almost every color aspect of the styles used cause me extreme eye strain.
Then, I picked up this game upon release. It was on a whim. I was certain that I would dislike it, in spite of the fact that the few reviews around at the time were very excited, it didn't seem like something I would like. The one thing that sold me on it was the constant joking the playerbase was getting at. What was this "determination"? I would find it. And find it I did.
Now I stand before you, a changed person. This game is great. All of the characters quickly begin to feel like your actual friends. Also, the music is awesome and feels like a throwback to the games I played on my uncles Gameboy when I was visiting my grandmothers house. The art style is actually really nice, and as you move through the different places in the game you'll begin to realize that the simple style was completely on purpose, as the locations have some of the best pixel art I'd seen up to that point.
I would recommend this game. Especially to people who hate the game just because other people liked the game. Try to go in without expectations. Imo, it's pretty great, and has left me with a number of memories that can still make me chuckle.
Good luck out there!

One of my favorite parts of this game is the unique characters you can play as. There are many classes that can be unlocked and played as, and they allow for different strategies and tactics while playing. Each time you die you get to choose your heir, and have a choice from three heirs with different characteristics that can be helpful or detrimental.
The castle you storm each run is filled with various enemies and is the first "stage" if you will, of the game. Three other "stages" surround the castle each run in the same configuration, but the rooms themselves are different every time. Each stage has it's own boss, and most runs you will come across one or two minibosses. There is gold to be found, armor and weapon blueprints, and runes that can enhance your character.
Every time you die, you start with an heir outside of the castle, and you can use the gold earned from the previous run to buy upgrades like new classes, or upgrades for classes, as well as upgrades to your HP, Mana for spells, crit chance, damage, and many other attributes. You can also buy different armors or weapons or runes that you find blueprints for in the castle. Once you enter the casle however, any money you have leftover will get taken away (the amount taken can be lowered by purchasing upgrades). Upgrading your character this way each time is probably one of the only aspects of this game that detract from it being called a rogue-like, however it is an excellent game.
I also recommend using a controller as I found the gameplay much easier and better with a controller, but a keyboard and mouse work also.

theHunter: Call of the Wild - Review after 30 hours of gameplay
TL;DR Skip to the bottom
This game feels like an early access game hidden beneath the guise of full release discussed in depth below.
theHunter: Call of the wild [First Impression]
theHunter: Call of the wild here-in referred to as CotW gives you an amazing first impression with it's stunningly beautiful graphical fidelity. The ambience of the soundtrack will make you feel totally immerssed in this hunting simulation style game. The wildlife feels, at first glance, realistic enough with their calls of mating, warning and pathing. It gives you just enough tutorial to throw you straight into the game to understand it's basic mechanics without overloading you, however, just too little to teach you how to play the game properly.
theHunter: Call of the wild [Maps]
Both the Lake and Hirchfelden maps will take your litterally hours to traverse around the borders of them with a variety of areas such as mountains, rivers, lakes, plains, and forests to explore for animals. So whether you are taking pictures with your ingame camera or hunting you'll have no shortage of beautiful terrain to walk through to do so.
Overall I'd rate the maps a stunning 8/10. While these maps are quite beautiful there are only 2 maps at the time of this review. If you spend any real amount of time in the game, you'll learn them like the back of your hand. They are not gigantic maps but they are big enough.
theHunter: Call of the wild [Progression]
It seems to be a growing trend in newer titles to have some form of progression system. Now while this works perfecly well with their leveling, skills and perks system it falls flat on it's face with weapons progression. To unlock higher end weapons you must use lesser weapons and their optics in harvested animals. Meaning you do not get the experience for your shots unless you track down your animal. It makes sense from how they implemented it but not why. There should be no need for progression on weapons. If I have the cash I should be able to purchase the weapon of my choosing regardless of the power of the weapon or view distance on the optic.
Overall I'd rate the progression system a solid 5/10. It's completely average with no real innovation though it does needlessly lock weapons behind a seperate experience system which to me is a negative.
theHunter: Call of the wild [Stealth]
CotW does have an intricate stealth system that works very well. You make noise as you move through grass, shrubs, bushes and trees making stalking prey a nice challenge for bow hunters and other close quarter hunters. It feels good to sneak up on your prey and take it down from stealth. Hiding in trees, bushes and tall shrubbery will also reduce your visibilty to animals making it an effective ambush location if you choose your spot well.
CotW does NOT have camoflague clothing that works with the stealth system. This means even if you buy the camoflague clothing, for a high price I might add, it does nothing but change how you look to other players as you play from a first person perspective. So unless you want to play CotW barbie dressup edition clothing does nothing for you and that is a real shame. If I'm hunting in real life, which I do, I buy camoflague to increase my chances of bagging that trophy whitetail. There is already a visibility reduction statistic built into ground blinds that could be attached to camoflague clothing. To me this is a simple and much NEEDED fix to make immediately.
Overall I'd rate the stealth system a very good 6/10. It's above average and does everything you'd expect it to. I've docked this from being better for the lack of real hunting camoflagues. A characteristic found in the much more venerable title of the same franchise, theHunter Classic.
theHunter: Call of the wild [Weapons]
CotW suffers from a serious lack in variety of weapons. You have 2 shotguns, 3 pistols, 3 bows, and 7 rifles. It's really quite pathetic. This compounded with the fact that each weapon of the same type has the exact same effective range is a complete joke. Every single rifle has the same effective range of 150 meters, that's it. As a military veteran of the united states army I can quite easily tell you that their .338 rifle has an effective range of over 500 meters and has confirmed hits at over that range. It's unacceptable at best. Weapons also suffer from poor audio balancing. When firing the .357 magnum pistol for the first time while wearing headphones at an average or above average volume level it will give you quite the startle. Where as the .223, .243, .270, and 7mm rifles all have a good balance of sound. The ammunition choices seem acceptable at first glance until you shoot a .270 round into a white tails lung and it fails to come out the other side or penetrate both lungs. I've had 1 shot using the soft tip ammunition penetrate both lungs in easily over 100 rounds fired into lungs. In real life soft tip expansion rifle rounds more often than not go clean threw the animal. They don't stop because they hit the shoulder bone either unless you're hunting something above the rifles weight class like a bison. The accuracy stats on these rifles is all over the place. As an example one of the lever action rifles has over 800% better accuracy than a BOLT ACTION .338 LAPUA MAGNUM! Have these developers done any weapons research whatsoever? Apparently not.
Overall I'd rate the weapons a lazy AF 1/10. There is no real weapon variety. The audio balancing is poor. The same range on all weapons is BEYOND lazy. The lack of realistic bullet penetration is pathetic and the accuracy ratings on some of these weapons is mind boggling inaccuracte.
theHunter: Call of the wild [Animal Artificial Intelligence]
CotW suffers from some of the WORST animal AI I have ever seen in a hunting game. As a former game developer and with a little exploration I was able to come to a logical conclusion.
|||
The following statement can be construed as hearsay as I do NOT have access to the games coding.
(I believe the AI to be run on a pathing map placed below the real map that the players walk on. I have seen this blank map and have reasonable suspition to believe that the cause of some of the horrible pathing of the animals can be attritubed to this.)
|||
Sooner or later you'll find animals that seem to walk completely in place without moving. Other times you'll find them running blindly into the same tree and sometimes for over 60 seconds. It's quite bizzare to watch an animal you've just shot at run at full speed, going nowhere, into a tree. I have also witness "sinking" animals where animals occasionally clip into the terrain. A bug common in theHunter series and still seems to be affecting the later titles as this bug is common around hills in both classic and CotW.
I've watched animals return time and time again to an area in which I have fired a rifle, shotgun and pistol in harvested the animal and watched them return to me without callers. We had believed animals to avoid hunting pressure areas but that does not seem to be the case 100% of the time. In fact it happens so frequently that I've managed to at one point harvest 6 animals within 50 meters of where i first shot 1, then the second, third, etc.
Overall I'd rate the Animals Artificial Intelligence at a 5/10. It's workable but could use some improvement.
theHunter: Call of the wild [Final Verdict]
While the game runs great on it's maximum settings and has very high quality ambience the game suffers from illogical design choices and lazy programming. The lack of working camoflague in a hunting simulator is unacceptable. The animals AI is servicable but needs work. The stealth system works good enough and is acceptable. The weapons system is a complete and utter joke.
Overall I'd rate it 5/10. I'll be on theHunter Classic until it's fixed.

There are three phrases I would use to describe Rogue Legacy.
The first is "difficult."
There are very few games produced today that are this difficult except when they are designed to be nearly impossible.  When you die, you actually DIE.  It's not a game over, but you continue the game as your next of kin.  Incidentally, if someone says they beat the game with their first character, they are most likely a liar.
For me, few games are difficult enough for me to start screaming and swearing when I die, while still being good enough and compelling enough for me to keep on going after 30 deaths.
The second is "consistently unique."
Being a rogue-lite, every time you enter the castle, the whole map is randomly generated.  By itself, that's nothing special.  Lots of games do that.  But when you combine that with the inherited traits of each offspring?  That's something new every time.  If your character is dyslexic, all in-game text is jumbled.  You have alzheimers?  Hope you don't rely on the map too much.  Dementia?  I won't give it away, but I will say yes, you ARE actually hearing that.
The third and final phrase is "%#&@!"
Refer back to point one.  Also point two if your character has Coprolalia.
Look for $3 this is about the best you're gonna do.

Borderlands makes me super aware that I'm playing a game-- in a good way. Staying highly amused by the NPC's behaviors, being entranced by the consistent art style of the series and being delighted at looting every inch of valuable scrap I see after violently ripping it from the corn-holes of murdered psychopaths makes maneuvering around Pandora a true delight. It allows me to voice my Gorilla-like aggression without polluting it's style with masculinity and overplayed 70s-era stereotypes of what a manly man (or woman) is. It's difficulty is scaled to a perfect amount that makes you, over time, grow and adjust to the hardness of the enemies just long enough to get comfortable before the next obstacle sodomizes you.
This is Pandora, the place where a pack of ravenous Skags trying to rip off your appendages is as normal as a springtime allergy. So what do you do, when you have allergies? You take an allergy pill. What do you do when you're faced with bloodthirsty skags? Bullets. Lots of them. The most hardened hunter on Earth is nothing compared to the average surviving individual on Pandora-- their badassery stems from the experience necessary to live longer than an hour in the wastes of the Borderlands.

Rogue Legacy is, as the name suggests, a Rogue-like RPG-meets-platformer. The objective is simple: fight, collect, die, improve and repeat. It uses its own repetitiveness to constantly evolve, improve and challenge your often flawed characters to progress further in the game... That's right. You have to die to live.
Rogue Legacy is probably my most underrated game. I've had this in my library for over a year, and have only just begun to play it properly! I recently picked it up for my Vita thanks to the PSN summer sale, and decided to give it a second go. Understanding the game mechanics right off the bat and having it running on a portable device is alot more rewarding than I originally thought, so I returned to my Steam copy. So yes, this review is over a year late, but I recommend Rogue Legacy.

There are games waiting in our libraries, waiting to be played, never being instaled. There are games we liked, but no more than that. There are excellent games, beautiful and with a great story. And then, there is Spec Ops: The Line.
This game is like a good glass of wine. You first taste it, enjoy the smell, the color. You then take a slip, and another one, tastier than the first. You begin to like it, to enjoy it. You continue slip after slip, enjoying it more and more. And then, at one point, the wine is gone. And you are left there, standing like an idiot, an empty glass in your hand, wondering what happened, trying to understand this strange feeling you've had. But the more you try, the less you can remember this bittersweet sensation in your mouth. This game will do that to you. It will bring you to strange, powerfull sensations and will suddenly leave you, feeling more alone, ashamed of what you are, wanting more, willing to understand. It is a must have for every player, as it will show you that videogames still can make you feel, and that sometimes, they are real art masterpieces.

I will say, I have played every Call of Duty to date, and Black Ops II just didn't please me.
There are several issues with the multiplayer, the most important one being the lack of dedicated servers. This leads to major lag issues with many people, myself included.
And there are pleanty of balancing issues with multiplayer. Some weapons seem too strong or too weak, there is hardly an inbetween. This results in only a couple weapons being used, as they are the stongest and there is no need to use others.
Maps are forgetable and complicated.
The zombies mode was quite an improvement from Black Ops. Zombies has always been my favorite part about Call of Duty, and I enjoyed what they have done with Zombies this time around.
However, there are a lot of issues with the main Zombies map, TranZit. The bus seems to be very buggy, as I find myself falling out of it when I was safely inside of it just a moment earlier.
And the multiplayer for Zombies has similar issues as multiplayer mode, there is a lot of lag.
However unlike multiplayer mode, the maps are very creative and memerable. I have only played TranZit and Die Rise.
And finally, the campaign mode. Unlike most people I actually play the story mode, and while most Call of Duty games (Mainly the Modern Warfare series) have a cookie cutter story, this one included, I found myself enjoying it. The actual story itself is rather boring, but the missions were fun. The addition of being able to customize your loadout in campaign is a nice touch as well.
Call of Duty: Black Ops II was a displeasing entry into the Call of Duty franchise. The campaign was enjoyable, as was Zombies mode, but multiplayer felt unfinished, with poor maps and unbalancing that has and never will be fixed. The game as a whole felt clumsy and not perfected for a PC.

I have a bit of a love/hate relationship with this game, yet I'm recommending it for one reason, and one reason alone, which you'll find at the end of my review. Note, I've played through the original LiS 6 times, and watched 25 (maybe more) entire play throughs from start to finish online.
It's a prequel to my favorite game of all time (I got a tattoo)... Yet somehow it feels so disingenuous, and incredibly unnecessary. Though there are little callbacks and references that are pretty neat if you catch them, which was nice.
To start, it's made by a completely different dev team, in a completely different engine... and it shows. Though the character models look way better, lighting and environmental visuals and effects take a hit, as well as performance. And it lacks the musical touch of jonathan morali, but the theme/menu music managed to strike a chord with me. Though the vocal tracks are all very same-y, and lack the perfect assimilation the tracks in LiS had into the experience. This is mainly because they're almost all from a single artist, who, to my understanding, made the tracks in tandom with the team solely for this game. ( which is commendable, but also probably to avoid licensing costs and potential royalties).
This causes a seeming lack of variety. All the vocal tracks also seem incredibly forced because they NEED to have the tracks because "LiS has licensed music tracks"! So instead of blending seemlessly with the experience, forever matching a certain song with a certain pivotal or immersive moment in your mind (ala "Something Good" at the beginning of Ep2, or "Obstacles" at the end of the first Episode after Max's revelation). Basically every track in BtS plays because someone LITERALLY plays it on a speaker, or through headphones, seemingly to hit a dev assigned music quotas per hour, or something. This happened a few times in the original ("To all of you", "got well soon", etc.) but it felt so integral in those examples, setting the stage for a raging party, Max receeding from the real world on her way to the bathroom (and opening you, the player, up to the entire experience to come), Max being snapped back to reality in Chloe's room, etc. It just feels so invasive and forced in BtS, almost painful.
But... Music aside, the most offensive, glaring issue plaguing this title, that makes it feel completely disconnected from anything we know as Life is Strange... is that EVERY voice actor was recast because of a strike that was taking place. EVERY. SINGLE. CHARACTER. Has a new actor. Why not wait a bit for a true to life (is strange) experience? Because they wanted to cash-in. If the devs truly cared as much as we're lead to believe (hell, as much as me) they'd have done so.
Ever go up to your friend that you've known for years, and suddenly they sound like a completely different person? They're not sick or anything, that's just how they talk now, completely different voice... No?? Me neither. But that's what it feels like with every single encounter with every familiar character from the original game. Right down to our main character, Chloe (if you can even call her that). They didn't even try to voice match with 95% of the characters, the only recast that I found to be acceptable was frank, with the vocal pitch and inflections being damn near perfect to the original iteration, it was easy for me to believe that was Frank.
But not for anyone else... It was such a jarring experience. I spent more time thinking about how different the characters sounded, and thus thinking about how they weren't the same characters, than I thought about what they were saying. It took me right out of the experience. Not that the actors are bad or anything, they just don't fit. It's like they replaced title actors in a film, and just expect you to play along like it's the same person (*cough* don cheadle in iron Man 2).
And secondly, another major issue... There's no real plot. I've finished the second episode of what's to be a 3 episode ride, and I just feel like nothing's happening. There's no stakes. We already know the outcome, we know what happens, there's no real suspense, or mystery. And what little there is feels incredibly manufactured for the sake of drama. Trying to tug on the feel strings like the first one through random plotpoints.
Which doesn't work, because you have to care about the story, and the characters. But when it feels like the characters are imposters and the story is pointless it makes it incredibly hard to give a damn. there's nothing important going on, Chloe has no risk, and again, as I've stated, there are no stakes. Not for Chloe, not for anyone. The original game had so much going on, REAL SH|T. People getting kidnapped, murdered, missing, drugged, beaten, time travel, a gigantic tornado, fuggin SUICIDE. Life is Strange had the intensity at 25/10 and it was all grounbded in a semi believable world (EVEN WITH TIME TRAVEL).
So... Why am I recommending it? With all it's faults... there are moments, fleeting, but inspiring, once per episode; that feel genuine. Pure Life is Strange at the core. Oddly enough these are simpler interactions with newly introduced characters (a game perhaps, or a performance ;), but during these moments... I forgot about all the issues I had with the game... I just got immersed in the experience. I was once again back at blackwell academy, I was once again apart of a world that I love. And it was amazing, albeit short-lived.
Is that a good enough reason to recommend this game to everyone? Absolutely not. I'd recommend you play the original instead, it's way better, by a landslide, even though it stumbleds at it's final episode. But, I recommend this game to you, if like me, you love LiS, and want for a moment to feel like you're back in that world, not even the whole time. Just for instances, but these instances are so sincere, and so enjoyable, that they carry my purchase alone.
Also, I'm happy with the length. If you're as observant and thorough as I am, then you'll get a lot of mileage per episode out of BtS. I've clocked 9 hours between 2 episodes, compared to 14-ish between the 5 in the original game my first run through.

My thoughts:
GOOD:
- Teamwork required.
- Scoring feels satisfying.
- Costumization.
- Good latency and lag compensation.
- Crew/Team Matches
- Easy to get into, hard to master.
- If you're good at the game in terms of skill you'll notice you beat people with a lot of P2W stuff but you'll probably lose anyways.

- MVP Rewards, the player that contributes more to the game/team gets awarded for it even if you lose.
BAD:
- Leveling is slow.
- No filters to sort out rooms.
- The game doesn't kick players that just stay there AFK (ex. You open a room and stay with it open forever without starting any game).
- No "click a button" Auto-Matchmaking to avoid room problems.
- It seems like there's low playerbase some times.
- A bunch of P2W stuff that you need to get better.
- Menus are a little confusing for new players but you'll get used to it.
- Should have a better introduction.
- Servers have problems, be sure you play on your closest region or you'll find yourself DCing or having lag problems.
*Overall it's really fun but difficult to get good at and understand how the game and systems work, give it a try!

A Unique Expierence (mild spoilers throughout)
Undertale is unlike any other game I've played before. Actually, I'm not even sure I can call this a game.It's really more like an interactive "choose your own adventure" story. While Undertale has some puzzles and battles scattered about here and there, what really sets this game apart and makes it shine is the writing. All of the stories discovered throughout the course of the game clearly have a lot of thought put into them. They don't just inform you, but they make you feel along with the characters as well. For instance. During the "walk of feels" in the neutral run - the way the story is spoken a little at a time by different characters actually makes you, the player, feel as though this story is being narrated by all these monsters affected by it. This aspect of narration just adds a layer of depth to the story and it reaches out, engaging the player in the story.
This leads to another great aspect of the game - the "choices matter" concept. Each battle faces the player with a choice - to kill or to spare - furthermore, the player also often has a choice when it comes to socalizing with other characters. They can choose whether or not they show compassion... or whether or not they listen to a character's backstory. And all these decisions can drastically affect the outcome(s) of the game. Through choices, you, the player, can end up being the hero OR the villian, and you get to see the benefits and consequences of each role, and each choice. (Though I must say, speaking of consequences, the game sure does do a great job making you feel terrible when you make too many bad choices... genocide run...)
Which leads me to the last point - personality. Toby Fox did such a great job giving each monster a unique personality. From the way they speak, to the stories they have, the game is fully capable of making the player feel many emotions twoards an 8 bit, pixelated drawing. The dialogue/stories aren't always optimal, but that is what makes the characters even more realistic - their imperfections. Furthermore, the game itself has quite the personality... espeically through Flowey, who tends to break the fourth-wall quite a bit, often refering to typical (often relatable) gamer and game sterotypes. It is a tad bizzare, but certianly unique and entertaining

Recommended, but barely.
Gameplay: Fun, furious, only moderately frustrating. It's like an Arkham Assylum game, without pretending the protagonist doesn't kill people. Some issues with counter timing, boss battles, and some of the car physics is ridiculous. Overall, this is a strong point of the game.
Visuals: Pretty good. Not as good as I would expect from such a recent game, but the areas are huge and there are virtually not loading screens outside of Strongholds.
Open World: Excellent. This is where the game shines, and makes up the majority of your play through. Lots of diverse activities,
Story: Cliche and cowardly. For the first three quarters or so, it felt like they were building to a big character  climax. Then you get there and the writers deliberately put the character right back at the beginning of the game. The last shot is almost the same as the opening shot, and the only difference is that a lot of people died between the two.
Other: A handful of inconsistencies bugged the crap out of me.
Post apocalyptic wasteland, right? Resources are scarce? And manufacturing is essentially non-existant. So where do all the cars come from? Seriously, I destroyed over 400 cars in a single play through. So who makes those things?
Then there are the people. I understand that Scrotus has access to a vast breeding pool and many war boys, but come on. I killed 2263 people in a single play through. Max is to the generation of young men in the Wasteland as World War One was to Europe; when the dust settled over one third were dead. That doesn't even count the crippled.
The Gastown Races are the two worst boss battles in the game. The "race" gives you 7:30 to win, but if you take longer than 1:00 then you won't win. The ensuing thunderdome battle is the longest and most tedious boss fight in the game. Like the pod race in Phantom Menace, the climactic action sequence is boring and tedious. If I hadn't had to press buttons, I would have fallen asleep.
How did Stank Gum survive me blowing up his truck? Seriously, how?! It makes no freaking sense, yet you see him two boss battles later completely unharmed. He's not even a cool enough villain to justify that sort of genre-breaking.
Summary: Enjoyable. The gameplay is fun, with some great "help the common man" missions in every area; these missions also help you, providing resources and shelter. The story is pathetic and nonsensical; honestly, I'd recommend stopping story missions after you get the V-8 engine, since it goes downhill from there. Lots of tough racing challenges for completionists. Decent leveling system.

A highly enjoyable action-platformer-roguelite-metroidvania (what a mouthful). It's got a lot of substance with many types of enemies, minibosses, traps, upgrades, and challenge rooms. The enemies range from racing pouncing wolves, to floating eyeballs which wink bloody tears at your position, to flail weilding suits of armor, to ghostly portraits being flung off the wall, as a few examples. Minibosses are usually suped up versions of regular enemies which sometimes have extra abilities and effects besides much increased attack and health. Traps include fireball launchers, cannons, spike traps, thin platforms, rotating platforms, and a few others. Challenge rooms are really cool. When you enter one you'll be given a random difficult objective. Sometimes you'll be racing through labyrinths, sometimes you'll be fighting multiple minibosses, sometimes you'll have to navigate a room properly without jumping or moving a certain direction. They can get really inventive and really rewarding.
As you play the game you loot gold and treasures. Both are saved until you die. When you resurrect you can spend gold to improve your lineage and grant your next offspring all manner of bonuses and abilities. Dashes, evasions, attack and defense spells, vampirism traits, and tons more. The game stays fresh by keeping you working to unlock and purchase new upgrades. When you get past the main upgrade screen, there is also a shop where you can pay (usually smaller increments) to equip new pieces of armor, and new swords, which also have lots of cool effects to check out when you re-enter the randomizing castle.
Since Rogue Legacy is both a metroidvania and a roguelike-and so exploration is important- I don't want to say too much more, but know that there are multiple ways to play, 4 main themed areas to explore, 5 really fun main bosses (and maybe some secret bosses), good music tracks, and a decent number of jokes and references peppered throughout. I'm really glad my brother recommended this. If you have any interest in exploration, challenging games, or action heavy sidescrollers this should suit you well. This game should also heavily appeal to anybody who has wondered what it would be like to play as a giant with IBS who is afraid of chickens and can telport as he races to explore a castle that 78 of his ancestors have died in to avenge them. 8/10 was quite a good ride with some replayability.

While Spec Ops is a difficult game to recommend based on its mediocre gameplay, performance issues, and frustrating controls the story packs a real punch and is the sole highlight of the game. The 'Do you recommend this game, Yes : No" is very limiting here because it depends. If you are looking for a good game this isn't it. If you are looking for one with a great story that is a military game no less than you found it. The developers had a message to send about war and the glorification of it and pulled no punches.
Game wise Spec Ops The Line suffers. I was constantly fighting with the controls and couldn't help but be bored to death whenever the shooting started thanks to the mediocre mechanics and bad AI. It came to the point where I was trying to rush through the game just so I could be done with it and that's a shame because it somewhat took away from the impact of the story.
The visuals are average and the aliasing hurt my eyes but it runs worse than Crysis 3. On a rig equipped with a 3770K, 16 Gigs of RAM, and a GTX 780ti I was getting frequent stutters, shaky mouse movements, and framerate drops.
With that said the creators of Spec Ops The Line clearly had a vision and they must have fought tooth and nail to make it happen. What starts off as a cliché military shooter ends up as something far more. The story is grim, depressing, bold, and a big middle finger to military games which rely on unquestioning patriotism and make war seem like it's fun and cool. It is not afraid to tackle the horrors of war and PTSD. It's designed to make you feel uncomfortable and it's about time a military game goes this route.
It's a shame then that there isn't a good game here to compliment the work put in by the writers. I am glad to have experienced Spec Ops The Line but it is not something I can easily recommend.

This is by far one of the most exciting, action-packed FPS games I have ever played, and it has reason for it. Such as:
1) The cast is likeable and hilarious. Especially Tiny Tina, I was laughing so hard when I heard her the first time.
2) The classes have absolutely no flaws in combat. The Assassin: Can cloak for a short amount of time. Good for distracting enemies and sniping. The Siren: Can phaselock enemies into a place. Good for eliminating bosses since they cannot move or shoot while active. The Commando: Can build a sentry turret. Good for clearing out waves of enemies. Finally, The Gunzerker: Can dual-wield any weapon in the game. Good for taking out enemies with far superior levels than you.
3) Guns. There are over a billion guns in the game. Ranging from Normal to Legendary. I forget the rarity color legend though. But I think it has over 6 qualities.
4) Enemies/Bosses. Most of them give you a challenge, but some you can take out with one shot. Enemies always respawn if you leave the area they are in and come back. Same with Bosses. Not all bosses respawn, but most of them do. Only the main bosses don't respawn, such as W4R-D3N, Bloodwing, Gluttonous Thresher, and so on.
And finally, 5) Goliaths. I absoulutely LOOOOOOOOVE leveling up Goliaths. For those of you who don't know what I'm talking about, I'll tell you. Goliaths are big, bulky behemoths with masks on them. Shoot of the mask, and they go on a frenzy, killing everyone in sight. They don't use their guns, luckily, so they can't really kill you unless you're too close.
If they kill someone, they level up. And each level they get, they need an extra kill to level up again. I love getting those Fatal GOD-liaths to just f**k up everyone in sight.
In my opinion, 11/10 IGN. Get this game NOW.

Having played for over 77 hours and found most of the lookouts and camps on both maps there are a few issues that players need to understand if they want to play this game. Shooting a deer in the head from under 20m away quite often leads to low blood loss and a long run over easily ove 30 minutes before finding the body, where as hitting a deer in the neck from almost any range will result in an instant kill. While it is a good game and obviously not fast paced it can be frustrating and can put some players off easily. The kills often seem to be worked out by the software as a roll of an imaginary dice and not based on any kind of balistics or hit box. The weather is good but the down side for the player is when it rains the rain is so loud you cannot hear any animals moving around but the animals can hear you from a vast distance unless you are stationary. When an animal is shot quite often the tracks will criss cross your path without you ever seeing the animal moving in that direction, i have found often after shooting an animal in an open field the track criss crosses the field even though i had watched the animal run straight away from me and out of the field. I am not saying this game is a bad game by any means but there are glaring issues that havent been addressed. The game portrays itself as a hunting simulator with weather,wind,noise,fatigue but the animals are quite often based on an arcade style. I would happily recommend this game as a game to relax with but not as a game that rewards for progress and skill.

This is a very fun, roguelike, platformer, where you hack your way through different parts of a randomised dungeon until you die. Then you spend your gold you earned through your run and upgrade your characters and repeat the whole thing until you are strong enough to take on one of the bosses, and ultimately the final boss of the game.

Borderlands makes me super aware that I'm playing a game-- in a good way. Staying highly amused by the NPC's behaviors, being entranced by the consistent art style of the series and being delighted at looting every inch of valuable scrap I see after violently ripping it from the corn-holes of murdered psychopaths makes maneuvering around Pandora a true delight. It allows me to voice my Gorilla-like aggression without polluting it's style with masculinity and overplayed 70s-era stereotypes of what a manly man (or woman) is. It's difficulty is scaled to a perfect amount that makes you, over time, grow and adjust to the hardness of the enemies just long enough to get comfortable before the next obstacle sodomizes you.
This is Pandora, the place where a pack of ravenous Skags trying to rip off your appendages is as normal as a springtime allergy. So what do you do, when you have allergies? You take an allergy pill. What do you do when you're faced with bloodthirsty skags? Bullets. Lots of them. The most hardened hunter on Earth is nothing compared to the average surviving individual on Pandora-- their badassery stems from the experience necessary to live longer than an hour in the wastes of the Borderlands.

A game that can be enjoyed at times, but the majority feels like its too easy or just not finished, with some major issues with scopes and animal AI that really drag this title into the mud. Stand hunting seems to be nerfed due to zones becoming less active when you kill an animal, or something. Feed/rest zones are too easy.
The AI is only barely challenging when hunting the hardest difficulty trophy, but feels like this should be the base difficulty almost, the rest is trash AI that ignores gunshots 100m away and their friends dying in a bloody mess at their feet.This game has promise but suffers as it seems clear the devs are focused on making money from DLC's rather than fix glaringly obvious issues, seems to be a lack of quality control.
The complete lack of an online competition system also leaves a massive gap in what thehunter classic provided.
Pros
- Pretty graphics
- almost everything can buy with in-game money
- large reserves
- nice sounds
- vastly increased animal draw distance and firing range (although the AI is dumb and just ignores when their herd members just drop dead.)
- larger herds and groups
Cons
- Terribly glitchy and incomplete binocular and scope controls (red dot sight moves at about 0.00001 degree per second)
- Very bad AI (nowhere near as fun or challenging as hunter classic, dont expect too much challenge)
- some parts of the map are completely empty of animals

- unrewarding animal scoring, antlers all look similar

- feels like an arcade game
