Alright, now that Apocalypse is out, I'll try and do my best to create an elaborate review of Black Ops II.
Let's start off with the campaign, I found it was kind of good in some ways, I mean it is really good, with a pretty decent story and the addition of you making the choices of getting a different ending, but I found that the characters didn't felt that good like it did in Black Ops 1, and as for a sequel story, I didn't like many of the old 20th century missions, there's probably too many of them in my taste, and in a mission with Mason, there's the "numbers" again, but that was just bad..
You can ride a horse, do a wannabe RTS things here and there, get to fly a jet, make your decisions on different events of the campaign, I think they're actually stepping up their game.
Multiplayer: Ooh boy this is the hard part, with success always comes the haters... As for the gameplay I found it was very fluid and smooth and the maps are amazing, with these "new" graphics. One reason I pick Black Ops and Black Ops 2 over the Modern Warfare Series (Excluding MW1) is the colors, this may sound weird, but indeed these games have clear colors, and bright ones too.
This game is like my pick and play if I'm in a good mood, since everytime I play I feel like I achieve something with the level system, or trying to get gold weapons, which is a pretty good system to get you busy for a long time.
Zombies: Alright so I'm a fan of Zombies in Call of Duty, in this one I could clearly see they were going for something different: TranZit, which was the worst map in my opinion. When on the bus, power station or going from one place to the other in the fog, the game has a slight chance of Crashing, and also the fact that not many people play in PC, I should've put this in the Multiplayer bit too, trying to find a match in Zombies takes around 10 minutes but don't get too excited if you find at least ONE person to play with, since the maps worth playing are HUGE, and there are quitters all over the place. I would recommend getting a friend to play with. The stock game comes with 4 maps, Tranzit, Bus depot, town, and farm, each one being a place in Tranzit as a stand alone map. These maps are boring once you've played them a lot, but No one plays Tranzit, because everyone plays Town, so the stock game in Zombies is really bad.
As for the buildables, I loved the portable engine to power up stuff, the Zombie Shield I never saw anyone use it and it is on all maps, which is the worst thing they could've kept for all maps...
As for Grief, No one plays it, I never played it, I didn't like it either, I rather play zombies in a coop way.
Revolution: I liked it, got it when it was coming out, 4 original multiplayer maps, a new Multiplayer weapon, the Peacekeeper which I used a lot, a very good zombies map, Die Rise, really felt like CoD Zombies.
... Oh and a new gamemode, wow I even forgot that existed because no one plays it, so I never got to play it, although the idea sounded pretty good, as for you turning into the zombie.
Uprising: Amazing Maps, a remake of Firing Range, a classic from Black Ops 1, and Mob of the Dead, probably the best zombies map in BO2 by far. Sadly, no new weapon or anything fancy.
Vengeance: Probably the only reason that I have to get it is the Cove map, everything else doesn't look convincing, and Buried looks too easy. I didn't get it, but my call is to wait until it goes on sale.
Apocalypse: Maybe the only reason to get this is Origins, a really fun map, although hard, but to learn everything hidden in origins is quite the job, and I really like it.  Only thing I didn't like is the combination of steampunk robots in a 1918 era with also the templars, just wasn't too good. As for multiplayer goes, 2 reused maps, not apealing, but I didn't have stadium from Black Ops 1, so that only makes 1 reused map, which isn't a big surprise Treyarch got lazy at the last DLC...

Undertale is a brilliant game, with unique gameplay and a snazzeh soundtrack.
The basis of the game travels deeper than meets the eye, so much so that it can be considered on a similar plane to shakespeare, just portrayed in a different manner. I love how the soundtrack reflects on the emotions and of the game itself, and what some may consider the easter eggs stop being easter eggs and start being the actual game with all the things they imply. The soundtrack flows so fantastically well that it is often pulled into itself to imply certain feelings and concepts of emotion and relationships between other characters.
The meta aspect of the game is brillant, the fourth wall is repeatedly broken down and reinforced with the fifth wall of a thin prosepect that this is just a game... The fact that the characters and story adaptively react to what you do, from killing goat moma then reloading the save so that she realises that you killed her, to the implications of potentially realising who you actually are as a person more than just a character go from more mundane effects to considerable levels of guilt over these few pixelated pieces of code (*yeilds fifth wall as a defence against feeling guilty*).
The deep story is intertwined with a series of puns and literal jokes that sometimes seem so hilarious yet so scary at the same time, this game is a god damn work of art!!
This is one of the very few games I have played through more than once, and one of the very, VERY few games I have played more than three times. That speaks for itself.
Overall, a snazzeh game with a snazzeh finish, also, dah cuetnez.

I'm enjoying this game a lot! The vehicle combat is by far one of the best I've ever experienced in a game. The out of vehicle combat is pretty standard to say the least, however the sound of a fist hitting a face never really gets old. The vehicle customization is great! You can almost play the game like an RPG based on your car, such as how fast it goes based on the armor so you could play as a tank that doesn't take much damage, or play as a really fast car that can't take a punch but can run away with the speed of Hermes. The game simply runs great, and looks great. The only flaw with this game is the side content that involves a lot of grinding, if you are a completionist I wouldn't want you to "complete" this game, it simply has you do the same thing over and over as far as scarecrows, salvage sites, mine fields, and sniper towers go they are all the same. The story isn't bad, the progression from Nathan Drake attire to Mad Max bad♥♥♥♥♥is very satisfying, and the little side story you get when you level up is pretty interesting. This game does a great job of capturing the "Mad Max" look and feel. If you like Mad Max I don't see why you wouldn't want to try this game.
TLDR: Get Game if don't mind a grind but still like good game elements.

I love games that make you think. Even more I love games that make you feel. As you might have read before, this game is an average third person shooter (at best). Although it was meant to be so much more. Just the concept of its story telling is reason to invest your time in this game. Spec Ops: The Line shows you the brutality of war. It shows you you the insanity of conflict. However,  it does not only shows you, it mocks you, if you decide to play on. It asks you with each step. "Are you ready to stop playing now?" And with every positive answer it rewards you with another brutal experience.
Many are angered that it doesn't give you a choice, but punishes you for doing things that are scripted, that you had no way to avoid. To that I say: "That is the point of this game." Not only that, it gets harder and more brutal to carry on, the game itself just starts to oppose you. In the beggining, on loading screen you might see some helpfull tips, but as the story goes on, the same loading screens start to remind you what horrible things you did.
10/10 will not play again.

I already played this game on 360 last year and even prestiged once. But as I wanted to just play multiplayer for free, I decided to buy both Black Ops 1 and 2, which I already enjoyed playing in the past. As I believe I have mentioned on the Modern Warfare 2 review, the PC version of Call of Duty has no automatic targeting like the console versions do, which makes the whole experience frigging harder. I guess, when the people say that you don't need any skills to play CoD, they are talking about the console version. But in the PC version, only the real skilled players can actually play. Even though I used to get real good scores in the 360 version, now I keep getting mediocre scores or I only keep dying. The PC version truly is the most challenging CoD ever. Probably the PC version of CoD is even harder than Counter-Strike: Global Offensive in my opinion (I do not know why, but it feels that way). Even though Black Ops II multiplayer is really fun both on the console and PC, there are not many people who play this game on PC unfortunately. Right now, there are around 7,000 people online? 360 version was getting around 200,000 people or more (Don't really remember but the number was high). Thanks to this, not many people play Domination and such, but mostly people are all gathered on Team Deathmatch. *Sigh* I guess I am not surprised as CoD seems to be a lot more popular on consoles. It's a shame, really, because I really love the maps of both Black Ops 1 and 2, and I wish there were more people playing BO2 PC multiplayer. So now, I should go out and pre-order Call of Duty: Ghosts for PS3 :P

Back in the day I was a huge city builder fan. I loved the old SimCity games where you could focus more on the outline of your city and make everything ”feel” good for you. Than the later games have added plenty of tiny functions that I never really liked that much. The micro management was never really THAT fun there. Prison Architect gives me that awesome feeling that those older city builders did, focusing on building and having fun rather than micromanagement.
I can build a prison that have a layout and style that I like. And once you've finished a huge chunk of the prison you can start to micromanage the different sections and rules of the prison and even though I didn't like that in the citygames I love it here! Becuase everything you change have an almost emediate effect on your prison.
I also love that this is one of those games that actually keeps getting updated! You get new things and new game rules to play around and the game is even getting a bit harder (and that's a good thing). Truly my only complaint about Prison Architect is the fact that once you've gotten far enough with your build it can be a bit slow. You're prison is safe, you're guard do their job and you keep getting money to advance babysteps forward. And that means waiting for that money you need to keep building. Some time ago you could even let the game run by itself to just get money and not really losing anything for doing so.
Overall a great city bu.... prison building game that will bring you hours and hours of gaming fun.

I'm enjoying this game a lot! The vehicle combat is by far one of the best I've ever experienced in a game. Strangly enough, Mad Max takes out a lot of the content from it's predeccesor Assasin's Creed Syndicate.  As a follow-up to a game that was already lowly reviewed it baffles me how Ubisoft would remove most of the previous staples in it's long-running series.  To begin with, it seems that most NPCs have been removed leavy an overworld that, while not outright stated, seems to take place somewhere in the Syrian desert in what appears to be the present day.  The protagonist Max Rokatansky is a modern day American Assasin working in Syria towards an unknown objective.  While missing he is missing the classic hooded robes worn by all previous playable characters, Max still provides that excellent gruff white male action that we were not certainly missing.  As for the story the open-ended approach shrouds the story to the point that after hours of playing I still do not understand.  From what I can gather, Max is driving along in the Creedmobile until he is attacked by white ISIS slaves and goes after a mutanted fictional re-imagining of President Assad.
Overall this game lacks...everything

I already played this game on 360 last year and even prestiged once. But as I wanted to just play multiplayer for free, I decided to buy both Black Ops 1 and 2, which I already enjoyed playing in the past. As I believe I have mentioned on the Modern Warfare 2 review, the PC version of Call of Duty has no automatic targeting like the console versions do, which makes the whole experience frigging harder. I guess, when the people say that you don't need any skills to play CoD, they are talking about the console version. But in the PC version, only the real skilled players can actually play. Even though I used to get real good scores in the 360 version, now I keep getting mediocre scores or I only keep dying. The PC version truly is the most challenging CoD ever. Probably the PC version of CoD is even harder than Counter-Strike: Global Offensive in my opinion (I do not know why, but it feels that way). Even though Black Ops II multiplayer is really fun both on the console and PC, there are not many people who play this game on PC unfortunately. Right now, there are around 7,000 people online? 360 version was getting around 200,000 people or more (Don't really remember but the number was high). Thanks to this, not many people play Domination and such, but mostly people are all gathered on Team Deathmatch. *Sigh* I guess I am not surprised as CoD seems to be a lot more popular on consoles. It's a shame, really, because I really love the maps of both Black Ops 1 and 2, and I wish there were more people playing BO2 PC multiplayer. So now, I should go out and pre-order Call of Duty: Ghosts for PS3 :P

Beat this game once, don't really see a need to play it again. The jist is that you're playing a roguelike/castlevania kind of game with generic-looking art. Anytime you die you move forward a number of years and your successor takes your place as the one to go into the randomly generated castle, with a randomly allotted class and traits. Why are we going into the castle? Beats me, I stopped remembering what the story is supposed to be about somewhere around a hundred dead heroes ago. Build up your stats by building up your castle with the money your ancestor left for you, then go in and die all over again.
The thing that keeps you hanging on is all the randomly generated stuff and the desire to build up your castle until you've experienced all the possibilities. Your character can be a dwarf, or have gigantism; they can be colorblind; near-sighted, far-sighted; have dysgraphia and be unable to reliably read anything; or any number of other hilarious traits that are all worth experiencing at least once. The classes you can get are minimalistic but have just enough impact on your play style to make every playthrough feel somewhat unique, and they get moreso as the game progresses, moving from the likes of Fighter, Rogue, and Mage on into more remarkable things like Assassin, Lich, and Dragon.
Problem? You've seen everything this game has to throw at you by the time you're in the second part (of four) in the castle. Most monsters are re-colors of earlier monsters. Bosses aren't really interesting to begin with, nor do they get more interesting. In fact, there's a certain ring of disappointment to emptying out a section of the dungeon and going, "Oh. Well, I guess I have to fight the boss now," knowing that even if the boss doesn't end your current run the aftermath certainly will. All the levels are random arrangements of procedural crap, and while early levels feel difficult-but-fair considering the game's trial-and-error approach, late levels feel like their randomized layouts and encounters were barely playtested and won't feel like they're worth the risk when you ran out of new stuff to try out ten hours ago.
I won't call this a masterpiece, but I'll say I got my money's worth of entertainment out of it and it's definitely worth a solid try.

I have been playing this game very consistently since having purchased it and I can say it is quite good overall.  It is an open world game enabling you to play on different reservations and explore different areas which contain different species of wildlife and obviously hunt them.  The area is quite large but it is limited.  I say this because due to its limitation, it will inherently becoming boring after a while, but only for some perhaps.  I have put in a lot of hours and still enjoy it.
The graphics and sound are excellent.  Beautiful lush vegetation, sounds of thunder, and incredible breathtaking views at some of the towers.  Put it on max, and it looks amazing.  There's definitely a calmness and peace to playing this game.
The gameplay consists of two kinds:  missions and open world.  In open world, which is what I mostly do, you can explore, shoot any animal, eventually unlock any weapons, discover landmarks, outposts etc.  There are challenges you can sort of create anyway.  It is a lot of fun--and challenging, to use the bow or shoot from long distances.  The missions enable you to rack up money and points and therefore level up a lot faster than killing animals in open world.  However, the missions can be frustrating, particularly the photo missions.  Sometimes, you will get pretty fed up with the missions and then the gameplay is just limited to open world and shooting animals.  It can get old, which leads to my next point.
As of right now, the game definitely needs more content.  There aren't enough animals, not enough weapons, not enough land.  There can be extended periods of time where there is nothing going on, no animals around albeit with greater strategy this can be avoided somewhat.  It is definitely possible that new maps, animals, weapons etc will become DLCs in the near future though.  Some users have suggested fishing.  I don't thinking changing the concept of the game is a good call; there are good fishing games out there.  It should stick to hunting and simply enhance the depth of that.  Right now the weather is either clear, foggy, or rainy.  Snow would be awesome.  Lots of potential with this game.

DLCs such as ATVs has been a good addition, as have tents and blinds.  There's definitely more that the developers could include however.  And some should be free.

There are some glitches that have detracted from the gameplay, but most have been remedied.  The animals sometimes run around in circles, previously you would get a vital shot and the animal would bleed profusely but not die.  These have been fixed but there are still some quirks.  Head shots for instance are tricky.  Sometimes the animal instantly drops, other times it trots off with a low bleed rate.  I'm not a hunter in real life but I just can't imagine this happening.
The controls are very good.  It's simple to use some things with a controller whereas other things like aiming and shooting you absolutely need to use the KB/mouse combo.  There are perks and skill points you can earn which help with your ability to down an animal, another cool feature.
Overall, I would recommend this game.  It is still relatively new; there hopefully will be more DLCs to come to enhance the gameplay.  For $30, it's still worth it.  If you can get this on sale, absolutely buy it.  You will not be disappointed.

I play rust almost every day, wasting numerous amounts of hours back to back farming, killing, building and laughing. The reason this game is so fun is because its so easy to play, after learning the fundamental basics that is. The game is continuously updated by the dedicated developers, that are releasing weekly wipes. Rust has many mechanics for survival, building, fighting, interacting, and even role playing!! This game covers a lot of aspects from a game where you want to spend many hours playing, it hardly gets boring.
And on top of all that its MULTIPLAYER aswell. Honestly could not have asked for a better game to invest almost 2000 hours in.
The main part of this game that is a really interesting mechanic, is that you actually have to trust people you decide to team up with, because at any moment they can steal from you, kill you, just about do anything to you, even lock you in a prison... This game is somewhat realistic, and exciting at the same time, some positive aspects of this game is that you spawn completely naked, which i find pretty amusing, as you can spawn with different size bodies, weather it be a female or male.
To begin in rust; you are given a randomly generated character (any race, any gender), and spawned in naked with nothing but a rock and a torch. The rock and torch are used to help you advance in this harsh environment, by smashing trees, rocks and animals you can gain resource and evolve out of the "naked" stage. You'll want to secure a location by building a base and expanding to a reasonable size, as not everyone is friendly and they will try and attack you and grab your loot while your not on. Expect to get raided in this game, no matter where you hide or how high you build, there will come a time when someone will be curious enough to slave away to get enough resources to breach and clear your base... and once you come back to an empty base you will go through 2 feelings. Anger, the feeling of lose because you have just been raided, all those hours, wasted for nothing. Then you'll go through acceptance.  Accept the fact that you got raided and its not the end of the world. You can do it, just get back out there with your tiny rock and start over again. At the end of the week, it all gets reset and you get to start it all over again and if they reset that week, then your time will eventually come, where everyone will be back on the beach with nothing but a rock.
Yes, rust can be played entertainingly for an hour a week and you will be presented with a ton of fun, unlike what other individuals who haven't played rust to the fullest, and experienced its full potential. No, you won't rule a server, however you wouldn't hope to play an hour of CS and wind up noticeably Global inside a singular week, yet you can even now have a ton of fun and discover things, similar to the way you can experience in other computer games.
Note, rust is difficult to be great at, yet it's as simple to get into like other games and the trouble and weight of knowledge makes the profundity and replay ability that other games just don't have. However other games  do, while as yet being less demanding to get into than those recreations. You don't need to make inquiries that leave you scratching your head in wonder why your bullets aren’t going where your crosshair is. You don’t need to worry about anything to play Rust, BUT, similar aspects are still in this game, and you can easily learn them and improve your skill.
The most compelling motivation I see Rust as one of the best recreations ever is that it simultaneously enables individuals to play an alternate reality inside a similar aspect. Because I play it for the pvp and rivalry doesn't mean others can't play it like they want to, and have a better time than I do. The stories and encounters you will have in Rust are incredible as you are continuously running into different types of people.
At the end of the day rust is just another one of those games that you can spend hours upon hours investing into the game just to have it wiped with a couple of days, but it’s all about the experience you get from the game, the encounters, the kills, basically everything that happens has its own meaning whether you hate the game because of that or you are sucked in more and more. This game is certainly worth buying and playing

To keep this simple, I'm going to only put in Pro and Con.
Pro:
~ Fun for Multi playing
~ Somewhat funny NPC conversations
~ Things explodes
~ The art direction is quite nice
Con:
~ The environment is extremely static. Nothing reacts to explosions or any other combat activities (Except barrels or animal crap)
~ If one inch of a floor pops out, it will stop you dead regardless on if you're running or walking. Seen NPC enemies spaz out from seeming nothing.
~ Unfriendly exploration for the maps. In another word, very restrictive limited map exploration options.
~ Mobs fights dirty and often unfairly in a predictable way.
~ Mobs would roll around and none of your shots will hit it until it stops rolling
~ Extremely low replay value. Same old story line, same old side quests, same old choices, same old rewards
~ The guns you find will not be enough and/or good enough for the job at hand. You will be forced to use the golden keys just to get to the next stages in game and prevent you from pulling your hair out from frustration.
~ Very low Legendary drop rate (Only found 1 Legendary drop rate in 165 hours of game playing)
~ Character outfits is extremely generic with mostly just color change options (unless you buy the DLC just to get a few more variations)
~ Spend $200,000+ on the slot machine, never got anything better than Blue weapons
~ Invisble boundry walls everywhere making it feel very trapped for a map
~ Limit options for cars to drive
~ If you die, all mobs including boss mobs will reset their health instantly
~ Mobs respawns too quickly (about 10 min)
~ Getting reincarnated by the machine after death takes so long to wait, unnecessary reincarnation cut scene.
~ Worth repeating: The environment is extremely static, doesn't encourage any interactions with the environment other than opening chests or blowing up barrels.
Would I recommend this game to anyone?
If you like blowing the crap out of thing in a mindless braindead fashion with a witty but rather linear story line, Yes, recommended.
Otherwise, No. Better games out there to play with and a better use of your time not to play this game.

Let me start off by saying that Undertale is one of the most interesting and funniest RPG’s I have ever come across. It’s been over a year since the game came out and became an indie darling in no time. But should you buy into the hype of Undertale?
Undertale is an old school JRPG created by only one person. It is a game where you can go on to the end without killing anyone or by stomping over everyone you come across. It puts you in the shoes of a lost soul who has fallen into the underground prison of monsters. From here you encounter a variety of characters who either help or hinder your quest to get back to the surface.
These said characters are the soul of Undertale as these are some of the most memorable characters you will find in a RPG. They range from funny to straight up sadistic and Undertale makes a beautiful transition between the two. Don’t take the funny characters for granted though, unlike most games where there are some funny guys who constantly crack jokes and nothing else,
Undertale shows you the second side of these characters. For example, Sans is a wisecracking skeleton who does not leave a single chance to make a cheesy pun but at the same he cares for his brother too much and wants to see him happy. His entire motivations revolve around his brother who is equally well thought out and has some of the best dialogues in the game. These characters make you care for them. You can either go with the Pacifist ending where you don’t kill anyone or be a genocidal maniac which legit turns into a full  blown creepypasta by the end.
In terms of gameplay, you usually fight using a floating heart to save yourself from attacks while using a modified QTE to pull off attacks of your own. This combat system is supported by an ACT system which is different for every enemy you encounter. If you choose not to attack an character during your turn, you can try to charm your enemy and make them comfortable enough that you can spare them.
Some enemies might want to flirt with you, some want you to pet them while others just want to eat your green veggies. This gives some of these random enemies a certain layer of dimension which is not present in other games. It shows that even monsters can have hearts and shows that even the random encounters can be given a personal touch.
Undertale is one of those games where even the littlest details and the most random characters matter and tell stories of their own. There are bleak as well as happy stories to be found out all over the world. An Ice Cream seller who wonders why doesn’t anyone buys his ice creams in winter while there is a guy who has never seen a single ray of the sun due to being stuck underground and tries to stay happy despite the grim conditions. There is an element of bleakness as well as a glimmer of hope in these characters and that is what makes Undertale special.
That’s not to say it does not have its fair share of problems. There is a lot of backtracking to be done here since the shops are located far away from each other and there is no apparent fast travel system present here. But that only makes you want to explore more and minor problems does not take away anything from the overall beauty of Undertale.
Undertale proves that not everything needs to be bright and flashy in order to look and play good. It has a very unique and charming art style which brings every environment present in the game to life. The character are well designed and do not feel generic even till the end of the game.
There are certain visual touches to the characters like winking or blushing which adds an unique charm to the said monsters. The game also transitions from charming to haunting quite quickly and it can leave you speechless when it does so.
Excellent. It has a perfect soundtrack to go along with the game and it changes the soundtrack according to the mood so subtly that you won’t even notice. The minor sound details and effects like a ba-dum-tss whenever San cracks a joke makes for some compelling experience.
Is Undertale the best game? No. But it is one of the best RPG’s I’ve played in a long time. Don’t go in expecting a thriller combat system or so because Undertale relies on its character and world building. There is a certain charm to the characters present in Undertale which is not found elsewhere and it is for them that you should buy and play Undertale the first chance you get.

As usual with Call of Duty games created by Treyarch, they are split up into the same 3 sections- campaign, multiplayer and zombies.
The campaign lives up to its predecessor- thankfully this time completing the task of not giving me a number filled epileptic fit at the most cruicial and interesting times of the storyline. The characters, especially the enemies, are bold and genuinely interesting, it's extremely rare in an FPS game to actually have an enemy one can relate and even to an extent, sympathise with. The way the missions travel back and forward in time is most pleasing and a welcome addition- sadly, the waste of time optional "strike force" missions drag the experience down as it's quite obvious they're just rushed filler content. Overall, the campaign is sort of what you'd expect- but with better story elements.
The multiplayer is just downright grusome. The removal of COD points and replacing it with this petty unlock system was an idiotic move in my opinion. If I rememeber correctly, we was promised something that would make this multiplayer different from the other Call of Duty games- what was that exactly? Diamond skins? Pathetic. If you're thinking about getting this game just for the multiplayer-don't bother.
Zombies was my favourite feature of World at War and lived up my expectations in Black Ops 1. Zombies is what separates Treyarch games from Infinity Wards, it is the key element in their success, which is why it pains me to say that it is terrible in Black Ops 2. I understand that they thought they had to spice the map layouts up a bit, but whatever moron decided that the way to do it would be to put a bus in there which moves you around from place to place, making the layout far too complex and downright chaotic should be fired instantly, jest me forget the individual maps without the damned bus which are covered in fire, preventing you from moving a metre without being burned. Call me a conspiracy theorist, but I actually think Treyarch purposely made the default maps terrible to force you to buy their optional nuketown map- which is, not so surprisingly, the only map which doesn't burn or force you to move around on a not so reliable vehicle. Disappointing, truely.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 (ETS2) is a 2012 vehicle simulation game developed and self-published by SCS Software. It features a massive game world spanning most of mainland Europe, the British Isles, and Scandinavia with each of the cities being connected by the beautifully recreated road systems such as the German autobahn roads.  The game also offers detailed simulation mechanics for hardcore sim players while also offering an alternative 'automatic' mode for the more casual players or beginners such as myself.
Although the game's primary and obvious gameplay mechanic consist of driving across Europe, it does feature additional mechanics to give the game a little more spice such as; a progression (level up) system where each level unlocks new cargos, trucks, upgrades and delivery conditions; Truck Company Management system where you manage a trucking company by purchasing / upgrading garages, trucks and hiring drivers to use them.
Start the game as a driver for hire and earn enough money to build your own trucking empire that will span the entirety of Europe.
+ Beautiful graphics with detailed truck interiors, world environment, and road systems
+ Good sound effects and assets
+ Europe is vast and well detailed  giving individuality to each location you visit
+ Good selection of trucks with a good upgrade and customization system
+ Various cargo and delivery conditions
+ Surprisingly contains a relevant progression (level-up) system
+ Garage and Truck Company management system
+ Offers different game modes to cater for both hardcore sim players, casuals, and beginners
+
+ Very fast load times (Even on a mechanical hard drive)
+ Live European Radio Streaming or custom music playlist using the in-game radio feature
+ Has a demo in the Store page for anyone who's not sure if this genre is to their liking
- Some micro-stuttering despite the FPS being above 60
- Low number of pedestrians makes some parts of the cities a bit empty
- Poor reward for manually parking a trailer (they could have at least given 100xp for it)
- Anti-aliasing is limited to only MLAA
+/- The game's overall concept is for a narrow/niche audience.
+/- The AI needs to attend a Road Courtesy and Discipline class. (Although this does add to the immersion since the player will have to exercise due diligence while driving)
Playing this game is surprisingly stress relieving and gives off a zen-like feeling while also offering a lot of other contents within the game world.
I can
this game at full price if you're a hardcore simulation fan but if not, I suggest you purchase this game on a sale. Either way however, I

which includes all available DLCs and Expansion Packs as well as SCS' other games such as Bus Simulator, Trucks & Trailers, and Euro Truck Simulator (1).
To be completely honest, I didn't think much of this game when I first bought it because I did not see the appeal in driving trucks around in a game without a plot or a story. I was, however, pleasantly surprised on how much I enjoyed the experience because what the game lacks in story (being a simulation game and all), it makes up for in solid gameplay, excellent presentation, and player-friendly game mechanics.

The biggest downside to the game, as you've probably seen, is the community. I'm willing to bet if the community was cleaned up, there would be much more positive reviews, but that frankly won't happen. So, the community is horrid.
The community is fine with mocking other players, should they be watching them on the featured match thing, or playing with them. The amount of bragging and downtalking is unreal. If there was a feature to turn the chat off, it would be a blessing.
Moving off the community, the game itself isn't bad. The game mechanics are rather solid, and the music (which isn't too bad, but can get old) can be turned off. Regarding the music, there supposedly is a surplus of songs, but for some reason only three will play in a loop, even when all of them are checked.

You're given enough room to make your character look decent by paying with in-game or real-life currency. That said, the voices for the characters are near the bottom of the barrel. Seeing as each gender only has three voices, and each are decent at best, and pretty bad, at the worst.
Shooting and defending are close to the same difficulty. Shooting can be kinda odd, seeing as the bar will sometimes mean literally nothing (you can for some reason still make a shot, if it's outside the green/yellow, and miss when it's in the green), or everything. Defending is equally weird, in that while it's done decently, it's not the easiest thing in the world to do, without a good deal of practice (like anything).
Finally, the servers themselves can be sketchy. You may join a room, and have everybody ready up. You might find another team to play, only for the game to stop the loading at thirty percent and send both teams back to their "lobby". There is no reason I've seen for this, besides the game being kinda weird. That said, it'll normally go away, after some time.
For the most part, the game is fine for what it is. The biggest drawback is the community, so if you're able to ignore the community, you'll probably enjoy the game itself.

I'll give Mad Max a thumbs up, but the predominant sentiment that I take away from it is that it could have been so much better.
There are moments of brilliance here padded by many hours of rote tedium. Mad Max's open world is filled with many things to do, but too many boil down to the same thing.  Past the half-way point, the game increasingly felt like it was populated more to meet some quota of "things to do" than to be an engaging game first and foremost. This wouldn't be too terrible if the side missions were largely avoidable, but the main storyline progression is fairly reliant on the resources and upgrades they provide.
Beyond the lack of variety in the general gameplay, there are several little annoyances, such as unskippable mini-cutscenes that occur for basic tasks such as filling Max's canteen or eating (which is equivalent to picking up a medkit).  These are short, but even so, they will happen many dozens or even hundreds of times of the course of the game, and even the tenth time I saw Max go into the same exact mini-cutcscene of him scarfing down some dog food, it was already too many.
The combat too, has problems.  It's "Batman combat", but unlike every other implementation of this combat I've seen, you can get hit while in the middle of an attack animation and counters are not an immediate interrupt.  This has the effect of making it somewhat more challenging, but in a way that feels cheap.  When every other game featuring this style of combat lets you break out of an animation for a counter, it feels broken when one game doesn't.  While I enjoy this style of combat, it is inherently repetitive, so the fights needs to be relatively quick to resolve and not too frequent.  Mad Max breaks both rules, you'll get into likely hundreds of fights over the course of the game and the enemies take quite a lot of hits, making them drag on too long.  This signiciantly contributes the game's feeling of tedium.
So what's good about the game?  The car combat for one.  Your car is a bit fragile at first, but building it up into a viable combat machine is rewarding and taking down conveys was always my favorite part of the game.
The game also does a great job of capturing the setting and making everything feel a bit unrealistically outlandish in a way that's quite intriguing, just like the films.
The success of the setting is also helped by the excellent graphics, which can be maxed out on a GTX 970 at 1080p and still maintain a solid 60fps. (Feels like a while since I've played a major title where you can do that...)
All said and done, I certainly don't regret the time I spent with the game, but I feel it would have worked better as a shorter, more focused experience.  Still, if you have any affinity for the Mad Max movies or its particular flavor of post-apocalypse, it's worth picking up on sale

To be honest with you, I just picked this game up because it was on sale. And looking at the metacritic score and the name itself I rather expected it to be another generic, mediocre shooter.
Oh boy, I couldn't have been more wrong!!
Gameplaywise it totally fits that description. It is a Gears of War-esque Shooter with slightly harsher damage model.
Graphics are typical PS3/Xbox360 stuff. On the other hand the Leveldesign, though linear, is well made and creates a atmospheric and breathtaking environment I often found myself starring at in appreciation.
AI is decent. Squadmates are actually useful, taking cover and supporting you. Enemy AI will use suppressive and cover fire and try to flank you and also use grenades to flush you out of cover.
Not gonna talk about MP. Yager studio themself said in an interview they didn't want it and they didn't do it. But Publisher 2K still made a different studio do it and shoe-horned it in...
So what is the BIG selling point of this game? It's narrative!
If "Apocalypse Now" (and for that matter "Heart of Darkness") was a game, this is what it would be like. You will see plenty of references and parallels but rest assured, the game isn't just a copy. It has a story in its own right and goes its own ways.
As the story unfolds the lines between good and evil will start to dissolve until there is nothing left. You are being dragged into a conflict you have no concept off and always left one step behind. It keeps spiraling out of control fast as things turn sour and♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan - mainly because of your own ignorance - while you also have to bear the dire consequences of your actions.
On the metalevel the game is toying with alot of our preconceptions about Shooters, how violence and morality is represented and going into some other really deep stuff if you start thinking about it.
SpecOps deliberately keeps giving the players red herrings, false targets and vague objectives and watches us kill again and again regardlessly. It says we need to blow up some people and we do it.
Because it is what needs to be done to accomplish the mission, right?  "We have no choice" like Cpt. Walker says. After all we are the good guys, fighting for a just cause with only the best intentions. Violence is a mere necessity.
Who would have thought those people might be unarmed civilians with children? And at the next loading screen you will be asked  “Do you feel like a hero yet?”
That effectively is what SpecOps is all about: to ♥♥♥♥ with your head and expectations. This game is a mind ♥♥♥♥ through and through.
Bottom line: don't let yourself be put off by it's looks, because there is more to it than it first seems. You should really give it a try! Chances are you won't be disappointed.

Let me start off by saying that Undertale is one of the most interesting and funniest RPG’s I have ever come across. It’s been over a year since the game came out and became an indie darling in no time. But should you buy into the hype of Undertale?
Undertale is an old school JRPG created by only one person. It is a game where you can go on to the end without killing anyone or by stomping over everyone you come across. It puts you in the shoes of a lost soul who has fallen into the underground prison of monsters. From here you encounter a variety of characters who either help or hinder your quest to get back to the surface.
These said characters are the soul of Undertale as these are some of the most memorable characters you will find in a RPG. They range from funny to straight up sadistic and Undertale makes a beautiful transition between the two. Don’t take the funny characters for granted though, unlike most games where there are some funny guys who constantly crack jokes and nothing else,
Undertale shows you the second side of these characters. For example, Sans is a wisecracking skeleton who does not leave a single chance to make a cheesy pun but at the same he cares for his brother too much and wants to see him happy. His entire motivations revolve around his brother who is equally well thought out and has some of the best dialogues in the game. These characters make you care for them. You can either go with the Pacifist ending where you don’t kill anyone or be a genocidal maniac which legit turns into a full  blown creepypasta by the end.
In terms of gameplay, you usually fight using a floating heart to save yourself from attacks while using a modified QTE to pull off attacks of your own. This combat system is supported by an ACT system which is different for every enemy you encounter. If you choose not to attack an character during your turn, you can try to charm your enemy and make them comfortable enough that you can spare them.
Some enemies might want to flirt with you, some want you to pet them while others just want to eat your green veggies. This gives some of these random enemies a certain layer of dimension which is not present in other games. It shows that even monsters can have hearts and shows that even the random encounters can be given a personal touch.
Undertale is one of those games where even the littlest details and the most random characters matter and tell stories of their own. There are bleak as well as happy stories to be found out all over the world. An Ice Cream seller who wonders why doesn’t anyone buys his ice creams in winter while there is a guy who has never seen a single ray of the sun due to being stuck underground and tries to stay happy despite the grim conditions. There is an element of bleakness as well as a glimmer of hope in these characters and that is what makes Undertale special.
That’s not to say it does not have its fair share of problems. There is a lot of backtracking to be done here since the shops are located far away from each other and there is no apparent fast travel system present here. But that only makes you want to explore more and minor problems does not take away anything from the overall beauty of Undertale.
Undertale proves that not everything needs to be bright and flashy in order to look and play good. It has a very unique and charming art style which brings every environment present in the game to life. The character are well designed and do not feel generic even till the end of the game.
There are certain visual touches to the characters like winking or blushing which adds an unique charm to the said monsters. The game also transitions from charming to haunting quite quickly and it can leave you speechless when it does so.
Excellent. It has a perfect soundtrack to go along with the game and it changes the soundtrack according to the mood so subtly that you won’t even notice. The minor sound details and effects like a ba-dum-tss whenever San cracks a joke makes for some compelling experience.
Is Undertale the best game? No. But it is one of the best RPG’s I’ve played in a long time. Don’t go in expecting a thriller combat system or so because Undertale relies on its character and world building. There is a certain charm to the characters present in Undertale which is not found elsewhere and it is for them that you should buy and play Undertale the first chance you get.

Great. The minute-to-minute action is satisfying, and the story arc is satisfying. I played a few hours of the first game, and I find the inclusion of characters from the first game enjoyable. Generally, it's unfortunate that DLC missions don't scale with player level. Playing the Mr. Torgue DLC at too high a level really wrecked it. I'm saving Captain Scarlett for my true vault hunter playthrough.

This game took me by surprise. I only purchased this game as it was on sale, and I figured a few extra achievements couldn't hurt right?
Well I have no interest in trucks I find myself playing this game and enjoying it. This game really does do a very good job of being a truck simulator. It is complete with customization options, plenty of DLC if you get bored of the base game, an excellent set of mods (Not from Steam Workshop) can be installed which can further enhance your gameplay experience.
If you are a truck fan, this game is almost certainly a must have. Someone who is a truck fan would absolutely love this game to bits.
If you're not a truck fan, you may, or may not like this game but if you can get it when it is on sale you should try it before mocking it, it actually does what it is designed to do very well.
Although, I'd highly recommend having a music player playing music in the background as the long drives can be a bit daunting without it.
As for its down sides.. I couldn't get the built in radio player to work on Linux at all with MP3 or radio streams as is apparently supported. Not a big issue for me as I just used another media player to have music in the background.
It can also be very resource intensive also so you may need quite a beefy system if you want to wack the graphic settings up.
So to break all this down into a nice pro/cons list:
Pros:
- Very well built simulation game. Does what it says on the tin.
- Has achievements/trading cards for those who may want them.
- Cannot be simply "beaten" in a few hours like most modern games.
- Has company management features built in allowing you to employ people, buy trucks etc etc etc.
- Trucks can be customized.
- Visually it looks amazing if your system can cope.
- Great modding community that offers many things the base game cannot.
- Multi-platform support
Cons:
- Very resource intensive mostly on the GPU and appears to only be using only 1 CPU core out of 8 on my system
- Framerate can drop in some locations for a few seconds.
- No built in multiplayer (Though can be added via unofficial mods)
- AI traffic can be pretty darn stupid at times and will happily ram you out of your lane if it wants your lane and then charge you for the privilege with a traffic fine.
Hmm, I wanted to list more cons.. but I honestly cannot think of any others. So I'm going to have to say.. yes I recommend this game :-).

To be honest with you, I just picked this game up because it was on sale. And looking at the metacritic score and the name itself I rather expected it to be another generic, mediocre shooter.
Oh boy, I couldn't have been more wrong!!
Gameplaywise it totally fits that description. It is a Gears of War-esque Shooter with slightly harsher damage model.
Graphics are typical PS3/Xbox360 stuff. On the other hand the Leveldesign, though linear, is well made and creates a atmospheric and breathtaking environment I often found myself starring at in appreciation.
AI is decent. Squadmates are actually useful, taking cover and supporting you. Enemy AI will use suppressive and cover fire and try to flank you and also use grenades to flush you out of cover.
Not gonna talk about MP. Yager studio themself said in an interview they didn't want it and they didn't do it. But Publisher 2K still made a different studio do it and shoe-horned it in...
So what is the BIG selling point of this game? It's narrative!
If "Apocalypse Now" (and for that matter "Heart of Darkness") was a game, this is what it would be like. You will see plenty of references and parallels but rest assured, the game isn't just a copy. It has a story in its own right and goes its own ways.
As the story unfolds the lines between good and evil will start to dissolve until there is nothing left. You are being dragged into a conflict you have no concept off and always left one step behind. It keeps spiraling out of control fast as things turn sour and♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan - mainly because of your own ignorance - while you also have to bear the dire consequences of your actions.
On the metalevel the game is toying with alot of our preconceptions about Shooters, how violence and morality is represented and going into some other really deep stuff if you start thinking about it.
SpecOps deliberately keeps giving the players red herrings, false targets and vague objectives and watches us kill again and again regardlessly. It says we need to blow up some people and we do it.
Because it is what needs to be done to accomplish the mission, right?  "We have no choice" like Cpt. Walker says. After all we are the good guys, fighting for a just cause with only the best intentions. Violence is a mere necessity.
Who would have thought those people might be unarmed civilians with children? And at the next loading screen you will be asked  “Do you feel like a hero yet?”
That effectively is what SpecOps is all about: to ♥♥♥♥ with your head and expectations. This game is a mind ♥♥♥♥ through and through.
Bottom line: don't let yourself be put off by it's looks, because there is more to it than it first seems. You should really give it a try! Chances are you won't be disappointed.

Rating: 8/10, would recommend! However, game still in alpha.
Despite being in development, the existing gameplay and potential of this title make it a wonderful experience. I'd recommend PA for anyone who enjoys "citybuilding", architecture, and/or sim games. On top of that, the addition of 'failure conditions' is a really wonderful way the developers added in a bit of action gameplay. Not only do you get to build whatever kind of prison you want, but if you "fail" a map, then you have to PLAY it. You join the ranks of inmates, and must go about serving your (randomly assigned) sentence.
The game runs great, although there are occasionally bugs, some of which can be a game ruiner. At time of writing, I believe we're on Alpha 26, so bugs are to be expected. The developer is pretty responsive to bug reports and feedback, so hopefully by beta release all the wrinkles will be smoothed out.
I consider myself someone who plays this game "casually": I play for fun and to see what I can accomplish, not as a content creator, or a power builder. I have logged so many hours in this game because it's just that enjoyable. Granted: there could be a more easily accessible guide for beginners, but there is a tutorial and the game design does help you figure things out effectively.
Mods are enabled and at least mildly encouraged by the devs, who have integrated Steam Workshop into the game. However, you don't necessarily *need* any mods to play. Most of the uploaded mods are cosmetic changes, custom content, or bug fixes, and the vanilla version of the game is perfectly enjoyable by itself.
When I mentioned before that you can build whatever kind of prison you want, I meant that sincerely. A village, a turtle, a fleet of boats, and a castle town are all maps currently shared in the workshop. If you want to get creative, you can!

The game starts out very simply. Build a prison for 8 prisoners. Sounds easy enough. Before you know it you have 100+ prisoners all with their own needs and you have to find a way to make money to keep the prison up and running. You have to choose how to run your prison from keeping you prisoners happy and event free (you get a bonus for days without incident.), try to accomplish grants or put your prisoners to work. This is on top of if you want to have min, normal, max security inmates coming in.

I've had this game in my library for quite awhile now. I've gotten the mixed ending, pacifist ending, and the "below" mixed ending. I rage quitted the genocide run because of my many failed attempts at the Undyne the Undying boss fight (seriously, ♥♥♥♥ her). Anyway, I decided to make a review of this game.
Undertale is somewhat special to me. I've bought it when I was pretty much new to Steam. My freind talked about it a few times, and I was interested. I'm not really into turn-based RPG games as I am to action/open world RPG's like Skyrim, but I gave it a try anyway. I was hooked to it. Everything from the characters, humor, music, atmosphere, story, and even gameplay felt so enjoyable to me. If you're just as sensitive as I am, then you might almost shed a tear, because this game is very emotional and has some really lovable/sad moments. Like most RPG games, you have a choice weither to be the good guy, bad guy, or both (I started off as a pacifist because I always start as a good guy in games). Undertale is somewhat unique to this system because it feels more "open-choiced" than most games I've seen. You'll get an ending depending on what choices you made, and this game has MANY choices.
This is sort of a bonus to this review, but if you're gonna look at Undertale's community before playing it, DON'T. It is as most people say: cancer. And I'm not just talking about the fans, I'm also talking about the spoiled haters who say stuff like "you're autistic" or "kill yourself" when they see people who have a different opinion than theirs. But you already knew the community is bad, like all other communities right? Judge the game itself, not because of the fanbase.
So, do I recommend Undertale? Well, if you're a fan of turn-based RPG's with a deep story and multiple choices, then yes, yes I do. I even recommend it for other gamers, such as myself.

Something that can truly be eye-opening. Spec Ops: The Line is one of those hidden trasures that comes along now and then. It's nice to see the AAA community try something different, and Spec Ops does just that and led me to many surprises one after the other.
It is easy to mistake this as some bad Call of Duty clone at first glance. I thought the same when I first saw it and I'm confident I'm not the only one. To avoid spoilers I will talk about what goes on in the game as little as possible, but there are certain subjects the story of Spec Ops: The Line touches on that throws a bit of the harsh realities of war into the face of the player.
I have talked to many soldiers, both currently active and those who were active. There is a consistent theme: there is no moral high ground in war. Spec Ops delivers on this very well. You are constantly given moral choices that don't seem to have a positive outcome either way, and you're constantly making decisions based off incomplete information, and it just sends things further spiraling downward to create the story masterpiece that is Spec Ops.
Since I can't talk more about the story without giving things away, you should stop reading this and buy Spec Ops now.

You play as a soldier fighting the good fight, fighting to save people and set them free from oppression. You, dear player, are the hero. Only you're not. The game helps you question why we obey whatever directives we are gives in any FPS. Why do we shoot these people? Are they all bad? Are we so morally superior that whoever we shoot is always the bad guy? Well, I suppose shooting people who are shooting at me is a pretty good way of staying alive. Fair point. But what about people who are not shooting at you? Spec Ops: The Line plays with your sense of self in a game and the fact that you identify with the character you play.
On the gameplay side of things (I did buy the game before it appeared on Steam), it does not play as smoothly as say a Call of Duty. However, whatever gripes anyone might have with weapons handling, it does not subtract significantly from gameplay in general.

Rating: 8/10, would recommend! However, game still in alpha.
Despite being in development, the existing gameplay and potential of this title make it a wonderful experience. I'd recommend PA for anyone who enjoys "citybuilding", architecture, and/or sim games. On top of that, the addition of 'failure conditions' is a really wonderful way the developers added in a bit of action gameplay. Not only do you get to build whatever kind of prison you want, but if you "fail" a map, then you have to PLAY it. You join the ranks of inmates, and must go about serving your (randomly assigned) sentence.
The game runs great, although there are occasionally bugs, some of which can be a game ruiner. At time of writing, I believe we're on Alpha 26, so bugs are to be expected. The developer is pretty responsive to bug reports and feedback, so hopefully by beta release all the wrinkles will be smoothed out.
I consider myself someone who plays this game "casually": I play for fun and to see what I can accomplish, not as a content creator, or a power builder. I have logged so many hours in this game because it's just that enjoyable. Granted: there could be a more easily accessible guide for beginners, but there is a tutorial and the game design does help you figure things out effectively.
Mods are enabled and at least mildly encouraged by the devs, who have integrated Steam Workshop into the game. However, you don't necessarily *need* any mods to play. Most of the uploaded mods are cosmetic changes, custom content, or bug fixes, and the vanilla version of the game is perfectly enjoyable by itself.
When I mentioned before that you can build whatever kind of prison you want, I meant that sincerely. A village, a turtle, a fleet of boats, and a castle town are all maps currently shared in the workshop. If you want to get creative, you can!

The game starts out very simply. Build a prison for 8 prisoners. Sounds easy enough. Before you know it you have 100+ prisoners all with their own needs and you have to find a way to make money to keep the prison up and running. You have to choose how to run your prison from keeping you prisoners happy and event free (you get a bonus for days without incident.), try to accomplish grants or put your prisoners to work. This is on top of if you want to have min, normal, max security inmates coming in.

Okay, let's get honest here. I loved the first Life is Strange. It had it's errors and fails, but I still love it. Right now I'm very confused what to say about LiS: Before the Storm. I'm just confused.
Without spoiling anything in the beginning, I want to say this: If you liked the first game and you don't have high expectations - go ahead and play this. If you are easily getting dissapointed - you should still buy this one, but imagine it's a different game, just in the same universe. Hard, but it will help you. And if you are looking for answers for the questions you have about the previous game - you can just click the "x" in the right corner, because "there ain't no answers here".
The feel of the game is different, but I am amazed and happy about the graphics. At least it gives the LiS nostalgia. Music isn't a huge plus for me here, except their own music made for game, and not the songs that they had in from others, if you know what I mean. If you are here looking to find out why and how f.ex.
, you'll be dissapointed. What got me mad as well is how the game was set. I enjoyed episode two, and it was the only one I kind of liked. First one felt too awkward in mood, and the last one is just... like I was watching a movie, not actually played a game. SOOOOOOO many scenes where they just talk and you have nothing you can say. SOOOOOOOOOOO many.... It's fine if you like it this way or want to know a bit more about Rachel. For me this game felt very rushed and didn't solve much from the previous game. I actually have more questions now than I had before. The whole game felt just rushed and, well, just to tell a story that we didn't really need in the first place. Okay, I'm just kidding. It's great to have a prequel, but I imagined it to be much better. I like the topic they focused on, and I like some of the characters, but many of them feel like not themselves.
Overall I recommand this game just because it's a LiS title

Rogue Legacy is a very enjoyable game. You progress through a castle finding chests containing money or blueprints, and survive as long as you can beating rooms, puzzles, and bosses until your death. Upon dying, a new heir to your family is chosen, and you play through a new castle with them. Previously earned blueprints allow for this heir to possibly wear better armor, earn better weapons, and the money you earn from your previous life carries over so that your heir may afford these new luxuries.
It's definitely a one-of-a-kind game, and I highly recommend it to any fan of platformers looking for a rogue-esque title.

I highly recommend this game, expecially if you can catch it on sale.

So, how do you review a game that simulates an actual job? I can see how the fantasy element of many games could offer escape into a world nobody could actually vist, but a game where with 6 months of lessons you could actually do it for real poses me a problem. And a solution.
Becoming a long distance lorry driver in the real world is not for me - I dislike motorways, parking, service stations, ports, railways, paying for huge amounts of fuel, working to deadlines, border crossings and a myriad of other things associated with driving for a living. However, this game smoothes out all of those issues - want to cross a border? Drive straight through. Want to fill up with fuel? Sure, that's 20 seconds of your life.
The experience is very hypnotic, the scenery magnificent and the other road traffic is slightly more sane than in reality.
This is not so much a game as an example of how much better real lorry driving could be if you remove the irritations of paperwork, fuel costs, border controls and everything else that makes driving a misery.
Highly recommended with one caveat - real roads are much worse than those you drive in the game.

Inside all of us, there's an unsatiable, yet unnoticed desire inside all human beings to drive giant trucks carrying heavy cargo. However, many are scared to go out into the real world to satisfy this need, as doing so would put their lives, others' lives, and the cargo carried in danger. But where can you expirement with a playground that is wide open, realistic, AND simulated? This game has and is the answer to that question.
Welcome to Euro Truck Simulator 2.
Now, when I first viewed this game, I was VERY skeptical to say the least. Then I saw the demo, thought why not, only 1000 megabytes. And boy was I hooked. It was a great ride (haha) with the demo while it lasted, but it only lasted for five shipments.
Then I got to contemplating. Is the price of this game worth it? As of now, yes! I am loving the game. It may not be for the hardcore Call of Duty players, but it sure can suit a wide range of other gamers.
TL;DR: Fun game, great price, definately worth it.
+Great graphics! The great textures help add to the feel of the game.
+Great little-things-that-most-people-don't-pay-attention-to; You actually have to press keys for turn signals, windshield wipers, etc.
+There are rules of the road! If you crush other cars you get fined, you also get fined for exessively going over the speed limit and running red lights!
-Sadly, you cannot exit your vehicle. I feel that if this was in the game it would make it to the top of my list. I'd love to park off duty, go and customize the clothing my character has, and be able to walk around my vehicle.
8/10, definately does it's job; it's simulating trucking! In Europe!

Ive been playing DayZ for years, and started when the bugs were at their absolute worse before the .60 update; you have to remember this game is in ALPHA but as I write this review on October 2017 the game is currently in .62 and while yes it still has its bugs its great to play! DayZ takes a LOT of in game Knowledge so my advice is this:
1. Learn the Map use your steam browser and go to IZurvive
2/ DayZ Wiki is your bestfriend
3. DayZ Spy is also Key you can see how many active people are online and the best servers to go
4. Occasional DayZ Reddit visiting to keep up with Devs and updates on game improvements
DayZ is just months away from finally hitting BETA after all these years of being in Alpha and while yes the game has been in Alpha for an extreme amount of time the game has improved massively and Beta will improve a lot of the bugs that people complain about! Will it be perfect? probably not but what makes this game great is the experiences and interaction with other people! Yes there are ♥♥♥♥♥♥TON of Bandits dont just trust anyone you meet but use your instict and gut to weave out who may be friendly and who isnt! If you know anyone that plays the game with experience, I highly recommend getting some coaching from them as they probably know all the ropes of the game. IF you do not know anyone or meet anyone in the game willing to show you around; there is also a subreddit for players to meet other serious players to link up and run through the zombie apocalypse. The interaction with other players is key to this game so making a friend YOU CAN TRUST is KEY to survival! But interaction with other players whether good or bad are a huge part of the DayZ adrenaline rush; one minute youre looting houses with a friend and the next youre hiding and boarding up in a nearby house because of the sound of footsteps or a gunshot off in the distance!
DayZ has a great RP ecperience for the servers and groups that stick to it! I would recommend DayZ Village by Barely infected they also have a website if you google them and enjoy the RP experience. DayZ has a beautiful RP experience when done right.
Zombies need a lot of work they are not anywhere near perfect as of right now! theyre more a chore then they are enemies; its the people not the zombies you should be worried about but the game has intense survival aspects from eating to making sure you dont get hypothermia! Searching for loot is key to survival on this game do not start getting discouraged if youre not finding any loot just stay away from major spawn poitns (mostly the coast, spawn points are also listed on the map website i mentioned above) so it is easier to find weapons and loot.
Yes this game is known as "the running simulator" but if you learn the game and where loot spawns it will be much easier for you to find things conveniently if you learn the best plaves to find them, remember the DayZ Wiki and IZurvive are your best friends!

There is nothing I can say any better than what has already said about this game.  The game mechanically is generic; a third-person shooter with some squad based combat with the added bonus of using the world around you as a means to fight, this being done thanks to the sandstorms and the trapped sand within the enviornments themselves.
Glass can be shot to cause an avalanche of sand to smother your enemies, or simply to blind and disorient while you go in for the kill.
But that isn't why it is mandatory that you play this game.
The narrative and everything used to frame it, even the very "generic" layer of the game is all done with the intent to drive home a story that while far from original (it is loosely based off of the novel, Heart of Darkness) has never been more personal.
This is easily the best version of the story I have ever come across, because while the movies and the books that portray it have done well and moved on to become classics, this is a version that is going to make it personal for you. You drive a truck,what can I say more?

Euro Truck Simulator 2 casts you as an up-and-coming truck driver in Europe. You start out doing freelance jobs for other companies who provide you with a truck for each job, eventually amassing enough money to buy your own garage and truck, which is when the game truly begins. Of course, you can always take out a bank loan, but if you want to stay debt-free, you have to work for that money. You can always take a quick job if you feel like it, but to gain access to the most powerful trucks you need to buy and upgrade them yourself, both visually and performance-wise.
After each job you will gain money, experience and truck upgrades. Experience can be used to level up your driver in various ways. For instance, you can put points into certifications for dangerous cargo or long distance driving to unlock more job types or eco-driving to reduce fuel consumption and the resulting costs.
Once you've got your truck company off the ground you can start expanding by buying more trucks, hiring drivers and more garages across Europe. The game doesn't offer much in the way of micro-managing you employees, but you can upgrade their trucks in the same way you upgrade your own and decide what attribute they should focus on levelling up.
Do note that there's no win-state in this game. It just keeps going while you expand your freight empire and if you want a clear goal you need to set it yourself.
When you're ready to hit the road you either pick from a list of available quick jobs or go the the freight market to find cargo to haul with your own truck. Quick jobs are great if you just want a quick fix, as you don't have to drive all the way to pick up your cargo. If you want the pure experience you buy a truck, pick a job and drive to pick up the trailer before embarking on your journey. Along the way you will need to follow the rules of the road and watch out for traffic. Any and all traffic offences will result in a fine, which can severely bite into your profits if you're not careful. While you can get away with speeding, there are speed cameras along most roads that you need to be on the lookout for. You also need to keep an eye on your gas tank and your sleepiness levels and pull into a gas station or rest stop when needed. When you arrive at your destination you can choose to park your truck yourself, which can be a true challenge in certain locations, or relinquish a handful of experience points by using auto-park.
One immersion breaker is that there is no real in-game economy to speak of. Everything stays pretty much static no matter what happens in the game and there are no realistic cargo chains (i.e. raw materials to factory, products to store). This will hopefully likely in the near future as the developer has created tools for creating such chains and has implemented a few in the Scandinavia DLC.
Since I'm so late in writing this review, I'm lucky enough to write it after the 1.17 patch was released. This patch brought plenty of changes to the graphical presentation, most importantly the lighting. The game is definitely no Project CARS, but it has absolutely been serviceable and is now even more so with the improved rendering engine. Some scenes are made absolutely gorgeous by it. World textures could definitely use some upgrades to make the game a look bit more realistic and some models look a bit basic, but overall the visuals of the game are just fine. Not mind-blowing, but they do the job well.
The trucks themselves are modelled in stunning detail, and the Mercedes-Benz New Actros that was released in patch 1.18 takes this to a whole new level. It's clear that a lot of love and hard labour has gone into the trucks and they are definitely the highlight of the game's presentation. The only downside to the models is that the switches and knobs inside the cabin aren't adjustable. I may have been spoiled by other pure simulators, but it would be a nice touch if you could actually use the physical buttons instead of mapped keys on a keyboard or controller.
The physics simulation leave a little more to be desired. The truck cabins don't sway as much as they ought, which is especially noticeable during roundabouts or when decelerating. Trailers don't
heavy, but just slow you down, and there's very little feedback from the road surface.
The sound design as a whole is serviceable. The truck sounds are of course very good, but the rest of the sound scape doesn't feel as fleshed out. Not that it matters all that much when you spend most of your time inside the cabin (which
the proper way to play), but it would be nice to have a some more prominent ambient sounds to instil a sense of place when you pull over and turn off the engine. If the truck sounds or road noise aren't to your liking, there are loads of mods available that remedy this.
The world design is generally pretty good. Areas like Great Britain and Switzerland feature some of the best roads and vistas the game has to offer, but some areas feel very bland, especially Germany, which unfortunately is the country you travel through the most because of its location. These areas have generic roads with generic intersections and generic city layouts. It all starts to feel very same-y when you pass the same copy-pasted intersection for the fifth time on a single haul. Some off/on-ramps are also very confusing, where one lane suddenly turns off the road without any heads-up. The signs don't always indicate correctly and these intersections are unrealistically common in the game.
The DLC that has been released is a lot better in this regard, but if you want to up the fidelity of the base game, there are a lot of map mods to try. ProMods is one of the bigger mods that add new areas to the game, but they are also currently in the process of redesigning a lot of the base game to get it up to scratch with the new areas.
The game also supports TrackIR and Oculus, but I haven't had any chance to try these features out.
The game supports keyboard & mouse, gamepads and steering wheels.
The controls for kb&m and gamepads are fairly straight-forward and work just fine. The wheels are way more interesting and you get a lot of settings to perfect your experience. Earlier, the trucks had some wonky wheel rotation properties, but a recent patch gave all trucks 900º rotation. I haven't found any settings I feel are missing, either. There are multiple sliders for different axes and FFB settings, all buttons are rebindable and there is a useful wizard for quick setup.
The force feedback feels a bit "grindy", though. I use a Logitech G27 and it feels like the engines struggle with providing resistance, almost like they're slipping on sand. This does not happen in other games, where the feedback is tight and grippy. I have no idea what causes this, and it doesn't seem like any of the settings fix it. It
and can give you a juicy jolt if you crash, but it's not what I've come to expect from force feedback.
Despite some technical flaws this is one of my favorite games. It's a solid package and great for a relaxing evening of driving.
If you can stomach long drives, gradual progression and being responsible for your own fun
on the open road, this game comes highly recommended.

So, do I recommend Undertale? Well, if you're a fan of turn-based RPG's with a deep story and multiple choices, then yes, yes I do. I even recommend it for other gamers, such as myself.
