Welcome to my review of game "theHunter: Call of the Wild". Today i'm gonna review one of the best games i've played in a couple of months.
I'm pleased that i can do it for you guys.
The story begins when i saw this game on steam sale on 13-14 of august or something, and during that time i was away from home so i couldn't buy this, because i don't have credit card yet. So i screw it. Then i decided to watch some videos on YT of this game and i felt in love. The graphics was amazing. I was in such a shock, that i bought it when i came back home and didn't even looked on the price,  just bought it. And... Guys, i'll never regret that bought. Down below i'm gonna leave infos in more schematic format, because i know you "readers" like it, just like me so let's go...
-Graphics: Shadow, textures etc. are master class in this title. This artwork gives you the feeling beeing in actual forest. That's quite amazing, isn't it? :D But, graphics can be good, but what about optymization? It's not very good, but only and so good. With my PC SPECS (which i have on my STEAM profile) i usually get 40-50 FPS on ULTRA (including ultra shadows which aren't automaticly turned on, so yea, my GTX 970 handles it pretty well. Day cicle is full and super long, so you don't need to worry about getting dark in half of your hunting ;-) Rain is also very well mapped. Amazingly breath taking rain... best i've ever seen in video games.
-Atmosphere (climat): It's one of the best created worlds in video games i've ever seen. Of course in video games in "simulators" category. You just need to see this by your selves, i can't describe it, you know it.
-Sounds: Masterclass there. Birds, worms, dragonflies, everything couses sound. And realy atmospheric sounds, which allow you to dive deeper in this world of hunting. Just like climat, you need to feel it by your own.
-Mechanics: Not the best, but allow you to not get frustraded or something. None of this, but they could have been more flattered you know. Tracking system is pretty easy, but entertaining either, so what do you need more to have fun in hunting game? Shooting is awesome. During every shot you feel that power coming out from the barrel of your gun and that's most important in hunting game, isn't it?
There are fast travel points, lookouts and much few more activities to discover, such as places' history and information about some events or things that happened on each map.
So.. when we're on maps. The locations you can visit are two. Each of them are HUGE. And i mean huge as hell. One's more european (poland, germany) and the other is more US.
Fauna changes with each map, so you won't get bored of one species of animals. You won't see them at all during the game if you sprint all game long, you cause too much noise. Be careful ;-). You can also but DLCs which are not necessary to have fun in the game. They're only little flavours on the top of a cake. Check them out, maybe one of them will get your attention. I personaly entertain the "Tents", but check them out either way. Weapon customization is not very rich. Only scopes and ammo you can shoot with. Nothing special. You have bunch of guns to shoot with, including bows, shotguns, pistols and hunting snipes. A lot of them to buy and test in front of you.
DLCs for now:
-Tents
-ATV(quads)
-and few free ones: bow, shooting range and character customization pack.
-Music: Just casual music to don't get you bored from hearing only world's sounds (which are not bad, but you know). It turnes on sometimes during exploration or random moments, i can't tell you by now.
-Story: Admit, who counted on story in hunting simulator ;-) No one, you can't hide yourselves. The story is only to make you doing some random stuff, like shooting fox by bow, which you wouldn't do at all with no constraint. So there are few people who give you missions, but they contact you by a phone, so you don't see them all game long. Only chats. Only faces you're gonna see during the game are:
-yours
-friend's, in multiplayer
So no that many :-P But who cares, it's hunting game.
-Multiplayer:
Very funny and hard at the same time. Co-op is realy cool. Not many interactions between players but game it's self makes it fun and intresting. Just find out buying it now on STEAM STORE, i bet you won't regret this as i don't  :-)
OVERALL: 9/10. REALY nice game ;-) I recommend it. and notice, when i recommend a game, it's worth a recommendation :D I bet you.
Cheers,

So you make a jail in this game. Yey. Build buildings and rooms that are used for various purposes all to make your prison... however you want, actually. After moving beyond the premise that you are building this unpleasant place, the game gives you significant amounts of freedom to choose what sort of unpleasant place it is. Will you make a rehabilitation center with classrooms, gardens, and plentiful opportunities to help your inmates? Or will you make an abyssal hellhole of concrete, armed guards, and abusive authority? You can make both in this game, and everything in between. As far as simulations go, the sort of creative freedom this game offers the player is exactly what all games of this genre ought to have. You can adjust everything from deciding what your prisoners do each hour of the day, the types of inmates you have in your prison, to what sort of punishments you deal out when those convicts decide to do something naughty like punching the cooks or trying to dig an excape tunnel through their toilet (eww!). There are nearly an endless amount of possibilities! :o
It's still in Early Access, but the game is very playable right now. I'm looking forward to seeing what else they will add, because what the game already has is excellent. Even if this game is apparently unfinished, you can still have lots of fun with it as you create the jail of your... choosing. XD
If you like simulation games where you build stuff, like SimCity or Tropico, then this is certainly a game worth looking into. Have fun!

Now, when I heard there would be another Borderlands, I had to admit, I was curious. After playing the first game, however, I realized this game wasn't really my thing. I loved playing as Roland, though. He was the reason I even got through the first one, get a team of four Rolands and you can steamroll through the entire game, because only two things survived in the first game: Everyone you've yet to kill, and Roland.
So I played the second game.
I've been a big fan of the art style for some time, as it's got its own watercolor-ink style that makes it look like it should come out of a comic book, which is very interesting to look at, and keeps my eyes occupied with how bored I typically am actually playing the game solo. This is not a game to play alone, unless you like Japanese RPGs, or grindfest Korean-type MMOs, but with guns, and much less a chance to hit anything if your gun is too farsighted or stupid (or Hyperion, which is basically synonymous.) Bullets veer off to the left and right at the start, and although I've had a few happy accidents where stray bullets killed someone or something I wasn't aiming at, I can say that it builds up to the constant nessesity to move towards better guns and overall equipment. Shields come with a cost to your health, some things feel at least a little stupid to even add, name generators sound like cringey (moreso than usual) Homestuck handles (greasyWeasel I feel, was entirely named so on purpose), and most things which feel less like a joke and more like a grab for attention, akin to a teenager waving their arms about, shouting "OH LOOK AT US WE'RE RELEVANT".
And you know what? That's okay. Because it's not about the stats, at the end of the day, (Badass tokens give you permanent buffs across all characters, Class mods can make the game not suck for you and your team) but rather, about working with your team, as a combined effort to be a horrible person to horrible people. Tons of great little moments add to the game, but I could've gone with fewer references to the internet at large ("jokes") and generally speaking, I'm not really paying attention to the game at large as much as I am a conversation durring, and you know what? That works. Music's not stellar, but it adds atmosphere, so it does its job right. My biggest problem is that the guy I'm stuck with in Co-Op is usually too drunk behind the wheel to drive properly, and I hate driving intensely in this game (unless I'm in the back of a bandit technical, hooping and hollaring as my Assassin buddy babysits two Psychos) outside of bumming a ride and blowing stuff up like it's an on the rails shooter.
In summary, I'm not one for loot and shoots by and large due to their tedium, but this is alright. The story's okay, but the characters really hold my attention more. At least a little mad about what happened in the story, but you know, that's why Handsome Jack is so good to hate. Not very replayable, unless you get someone to power level you, or you're mucking about with friends.
6/10, if only for the Co-Op capabilities, and how fun it is to play when you could not care less, or not entirely sober. Lots of fun content (coughcough-DLC-coughcough), with (in my opinion, poor -or even not enough- execution) a lot of missed opportunities. I don't see myself playing this again after I beat it the first time, making the customization feel at least a little stupid (though, a great addition) for what you have to go through, and ends up feeling as hollow and empty as unlocking an achievement.
In short: It's okay. Could've been better, but then, it also could've been made by EA. So at least there's a silver lining.

This game I therefore would not reccomend to someone who does not have skill or patience as it is a bit of a grind. That being said it is very satisfying to beat a boss or get to a new area, so much so that it makes the struggle worth it, a bit like a 2d dark souls. The characters or heirs that you choose with each new life have witty traits that will change the way that you play the game, and as you build your manor you will unlock more classes to choose from, thereby changing the playstyle of your run, overal I would reccomend this game to people who like challenges and exploration. 8/10

I suck at reversing the trailer (even though I'm getting better at it) but that's not the game's fault. There's really quite a lot to recommend in this game, so I'll get to it.
Pros
1. Very realistic driving simulation, from game pad and joystick support, to manual gear changes, faithful replicas of various brands of trucks, etc.
2. Somehow they compress time -- a 4 hour journey can be completed in 30 minutes of real time game play. This was one of the biggest questions I had before buying this game since I didn't want to be stuck at the wheel for hours at a time. I don't know how they do it, but they compress driving time very well, so that you feel the longer deliveries but at the same time don't burn an afternoon travelling a simulated highway.
3. Great graphics and physics engine -- rain, cloudy skies, wiper action, water drops on your windshield, headlights, all nicely represented.
4. Some RPG elements included -- running your own trucking business, buying vehicles, hiring drivers, all add a nice touch to what was supposed to be just a sim.
5. The most amazing thing to me is: the landscape and the scenery look real! I don't know how they mapped thousands of miles of roads, signs, landmarks, scenery, etc. but they did a damn fine job of it. You really feel like you're in Europe!
Cons
1. Kind of steep learning curve, figuring out the driving controls/keys, had to keep pausing and checking the game setting options (there are a LOT of functions). I wish this part could be covered in a tutorial of some sort.
2. A sandbox / practice mode would have been nice. You literally get thrown into the driver's seat from the start. But I guess some people like jumping in right away, but some like me prefer to have a decent understanding of all the controls first.
Although I'm not as good a driver as I want to be, I'm actually having fun (minus the tickets and accident citations)!
Recommended!

Liked: graphics are nice, spawn rate of resources pretty good
Disliked: lack of any kind of permanence for stockpiling, STEEP learning curve, no way to delete parts of a structure you make, getting to any type of sophistication takes hours unless you're near a harbor or some other type of monument (even then it still takes an hour or so).
A great deal of the game feels like wasting time. What was great about Minecraft is that you could become sophisticated in a relatively small amount of time and not feel like after spending hours building something up, you have a veteran player come in with a freaking rock and kill you since you're still learning the game. It would be like having a person spawn and be able to kill you with punches in 10 seconds and take everything from you and your base. If you like starting from scratch each time you spawn into the world, this game is for you. Otherwise it feels like counter strike with building crap and nudity, and without money or any kind of store to gear up and get back in the game without spending another couple of hours gathering, smelting, burning, etc to try and get back to where you were. Some people really enjoy the grind; I got out of MMOs precisely for that reason. And in MMOs you generally get to keep or secure what you've already attained to a certain degree which Rust does not allow you to do.
There is no tutorial, no real resources available online, so anyone who's played even a few hours more than you has an infinite edge, and you'll find yourself resetting over and over again. In my experience, gamers are unreliable so the ability to create your own map and not play with other players to get the hang of the game mechanics would be very helpful. As it stands after 5 hours play time I was still unclear on how to rotate objects for a structure.
There are also incomplete instructions on items for game mechanics, and hell the refinery even mentions ore and smelting... you'd think charging $20 for a game that they can get some text descriptions correct.
Overall, I was not a fan of this game. Being a working professional I have only 15-20 hours per week to play games, and having no way to secure progress to any degree other than banding together with a clan who expects you to play a certain minimum amount of time and have a certain number of hours clocked in the game is infuriating and really sucked the enjoyment out of the open world gathering and crafting.
So, two very definite thumbs-down from me.

Fans of the old and new movies alike will instantly recognise the setting and (art)style, largely copied from the third movie (Fury Road). You play the protagonist Mad Rockatansky, or "Mad Max", in a post-apocalyptic wasteland at some former coast of Australia, looking for his homeland which he mysteriously calls "the Plains of Silence". Already at the start of the game, in the intro, he gets robbed of his V8 car "Interceptor" and posessions and over the coarse of the game he tries to get back his car (or build a new one as he soon discovers), avenge the man responsible (Scabrous Scrotus) to then continue his journey. On his way he encounters the many War Boys of Scabrous Scrotus, and a fellow war lord Stank Gum with his War Boys, and also some allies whos help he can use all too well.
The graphics in this game are pretty well done and optimised. Although of course this game is not full of lush bushes, animals and other stuff that can burden your graphics card a lot, it still feels like a beautiful vast outstretching desert full of artifacts of a past history that runs really well and smooth. Scattered around the landscape you find, next to rock formations and tire tracks, the remnants of a lost world: rusty shipwrecks, former oil drill platforms, crumbled bridges, ruins of factory buildings, docksides, harbour cranes, so on and so forth, reminding of a life long gone where there was still plenty of water and food to go around. Collectibles scattered throughout the world will hint you to it and what might have happened.
So how does it play? After meeting your first few characters you find yourself quickly driving around a LOT in your newly acquired ride looking for scrap, the main currency in the game. Scrap is used to upgrade your car, lovingly called the 'Magnum Opus' by Chumbucket whom you meet at the start of the game and likes to express everything in a religious but car related fashion, and scrap is used to unlock some abilities and gear on Max. By completing activities like achievements, do x times this or x times that, or races you will earn Griffa tokens. These can be spent when you visit Griffa to upgrade some perks. These perks will add extra scrap ontop of what you pick up, or makes you consume less fuel, et cetera.
Of combat in this game are two kinds: on foot and in the car. That's right, car combat! Early in the game Chumbucket will fabricate a harpoon for you on the car that enables you to rip off doors, tires, bumpers or snatch the driver right from his seat! Despite the limited tools you get for the car to use, car combat in this game is the most fun. Chasing down Scrotus' convoys going high speed, picking off cars left and right watching them tumble and turn into big balls of fire (Michael Bay would approve!) feels exhilarating!
On foot the combat is much the same like the Batman games, for those familiar with it. Max can pick up a few weapons but they always have a (very) limited lifespan. This can be elongated by the perks at Griffa, but you'll generally be fighting with your fists. Even the little shivs Max carries can only be used once for a finisher and not always be looted back from the corpses. Max also carries a shotgun, but the ammo is rather limited, even with all upgrades unlocked. All-in-all the combat in the beginning feels powerful, it feels as if more could have been done to make it more interesting and less repetitive in the long run. Every boss fight of the Top Dogs in the world is almost completely the same and requires no imagination. Once you figured out one, you know how to beat them all. Such a pity!
Story wise this game is as dry as the world it plays in and as shallow as the water collectors. There is very little character development, of either Max or anyone he encounters. Then again, Max is a rather selfish man with little empathy for others. At least that's what he wants to make himself believe. Griffa, the fella Max visits to upgrade his perks every now and then, sometimes puts question marks at his deeds to make him rethink, but that's about all the hints Max (and the player) gets.
The game is a good looker, runs very well, and fun to play if you like to drive an aweful lot through miles and miles of desert land in a world fueled by the atmosphere from Mad Max: Fury Road. Car combat is most fun, combat on foot is a little too familiar and not much depth. Story is very short and paper thin I'd say, compared to games like Witcher 3. If you like the car bit, it can be worth your money. If you seek something full of story and rich hand-to-hand combat, you will be disappointed.

My feelings on Undertale is complex, but I believe that people can both like and dislike this game fairly easily.
I like the premise the game; it's simple and easy the follow: monster and humans once lived in harmony, humans didn't like that monsters were capable of absorbing SOULs, drove the monsters away and sealed them underground. A human falls into the underground and you have to guide them through to find a way out. Not memorable, but some of the characters and art style throwback to the SNES and Genesis age is quite impressive.
The gameplay is quite creative as well, using a semi-turnbased RPG system where you and your enemy take turns performing actions or attacking, while you can dodge enemy attacks in real time. This adds a new layer of difficulty in what we normally expect from RPGs, but has a nice enough difficulty curve to avoid it being brutal.
The difficulty, however, is where I begin to question the design choices. I don't expect every game to have a layer of difficult fights, but I do appreciate the difficulty being CONSISTENT. By now, most of you know that the game has three main paths: true pacifist, neutral, and genocide. depending on which path you select depends on how well the difficulty is handled. If you try the neutral route, you get enough LV to stand against more difficult battles while also breezing through the normally easy ones. This keeps the difficulty roughly the same throughout. Not bad, but not recommended. The true pacifist route sees that the fights become gradually more difficult and more complex, and without room for LV, the difficulty spikes in some areas is understandable. However, the way that the final fights are set up for both the neutral and pacifist fights make it so that all that you learned is nearly pointless. The genocide route is roughly consistent in its battles; and by that I mean that literally ALL BUT TWO FIGHTS ARE ACTUALLY DIFFICULT AT ALL!!!! It's fine to have easy fights, but you have to make the fights have some complex mechanics to back them up. Sure, it proves that monsters are no match for humans, being consistent to the lore of the game, but only two monsters stand up to you at ALL!?!? I call BS, I'm sorry, but I do.
The characters in the game, as I mentioned earlier, are also fine, but most of them feel one-dimensional or lack luster. Asgore, Papyrus, and Undyne suffer the most from this. They aren't bad, but they could've had a lot more improvement. I believe that Sans and another character whom I won't spoil are the most three-dimensional, but for their own separate reasons. Toriel is close, but didn't quite hit the mark.
The battle is unique as I mentioned earlier, but with most battles being easy, most people don't appreciate it much. There are four options: Fight, Act, Item, and Mercy. If the player ACTs in a particular way, then the player can spare them. Using an ITEM allows the player to switch between gear and heal their HP. FIGHTing sounds just like you think it does: hack away until a monster's dead. What's really interesting is that depending on how many you spare, and by extension kill, affects how the story will turn out.
The only other thing is general presentation, including art and music. For being done by a single man,  both are extremely well done. Character models look fabulous, the scenery is consistent and beautiful, and I just have fun frolicing down the paths of the areas like Snowdin. The music was so closing to being in my top 5 greatest gaming soundtracks, but didn't quite make it. The big reason is because of the area themes which are remarkably dull, surprisingly. They aren't bad, but they aren't memorable personally. However, a lot of area music is memorable in any other game, so I guess I can't punish Toby Fox too much here. However, the boss fight music is on a whole other level. Having hits like Megalovania, Battle Against a True Hero, Hopes and Dreams, and Bonetrousle, the music has you coming back to fight these guys again and again just to hear where they originated. I personally took at least two minutes at the beginning of each fight just to let the music sink in. If for nothing else, the music alone can constitute reasoning for playing this game.
My final thoughts: I like the game, trying to break normal playing conventions, breaking the forth wall, pretty solid humor, an extraordinary score, and so on. However, the game can become too easy in some cases, the battle system eventually repetitive, and a vast majority of areas and characters left... unmemorable. Not too mention this game harbors about 10 hours of gameplay before you do just about everything it can offer. Maybe even less if you adjust to it quickly. But for its price, I'll let it slid. I can't complain about the game, but even for ten dollars, be sure that everything I just described sounds like the game you'd enjoy. Worst case scenerio, you only spent $10, and you can wait before you get more money for another game. This game still gets a solid 7.9 out of 10. Good, but far from perfect.

This was the most enjoyable, addicting, and challenging 30hrs I've spent platform gaming in some time. I'll throw my recommendation on the massive pile of recommendations this game already has. I got hooked quick and didn't stop until I hit the top. I don't normally 100% games or pay attention to "achievements" but I went all out on this one! I couldn't help myself, it is that good.
I got it on a steep sale of 2.99USD but 14.99USD is not unreasonable for what you get out of it. (But of course still wait for a sale of some sort.)
Now if I had to FORCE out a complaint or two at gunpoint they would be;
1. Be very aware that every time you beat the game the difficulty will increase substantially. I think I was ahead of the designed curve on my first and second finishes which made my third playthrough feel more like punishment for beating the game rather than any reward. Some thirty or so ruthless deaths later I had stockpiled enough gold to unlock some perks that helped with this issue and I got back to enjoying the game. Other than that issue this game actually avoids ever turning into too much of a "grind". Really scales super smooth.
2. Certain enemy's detection of the player kind of eliminates the perceived appeal of a few specials and dashes. You would think you could use a dash to the opposite side of a turret to land a quick strike but it will instantly be facing and firing on schedule at you the exact pixel you cross over.
Neither are real issues, just trying to find a negative for argument's sake. But honestly, this game is darn near perfect for what it is.
Buy without apprehension and enjoy!

Fans of the old and new movies alike will instantly recognise the setting and (art)style, largely copied from the third movie (Fury Road). You play the protagonist Mad Rockatansky, or "Mad Max", in a post-apocalyptic wasteland at some former coast of Australia, looking for his homeland which he mysteriously calls "the Plains of Silence". Already at the start of the game, in the intro, he gets robbed of his V8 car "Interceptor" and posessions and over the coarse of the game he tries to get back his car (or build a new one as he soon discovers), avenge the man responsible (Scabrous Scrotus) to then continue his journey. On his way he encounters the many War Boys of Scabrous Scrotus, and a fellow war lord Stank Gum with his War Boys, and also some allies whos help he can use all too well.
The graphics in this game are pretty well done and optimised. Although of course this game is not full of lush bushes, animals and other stuff that can burden your graphics card a lot, it still feels like a beautiful vast outstretching desert full of artifacts of a past history that runs really well and smooth. Scattered around the landscape you find, next to rock formations and tire tracks, the remnants of a lost world: rusty shipwrecks, former oil drill platforms, crumbled bridges, ruins of factory buildings, docksides, harbour cranes, so on and so forth, reminding of a life long gone where there was still plenty of water and food to go around. Collectibles scattered throughout the world will hint you to it and what might have happened.
So how does it play? After meeting your first few characters you find yourself quickly driving around a LOT in your newly acquired ride looking for scrap, the main currency in the game. Scrap is used to upgrade your car, lovingly called the 'Magnum Opus' by Chumbucket whom you meet at the start of the game and likes to express everything in a religious but car related fashion, and scrap is used to unlock some abilities and gear on Max. By completing activities like achievements, do x times this or x times that, or races you will earn Griffa tokens. These can be spent when you visit Griffa to upgrade some perks. These perks will add extra scrap ontop of what you pick up, or makes you consume less fuel, et cetera.
Of combat in this game are two kinds: on foot and in the car. That's right, car combat! Early in the game Chumbucket will fabricate a harpoon for you on the car that enables you to rip off doors, tires, bumpers or snatch the driver right from his seat! Despite the limited tools you get for the car to use, car combat in this game is the most fun. Chasing down Scrotus' convoys going high speed, picking off cars left and right watching them tumble and turn into big balls of fire (Michael Bay would approve!) feels exhilarating!
On foot the combat is much the same like the Batman games, for those familiar with it. Max can pick up a few weapons but they always have a (very) limited lifespan. This can be elongated by the perks at Griffa, but you'll generally be fighting with your fists. Even the little shivs Max carries can only be used once for a finisher and not always be looted back from the corpses. Max also carries a shotgun, but the ammo is rather limited, even with all upgrades unlocked. All-in-all the combat in the beginning feels powerful, it feels as if more could have been done to make it more interesting and less repetitive in the long run. Every boss fight of the Top Dogs in the world is almost completely the same and requires no imagination. Once you figured out one, you know how to beat them all. Such a pity!
Story wise this game is as dry as the world it plays in and as shallow as the water collectors. There is very little character development, of either Max or anyone he encounters. Then again, Max is a rather selfish man with little empathy for others. At least that's what he wants to make himself believe. Griffa, the fella Max visits to upgrade his perks every now and then, sometimes puts question marks at his deeds to make him rethink, but that's about all the hints Max (and the player) gets.
The game is a good looker, runs very well, and fun to play if you like to drive an aweful lot through miles and miles of desert land in a world fueled by the atmosphere from Mad Max: Fury Road. Car combat is most fun, combat on foot is a little too familiar and not much depth. Story is very short and paper thin I'd say, compared to games like Witcher 3. If you like the car bit, it can be worth your money. If you seek something full of story and rich hand-to-hand combat, you will be disappointed.

This review is written with 43 in game hours worth of experience.
Mad Max is a beautiful game with lots of stunning scenary. Whether it's the vast emptiness of The Underdune or the rocky canyons of Cadavanaugh. What's infront of you never fails to take your breath away. Coming across another heavily defended oil camp always brings a spark of joy, even if that spark comes with an explosion of fire.
When it comes to sound, the developers have excelled in creating a rich enviroment. The engine sounds are amazing and very realistic, but never to intrusive when you are powering through the Wasteland.
Unfortunately the game
lacks a bit in the story department. The game starts you off right in the action. You will be pit into a fight with the self proclaimed leader of Gas-town, Lord Scaborous Scrotus. After the fight you shortly meet your first main allies, Chumbucket and Dinki Di the dog. Character development is at a minimum but when it does happen, it hits you in the heart. Max himself is a pretty big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at the beginning but by the end I was justifying his actions where the game didn't have to. One thing I will note is the ending
You are given Max's iconic car, jacket and shotgun. This is a nice nod to the original movies. This is not the problem though. In the ending some major things happen that I will not spoil, the problem is that once you go back to the open world, these events have had no affect on the world with multiple very dead characters being miraculously alive.
I love the gameplay in Mad Max. It is all about your car as you drive around the wasteland. Vehicle combat is as satisfying as you would expect from a game about Mad Max and ground combat is very fluent. The map is very large and packed full of activities to do to lower the threat of Scrotus. The upgrade system is very simple to use. During your adventures you find scrap which is used to either give Max a boost in armour or attack or add to your magnificent car. The wasteland is ruled by 5 factions, most of which you can befriend and help for rewards such as having your fuel, water, or health replenished at a moments notice. These factions are Jeet's, Gutgash's, Pink Eye's, Deep Friah's and The Buzzards. Whilst it is enjoyable having all of these factions, it would have been nice to see some more interaction between them, seeing as they all have their respective areas.

this game is it's own beast and most certainly not for everyone.
first off: you need a lot of time and patience for this. and i mean: a lot! most noises will scare game off and you will basically start from scratch and lure or track them right again. so using the ATV may be fun and quick but is only really useful (and more or less essential) to unlock fast travel points from which you can then start exploring on foot. and even then: don't run around too much either. every ground surface and shrubbery will make the appropriate noises and wind coming from the "wrong" direction can quickly give you away.
so take it slow, go for a walk, enjoy the beautiful environment and more or less let the animals and missions come to you.
call of the wild features one of the most stunning open worlds i have every seen. amazing lighting, beautifully rendered foliage and a in general just very detailed map will make you wanna explore. and that's what you will be doing most of the time. both maps are HUGE and will keep you busy finding all the locations that give you lore, fast travel points to stock up or rest and positions to set up deer stands. when it comes to sheer visuals there are very few virtual worlds that can compete. horizon zero dawn and the witcher3 are the only ones that come to mind.
on the other hand tho: there is very little to do except finding said locations for xp and fast travel. there is a few collectables like shed antlers etc, but that's about it.
the focus is (unsurprisingly) on tracking and shooting animals. and that's perfectly fine. the game tries to add some extra things like photography missions and somesuch, but that's about it. after all this is a hunting simulation so it makes sense, but some may be disappointed by the lack of anything else.
but don't worry: that's quite a lot to master. you can unlock weapons, skills, perks and other equipment that will help you to make it easier to track, lure and ultimately kill and harvest game.
mostly the AI is good with a few exceptions here and there, but if you don't prepare properly, pay attention to sound, wind and positioning you will not get anywhere because the animals will hear, smell or see you from quite some ways away and bolt to not be seen anytime soon.
tl;dr:
pro:
+ visually gorgeous world
+ amazing sound with good 3D-positioning
+ two huge maps to explore
+ unlockable skills, perks and equipment
cons:
- not much interaction with the world except exploration and shooting
- a very few bugs here and there: AI messing up or environment floating in the air etc.
- ATV is a must have and should not be extra DLC
so in short:
if you feel like a chilled walk in an amazing vision of the wild and occasionally hunting animals you will enjoy it. patient snipers and stealth veterans should consider getting this.
if you are not really patient enough and don't have the time to sit in a spot for a few minutes doing basically nothing, this is most likely not for you.

For all the talk about games as art few AAA titles really aim to be more than entertainment, the equivalent of Summer Blockbusters that fill the screen with gorgeous visual set-pieces but fail plots or characters more developed than those of mustache-twirling villains plotting for power for powers sake (see Call of Duty Kevin Spacy for reference).
Spec Ops the Line plays with these conventions amazingly; a few levels in and it's a typical (competent but not outstanding) cover-based shooter with a niche trick of having sand as a usable environmental weapon. As it progresses it becomes so much more; a critique of war, of making a game of war, of people who 'play' at war, of nationalism and the idea of right and wrong when it comes to ending life in all sorts of circumstances.
To discuss the plot directly would be to undermine the power of progressing through the narrative oneself and I'm forever grateful that this is one experience I got to have spoiler-free. I can't say it was pleasant, but I can say I'm grateful to the developers and writers for not backing down and following the story to the conclusion it needed. If the 'Call of Duty' and 'Battlefield' franchise are 'Boy's Own' comics then this is 'All Quiet on the Western Front'.
It doesn't need multiplayer and it really doesn't need the 'Spec Ops' title-prefix, it does need support and wider recognition, and it's something I recommend for anyone who who considering a military career as a result of their CoD-obsession.

This game is soooo close to being an amazing game. It has everything you want in a F2P game: good gameplay, good graphics, a fairly decent community, and regular updates and changing events to keep you coming back.  However, it also has P2W microtransactions, the one thing that makes so many of these F2P so unappealing to people.
When you start the game, you can create a character in any of the 5 positions in basketball.  You'll also notice that there are tabs, each one signifying the different types of players.  The most basic is just named with the same name of the game.  The other tabs have various "Special Characters" that you can buy for $15 if you don't have a coupon to make it free.  If you are new, you may not notice much different with these "Special Characters" except for a different skin.  However, these "Special Characters" gain a +40 stat boost that you can use at will when you purchase them.
To put this in perspective, you gain +2 stat points every time you level up.  That means that if you pay $15, you can basically gain 20 levels worth of stats.  The max level cap is 50.  No matter how long you play, a basic character can never be as good as a paid character because of this, especially since this game's mechanics relies upon stat advantages and you can only be on specific servers for about 10 levels.  Even if you are a normal character at the top range of levels for your server, you will still be worse than a special character just getting into a server.
You can be in a great position to block a dunk, but if you have a lower Tussle stat than the other character then you will be ran over.  The higher Long Dunk stat you have the longer range you can dunk from and the higher (vertically) your dunk is.  Needless to say this means Special Characters can end up dunking from the top of the key from a standstill, something that I have yet to see in real basketball.  The greater Middle and 3 pt. shot stat you have means that you'll have a greater chance of making the shot even with "Active Defense", the greatest defense you can have on a shot other than a straight up block.  This means that you can be all over your mark, but unless you can get a block you may as well not even be covering your man.  The game even breaks at a certain point when the stats get high enough.  The tutorial makes it clear that you can't block or steal from behind a player, yet I've seen so many "Special Characters" do that exact thing simply because their Steal or Block stat is noticably high.
This isn't even taking into account the paid stat boosts you can get from clothing, the more stat-awarding "toys" you can buy with real money, and having the ability to get more stat-improving cards with real money.  Even the VIP system is broken, giving them extra skill slots, an XP boost, the ability to kick ANYONE from servers (including the host), and other minor tweaks.  Yes, you get a 50% XP boost for paying real cash for a VIP upgrade, giving those with money an even greater advantage.
This is why F2P games fail.  You won't notice this at the lower levels, and you'll have some fun times, but when you get to the higher levels there are less and less basic characters, only leaving the specials to destroy the court.
Regardless, if you can look past this, I recommend this game to anyone who likes basketball or wants to get into it.  To anyone looking for competetive play based entirely on skill though, I strongly urge you to look at other games and only play this for the arcade feel.

Ok, so I finally did it. After about a year of fighting with myself and reading all the negative reviews, I took the proverbial plunge and bought the game. I wish I could say this is the greatest survival game of all time or even the worst but instead I'm at a crossroads. I have roughly 230 hours on Miscreated and I just purchased DayZ last night and I put 6 hours on thus far so I tried to keep this as subjective as possible as I am very much in love with Miscreated.
The point I would like to make is this, for a game that has been early access for years, has had persistent bugs throughout it's development, and still is a frustratingly buggy POS, despite all of that, it has a huge fan base. The reason being is the immersion. You feel lilke you're all alone in a wasteland because of how huge the map is. You feel like you are fighting for survival because of how sparse the "loot" is. That being said there is so little in so much...I spent 6 hours playing on a high population server and never saw a single person. I traveled from town to town and searched every building high and low for things to survive to always come up frustartingly empty handed.
The bugs will get under skin as you play and all of a sudden your frame rate drops below 5 FPS or you get stuck in a corner of a house.
The melee combat leaves something to be desired but is better than most other survival games. Due to the difficulty of finding ammo and decent weapons I only shot off 3 rounds in a days worth of gaming but the physics and "feel" is on point.
Surviving without dieing is, of course, the greatest aspect of this game. I loved trying to survive. I've died from bleeding out, hypothermia, sickness, falling, etc. in less than 24 hours of gameplay and it was awesome!! Then throw zombies into the mix and holy sh*t you have an action packed fight for your life!! I could only imagine how adding friends or enemies into the mix would be even more of a game changer...
In conclusion, this game is unfinished. It has the potential of being one of the greatest survival games of all times if the developers would push it...instead if feels like they all but gave up. The atmosphere is great! Dare I say better than Miscreated's? The gameplay is clunky but supposedly they are fixing that when Beta finally comes out....hopefully in the next decade. I'll give this game a thumbs up just because I have faith in the final product, if it ever comes...if they finish this game and give it everything it deserves/needs this would be the benchmark of all survival games for a very long time.

My feelings on Undertale is complex, but I believe that people can both like and dislike this game fairly easily.
I like the premise the game; it's simple and easy the follow: monster and humans once lived in harmony, humans didn't like that monsters were capable of absorbing SOULs, drove the monsters away and sealed them underground. A human falls into the underground and you have to guide them through to find a way out. Not memorable, but some of the characters and art style throwback to the SNES and Genesis age is quite impressive.
The gameplay is quite creative as well, using a semi-turnbased RPG system where you and your enemy take turns performing actions or attacking, while you can dodge enemy attacks in real time. This adds a new layer of difficulty in what we normally expect from RPGs, but has a nice enough difficulty curve to avoid it being brutal.
The difficulty, however, is where I begin to question the design choices. I don't expect every game to have a layer of difficult fights, but I do appreciate the difficulty being CONSISTENT. By now, most of you know that the game has three main paths: true pacifist, neutral, and genocide. depending on which path you select depends on how well the difficulty is handled. If you try the neutral route, you get enough LV to stand against more difficult battles while also breezing through the normally easy ones. This keeps the difficulty roughly the same throughout. Not bad, but not recommended. The true pacifist route sees that the fights become gradually more difficult and more complex, and without room for LV, the difficulty spikes in some areas is understandable. However, the way that the final fights are set up for both the neutral and pacifist fights make it so that all that you learned is nearly pointless. The genocide route is roughly consistent in its battles; and by that I mean that literally ALL BUT TWO FIGHTS ARE ACTUALLY DIFFICULT AT ALL!!!! It's fine to have easy fights, but you have to make the fights have some complex mechanics to back them up. Sure, it proves that monsters are no match for humans, being consistent to the lore of the game, but only two monsters stand up to you at ALL!?!? I call BS, I'm sorry, but I do.
The characters in the game, as I mentioned earlier, are also fine, but most of them feel one-dimensional or lack luster. Asgore, Papyrus, and Undyne suffer the most from this. They aren't bad, but they could've had a lot more improvement. I believe that Sans and another character whom I won't spoil are the most three-dimensional, but for their own separate reasons. Toriel is close, but didn't quite hit the mark.
The battle is unique as I mentioned earlier, but with most battles being easy, most people don't appreciate it much. There are four options: Fight, Act, Item, and Mercy. If the player ACTs in a particular way, then the player can spare them. Using an ITEM allows the player to switch between gear and heal their HP. FIGHTing sounds just like you think it does: hack away until a monster's dead. What's really interesting is that depending on how many you spare, and by extension kill, affects how the story will turn out.
The only other thing is general presentation, including art and music. For being done by a single man,  both are extremely well done. Character models look fabulous, the scenery is consistent and beautiful, and I just have fun frolicing down the paths of the areas like Snowdin. The music was so closing to being in my top 5 greatest gaming soundtracks, but didn't quite make it. The big reason is because of the area themes which are remarkably dull, surprisingly. They aren't bad, but they aren't memorable personally. However, a lot of area music is memorable in any other game, so I guess I can't punish Toby Fox too much here. However, the boss fight music is on a whole other level. Having hits like Megalovania, Battle Against a True Hero, Hopes and Dreams, and Bonetrousle, the music has you coming back to fight these guys again and again just to hear where they originated. I personally took at least two minutes at the beginning of each fight just to let the music sink in. If for nothing else, the music alone can constitute reasoning for playing this game.
My final thoughts: I like the game, trying to break normal playing conventions, breaking the forth wall, pretty solid humor, an extraordinary score, and so on. However, the game can become too easy in some cases, the battle system eventually repetitive, and a vast majority of areas and characters left... unmemorable. Not too mention this game harbors about 10 hours of gameplay before you do just about everything it can offer. Maybe even less if you adjust to it quickly. But for its price, I'll let it slid. I can't complain about the game, but even for ten dollars, be sure that everything I just described sounds like the game you'd enjoy. Worst case scenerio, you only spent $10, and you can wait before you get more money for another game. This game still gets a solid 7.9 out of 10. Good, but far from perfect.

As a prequel story, Life Is Strange: Before the Storm is surprisingly relaxed about filling in gaps of time. Instead, it focuses on the ways one small decision can set off a devastating ripple effect. Even something seemingly benign, like Rachel Amber bringing Chloe along to play hooky, kickstarts the chain of events we know inevitably shatters lives and families.

So far this game has not been any less that what I have come to expect from Square Enix. I love the rich diverse storyline of the first game, and am so far enjoying this one. The characters and story are so intricately written that it is incredibly easy to become so immersed in it that you forget this is actually fiction. The characters feel so real, and their portrayal is so raw and honest. They are relatable and I think almost anyone who plays this game will be able to relate to the characters and situations in one way or another.
I was already familiar with one of the main characters, Chloe Price, from the original life is strange game and have a definite soft spot for her. Getting this extra insight into this particular character and the events leading up to Life is Strange really feels like you are being taken on a journey of not only watching the characters grow and discover themselves, but of self discovery too. When you find certain aspects of the game provoking particular emotions, you can't help but relate some of the experiences to your own. I believe that anyone can play this game and find something they can relate to and reflect on.
As part of a community which likes to share thoughts and opinions on this game there are conflicting opionions based on each person's perspective. From what I have read from other people's perspective of the characters and situations in this game, I have seen so many people from many different walks of life and different personal situations, but no matter who they are or which characters they felt more strongly towards the one thing is clear. This game will always surprise you and anyone can enjoy it.
I, along with many others, are highly anticipating the final chapter in this episodic rollercoaster. We have laughed, we have cried, and everything in between. We are ready to see how empty Hell really is.

This review is written with 43 in game hours worth of experience.
Mad Max is a beautiful game with lots of stunning scenary. Whether it's the vast emptiness of The Underdune or the rocky canyons of Cadavanaugh. What's infront of you never fails to take your breath away. Coming across another heavily defended oil camp always brings a spark of joy, even if that spark comes with an explosion of fire.
When it comes to sound, the developers have excelled in creating a rich enviroment. The engine sounds are amazing and very realistic, but never to intrusive when you are powering through the Wasteland.
Unfortunately the game
lacks a bit in the story department. The game starts you off right in the action. You will be pit into a fight with the self proclaimed leader of Gas-town, Lord Scaborous Scrotus. After the fight you shortly meet your first main allies, Chumbucket and Dinki Di the dog. Character development is at a minimum but when it does happen, it hits you in the heart. Max himself is a pretty big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at the beginning but by the end I was justifying his actions where the game didn't have to. One thing I will note is the ending
You are given Max's iconic car, jacket and shotgun. This is a nice nod to the original movies. This is not the problem though. In the ending some major things happen that I will not spoil, the problem is that once you go back to the open world, these events have had no affect on the world with multiple very dead characters being miraculously alive.
I love the gameplay in Mad Max. It is all about your car as you drive around the wasteland. Vehicle combat is as satisfying as you would expect from a game about Mad Max and ground combat is very fluent. The map is very large and packed full of activities to do to lower the threat of Scrotus. The upgrade system is very simple to use. During your adventures you find scrap which is used to either give Max a boost in armour or attack or add to your magnificent car. The wasteland is ruled by 5 factions, most of which you can befriend and help for rewards such as having your fuel, water, or health replenished at a moments notice. These factions are Jeet's, Gutgash's, Pink Eye's, Deep Friah's and The Buzzards. Whilst it is enjoyable having all of these factions, it would have been nice to see some more interaction between them, seeing as they all have their respective areas.

Mad Max is an open world action game that is staggeringly well optimised. The core gameplay loop of driving around, fighting off patroling vehicles and frequent brawling remained enjoyable for me throughout the entire experience. In addition the game world is easily one of the best in the genre, taking the lifeless wastes of the Mad Max universe and making them interesting and visually unique, no world in gaming looks quite like this one.
As great as the good parts are, the bad is of equal magnitude. The core gameplay is fun, but the structure that gameplay sits in is the worst in the entire genre, the dull routine of clearing camps, and other markers on the map got old by the end of the first zone and the structure never really improved from there, locking off entertaining upgrades behind this filler content would be a fine move if the filler wasn't so boring.
In addition, much like other games sharing the Arkham/Assassins creed style parry counter combat system, I predicted that I'd have to gimp myself to make the combat entertaining. Even with intentionally not taking certain upgrades and fighting subotimally, the hand to hand gameplay fails to hold up as well as the vehicle combat, fistfights can be made entertaining, but all of the engagement has to come from the player, the combat system itself lacks Shadow of Mordors capacity for self tailored difficulty.
Despite the serious shortcomings of the filler content, the main campaign is a ton of fun, though it is gated off by the godawful map marker clearing. If the game is on sale or the world is particularly enticing to you, I'd recommend picking it up, if not, don't waste your money, while the good in this game is really good, the bad is horrendous.

It is a good game, though very repetitive when it comes to the area clearing, the main story is a bit short as it pretty much revolves around you building your car and once your done you pretty much go into the final boss sequence.
As far as replay value goes, there isnt any as there arnt any real choices that could make the story unfold differently.
With all that said and done it is a decent game, which runs well and it did not crash once, which looking at most AAA games is nothing short of a miracle.
Is it a good game? Yes
Is it worth £35? Probably not, but i have spent more on worse before.

This is a good concept.  The game itself is a lot of fun.  If it had been developed by an experienced, competent design team using industry standards, it would be absolutely amazing.  I don't want to give this a thumbs-down, but I cannot in good conscience recommend this game unless you enjoy single-player games that lack both a "pause" and a "save" function.
The world in the game is beautiful, and the game is challenging and fun to walk around and track animals.  There are a few missions/quests, enough to give you something interesting to do, but you still have the freedom to walk around on your own, and to take targets of opportunity.  There is also a process for unlocking better weapons and ammo as you increase your score, and this along with the need to earn money in-game by making kills, gives you rewards to keep playing.
However, there are several serious problems with this game.  There is currently no pause feature.  This sounds like a minor omission until you realize that real life often does intrude on gaming.  Maybe you have dinner in the oven, or you have to take medication, or family members call, or you have to use the bathroom, or any number of things.  With most (single player) games, you take for granted that you can hit Pause and do your business, and come back to the game and continue.  Not in theHunter COTW.  Even if you hit the Esc key to bring up the menu, even if you're browsing through the in-game help or changing settings, the game continues to run and things continue to happen around you.
Another problem is that the game does not feature TrackIR, even though its predecessor did, and the devs have no plans to add this capability.  Instead they have integrated something called Tobii Eyetrack.  Virtually every other game that calls itself a "realistic simulation" uses TrackIR, so most of us who enjoy this sort of game already own TrackIR, and it would add a lot of immersion.
However, one of the biggest problems with this game is the save feature: there is no save feature.  The game saves automatically, which is nice...until you lose power in a thunderstorm while playing, and the next day you find that the game doesn't recognize the save file even though the save files are very clearly still on your computer, the game only gives you the option to start a new game.  Oh, and to make it even better, if you decide to start a new game, it overwrites the save files already on your computer.  That's because there is no ability to save-as, no ability to have multiple save files.
After 15 hours of play, I am not going to start a new game.  Unfortunately, after 15 hours I am also not eligible for a refund.  This game is nice, but the developers are clearly amateurs.  I don't mean that as an insult, I simply mean that they do not adhere to basic industry practices and standards.  This is sad, because it is a very nice game, but unfortunately incompetent developers are one bug that cannot be fixed.

For all the talk about games as art few AAA titles really aim to be more than entertainment, the equivalent of Summer Blockbusters that fill the screen with gorgeous visual set-pieces but fail plots or characters more developed than those of mustache-twirling villains plotting for power for powers sake (see Call of Duty Kevin Spacy for reference).
Spec Ops the Line plays with these conventions amazingly; a few levels in and it's a typical (competent but not outstanding) cover-based shooter with a niche trick of having sand as a usable environmental weapon. As it progresses it becomes so much more; a critique of war, of making a game of war, of people who 'play' at war, of nationalism and the idea of right and wrong when it comes to ending life in all sorts of circumstances.
To discuss the plot directly would be to undermine the power of progressing through the narrative oneself and I'm forever grateful that this is one experience I got to have spoiler-free. I can't say it was pleasant, but I can say I'm grateful to the developers and writers for not backing down and following the story to the conclusion it needed. If the 'Call of Duty' and 'Battlefield' franchise are 'Boy's Own' comics then this is 'All Quiet on the Western Front'.
It doesn't need multiplayer and it really doesn't need the 'Spec Ops' title-prefix, it does need support and wider recognition, and it's something I recommend for anyone who who considering a military career as a result of their CoD-obsession.

Ok, so I finally did it. After about a year of fighting with myself and reading all the negative reviews, I took the proverbial plunge and bought the game. I wish I could say this is the greatest survival game of all time or even the worst but instead I'm at a crossroads. I have roughly 230 hours on Miscreated and I just purchased DayZ last night and I put 6 hours on thus far so I tried to keep this as subjective as possible as I am very much in love with Miscreated.
The point I would like to make is this, for a game that has been early access for years, has had persistent bugs throughout it's development, and still is a frustratingly buggy POS, despite all of that, it has a huge fan base. The reason being is the immersion. You feel lilke you're all alone in a wasteland because of how huge the map is. You feel like you are fighting for survival because of how sparse the "loot" is. That being said there is so little in so much...I spent 6 hours playing on a high population server and never saw a single person. I traveled from town to town and searched every building high and low for things to survive to always come up frustartingly empty handed.
The bugs will get under skin as you play and all of a sudden your frame rate drops below 5 FPS or you get stuck in a corner of a house.
The melee combat leaves something to be desired but is better than most other survival games. Due to the difficulty of finding ammo and decent weapons I only shot off 3 rounds in a days worth of gaming but the physics and "feel" is on point.
Surviving without dieing is, of course, the greatest aspect of this game. I loved trying to survive. I've died from bleeding out, hypothermia, sickness, falling, etc. in less than 24 hours of gameplay and it was awesome!! Then throw zombies into the mix and holy sh*t you have an action packed fight for your life!! I could only imagine how adding friends or enemies into the mix would be even more of a game changer...
In conclusion, this game is unfinished. It has the potential of being one of the greatest survival games of all times if the developers would push it...instead if feels like they all but gave up. The atmosphere is great! Dare I say better than Miscreated's? The gameplay is clunky but supposedly they are fixing that when Beta finally comes out....hopefully in the next decade. I'll give this game a thumbs up just because I have faith in the final product, if it ever comes...if they finish this game and give it everything it deserves/needs this would be the benchmark of all survival games for a very long time.

If you like car combat, this is definitely up your alley. If you’re a big Mad Max fan, go ahead and take a look. If you like open worlds filled with activities to complete, this is your jam. This game is an amazingly good hybrid between roguelikes and platformers. It retains many aspects from roguelikes, such as randomly generated dungeons, tons of bad guys after your head, and permanent death, all of which are integrated almost flawlessly. Though, it's not as difficult as many roguelikes, but it can be at times.
The platforming is solid, but it takes some getting used to. One particularly important ability is the downward strike in the vein of Duck Tales or Zelda 2. Some platforms can only be opened by doing this, and you have to time it JUST right to get it open. Again, it's a bit frustrating at first, but you do eventually catch on.
I think the heir system is alright, albeit a little bit unnecessary. Most of the traits the children can have are aesthetic, such as seeing everything in black and white or seeing everything flip around a la Paper Mario. However, the slightly rarer ones do affect gameplay, such as the inability to use the map, or the ability to keep the platforms open. Though, most of the time you pick the 'normal' characters; ones whose traits don't matter that much. In other words, the characters feel almost the same. If it wasn't for the varying classes each child could have, the heir system would be almost worthless. The classes are what actually make the children unique, as all classes are upgradable once and each has different strengths and weaknesses. A Geologist, for example, is an upgraded Miner who can see all chests on the map, as well as having a hefty bonus on collected gold. S/he suffers from lack of fighting potential, though. These, in combination with the aforementioned traits, make a good and fairly varied heir system.
The actual gameplay itself is surprisingly addictive! Even after your character is killed, you'll want to immediately start a new character and spend all the gold you had from your previous character. Upgrades and armor last forever, so there is always a sense of progression with each life. Furthermore, you can buy runes which give you more special abilities you can tinker around with. I'm not going to spoil much of the gameplay, but I'll just say that there is a TON of replay value in this game.
As far as the story goes, it just drops you little crumbs of it as you play, which is a good thing because it provides additional incentive to keep playing. Each diary entry often foreshadows what you will go through and what you can expect, so no need for external guides. Though, it doesn't spoil absolutely everything, leaving you to find some things out on your own.

It's fine, and certainly has massive potential, but the fact that its selling for 30-50 dollars depending on how loose your pocket is and has already raised 10 million is troubling.  It will never be a 10 million dollar game, and isn't worth 30 dollars in its current state.   People should be waiting or looking elsewhere.
There are bugs, and I know I am not allowed to complain about bugs in an alpha game, but I am going to hammer on this:
The project is funded.  Beyond funded.  This game has the look and feel of a 2 man prototype.  They need to produce something worthy of the funding they received and I am not sure they aren't getting distracted by side projects already.  Did they want 10 million of funding for THIS game?  Not a lot of people have the fortitude to stick it out like Tarn Adams and Dwarf Fortress, and that game isn't even funded properly.   Now I am not saying they shouldn't take profit away from their project, but that is where over funding from the start gets into tricky territory.  When would you be ok with them stopping?  What if they made a 2 million dollar game and took the 8 on to other projects that have nothing to do with what you originally funded?
Some people will be fine with that.   Some people will be upset with them not following through with the demand they are milking.  Even others will be happy just to have the chance to be a part of the cult of personality that video gaming is turning into.  The next film everyone saw so they can talk about it around the water cooler (or reddit boards).
Just remember, people already want minecraft money when making an indi game.  The quality of game that comes out of this will dictate profit margins a great deal in the industry going forward.   Don't be confused that you are going to get every penny thrown at this game going back into it and no one is going to get a rebate based on the quality of what comes out.
Personally for 30 dollars and the option to spend 50 I expect oceans more content than what is present.
Is the game fun?  I have had similar levels of fun with a free flash game, though I have certainly paid more for less.  It's an "interesting" game in the parts that are fleshed out (inmate personality, logistics) and shallow but functional in the parts that aren't (progression, finance and prison services like medical care and prisoner reform).
When I say its "interesting" I mean that I believe the game has done a smart job being ambigous with feedback.  A lot of players aren't into this.  They want to know every + and  -, but I think when feedback points you near the target it creates better story telling through engaging your imagination, allowing you to tie importance to something that may not be optimal but is still beneficial.  It's engaging until you run into a motivational wall of not being able to affect the change you want any longer.
It's a clean game with smart graphics and, if user generated content is catered to, could be a real game changer.  I can't give it points for something it doesn't do yet.  The game is playable, hard but simple and ultimately as bug riddled as any alpha out there.  There are some interesting things going on under the hood, but just glimpses.  But its funded, so the ball is in their court and no amount of throwing money at this is going to change the outcome.
It hasn't been worth what I paid for it (even on sale), nor a satisfying experiance from a purely gameplay standpoint.  The most I got out of this was the chance to see the hype and write this review.   Hopefully this game doesn't turn into DF9 redux.

Mad Max is an action, open-world game that sends you inside one of the best movie of 2015. Usually, I tend to avoid games based on movies, because more than often they are rushed titles whose only purpose is to sell using the name of the movie. So, what happened that made me change my mind about buying such a potentially bad game? Mainly, Steam reviews. With a solid 90% positive reviews I thought to give the game a chance, besides I'm also a big fan of Mad Max movies, a post apocalyptic genre lover and the game was 66% discounted during Christmas. I bought it and it was a real, amazing surprise.
TECHNICAL ASPECTS
***GAMEPLAY 8/10
Mad Max gameplay is amazing, but unfortunately it is flawed by some aspects that may bore the gamers. As I said, the game is open-world, Max can travel by foot (not a very good nor smart idea), by car (best idea) or by fast travel (anti-boredom idea). Why is fast travel anti boredom? Simply because the world is HUGE, it's like Skyrim but in a desert with almost no life, so even with a car, but nothing to do it gets boring. The environment is really well made, don't get me wrong, I tried to avoid using fast travel (I'm not a big fan of it), but if you want to 100% complete the game, traveling, even with your fastest car, becomes a nuisance.
Now, let's talk about fighting. Take the Batman Arkham franchise, strip the Bat of it's costume, grow Wayne a big bushy beard, give him some ragged clothes, a double barrel shotgun and throw him in a desert, done ? Good, you now have Max, a man that fights (kinda) like the Gotham vigilante. What is great about this in Mad Max is that you can perform some finisher moves depending on the environment. Is your enemy with his back against a wall ? Grab his head and smash it on said wall. Is your enemy the sniper in that tall tower that just blow up one of your car tires? Find a way to sneak up on him and push him over the ledge of his tower, no more sniping for you ... Baiatch ! Do you like the sound of your shotgun? Grab an enemy and gut shot him... again, and again, and again, and ... damn I ran out of ammo.
Once your enemies are all dead you can go back to your car and chill out... wait no ... a war party approaching !!! Fighting in Mad Max doesn't end when you enter your car, it really begins there. If you have seen the 2015 movie you know what I'm talking about, if not go buy the DVD and then buy the game (I'm not joking). Car fights are almost exactly like the ones you see in the movie: ramming, grinding, burning, harpooning, blowing up tires, fuel tanks or drivers. The only problem about cars is that the game doesn't like to see cars upside down, so whenever you flip your car and start sliding on your hood, some mystical force flips your car back on its wheels.
All of this you'll be able to do by buying the right upgrade for Max or the car, there are a lot of them. For Max there are the classic upgrades : better armour, more HPs, special combos, etc. For the car there are car bodies, tires, ramming grills, engines, hood ornaments, harpoons, spikes (to impale enemies that try to jump on your car) pipes that shoot flames and much more. Each upgrade will cost you scrap (the currency of the game), you get scrap by completing missions, looting enemies or locations and by destroying enemy vehicles. It is hard to have enough at the beginning, but doing side missions helps you a lot and eventually you end up having more than you need.
Last thing I'll explain about gameplay is what made the Steam reviews drop from 97% positive to 90% : the lack of diversity for what concerns side missions. In Mad Max you have the possibility of roam free around the map doing things like destroying enemy convoys or liberating outposts. Although these things are fun and give you the opportunity of doing something other than the main quest, they are basically all the same, they just get a bit harder the more you go on. These enemy outposts for example, are different only in their appearance, one is inside a chasm, while another was built on an abandoned oil rig. The problem is that you always have to do the same thing, fight your way among enemies and blow things up or kill the boss. Here, the bosses, or I should say "big guys who look all the same except for the colour of their clothes", this is the worst thing of the game, these guys are supposed to be generals, not cannon fodder, so I expect them to be unique, to fight in different ways, to die in different ways, well... no, they are all the same, they fight all in the same way, and you kill them in the same way.
***STORY and LORE 9/10
It's not the main thing of the game obviously, but I guess it's noticeable by the fact that I wrote a poem about the gameplay and almost nothing about the story. However, it is good, not excellent but good enough, it follows up the event of the movie but doesn't cross them, so the game and the movie remain separated but in the same context. It also seems that George Miller, the director and inventor of Mad Max, supervised some aspects of the game, the lore in particular, I've read that he likes the idea of being allowed to explain things (in a game for example) that you cannot explain in a movie (for obvious reason of time). So, when going around doing quests you come across some "relics" that give you hints on what happened to the world. When you start the game you may think you're in a desert in Australia, but it's not just a desert it's
.
If you want a short summary of the story keep reading (I won't spoil anything important)
The game starts with Max driving his beloved Interceptor, you get attacked by Scrotus (one of Immortan Joe sons) you manage to kill Scrotus but your car gets stolen and scrapped. Then, you encounter a hunchback named Chumbucket, a blackfinger (title given to those who are skilled mechanics), who wants to help you because he says to have seen you in a vision and thinks you're the "Saint" (an envoy of the goddess called Angel Combustion). He builds a new car, the Magnum Opus and comes with you to help you get a V8 engine that is supposed to allow you to continue your journey through the desert.
During the game you come across other characters, some crazier than others, who help you if, of course, you help them first and you do that until you reach Gastown. What happens then, I let you discover by yourself.
***GRAPHICS 10/10
Amazing, nothing less. Even though it's not perfect I give the game a 10 because it runs at a steady 60fps on (Mad)Max settings 99% of the time, I dropped under 50 only twice, but there was really a lot going on on screen. The game is so well optimized that makes other AAA games look bad. Everything about the environment is unique, each region has its unique features and look. You don't have the impression of being in the same place, even though you're in a desert with only rocks, sand and some scattered ruins, but what really shines here are the storms.
Storms are random events that can occur when you are out in the open, your companion Chumbucket will scream "Storm approaching !" and will point in that direction, you move the camera and you see it : a front of black clouds of dust moving towards you at incredible speed. You may try to outrun it and find somewhere to hide, but you'll miss all the fun, so pedal to the metal and run inside the storm. Everything turns black for a second, the wind howling covers even the sound of the engine, lightning starts falling from the sky and you have to steer to avoid being hit... it is so damn fun, if you manage to find some crazy enemy inside a storm is even better.
***SOUND 9/10
I'm running out of space to write so I'll just say that sound is great: engines, explosions, bone breaking or dislocating, car grinding to each other. Best part of it is voice acting.
OVERALL SCORE 9/10
