"I thought my duty was to protect this city from the storm. I was wrong. I have to protect it from you."
The debate of "Games as Art" has been raging for as long as any gamer can remember without any sort of certain or definite answer. Well, if one thing is certain, it's that if games are art, then Spec Ops: The Line is Dada. It is anti-art. It is that which kills art. It is the destroyer.
From early on, the game makes this clear. It takes every trope and cliche from modern-based military themed shooters and turns them completely on their head. Instead of shooting anonymous brown-faced people, you're shooting Americans. Instead of watching your character suddenly evolve from a basic-fresh recruit into an elite badass soldier, you watch your character gradually devolve from a level-headed everyman soldier into a bloodthirsty and delusional psychopath. Instead of having bottomless reserve of neverending 5.56 NATO rounds for your M4A1 Carbine with which to mow down legions of enemy soldiers, you get just enough ammo to contemplate saving a bullet for yourself. Instead of moral choices, you make immoral choices. Instead of choices at all, you are given none. Instead of enjoying yourself and being inspired by the game's story and message, you'll find yourself suffering through it until you're caked in blood and dirt, kneeling over the toilet and attempting to retch up what little remains in your stomach.
Instead of encouraging you to keep playing, the game informs you, quite early, that the only correct response to all of this is to turn off the game and stop.
"No... This is wrong! We did this part already!"
In terms of gameplay, The Line is in every way, shape, and form the definition of a generic third-person cover shooter. There is nothing to be surprised about here. It could be argued that this generic playstyle is integral to communicate the game's message, but it could also be argued that the game attempts to, as RPS put it, have its cake and eat it too. Take from that what you will.
If you enjoy third person shooters, you'll probably somewhat like the gameplay without being impressed by it at all. Otherwise, you'll most likely suffer through the gameplay in order to experience everything else The Line has to offer. Luckily, a good difficulty variance exists in the game to boost accessablity if nothing else, with the lower difficulties providing a simplistic and easy to slog through gameplay and the higher difficulties being nail-bitingly tense and brutal. Some squad-based tactics are also introduced at some points, but these don't do much to shake up gameplay at all. Rainbow Six this is not.
"I never wanted to hurt anyone..."
"No one ever does."
Spec Ops: The Line is awful, brutal, horrible, and disgusting. And yet, this is all a good thing. It is more than just a game, it is an experience. This game will affect you in ways that other games could never even dream of doing. You will not enjoy the way that this game makes you feel, but that is in fact the most important reason that you could play it.
Games like Journey, Proteus, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons, and other recent titles like them have shown us that games can be inspiring, beautiful, thought-provoking, and heartwarming in ways that only videogames can be. Spec Ops: The Line shows us the polar opposite of that: that games can be brutal, ugly, unforgiving. That they can tell a story that does not inspire you, but rather destroys you, fills you with disgust and self-doubt. A game can show you how far you can fall. It can show you that no matter how hard you might try, you can't always save yourself.
Because once you cross The Line, there's no coming back. There's no chance for redemption. You have to learn this. You have to accept this. If you don't, well...

Cinnamon Buns
You will need:
Dough:
1/4-ounce package yeast
1/2 cup warm water
1/2 cup scalded milk
1/4 cup sugar
1/3 cup butter or shortening
1 teaspoon salt
1 egg
3 1/2 to 4 cups all-purpose flour
Filling:
1/2 cup melted butter, plus more for pan
3/4 cup sugar, plus more for pan
2 tablespoons ground cinnamon
3/4 cup raisins, walnuts, or pecans, optional
Glaze:
4 tablespoons butter
2 cups powdered sugar
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
3 to 6 tablespoons hot water
Steps:
Heat oven to 350 degrees F.
In a small bowl, dissolve yeast in warm water and set aside. In a large bowl mix milk, sugar, melted butter, salt and egg. Add 2 cups of flour and mix until smooth. Add yeast mixture. Mix in remaining flour until dough is easy to handle. Knead dough on lightly floured surface for 5 to 10 minutes. Place in well-greased bowl, cover and let rise until doubled in size, usually 1 to 1 1/2 hours.
When doubled in size, punch down dough. Roll out on a floured surface into a 15 by 9-inch rectangle. Spread melted butter all over dough. Mix sugar and cinnamon and sprinkle over buttered dough. Sprinkle with walnuts, pecans, or raisins if desired. Beginning at the 15-inch side, role up dough and pinch edge together to seal. Cut into 12 to 15 slices.
Coat the bottom of baking pan with butter and sprinkle with sugar. Place cinnamon roll slices close together in the pan and let rise until dough is doubled, about 45 minutes. Bake for about 30 minutes or until nicely browned.
Meanwhile, mix butter, powdered sugar, and vanilla. Add hot water 1 tablespoon at a time until the glaze reaches desired consistency. Spread over slightly cooled rolls.

There's a bit of frustration in the beginning until you start getting some upgrades under your belt, at which point you can start to survive more than thirty seconds in the castle.
However #1: The plot falls a little flat, which wouldn't be a concern if they had just left it out, because let's face it, you don't really need plot in a roguelike.  But since they took the time to give us journals and clues and a cohesive storyline, why make it so pointless in the end?  When the boss asks why you're attacking him, I don't actually have an answer.
However #2: The game expects a much higher uptake of skill than I necessarily experienced.  I'm not a n00b by any stretch, but apparently I'm not hardcore enough for this.  As soon as I tried the New Game+, I saw that the enemies had gotten exponentially harder and equally unfun to deal with.  So if you're looking for long-term play this is only fun if you like frustration.

It's definitely worth picking up the complete edition, but I'd say only on a steam sale. Three of the four DLC packs are good, but there's one that is just sort of boring, and the only real saving grace it has is it's commentary and dialogue. Gunplay is tight, the flashy nature of the game makes you feel good, and later in the game in Ultimate mode the difficulty increases drastically, bringing a welcome challenge to the otherwise easy campaign.
Like any MMO or likewise style of game, however, the endgame becomes less about completing story missions or quests and entirely about raiding bosses for their best loot drops. This would be a great feature of the game if not for the downright ridiculously easy way to duplicate items from other players, who seem more than willing to do so. This breaks the game for me in a sense, but in the long run I suppose it's really just a minor annoyance.
In short, get the game if you like grindy MMO types of games, but don't expect a long campaign. The game's more about playing with others and killing stuff, which let's face it, is all anyone really wants.

This game took me by surprise. I only purchased this game as it was on sale, and I figured a few extra achievements couldn't hurt right?
Well I have no interest in trucks I find myself playing this game and enjoying it. This game really does do a very good job of being a truck simulator. It is complete with customization options, plenty of DLC if you get bored of the base game, an excellent set of mods (Not from Steam Workshop) can be installed which can further enhance your gameplay experience.
If you are a truck fan, this game is almost certainly a must have. Someone who is a truck fan would absolutely love this game to bits.
If you're not a truck fan, you may, or may not like this game but if you can get it when it is on sale you should try it before mocking it, it actually does what it is designed to do very well.
Although, I'd highly recommend having a music player playing music in the background as the long drives can be a bit daunting without it.
As for its down sides.. I couldn't get the built in radio player to work on Linux at all with MP3 or radio streams as is apparently supported. Not a big issue for me as I just used another media player to have music in the background.
It can also be very resource intensive also so you may need quite a beefy system if you want to wack the graphic settings up.
So to break all this down into a nice pro/cons list:
Pros:
- Very well built simulation game. Does what it says on the tin.
- Has achievements/trading cards for those who may want them.
- Cannot be simply "beaten" in a few hours like most modern games.
- Has company management features built in allowing you to employ people, buy trucks etc etc etc.
- Trucks can be customized.
- Visually it looks amazing if your system can cope.
- Great modding community that offers many things the base game cannot.
- Multi-platform support
Cons:
- Very resource intensive mostly on the GPU and appears to only be using only 1 CPU core out of 8 on my system
- Framerate can drop in some locations for a few seconds.
- No built in multiplayer (Though can be added via unofficial mods)
- AI traffic can be pretty darn stupid at times and will happily ram you out of your lane if it wants your lane and then charge you for the privilege with a traffic fine.
Hmm, I wanted to list more cons.. but I honestly cannot think of any others. So I'm going to have to say.. yes I recommend this game :-).

This game has a rather short main campaign, and the gameplay can get somewhat repetitive (duck, shoot, reload, rinse, repeat). That said, I did actually enjoy the gameplay for the most part. However, the story is the best part of this game. I probably enjoyed it more because I went into it without knowing much of anything about the plot, so I won't say anything that would potentially spoil any of the surprises. I will say that it is pretty mind-bending. The player gets some interesting and difficult decisions to make, but unlike most "player choice" games, there's no menu screen that comes up - the choices just happen naturally in the flow of the game. Sometimes you don't even realize that you could have made another choice until you go back and read the achievements list. The voice acting is well done, music really adds to the atmosphere, and the game environment is just beautiful. (Note: If you don't like gory/disturbing images, maybe not the best game for you.) Overall, definitely recommend.

Mad Max is an action, open-world game that sends you inside one of the best movie of 2015. Usually, I tend to avoid games based on movies, because more than often they are rushed titles whose only purpose is to sell using the name of the movie. So, what happened that made me change my mind about buying such a potentially bad game? Mainly, Steam reviews. With a solid 90% positive reviews I thought to give the game a chance, besides I'm also a big fan of Mad Max movies, a post apocalyptic genre lover and the game was 66% discounted during Christmas. I bought it and it was a real, amazing surprise.
TECHNICAL ASPECTS
***GAMEPLAY 8/10
Mad Max gameplay is amazing, but unfortunately it is flawed by some aspects that may bore the gamers. As I said, the game is open-world, Max can travel by foot (not a very good nor smart idea), by car (best idea) or by fast travel (anti-boredom idea). Why is fast travel anti boredom? Simply because the world is HUGE, it's like Skyrim but in a desert with almost no life, so even with a car, but nothing to do it gets boring. The environment is really well made, don't get me wrong, I tried to avoid using fast travel (I'm not a big fan of it), but if you want to 100% complete the game, traveling, even with your fastest car, becomes a nuisance.
Now, let's talk about fighting. Take the Batman Arkham franchise, strip the Bat of it's costume, grow Wayne a big bushy beard, give him some ragged clothes, a double barrel shotgun and throw him in a desert, done ? Good, you now have Max, a man that fights (kinda) like the Gotham vigilante. What is great about this in Mad Max is that you can perform some finisher moves depending on the environment. Is your enemy with his back against a wall ? Grab his head and smash it on said wall. Is your enemy the sniper in that tall tower that just blow up one of your car tires? Find a way to sneak up on him and push him over the ledge of his tower, no more sniping for you ... Baiatch ! Do you like the sound of your shotgun? Grab an enemy and gut shot him... again, and again, and again, and ... damn I ran out of ammo.
Once your enemies are all dead you can go back to your car and chill out... wait no ... a war party approaching !!! Fighting in Mad Max doesn't end when you enter your car, it really begins there. If you have seen the 2015 movie you know what I'm talking about, if not go buy the DVD and then buy the game (I'm not joking). Car fights are almost exactly like the ones you see in the movie: ramming, grinding, burning, harpooning, blowing up tires, fuel tanks or drivers. The only problem about cars is that the game doesn't like to see cars upside down, so whenever you flip your car and start sliding on your hood, some mystical force flips your car back on its wheels.
All of this you'll be able to do by buying the right upgrade for Max or the car, there are a lot of them. For Max there are the classic upgrades : better armour, more HPs, special combos, etc. For the car there are car bodies, tires, ramming grills, engines, hood ornaments, harpoons, spikes (to impale enemies that try to jump on your car) pipes that shoot flames and much more. Each upgrade will cost you scrap (the currency of the game), you get scrap by completing missions, looting enemies or locations and by destroying enemy vehicles. It is hard to have enough at the beginning, but doing side missions helps you a lot and eventually you end up having more than you need.
Last thing I'll explain about gameplay is what made the Steam reviews drop from 97% positive to 90% : the lack of diversity for what concerns side missions. In Mad Max you have the possibility of roam free around the map doing things like destroying enemy convoys or liberating outposts. Although these things are fun and give you the opportunity of doing something other than the main quest, they are basically all the same, they just get a bit harder the more you go on. These enemy outposts for example, are different only in their appearance, one is inside a chasm, while another was built on an abandoned oil rig. The problem is that you always have to do the same thing, fight your way among enemies and blow things up or kill the boss. Here, the bosses, or I should say "big guys who look all the same except for the colour of their clothes", this is the worst thing of the game, these guys are supposed to be generals, not cannon fodder, so I expect them to be unique, to fight in different ways, to die in different ways, well... no, they are all the same, they fight all in the same way, and you kill them in the same way.
***STORY and LORE 9/10
It's not the main thing of the game obviously, but I guess it's noticeable by the fact that I wrote a poem about the gameplay and almost nothing about the story. However, it is good, not excellent but good enough, it follows up the event of the movie but doesn't cross them, so the game and the movie remain separated but in the same context. It also seems that George Miller, the director and inventor of Mad Max, supervised some aspects of the game, the lore in particular, I've read that he likes the idea of being allowed to explain things (in a game for example) that you cannot explain in a movie (for obvious reason of time). So, when going around doing quests you come across some "relics" that give you hints on what happened to the world. When you start the game you may think you're in a desert in Australia, but it's not just a desert it's
.
If you want a short summary of the story keep reading (I won't spoil anything important)
The game starts with Max driving his beloved Interceptor, you get attacked by Scrotus (one of Immortan Joe sons) you manage to kill Scrotus but your car gets stolen and scrapped. Then, you encounter a hunchback named Chumbucket, a blackfinger (title given to those who are skilled mechanics), who wants to help you because he says to have seen you in a vision and thinks you're the "Saint" (an envoy of the goddess called Angel Combustion). He builds a new car, the Magnum Opus and comes with you to help you get a V8 engine that is supposed to allow you to continue your journey through the desert.
During the game you come across other characters, some crazier than others, who help you if, of course, you help them first and you do that until you reach Gastown. What happens then, I let you discover by yourself.
***GRAPHICS 10/10
Amazing, nothing less. Even though it's not perfect I give the game a 10 because it runs at a steady 60fps on (Mad)Max settings 99% of the time, I dropped under 50 only twice, but there was really a lot going on on screen. The game is so well optimized that makes other AAA games look bad. Everything about the environment is unique, each region has its unique features and look. You don't have the impression of being in the same place, even though you're in a desert with only rocks, sand and some scattered ruins, but what really shines here are the storms.
Storms are random events that can occur when you are out in the open, your companion Chumbucket will scream "Storm approaching !" and will point in that direction, you move the camera and you see it : a front of black clouds of dust moving towards you at incredible speed. You may try to outrun it and find somewhere to hide, but you'll miss all the fun, so pedal to the metal and run inside the storm. Everything turns black for a second, the wind howling covers even the sound of the engine, lightning starts falling from the sky and you have to steer to avoid being hit... it is so damn fun, if you manage to find some crazy enemy inside a storm is even better.
***SOUND 9/10
I'm running out of space to write so I'll just say that sound is great: engines, explosions, bone breaking or dislocating, car grinding to each other. Best part of it is voice acting.
OVERALL SCORE 9/10

Releasing a movie tie-in game usually goes one of two ways: either it’s a rush job thrown out with the movie to get some quick bucks, or the developer actually has the time it needs, regardless off the potential loss of income because of a later release date. Thankfully, Warner has allowed Avalanche the time to make a solid, vast open-world that is a lot more fun than the colour palette might suggest.
And there is an enormous amount going on in Mad Max; just so many systems operating at once. You can upgrade Max, or his beloved car, The Magnum Opus, whenever you like from the pause menu with scavenged scrap (the currency that runs the world), but there are core abilities that you can only level up using tokens received from completing challenges. These are the important ones, really, as they increase things like Max’s strength, or health, or even how long a full tank of fuel might last. But you can only upgrade these at set locations. They’re not hidden and are on your map, but it’s a little odd to have a conceit like this in play when there are so many moments that flaunt how gamey it is.
Take Max himself, for example. Once the car takes a certain amount of damage you’ll have to get out and wait while your companion, Chumbucket, fixes it up. But the enemies don’t care, and will keep coming at you. The AI here is quite smart (elsewhere they will expertly dodge you as you drive around engaging them), and will just try to drive right over you, but if you have a decent amount of health, you’ll stagger a bit but not die. After a few dodge rolls and a bit of running round in circles (get used to doing this, by the way), you can jump back into your ride and get moving, harpooning a Wastelander out of his car to certain death.
These moments are as stupid as they are cathartic. The way you can take damage is obscene, but all is forgiven when you enter slow-motion, harpoon a guy right in the chest and tap circle to quickly pull him from his vehicle, whereby he whips towards you, which lets you ram him head-on. The harpoon gun is a triumph, and the most Avalanche thing here. Driving around firing it into sniper towers and pulling them down never gets old, and the sniper rifle mechanic is interesting, too. Rather than giving you a sniper to run around with like the shotgun you have, it’s fired from the back of your car. Chumbucket can drive the car for you (though you control it) and you can creep up to enemy bases, slowly picking off their snipers. Again, it never gets old.
Thankfully the wasteland survival ideas are well implemented. Water is scarce, sure, but most of the time you’re in a situation where you’ll need to use it to heal, it’ll be some kind of stronghold (small or large) so there will be a tap, or pool to fill up your flask. Gas is needed to keep your vehicles running, but it takes a while to use it, and again, tanks can be found at populated areas. In a nice touch, you can put a spare canister in your boot just in case you run your tank dry, but you can also pick it up and throw it at enemies, exploding it with a shotgun burst.
The combat is the Batman Arkham melee method that, quite honestly, I’m nowhere near tired of. Mad Max’s world is a brutal one, and although you can happily pummel away at combos with the square button, and counter with triangle, things are mixed up with the addition of unlockable extra moves. A particular good one (early on) is simply to hold the attack button after two hits for a strong finisher. You can pick up weapons and integrate them into your move-set, too, and if you’ve collected any shivs you can finish people with them. Or, should you buy the skill, you could just get in close for a shotgun to the gut – it’s a one-hit kill, obviously. It makes for a violent, bloody system that feels damn good.
Car combat is less successful at first, but not bad. Depending on how upgraded your vehicle is, you can use the harpoon to differing degrees of success, but you can also target the red barrels in the trunks to quickly blow them up. On top of that, another option is to simply ram into your enemy – which has varying degrees of success depending again on what you’ve spent your scrap on. There’s a lot of car combat, though, and the slow motion aiming is a Godsend that removes most of the frustration. But you’ll have to get used to it, as you’re a sitting duck if you leave the Magnum Opus for too long.
It’s a very a-typical open-world game, in many ways, but one that’s faithful to the source material, especially when it comes to the characters. Max is an utter♥♥♥♥♥♥ but a badass with it. No matter what people do to help, he’s never nice to them. You could argue that this is because of the harsh, barren world he inhabits – everyone here wants to kill you, or use you for a deal. But the character you warm to the quickest is Chumbucket, so it’s hard to hear Max continually abuse him with his negativity. The voice acting is fine, for the most part, but the downtrodden, gruff Max is a little hard to like. It’s a very comic-book like universe, and the people are designed to match: burnt skin, tattoos, and even one guy who has razors cut into his skin – I’m not sure if that’s for effect or so he can keep his face beard-free.
What Mad Max does best, however, is never, ever take itself seriously. The opening cut-scene (which I won’t spoil, obviously) is over the top, but also features a gruesome chainsaw scene. As you take control for the first time and realise the person in that scene isn’t dead, you realise exactly what kind of game this is. There’s no logical reason how he can be alive after what you saw, but there it is, and he’s the main antagonist you’re fighting back against.
The story is generally fine, but nothing special. Most main missions see you have to chase something down and take someone out, and although there’s an attempt to make you care now and then, it falls flat. The fun is to be had just exploring, maybe getting caught in a horrendous storm that nearly takes your life.
Technically, there are a few frame-rate hiccups that are seemingly par for the course with open world games, but otherwise the only way Mad Max suffers is because of the source material. Fire, sand, metal – the trifecta of the world. You can’t blame Avalanche for keeping to that, but it does sometimes make for a bland looking game. There are some excellent moments, though, like those storms, or when night is setting in and it gets cold. Particle effects and explosions are fantastic, and there’s a real sense of style despite the brown look, especially when it comes to the gorgeous sky.
Mad Max is a fun game. You’ll happily lose an hour or two here and there, and feel great about it Nobody quite does that open-world charm like Avalanche, and the harpoon never stops being a source of mirth. The combat is great, and if you’re after an open world third-person title, you could do a lot worse.

This game has a rather short main campaign, and the gameplay can get somewhat repetitive (duck, shoot, reload, rinse, repeat). That said, I did actually enjoy the gameplay for the most part. However, the story is the best part of this game. I probably enjoyed it more because I went into it without knowing much of anything about the plot, so I won't say anything that would potentially spoil any of the surprises. I will say that it is pretty mind-bending. The player gets some interesting and difficult decisions to make, but unlike most "player choice" games, there's no menu screen that comes up - the choices just happen naturally in the flow of the game. Sometimes you don't even realize that you could have made another choice until you go back and read the achievements list. The voice acting is well done, music really adds to the atmosphere, and the game environment is just beautiful. (Note: If you don't like gory/disturbing images, maybe not the best game for you.) Overall, definitely recommend.

Well ... Just finished this  ... How could I describe my feelings now ? Disgusting ? Yeah, it made me feel like this guy you control in the game. And, well, it's a good thing. It shows I've been trapped by the plot. Our character learns things the hard way and you must be feeling bad for him. The strength of this title is to show another approach to war. There's no hero here and, like in real life, you'll find that civilians are always the first victims. You understand this shooting game has a plot. A strong one. You like it or not, but you must feel concerned.
For the gameplay, I found it pretty decent. It's a scripted game, you'll have to follow the path from the start to the end. This path serves the plot of the story (with a fairly large amount of cut scenes to push you more into the story). IA does its job quite well, enemies and mates are smart enough. The soundtrack is really good. Voices (localised in french for my version) are incredible and graphics (got one or two bugs) are good enough as well.
When it comes to lifetime, I think best players could finish it in less than 6 hours while average ones should need 8-9. It's short. Yet it worth it.
Whithout this detailed plot, it could be just one more (above average) shooting game. But, there's its story and its soundtrack, it adds a lot to the pleasure and it makes this title a must have.

I started playing Rogue Legacy on a whim one day when none of my co-op friends were online and immediately got sucked into it. I really like pretty much everything about this game and would recommend it for pretty much everyone.
The gameplay is solid, if you like 2D sidescrolling games. The combat is fluid, and the enemies are diverse. The different classes you unlock also give you some diversity in gameplay style and allow you to pick what you prefer (tanky vs fast vs magic) I really enjoy the presentation as well as the art style is clean and congruous, but they aren't afraid to play with things for fun.
What really sets Rogue Legacy apart though is the character selection. As with a proper rogue-like, you will be dying a lot. Like, a lot. And once you do, you are giving the option of picking between 3 successors, with random rolled characteristics. The traits are interesting and add a really fun element to the game. I don't want to go into detail about what they do because it's fun to discover them, but it's a nice design that keeps the game fresh.
Speaking of rogue-likes, this is how they should be. You expect to die constantly, but I rarely find it frustrating because that's part of the experience. The goal isn't to finish everything in one life, it's to live long enough to collect loot and gear to unlock permanent upgrades for your lineage. Thus, each attempt gives you a slightly better chance at getting farther the next time. The scaling works really well too. You will slow creep farther and farther into deeper areas, sometimes without even realizing right away that you're making progress. I'm finding that balance to be well executed as I can reasonably proceed to harder areas around the time I'm starting to find the area I've been playing in too easy.
This is a game that it's easy to get sucked into. I often find myself playing for an hour or two longer than I planned on because I've unlocked something new and say "just one more run before I quit" several times in a row. It's fun, amusing, challenging, and gives you something to work towards. You really can't ask for more than that.
Rogue Legacy is love, Roge Legacy is life, Rogue Legacy's hair smells very nice.

Great game that offers a challenging rogue experience, but also allows you to continually progress.  Each run through the castle is almost guaranteed to get enough gold to progress.
The only downside was the control layout on the keyboard.  I ended up remapping the keys because it was really awkward at first.  I assume most people use a controller to play this, so maybe the experience is better with one.

This is not a rogue-like. The only real similarity this game has with the original Rogue rpg is the permadeath aspect, and even then the game's upgrade system almost encourages you to die. But that's just arguing semantics for a game that has much worse problems than not being enough like an old ascii rpg.
The levels are not randomly generated, they're just randomly placed. This wouldn't be so bad if the individual rooms weren't so poorly designed. Add to that the permadeath aspect, and the rooms start to get repetitive real fast.
Combat in the game is fairly bland, with a lack of power behind your attacks. The mid air + down strike isn't as seemless as it could've been.
The only real enjoyable part of the game is upgrading your castle. The carrotstick of "just one more upgrade" kept me playing for long hours at a time, despite my problems with the game. Once I hit the wall where I could no longer continue upgrading my castle without large piles of money, I realized that I wasn't actually enjoying the game itself, just the feeling of getting closer to the figurative carrot. It was then that I realized I had better things to do with my time, and better games to play through instead.

Every visit to Arcadia Bay gives me the similar feeling - I'm happy I'm here because of all town's beauty and cosiness, but I become sad when I remember all these stories that happened here..
So, what is this game about? It is set in 2010, 3 years before the original story of LiS. You play as Chloe who's trying to get through tough times. She misses her best friend who moved to Seattle. She argues with stepdad and she is not always polite with her mother. She feels abandoned. But one day Chloe's life changed when she met someone who made her not alone anymore. Someone who saved her life. Someone who became Chloe's angel.
Seriously, don't you want to know more about Chloe and Rachel and their friendship?
What are differences between original game and prequel? You don't have a special ability like rewinding time. But you have some new features:
- "Backtalk" - risk/reward conversation mode that allows you to use arguments and insults to get someone to do what you want.
- an option to change outfit. Yes, you can finally choose from various outfits for Chloe.
- you can see current objective written on your hand.
- some sort of audio player which allows you to listen to official game soundtrack.
Otherwise, both games are pretty similar. Same game mechanics, same style of dramatic storyline, same music genre, same characters and same emotions. Write "Letters to Max" which is equivalent to Max's Diary, make graffiti instead of making photos and feel sad and lonely after completing another episode.
Also I can't thank "Daughter" band enough for the amazing
that fits perfectly with game's atmosphere.
So, is this game a totally worthy prequel to the original game? Absolutely. If you love "Life is Strange", you'll love BtS too. No doubt.
Thank you, Deck Nine.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is an amazing simulator. A nice range of trucks, with lots of customization options available.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 takes you all across Europe, through winding hills and up speeding highways.
You start from the bottom, and work your way up to 1 private truck, you can then go on to own your own massive logistics company.
What makes this game really amazing is the fact that there is a great FREE mod called Euro Truck Simulator 2 Multiplayer. This awesome mod allows you to play with up to 2000 other players on different servers around the world. It really makes it social, and not so lonely when driving those long roads.
World of trucks website, also allows you to customize your avitar with custom pictures, you can even change your plate and show off your trucks to the world, just imagine a Facebook of TRUCKING.
I highly recommend this game, for people that enjoy driving in particular, people who like business and progression.

TL;DR : Paying gives slight advantages which will increase probabilities of things like shots, stealing, blocking, speed, etc. but ultimately skill overrides all of this.  I have paid nothing, and still whoop players who have spent cash on this game.  There's a lot of trash-talking, but show me a competitive game without that.  If arcade style hoops is your thing, this game is really fun, and the price is right.
Do you remember NBA Jam. or more recently the NBA Street series? This is an online, 3v3 version of those games.  There are no rules, no fouls, but it's so much fun and an enjoyable arcade style basketball game.  Just to address a few issues though:
Some games have had lag spikes that are annoying, but most of the time fix themselves within 10 seconds or so.  Other times, there are glitches such as the ball being unable to be picked up, passed, shot, in which case you will be waiting for the game clock to expire, and whoever had the highest score before the glitch will win.
Is this game pay-to-win?  Somewhat, but not really.  There are a lot of little stat boosts you can buy with money, but most of them can be earned by playing the game and earning in-game currency as well.  There are "special" characters which start with additional stat boosts, but you can also earn one of these for free by reaching level 50 with any character.  Ultimately, do people who cash have a slight advantage?  Definitely.  But no amount of cash can make you a good player, or let you win all the time.  This game still relies heavily on skill, predicting your opponent, and your general ability to play good offense and defense.

I am a hunter IRL. This game made me feel as if I was in the field at an outfitter. The realism is amazing. The way the various animal species act is very realistic as well.

This game is so good for the first seven or eight hours that I'm genuinely mad the formula falls apart and it becomes tedious.
Yeah, the game is clever and charming and the unique take on the Metroidvania genre is initially intriguing. Unfortunately all that charm is just a veil that hides the fact that the game is 95% grinding. Once I'd played with all the classes and all the possible traits a hero can have there wasn't much left to hold my interest. All you're doing is repeating the loop of searching out the chests and gold until you die and you can spend it on upgrades. You keep repeating that until you're bulky enough to take on the boss. The more you play the larger the area you search through in each run becomes and the upgrades cost more meaning subsequent runs take longer and longer while giving you less and less returns. The worst is going through a whole run just to upgrade your weight capacity so after another run you can buy and equip a new weapon or armor. There's  just not enough to see and do while grinding over and over to justify how long it takes. Each area of the castle is pretty much the same as the last only with recolored enemies.
Similar Rogue-likes/lites/whatever you want to call 'ems like Spelunky and The Binding of Isaac are compelling because you know you always have the capacity to win and your own personal skill level is the limiting factor. Rogue Legacy's tougher areas are filled with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t rooms that are so loaded with enemies charging at you and spewing bullet-hell death that you're pretty much required to grind to a certain point just to be able to have that area available for grinding in. It's a very boring cycle because the game lack any feeling of progressing. Unlike a traditional Metroidvania game you're not exploring to open up new areas and get items that will give you access you new parts of the world, you're just hoarding gold for upgrades. That sucks. And once all the classes are unlocked all you're playing for are marginal stat upgrades and that sucks even more.

This is an excellent old-school arcade-ish action-platformer with stellar production values and great (but difficult) gameplay. You've read the other reviews (I assume), so I'll just add a few thoughts (and gripes).

Like so many retro gamers, I've been having trouble trying to find games that properly capture the true "metroidvania" feeling that we know and love. Castlevania isn't the same anymore, Metroid is an afterthought and a tool and Super Smash, and all other similar games have fallen off the radar. I can't say that Rogue Legacy is the new king of the style, but it's a solid game that fills the void.
= Graphics =
Fluid 2-D graphics, reminiscent of SNES. Do I need to say more? No cell-shaded characters, no selective lighting, and no other random gimmicks. Some children in the game do have traits that affect visuals, such as 'retro' vision, as seen in the images above. But that's still a pretty cute thing to see once in a while.
= Music =
Nothing special really. It's there. It's background noise. I usually keep other stuff on in the background to get me pumped up against a boss. Castlevania of course works well here.
= Gameplay=
The thing that kept me hooked for roughly 20 hours (with more to come, that was only my first game) was its fluid gameplay. This isn't like early metroidvania games where you had to get a running start to make any jump, nor do you have to hit that 'perfect angle' to get onto a ledge or attack an enemy. I used a gamepad and I was making split-second movements constantly to avoid attacks and traps. It's very responsive and smooth.
Gameplay gets a tad repetitive, to be honest. Sometimes you get an offspring that's doomed to fail so you know ahead of time you won't get much use out of them. The point of the game is going to each area, and there are four, all connected, with their own bosses. you beat the bosses, you open that shiny door int he beginning. It gets tiring venturing to each location just to beat the boss, as you might stumble across a difficult room when you think you have a child that could actually take on a boss...then you die. Rinse repeat. Luckily, the castle's map is randomly generated, so it's different each time.
= Lasting Appeal =
It'a metroidvania with randomly generated maps, tons of ways to improve your character, and each new game+ gets more difficult. If you like SNES side-scrollers, then you'l play this more than once.
= Verdict =
Safe to say I adored this game. It can be repetitive and frustrating with difficult bosses, but the leveling up system of looting gold and buying upgrades is oddly addictive. It's full of references and homages to classic games, but doesn't rely on them as a crutch. This is probably one of the best side-scrolling games I've played since the GBA castelvanias.

Reviews for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
---
With regard to accessibility for deaf/hoh gamers, I give Black Ops 2 8/10 single player and 6/10 multiplayer.
Gameplay
I am an avid FPS gamer.  Like any FPS, you will get killed by things you did not know were coming.  Even the most well-captioned FPS game will have uncaptioned audio cues for imminent danger.  That said, Black Ops 2 does okay in this category, but doesn't break the mold.
Subtitles/Text
Subtitles for single player are just subtitles - no captions - but they help tell the story.  I do feel that they are a little slow, though, for key moments when you have to react quickly.  For multiplayer, there are no captions or subtitles.  You are on your own.
Chatting/Communicating
BO2 allows text chat, but most players make use of voice chat in my experience.  In the lobby, you can ONLY use voice chat - there is no input for text there.
Not a fan of multi-player, but I enjoyed the single player story!

I loved the pace and story of the original Life Is Strange game. It had so many twists and turns cleverly masked in plain sight and such a gripping story that was layed out spectacularly.
Before The Storm has many of the same elements as the original Life Is Strange but it's pacing and emotional aspects seem off. To start off. Where Life Is Strange was much slower, it built an emersive world with believable (though writing was at times cringy) characters. Before the Storm is a much more fast paced game, going though the emotional highs and lows, and through the character interactions and developments rapidly. The problem is, even though it has two less chapters than Life Is Strange, it doesn't need to pace itself so rapidly. It feels like Deck Nine is trying to cram 5 chapters into 3, which causes a lot of the character and emotional development to move so rapidly and at times illogically. Many of the moments I should be connecting to the characters fall short due to this pacing issue.
Outside pacing, the game, as metioned before, holds many of the same qualities as the original though not to the same standard all the time. Still a splendid game

Начав играть поздним осенним вечером, расслабившись и налив себе ароматный кофе, уже через 2 часа я имел рект. Именно, что рект. Потому как не давали выбратся с пляжа. Имея в одной руке камень, а в другой руке причинное место, ты оказываешся против полностью вооруженных людей сидящих на вышках. Многие голожопы отчаивались и убивали друг друга прямо на месте респа, кто-то оказался в этом весьма успешен, и вскоре образовалось целое племя из таких матерых голожопов под моим предводительством. Мы делали копья и убивали свежереснувшихся, запасаясь человечиной, и конечно продумывали план побега с пляжа.
Вокруг пляжа в радиусе 500 метров был полукруг из стен и вышек, но так как хозяивами были несколько человек, то имелись дырки в пересечении зон их влияний. На выбранном нами участке стены обычно стояли 3 человека с болтами, наслаждаясь этаким тавер-дефенсом. Сделав пару пробных вылазок мы обнаружили, что ночью стреляют только двое, а третий долбился в глаза в темноте, это впоследствии сыграет нам на руку. Один человек из пяти, с третьего захода даже попал за стены, но обнаружил там минное поле из капканов и собственно мин.
На третью ночь мы были готовы, в нашем запасе было 10 человек с копьями и 5 голожопов. Голожопы были набраны под страхом многократной смерти и были нашим арьергардом (пушечным мясом). Выдвинувшись с пляжа рассредоточенным порядком, под шквалом двух болтовок, до стен добежали только 3 голожопа и 7 копейщиков. Перед нами стояла задача быстро преодолеть минное поле - тогда мы выстроились гуськом, пустив вперед оставшихся голожопов. Их хватило ровным счетом на сто метров, дальше рисковали мы сами. Очень помогли запасы человечины, у каждого было по 3 стака. Дойдя до половины мы услышали как по нам начали стрелять сзади, по этому мы пустились бежать в рассыпную остаток пути. Вокруг стали взрыватся мины и сщелкать капканы, люди падали один за одним.
До леса, которой был границей минного поля, добежали только двое - я и еще один человек-копейщик. Наконец мы были свободны. Мой спутник крепко выругался и отправился восвояси. Я остался один, ох***я с такого начала игры на серве. Теперь мне предстояло построить дом.

Still, I would rate this game as one of the top 3 games I've ever played.

I am a hunter IRL. This game made me feel as if I was in the field at an outfitter. The realism is amazing. The way the various animal species act is very realistic as well.
This is a game that takes patience, but of course, you would encvounter more game than you would in real life, because it is a video game afterall. But it is very simulation like as much as possible.
I found myself very relaxed, enjoying the anticipation of stalking.
It has perks, skills, and you can level up your hunter, as well as their skills on each weapon type: rifle, hand gun, shotgun, and bow. I really enjoyed the bow, as it is a challenge to draw the prey in, and get them at a short range.
I would like to see improvements in the varmint hunting, however: foxes and coyotes.
I seriously enjoyed the beautiful landscape, moving around on the 4 wheeler ATV, and just the whole free roaming aspect of it. Buying new equipment for upgrades, all of that.
What can I say? Just don't compare this to "The Hunter: Classic", because this is leaps and bounds, light years ahead in quality. This is the king of hunting games right now, and as many hunting games as I have played, IMO, this is the best ever.

This game is suprisingly good, if you can switch from FarCry to a hunting, and "enjoying a trophy" - mode. The skill tree really makes a difference. If you just run full speed through this, you won't see much, because the entire forest will run away ;-)

Simple things as the "walking sounds" are absolutely fine in this game, compared to many others.
Critique: This base game needs much more, to keep you going after you got the most important skills. New DLCs, (the ATV/quad DLC is very useful, the fast-travel tent also very good), but this is just for convenience. This needs more animals, maybe brown bears, grizzly..., birds you can pick (not just call rabbits critters like rats without trophy), maybe add taxidermy to mount trophies in a / your lodge, like with the classic game, trophy snapshot is missing.

This game is one that seems like I haven't spent a huge amount of time on, but I've played it on two separate accounts and have obviously beaten it or I wouldn't be talking about it. It's great for killing time, but not for much else. I hope someday people understand that there is a difference between difficulty derived from reaction times and strategy, and a game being cringe-worthy to operate. This is the latter. Your character can barely swing a sword in the right direction, let alone in any kind of useful arc. If you have enemies directly above you, you're screwed since the delay between attacking and jumping either means you're going to jump into the enemy above (Most enemies are made of razor-blades so you'll get hurt that way) or you can attack and not jump, and hope the enemy doesn't time your swing and run into you.
I don't get it, why do people make games wherein your character is a huge gaping vag? They think that it's a valid form of difficulty? I know not everyone realizes this, but you can play a difficult game with capable characters that can attack where you actually intend the instant you press a button. No joke: in this game you have to move in the direction you want to face without swinging in order to attack in that direction. So if there's an enemy right next to you, your only choices are get hit or run away. Because you aren't turning around to attack unless you want to run right into the enemy.
Essentially I'm just annoyed with everything about this game that reminds me of every gaming cliche I hate, and if there was something stronger than deleting it I would do it in a heartbeat. That's why I'm writing this review, because there isn't an option to delete and take a dump on the designer's desktop.

Rogue Legacy is the perfect example of what happens when the controls for a platformer are well-established. As of this review, it is one of my most enjoyed platformers.
+Controls - Very well established, responsive, not necessarily without flaws, but still feels very good to play...
+Creativity - A lot of thought was put into character traits, skills, monsters and terrain. Each of these make every playthrough feel fresh even if it retains the same gameplay mechanics every time.
+Gameplay - Simple, but fun. Skills and class abilities allow you to approach each situation differently each time. It does come with one small drawback: it may feel awkward the first time around.
+Art - what can I say, it's well done... at least for me
+Music - good, not too good though...
+Backstory - ERMAHGEHRD story in a platformer... don't need it! herp derp blah blah... okay it's not exactly the best story, but it was good enough to keep me playing and keep me searching for the diary entries.
+Classes - okay so this should be part of "Gameplay", but it was so well done it deserves a separate mention... My favourite class would definitely be the Spellsword... and NO, there are PLENTY of reasons NOT to play Spelunker/Miner
-Bosses - Let's be honest, it's easy to beat the bosses first time around... even more so if you've over-leveled which is not hard to do after some time... However, beating a boss unlocks a more challenging version of the fight with that boss, though some of you Hyper Hardcores probably still find that easy... Fighting through the levels presents a bigger challenge than actually fighting the bosses. Strangely though, this never bothered me.
-Grindy - If you don't like the gameplay or don't get a feel for it early on, it's going to feel like this. I'm sure some players will think that they should max the gold related skills first, but I disagree. (I'd recommend to get "Hokage" early on.)
-Randomization - the fates sometimes feel like toying with you, using rooms that you know you cannot access without a particular trait...(Minor)
-Flexible Trait - WHY is this even a trait? This was one of the key bits missing from the wonderful controls. (Minor)
Recommend? Yes, to anyone who enjoys platformers from the fun casuals to the hyper hardcores...
Yes, to anyone who is looking for their first platformer...
Yes, if you need to wash down the taste of horrible controls in platforming games *ahemtheybleedpixelsewahem*
Don't get if: well, honestly I can't come up with a reason not to recommend it right now... I probably won't find one

I will break this review into 3 parts; Gameplay, Graphics, and Story.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay is coverbased, thirdperson. Similar to Gears of War, but not quite the same. I was glad to find that this game didn't do what most games fo when they want to make themselves more difficult. That being giving baddies more hp and more DPS. It only takes a single dirrect burst to drop most baddies (save armoured heavies encountered later in the campaign) and same goes for you. YOU ARE NOT BULLET PROOF! nor can you carry thousands of rounds of ammo, you have to conserve and make shots count. You need to take cover in order to survive, and the cover system is fluid after you get the hang of it. The game uses the setting of desert storms to allow you some environmental effects. You can shoot out windows piled up with sand to burry enimies, knock out glass floors when your on top of a building, and more besides. It is used often enough to matter, but not enough to become a gimic.
GRAPHICS
These are nice enough, for when they were made. Because of the desert setting, extra attention is paid to color and lighting. It has amazing effects for the story. Animations are exelent with one exeption: the main characters face. It does not match the voice at all which is a shame because the voice acting is exelent, and even in cinematics, remains wooden and lackluster
As the story progresses, the colors textures, models, and even the voices, change to accomidate the story, to great effect I might ad.
STORY
This is NOT an action shooter. It is in fact, a "horrors of war" game. Now it is Very difficult to pull off a Horrors of War MOVIE without it turning into action-porn, and conveying the war drama effect in a GAME is downright impossible. But these guys DID IT! and did it DAMN GOOD TO, THANK YOU 2K!. The story is inspired heavily by Heart of Darkness and it's film adaptation Apocalypse Now. It's a lot like watching the chestburster scene in Alien. You can't stand to watch anymore, but you JUST CAN"T LOOK AWAY! After the the first big morals bender (No spoils, but I will say it involves white phosphorose) I actually started to hate myself for my actions. They say that you either die a hero, or live long enouth to see yourself become a villain, and you live very long in this game. psych stuff shows up after a while, just to complete the horror (the horror). make no mystake, it's not a scary horror game, but it is horrifying beyond belief in it's own way.
My only complaints are little nitpics over realism that nobody ever gets right anyway (characters ziplining on their bare fingers, being thrown out of helicopters, falling through floors, and brushing themselves off. nobody ever needs water [even though dehidration becomes a plot-point] etc.) Otherwise, I rate this game 6 out of 5 stars :)
A game that isn't afraid to take the ugliness of war and shove it right in your face.

Mad Max is a third-person action game made by Avalanche Studios and published by Warner Bros. Although WB are getting a lot of hate for abandoning Batman: Arkham Knight and Mortal Kombat X on PC, this game is not the case! Avalanche Studios optimalised the game for PC perfectly!
What surprises you for the first time immediately, is the game world. It's not as big as in Just Cause games, but that doesn't matter, it's still huge. You'll be able to explore through the wastelands, see all 50 shades of sand, kill many mad warriors meanwhile and collect tons of scrap.
Scrap is the resource (or the currency) that is used in Mad Max for everything - you upgrade your weapons, your car or even Max's clothes with scrap. And there's plenty of upgrades for everything, so if you don't plan to get 100% achievements, you won't even unlock every upgrade the game offers. But the scrap isn't the only thing you need for unlocking the upgrades, most of advanced ones also require completing a specific mission or a simple task, like: Lower the antagonist's (Scabrous Scrotus) influence in area by taking over his camps or destroying his scarecrows (pylons that should let people around know who rules in the wasteland).
While you can have about 5 basic car constructions (upgradable in any way you want) there are many more vehicles in the game, and you can control all of those! You'll find use for them in racing (death runs) that offers few types of races.
The combat is similar to Batman Arkham series, with many similar animations (punching, kicking and jumping groups of enemies) and practically same controls. You mash the left button for attack and when anyone in the enemy group attacks you, you have to parry the attack with right button. With exception for knife attacks and finishing moves, that's all. Anyway, it's not any significantly hard and it's fun.
What's also a great pro of the game is the attention for details that aren't mentioned much when people talk around the game. There's a specific weather (random) event that'll make you impressed, but I don't want to spoil the details. Through the world you'll explore, you'll be finding photos of the old world (before the sandpocalypse), usually with something written on the back side. Those lead you (and the Max) to thinking about what in the game world is already lost.
The story is not bad for a game based primarly around combat, racing and exploring, it even tries to play with your emotions. But it'll most probably fail, because Max is stonehearted, so you'll get over all bad events like it was nothing. There's few really interesting characters that have interesting backstory, but there's also characters that you meet without any proper explanation of sympathies.
I think that every player will be really excited to explore everything in the beginning, every small camp with scrap. But that doesn't last forever and most players will later find the "breaking point" where they found exploring being too much repetitive, leading to sticking just with the main story missions (they'll require you to do some regular exploring few times anyway).
The content recycling in the game (repeating enemies, camps etc.) is made delicately, with exception for one thing that ended up pretty bad - the bossfight(s). There are many bossfights in the game (especially for the side exploring - beating the Top Dogs) but they all are the same, the bosses even still use the same weapon! Only thing that changes is the arena where they fight and number of other NPCs that spawn around to help the boss.
The world of Mad Max has a day/night cycle, which is great but feels half-baked with the fact that you can't rest until specific part of the day comes. As there are few missions that requires to do them at night, you might end up having to do something else for about 90 minutes, while waiting for night.
In the end, I was really entertained for more than 20 hours thanks to Mad Max. As a current AAA game I got enough satisfaction out of it and even though I have not found motivation to complete everything that's not mandatory in the game, I still think it's a great game and definitely deserves my recommendation.

So, now that I finished the game 100%, I can properly and thoroughly review it.
It should be noted that the game has a somewhat faint connection to the movie, and it's probably a good thing - game devs had a greater freedom in terms of things they could make.
Before you read the review, you should understand that this is a sandbox game with all the cliches and quirks sandbox games have: lots of collectibles, vast map, going from A to B, killing X enemies. I do not mind such gameplay, if the game provides something in return for my struggles, and Mad Max delivers.
What I loved about the game:
As you can see by the amount of hours I spent in the game, I found a lot of elements of the game appealing, but these come to mind as gems. However, there were some little problems that reduce my final grade a little bit.
You can see that most of my complaints have the same basis - lack of content. The game could be much better if the devs tried to introduce a little bit more diversity to the enemies, Max's moves, and Wasteland missions. However, you will only start noticing the abovementioned problems after 8-10 hours in the game, which means that you pretty much already get a good value from it.
Final grade: 8/10.
If you are a fan of Mad Max - play it. If you are a fan of sandbox games - play it. If you like dark, gritty, post-apocalyptic settings - play it. It is all-around good game, and you probably won't regret getting it.

My mum said to me that I am too loud when playing games and I need to stop screaming things down the mic at 3am.
So I decided to buy theHunter: Call of the Wild, hoping it would calm me down. And it did!
Slow-paced, relaxing game that can be very rewarding. Looks absolutely stunning, too! I haven't yet come across any bugs/glitches and as far as I can tell the gameplay is quite realistic.
I have never hunted in real life and I would never want to, but in game-form it's really fun!!! Aside from being an enjoyable game to play, it's also taught me a lot about hunting in real life; tactics used, what weapons/ammo is used for each animal, and most importantly the ethical issues surrounding it, and how hunters deal with them.
Big thank you to the devs for making this game! Although I haven't played theHunter: Classic, I have found a lot of the negative reviews around that game come from micro-transactions and subscription fees: this game has nothing like that, and it is a standalone purchase (with a couple cheap DLCs), once you buy this game you get all the current maps, weapons, ammo, callers, lures, etc... and they can all ONLY be unlocked through game progression - which is good I think.
I will be honest though, this game has inspired me to try theHunter: Classic, which I have read is a bit more realistic and has more variety (especially varmints and birds), so we will see how that goes.
I can only think of two cons with this game:
> There are no birds to hunt (which is a shame, because the shotguns are really nice to use)
> There is not much variety in terms of hunting varmints. There is only 1 type on each of the maps (Red Fox and coyote) that give any reward for hunting. You can shoot the squirrels and rabbits running around, but they do not give any sort of rewards, or recognition that you killed it. This is a shame because I think the smaller animals are the most fun to track down!
Both of these cons are very personal gripes that I expect will be fixed with upcoming DLCs, which I don't mind. There is enough in the game to keep me entertained until then!

Spec-Ops: The Line is a squad-based third-person shooter, but really this is just a cover-up. The game is actually an experimental arthouse game that tries to challenge conventions of the modern game industry, narrative, and ask the player what they really want from games.
Spec Ops: The Line is the 11th game in the Spec-Ops series, but you'd be forgiven for not knowing that, as the series wasn't particularly great and hadn't had a new entry in its series in over 10 years before this game came along. However, Spec-Ops: The Line is more of a stand-alone game, and you need no knowledge of the previous Spec-Ops games to enjoy it.
You play as Captain Martin Walker, who comes into the town of Dubai under fictional settings that its been ravaged and left for dead by rampant sand storms and riots in the town. A US team, known as the 33rd, was sent there to help keep things under control. The last the city and the 33rd team were recorded doing was trying to form a caravan to help save the survivors of the city. However, all contact was lost, and the city was declared a no-mans land, with access to the city barred off by the UAE government.
Our main character, Walker, comes in with a small team, with the only other members being Lieutenant Alphonse Adams and Staff Sergeant John Lugo. Walker has a personal stake in all of this... The leader of the 33rd, Colonel John Konrad, is a personal hero of his, someone who saved his life on the battlefield. This man changed Walker's life, and is the sort of man Walker inspires to be. So when a communication message from Lugo gets out, he takes on the mission very personally, and is determined to do whatever it takes to save him.
Spec-Ops: The Line is a very beautiful game. Countless scenes and imagery are backed by fantastic artistic design, and one sometimes can't help but to just sit-back and appreciate the aesthetics of it all. The characters are well animated, the effects of things like sand and water are impressive, there are some gorgeous overlooks of the city at various points in the game, and visually stimulating environments that range from theaters to malls to aquariums to the natural desert itself.
The soundtrack is also very stimulating. The game features a variety of licensed music, ranging from Hush by Deep Purple to Star Spangled Banner by Jimi Hendrix. The original soundtrack is also rather interesting, featuring rather ethereal sounds, industrial, and pseudo-rock to home in the tones of each scene. The voicing is handled fantastically, and fits each character rather perfectly.
But there is something looming over Spec-Ops: The Line almost the entire time that may turn off a lot of people. The game isn't really all that fun to play. It's serviceable and not badly made, but something about it makes the gameplay never really a fun experience. And as odd as it may sound, I think this is what the developers were going for. There comes a tedium to the combat, a sort of unfeeling to it all. It can be a struggle at times, and there are some moments that are really cool from a visual stand-point and conceptually so, but it still somehow remains unfun.
Also as someone who played the whole game on hard difficulty, I recommend you do not. I usually play games on the hardest difficulty available as I find it fun to be challenged, but in the case of Spec-Ops I'd argue it actually actively worked to try and make me enjoy the game less. I wasn't having fun with the harder challenges, it didn't feel satisfying to overcome difficult segments, and it caused me to repeat several segments over-and-over again, and not in a way that it was enjoyable.
But I'd still say Spec-Ops is worth experiencing. While the game poses as a third-person shooter, and there is definitely third-person shooter gameplay here, that isn't at the same time really what the game is or is about. Talking about Spec-Ops is difficult, as I believe it is best to go into it without knowing almost anything at all. But at the same time, there is a tedium, a drudgery to pull through in the game.And that arguably is part of the game, and is part of the point of the game and its themes. Spec-Ops has a lot of thought put into it, and is a case where the narrative, atmosphere, and overall experience is much stronger than the gameplay.
Here's an odd analogy; This game is essentially to Shooters what Silent Hill is to Survival-Horror or Braid is to platformers. The games are well-made, but gameplay isn't the focus. Other elements take the lead, and the games have rather strong emphasis on its other elements. The gameplay without these other elements is arguably rather lackluster, or kind of tedious. But with the other elements, the games rise from this to become a rather interesting experience in game form. Some may never see the enjoyment of a game that isn't fun to play from a gameplay perspective, but if you can, there is a lot to love in Spec-Ops: The Line.
It's depressing, sometimes hard to swallow, and you may not honestly understand everything the first time you play it. However, it is likely to stick with you, and really delves into a sort of symbolic social message on shooters and war, and how the general public see's it. It's not very fun, but Spec-Ops is still an experience worth undertaking.

It's definitely worth picking up the complete edition, but I'd say only on a steam sale. Three of the four DLC packs are good, but there's one that is just sort of boring, and the only real saving grace it has is it's commentary and dialogue. Gunplay is tight, the flashy nature of the game makes you feel good, and later in the game in Ultimate mode the difficulty increases drastically, bringing a welcome challenge to the otherwise easy campaign.
Like any MMO or likewise style of game, however, the endgame becomes less about completing story missions or quests and entirely about raiding bosses for their best loot drops. This would be a great feature of the game if not for the downright ridiculously easy way to duplicate items from other players, who seem more than willing to do so. This breaks the game for me in a sense, but in the long run I suppose it's really just a minor annoyance.
In short, get the game if you like grindy MMO types of games, but don't expect a long campaign. The game's more about playing with others and killing stuff, which let's face it, is all anyone really wants.

When I first started playing Rogue Legacy I didn't see the light at the end of the tunnel. No matter what tactics I employed, or how cautious I was, the game never failed to mercilessly punish each tiny mistake I made sending me to start the entire process over again. I had no hope. Despite this loop of assured failure I struggled on. Partly because no game can defeat me, but more importantly because Rogue Legacy would not let me go. Each death meant a quick check of the castle, the vendors and then paying the doorman everything I had simply to enter and die once again.
Rogue Legacy is a fantastic representation of 2D metroid style games mixed with a generous helping of you-gotta-earn-it. It's controls are smooth and responsive making YOUR mistakes all the more frustrating. It's entirely unapologetic for absolutely mashing the player until they finally learn the fundamental lessons of the game and that's what makes it great. If you're like me you're going to want to quit this game and curse its existence only to be pulled back in by it's beautiful blend of action and character. The castle that you traverse is procedurally generated each time you enter with a new decendant but never suffers boring, bland, or poor design which is a testament less to the durability of it's systems and more to the cast of characters inhabiting this shifty environment. You have to learn what they are and what they do to have any hope of defeating them. You might be able to run from room to room casually slaying all the monsters contained within, but eventually the game will test your knowledge and set what are basically living traps as rooms full of various creatures advance from all angles, working in tandem to bring you down. With a proper understanding of your enemies you'll eventually be able to build very satisfying strategies that are every bit as dynamic as the obstacles the game throws at you.
If you're a fan of side scrolling exploration games such as Super Metroid, or anything there-after labelled "metroidvanias" then chances are you're going to enjoy this game. It's a unique and interesting take on the genre that feels very fresh and engaging. Above all the rewards for victory, small or large, are absolute and those moments dominate the silent rooms filling every corner. The sensation of action satisfaction from thoroughly dominating your foe, with the knowledge of your foe, will drive every future success as well as mend any failure until you've fought and won your very last battle.

There are some serious flaws with this game.
First of which is that the campaign is boring. I never cared about a Call of Duty storyline since the second Modern Warfare and this one does not stand out.
Secondly, the multiplayer is incredibly annoying, and if you are relatively good with shooters, that doesn't matter. I can (when i'm not hungover or stressed out) get top of the team in games like Counter-Strike, Battlefield, and even Day of Defeat, games that are considered more difficult than Black Ops 2. Skill from other games does not carry over to this one. The playing field is so leveled that you could call it a bottomless pit. Hell, someone with no experience concerning shooters can (after getting familiar with the ebb and flow of the controls and overall structure of the game) demolish people who actually have skill. With the utterly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ decision to include things like target finders, select fire, etc. anyone can pick this game up and do relatively good.
Finally, zombies. Yes it is a "unique" gamemode. Yes I enjoy it. That doesn't mean you can say it fantastic or better than games like Left 4 Dead or Killing Floor; games that are head and shoulder over this overly repetive, luck-based and deathly annoying survival thing. When I care so little about a game (yes, for the sake of not trying to conjure synonyms for gamemode) that I don't even remember (or care to) prices for certain guns, perks, ♥♥♥♥, whatever, that should support the argument that this is boring. I want to like it, but when i've played games like Killing Floor or Left 4 Dead, Zombies in Black Ops seems petty and worth burying.
Seems all negative eh? Well, just because I have problems with Black Ops 2, that doesn't mean I don't have fun. You see, the fun you can have with Call of Duty is mindless, stupid fun that does not require usage of more than a single brain cell. As long as you can turn off your brain, you can have fun with this. BUT, you must remember to turn it back on when you are done playing it - especially if you are discussing its merits or lack thereof.

What I like about the Game as of December 21 update 0.5/0.5.1:
> Graphical Options have been expanded: The game has some more qaulity to it now.
> Costume Customization: Always a plus and an added bonus for creativity and character Differentiation/Distinctness.
> Fixed the easily broken moves such as the scoop (Hold "X" and tap "A" near an opponent to break physics) and the Star Fish (Curl in a ball sometime holding "X" or "B" and just repeat taping "A" to flop in your curled state laying waste to any attackers dumb enough to get in range of you), this is a good thing since these moves alone ruined the fun with how abusive they were.
> Displays controls on loading screen.
> Able to Tackle/Dive by sprinting and pressing "B".
>The level backgrounds have been reworked and look a bit more asthetically pleasing.
> And...uhhhhhh...the blimp level is actually better somehow.
What I do NOT like about the Game as of update 0.5/0.5.1:
> The Price: I can't complian personally getting it for free but even I can gauge that I would not of payed 20$ for this fun but broken mess, especially now as of the 0.5 and 0.5.1 update.
> The Graphics: While in a sense are more asthetically pleasing..at the same time they don't feel right. The transition has taken such a different tone in 0.5/0.5.1 in the way of its graphics style.
> The Reworked Stages: Somehow feel inferior now, I do like some of the asthetics but just like the graphics the stages feel off somehow. They don't feel nearly as fun to brawl in for many reasons I don't quite know how to explain.
> The Physics: Before they were a little rediculous, clunky and abusive but that rare moment you landed and drop kick or a flying super upper cut was somehow a game changer, ender or just "Holy Sheet!" moment, somehow it made it fun having that moment you or your friends get launched into the ceiling or wall by a rare generic falcon punch or kick.
The physics now seem not only clunky still but bland, heavy and just not effective. Really the only effective meas of offense and just wildly punching and jumping, It is so akward now to land a drop kick and it rarely happens, I mostly just flop to the ground after an air spasm that was suppose to be a drop kick, granted headbutt is still just about as effective but now nearly anything will knock you out, even the gentle caress of a babys hand across your cheek."
> The Online: Currently is a mess. Joining a game was a nightmare without a connection issue and once in it was extremely lagged behind in responses and just laggy. People literally would drag themselves into death by accident while holding onto someone.
> The Utterly annoying balloon scoring system after a round: It's slow, too slow, it's not needed.
> The Buoy does not load. Ever. (this may not be a problem for everyone)
"Before this update I loved this game despite it's obvious funny and rediculous flaws and honestly the only thing I would of changed were the over abusive Scoop and Stafish technique. It is great the game is trying to overall inprove but the formula has been watered down and slapped with a fancy label now. Undertale is a videogame that takes the players knowledge of videogame tropes, and uses that agents the player in clever ways. Undertale is a videogame in the “RPG”, or Role Playing Game, genre typically in an RPG the player is on some sort of quest, and along the way they fight enemies to increase their stats, LV, and XP which usually stand for levels and experience. RPGs also tend to have “turn based combat” meaning you and your opponent take turns while fighting, this is the style Undertale uses, but with a few twist. For example during your opponents turn you can doge their attacks in a Mimi-game like sequence that has you controlling a heart trying to avoid the attacks from your foe. The game also takes a “Pixel art” art style, somewhat recreating the feel of an older style NES game. If I had to say what the overarching theme of the game is, it’s that actions have consequences.
