Spec-Ops: The Line is a squad-based third-person shooter, but really this is just a cover-up. The game is actually an experimental arthouse game that tries to challenge conventions of the modern game industry, narrative, and ask the player what they really want from games.
Spec Ops: The Line is the 11th game in the Spec-Ops series, but you'd be forgiven for not knowing that, as the series wasn't particularly great and hadn't had a new entry in its series in over 10 years before this game came along. However, Spec-Ops: The Line is more of a stand-alone game, and you need no knowledge of the previous Spec-Ops games to enjoy it.
You play as Captain Martin Walker, who comes into the town of Dubai under fictional settings that its been ravaged and left for dead by rampant sand storms and riots in the town. A US team, known as the 33rd, was sent there to help keep things under control. The last the city and the 33rd team were recorded doing was trying to form a caravan to help save the survivors of the city. However, all contact was lost, and the city was declared a no-mans land, with access to the city barred off by the UAE government.
Our main character, Walker, comes in with a small team, with the only other members being Lieutenant Alphonse Adams and Staff Sergeant John Lugo. Walker has a personal stake in all of this... The leader of the 33rd, Colonel John Konrad, is a personal hero of his, someone who saved his life on the battlefield. This man changed Walker's life, and is the sort of man Walker inspires to be. So when a communication message from Lugo gets out, he takes on the mission very personally, and is determined to do whatever it takes to save him.
Spec-Ops: The Line is a very beautiful game. Countless scenes and imagery are backed by fantastic artistic design, and one sometimes can't help but to just sit-back and appreciate the aesthetics of it all. The characters are well animated, the effects of things like sand and water are impressive, there are some gorgeous overlooks of the city at various points in the game, and visually stimulating environments that range from theaters to malls to aquariums to the natural desert itself.
The soundtrack is also very stimulating. The game features a variety of licensed music, ranging from Hush by Deep Purple to Star Spangled Banner by Jimi Hendrix. The original soundtrack is also rather interesting, featuring rather ethereal sounds, industrial, and pseudo-rock to home in the tones of each scene. The voicing is handled fantastically, and fits each character rather perfectly.
But there is something looming over Spec-Ops: The Line almost the entire time that may turn off a lot of people. The game isn't really all that fun to play. It's serviceable and not badly made, but something about it makes the gameplay never really a fun experience. And as odd as it may sound, I think this is what the developers were going for. There comes a tedium to the combat, a sort of unfeeling to it all. It can be a struggle at times, and there are some moments that are really cool from a visual stand-point and conceptually so, but it still somehow remains unfun.
Also as someone who played the whole game on hard difficulty, I recommend you do not. I usually play games on the hardest difficulty available as I find it fun to be challenged, but in the case of Spec-Ops I'd argue it actually actively worked to try and make me enjoy the game less. I wasn't having fun with the harder challenges, it didn't feel satisfying to overcome difficult segments, and it caused me to repeat several segments over-and-over again, and not in a way that it was enjoyable.
But I'd still say Spec-Ops is worth experiencing. While the game poses as a third-person shooter, and there is definitely third-person shooter gameplay here, that isn't at the same time really what the game is or is about. Talking about Spec-Ops is difficult, as I believe it is best to go into it without knowing almost anything at all. But at the same time, there is a tedium, a drudgery to pull through in the game.And that arguably is part of the game, and is part of the point of the game and its themes. Spec-Ops has a lot of thought put into it, and is a case where the narrative, atmosphere, and overall experience is much stronger than the gameplay.
Here's an odd analogy; This game is essentially to Shooters what Silent Hill is to Survival-Horror or Braid is to platformers. The games are well-made, but gameplay isn't the focus. Other elements take the lead, and the games have rather strong emphasis on its other elements. The gameplay without these other elements is arguably rather lackluster, or kind of tedious. But with the other elements, the games rise from this to become a rather interesting experience in game form. Some may never see the enjoyment of a game that isn't fun to play from a gameplay perspective, but if you can, there is a lot to love in Spec-Ops: The Line.
It's depressing, sometimes hard to swallow, and you may not honestly understand everything the first time you play it. However, it is likely to stick with you, and really delves into a sort of symbolic social message on shooters and war, and how the general public see's it. It's not very fun, but Spec-Ops is still an experience worth undertaking.

I HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who enjoys driving simulators, drives trucks for a living or just enjoys trucking as a whole. There are so many great features to this game and awesome upgrades from the original Euro Truck Simulator that it is awe inspiring. There are a couple cons, yes, but they are FAR outshadowed by the pros.
PROS:
GREAT truck selection. From Volvo to DAF, from MAN to Iveco, from Renault to SCANIA, you are completely covered.
All trucks are able to be customized in a plethora of ways
Driving is fun with your trucks performance affected by the weight of the load in realistic fashion i.e Engine working harder while going uphill, takes longer to gain momentum with a full load from dead stop etc
Graphics are nice and clean for trucks themselves as well as the loads you haul
Expansive map
Many many more
CONS:
Steering can get a bit clunky without a steering wheel. (I use keyboard and controller in varying degrees as I can't justify laying down close to $100 for a steering wheel to play a single game)
Game time can become a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when you try and figure out how far you can drive and how much you have to do before the day ends and your loan installment is taken from you
NPC driver AI can be a bit stupid at times
Towns are not very well fleshed out in places and highway driveby areas are rather plain and dull
All in all though, I highly recommend the game as it is a great way to unwind from your day while you wind up gears and truck on down the highway leaving all your problems behind like a lot lizard at the truck stop.

Wow, you guys are rather butthurt aren't you?
Asides the bugginess and broken mechanics, the game is how it should be.
It's raw, gritty and unforgiving; exactly how I'd expect a mass apocalypse to be. I don't want to be in a post-event world where I'd see people every other minute. It SHOULD be empty.

. I'm a survivalist. I don't shoot unless I absolutely have to, to
. I survive for weeks and weeks irl like this, until I get killed by a glitchy zombie... or falling off a roof rather stupidly, or eventually being killed by another player because of a stupid mistake I made.
Point I'm trying to make is, play this game as a 'survivalist', bring your friends or try to make new friends (yeah, it's possible), scavenge for that wasteland gold, avoid confrontations the best you can and if you can't, try to negotiate. If you get bored of it, then I think you enevitably answered the question of whether or not this game is for you.

Ok first let me tell you that this is one of the most fun(ny) and unique multiplayer games I've played in a long time. There are a lot of crazy and random things that can happen in this game and they can create some really tense and epic moments. Here is the problem I have with this game though:
It's broken. Let me tell you that I've invested in many Early Access, Alpha, and Beta titles on Steam and abroad. I can handle constant crashes, gamebreaking glitches, and just about anything you can throw at me as long as I can at least PLAY your game. However, this game is broken

Well, mostly multiplayer. Of course you have your standard Alpha game issues across the board. Your crashes, infinite loading screens, physics glitches (which are actually more funny than anything, even if they cause you to lose a match), and the works. Here was the final nail in the coffin that caused me to leave this game a negative review.
A friend and I, excited to play this extremely funny fighting game, hopped into a "party" together. I searched for a match. Most servers were either full or had 7 of 8 slots filled.
{- Problem #1: Not enough servers for players in the US.}
By chance, within a few minutes, a server in our area (I live in Georgia, she lives in Texas) with 6/8 players opened up. I quickly jumped on the opportunity to snatch it up for my friend and I. I got in! I search among the heads in the game and press the button that shows the name tags and she's nowhere to be found. "Did you get in?" I asked her. She said no. I quit and return to the lobby.
{- Problem #2: Buggy party and matchmaking systems}
I try several more times and one of 4 things happened
:
1. "Could not connect to server", despite the fact that there were already people on it.
2. One of our games crashes
3. We get to the loading screen, but it's one of those infinite loading screens (I had a few of these before I tried to play with her so I knew how to identify them).
4. The server somehow filled up while we were connecting.
{Problem #3: No private matches, or starting your own server lobbies through peer-to-peer that other people can join later.} <-- You can host your own server, but I was sure my wifi was not strong enough to host for this game, especially not the week I wrote this.
5. It was a bugged server for players in the US that offered no information about itself in the server browser. These are typically incredibly laggy and have bots on them for some reason.. I think. Note: I was making sure to disable unofficial servers each time I searched.
{- Problem #4: See #1 PLUS, Not enough WORKING servers for players in the US}
We spent the better part of an hour trying to find a game, and it never happened. If you have a brother or sister, or some friends and people with Xbox Controllers to screw around with in person, you can play it. However, as of now, you can forget about playing with your Steam friends. Even if you're just looking at it to mostly play Local multiplayer, don't buy the game. Not yet. The developers seem to be pretty active, updating the game regularly and quickly when severe issues make themselves present. Get it when it's stable enough to play, or at release. Let us early adopters handle this bad boy for now and take all the anger and frustration for you.
EDIT: I tried this again later with a friend I met in the game who added me randomly but the whole time, my hopes were low. That time, we got into a server but of course it was laggy and the action would freeze and resume every second like clockwork. We left that server because the experience was terrible, and were never able to find another server since. What's ironic is that maybe 10 - 15 minutes after the guy added me, my game crashed. My first thought was "Welp, that guy was cool, too bad I'll never be able to play with him again!", then I chuckled to myself the way a hyper-masculine dad would who's tried for all his son's life to get his son into sports, only for the son to tell him he's gay and wants to sing for a living.
To the developers, if you're reading this: Please, PLEASE prioritize fixing the almost unplayable online multiplayer over all other things for the time being. We can't playtest the game if we can't
the game.
Don't make the same mistake I did by seeing these issues all over the reviews section and believing they won't happen to you. They will. Just wait until the multiplayer reaches an acceptable level of stability. When that happens, I will absolutely change my review, because if it weren't for those issues, I would completely recommend this game.

I'm gonna be honest, Life is Strange: Before the Storm is even better than the first Life is Strange because there CLEARLY are improvements over the first game, from a technical side to a story-telling one.
Since the game was being developed by a completely different team from the first one I admit I had set really low expectations, as I expected it to be an attempt at milking the game by the publisher, while providing a lame story with lame interactions in the hopes that people would buy another game simply because the Life is Strange brand.
And boy was I wrong.
The story itself is fantastic, the characters are well-designed and the dialogues are brilliant! Character animations also greatly improved so did the lip-syncing!
As opposed to the first game, the developers spicied things up a little: there's no more time rewind, so you better do good choices, and there's the Backtalk mechanic that allows you to win conversations by finding the right "roast" to say at the right moment, in a limited amount of time.
I admit, I only don't like the fact that Chloe's original VA isn't in the game, but that was due to a SAG-AFTRA strike (which ended just recently). I also found the start of the game's dialogues really, really awkard, but that might just be a personal opinion.
Aside from all of that, the game, still, is perfect.
The developers still keep amazing me because they paid attention to so many small details and references to the first game. This wasn't an attempt at milking the franchise at all, this is pure gold. They also understood they needed more "fanservice", such as the option to make two characters fall in love or not.
You should completely get it, even at full price with all the premium stuff like Mixtape Mode etc. because the game is seriously worth it. I pre-ordered it at full price because I admit I was hyped as a huge Life is Strange fanfag.
Thank you, Deck9.

The story to this game is pretty simple, but manages to still be interesting; particularly the lore found in some caves a little ways into the game. I found its music to be simply fantastic, and the absolute best thing in the game for me; especially the music to any boss battles. Some of the characters did have a bit of charm to them and I smiled a few times here and there while playing. The graphics, though simplistic, got the job done and gave the game a unique look. Some people might complain about graphics, but I found them to get the job done just fine here.
However, the gameplay itself - e.g. actually playing - was the most unenjoyable part of the game for me. You can either kill everything, kill a few things, or kill nothing. I went with the very latter, because I had heard from multiple people that it is far easier than killing everything,  and that it's more rewarding. Not only that, but the characters all seem to be rather friendly even if they don't seem to be at first, so sparing them seems like the right thing to do. You walk about, solving simple puzzles and either fighting or choosing non-combat "actions" like petting or laughing in combat to get the monster to not want to fight any more, then spare them. Healing items make boss fights less difficult, but I still found them incredibly challenging.
That brings me to my main source of dissatisfaction with the game. The rest of the gameplay was just okay to me, so when the battles ended with me on a gameover screen time and time again, those occasional smiles the game gave me were vastly outweighed by scowls and myself exclaiming obscenities while filled with rage. There is no difficulty setting I can lower, and the game's bullet hell core means skill and talent will make one player adore the game, and another despise it.
I am not, nor do I claim to be, any good at this or most kinds of games, but I do enjoy playing them and finding my own ways through them. However, if you are as bad as I am at bullet hell style, then healing items, memorization of attack order, and trying your best simply won't do. You may never be able to "git gud" enough, and no clever means exists of circumventing dealing with the bullet hell.
I hear the game's community is supposed to be the bane of the universe, though I haven't experienced it yet myself. By posting this negative review, however, I do anticipate witnessing it firsthand, though. I recommend games I enjoyed my time with, and the overwhelming amount of my time with this game was spent finding it simply "okay" or seething with anger, and the latter leaves me unable to like or recommend such a game.

TL:DR at the bottom.
First of all: Don't let the overwhelmingly positive rating fool you. I give you my word, it's definitely NOT that good. Especially at the full price. Spend your money elsewhere.
That said, I think the main reason this game got the overwhelmingly positive rating is because of the lack of proper car combat games. Fair enough, it's a proper car combat game. But that's IT. That's the only throphy this game deserves.
Here comes a whole mountain of cons:
- - - It's not Mad Max. No, sir. If you watched the movies, you will remember that fuel was the sole precious thing on the face of earth. And water. And the huge nothingness of the post apocalyptic desert.
Well, in this game. fuel is EVERYWHERE. WTF? You never ever, ever run out of gas. Which is ridiculous for a Mad Max game. Seriously developers what the ♥♥♥♥? What kind of Mad Max universe is this? Why is fuel and water everywhere? Might as well put up a ♥♥♥♥ing Walmart in the middle of the desert so we can more comfortably shop and restock our homes. - - -
- Need fuel? EVERYWHERE.
- Low on water? Oh that's not a problem at all. Just refill at one of the three strongholds or one of the thousand loot camps lying around.
- Health low? Fast travel to a stronghold or drink water. Or eat♥♥♥♥♥♥ which is everywhere.
- OK let's say you need to upgrade your car. You need scrap to upgrade everything. So where do I get scrap? WELL SCRAP IS EVERYWHERE, SO NOT A PROBLEM.
- Strongholds: Just step into a stronghold to refuel your car, refill your canteen, ammo belt, your cars rockets, and fill up your health bar. Uh, what is the point of all that then?
- Anyway moving on. The story SUCKS. Honestly who wrote this piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ They were either screenwriting students fresh out of college, or they were high on marjuana. Let me summerize the story for you without major spoilers.
- Max is attacked and loses his car.
- Starts making friends.
- Do a couple of errands for those friends.
- Friends say there is a race going on in Gastown, with a prize V8 engine. (Who the ♥♥♥♥ gives away a V8 engine in a car-founded post apocalypse world is beyond me)
- Max wants the V8. So he joins the race.
- Max wins race, gets the V8.
- Oh no, one of his friends is captured.
- Max chases the evil doer.
- Max kills the evil doer.
- End credits.
- What the ♥♥♥♥?
I expected much, much, MUCH more from this game. Even as I realized that the game's resource management is bullcrap, I still had faith in the main story. But that sucked too.
Now onto the good stuff:
+ Spectacular explosions and car combat mechanics
+ Multiple ways to hurt a vehicle
+ The car handling is not absolute arcade. It's kind of a mixture of sim and arcade. Would have been better to have manual transmission with sim-like handling, but hey, they're trying to appeal to the majority of players so, players like me have to sit in the dark.
+ Beautiful ocean floor wasteland.
+ Consistent stuff with Mad Max films here and there.
+ Collectibles (if that's your thing)
+ Minor vehicle modding
TL:DR
Cons:
- Abundantly rich resources make no sense in a Mad Max universe
- Story sucks and is ridiculously short
- Absolutely terrible voice acting, especially on Max
Pros:
+ Good graphics
+ Spectacular explosions and car combat mechanics
+ Two creepy underground missions were nice (out of 15 in total)
+ Beautiful wasteland to explore
+ Consistent stuff with Mad Max films here and there. ("Two men enter one man leaves" was a nice touch)
+ Collectibles
+ Minor vehicle modding
Verdict: Aiming at profits require you to appeal for the most people. Well, most people love Hollywood films and action games with little skill required. So that's exactly what this game is. A very bad repetition of the last Mad Max movie. I expected a lot more, but this is what we have so it's gonna have to make do. Maybe the next installment will be better. All in all, it deserves a thumbs up. But only buy on sale.

A lot if not the majority of the base game will include you walking, crawling and stalking your choice of game, whether that be Roe Deer, Wild Boar or any of the other animals in the wild. You have the ability to track your target animals and get information off of their traveling, eating, sleeping and other habits, also if you have shot, but not killed an animal you can find blood splatters that will tell you if they are vitally wounded or not making it more interesting to track down your target. Running is in the game, but often it is best not to use if you want to avoid alerting and scaring away potential animals. Though it is useful especially if you are just exploring new terrains. The stealth aspect of the game works well and will force you to be patient in order to successfully get a kill. There are useful tools you can use including scents to cover your natural human smell as-well as animals 'calls' to attract whichever animal you are hunting. There is a 'story' mode in single player where you will be asked to do tasks including take pictures of animals as-well as just shooting animals (sometimes with a certain gun) in particular locations around the map. You can disable these story mode messages in the options which is a nice feature if you just want to freeroam. Early on you will want to find an outpost so you can resupply and have a place to fast travel to as this is very important. the outposts can be found from just exploring and often are easier found if you find a lookout post to get a layout of the land. At the beginning of the game you will have only one rifle some deer attracting devices with not much other weapons/gear and you will have to level up to get more options for guns and equipment. There is a perk system aswell as a skill tree you can level up for whatever you play-style is. There are two maps to choose from and both have different animals to choose from to hunt. As-well, there is a multiplayer mode with up to 8 players that is accessible after you get your first outpost in single player. While this mode is fun, it is inconvenienced by the fact the host of the server will be free to fast travel to whichever outposts they have traveled to in single player so long that they have discovered the outposts. The problem is that if any other players join the host and don't have certain outposts unlocked in their singleplayer that the host has unlocked in their game, the nonhost player will be unable to fast traveled and be forced to walk to whichever outpost the host fast traveled to. This problem is remedied by either just walking to all outposts in your single player world before considering playing multiplayer which will take considerably long considering the maps are rather large. Alternatively you could purchase the ATV dlc, though this feature feels like it should be included in the base game rather than a premium item that is only accessible through a micro-transaction.

The game was made using the Apex Avalanche Open World Engine and it looks great regardless of which graphics settings you use. While using higher graphics settings all of the vegetation is thick and bustling and the scenery truly pops and gives a great sense of immersion in the game world. If you are on a lower end machine though, you can turn down a great amount of the post-processing effects as well as vegetation and shadows and still be left with a very visually pleasing game. What I really appreciate in their graphics setting menu is that they tell you what level of a performance impact all the settings do for you so you can gauge what type of performance you would gain from turning down some settings.
The audio is where this game shines a great deal. The sounds you will experience are so immersive. Every little leaf, twig and rock on the ground will give a satisfying sense of you being on said item. The weather as-well sounds are very impressive, whether it be a little wind or a horrendous thunder storm. All the sounds in this game sound perfect. When in multiplayer as-well if your hunter friends are firing at game far from your location you can hear the booming echoes of their shots echoing through the terrain. All animals have their own unique voices and if you are lucky enough to get close enough to listen to them you will truly appreciate the clarity in the animals voices. The only thing you may get sick of relatively quickly is the in-game music. While after initially hearing the beautiful songs you will indefinitely appreciate how smooth and well fit they are in this game. You will soon hear them repeat very frequently and will likely just disable them as they do become quite a distraction the more deep you get into the game.
You're a hunter who has free roam to two reserves including Layton Lake District, a map modeled on the North American Pacific Northwest, and Hirschfelden, a recreation of a European farmland type area. Your main objective is focused around tracking and killing animals in order to gain more points to get better gear to hunt with.

While there are some problems such as not including the atv with the base game and it being a micro-transaction, aswell as some minor nuisances in multiplayer such as the fast travel problem and some of the animals in multiplayer servers seemingly having an infinite amount of health which really takes you out of the game. I do believe this game is great especially for the patient minded players in mind. I do believe if you have or even have not hunted in real life you will find this game to be a great attempt to capture the essence of that experience. I recommend this if you don't mind tracking animals for long periods of time, or luring game to you in hopes of getting that perfect shot. If you are looking for something faster paced and action oriented then this game likely is not for you.

This is a great one! Granted, gameplay itself can get a bit boring at some points, given the large amount of equal looking enemies and always the same goal to get to a certain place with guns blazing. This is not a realistic military shooter (but neither are COD and MoH), but more like an almost casual feeling action game. The most specular feature of this game is its story. Located in a fascinating and original setting, this game offers a profound plot almost without logical breaks. The game has often been called the Apocalypse Now of gaming. Taking the psychedelic guitar soundtrack and the audio logs of the crazy commander into account, this is a resemblance, the team certainly aimed at and perhaps they even did it a bit too much. But then again, can there be too much of Apocalypse Now? If your answer is no, you should definitely give this game a try!

TL:DR at the bottom.
First of all: Don't let the overwhelmingly positive rating fool you. I give you my word, it's definitely NOT that good. Especially at the full price. Spend your money elsewhere.
That said, I think the main reason this game got the overwhelmingly positive rating is because of the lack of proper car combat games. Fair enough, it's a proper car combat game. But that's IT. That's the only throphy this game deserves.
Here comes a whole mountain of cons:
- - - It's not Mad Max. No, sir. If you watched the movies, you will remember that fuel was the sole precious thing on the face of earth. And water. And the huge nothingness of the post apocalyptic desert.
Well, in this game. fuel is EVERYWHERE. WTF? You never ever, ever run out of gas. Which is ridiculous for a Mad Max game. Seriously developers what the ♥♥♥♥? What kind of Mad Max universe is this? Why is fuel and water everywhere? Might as well put up a ♥♥♥♥ing Walmart in the middle of the desert so we can more comfortably shop and restock our homes. - - -
- Need fuel? EVERYWHERE.
- Low on water? Oh that's not a problem at all. Just refill at one of the three strongholds or one of the thousand loot camps lying around.
- Health low? Fast travel to a stronghold or drink water. Or eat♥♥♥♥♥♥ which is everywhere.
- OK let's say you need to upgrade your car. You need scrap to upgrade everything. So where do I get scrap? WELL SCRAP IS EVERYWHERE, SO NOT A PROBLEM.
- Strongholds: Just step into a stronghold to refuel your car, refill your canteen, ammo belt, your cars rockets, and fill up your health bar. Uh, what is the point of all that then?
- Anyway moving on. The story SUCKS. Honestly who wrote this piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ They were either screenwriting students fresh out of college, or they were high on marjuana. Let me summerize the story for you without major spoilers.
- Max is attacked and loses his car.
- Starts making friends.
- Do a couple of errands for those friends.
- Friends say there is a race going on in Gastown, with a prize V8 engine. (Who the ♥♥♥♥ gives away a V8 engine in a car-founded post apocalypse world is beyond me)
- Max wants the V8. So he joins the race.
- Max wins race, gets the V8.
- Oh no, one of his friends is captured.
- Max chases the evil doer.
- Max kills the evil doer.
- End credits.
- What the ♥♥♥♥?
I expected much, much, MUCH more from this game. Even as I realized that the game's resource management is bullcrap, I still had faith in the main story. But that sucked too.
Now onto the good stuff:
+ Spectacular explosions and car combat mechanics
+ Multiple ways to hurt a vehicle
+ The car handling is not absolute arcade. It's kind of a mixture of sim and arcade. Would have been better to have manual transmission with sim-like handling, but hey, they're trying to appeal to the majority of players so, players like me have to sit in the dark.
+ Beautiful ocean floor wasteland.
+ Consistent stuff with Mad Max films here and there.
+ Collectibles (if that's your thing)
+ Minor vehicle modding
TL:DR
Cons:
- Abundantly rich resources make no sense in a Mad Max universe
- Story sucks and is ridiculously short
- Absolutely terrible voice acting, especially on Max
Pros:
+ Good graphics
+ Spectacular explosions and car combat mechanics
+ Two creepy underground missions were nice (out of 15 in total)
+ Beautiful wasteland to explore
+ Consistent stuff with Mad Max films here and there. ("Two men enter one man leaves" was a nice touch)
+ Collectibles
+ Minor vehicle modding
Verdict: Aiming at profits require you to appeal for the most people. Well, most people love Hollywood films and action games with little skill required. So that's exactly what this game is. A very bad repetition of the last Mad Max movie. I expected a lot more, but this is what we have so it's gonna have to make do. Maybe the next installment will be better. All in all, it deserves a thumbs up. But only buy on sale.

I played this game the first time ever when I pirated it. I pirate a lot of games. I've pirated every game I've ever played, and the most important thing to take from this is I only purchase games on Steam that I've aleady pirated and love, so that I can support the developers. The lone exception is when I purchase a game bundle for like $4, and it's usually because one of the games was one I pirated and loved.
Rogue Legacy is not just one of those games, it's the defining example. There are only three other games I've loved as much, the first being Super Metroid, the second being Deus Ex (Original), and the third being LoZOoT. My Steam counter right now only shows 10 hours of playtime, but before I bought this game, I pirated it. And I played it for maybe a hundred hours in total. I can't get over it, it's just so damn great!
First off, the platforming is insane. You 1-3 shot all enemies except Uber enemies, Mini-Bosses, and Main Bosses. On the contrast though, unless you're playing a tank class, they also 1-5 shot you! You can't mess around, they will eat you whole in the beginning! But as you play, you get coins, and when you die, you spend those coins in a massive system that extends its way into infinite New Game+ modes. For example, you can upgrade your HP 75 times! There are like, I don't know exactly... probably 12 classes, plus 12 upgraded forms of those classes, plus 30 stat boosts that can all be upgraded 75 times as well.
The upgrading really feels intuitive and like your choices mean something. Do you keep dying a lot? Buy more health and play as a Barbarian King/Queen! Use your Fus Do Rah (It's spelled that way) to knock projectiles away! Do you wish you could use Time Stop for longer periods? Play as an Archmage and use your huge MP pool to freeze time and whale on bosses!
The platforming is perfect too. It's exactly like what I always wanted in a GOOD MMX1-3 sequel. In fact, the platforming is even better than Megaman. It's better than even Metroid, because every jump feels incredibly responsive thanks to pixel-precision movement. You can slightly tap left or right to move a pixel or two over. It feels RIGHT.
If this game is on any kind of sale, get it. If it's not, get it anyway. Support these developers, and join in the throng of people begging for a fully realized sequel.

If you like metroidvania style games then this is your game.
Modern roguelike platforming from the last milenium, you pick one of three random combinations of class, genetic problems, and spells and head into the castle/dungeon. Each time you die your progeny takes over with whatever gear you've collected. Whenever you start a new character you can also use the money your last generation collected to buildup your own household, by improving on classes and things that provide stat bonuses. You can also build new equipment/runes from plans that were previously found. The castle becomes randomized on each playthrough unless you are willing to accept a penalty of only keeping half the cash you pass on. As you play you will find new spells, collect blueprints for new gear, and beat bosses in different parts of the castle that pave the way for you to complete the game.
I beat the game on the DRM-free version, but the steam version seems to have all the same things, plus all the steam specific stuff (achievments, cards, etc).

Original review:
So it is a mixed bag. If you insist on buying games that are relatively bugfree, skip this one. While it usually runs smoothly in SP, MP is rather buggy as of today. Our co-op sessions are regularly cut short by bugs.
If you don't feel like supporting somewhat shady DLC schemes, you should skip it too, I guess. The tent DLC feels like something that "should" have been in the base game.
Shooting in this game is decent. Something though is clearly wrong with how bullets interact with the animals. Stationary animals are fine, but animals in (rapid) movement seem to have issues with the hitbox not aligning correctly with the 3D model. Shots NEVER penetrate the target for some reason, and therefore all weapons feel strangely underpowered.
Talents and perks are full of useless stuff. A complete overhaul of both talents and perks would do the game good.
Progression isn't deep at all, and so you don't unlock everything too quickly they just amped up the required XP to unlock things. Not a fan.
Cons aside, this game is pure eye candy. I don't think I have ever seen landscapes more gorgeous than  in this game. The sound design is amazing too. This is easily the most immersive game world I have ever seen.
So, some parts of the game feel like they were done by unwilling interns and others are in a league of their own. Overall though, this is a clear DAUMEN HOCH.

I got this game on my other account in 2013. This was the first computer game that I played.. erm too much on. My friends were all confused on how I could play this game so much, I mean I could barely explain it. When I first started playing, it was on some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Mac at like 25 fps. This game is always a love hate relationship, as angry as I can get at this game, the good times have always been worth it. That feeling of scrapping by a win in pvp, getting some sick gear, and generally destroying is unmatched in rust. I have not played any other game that gives such a satisfaction as getting that head crunch is. As far as rust has come when it comes to being a better game now, then when I used to play it a lot more. The game is better now in almost every single aspect, but I still wish I could go back to the early days when the game was much different. The original map was amazing, everyone being that same naked bald man was just silly, but in a good way. Guns were not random, they shot where you aimed, and it was very hard to be good with gunplay, but it was amazing. The feeling of pulling a pipe out of your♥♥♥♥♥and killing a full kev was absolutely amazing, I will always love this game. The community has just about always been the same. Brutal, hard learning curve, and unforgiving. Any moment your base, everything you've worked on for days, can be taken away from you, and you can do the same to others. One controversial thing about rust now, is the component system over blueprints. Blueprints were random, but in those rad town crates you could actually get guns and gear which was great, now you can't. Components are overall better, but I really do not like the fact that there is no gear that can be looted in rad towns. Another complaint about rad towns now is that most of them are useless, like power plant for example. The only good places to loot curently are dome, and airfield, most radtowns have almost no places to get good crates and pvp. These rad towns should definetly get a buff. In old Rust, clans didn't rule servers as much, there were more solo players and very small groups. Sometimes new rust can feel much more like a grind. Now one of the biggest things I have to say about new rust is the amount of different buildings you can make, the pure customization and freedom. People can be so creative with base building now, over simple tall, square houses like in Legacy. One problem with that however, is it can make raiding larger bases almost impossible because of how much explosive would be needed. Overall, the new Rust is a MUCH better game, but Legacy has such a special part in my heart. Oh and uhm... buy this game, best 15 dollars at the time I ever spent, right next to csgo.

Prison Architect is a time eater that hasn't captured and enraptured me since the first time I played SimCity 4, and there're a lot of reasons why; it's an open ended building sim game that has a billion goals to choose from even if it's just "I want a prison where all the solitary confinement cells are 1x1 units and no cell will have lights" or "My staff will have the bare basics while my prisoners are treated like kings".
It's a little clunky to get into so I'd recommend watching some Let's Plays to get a bit of an idea of the controls and the UI layout, but most likely you'll be playing by experience, scrapping prisons and building newer, better ones as you learn and play.
All this said, however, the game is in Alpha build, so sometimes things can not go the way you want them to, for example all my prisoners wanting to go to a canteen that wasn't functional yet, was still technically outside, but because they wanted to go to it, the guards let them right out, boom, empty prison and $1k expenditure every day. However
this game is in Alpha, it's unclear whether this is my fault or something not yet given full functionality, it's a work in progress, it'll have a million bugs.
For an Alpha game, Prison Architect looks ready for the market already, I was expecting really heavy whiteboxing and spontaneous crashes but this game runs smooth as a baby's bum (until it goes "STOP, I'm autosaving" then carries on), and as a good dev should, Introversion have kindly told you when things aren't finished in the detail of any object or function.
I spent less than £7 on this game, but having played it, I would easily pay the £19.99 full price.

I consider myself someone who enjoys the FPS and cover based combat genre but I'm not exactly in it for the competitive multiplayer, the single player stories tend to be far more compelling for me, even though more often than not they're not stellar.  But this game is amazing in it's horror and the deeper inflection of the psyche of soldiers.  The terrible things that they see and do, and how it affects them long term.  It's a horrible, sickening story, but in the most amazing ways.  It is deeper and far more intelligent than any shooter game I have played.  The controls are not as solid as Gears of War or CoD, but it is worth it in the experience that it provides.  Highly recommended by anyone, especially FPS fans.  Fair warning, nothing you've seen in the CoD franchise is nearly as morbid and heart wrenching.

Between the desk top launcher and the steam version, I have logged over 2000 hours on TheHunter Classic. Due to my love of that game a friend bought me a copy of COTW in a steam sale since they thought it would be a game i would love.
WRONG... I am sorely dissapointed in COTW and the six hours I have spent playing it would have been better spent doing some other more enjoyable activity like getting a root canal or stabbing myself in the face with a fork.
I will do my best to list the pros and cons of the game in hopes that perhaps it may be possible to explain my bland experiance...
PROs:
Good graphics (ran smooth as butter on ultra settings on my GTX970M)
Good animal models (though see below for issues with them)
Plausable sound and scent effects on animals
large sandbox / open world maps
cons:
'Doc' the game warden never shuts up
animals seem to come in size tiers and any animals of the same species and size tier are identical 3D models and skins
General lack of clarity on the controls and inventory  (even with tutorials)
moving at a crouch is the speed of a snail on qualuuds this means either choose to walk erect and scare off everything or move crouched and never get anywhere.
avatar figets constantly (inspecting rifle, polishing PDA with sleeve etc.)The pillars of hunting are silence, patience and stillness, this figeting breaks immersion.
Items like tents and blinds must be bought as DLC
Animals regularly become passive and simply stand around as you walk up and can literally push them around.
point blank shots are the same as long range shots for damage, kinetic dump etc.
damage model makes the .243 woefully weak and unrealistic (think nerf darts)
small number of species
there is more but I don't want this to start sounding like a hate rant
over all I think they have something that could be a heck of a game but in its current state this game is mostly flash and little  substance. I am sure the stellar experiance I have had with THC has caused the shortcomings of COTW to seem far more glaring to me so perhaps I am biased or had unrealistic expectations.

The story to this game is pretty simple, but manages to still be interesting; particularly the lore found in some caves a little ways into the game. I found its music to be simply fantastic, and the absolute best thing in the game for me; especially the music to any boss battles. Some of the characters did have a bit of charm to them and I smiled a few times here and there while playing. The graphics, though simplistic, got the job done and gave the game a unique look. Some people might complain about graphics, but I found them to get the job done just fine here.
However, the gameplay itself - e.g. actually playing - was the most unenjoyable part of the game for me. You can either kill everything, kill a few things, or kill nothing. I went with the very latter, because I had heard from multiple people that it is far easier than killing everything,  and that it's more rewarding. Not only that, but the characters all seem to be rather friendly even if they don't seem to be at first, so sparing them seems like the right thing to do. You walk about, solving simple puzzles and either fighting or choosing non-combat "actions" like petting or laughing in combat to get the monster to not want to fight any more, then spare them. Healing items make boss fights less difficult, but I still found them incredibly challenging.
That brings me to my main source of dissatisfaction with the game. The rest of the gameplay was just okay to me, so when the battles ended with me on a gameover screen time and time again, those occasional smiles the game gave me were vastly outweighed by scowls and myself exclaiming obscenities while filled with rage. There is no difficulty setting I can lower, and the game's bullet hell core means skill and talent will make one player adore the game, and another despise it.
I am not, nor do I claim to be, any good at this or most kinds of games, but I do enjoy playing them and finding my own ways through them. However, if you are as bad as I am at bullet hell style, then healing items, memorization of attack order, and trying your best simply won't do. You may never be able to "git gud" enough, and no clever means exists of circumventing dealing with the bullet hell.
I hear the game's community is supposed to be the bane of the universe, though I haven't experienced it yet myself. By posting this negative review, however, I do anticipate witnessing it firsthand, though. I recommend games I enjoyed my time with, and the overwhelming amount of my time with this game was spent finding it simply "okay" or seething with anger, and the latter leaves me unable to like or recommend such a game.

I picked this game up while it was on sale a few weeks ago.  The game is a real-time light roguelike with retro-style graphics and music where the goal is your basic dungeon crawling setup of complete the branches and bosses of the dungeon, then fight the primary antagonist.

The twist of the game is that you start off playing as a pretty generic character on you first attempt until said characted dies, then play as one of the character's three children for your next attempt, then one of that new character's children, blah blah blah, etc, etc.  The complexity and uniqueness(not sure if that's a word) of the game comes from the various genetic traits that may be inherent in the children you pick.  Traits, such as color blindness, ADHD, gigantism, are modeled off their real-life counterparts and give your characters various benifits or drawbacks, but often have a mix of both advantage and disadvantage.  This feature causes you to very quickly develop an adaptable playstyle as you progress through the game, learning what traits are beneficial in what situations.

I enjoyed the variety and replayability that this feature provided and felt like it was one of the more original ideas I've ever come across in a roguelike.  I definitely enjoyed playing this game and will probably return to start a new legacy sooner than later.

First of all whoever coined the term "Roguelike" should be shot.
That aside, Rogue Legacy is a short 2d (I refuse to say roguelike) platformer with some twists. As probably ever other review tells you, your hero changes to your next heir when you die and the heir has the potential to be born with some positive or negative traits. You level by dying which is a strange system in itself. The castle randomly changes with every heir unless you choose to pay a fee to save your previous layout with the "Architect." Each heir retains stat and armor upgrades your previous heirs had. As your characters get stronger, so do the mobs.
Pros:
- Harder than most platformers. The difficulty level was perfect for me, not rage inducing, but hard enough to be of a challenge.
- Castle layout changes and different challenges spawning kept the maps interesting.
- Well planned bosses, except the last boss was kind of easy...
- Addictive
Cons:
- If you're used to old school platformer controls, this feels nothing like them. Slow attacking forces you to play very differently.
- Mage classes don't really feel like mage classes.
- Can't hold the d-pad down + attack like in Adventures of Link. Downward attack doesn't hold. Lasts for only a split second.
- Game balance could use some work as sometimes the scaling just felt off.

I was loving everything about this game, and I was ready to rave about it and suggest it to everyone.
Then I hit the apparently well known kitchen/cook bug...
My cooks, no matter WHAT I do on certain prisons absolutley refuse to cook anything. It doesn't sound like a big deal, but it completley dismantles and breaks your game.
There isn't any point of building these prisons when a simple glitch like this makes it useless. Prisoners riot, nothing gets done, and I have tried everything to fix it. I've dezoned, rezoned, put equipment before and after zoning, switched rooms, switched back, rezoned and dezoned the canteen, fired the cooks and hired them back several times, changed my delivery place as many times as I can think, dumped ALL the ingredients and tried to get them back, changed the food quality up and down several times, adjusted the regime to try to make it work. I even went in the safe file to see if food was enabled and it is.
It's sad that such a stupid glitch can make a great game completly worthless but it does. No one is going to want to invest hours into this game to get derailed by this unfixable bug.
The only other minor issues I have had were easy to work around, but this is truly a game breaking bug.
At the moment, I am going to have to give this a negative review, despite wanting to praise this game. The developers seriously need to look at the food and food creation mechanics and do something about this.
If you can pick this game up on sale for under 6 dollars, I would say go ahead, but do NOT pay full price.

Whilst not overly original and a bit on the easy side, Mad Max is a highly fun romp with smooth mechanics and enjoyable gameplay. Fans of modern open world games will feel right at home in the game, and though the driving mechanics feel a bit clumsier than in, say, newer GTA's, driving around and engaging in car battles is fun. Close combat, of which there is a bit more than is fitting for the franchise, is in the typical Batham Arkham-games vein, and works well but quickly becomes far too easy once you learn the ropes.
Graphically the game is nice, with the post-apocalyptic desert looking eye-pleasing but still unwelcoming, and details such as maggots crawling in corpses (you can eat the maggots!), dissected bodies dangling as trophies, houses built of debris and stuff like that make the setting right. However, much of the setting is just gloss and the grim reality of the Mad Max world doesn't translate into gameplay mechanics; there's fuel aplenty, water is easy to find, there's no shortage of ammunition, and so on.
I wouldn't say Mad Max is a _great_ game, but it's still very much worth playing as long as you don't expect a groundbreaking entry into the overpopulated genre of open world action games.

Really not sure about this Game... It HAD potential, but I think a lot of it was missed. For me, the Game had more Negative aspects to it. I'd only recommend this during a Sale, and only recommended for someone who wants a Game to mess around in.
The Story itself is extremely short with just 15 Missions which take no time at all to complete. Not only is the Story short, but it just bored me and not once did I really even care for it. It just felt like an empty shell. The only thing that made this Game have some length was the fact you have to complete tasks to unlock Story Missions. Complete so and so amount of Wasteland Missions, complete so and so amount of Stronghold Projects.
None of the Characters were interesting, and although the Voice acting was decent, the cut scenes were just short, and quick to the point with no context.
Surely the Gameplay would make up for it though. Unfortunately the Gameplay is hindered with the horrible Auto Camera [slow Manual Camera], and slow response on the Controls which felt like it had a slight lag after pushing in a direction.
The Game has the usual Assassins Creed style combat, punch punch, counter when you see the Marker, but unfortunately, the Game doesn't allow you to turn the Counter Markers off, which just makes the combat so easy and boring after awhile. Infact, NOTHING in the Game was a challenge... Apart from fighting the Camera and Controls.
The Game has 9 Boss Fights in total, 3 with Scrotus [the Main boss] and 6 "Mini" Boss Fights. However 4 of these Bosses is someone wielding a large Mace, ALL with the same animations, and same method to defeat [wait for him to charge, roll, start punching]. The remaining 2 are duel wielding daggers, again, same animations, same method to defeat [roll, counter when you can]. It is just absolutely lazy development.
Come across a door you need an explosion for? No worries, just look 5 meters away and there will be a well placed Fuel can for you... Speaking of Fuel cans, WHY does the Game even have Fuel for the Car? The first and ONLY time I Fueled my car was at the start in the Tutorial, after that you will never really need to. I only completed my Project for auto Refueling in Jeets Stronghold [the first one which I never went to afterwards], and none of the others.
Being an Open World Game though, there would be tons of things to do right? Here is what you can do;
- Death Runs [Racing]
- Scavenger Locations [You will encounter a max of around 3 enemies, and 2 pieces of Loot].
- Minefield [Use your Dog to locate a few Mines].
- Camps [Destroy either Transfer Pumps, or Oil Tanks to complete].
- Scarecrows [Destroy them to lower Threat in the Region. Takes a max of 10 seconds to do].
- Stronghold Projects [Complete Projects for Strongholds to give free Ammo ect. You will come across these in Camps and Scavenger Locations].
This is around 90% of the Game. For an Open World, it just isn't much variety. The only thing that was half decent to do were the Camps, but this was countered with the simplistic Combat, and horrible Camera.
A couple things I enjoyed were Harpooning people from my Car. As fun as this was, after your Harpoon hits, your Camera will follow your Target, even after you correct it. This will usually end with you Driving into a Wall beacuse you can't see where your going.
The last 2 Missions were just great. It's the only time through the entire Game, that I felt something for the Story. The dialog, and the Gameplay were fantastic, and it really is a shame that the rest of Game was not at that level.

After playing the game, I can't say that I understand the praise it gets.
The good:
-Music was solid (although the same can be said for a lot of indie games these days)
-Succeeds at being funny
-Lots of meaningful choices that affect future events in a natural and believable way
-Every battle/encounter feels different
The meh:
-Visual design is somewhat underwhelming compared to some of the truly inspired 2D RPG indie games that have come out in the last decade
-You can't get a "good" ending unless you play the game all over again. In my first playthrough (with no knowledge of how the endings work) I went almost purely pacifist, bar sparing a few guys and accidentally killing a weak monster at the beginning. To be told that I have to do it all over again just to have a decent ending is pretty frustrating. Luckily there's enough unique elements in the pure pacifist route to keep things fresh.
The bad:
-Bullet. Hell. When it comes to bullet hell, there is a *very* fine line between fun and frustrating. Undertale manages to stay on the fun side most of the time, but the boss battles require many attempts. Some would argue that that's to be expected of a boss battle; personally, I'm here to experience a story, not to spend half an hour memorising movement patterns.
-Worldbuilding is weak. A "library" with barely 3 lines of useful information. A few vague references towards monsters who want to see the stars. A couple of mystical tablets on the walls that explain the history of the Underground. It's so weak that one wonders if the tablets are just propaganda/myth (a genuine possibility when you consider that the library was terribly misinformed about the human world). We're told that the capital is overcrowded, and that society is in decline, but we're never actually *shown* these things.
-Shallow characters. The main characters get maybe 100 lines of dialogue, and half of that is comedy. Most of them show up for their alloted role in the plot, and then essentially disappear until the ending. One cannot reasonably expect much depth here, and yet people are claiming to relate deeply to these characters? Maybe I've just been reading too much Tumblr.
Undertale isn't a bad game, but I fail to see what it brings to the table over, say, a well-written visual novel. I felt no particular emotional impact. Honestly I'd rather just listen to the soundtrack by itself.

First of all whoever coined the term "Roguelike" should be shot.
That aside, Rogue Legacy is a short 2d (I refuse to say roguelike) platformer with some twists. As probably ever other review tells you, your hero changes to your next heir when you die and the heir has the potential to be born with some positive or negative traits. You level by dying which is a strange system in itself. The castle randomly changes with every heir unless you choose to pay a fee to save your previous layout with the "Architect." Each heir retains stat and armor upgrades your previous heirs had. As your characters get stronger, so do the mobs.
Pros:
- Harder than most platformers. The difficulty level was perfect for me, not rage inducing, but hard enough to be of a challenge.
- Castle layout changes and different challenges spawning kept the maps interesting.
- Well planned bosses, except the last boss was kind of easy...
- Addictive
Cons:
- If you're used to old school platformer controls, this feels nothing like them. Slow attacking forces you to play very differently.
- Mage classes don't really feel like mage classes.
- Can't hold the d-pad down + attack like in Adventures of Link. Downward attack doesn't hold. Lasts for only a split second.
- Game balance could use some work as sometimes the scaling just felt off.

On the fence about this one. I LOVE the concept of it and it's base mechanics are fantastic:
- Castle layout is randomized, or can be locked down at a penalty.
- The heir system, and the various traits they can have.
- Upgrades and armor/rune selections allow for interesting playstyles.
- Graphics are simple but pleasant.
- Enemies/bosses usually have good variation.
When you're in the groove of things, it can be very enjoyable. But I have to acknowledge its downfalls...
Perhaps most notably, there seems to be a noticeable delay (~0.1/~0.2 seconds) between the time I hit a button, and when the corresponding action happens, which matters like crazy in crowded rooms. Which is worsened as a result of being hurt simply by contact with most enemies.
The game seems
considering what's happening on screen. I can run
at a steady 30 FPS, but I enter a room in Rogue Legacy with 10-20 enemies and suddenly I'm experiencing a lower framerate? Even with all other programs closed AND the shader effects reduced? Particularly noticeable with most of the post-effects, which sucks when that particular heir is the only one with the class that you want.
The use of money in Rogue Legacy is...deceiving. You quickly realize most/all of your leftover money will be taken from you. So, you feel inclined to use any money you can after death...but each upgrade purchase makes EVERY next upgrade cost more. Adding insult to injury, some of the classes you've spent good money on, are not balanced with the rest. And to make it even WORSE, you want to get each upgrade once to build up the manor and see the other upgrades, but meanwhile you're not only using your well-earned money on some upgrades that will only marginally help you, you just made every other useful upgrade more expensive. Oh, and there's no reset on the upgrades. Which would be fine, IF the global-incremental upgrade system was removed.
"Oh cool, extra health and mana. Wow these can go up to 75, I should put some points into them and then I'll still have enough to get some of those side upgrades..."
As if the game wasn't already difficult enough, most enemies hurt you simply by touching them, which is absolutely unnecessary, and reeks of lazy game design. I don't care if the game is trying to be 'retro', there's too many kinds of enemies for this to be an acceptable method of damage on top of their other attacks. It's completely fine if an enemy has something like spikes pointing at you, or if they're made of fire. But no, that's not the case most of the time and feels extremely disappointing considering they could have simply given the enemies more actual methods of attack.
There's a difference between challenging gameplay, and superfluous difficulty just for the sake of making the game
more challenging . If they made a sequel and some of these fundamentals were more forgiving, I'm sure I would thoroughly enjoy it.

I've been playing The Hunter series since 2009 when it came out... The original had some really nice animals, arguably better weapons but the paid subscriptions killed me off eventually.
This new COTW is great, I am an avid hunter and outdoorsman in my personal down time - this almost gives me a bit of an escape from reality at home with headphones on, slink around the hills for half an hour, hunt some deer / elk / moose / bears etc then close it down.
Like some people have said, the deer are unreasonably good listeners! They can hear you from 400km, which is brutal. There are a heap of animals around but you generally only catch a glimpse of them running off in the distance between some trees unless you're basically crawling everywhere.
The Quad Bike DLC is awesome, but has changed the game a lot. I like them to get around and go to all the lookouts / unlock all the outposts but other than that they make hunting a waste of time, everything nearby clears out. Tents are convenient, that's about all.
The firearms, are fairly crap... They're unfairly balanced, don't do realistic damage, you can go prone but still have offensively useless muzzle / sight picture control... The external and terminal ballistics of the ammunition are light on making you often wound and then be forced to track even female fallow deer for kilometers sometimes which is rubbish.
This game could REALLY DO WITH SOME more modern, practical rifles - eg a Bolt Action 300WinMag / 7mm Rem Mag / 6 or 6.5mm Creedmoor or 260Rem for the Elk and other deer. .300RUM / .338LM / SAUM etc for ELR hunting and maybe a couple of Semi Auto .223 / 300 Blackout for foxes / pigs etc... The hippies and european naturalists get their hooks into the weapons and get into a tiff which is frustrating, they don't want to add any reasonable firearms (listed above) because it doesn't fit their demographic back home, get over it. Add them in, if you don't want to use them then dont... For everyone else, they're another option.
In summary, I love this game but it's a bit one dimensional still. The damage should be increased proportionally, the firearms should be modernised to reflect the rest of the western world. Probably my favourite game.

Rogue Legacy has an interesting combination of elements, all of which I liked. Combat is simple but varied. Controls are shallow but tight. Aesthetic is retro but modest. Essentially a game of Castlevania dungeon crawling through procedurally generated levels with short-term single-life character abilities and long-term RPG upgrades that you achieve quicker the better you loot in each run. I liked it a lot, but interest waned when I neared the end of the unique abilities to unlock and noticed that to succeed further in areas where the monsters are multiple times harder I’d have to grind for passive upgrades for likely a long time, “nah, I’m good”. The novelty-drip ran dry, I had my fill and felt it was well worth the asking price and with even more content in the (sorta) end-game makes this an easy one to recommend.

In Rougue Legacy, you play as a family bloodline relentlessly attempting to infiltrate a castle (Or something like that). The platforming gameplay is fluid, the bosses are relentless, and each heir is unique to themselves.
Each and every time you die, you can choose to upgrade your manor, before taking the plunge as your new heir. The loot collected by your deceased predecessor will be used to upgrade all aspects of your future characters.
As stated by the trailer: not all hero's are born equal - and that, in a way, is true. Every time you restart, you're presented with three heirs. Each heir has attributes and modifiers that can be anything from quirky, to outright odd (looking at you alektorophobia).
Overall, I had a good experience with this game, and haven't even completed the second boss yet (I think there are 4). But whatever the case, Rogue Legacy is a solid title from Cellar Door Games.

After playing the game, I can't say that I understand the praise it gets.
The good:
-Music was solid (although the same can be said for a lot of indie games these days)
-Succeeds at being funny
-Lots of meaningful choices that affect future events in a natural and believable way
-Every battle/encounter feels different
The meh:
-Visual design is somewhat underwhelming compared to some of the truly inspired 2D RPG indie games that have come out in the last decade
-You can't get a "good" ending unless you play the game all over again. In my first playthrough (with no knowledge of how the endings work) I went almost purely pacifist, bar sparing a few guys and accidentally killing a weak monster at the beginning. To be told that I have to do it all over again just to have a decent ending is pretty frustrating. Luckily there's enough unique elements in the pure pacifist route to keep things fresh.
The bad:
-Bullet. Hell. When it comes to bullet hell, there is a *very* fine line between fun and frustrating. Undertale manages to stay on the fun side most of the time, but the boss battles require many attempts. Some would argue that that's to be expected of a boss battle; personally, I'm here to experience a story, not to spend half an hour memorising movement patterns.
-Worldbuilding is weak. A "library" with barely 3 lines of useful information. A few vague references towards monsters who want to see the stars. A couple of mystical tablets on the walls that explain the history of the Underground. It's so weak that one wonders if the tablets are just propaganda/myth (a genuine possibility when you consider that the library was terribly misinformed about the human world). We're told that the capital is overcrowded, and that society is in decline, but we're never actually *shown* these things.
-Shallow characters. The main characters get maybe 100 lines of dialogue, and half of that is comedy. Most of them show up for their alloted role in the plot, and then essentially disappear until the ending. One cannot reasonably expect much depth here, and yet people are claiming to relate deeply to these characters? Maybe I've just been reading too much Tumblr.
Undertale isn't a bad game, but I fail to see what it brings to the table over, say, a well-written visual novel. I felt no particular emotional impact. Honestly I'd rather just listen to the soundtrack by itself.

I'm not going to bore you with plot lines and such, there are thousand other reviews out there to accomplish that.  What I am going to talk about is the ~50 hours I have in the game so far and why you need to play this.
I'm a huge fan of story, characters, environments.  I seek out these games.  All time favorite, KoTOR, runner up, Grim Fandango.  I enjoyed Borderlands though the hyper stylization grew old pretty quick.  Rage was another but too much on rails for me to enjoy.
To put it bluntly, this game, this story, these characters, the environment, the voice acting, the attention to details, all the "filler" in environments make sense on where you are at, all done very professionally, wow it shows.  For example, part of the game is in a dried up ocean, the bad guys keep people in cages, what kind of cages, crab cages of course.  Something that would be salvaged at the bottom of the sea.  Everything pulls you in and entertains majestically and the developers are faithful to the world they create.
I'm also a dungeon crawler by heart.  Every little nook, cranny, side quest does not get past me.  I'm methodical.  Plenty of "Easter Eggs" some would call them to enjoy.  To me, it's yet again how the developers tie the story into our own lives.  Not corney or out of place, but very well done that just flows with the world they created, an extension of our world, our history.  This game rewards me in ways that I haven't felt since KoTOR.
The combat in this game is visceral, absolutly the best hand to hand mechanics I have ever played.  Animations, interactions, choices, just superbly done.  Two favorite memories so far, running away from a pack of bad guys, I climbed a ladder only to find a fuel can at the top.  Heard the group taunting me.  Lit the fuel can, dropped it down the ladder, WITNESS !!.  Second, got forced out of my vehicle, enemy vehicle closing in on me fast.  He hit his boost just as I was prepping to try to dodge him and his vehicle exploded in a huge fireball just a few feet in front of me and scrap fell all around me where I stood.  Took me a few seconds to comprehend it all.   I happened to wander unknowingly into a mine field and the bad guy drove right over it.  Totally random chance, scene right from a movie, super intense moment with a dollup of irony makes for a light hearted moment at exactly a pivotal time.  This is good stuff folks.
You will see some repeats in the game, it's own version of farming, to "fill in time" I would say in the game.   Of course I would of loved to see more uniqueness but there's only so much time and money for development.  It's obvious where they developers decided to put their resources and I can applaud them for that, forgive for some of the downfalls.
Some of the story lines seem misplaced.  By the time you get to them and complete them, the reward, well, would have been very useful much earlier in the game but now it's just another checkmark on the quest log.
I'm not a fan of mini-games in a game.  There's a side area where you can "Race" either bots or online through various "Race Centric" contests.  I'm thankful the Developers decided to leave it as a "add-on" to the story and not require it.  For me, just getting around the world there's enough driving, racing, smashing to satiate any appetite.
This is an "A" rated title, no doubt in my mind.  Play this game, focus on the game, watch everything and you will be surprised over and over again at all the little details that just make this game, well, Valhalla.

A fun, and enjoyable game.
Do NOT get hyped about this game. Take it slow and enjoy it, do not expect overly great things from this game.
It is 100% singleplayer with the only real multiplayer aspect being race times.
For an open world game, this game is very cinematic. Not just in the story, but also in how you destroy vehicles and watch them burn. A lot of really nice cinematic moments.
Pros:
1. Really really well optmized. Even on my weaker pc, the game handles pretty well with minimal frame drops.
2. Not too overwhelming of an open world game. I personally dislike open world games. I love the concept of them, but they don't do well with the balance between story or side missions and then fill them with meaningless collectables. This game balances the two and makes it feel like you can 100% the game within 100 hours. I like to take my time with games, specially ones that are single player and story driven (hehe). So I do recommend playing this game if you have time to spare and just enjoy the wasteland. It's definitely one that open world gamers will chew up really quickly. I, not being an open world gamer, took my time to enjoy what the game offers before finishing the story missions.
3. Tons of destruction: This game will constantly put you in fights throughout the wasteland. It's a little annoying at times but it's not too bad. More-so when you have your ride geared up. I've yet to get bored of destroying vehicles and watch them fall off cliffs and exploding.
4. Gorgeous: It's just a lovely, beautiful game with a ton of epic camera angles. I could probably spend a day driving through the wasteland and taking snap-shots of Max standing over a cliff and looking over the wasteland.
Cons:
1. Repetitive: I know this is a constant complaint about this game but it truly is repetitive. The boss fights are pretty much carved out of everything you've already done in the game, just with more health. It's still a fun game but I would've liked to see some more variations. About halfway through the game, you can experience almost everything it has to offer.
2. Story/side missions not replayable: I love replaying missions from my other games like Max Payne. Again, I'm not an open world gamer so this really does bug me a lot when I can't replay an epic mission.
3. A bit short: This is a double-edge sword. The game is fun but it is short with content and story. Just about any open world gamer will complete this game relatively quickly. If you don't play that many open world games or if you want to play open world games, I'd recommend to start with this one. Even for me, the story was too short and although it had some really cool moments, it didn't quite reach my expectations.
4. Not enough racing: So this is more of a car-combat game, like Twisted Metal. So although racing is part of this game and there are a few races to play, it focuses more on the vehicular combat. I'm a bit mixed about it and I feel they could've been a little more aggresive with the races.

If you like nature and hunting, this is the game to get. No game on the market nails down the atmosphere like this one does. In my objective opinion, it has the best looking "nature environment" i have ever seen in a game (the playermodels do feel a 'bit' more Cartoonish).
CAUTION:
if you are a 'run and gun' type of player, this has little to offer you. Also seeing the relative scarcity of animals, you will be walking alot. LIKE ALOT. I personally dont mind because i get immersed into the scenery and audio, hiking simulator. XD
If you play it smart ( aka dont keep running everywhere and scare all the animals away), you can stalk or lure animals pretty fast.
Just keep in mind to make your first shot count. This is no zombie shooter game. Try going for the lungs at the beginning, then gradually learn to hit more smaller vital spots. (this is for the noobs who would stalk an animal for 30m then miss the shot because they went for a headshot, then ragequit and refund)
At launch there were some problems with animal AI (they kept getting stuck in trees and bushes) and some UI problems.
These have been fixed and many other things (however some smaller bugs remain). To be honest i dont like the quests, some are even ridiculously hard (like making a valid photograph of  3 bears in a certain zone)
The business model however is deceitful . . . Unlike their previous titel 'Thehunter' that has microtransactions for every little piece of content, "Thehunter: call of the wild" was advertised as an "one time purchase" , ok no problem even though i knew they would add new reservations as dlc (currently 2 ingame).
Acceptabel
NOPE,
they added some basic stuff that should have been in the core game as "free dlc" and started pushing some core game mechanics as "PAID dlc", custom spawn/fasttravel points (tents) and motorized transport (atv).
Conclusion:
transport and cutom spawn/fasttravel points as DLC.
Whats the next step in the game development world, selling the ability to save a game as 'DLC'. Yep lets chop the whole game into dlc. The ability to run, the ability to reload, the ability to harvest an animal. ALL DLC
I like this game, really. But i currently cant support the business model of the developers. ONCE they start selling 'actual EXTRA content' as DLC and setting the core mechanics they are currently selling to "free". I will give this a upvote.

After at least 500 hours in the SA alone and well over 1000 uncounted hours in the Mod, after trying my hand at almost every aspect of this game
, I rank it above every other multiplayer SURVIVAL shooter out there. Now, before I go into my personal experience, I'd like to give my opinion on some common complaints...
--My Answers to Common Complaints--
--Rant End--
--Here's the Review--
Now, as for my personal viewpoint on the game:
Possibly one of my most valuable gaming experiences to date. Right next to the Soulsborne franchise and the Elder Scrolls. It has taught me many new ways to look at games,and has given me a newfound appreciation for dedicated game developers.
I still remember my first days in the vanilla mod (mid-late 2011), blindly running through the woods with nothing but an axe, scared out of my mind. I remember finding my first gun, car, helicopter etc. I loved it.
I loved the thrill of gunfights, the slow patience of stalking prey(be it man or beast), the relief of a life-saving bloodbag. The satifaction of a geared character, stocked based and a high survival time. And the great sadness of having them lost.
No game has made me feel so invested in my time and character before.
And I find that the Standalone has kept these feelings as flush as the first times I started playing. I still jump at the unexpected gunshot, I still feel a chill when encountering other players (friendly or not), I still feel the satifaction of a long lived character and the sadness of having them die. This game does this better than any other I have ever seen.
There is no other game that does what DayZ does, the way it does. And that is why I love it.
If anyone is interested in a slow, intense, gritty, paranoia inducing beauty of a sandbox with no safety net, they should play DayZ.
Don't let the rough exterior deter you. Diamonds lie beneath.
