Rogue Legacy certainly is an interesting game that brings some new ideas to the table.   It's a difficult but fair rogue-lite action platformer that has a 'one more run' type of addiction to it. It's hard to put the game down because the more you play, the more determined you become in beating it.
The big selling point of the game is the legacy part of the game. You play as a family of heroes who are on a quest to conquer a cursed castle in hopes of gaining an item that can heal all ailments and inperfections. However, contrary to the idea of a perfect hero. Your family legacy is anything but perfect. Every hero in your family has their highs and lows.
Anything from knowledge of advanced magic to having severe cases of schizophrenia.  The combos in your bloodline are seemingly endless and what you get every time is a luck of the draw.
Furthermore, having defects isn't always a bad thing. For example, traits like A.D.H.D makes you move faster which could be handy in dodging attacks.
You can also upgrade your castle to gain advanced abilites for future generations of family and their class layout. You can even lock down the cursed castle layout and stop it from randomly generating each time. But by doing so, you forfeit a huge chunk of the gold and treasure gained on the run.
There is so many features and content in this game that it would take forever to explain in fine detail. But I will say this, for fifthteen dollars.  You get a lot from this game.
Though, the biggest problems with this game is that I wish the game wasn't so reliant on strictly the keyboard. It's not impossible to get used to, but it's uncomfortable and akward to have your fingers clustered around the damn keys. You can use a controller, but still, at least let us use the mouse for attacks. I frankly don't understand the developer's logic with this.
Accessiblity is key, give your players freedom to customize controls to the mouse and keyboard alike.
Also, the music while good can start to get a little repetative to listen to after a while.

Other than that, I fully recommend Rogue Legacy.

I must admit, when I bought this game I haven't expected anything from it. Friend bothered me just enough, it was also actually on sale, so I decided to give in and get it. To put it shortly? One of the best decisions of my life when it comes to gaming.
The game is an FPS with RPG elements. The talent trees remind you of oldschool WoW, as you talent in of the three available talent trees on every level you gain. Also, as mentioned before, the quest, leveling and even item management are all present in a game. You will find yourself replacing shields, guns and grenades for these on higher levels all the time. You will probably also end up farming at least several bosses to get shiny (and, in some cases, extremely powerful) legendaries.
Each of the six available characters/classes (however you prefer to call it) have their own unique ability, which is unlocked somewhere around middle of the first map, once you reach 5th level. Each of these plays differently, and depending on who you play you will probably find yourself adopting different tactics. Which is good.
Storyline itself is at least pretty decent, if not actually good. The game setting (a wild west in SPAAACE) makes it even more interesting. Most characters are cool and memorable, but an obvious big star of this game is the main villain: Handsome Jack, whose character was loved by many, including me. This guy is so deliciously evil, that it's really easy to love to hate him!
The game also isn't completely perfect, on many places grind and slow making quest after quest without advancing storyline were very tedious, to the point where I actually decided to skip all of the optional quests and go with main plot. Good thing is, that even if you do that (and you shouldn't, as you will probably find yourself badly outleveled later on) the main plot still isn't that short.
Also, the best part of the game is clearly Tiny Tina's Dungeon Assault, which for me itself was much better than main part of the game, but that's just an opinion. For hours of fun and actually somewhat challenging gameplay here goes a big RECOMMENDED from me.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a leisurely driving game. You find jobs, pick up loads, haul them, and park the trailer on the other end. Along the way you'll follow your GPS, watch some beautiful sunrises, and watch the scenery pass by. Eventually you'll amass enough wealth to buy your own truck (and keep more profits), expand your garage, and then your fleet, and hire other drivers. But the real fun is listening to the wealth of internet radio stations the game has pre-programmed. When you're cruising over the mountains of Bavaria with Johnny Cash piping through the speakers (and a beverage of choice in your hand), you'll get why this game is fun.

So a lot of people rave about the game's playability and optimization.  Those are all great - don't get me wrong, but since it's already been covered I'll talk about something else.
The characters in this game are superb.  Well-written for one thing, but more importantly they fit into the story in a believable way that actually fits and enhances the gameplay.  In this game is a sidekick who is actually useful, who you don't have to babysit, and who becomes and intuitive part of your team, and an integral and plot-driving part of the story.  The battles are fast, brutal, and exciting, especially the convoy attacks.  Your character levelling system really makes a difference - as Max and his car get progressively scrappier, you can tackle greater challenges.  And unlike many other RPGs, those great challenges are thrown in your face from the beginning, so there's a crucial point in the game where you find yourself not running from battles anymore, but fighting and winning.  Glorious. . .
Add to the the glorious care taken to recreate this post-apocalyptic wasteland, staying true to the films while adding new content that fits with the lore, and you have a game that lets you experience a deeply satisfying story.  I rarely go for 100% completion in games, but the world of this one is so rich and fun to play around in, that I couldn't help myself and unlocked everything I could.
Definitely get this!

Some games are perfectly functional, and yet they leave you weirdly unexcited. They have few apparent flaws, but they don't really excel in any department either. Those games make it apparent that one important feature is missing from Steam reviews: the thumb pointing to the side.
The Mad Max movies popularized the post-apocalypse as a setting and left a stylistic imprint along the way. Many of the things you saw in the movies became a staple of post-apocalyptic fiction in general: vast and empty landscapes, moral decay, lack of resources and violence in all shapes or forms. Mad Max also gave the characters populating such an environment a distinctive look: Wasteland dwellers didn't just dress in torn up jeans or ripped shirts, they rather wore something between football gear, hardware store and BDSM fetish - something many fictional works borrowed from. In a way, games like Fallout, Rage or Borderlands are Mad Max games in spirit. Finally, the OG gets his own (current-gen) game and the result can be described as a big and resounding "eh".
Even if you never laid hands on Mad Max before, chances are you already played it. The game incorporates two of the most
popular features of this generation: open world and Arkham Asylum style two-button combat. Since this is Mad Max, vehicular combat also plays a big role in this game. In fact, your ultimate goal is to acquire enough currency to turn Max's car into a spike-ridden monstrosity capable of defeating the local warlord. To do so, Max can engage in a multitude of activities, be it racing, attacking enemy convoys or taking down bandit camps. Plus, there are possibly hundreds of locations Max can loot for small rewards.
Mad Max is not just any sandbox game - it's THE sandbox game. With all of the genre's pros and cons amplified. To the max.
The big drawback of those games is that the large quantity of activities goes at the cost of their quality, leaving you with a large selection of missions that get repetitive fast and simply aren't that interesting in the long run. It doesn't help that you need to do them dozens of times.
Here's the thing: The game's mechanics are competent and don't have any apparent flaws apart from the lack of depth. After a while, you will develop a nice and steady flow, taking out one bandit camp after another, even though you don't enjoy yourself as much as you think you should. At some point, you will develop that MMO tunnel vision, eyes set on the next upgrade, which will be enough to keep you going. The mechanics are simple, but don't require any finesse, strategy or skill. As you play, your mind will wander off frequently. Maybe I should go swimming, you will think. You will catch yourself pondering life and its existential tribulations to the sound of exploding cars and cracking bones. Eventually, you will awaken from your trance.
The only times I stumbled over some honest fun was during the car chases, but even they got tiresome after common enemies received multiple layers of armor and started attacking in groups of three - often when I was in a hurry to get somewhere. Meanwhile, the missions in which you are supposed to attack a convoy are possibly the closest you will get to a breathless chase depicted in Fury Road.
Mad Max is by no means a bad game and more of an example of somebody trying excessively hard to play it safe. It's vanilla ice cream. It's Coldplay. It's jeans and t-shirt. Only the visuals manage to impress since the game is nice to look at and runs without any hiccups.
This may sound like a thoroughly negative review, but it comes down to what you want from the game. If you expect a strong movie tie-in, you will be severely disappointed. However, if you often find yourself with a couple of hours to kill, Mad Max is the game for you. It will keep you busy for hours upon hours.
Busy. Not necessarily entertained.

Let me begin by saying that although picking your class has changed quite a bit, this game is still COD through and through. I enjoy playing the game, and it seems to reward smart gameplay more often than not. I feel though that Treyarch needs to look into polishing the mechanics more. There are some glitchy things that happen every so often that makes you question how much time is dedicated making sure their engine and game mechanics work like they are supposed to. Connection is much improved over the last 3 titles. Set your max ping to 50 and you should be good. I really appreciate the efforts to ban cheaters and keep this game updated with regular patches and what not. It's perhaps the redeeming title of the series and one that feels almost as good as COD4 did when I first played that game. The two are obviously not comparable, but I can say this is the most fun I've had playing COD since then. That being said the franchise is a bit tired for me, so it's hard to keep playing it without getting bored of the same things. If you enjoy arcade shooters and you're not burned out on COD, this is definitely a buy. The next IW should be coming out soon, but I'm not sure how excited I am for it as MW3 was a complete dissapointment.

This is by far the most difficult game I think I've ever played. It's up there with Icaruga and Ninja Gaiden. This whole game was set up to basically show you how disappointing the rest of your time playing it will be. Don't get me wrong, I like hard games, but this one is just a little too "randomly generated" for me. I'll explain after I give a quick summary below of the strong points and weak points of the overall experience.
Turning, at least with the keyboard, seems a little inconsistent. In Binding of Isaac when you turn left, you turn left, you are immediately looking and aiming in a direction when you hit that button. In this game, you sometimes just don't turn around and attack in the direction you want. The character control is kind of like starbound or terraria only without the smoothness. There were times I died simply because my character seemingly would NOT turn in the direction I needed to attack in. I don't have a controller so I don't know if this is just because of the keyboard or what. Either way, I don't like it.
Skills and classes are pretty spot on. The way you level up and collect gold to unlock additional items and enchantments is really great and it gives you the impression you're improving your character. These skills are also not just little things you add and forget. When you get a rune that absorbs health on enemy kills the game changes in a big way. Little upgrades make the world of difference. I feel a lot of games lack this kind of experience.
Gameplay. ♥♥♥♥ me in♥♥♥♥♥ If you've played Terraria, Starbound, Binding of Isaac, Legend of Zelda, FTL, or generally any game where you have one life and play through it til you die, you will realize this game takes those concepts and just takes a giant♥♥♥♥♥♥on your expectations. There is no hand holding. There is no difficulty ramping. You don't start in zone 1. You start in THE ZONE. The only level of difficulty this game has is based on luck. To put it in perspective it'd be like going to the gym to take some boxing lessons and you find that your sparring partner is Mike Tyson one day and a 8 year old girl the next. As an example: My first room. My FIRST room as in I did the tutorial and started the game. I went in and was assaulted from 6 directions. I was attacked by a zombie, a purple ball, a star that shot fireballs, a painting, and the only place to dodge had spikes. I killed one enemy and took a beating and died in the first room. My second "life" I entered a item room, got a spell or something, next room had a red telepad. I took it and went to a place where there were giant mages who shot huge fireballs and took 10 hits to kill. Oh by the way there were 3 of those the second I spawned in. My fourth run was basically over by the second room because there was a wall of fireball shooting things and 2 flying paintings that mauled me instantly.
So if you get this game don't think you're going to have easy rooms at first with maybe one or two enemies who casually stroll towards you or throw♥♥♥♥♥♥at you. When I first caught a glimpse of this game, I was not intrigued. Sure, the setting seemed original, but I was under the impression that the protagonist/s would be all "hooaah" US soldiers and they were there to fight the local populace. Which, in essence, is a massively overplayed and saturated narrative. Once I played the game, I realised that I made a mistake. I doubt I was ever THIS wrong in my overall assessment of a game before.
The story line, albeit heavily influenced by the last (or pre-last?) century novel "The Heart of Darkness", manages to remain fresh and relevant, at least in terms of modern military conflicts. I have not been this satisfied by a shooter narrative since Half Life 2. The writing is simply excellent, furiously paced, with twists coming left and right. The voice acting? Phenomenal. The whole cast is a sight to behold (or to hear), but...Nolan North..If I ever were to give out an Oscar for voicing a game character, this would be the case. Cpt. Walkers transformation is simply breath-taking. Sure, in other games, the break-down of a character is often portrayed visually, i.e. blood, torn clothing, injuries..But here, its mainly mental, in the voice. The first time you will hear Walker bellow "Kill is f*cking confirmed", you will know exactly what I mean. 11/10 and then some.
Visually, its rather a mixed bag. But by no means a BAD mixed bag. Vistas and environments are engaging and beautiful, no qualms there. But maybe sharper/more detailed textures or effects would have been the proverbial icing on the cake for maximum immersion. Either way, you will not be dissapointed, it IS a pretty game.
Soundtrack wise, this game is a gem. The guitar riffs, as well as the licenced songs from the Vietnam era and what not fit the story and setting like a glove. Small spoiler: When I first encountered the enemy in a certain level, and the accompanying song was "Hush", I knew right there that this game clearly knows how to hit my good buttons :). This is an A-class soundtrack in my book.
The controls (keyboard) are quite clunky, i.e. on the harder difficulties you will be furious at some points :). It is clear that the game, at least control wise, was mostly intented for consoles. This would probably be the main problem within the game, at least in my opinion.
So would I recommend this game to you? Absolutely. This is truly a breath of fresh air in the TPS/war shooter genre. The creators have shown the game industry that new, fresh and uncompromising ideas DO have a place in todays oversaturated, generic shooter market, and CAN make a difference. I only wish that more games such as this are released more frequently.

Despite what the reviews below said, in its current state I could get this working ... if you ignore the 'quick play' online, use the server list, pick ones with a few spaces and try a few times, I eventually got in. Not ideal, but not totally broken (for the UK at least).
My reason for not recommending is to do with the game itself ... it's just not that fun (build 0.5) and doesn't feel like it'll ever be a game worth the price they're asking. The problems? Trying to look past the current build and at what will be in the finished game it's just hard to see what will be here. The characters are non-responsive to the controls. This is what makes for the hilarious clips, but it also makes it a game that's always going to more fun to watch than to play.
There's also not a lot of scope for expansion beyond more maps ... the game is people pushing/punching/kicking/lunging at each other until you're the last one no longer on the map. Whether you're on a blimp or a train station, the premise is the same with only the backdrop changing. Ok, on the scaffolds you can cut the cables, but the maps are so small it doesn't take too long to suss these things out, and if someone else is doing it you can see it coming. Maybe Steam Workshop can help to pad the number of maps out but even now it's not the quantity that's the issue, it's just how little effect they really have on the game.
I guess it just feels a bit too deliberately mindless ... again, makes for very funny viewing, but then why pay out when you can watch the collection of YouTube clips.
That said, if you have a party of 6, all on a voice chat, or you're playing local you'll definitely get more out of it than if you've got 3 or less where the novelty will wear off quite quickly. After about 10 minutes of actual gameplay, I'd seen all the maps, kind of got a handle of the controls and felt like I was doing the rounds.
There are a lot of current build problems that are listen below. The controls are quite (possibly deliberately) fiddly, the online servers are hit and miss and when you get into them there's often lag (not in an FPS way, but in the form of a delayed reaction). Fair to say these will probably be fixed over time.
If this was less than a fiver, my main gripe would be gone and I'd be on the fence of whether it's worth getting or not. But 10 in a sale, and 13 at early access price ... too much, sorry.

TL;DR - It's a good game that is too busy drowning in a molasses pool of grinding. Enjoy grinding for days? This is the game for you.
The concept and platforming is fantastic. But Rogue Legacy is nothing short of a grind simulator.
This game's greatest flaw is that the game's "difficulty" is simply making you grind out coins. Sure the story is charming at first, and the concept of your heir taking over when you die is amazing, but take that away and you've got a good platformer that wants you to keep throwing yourself at it in hopes that you die with enough coins to level up something and come back as someone else.
This concept wouldn't be so bad, if it wasn't the sole focus of this game. Go in, get money, die with enough money to upgrade a skill, and rinse repeat until you've reach a high enough level to move onto the next zone.
Don't have enough money invested into your skill tree before you went to the other zones? You're going to have a bad time... You'll also probably be pummeled into the ground because the level differential is massive.

Rogue-like games only work if there is a sense of progression, even in the face of defeat. While Rogue Legacy offers this sometimes, I mostly find myself back at my manor with absolutely nothing to buy after my previous run. Now, this normally wouldn't be an issue in rogue-like games... but you MUST give up all of your gold EVERY time you enter a new castle. This completely negates the whole "progression" aspect of rogue-like games. It makes dying prematurely TRULY a bad thing, because if you are just 10 gold short of that upgrade you want, too bad. Charon takes it all before you play again and it makes you start from scratch. I mean, think about it. What if an RPG sent you on a quest, and if you didn't gain a level during that quest, you lost all the XP you earned towards the next level? That's what Rogue Legacy feels like. Not a never-ending sense of progression, but countless instances of "Dang, another wasted run." It's truly a shame how a single misplaced mechanic completely ruins this game for me, because in every other aspect, it shines. I wish I could recommend Rogue Legacy. But because of Charon's greed, I sadly cannot.

TL:DR Version: It's a good solid game with a 4th wall breaking meta narrative on the nature of shooters that ultimately hurts both its story and intended point, but is still something worth experiencing.
Originally when this game came out, it's marketing convinced me that it was another shooter where you killed the "evil Muslims". That they were just arrogant for building that city in the middle of the desert and so on, that I entirely skipped the game and looked on it with scorn. Spec Ops games previously have never given me much reason to think otherwise.
Yet a friend gave me a free copy of the game and I was pretty starved for a good shooter so I gave it a go and what I played ultimately surprised me as much as it confused me, but more on that second part later.
Spec Ops combat is run of the mill on paper. You have guns, you have enemies, you have cover, and you have regenerating health. What sets the game apart is how well it executes each of feature. To say the guns handle well is an over simplification, each of the guns fulfills a unique niche and feel and you quickly develop favorites, followed by attachments to those favorites.
Enemies come sporting some of the better AI I've experienced in shooters along with fluid motion and a sense of self preservation that games like Call of Duty simply lack. They are what make ducking into cover fun. Cover shooting mechanics won't surprise you, but they are as solid as the rest of the game.
My only real complaint about the game is how it trips itself with its own meta narrative on shooters themselves instead of military misadventures or the idea of being a hero. This leads to a lot of confusion at the end of the game that is entirely intentional on the part of the developers. Spec Ops the Line's entire story is literally left up for the player to decide what exactly really happened.
While this is an experience that is worth experiencing it also leaves a profound sense of confusion and a lot of questions that the game could have avoided by not breaking the 4th wall as subtly as it did and went with a more down to earth commentary. It's rather sad, as the game's natural story arch with all its horrific events would have sufficed as a means of getting their point across, but that point becomes rather lost in the confusion and is only discoverable by going online and reading an interview.
Still the game is solid, even if the story harms it a bit from a game standpoint, so I recommend this game, but only to those who can deal with the meta nature of the game. COD fans, you will probably not like this game.

Hey everyone this is WohlfePac and this is my review for The Hunter Call of the Wild. First off this is a really fun game. I love hunting in real life and this game goes right along with that. You get rifles, shotguns, pistols, compound bows, and all kinds of tools and calls. Pros: It's a great open world experience. The graphics are pretty good and the calmness of walking through the woods is very relaxing. I tend to play this game when i just want to relax and not have people jumping out of every corner trying to kill me. I really like the tent and blind dlc. I don't use the. Blinds very much but the tent allows you to buy stuff from pretty much anywhere. You don't have to run back to your cabin to buy or store something, you just drop your tent, step inside and buy something. You can also sleep there too which is really handy. You can also fast travel back to it if you get too far away. The gun mechanics are very good and I don't mean to brag but I killed a deer from over 200 yards away. I'm excited for the atv dlc because it's a huge map and just walking somewhere takes forever! Luckily I'll be picking that up once it releases.
Cons: there are a few cons and one of them being the map has a small glitch that when u set a way point it doesn't put it on the spot where you clicked on, it puts it just off to one side of it or just below it. Doesn't seem bad but when u get where u wanted the marker is about 100 yards away from where u wanted it (a little exaggerated but still frustrating). Also it seems kinda stupid to have to pay to sleep. Yea and it's not very cheap. I think it was just under 200 credits just to sleep. I'm hoping they'll remove this in an update. Also there are only 2 bows, 6 rifles, 4 shotguns, and 4 pistols to choose from. No crossbows or black powder guns which are very popular for hunting these days. If there could be more of a variety in the game that would be great. Also it's not a survival game; no crafting, no building, no food consumption. This isn't really a problem but when you have an open outdoor world and all you do is shoot animals, buy guns and shoot more animals it gets kinda boring. Also very limited customization for your character. You can change the gender from make to female but the only thing you can change after that is the color of your camouflage jacket and pants. And you can't even see your character. Not even the arms. And the other colors besides the stock ones are expensive like 5 figure expensive. And when you can't even see it it makes no sense. What they should have done was make it so you can change your hat,boots, jacket, etc and allow a third person view to see your character. Maybe add safety harnesses and other add-ons to make your character unique. Maybe we can make some of this stuff in some kind of crafting table or something. Anyway the game is pretty fun and it's definitely worth getting but don't expect a super exciting experience. It's more relaxing than exiting and that's ok sometimes we need a break from the action and take things slow once in awhile. So that's my review thanks for reading and I'll see you guys next time bye bye!

What can I say? if you don't know what the Borderlands series is about or never played it then where have you been?

While BioShock Infinite might be the best game I have ever played, Borderlands 2 is the absulutely best in terms of overall player experience. I have never ever had so much fun as when playing this game. Beautiful graphics, entertaining storyline, probably the best voice acting in all of video game industry, some of the greatest character designs ever made (Claptrap, Tiny Tina and especially Handsome Jack), immense amounts of loots (there are literally millions of guns you can choose from) and excellent replayability. The game has about 200 hours of gameplay if you wish to level a character entirely, which is a lot, but I guarantee you, they will be some of the best moments of your gaming life.
A lot can be said about maturity of the content of the game as well. A lot of harsh language, sexual innuendos and things that would be disgusting in other games (cannibalism, torture and so on) is present, but the game is incredibly mature and deals with all of these themes in a very respectable way, which is further supplemented by the perfect graphics. Not only that, but the game also packs striking thoughts and supports LGBT rights, goes against domestic violence (I will never forget Mr. Torgue saying his best quote ever: "YOU BETTER TREAT MOXXI NICE! NOTHING IS MORE BADASS THAN TREATING A WOMAN WITH RESPECT!"), regards personal insecurity and many many other important topics in our current society. It does all of this with grace. There is even an NPC created specifically for a now-deceased Borderlands fan - and that is just one of many examples of how great the developers are. Honestly, Gearbox Software staff are some of the best people I have ever had the pleasure to meet.
The humour in the game is also something that cannot be possibly overglorified. Not only you will find references to just about every game and pop culture theme ever to be made here, but the dialogues are incredibly funny even when discussing important things. The way the game makes fun of itself is something that absolutely captured me. ("Torgue weapons ALWAYS fire EXPLOSIVE ROUNDS. They are also LOUD and require EXCESSIVE use of CAPITAL LETTERS") The fourth wall is broken all the time, but it is done in a so incredibly funny way that it feels so, so right. ("Hey guys, remember the old Crawmerax the Invincible?" "Sure, we exploited his glitches for HOURS! Oh, Pearlescents!")
The DLCs are all worth is as well, as they add a lot to the story and offer a lot additional content. Tiny Tina's Assault on the Dragon Keep is probably the greatest DLC ever created for any game ever. The amount of references, fun and interesting enemies present here are incredible. If I had to choose a single game out of all of them and spend the rest of my life playing it, it would be Borderlands 2.
Would I recommend this game? No. No, I do not recommend you to buy this game. I recommend you to head to the Store and buy the Borderlands GOTY Edition, Borderlands 2 GOTY Edition, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel and it's Season Pass and The Tales of Borderlands as well. Buy the entire franchise. Just. Do. It. Also, write a love letter to Gearbox Software and thank them for creating the best game franchise currently to exist.

When I first started the original Life Is Strange, I didn't really know what I was expecting. I just felt like playing a "Choice Matters" game and I heard good things about it, but also some bad things. All in all, I was blown away by the game though and it quickly made its way to the top of my list of all time favorite games. Naturally, I also had my problems with the game, but I could overlook them since I liked it so much.
Then Life Is Strange: Before the Storm was announced (along with another unannounced LIS Project) and I was ecstatic. I liked Chloe as a character and I was thrilled to find out more about her story.
Now, bear in mind that this review is written as of Episode 2, which has been out for a few weeks now, but nevertheless, here are my thoughts.
The positive things:
Right from the start the love for the characters and settings is seen. Deck Nine understands the world that DONTNOD built and they put in stuff like characters or little easter eggs that would also fit perfectly into the "first" game. Chloe comes off as believable and you can notice the habits that would eventually evolve and become stronger over time. Rachel is an amazing character that I would've loved to see more of (more on that later) and the other miscellaneous characters find their position in the world rather well. To round it off the story is decently written, a few mistakes here and there, but overall it's a good experience so far. Additionally, this game is supported and - in parts - carried by a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack by Daughter.
The negative things:
A few key mistakes that the "first" game made are still here, which mostly boil down to some questionable writing. Characters that would not make that decision for any logical reason ever, cringy or awkward dialogue for the sake of cringy/awkward dialogue and some motion capture movement that makes no sense at all. I understand that this is a video game and a story about teenagers, but forcing it makes it feel more out of place at times than not having something like that in there. It just seems like the developers have a hard time when deciding how to balance these moments.
I don't think this point fits in with either positive or negative but here goes:
I wish there was a way to retcon the whole Life Is Strange story after experiencing the first two episodes of Before the Storm. If you read this review before playing either of them, please do yourself a favor of playing this one first. You might not understand some of the references, but it will make the experience so much better. My main point here is that I would've loved to see more of Rachel and I just don't feel like only having her in three episodes in Before the Storm is doing her character justice. She's super likeable. With retconning the stories of both games, you could make a really coherent and well crafted story, minus most unnecessary cringy moments and it would make the impact of some scenes from the "first" game so much better.
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely, yes. If you're looking for a story with characters you can fall in love with (figuratively) and you don't mind a few cringy moments or some shotty writing, this is the game for you. But please, do yourself a favor and play this one first.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person shooter telling the story of US captain Walker, who is sent to Dubai to investigate the failed evacuation of the city after it has been hit by several huge sandstorms.
Gameplay-wise, Spec Ops is your average tps: you need to master taking cover in order to survive and use the game's environment to your advantage (explosives, sand drops, ...). Althought the enemies are kind of repetitive and the various encounters basically the same, the title is entertaining and playable enough. It also spots an average lenght (five or six hours, on an average).
The strongest suits of Spec Ops: The Line are its visuals and atmosphere. The plot and the situations you will find yourself in are basically severe deconstruction on the most abused cliches of modern military shooters. The sanity slippage suffered by the protagonist and the general lack of choices in some instances just add to general surreal theme of the title.
All in all, Spec Ops: The Line is a very atmospheric game and a good gaming experiment in its own right

cons:

The best way to describe the feeling I have about this game is that ... I am pleased.
I admire the world. The post apocalyptic desert with scarce resources and people a half way or more closer to becoming an animals.
The graphics and easiness that my computer dealt with it (2yrs old PC with Radeon R9 200) is really impressive.
I love the locations. Their diversity, they looks, their climate. The biggest surprise that you can make so much out of sand, dirt, stones, rocks, rust and scrap and maybe a little bit of human flesh as decoration. Hands down the best part of the game. I am really impressed with e.g. camps (the ones you take over). Surprising how different they are.
I really like the story. It is not long but both main story missions and wasteland ones are really good. One disadvantage is that there is not as many of them as it should be ... for my taste.
I quite enjoy the cars, their looks, the feel when driving, the scope and selection of modifiers they have and the battles in them. Also the possibility to free-roam almost everywhere is quite satisfying.
I also really liked the characters. There is not much of them but they are created quite well in regards of looks, characters, behaviour and dialogues. Max included.
The amount and quality of opponents is also more than enough.
The melee fights was something I had some problems with in terms of having fun but when I got used to it and developed my main character I started to have some enjoyment out of it. Keep in mind it is just not my kind of thing.
Now the things I do not like. The repetitiveness of other than main story and wasteland missions. Most people will find it tiresome and too boring after a while (mine sweeping yay). I stuck with it cause of other things (mentioned above). It is something many sandbox games are struggling with and Mad Max tries to balance it with other qualities. Nevertheless it is not the best result.
I do not like the bugs. Only good thing about them that there is not much of them and are mainly a minor ones. The game only crashed once so with over 90 hours it is quite a good result.
Boss fights. They are almost the same with little variety to actual fights (shotgun and shivs ftw).
General difficulty. You cannot change it and most of the time I found this game quite easy. There are some difficulty peaks (main story boss fight) but I died like 10 times and mostly cause I wanted to test out some things not of actual challenge.
And there it is. My recommendation? If the post apocalyptic world is your thing, you like the carmageddon style of driving and beating people with your fists makes you smile then go for it ... or if it is below 5€ ... then pick it up even just for the main story (around 20 hours).
EDIT: ... and I even cried once ...

Hey everyone this is WohlfePac and this is my review for The Hunter Call of the Wild. First off this is a really fun game. I love hunting in real life and this game goes right along with that. You get rifles, shotguns, pistols, compound bows, and all kinds of tools and calls. Pros: It's a great open world experience. The graphics are pretty good and the calmness of walking through the woods is very relaxing. I tend to play this game when i just want to relax and not have people jumping out of every corner trying to kill me. I really like the tent and blind dlc. I don't use the. Blinds very much but the tent allows you to buy stuff from pretty much anywhere. You don't have to run back to your cabin to buy or store something, you just drop your tent, step inside and buy something. You can also sleep there too which is really handy. You can also fast travel back to it if you get too far away. The gun mechanics are very good and I don't mean to brag but I killed a deer from over 200 yards away. I'm excited for the atv dlc because it's a huge map and just walking somewhere takes forever! Luckily I'll be picking that up once it releases.
Cons: there are a few cons and one of them being the map has a small glitch that when u set a way point it doesn't put it on the spot where you clicked on, it puts it just off to one side of it or just below it. Doesn't seem bad but when u get where u wanted the marker is about 100 yards away from where u wanted it (a little exaggerated but still frustrating). Also it seems kinda stupid to have to pay to sleep. Yea and it's not very cheap. I think it was just under 200 credits just to sleep. I'm hoping they'll remove this in an update. Also there are only 2 bows, 6 rifles, 4 shotguns, and 4 pistols to choose from. No crossbows or black powder guns which are very popular for hunting these days. If there could be more of a variety in the game that would be great. Also it's not a survival game; no crafting, no building, no food consumption. This isn't really a problem but when you have an open outdoor world and all you do is shoot animals, buy guns and shoot more animals it gets kinda boring. Also very limited customization for your character. You can change the gender from make to female but the only thing you can change after that is the color of your camouflage jacket and pants. And you can't even see your character. Not even the arms. And the other colors besides the stock ones are expensive like 5 figure expensive. And when you can't even see it it makes no sense. What they should have done was make it so you can change your hat,boots, jacket, etc and allow a third person view to see your character. Maybe add safety harnesses and other add-ons to make your character unique. Maybe we can make some of this stuff in some kind of crafting table or something. Anyway the game is pretty fun and it's definitely worth getting but don't expect a super exciting experience. It's more relaxing than exiting and that's ok sometimes we need a break from the action and take things slow once in awhile. So that's my review thanks for reading and I'll see you guys next time bye bye!

Spec Ops surprised me. It also shocked me. Not because it is a bad game. In fact it is an amazing game. The reason Spec Ops surprised me and shocked me was because of its story. In the first hour or so you will be thinking "This is a game that is trying to be Call of Duty", which it does but for good reason. It takes the FPS and 3rd Person Military shooters we know and, in a few hours after the game starts, questions you why you like those games so much. Questions like "Why do you like raining fire down upon you enemies" and "Are you sure you want to be a hero?” These questions the game then goes on to answer for you. Without spoiling anything, at the end of the game I loved and hated the game. It gets you thinking "What happened?". Then you play it again to try and understand and start noticing subtle hints.
As for Gameplay mechanics, it is quite like your Gears of War type games, with the cover system and shooting mechanics. You AI buddies help and awful lot and are pretty smart. The terrain can sometimes be used again your opponents and you have a few different selections of guns to choose from, each feeling different. The voice acting is spot on and you will recognise the main characters voice immediately.
Buy this game, as its story is one of the most disturbing and thought provking in a game I have played and is one of the few games that holds me, the player, acountable for my actions throughout the game.

The best way to describe the feeling I have about this game is that ... I am pleased.
I admire the world. The post apocalyptic desert with scarce resources and people a half way or more closer to becoming an animals.
The graphics and easiness that my computer dealt with it (2yrs old PC with Radeon R9 200) is really impressive.
I love the locations. Their diversity, they looks, their climate. The biggest surprise that you can make so much out of sand, dirt, stones, rocks, rust and scrap and maybe a little bit of human flesh as decoration. Hands down the best part of the game. I am really impressed with e.g. camps (the ones you take over). Surprising how different they are.
I really like the story. It is not long but both main story missions and wasteland ones are really good. One disadvantage is that there is not as many of them as it should be ... for my taste.
I quite enjoy the cars, their looks, the feel when driving, the scope and selection of modifiers they have and the battles in them. Also the possibility to free-roam almost everywhere is quite satisfying.
I also really liked the characters. There is not much of them but they are created quite well in regards of looks, characters, behaviour and dialogues. Max included.
The amount and quality of opponents is also more than enough.
The melee fights was something I had some problems with in terms of having fun but when I got used to it and developed my main character I started to have some enjoyment out of it. Keep in mind it is just not my kind of thing.
Now the things I do not like. The repetitiveness of other than main story and wasteland missions. Most people will find it tiresome and too boring after a while (mine sweeping yay). I stuck with it cause of other things (mentioned above). It is something many sandbox games are struggling with and Mad Max tries to balance it with other qualities. Nevertheless it is not the best result.
I do not like the bugs. Only good thing about them that there is not much of them and are mainly a minor ones. The game only crashed once so with over 90 hours it is quite a good result.
Boss fights. They are almost the same with little variety to actual fights (shotgun and shivs ftw).
General difficulty. You cannot change it and most of the time I found this game quite easy. There are some difficulty peaks (main story boss fight) but I died like 10 times and mostly cause I wanted to test out some things not of actual challenge.
And there it is. My recommendation? If the post apocalyptic world is your thing, you like the carmageddon style of driving and beating people with your fists makes you smile then go for it ... or if it is below 5€ ... then pick it up even just for the main story (around 20 hours).
EDIT: ... and I even cried once ...

Rogue Legacy is a 2D action platformer that is categorized as a roguelike (Which means it has procedurally generated levels and permanent death). Rogue Legacy isn't as unforgiving though as other roguelikes because it adds in some RPG mechanics which make your impending deaths easier to swallow.
At the start of Rogue Legacy, you are a no name sword-wielding hero who is trying to conquer a castle and you have no idea why. As you go through the castle you'll find journals randomly strewn about that help piece the story together but for the most part the narrative is in the back seat throughout your adventures (Which is alright since the story isn't that in-depth to begin with).
After an hour or so of playing I was hooked with that thought in the back of my head "Just one more run.... after this one I'm done... Eh, one more can't hurt". The controls feel tight and the mechanics are solid and enjoyable with a variety of challenge rooms/events you'll encounter throughout the castle. The castle of Rogue Legacy is split into four separate sections which are very distinct in aesthetic, difficulty and feature a unique boss to that section.
The thing that sets Rogue Legacy apart from other roguelikes is the way in which death occurs. When you die (Which will happen a lot at first), you get to choose a new heir from three choices which you get to attempt another run through the castle with. Each of the heir's can have a randomly assigned genetic trait which will affect how the game either plays or looks. Discovering every trait and what each one does was pretty fun, so I won't spoil the surprises and upsets that come with them.
Another unique part of your death is that your future characters (Heirs) get stronger in whichever way you choose. While you progress through the castle you'll collect gold from chests/enemies. You then get to spend that gold at your manor after choosing an heir and you can invest in a number of things, from your stats to your armour or unlocking new classes or buying new equipment/runes. It's not impossible but for a first run through Rogue Legacy it's really unlikely that you'll beat the game without having at least several dozen upgrades purchased (Because of how weak your initial characters are). The feeling of progression through boosting your characters overall power is pretty satisfying and can get pretty addictive.
Near the end of Rogue Legacy once your character is powerful enough to do most of the castle without dying you'll have beaten all the bosses and unlocked the final section of the castle. Beating the boss there will not only end your Legacy but you'll have the option of continuing on to a harder castle where the gold gains are increased (It's a NG+ that just scales enemies damage/hp and rewards up).
For the most part I really enjoyed Rogue Legacy. The RPG mechanic is pretty good at giving you that "Just one more run...." factor. But after you beat NG+ a few times and you have all manor upgrades maxed out and equipment/runes bought there's not much to look forward to. Unless you enjoy pushing yourself to see how far into NG+'s you can go, just beat it a couple of times and enjoy the journey.

This is easily the best game I've ever played. You shouldn't go into this game for gameplay, it isn't anything new but it works perfectly fine with guns being relatively fun to use and enemies having good AI. At times you will find yourself dying a little too quick while some enemies feel like bullet sponges, but that's about right considering how little you wear while they are fully armoured. Now that we're done with the gameplay, the story is the real hook to buying this game. You will find yourself in a gripping story where you are put though many different situations to test your morality, most of which are no win scenarios and give no obvious good choices making you feel worse the more you play. The game is not black and white but rather the complete opposite with the game itself questioning you on whether or not you're really the hero as you fight your way through an entire army in order to find Konrad and end the nightmare he brought to Dubai when him and his soldiers were unable to evacuate this forgotten city. As the game progresses both you and the main protagonist will start to question what's really happening and your current mental state until you reach the ending which left me in such shock that I was left speechless and felt the need to replay the final mission numerous times to see all the endings. I personally felt dead inside after my first run. By the end of my experience I encountered so many twists and turns I didnt know what to expect next and after everything was over, I wanted to go back through the game and make different decisions from my first run to see how my teammates, myself and how everyone around me would react. Overall This was the ultimate video game narrative I've ever experienced and found it more than worth my time, this game took me about 8 hrs to complete due to some moments that took me a few too many tries, keeping it from being fun at all times, but for most people this shouldn't be much longer than 6 hrs though for most who play it on normal difficulty. I found that this game's length was excusable due to the fact that it was so immersive it felt at least twice as long. In the end this game has the best narrative in just about any game I have played so far including Telltale's Walking Dead games and it conveys a great message for the players, making this more than worth the cost.

The best way to describe the feeling I have about this game is that ... I am pleased.
I admire the world. The post apocalyptic desert with scarce resources and people a half way or more closer to becoming an animals.
The graphics and easiness that my computer dealt with it (2yrs old PC with Radeon R9 200) is really impressive.
I love the locations. Their diversity, they looks, their climate. The biggest surprise that you can make so much out of sand, dirt, stones, rocks, rust and scrap and maybe a little bit of human flesh as decoration. Hands down the best part of the game. I am really impressed with e.g. camps (the ones you take over). Surprising how different they are.
I really like the story. It is not long but both main story missions and wasteland ones are really good. One disadvantage is that there is not as many of them as it should be ... for my taste.
I quite enjoy the cars, their looks, the feel when driving, the scope and selection of modifiers they have and the battles in them. Also the possibility to free-roam almost everywhere is quite satisfying.
I also really liked the characters. There is not much of them but they are created quite well in regards of looks, characters, behaviour and dialogues. Max included.
The amount and quality of opponents is also more than enough.
The melee fights was something I had some problems with in terms of having fun but when I got used to it and developed my main character I started to have some enjoyment out of it. Keep in mind it is just not my kind of thing.
Now the things I do not like. The repetitiveness of other than main story and wasteland missions. Most people will find it tiresome and too boring after a while (mine sweeping yay). I stuck with it cause of other things (mentioned above). It is something many sandbox games are struggling with and Mad Max tries to balance it with other qualities. Nevertheless it is not the best result.
I do not like the bugs. Only good thing about them that there is not much of them and are mainly a minor ones. The game only crashed once so with over 90 hours it is quite a good result.
Boss fights. They are almost the same with little variety to actual fights (shotgun and shivs ftw).
General difficulty. You cannot change it and most of the time I found this game quite easy. There are some difficulty peaks (main story boss fight) but I died like 10 times and mostly cause I wanted to test out some things not of actual challenge.
And there it is. My recommendation? If the post apocalyptic world is your thing, you like the carmageddon style of driving and beating people with your fists makes you smile then go for it ... or if it is below 5€ ... then pick it up even just for the main story (around 20 hours).
EDIT: ... and I even cried once ...

Mad Max is one of my favourite games of 2015.
I was pleased to hear prior to purchase that the game was very well optimised, on a GTX 970 I can run everything on max settings and still maintain around 105fps. The story is really well done and resembles the same atmosphere felt in the film.
The characters are all fantastic and the voice acting is really one of the best I've ever seen in a video game.
Pros:
1. Probably the most well optimised game I've played ever.
2. Excellent setting, there's lots of post-apocalyptic games but none that focus on cars and car modifcations to the extent that Mad Max does.
3. Upgrade system is truly wide an deep. Not only do you have different tiers of unlocks for everything on your car but also for Max himself. There are also some hidden unlocks provided after completion of the story that were a very nice touch.
4. Combat system is basic but very satisfying with the upgrades you can give Max to give him more of an edge while fighting.
5. Open world do as you like. You can in theory do a bunch of challenges that gets Max to highest rank before completing the majority of the story and stronghold missions. This leaves you with a very easy path to finishing the game though.
Cons:
1. The game can get a little repetitive with scavenging from camps, finishing top dogs, oil camps and stank gum but these things are ofset by the long term rewards you get for completing the areas.
2. Stronghold missions tended to be a lot less fun and interesting than the story missions. Sometimes story missions unlock upgrades where you already have the next tier of upgrade.
3. Once you finish the game if you're still trying to finish up the upgrades to your V8 (final cost for all the V8s is well into > 10000 scrap) scrap tends to be harder to comeby in larger amounts. I also found that mobile scrap transports are very rare in the same limiting your ability to find them on the roads.
All in all I loved Mad Max from start to finish. It doesn't have any annoying second launcher or DRM, you have the option to get WBPlay (ie its not forced down your throat) and overall is a well rounded game.

This game has a lot of potential, and despite its current state I had a lot of fun playing with friends (it's no fun in singleplayer yet). The game is easy to play, but tricky to master; accessible and entertaining for all ages.
However, once we started playing seriously we found the game became tedious. We couldn't figure out how to interact properly with our environment, finding jumping and climbing to new areas too difficult; and being unable to use items as weapons.
What we'd like to see is:
1. More levels, more interesting/imaginative levels - the turbine and chute levels were personal favourites because the other environmental factors kept the game interesting.
2. More fighting ability - I was unable to land a satisfying blow on my opponent as the attacks were too weak. This should be coupled with an ability to block along with the existing mechanics of grabbing and crouching/crawling to evade attacks.
3. More objects / level interaction - I want to be able to pick up things and throw them or swing them as a weapon, place obstacles in the way for others, maybe push buttons or pull levers to trigger a trap
All in all given the early access status, I'd still recommend this when it's on sale provided you have friends to play with.

This game is hard for me to review. I spent quite a bit of time on it, and I did enjoy most of the time I spent on it, but at the end of the day I feel like this game also has a lot of missed potential.
Honestly, the game is buggy. It's not even a bug or two here or there; there are fundamental problems with the engine they used, where if you do something like prone on a cliffside, you literally clip through the ground and see the bottom of the map.
Also, there's just a lot less gameplay in this game than I was hoping for. There's a lot of weapons, but many of them are just a grind to unlock. Weapons are straight up better than one another. There's very little reason not to use bolt-action rifles as opposed to anything else. There aren't very many animals to hunt, and a lot of them (like moose, Roosevelt elk, whitetail deer, and blacktail deer on the Layton Lakes map) behave pretty much the same; the only big differences are the distance in which they react to sound and their average herd size. This makes it very easy to "play out" the game like I did - there's basically a hard cap on the number of interesting things there are to do.
Multiplayer is a monstrosity, with very few working features (for instance, you get nothing for any of your kills until you are in the same region as the host; it's been like this since multiplayer started working, which it basically didn't at launch, and hasn't been fixed yet) and a pretty awful community. The server browser is an absolute joke as well.
But somehow, this is the pinnacle of hunting games at the moment. Most of its competitors are ridiculously arcade-y, with little replay value. The ballistics in this game are actually very impressive - different bullets drop different distances at range, for instance.
Maybe I just expected something more out of this game. If you took the physics, multiplayer, and weapon selection of the original theHunter, and combined it with the graphics, increased range, and payment model of this game, you'd have a pretty ideal hunting game. And like I said at the beginning, I did enjoy the time I put into this game; it's the fact that I enjoyed the time I put into this game that leaves me wanting more. So I'm giving it a thumb's up, because I felt I got my money's worth, but I definitely think this game is a heap of lost potential.

7/10 - Where to begin.. Mad Max is an enjoyable game to play without thinking. Turn off your brain and shoot things, punch people, blow things up. Travel from one objective to another. I'll destroy this convoy, I'll blow up this scarecrow, I'll go to this location and pickup the collectibles. Do this repeatedly, this is Mad Max.
The story is decent, but short and few inbetween it's roughly 30 hours of playtime (50 for avid completionists).
The combat is similar to the Batman Arkham series so it's enjoyable enough.
Driving: The car mechanics are poor and clunky; it's overall quite bad. The main enjoyment comes from upgrading both the car and Max, adding stronger attack/defence, weapon capabilities etc.
The environments are bland and filled with nothing most of the time. Sometimes it's pretty to stop at certain locations and admire the sun setting or some mountains in the distance, but the majority of the time there's nothing, just sand and more sand.
Overall the game is fun, yet contains heaps of tedious collectibles and does nothing new to push the open world genre forward. I'd say look into it, if you've exhausted better open world games before it.

Let's get this straight: Rogue legacy is not a bad game, Rogue Legacy is not a game with sub-par graphics, audio, visuals, or anything! It has only one rpblem, but this problem ruined it for me.
I know it sounds weird to say that a roguelike has no replay value, but it really doesn't. First off, the only really unique quality it has is that it has character traits, which have been done before. Once you beat the final boss, it just feels like there isn't much to do. There isn't enough variety in the enemies, and more importantly, the characters. All the traits do is hinder you somewhat and that's it! They don't make it feel like an entirely new character, just one with a different disability. I wouldn't recommend this game, but some people will like it.

I can't help but give this game a not recommended. It actually pains me to say that a little bit, because there's so many good parts to Rogue Legacy.
The gameplay is tight, the leveling system is great, the platforming is well executed. Its just that the game's not fair. The fairy chests are almost impossible to get, and very necessary for progression. More often than not, a playthrough will not result in any sort of upgrade. And, there a bunch of rooms that you'll jump into that will immediately screw you over, but because its a rogue-like, means that you couldn't have done anything about it. I can't count the times that I jumped into a room and immediately fell on spikes with no way of knowing that was going to happen. It almost seems like the devs are just messing with you.
That's not to say that there aren't people that I would recommend this game to. Its just that I would only recommend it to very specific people. If you want something you can bang your head against for several hours and don't mind that the game is about as fair as a two-headed coin, than by all means, get it. If you're looking for anything other than something that's wall-punchingly infuriating, you'd probably be better off looking elsewhere.

I liked this game alot.
It's "2DEEP" at times, and tries pretty hard to make you feel like a terrible person for playing it. There's a big argument over the game, mainly that "you could've quit playing at any time!" but ultimately, there's alot of choices that you can't do anything about. The White Phospherous sequence comes to mind. As well as the inability to listen to your orders to not go into the city.
But then there's scenes where you do get a choice, and if you make the wrong one, you will feel like a terrible human being. There's a sequence where you need to disperse a crowd of civilians. Most people will just open fire and slaughter them, but you can fire into the air to get them to leave peacefully.
Stuff like that really makes this game have a unique feel to it. The small touches and attention to detail are fantastic, and really support the game's storyline. The protagonist, Walker, is very much not a hero, as you'll come to find out.
The gameplay works, it's nothing special for a cover based TPS game. It does what it needs to do as a vehicle for the story.
The multiplayer is tacked on, and the devs themselves didn't want to even have a multi-player aspect in the game. The end result is a forced, muddy mess of a game. I would look elsewhere for multiplayer action.
It's not as clever as alot of people make it out to be, but it's a very self-aware and meta game  none the less.

7/10 - Where to begin.. Mad Max is an enjoyable game to play without thinking. Turn off your brain and shoot things, punch people, blow things up. Travel from one objective to another. I'll destroy this convoy, I'll blow up this scarecrow, I'll go to this location and pickup the collectibles. Do this repeatedly, this is Mad Max.
The story is decent, but short and few inbetween it's roughly 30 hours of playtime (50 for avid completionists).
The combat is similar to the Batman Arkham series so it's enjoyable enough.
Driving: The car mechanics are poor and clunky; it's overall quite bad. The main enjoyment comes from upgrading both the car and Max, adding stronger attack/defence, weapon capabilities etc.
The environments are bland and filled with nothing most of the time. Sometimes it's pretty to stop at certain locations and admire the sun setting or some mountains in the distance, but the majority of the time there's nothing, just sand and more sand.
Overall the game is fun, yet contains heaps of tedious collectibles and does nothing new to push the open world genre forward. I'd say look into it, if you've exhausted better open world games before it.

All in all it's a really good game, but what it could have made great would be to have more variety in the rooms that are randomly stitched together.  After some 10/20 hours you have seen them all and there are no surprises anymore. I never understood why game developer don't offer basic tools or integrate the steam workshop in these kind of games. It would really help boosting the replayability.
I play it anyways, because the game mechanics are rock-solid. The jumping is smooth, the difficulty rises in a good manner and the enemies are fair.
The (gamepad) controls are great, except that the way you can attack is a bit odd in my mind. It is hard to explain without playing it, but you can attack "backwards", meaning that when you attack and go in the opposite direction, you kind of "slide back" instead of turning (you have to do this very fast). This is no glitch, since at least one character trait disables this "behavior". Also, this behavior is required to unlock the contents of some chests. I don't know what to think of this... having played old-school JnRs, this style of control is a bit weird and takes a while to get used to, especially when you're in a hassle and instead of dealing a blow to an enemy that is behind you, you can accidentally "slide back" and instead of hitting it, you run into it...
Also I think it's extremely annoying not being able to look up or down like in 2D-JnRs from the 90's (you stand still, hold up/down and you can look a bit up or down respectively). Somedays it just sucks to be alive.
Your entire life, defined by a Castle.
A Castle filled with hatred for all who explore it.
Whether it's by monsters or traps, you're going to die, just like your ancestors.
When your children come of age, they will lose their lives to this castle as well.
Upon starting Rogue Legacy, you're bound to ask yourself "What does everyone see in this game?" You'll walk into a room, and there will be wizards filling the screen with projectiles. This isn't a 2D shooter, and your hit-box is your entire body. Along with the wizards, there might be spiked floors, a couple knights, some evil paintings, and bone-tossing skeletons. Your options consist of finding another way around, attempting to fight your way through, or you could just die. Better luck next time right?
With Rogue Legacy, maybe next time will result in better luck. The keyword is in the title: Rogue. Unless decided otherwise, the layout of the castle is always random. The goal is to find each of the four boss-monster lairs to open the way to the finale. There are multiple areas to explore, and each room contains a multitude of possibilities. Your next attempt may result in more treasure, less frustrating enemy combinations, or it could be even worse and you'll die before you manage to explore three rooms.
Unlike its inspiration, Rogue Legacy isn't entirely sadistic. Your stats & equipment are carried over no matter how many times you die. Before the beginning of each adventure you can use the gold acquired in the last ill-fated adventure to purchase upgrades. These run the gamut of stat-gains, new classes, better equipment as well as ability-bestowing runes, and a few other niceties. Basically, you're expected to die. Unless you're completely miserable at the game, eventually somebody in your lineage will complete it.
However, don't confuse this method of game-design with "I have to grind until the game lets me win."
Rogue Legacy is primarily an action-platformer, meaning your reflexes and quick-thinking are just as if not more likely to keep you alive as a dozen health & armor upgrades. The controls are quite reasonable and extremely versatile with the right combination of runes. Also, if money isn't your immediate concern, weaving in-between the monsters and their attacks can be really enjoyable.
As we've come to expect, merely beating the game isn't enough. There's a new game +, then a ++, and it just keeps going. Each subsequent play-through has stronger enemies, more dangerous traps, and so on. To add to this mounting absurdity, there are a handful of optional bosses to contend with. These ultra-difficult clones force you to use specific class/stat combinations. Since grinding is out of the question, you really have to use every tool to have a chance. Honestly though, it's more frustrating just to trigger these fights. Since the layout is random, there's a high possibility that you won't find the necessary keys. Access to these battles involves finding statues and offering up a prayer (why you would pray for a headache is anyone's guess). Sometimes these statues simply don't spawn, or you don't survive long enough to find them.
More than anything else, if you're going to play Rogue Legacy, see it through to the end. It's an addictive game and well-designed, but trust me on this. Play this game as much as you're willing to stand, then uninstall it, hide it, bury it deep. The one day you revisit this game, load your NG+++++ character, and get dropped in seconds by more bullets than Dodonpachi, all you'll think is "What did I ever see in this game?"

Rogue Legacy, as the title suggests is a Rogue-like. It's got randomly generated elements here and there with psuedo perma-death (You keep everything but your character when you die) which brings in it's 'Legacy' system. This Legacy system allows you to pick another hero, a child of your previous one and they inherit any stat boosts, items or runes (abilities). The overall concept of the game is that you must spawn various heroes to grind your way up to defeat various bosses in order to complete the game. This is one of the weaker points of the game in a way however. If you do not like repetivity then stay away as for the first 20-ish lives (depending on how good you are and how much gold you get) especially, you will constantly loop through the first area just learning the mechanics and enemy types and also trying to defeat the first boss. I have to admit it was a little frustrating and I could only manage like 5 runs before needing a break. It's not all bad though, as when you die you keep any gold you rustled up and that is then used to upgrade your castle (It's an upgrade system that unlocks more as it grows, like a skill tree) You can increase stats such as health, mana, damage and even unlock new class's for your future heroes as well as giving them extra abilities. There's a fair amount of upgrades to choose from so you can tailor it to your personal preference for the most part.
Okay, so let's talk mechanics and gameplay (a bit more in depth) So, as already prefaced, Rogue Legacy has you enter a randomly generated dungeon to face off against various enemies and bosses. The combat is quite simplistic and yet a bit difficult to master, especially downward attacks in my own experience. (This is with a keyboard by the way) Much like the controls themselves it's somewhat tight and has a nice feel to it. You are also given a spell and a class ability to play with which vary in strength and usefulness. The spells are selected at random at the start so this can be a factor which makes you pick Lady Chun Lii III (this game also has references) The Barbarian Queen over Sir Charles the Assassin. The spells are more-so a personal preference of what each person likes and also what you intend on doing with that character as some enemies and bosses are easier to fight with certain classes and spells. Another Mechanic which I have yet to talk about with the Legacy feature is that the characters each have traits, some of these effect the game visually, others gameplay-wise and some just comical. You can have a Giant, a Dwarf, a skinny person, someone who is colour-blind, someone who is permanently roided and the list goes on. Some of these have little effects such as IBS which just makes the character do fart sounds when jumping or dashing. Other traits such as Dwarfism allow for you to get into secret areas for free loot and other little shortcuts. This brings me to another element of the game which is Blueprints and Runes. As you explore the Dungeon you will encounter many a chest, these contain, gold or blueprints with special chests containing stat boosts and Runes. Any blueprint you pick up allows you to craft some new armor and any rune you pick up grants you the ability to add an ability to your character. The Rune Chests come with a price however as you must find them hidden in certain locations or you must complete challenges. Some of these are easier than others. There a many varying abilities which can be stacked to become more powerful, this further adds to that personal customization to play in a way that suits you.
Time for Graphics, Sound and Aesthetics. As you can see from the screenshots and trailer up above, the game does not boast any amazing graphical fidelity, it is quite basic. The Aesthetic however is rather quite pleasing to the eye and has a rather Paper Mario feel to it. When the sprites turn around they flip sides.  It's a nice little nod and it looks quite neat. The designs on the enemies and locations are all pleasant to look at and you can usually tell an enemy from the background (There are enemies that are paintings which can catch you off guard if you don't notice them shaking). The sound design for most of these areas is awesome and is definitely one of the top points of this game. Each piece fits it's location and is enjoyable to listen to. The sound effects of taking damage, dashing etc are well suited and feel right.
I know I have yet to mention it but there is also a story behind Rogue Legacy. I'm not going to spoil it but basically there's an adventurer much like yourself, who's traversing the dungeon. As he goes about, he leaves journal entries behind which allows you to read his story and gives you hints on where to go and such. It's a nice way to add a story to the game which isn't entirely necessary. Also, this guy who's leaving these journals must be pretty good at the game as he goes through the entire thing without dying which is literally impossible for the player. Throughout the game there are also paintings that the devs have left of their previous games with some insight into them. It's a quiant touch that is interesting to read if you are interested,
So that's Rogue Legacy, I would definitely recommend it if you enjoy Rogue-Likes, Dungeon Crawlers or MetroidVanias as this game is a mash of the three. It's a fun 10 hour + raunch through a trap filled, enemy infested loot dungeon that will have you dying for more.

First off, BUY AND PLAY THIS GAME!, It's absolutley fantastic!
Secondly, here's why:
The story is simply too original to describe, People may overlook this game as a basic mil-spec shooter, but it is NOT! The main focus here is the EFFECTS of war on the soldiers not the shooting, although the mechanics work great and the gameplay feels solid too. The story follows 3 soldiers stranded in a dying Dubai, a Dubai they thought they were there to save. Surrounded by a raging sandstorm that is too strong to break through they fight their way through hostile sand covered streets and buildings to reach their goal of saving the civilians trapped there. Although nothing is what it seems.
The twists and turns the story takes almost put the writing of games like Bioshock and GTA to shame.
reviewed the game in their "The best videogame stories ever" article and I feel a direct quote would be sufficient:
"Military shooters don't often rank high on the narrative front, usually favoring gung-ho G.I. Joe antics and flag waving over character development. And, at first, Spec Ops: The Line falls right in line with that stereotype--you take control of Walker, a soldier sent into a sandstorm-ruined Dubai to find a missing general. But as time goes on it becomes more and more obvious that there's something more devious afoot, and the shooter's story transforms from run-of-the-mill to one-of-a-kind.
What unfolds is a damning criticism of shooters themselves, questioning everything that gamers have grown accustom to. Walker's journey sends him marching into the nucleus of the genre, playing with the storytelling in ways no other game has. By the end you might feel anger or sadness, but the important thing is that you'll feel something, and that's pretty rare in military shooters."
I truly feel anyone who can play a shooter, even poorly, NEEDS to experience this game!
Side note, I know it reads out I only have 2.5 hours, but most of the time spent playing through the SP was offline while my internet was disconnected lol.
