This game has so much to do. Unfortunately, most of it is boring, tedious filler.
Graphics:
All credit to the devs; the game looks beautiful and runs great on a wide variety of machines. Although there's a sound issue that hasn't been patched (more on that later). Draw distance, exploisions, particle effects. All top notch.
Controls:
Some of the worst gamepad controls I've ever experienced. The button mapping is non sensical (RT to run LT to jump?). The auto aim is horrible. The crosshairs stick to targets like superglue. When you want to aim at a different target you have to use a ridiculous amount of thumbstick input to switch to a different target and when the cross hairs finally breaks free, your aim goes careening off in one direction because of how much input you had to use. You can use the mouse to aim perfectly well, but I'd rather deal with the horrible aiming than the clunkiness of steering with a keyboard. Sniping suffers from the same auto aim problem but luckily you're stationary so the mouse works fine. Aiming while driving isn't something you actually have to worry about anyway. You can just push the B button and Cumbucket will shoot the most desirable target for you.
Gameplay:
The map is absolutely peppered with activities. Most of which get repetitive really fast. Scavenging locations are next to worthless unless they have a project part (you can track the location of project parts via strongholds so you don't have to keep checking locations looking for them). The ammount of scrap these camp contain isn't worth the time to collect. This is especially true considering there are several ways of collecting scrap faster. For example, in a storm you can easily collect 1200 to 1800 scrap. After looting a scavaging location you'd be lucky to get 18 scrap. Dismantling camps was fun for a while but gets repetitive before too long. The combat is overly simple. It's not quite as easy as the Arkham series. You have to actually face in the direction you want to attack and you don't do 20ft forward rolls all over the place auto targeting enemies in a different zip code. However, you could still probably win a majority of the fights by repeatedly smashing the controller into your face. There are "Top Dog Camps" where you have to take down a different boss each time. By "different each time" I mean exactly the same character model, with exactly the same moves, but colored slightly differently. It's not a challenging fight the first time, certainly not the fifth time. Resources are plentiful. I never even had to think about gas because I never came close to running out. Vehicle combat looks fantastic but mechanically it's very meh. Bump em a few times or just pick a weapon and press the B button over and over. No aiming required, that's done for you. Damage to your vehicle isn't a concern. If you loose all your car's HP you just have to get out and Cumbucket fixes it in no time. There's no penalty for death except for restarting at the last checkpoint which will cost you a few seconds to a minute or so. You won't be dying often anyways. Worst of all though is how few main missions there are. There's maybe a dozen if you count the shorter segments some of the missions have. What you do on these missions usually doesn't vary drastically from what you do in the side activities anyways. I spent a good deal of time doing the side missions to upgrade my car so I didn't have to worry about it towards the end of the game. I figured I was less than halfway through since I just unlocked the V8. I had the car almost completely upgraded and was relieved that all the busy work was done and I could finally continue the main missions. I drove to the next story mission and I discovered that it was the last mission. The final battle was easy and so anticlimactic. The ending sucked. There was no need to upgrade the car as far as I did.
Story: Your car has been stolen. You must upgrade your new car with the help of your companion Cumbucket. That's the whole story. There's a small sub plot but there's no time for it to develop and it's shallow as a kiddie pool. I don't really care though. Story in a video game is like story in a porno. I expect it to be there but I don't really care if it's good. Most of the time I'd rather skip to the action.
Replayability:
Probably a lot if you're a completionist. Very little if you don't enjoy doing the same few tedious activities dozens of times.
Performance:
Again, the game looks and runs great but myself and others have run into a sound glitch. On my machine the ambient sound effects (wind, construction noises) cut in and out constantly. Locking the game to 60 fps fixed it for me.
I can't recommend this game any less. It's not worth $60 especially when there are so many better games in the open world genre alone.

A rollercoaster ride through a storyline of guilt and revenge, Black Ops II opens a new, dark chapter in the lives and military careers of Frank Woods, Alex Mason and Jason Hudson, the protagonists of the original Call of Duty: Black Ops.
The game features two narrative levels, one in the past (1980s) explaining the fateful and tragic events that caused Nicaraguan Raul Menendez to go on a decade-long voyage of vengeance and redemption, and one in the future with David Mason uncovering the mystery behind an imminent catastrophe.
Black Ops II also features storyline choices and different outcomes, optional missions and pre-mission loadout selection as well as campaign mission challenges.
In addition to this extensive singleplayer content, the game also comes with full-fledged co-op Zombie game modes and deep competitive online multiplayer.

(Spoiler-Free review here!)
UNDERTALE is an amazing, humorous and story-rich RPG-like game. With a beautifull soundtrack, amazing storyline, unique gameplay and well-written characters.
At first it didn't really appeal much to me when it first came out and I didn't pay much attention to it either.. But it eventually became very popular and highly reviewed. So I eventually decided to buy it in the Christmas Sale to check it out. And boy, this game is quite an experience!
(The Plot of the game)
You're playing as a Human child, who fell down into the Underground.
The Underground is a place where Monsters live, creatures who once lived with the humans above but where forced to flee to the Underground due to a war between the humans.
Your goal here is to find your way back home through an astounding journey through the mysterious Underground. You'll face dangers and hardships, but you'll stay determined!
Thus begins your tale in the Underground, your Under-Tale.. get it??... ..
(The characters)
UNDERTALE has a varied number of characters, each with their own unique personality's, you'll encouter throughout the game. As mentioned above, I won't spoil the game. But what I can tell you is that these characters will make your joruney great, for they are well-written and you'll easily create a bond with them.
(Aspects of the game)
One of best aspects of the game is the emotional experience you'll recieve during your journey in this land of mystery. And have to say, it doesn't happen often that a game could make to the brink of tears.
You will laugh, you will cry. You'll be angered and you'll be horrified. But the most important ting is that you'll have fun!
During your travels you'll be encoutered by all types of creatures and you get to meet Monsters.
This takes us to another apsect that makes this game so great: Choosing the fate of others.
You see, UNDERTALE is an turn-based RPG. But it isn't just a regular RPG, for this game has a unique feature of battling where you can dodge attacks from enemies. And instead of the old xp-grinding killing sprees, like any other RPG's, is UNDERTALE letting you decide the fate of others by having an option to SPARE an enemy. This spare option can be used to make friends with the characters you'll encounter.
These choices are one of the most importand features tough, for it determines on how the game will end.
(Verdict)
I highly recommend UNDERTALE to anyone I know!
UNDERTALE is one of the very (very) few game wich took me on an emotional journey. The choices you'll make throughout the game will determine the way the game will end for you, making the experience personal.
Everything from this game is truly magnificent. From the story, to the beautiful surrounding, to the enjoyable characters and the amazing soundtrack! (I highly reccomend buying the soundtrack with the game btw..).
I assure you that playing this game will give you an unique experience. And most importantly: fill you with *determination*!
9/10
UNDERTALE lives up to its popular and highly reviewed reputation. And if you're wondering whether you'll buy the game or not, I highly reccomend it. This game is worth the price!

While suffering from quirky controls (for example, the run button - default spacebar, seemed at times like it was stuck and when I pressed it once, it had me run into a crowd of enemies; at other times, it felt like I was stuck to the wall like flypaper and couldn't run away from a thrown grenade), this was one of the first FPS that actually had me regretting some of the actions I've done, rather than acting like a blind pawn in a rush toward the next objective (cough, CoD, cough). Let's just say that a certain group of people would have still been alive, if I had known I could have spared their lives without murdering them in cold blood.
Of course, it is a welcome (and creepy) change of pace when the game starts addressing some messages to you, the player or "special guest", during the loading screens toward the end about some of the moral choices you made earlier in the game ("The Army does not condone the killing of unarmed civilians, but it's only a game, why should you care?")
A somber storyline with actually difficult enemy firefights (i.e. heavies), not to mention endings that made me feel like I completed the game rather than act as a setup for a sequel. makes this game worthwhile to rise to the top among other FPS of this time. What will Yaeger Development think of next?

Game reminds me a LOT of Binary Domain; another third-person shooter (wall humping and military lingo included) with average gameplay and a fantastic plot. I'm not gonna dwell too long on the game mechanics. It's typical stuff with nothing impressive or worth mentioning. This is one of those games that's more about everything BESIDES the gameplay, which says more about the writing than anything negative about the gameplay. I will only complain about one thing: the game has mechanics that are severely underused. Specifically, silencers, which would let you sneak around getting kills if the game dedicated more to that aspect.
Anyway, the plot is fantastic, and its SPECTACULAR how it handles good and evil. Ultimately, the paradigm (big word alert) is meaningless here; everyone has their motives and reasons for doing what they do. The game weaves a complex narrative that ultimately pins you as neither a 'good guy' nor a 'bad guy'; you are merely someone doing what he believes is right. Emphasis on ''believes'' because all supposedly moral actions in this game are subject to questioning.
I love the title for that alone. I love when villains are given motives and reasons for their actions other than ''I am bad raawr come get me in my evil evil castle''. They took it a step further by making the protagonist's morality ambiguous as well, and you get to shape some of it along the way. There are some segments where you have to make choices, and the writing makes it so that each option in these segments is a valid choice. Moral choices in games tend to boil down to ''kill grandma; don't kill grandma'', so there's never really any critical thinking involved; developers take note, this game does it right.
I could go on and on about how the pacing is done very well and how I love the narrative. But I'll end on a few unrelated notes:
-For a console game this♥♥♥♥♥♥looks great. This dude's bald head is so...so
.
-The menu changes as you play the title, which is a cool touch. It's little things like that that give a title some flavor.
-The game is loosely based on an old novel from the 19th century. So, like Binary Domain, it isn't exactly original.
-You might not get sound in pre-rendered cut-scenes. It's a bug having to do with NVIDIA cards or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ Anyway, the fix is insanely simple and there's a thread on the forums about it. Or you could watch pre-rendered stuff on youtube.
The game's pretty short and straight-forward. I love strong narratives so I can't recommend this enough. And while you're at it, pick up Binary Domain as well.

This game has so much to do. Unfortunately, most of it is boring, tedious filler.
Graphics:
All credit to the devs; the game looks beautiful and runs great on a wide variety of machines. Although there's a sound issue that hasn't been patched (more on that later). Draw distance, exploisions, particle effects. All top notch.
Controls:
Some of the worst gamepad controls I've ever experienced. The button mapping is non sensical (RT to run LT to jump?). The auto aim is horrible. The crosshairs stick to targets like superglue. When you want to aim at a different target you have to use a ridiculous amount of thumbstick input to switch to a different target and when the cross hairs finally breaks free, your aim goes careening off in one direction because of how much input you had to use. You can use the mouse to aim perfectly well, but I'd rather deal with the horrible aiming than the clunkiness of steering with a keyboard. Sniping suffers from the same auto aim problem but luckily you're stationary so the mouse works fine. Aiming while driving isn't something you actually have to worry about anyway. You can just push the B button and Cumbucket will shoot the most desirable target for you.
Gameplay:
The map is absolutely peppered with activities. Most of which get repetitive really fast. Scavenging locations are next to worthless unless they have a project part (you can track the location of project parts via strongholds so you don't have to keep checking locations looking for them). The ammount of scrap these camp contain isn't worth the time to collect. This is especially true considering there are several ways of collecting scrap faster. For example, in a storm you can easily collect 1200 to 1800 scrap. After looting a scavaging location you'd be lucky to get 18 scrap. Dismantling camps was fun for a while but gets repetitive before too long. The combat is overly simple. It's not quite as easy as the Arkham series. You have to actually face in the direction you want to attack and you don't do 20ft forward rolls all over the place auto targeting enemies in a different zip code. However, you could still probably win a majority of the fights by repeatedly smashing the controller into your face. There are "Top Dog Camps" where you have to take down a different boss each time. By "different each time" I mean exactly the same character model, with exactly the same moves, but colored slightly differently. It's not a challenging fight the first time, certainly not the fifth time. Resources are plentiful. I never even had to think about gas because I never came close to running out. Vehicle combat looks fantastic but mechanically it's very meh. Bump em a few times or just pick a weapon and press the B button over and over. No aiming required, that's done for you. Damage to your vehicle isn't a concern. If you loose all your car's HP you just have to get out and Cumbucket fixes it in no time. There's no penalty for death except for restarting at the last checkpoint which will cost you a few seconds to a minute or so. You won't be dying often anyways. Worst of all though is how few main missions there are. There's maybe a dozen if you count the shorter segments some of the missions have. What you do on these missions usually doesn't vary drastically from what you do in the side activities anyways. I spent a good deal of time doing the side missions to upgrade my car so I didn't have to worry about it towards the end of the game. I figured I was less than halfway through since I just unlocked the V8. I had the car almost completely upgraded and was relieved that all the busy work was done and I could finally continue the main missions. I drove to the next story mission and I discovered that it was the last mission. The final battle was easy and so anticlimactic. The ending sucked. There was no need to upgrade the car as far as I did.
Story: Your car has been stolen. You must upgrade your new car with the help of your companion Cumbucket. That's the whole story. There's a small sub plot but there's no time for it to develop and it's shallow as a kiddie pool. I don't really care though. Story in a video game is like story in a porno. I expect it to be there but I don't really care if it's good. Most of the time I'd rather skip to the action.
Replayability:
Probably a lot if you're a completionist. Very little if you don't enjoy doing the same few tedious activities dozens of times.
Performance:
Again, the game looks and runs great but myself and others have run into a sound glitch. On my machine the ambient sound effects (wind, construction noises) cut in and out constantly. Locking the game to 60 fps fixed it for me.
I can't recommend this game any less. It's not worth $60 especially when there are so many better games in the open world genre alone.

Hooo boy here comes Undertale flying in. Where to start with this one? It's more than meets the eye, if you catch my drift.
As far as RPGs that feel like they were made in a program that's called Role Playing Game Maker; few have stuck around long enough to capture my attention. Here comes this curious little game, that's garnered quite the following; and the following is still there. Drawing pictures. Making memes. Being nerds. Kinda reminds me of the homestuck folks, but somehow more acessable and less unbareably niche.
So let me tell you about my experience as a lay man. I dropped money on this game because I heard good things about it. That and the fan base persists as it does, which is either a sign of the worst thing in the world, a horribly mediocre thing in the world, or the best thing in the world. Ok, I can tell that the fans don't factor in the game a lot; but it is telling that something like this was able to sustain attention while looking like some kind of freaky child of Yume Nikki and Earthbound, but somehow not inventive or interesting enough to imitate either of them.
They knew they were making memes! And accessible memes at that! The dogs! The weird cat things! Here's my biggest issue: the game suffers from a lack of direction! BAM! Yeah, everything looks cute and all the monsters look like lovable stuffed animals, so what? Wait until you're smack dab in the middle of an actually good bossfight, and you have to worry about if you're going to kill a monster; or questions about your morality when you're actually confronted with someone who intends to kill you. Kinda ♥♥♥♥s with the whole tone, doesn't it?
Who was this game made for? The babbys? Look, there's some pretty heavy subject matter here. It doesn't matter how hard you try to distract me with beating up vegetables, or throwing stupid memes everywhere. Spec Ops: The Line.
To start of with I throught this game was just one of those games were everyone would ignore it, and it would just quietly past by in the corner. But no this game is a hidden gem, here is why.
Spec Ops The Line is a 3rd person shooter, with a cover system. But Unlike the rest, this one is more story driven, this makes a massive difference to the way this game plays.
Graphics, this game looked stunning when it first came out, and it still does now. The Devs really put alot of attension to detial and passion into this game..
The charators look good and they animate very well, voice sync is pretty much perfect to lip movement etc. The guns you can tell what they are, but remember this is a 3rd person shooter.
Finally the envirment, just wow, however word of warning which comes with a spoiler alert...This game turns...Dark and sinister quite quickly, now I did warn you that this one is different.
Sounds, the weapons sound belivable, but when playing I m spending most of my time not getting shot than I am admiring the sound of the weapons. Explosions have a bassy smooth boom to them, the envirment itself when not in a fire fight is quite quiet all you can hear is the wind howling around the buildings and things moving about in the wind.
Music is quite unnoticable during quiet stages of the game, just your standard low intensity tranquil music, till later in the game were the music turns, darker... the firefights the music does pick up but its over showed by the firefight itself.
Last, voice acting. These are fantasic I mean they would be, this is a story driven 3 rd person shooter. You can even hear the mood in the voices they are that well done.
Story, without giving away too much, this game is based in a storm ridden dubia, you are leader of 3 Spec ops trying to find survers and the "dammed 31St"..But what you acturly find is..a place full of chaos, and civial war. This is all I m wanting to give away.
Gameplay, as I said this game is a 3rd person shooter. To that point it plays like any other, it does have a cover system and the controls are tight mostly( althrough they are simifyed for consles) so one button does 3 different things basicly..This can cause issues but I get that.
As for its gun play it is very tight, and when one knows how the game works and how to move and get the cover system to work with you, than you are in for a great time. I almost forgot to mention about the basic squad commands, but your AI ( and the enamy ai) is pretty good they can take care of themselves and take down thier foes.
Now as I mentioned this game takes a turn, and turns very dark..What I mean is this you get some very odd choices, even through the gameplay is liner its not do this this this..It lets you chose. But in general the devs want you to see the choas and the darkness here, and its that which gives this game a personalilty.
Conclustion
Spec Ops the line is a great 3 rd person, and it has a great story to back it up, and the way it delivers that story, with great voice acting..Its a great expierance and a joy to see it.
This 3rd person is going to be very hard to beat and has alot going for it I feel.

This is a well known game, is not in need of additional reviews, so I will just correct some of the misunderstandings about this.
1) This is NOT a roguelike. Yes there are some similarities, "Rogue" in the name, you have only one life at each play, and a bit of randomization.
There are also many features of this game which makes it not a roguelike.
a)
It lacks proper RPG gameplay, since each class has only two upgrades and these upgrades are for between playthroughs not included in them. so you get stronger each time you die, but your strength is constant for only one gameplay time.
b)
Bosses are predefined. Some memorization or... grinding is required for a usual player. Reflexes do matter, also your grinding time. Mostly, your strategy does not.
c)
Yes, there is grinding. SInce there is persistance between lives. The game also gets harder by your newly bought upgrades, but it scales a bit slower, so yeah you are expected to grind as hell.
d)
since I already said that ur strength wont increase between two deaths, after getting enough "level"s rushing through bosses is a viable strategy. Think about average roguelike and you will see that calling this game a roguelike just because it is hard, semirandomized is stupid.
e)
Apart from looping with ever getting harder enemies, this game has a goal. So you can finish it. By finishing I am also meaning, being done with it, in like 20 hours or so. Yeah there is replayability, but you will be grinding the same stats all over again.
2) Saying this is not a roguelike is not a negative criticism like many thinks, just a categorization.
It is a nice game, I enjoyed playing it, and finishing it. Mechanics are weird, most are solid. I had my fun. For me Barbarian and Shinobi seemed much more stronger than the others but I guess they are actually balanced. Music were quite nice, atmosphere is also nice. Not many are on with me with this I guess, but writing in Prince's Journal was quite high quality material, and one of the strongest aspects for me. I kept playing until I see the end of the journal, and slowed down afterwards. There are some unique mechanisms like Architect, and insanity in the fiber of the Castle is really well thought. So a well designed cross genre platformer, I am satisfied with what I got.
TLDR: This is NOT a good roguelike. This IS a good game.

Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a very moving successor to the original series. It is easy to identify with the characters and find oneself immersed in the storyline. For anyone who loved Life is Strange this game should be one that you would also find enjoyable!

When the game was first announced, I was a bit hesitant. An unknown developer taking on a prequel for Life is Strange? Without the original voice actors? It seemed like it was just going for a quick cash grab or was going to be a trainwreck.
I was very happy to be wrong.
The game isn't complete yet. At the time of writing this, only two out of the three episodes have released. But those two episodes have been excellent so far. The writing is on point. The dialogue is wonderful, the characters are fully realized, and some of the choices are genuienly tough. The backtalk mechanic is fun and perfectly suits Chloe. It doesn't feel like it's set apart from the Life is Strange universe - it feels like a natural addition to the whole thing, and really makes me wish that Deck Nine will get more chances to write games in this universe.
The music is also exceptional. The ambient soundtrack and the musical soundtrack have both been fantastic so far.
That's not to say that it's perfect. For the most part, I like the voice acting, but some voices are just so different from the original game that it's hard to get past. Chloe is no longer voiced by Ashly Burch, and while the replacement does a good job, there are moments where it takes me out of the game because it doesn't sound quite right. Some characters, like Dana or David, sound completely different.
The story also feels a bit too fast at times as well. WIth only three episodes total, it feels like there's a lot of things to wrap up by the final episode. I feel confident that they can pull it off, but I can't say for certain. There's also a handful of elements that don't line up with the original game and how they were described there, but it's nothing that's big enough to ruin the experience for me.
So far it's been a great experience and I'm glad to have been proven wrong about my initial misgivings. I'm definitely looking forward to the final episode and the bonus episode that will follow. If you liked the original game, you'll definitely enjoy this one. It really offers a unique insight into Chloe's character and what her life was like before Max came back into the picture. I never thought I'd fall in love with Rachel Amber, but much like the rest of the town, I just couldn't help myself.
A really awesome game with a lot of choices. Despite the whole outcry because of anti-piracy software this is a very solid game that actually develop the characters more than some other games.

This game has great progression and a variety of utility options.  There are many design strategies for buildings you can think of, or find online.  I really enjoyed learning about the mechanics and materials, and playing with a massive amount of people that can vary from friendly to kill-on-sight.  Each play session is different because you'll always have different encounters, whether it's accidentally stepping on territory owned by a clan, running out of supplies and dying by nature, or unexpectedly running into a bear.
The downside of this game for me was when I finally learned pretty much everything, and I realized something: there is virtually no way to fully protect your gear and home from other players.  There is always a way for people to find a way to either destroy, or infiltrate your base.  Whether its C4, or even rocket launchers-- any wall, any door, can be broken.  So you can never really rest assured that your gear is safe.  That reason alone makes this game a whole lot harder later.  You have to be prepared to lose everything at any point, and the only exception to that is if you join a large group/clan.
Solo/duo gameplay is fun, but only if you don't care about sustainabililty.  Server hosts understand that this is a thing, so most servers are wiped clean every week or two.  Basically, this game isn't about long-term progression.  If that's what you want, this isn't for you.  Honestly, I think this game would be more interesting if it did something like survival of the fittest, starting with a set amount of players, and if you die you're kicked off the server until the next cycle.  That way the game fully embraces its short-term playstyle.  Instead, you're given this false sense of security with elaborate building possibilities and extensive upgrading, which is essentially all pointless if someone passes by your house with a few C4 explosives on hand, which unfortunately is common.
All this being said:  this game is fun.  Is it worth checking out?  Yes.  Is it a game you can sink endless hours into?  Yes.  Do I recommend it? ..Yes.
Just don't get the wrong idea.  You won't live long.  You're never safe.  Don't get attached to your accomplishments.  Cause odds are you'll log back in tomorrow and you'll be either raided, or dead.

TL:DR - It's open world, but there's no story to speak of.
I'm about fifteen hours in so far. It feels like the open world is there but the game is missing.
PRO: The desert is beautifully made, and the day-night cycle brings some lifelike and pretty sunsets and sunrises - if this is the world post-apocalypse, well, maybe it won't be all that bad.
CON: Quite simply, there's not much variety. You drive from place to place and when you encounter something you either fight with it if it moves, or ram it with your car if it doesn't. There are perhaps four types of encounter - other vehicles (easiest dealt with by ripping off a wheel with the harpoon), generic thugs (hit, parry, hit, parry until everyone else is dead), desert wanderers in need of water (give water) and watchers conveniently positioned outside big enemy camps to give you information. There are no puzzles to solve, nothing to figure out, no dialogue options, and thus far precious little storyline either.
Most of what goes on is completely inexplicable:
- The big chief has fuel convoys roaming the world, only they're not going anywhere but rather driving tight, pre-defined routes such that they lap about once every two minutes, never stopping to pick up or drop off fuel.
- The deserts are full of wanderers, none of whom have any water, but none of whom have thought to head for a friendly stronghold either.
- When you're running low on health, you can recover by eating a handy open can of dog food. Well, great, but the desert you're in was once the sea. Why was the sea full of tins of dog food?
- Part of what storyline there is involves bulding up your car (of course). Parts are very scarce, and you appear to be the only person besides the bad guy factions that actually has a vehicle. So you'd think that every truck you met would be unique, right? Wrong. Enemy vehicles - well, somehow the sea bed looks to have been full of old VW Beetles just waiting to be customised. Were Beetles a big thing in Australia? Will the great world-ending nuclear war somehow be presaged by a revival of the Beetle custom scene?
In summary, if you like to drive and to punch people, you might enjoy this for a little while, but no effort has been made to create an immersive story-driven experience or to give any sort of meaning to the various repetitive mini challenges that make up the bulk of the gameplay. Save your money.

Spec Ops: The Line.
To start of with I throught this game was just one of those games were everyone would ignore it, and it would just quietly past by in the corner. But no this game is a hidden gem, here is why.
Spec Ops The Line is a 3rd person shooter, with a cover system. But Unlike the rest, this one is more story driven, this makes a massive difference to the way this game plays.
Graphics, this game looked stunning when it first came out, and it still does now. The Devs really put alot of attension to detial and passion into this game..
The charators look good and they animate very well, voice sync is pretty much perfect to lip movement etc. The guns you can tell what they are, but remember this is a 3rd person shooter.
Finally the envirment, just wow, however word of warning which comes with a spoiler alert...This game turns...Dark and sinister quite quickly, now I did warn you that this one is different.
Sounds, the weapons sound belivable, but when playing I m spending most of my time not getting shot than I am admiring the sound of the weapons. Explosions have a bassy smooth boom to them, the envirment itself when not in a fire fight is quite quiet all you can hear is the wind howling around the buildings and things moving about in the wind.
Music is quite unnoticable during quiet stages of the game, just your standard low intensity tranquil music, till later in the game were the music turns, darker... the firefights the music does pick up but its over showed by the firefight itself.
Last, voice acting. These are fantasic I mean they would be, this is a story driven 3 rd person shooter. You can even hear the mood in the voices they are that well done.
Story, without giving away too much, this game is based in a storm ridden dubia, you are leader of 3 Spec ops trying to find survers and the "dammed 31St"..But what you acturly find is..a place full of chaos, and civial war. This is all I m wanting to give away.
Gameplay, as I said this game is a 3rd person shooter. To that point it plays like any other, it does have a cover system and the controls are tight mostly( althrough they are simifyed for consles) so one button does 3 different things basicly..This can cause issues but I get that.
As for its gun play it is very tight, and when one knows how the game works and how to move and get the cover system to work with you, than you are in for a great time. I almost forgot to mention about the basic squad commands, but your AI ( and the enamy ai) is pretty good they can take care of themselves and take down thier foes.
Now as I mentioned this game takes a turn, and turns very dark..What I mean is this you get some very odd choices, even through the gameplay is liner its not do this this this..It lets you chose. But in general the devs want you to see the choas and the darkness here, and its that which gives this game a personalilty.
Conclustion
Spec Ops the line is a great 3 rd person, and it has a great story to back it up, and the way it delivers that story, with great voice acting..Its a great expierance and a joy to see it.
This 3rd person is going to be very hard to beat and has alot going for it I feel.

Life is Strange & Life is Strange: Before the Storm are games you need to play to understand why people love them so so much. You just can't judge them by looking in from the outside, you need to experience them from the inside. So much more than a game, I would call it a Journey.
Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a prequel to Life is Strange, a prequel you must play after the game it is supposed to precede (in my opinion). You will get so much more from both games this way.
The story follows a teenager who believes the World is out to punish her, has lost faith in everything and is on the road to self destruction. That is until she meets someone who will change her life forever, for better or worse.
The characters, World and story are well written, designed and executed perfectly. They all just knit together so well. Envision your favorite book, film and music all entwined into one package and that still would not do it justice.
Easily makes it into my favorite games of all time, highly recommended. Well done to the Developers, Artists and Actors, incredible work. I look forward to all future Deck Nine games.

I had pre-ordered the Deluxe version of the game a couple months before release and have been playing the episodes as they have been released. (No spoilers.)
EDIT: Have played Episodes 1, 2 and 3.
Also, warning about those who have not played the first Life is Strange.
There is a MAJOR spoiler that they put at the conclusion of Episode 3 involving Rachel Amber.
For those who worry about it only being three episodes, I should mention that the question of why came up during the panel too. I remember that a person had asked if Square Enix had limited Deck Nine from the amount of episodes they could have, and they actually insisted that was not the case. They said that when they came forward to look into writing a story, they felt that three episodes would be more than enough.
And I think it's pretty clear that in each episode, A LOT happens.
Have officially finished all three episodes and I can safely say that the story feels complete by the end.
The music is also sublime. The styles and tone differs a little slightly from the first game and is clearly fitting towards Chloe, and I think Daughter composes some beautiful songs that really complete the mood for a lot of scenes in the game. (There is also a song that was written and performed by the developers of Deck Nine in the game which is supposed to be the "demo" of Pisshead.)
Visually, the game retains a lot of the style of the original, though upon closer examination, you can also find that they improved a lot of small things like the idle and secondary animations of the characters as well as facial expressions. The game also has a lot of beautiful moments and is great to explore through. Deck Nine has also kept the "pondering" moments that were in the original game where Chloe will sit and take in the scenery with music playing and her just thinking about the current situation. (And these moments can be stopped short or skipped at anytime if people want to.)
I think the other thing I enjoy is the attention to the character development. Rachel's characterization is probably the most fascinating and it matches well with what you find out about her from Max's pov in the first game. Being able to see things from Chloe's perspective also changes a lot in how you view her later actions in the first game too. And I think what I appreciate most is that Max is constantly mentioned passively by Chloe despite being largely absent. (Be sure to check Chloe's journal throughout each episode as things will change depending on the situation!)
As for Deluxe Version and how it goes so far, I think it is quite nice.
I enjoy having the extra outfits for Chloe to play through and I am also enjoying the Mixtape Mode where you can listen to music and watch Chloe chilling out in her room. I think as a pre-order it's not totally necessary considering we haven't gotten that "Farewell" episode yet.
When the game is on sale, I think people would enjoy it though. Wait a bit and see how everything pans out before committing to the Deluxe Version.

Call of Duty разделена на три части: одиночная кампания, мультиплеер, кооперативный режим с зомби.  В игре мы играем в разных временных промежутках и от лица двух героев мы наблюдем за развитием сюжета. Игра предоставит нам некую свободу действий и даже несколько концовок.  В игре используют движок IW 3.0 engine, обновленный модификациями. В глаза бросается консольное бремя и древность движка. Движок дополнен яркими красками, спецэффектами и текстурами. В результате мы видим красивую картинку. Моя оценка 9/10.
В мультиплеере мы видим, что появились новые карты, режимы, оружие. Сражения будут проходить в 2025-м году, где игрокам предстоит сражаться, используя большое количество разнообразной техники. Роботы, беспилотники, фантастическое оружие — все это станет частью мультиплеерных матчей. Моя  оценка 9/10.
В кооперативном режиме борьбы с зомби появились новые режимы. Четверо игроков могут столкнуться с ними в «Выживании», «Проблеме» и «Транзите». В первом режиме мы отстреливаемся от зомби на определённой карте до победного. Во втором две команды соревнуются в том, кто лучше стреляет. В третьем команда от карты к карте путешествует на инфернальном автобусе, управляемом роботом. Моя оценка 7/10.

Switching the resolution to my NVidia's dynamic screen resolution OR the native screen resolution made it unusable due to the false mouse positioning mentioned earlier. Regrettably, I'm about to try the game out despite all these problems. Will update the review later.
[Final Update]

Club Penguin is a massively multiplayer online game (MMO) involving a virtual world containing a range of online games and activities, created by New Horizon Interactive (now known as Disney Canada Inc.) using SmartFoxServer.[1] Players use cartoon penguin-avatars and play in a winter-set virtual world. After beta-testing, Club Penguin was made available to the general public on October 24, 2005[2] and has since expanded into a large online community —growing to the extent that by late 2007, it was claimed that Club Penguin had over 30 million user accounts.[3] As of July 2013, Club Penguin has over 200 million registered user accounts.[4]
While free memberships are available, revenue is predominantly raised through paid memberships which allow players to access a range of additional features, such as the ability to purchase virtual clothing, furniture, and in-game pets called "puffles" for their penguins through the use of in-game currency.The success of Club Penguin led to New Horizon being purchased by The Walt Disney Company in August 2007 for the sum of 350 million dollars, with an additional 350 million dollars in bonuses should specific targets be met by 2009.[5]
The game is specifically designed for children aged 6 to 14, however, users of any age are allowed to play Club Penguin.[6] Thus a major focus of the developers has been on child safety,[7] with a number of features introduced to the game to facilitate this — including offering an "Ultimate Safe Chat" mode, whereby users select their comments from a menu; filtering that prevents swearing and the revelation of personal information;[7] and moderators who patrol the game.[8] The game has been criticized for teaching consumerism[9] and allowing players to "cheat".[10]

for a piece of assessment I had to review a game and I chose Rogue Legacy.
This assessment was for CIU 110 and had to be roughly 500 words so there is a lot of reading...
Rogue Legacy is a 2d rogue-like action platformer RPG in which you enter the castle Hanson looking for a way to cure the king and be made next heir to the throne.
The game is set in a medieval time period that contains myths and magic and you’re son to a knight who disappeared in the castle Hanson and are  most likely afflicted with a condition such as Alektorophobia, (Fear of chickens) Coprolalia, (Similar to Tourette’s) or even dwarfism (shorter than usual) to name a few. So, as the only reasonable decision you give all your wealth to Charon the gatekeeper and enter the castle yourself.
Almost inevitably players will notice the rogue-like elements around the time they notice the platforming element, as you will die a lot and very often. By default the mechanics are easy to understand and won’t take much effort to remember, with any complex mechanics being explained so they can be mastered easily. A much greater emphasis would be needed on spacing as all enemies deal full damage on contact and can easily overwhelm the player, although a much greater number of enemies will simply wait for the best time to attack in an effort to kill you with a barrage of projectiles, without moving at all. If the player is having difficulty they can spend gold earned each life towards upgrades to their home keep to give themselves access to new classes which the player may potentially be allowed to select on dying(if you die you play as your heir after). The player also has the option to get a permanent buff to a statistic such as health or mana for example (there are several other stats). If the player would prefer they can also purchase new pieces of armour or runes that give the player new abilities, but this requires schematics acquired from dungeon chests.
In Rogue Legacy random chance is used to decide a great number of always changing variables, which is extremely prevalent as a feature of the game. Not only does the players heir get to be one of three potential candidates, all of which are randomly rolled, but the entire castle can be made to be completely different every time the player dies. Schematics are found throughout the world in chests but only a few chests actually guarantee them, instead there is a random chance that each chest can contain a schematic with a much higher chance that they contain only gold, or a single health or mana item.
So far this would have given mainly a view of mechanics and player experience, but there simply isn’t much focus on the story of rogue legacy. The story is revealed to the player by way of journals of a fellow knight who is going through the same journey. As for aesthetics, while the game has no stunning visuals, bosses can be quite daunting and projectiles and threats stand out vividly against interesting backgrounds that allow a player to easily recognise what actions they should take to pass through the sections of the castle Hanson unscathed.
Altogether Rogue Legacy is successful in creating a complex and expansive adventure with a surprising amount of replay value, the story although short felt immersive and believable.

Enjoyed the game though came to it with mixed feelings based on some reviews which concluded how mediocre it is. I can't say I agree with those reviews.
It does take a bit of grind to get to the unlocks but it doesn't get too repetitive. You probably can't just speed through the main storyline without doing the RPG thing or you'd be pounded by the end game enemies. On the plus side, vehicle combat is fun, though a bit simplistic. Keyboard driving is a bit jerky at times - you can spin out for holding down the directional key for 20 ms too long (exagerating). Ground combat is also fun - if you played any of the Batman games, you'll feel right at home. Story itself is not exactly a masterpiece and somewhat follows original Mad Max. It's nice to see a game where health doesn't just regenerate on its own but you have to manage water and find food sources to restore health.
There's a few bugs in the game through nothing game braing. Sometimes the bugs manifest as hilarious glitches. Things that have happened:
- When harponing the ground enemies from the car and you yank the harpoon back, the enemy sometimes get smashed into the car and gets stuck in between doors, windows or on spikes. Ragdol physics sometimes provide a great deal of fun before the imposter is dislodged
- When leaving the car, sometimes and for no aparent reason, yourself and the car get ragdolled. Funny to watch, not so fun when there's enemies about and Max is hurdling through the air.
- one of the enemies in a camp got stuck behing a fence so I went about collecting scrap. He somehow magically teleported out and started whacking me out of nowhere
- occasional glitches where enemies and cars dissapear / spawn, enemies glitch around battlefield to be in position for execution move
- a storm that never stopped. Ended up quiting to loading screen and reloading a save which fixed it
In summary, there's lots of fun things to do, sotry line isn't too bad. Not sure about the re-play value, perhaps in a years time? Oh - there's not multiplayer which is how it should be, at least they focused on single player experience.

I got this for free - I would never have bought it otherwise.
The game surprised me with its story and depth.
On the surface it is just another cover-shooter - nothing you have not seen before. But the story and premise is something else, and quite worth your time. Consider it more a cinmetaic experience that you are playing through. The story is well integrated in the actual gameplay, and cut-scenes are not invasive. You'll also find intelligence along the way, that further deepens the story. The voice acting is very well done.
It is very impressive graphically though, and many scenes are beautiful. Detailed face-expressions help the game make it emmotionally immersive.
You are often faced with tough choices that you don't want to make. In the end it does not seem what choice you make, but it still leaves a heavy impact on you.
The combat and mechanics are still good. Guns behave and sound well. The cover mechanics are ok. Sometimes you don't end up doing what you intended to do, but it workds most of the time. Your companions and AI chatters a lot, giving you good intel on the battle field, also further immerse you in the tone and feel of the game.
I like that the enemy has been given a voice and humanity too - you won't always want to attack them.
It seems to be designed with a controller in mind, and it works ok, but mouse and keyboard is still the better experience.
This game is about the story - and does not seem to have any replayability. Mechanics are good, but nothing new. Multiplayer is not really interesting, but the main game was a good experience that kept me hooked through the whole campaign.
Reckommended.

Right off the bat, I can say with confidence that this time around. Activision/Tryarch actually gave a crap about it's singer player experience with this game. The story and plot is engrossing, the characters well rounded, and you actually feel emotions for the first time in a CoD game about what happens to it's characters throughout the game, as well as a villian that actually makes complete sense and you get a feel for as the game fleshes him out the more the story goes on. As for the Multiplayer, it's both good and bad, some new tweaks with weapons, attachments and scorestreaks  are welcome additions, but the hit detection is still hit and miss and some weapon combos are OP as per CoD style. Maps are also hit and miss with some feeling too cramped and too many choke points that make you dread to play. While others are so open, you will be afraid to move half the time for fear of having your head blown clean off by a sniper. Zombies is still fun as ever with a group of people in constant communication with some new twists and turns, but nothing too wildly different from the norm of Treyarch's usual games. Even though BLOPS 2 isn't the savior of the entire CoD franchise like so many were lead to belive, it's Still a boat load of fun when you get bored of other high intensity FPS games, and want somehting fast and served hot to kill the time. I highly enjoyed the singleplayer campaign, so if anything definitly try it out for that portion alone. If you are Looking for a well rounded arcade shooter with a side of meat for the SP side of things?  look no further.

I'm sad to give this game a negative review, but after the last gaming session with my friends I'm terribly disappointed in the Game's development process.
So the first time I've picked up Gang Beasts was probably a year ago (maybe even longer). I invited some friends over we played it all night long. It was fun(ny) as hell and I was telling my Friends that the game is still in development so we started to eagerly speculate about all the features that moght be added to the game soon (maybe even the planned "co-op campaign" mode)!
Just recently, we were sitting on the couch again and we tried out Gang Beasts (again) - but the disappointment was huge. Framerate drops, many more glitches, worse controls(?), not a single new feature. Yes, we were playing the beta branch, which was probably our mistake, but still: Not a single new feature.
Yes, they added an online mode, but I am obviously one of the very few players that thinks that not every f****** game needs an online mode. Gang Beast's short description in Steam is still "Gang Beasts is a silly local multiplayer party game..." - and that's what the game was designed for in the first place! "Party game" means that you can play it with some friends in the same room, while drinking a beer or two (or eight), yell and laugh at each other. I don't understand why people need to play it online with people they don't see or even know. It takes away 90% of the fun. I love online games in general, but I just think that some games (including this one) are meant to be played on a single screen with your friends beside you.
Another thing most people don't consider/know is that a network implementation often requires streamlining core features, especially physics related ones (in order to keep the network traffic -> latency low). In a physics based game, this might be very hard to pull off or require core mechanics to be simplified.
The outcome of the decision to implement online multiplayer is that we now have a core game that is more buggy than a year ago with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥, broken online multiplayer mode. If players wouldn't have begged for online multiplayer, we maybe would have had a solid core game with more maps, modes, features, and maybe even the planned co-op campaign mode by now!
With the pace and direction the development process is heading, I've lost my faith in Gang Beasts. I also don't recommend the game at its current state and price.

A REVIEW BEFORE THE STORM (Episode 1 Only)

Intro
If I were to pick a game that would relate to me the most in the current day and age, it'd be Life is Strange Before the Storm. While Life is Strange was about how Max could use her powers to overcome various problems and rekindle her friendship with Chloe, Before the Storm is about Chloe having to live a life without her father, William, and having to face the world without him.
Story
Before the Storm follows the distressed Chloe trying to adjust to a life without a father figure to guide her. The episode starts off with an under aged Chloe who tries (and successfully) enters a "Firewalk" concert by haggling with a bouncer (even now in the very start of the game, it's very easy to tell that Chloe is very troubled where we have the ability to tag a RV, steal money, and even buy drugs). Once in the concert, Chloe finds herself meeting Rachel who saves her from a couple of baddies, one heck of an intro for a character who was such a mystery in the previous installment. Rachel befriends Chloe and from there, the game kicks off. To refrain from spoilers, the rest of the episode is just as great as the intro. From a simple run in with David, her stepfather, to scenes with Rachel, Life is Strange Before the Storm definitely packs a punch in the drama department and a certainly hard one at many moments in the game. Now, I'm not saying it doesn't have its weak points, Before the Storm most certainly goes on its tangents at points, but what game doesn't? Overall, the story in this episode is definitely something to write home about.
Gameplay
Much like its predecessor, Before the Storm handles similarly in controls and feel, the only difference being that the rewind button is now replaced with an objective marker and the big fat elephant in the room, no time travel or powers of any sort. Another nice addition to Before the Storm is its "Backtalk" feature which allows Chloe to unleash her inner rebel and well, talk others into submission. It essentially allows the player to tell NPCs to back off or let them pass through, etc. Other than that, not much is added to separate the gameplay of Before the Storm and Life is Strange.
Atmosphere
Not only does this game have an amazing story, it also has the perfect atmosphere to immerse yourself in. The art style is much akin to Life is Strange and is perfect for this type of story and world. It's so good that at many moments in the game, you just want to put down the controller, sit, and stare and revel at the beauty. To add, the soundtrack is a perfect addition to the atmosphere, Daughter did an amazing job in composing the sounds to express teen angst, something that Chloe and many other characters show as the story unfolds before us.
Conclusion
Before the Storm is definitely a great entry and very much lives up to my expectations and to that of many others. Decknine definitely did an amazing job on this game and I commend them for that. I'd recommend you buy it as soon as you can, I guarantee that you'll have an amazing time playing.

When I first heard about Life is Strange: Before the Storm, my initial reaction is, "Really?". I was skeptical at first due to it being handled by a different developer, especially if the developers have not alot of experience in the story telling genre and no time traveling mechanic which draws in to Life is Strange in the first place. I bought it due to obligations as I absolutely love the original Life is Strange, and I was pleasantly surprised. It being a prequel and following the struggles of Chloe and Racheal is a rollercoaster of emotions. The 'trying to be hip and cool' dialogue returns which I grown to love returns.
The story takes focus on Chloe Price and her struggles of her life due to the death of her father and losing her childhood friend. Then the story shifts focus to Rachel Amber, bringing her own troubles to the tabel and both of them have overcome the trouble. What I like about this game is that it does not entirely focus on Chloe and Racheal but also the characters which resides in the world of Life is Strange. I was relieved that the characters of Life is Strange returned to the prequel, even if it is a slight mention or a brief apperance and also some new characters created for Before the Storm which I also taken interest. Yes, there is some retcon or oversights due to it being a prequel and being made by a seperate team, but it is minor to not detract from the experience if you are a returning Life is Strange player. The story so far keeps me invested and hopefully we have a nice conclusion in episode 3.
The game is mechanically alright, instead of the wierd mouse controller schema in the original Life is Strange, it goes with a simple button map. The game seems to run at a decent frame rate and does not have any glaring issues as compared to the first release of Life is Strange. The soundtract is the most calming and also pumping which I listened to everytime and the indie group who created the soundtrack specifically for Before the Storm is top notch.
Life is Strange: Before the Storm might turn off to some people due to the dialogue and the angsty nature of the teenagers but if you were to overlook those, you will be in for a ride.

I think just like many others Life is Strange fans, I was a bit apprehensive about Before the Storm being developed by a different studio (Deck Nine) than the previous game (done by Dontnod). Man... I couldn't be more wrong. Deck Nine is doing an exceptional job, I'd dare to say it's even better than the original Life is Strange.

I got this for free - I would never have bought it otherwise.
The game surprised me with its story and depth.
On the surface it is just another cover-shooter - nothing you have not seen before. But the story and premise is something else, and quite worth your time. Consider it more a cinmetaic experience that you are playing through. The story is well integrated in the actual gameplay, and cut-scenes are not invasive. You'll also find intelligence along the way, that further deepens the story. The voice acting is very well done.
It is very impressive graphically though, and many scenes are beautiful. Detailed face-expressions help the game make it emmotionally immersive.
You are often faced with tough choices that you don't want to make. In the end it does not seem what choice you make, but it still leaves a heavy impact on you.
The combat and mechanics are still good. Guns behave and sound well. The cover mechanics are ok. Sometimes you don't end up doing what you intended to do, but it workds most of the time. Your companions and AI chatters a lot, giving you good intel on the battle field, also further immerse you in the tone and feel of the game.
I like that the enemy has been given a voice and humanity too - you won't always want to attack them.
It seems to be designed with a controller in mind, and it works ok, but mouse and keyboard is still the better experience.
This game is about the story - and does not seem to have any replayability. Mechanics are good, but nothing new. Multiplayer is not really interesting, but the main game was a good experience that kept me hooked through the whole campaign.
Reckommended.

The shooting is fine although I did find picking up weapons, ammo or grenades a bit clunky at times (Once again due to the them being mapped to the same button which is also used for reloading).
All things considered I would definitely recommend this game. Mostly for the experience it provides.

Rogue Legacy is a game where you enter a mysterious castle called Castle Hamson in search for a cure for your father's serious wounds because you'd heard rumors that there was a strange object in the castle that could cure anything!

Wild boar. Blacktail deer. Roosevelt elk. European bison. Beautiful, majestic creatures, all of which I’ve killed with a big gun in The Hunter, a semi-realistic hunting simulator set across two vast rural landscapes in Germany and America’s Pacific Northwest. But you can’t just sprint around firing your rifle like a Call of Duty protagonist: you have to be slow, quiet, and methodical if you want to bag one of the many furry trophies on offer.
Being a simulator, there’s more to a successful hunt than pointing your gun at the first creature you see then shooting it. There are a lot of places in the woods for an animal to hide, and your first job is usually tracking one down, which can take a while. As you creep through the trees you’ll see tracks highlighted on the HUD. Interact with them and your character will use his magical hunter senses to determine which direction the animal is moving in. Then it’s just a case of patiently following the tracks, trying not to make too much noise, until you catch up with it. But that’s only half the battle.
Walking quickly or through thick brush will alert the animal to your presence. If this happens, the best thing to do is crouch and move slowly. But the problem with this is that The Hunter is a game largely about quietly stalking animals, which means you spend most of it crouching and edging through the forest at an incredibly slow pace. I enjoy a slower-paced game, but it’s too ponderous even for me. And if you spook an animal it’ll sprint away and remain in a state of alert for a while, meaning the chances of finding them again are quite slim. This does give the game a nice sense of tension, and makes it genuinely challenging, but it requires—no, demands—an extraordinary amount of patience.
Once you’ve successfully cornered your prey, it’s time to shoot it. But even this comes with its own set of challenges. If your heart rate’s up from running, your hands will shake and make aiming more difficult. The wind is also a factor, affecting your accuracy. And even if you hit the beast, you might just clip its leg, and it’ll run away in panic. You can follow the blood trail to finish it off, but this has a negative impact on your final score. The best kills in The Hunter are the quick ones, preferably as a result of hitting a vital organ.
There are other factors to consider too. Animals will give a warning call if they sense you nearby, meaning they’ll be more likely to flee if you get close. Skulking behind trees and bushes will make you harder to spot, but the rustling will scare your prey. And your score for killing an animal is even determined by how ethically suitable the ammunition you used was. There’s a lot going on here, making it a fairly deep simulation, but at the expense of some accessibility and, crucially, fun. Actual entertainment is sparingly drip-fed in The Hunter, which makes playing it, for the most part, pretty tedious.
Weirdly, what I enjoyed most in The Hunter wasn’t the actual hunting, but the world. It’s a gorgeous game, and one of the most convincing digital recreations of nature I’ve seen on PC. The autumnal forests feel wonderfully organic, with foliage swaying in the wind, motes of pollen floating through the air, and realistic lighting and shadows courtesy of the engine’s global illumination tech. The sound design is fantastic too, from the crunch of dry leaves under your feet to the gentle chirp of birds. It’s so nice that it’s almost a shame you have to ruin the peaceful, serene ambience by shooting animals with a gun.
I love weird, niche simulators like this, but besides enjoying hiking through its stunning wilderness, I found The Hunter far too dull to hold my attention. But that’s exactly why some people will like it, so you’ll have to decide if you’re the type of gamer who can endure prolonged periods of inactivity for short, sweet rewards. It does at least have some depth and scope for mastery, and tracking and killing tougher animals like black bears is a genuine test of skill. But the real test is ultimately staving off boredom.

theHunter was generally one of my most favourite games growing up as a kid, while I did not have the cash to get the memberships to buy guns, licences and ammo, I did enjoy hunting with the free stuff. With this game my dream of hunting all the animals I can with whatever weapon I want came true, without the Pay To Win aspect I can thoroughly enjoy playing the game without limitations, if I want to go shoot a moose I can.
theHunter: Call of the wild also has the most beautiful graphics I've ever seen, the beautiful scenery just takes me away, I usually forget about the hunting while I explore the landscape.
The mechanics are also very interesting. having to keep an eye on your heart rate, wind direction, noise and visablity, it makes it out to be a very realistic experience.
The animals react realistically to what you do, if you make too much noise they will look in your direction, often giving off a warning call, if you stay still and don't move or make a noise they will eventually go back to what they were doing.
If the wind is blowing in their direction they will react to the smell of you and will move away and even flee. It makes me think and plan ahead.
In a quick summary-
Pros--
-ONE TIME PAYMENT! (Apart from the DLC's that is)
-Realistic effects on noise, scent, heartrate
-Beautiful scenery
-Seemingly realistic animal behaviours and patterns
-Beautifull models on guns and animals
-Lots to explore
-Nothing seems forced or unrealistic about the landscape or its design
-Missions, sidequests and small things to do to keep you entertained
Cons--
-No "competitions" from what I've seen (Tell me if I am wrong)
-Quite a few bugs here or theres, animals acting out
-Not enough customization on characters
-Not enough outfits, camoflauge and such
-DLC's should not be so small and pricey, instead make bundles if you want to make DLC's, put the AVA's and Tents in the same pack as they're both methods of fast travel in the first place.

A few difficulty spikes (one in particular - grr) are the only things that I'd complain about with this rather hidden gem.
The 3rd person shooter gameplay from minute to minute is solid if a touch clunky at times, but mostly works well. Firefights are satisfactory on the whole with a good balance between player power and AI challange. Enemies appear to move, shoot and behave intelligently on the whole, occasionally flushing you from cover with a well aimed grenade! Cover is plentifal however, and generally affords good protection. The levels are fairly linear but usually there are several routes available in a confrontation, allowing you to flank the enemy and gain the advantage while your teammates provide covering fire.
Where the game really surprises is in the story. What appears at first to be very standard disenguage-brain fodder, quickly heads in a darker and more surprising direction. It complements the atmospheric visuals well and lends a menacing overtone to the whole environment. Suffice it to say it is one of the few game stories where I really wanted to find the outcome, and then to replay to find all the alternative endings.
Overall this is a real surprise. A solid 3rd person military shooter with a dark and enguaging story that will hook you in and drive you through the campaign.

Rogue Legacy. A tough platforming roguelike with a pixel art aesthetic. In case you're not familiar with the game, it involves exploring an enormous castle over several generations. All the while you explore for loot, fight difficult enemies and cope with ridiculous traits like ADHD and dwarfism. But the question is...is the game worth your money?
Gameplay
For starters, throughout the entire experience I had trouble coming to terms with the game's controls. Your character is floaty, your attack has an awkward delay and maneuvering your way around enemies is frustrating at best because of your odd hitbox. I constantly found myself smashing into enemies and obstacles, so I often picked the sturdy barbarian and paladin so I could have runs that lasted longer than 30 seconds. And that's a shame, because one of the major selling points of this game is the sheer choice you're given with each new generation. I would've loved to play as a magic-using class, but their low HP and attack makes the game nigh-unplayable. But asides from the physics themselves, the mechanics fairly well-executed. The manor upgrade system adds a lot of customization to your playstyle and you'll get to see a lot of cool spells even if you don't play as magic-users.
Art
To be frank, Rogue Legacy is an ugly game. 7even is a very competent pixel artist, and if you browse his PixelJoint gallery you'll find some very nice art. Unfortunately, none of the effort he put into his previous work shies through in Rogue Legacy. Shading is blobby, animations are jerky and lazy gradients can be seen on some graphics. And that's not even addressing the elephant in the room here...Rogue Legacy's eagerness to recycle graphics. I sure hope you like fighting knight enemy, skeleton enemy and wizard enemy, because you'll be fighting at least a dozen different varieties of each! Oh! But sometimes, they're a different color! Or they're stretched so huge that the pixels would be a choking hazard for small children! What amazing variety!

Sound
In retrospect, I actually thought the soundtrack was pretty great! There are only 4 different level themes, but each one is quite lengthy and memorable. The soundtrack smoothly blends medieval, electronic and chiptune aesthetics, and you'll probably never get tired of the songs. The game even randomly spawns jukeboxes, which let you change the area music you're currently listening to! The sound effects are also nice, and they do a good job of giving you a heads-up to enemy attacks. They've got a lot of punch to them, and there are even unique sounds for the female characters.
Overall
Rogue Legacy is a flawed experience at best. The concept is unique, replayability is great and the sound is solid, but the game's execution is quite poor. If Cellar Door Games had focused more on controls or handled the art direction better, the game would have been nearly flawless. But the little things just add up and make the game pretty frustrating overall. If you're a hardcore fan of roguelikes or Castlevania, you might see past this game's flaws and enjoy it as a whole. But for everyone else, save your money for a better game like Spelunky.

So i kind of wanted to withold doing a review until the game was complete especially after the good, but not out of the ballpark amazing first episode. Now after the second episode, i guess i just have to say my piece (will probably update after the third and bonus, if it changes my opinion).  There was a lot of apprehension about where a prequel With Chloe and Rachel could go, becuase ultimately we know what happens to them already (if you have played Life is Strante: Season 1, and you really should do that beforehand).
But i was intrigued, because i fell in love with Life is Strange, and i wanted more, i wanted to know more about these characters i so felt connected to. And while the voice actors strike, the change of developers, and the prequel stigma all made me cautious, i still took the plunge with the deluxe edition.
And let me tell you it was so worth it. Chloe's voice actress, Rhianna DeVries does a more than fantastic job filling in for older Chloe actress, Ashley Burch (who assisted in the dialogue and voice coaching for Chloe). Her take is definitely so much more rebellious teen, and it works well i feel. I am still undecided who i like better for the role, coming down to what game i played (and what voice i listened to) last, i guess.
Rachel's voice actress, Kylie Brown, also is really perfect in emoting and just seems to fit her character very well. It is so refreshing to finally put an actual character to the face, and Kylie pulls that off effortlessly. Everybody else fills in their shoes admirably (and it helps that pretty much nobody pulls double duty, unlike the first game), and the new characters are very well spoken too, with the possible exception of Samuel, who is just horribly stilted, but that is excusable. So that is one concern assuaged.
As for the prequel aspect, it was a great choice by Deck Nine to set this three years in the past, and come out and say we will not deal with Rachel's disappearance, so they could craft their own story. And that story is all about Chloe's and Rachel's friendship/love. And that is what really suprised me, because it is done so beautifully. While episode may have seemed rushed, in the context of two lonely troubled teenagers, it may be not so far out, but the episode two writing, the connection these two developed, it just feels so right. I was initially leery that they went day by day with the episodes again, and i felt they should have maybe kept them weeks apart to let the relationship build organically, but after the Tempest scene, i think it was the right choice. It felt right. Those two are just complimenting each other, filling a hole in their lifes that nobody else could, it seems they are destined for each other.
And that brings me to the writing. Dontnod created a whole slew of intriguing and multi-dimensional characters with Life is Strange, and handing it over to another studio had the risks of them not understanding the intricities of the world we loved. But Deck Nine actually did an admirable job. There are some inconsistencies here and there, but they do not take away from the story told in Before the Storm, and as always some leeway must be given. In fact if we take this story on face value, the writing is simply awesome. It is clearly (much more so than Life is Strange) a coming of age and coming out story. Obviously you can follow the just "friendship" path too, but the depth of the game comes from love, or unrequited love from either side. And even in the limited timeframe it is presented to us, it feels organic and believable for those two characters.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game for the emotions (and of course the first game as well, although that is much more tragic in content, here at least you have a glimmer of hope). Probably not for the shooter crowd, but anybody interested in exporing their inner selves should give this a look.

The review tries to point out some of the problems in a funny way, if you can't get it I seriously doubt your comprehension skills, yet I decide to put it in another way.
1. The hearing of animals is clearly overpowered, comparing to other senses. For example, the boar and deer should have the smell as their strongest sense yet I got heard by them way more frequently than smelt by them. In some circumstances myself can't even hear my footstep clearly yet the animals can hear them with ease. The propagation of sound does not seem to be affected by factors such as hills and existence of trees so i suspect that they just programmed it only related to the distance.
It is extremely frustating when you are hunting a high-value target since they have stronger sense.
2. The movement system of the game is problematic as well. The fast travel randomly reset your continuous hunting score (can't figure out when the score is reset) so you have to walk A LOT if you aim high scores. The speed of walking and jogging is too slow which makes your sweeping very tedious and boring (unless you buy the shiny AVT) . Warning to new buyers: Walking in this game = ramble in real life , runing = walking in a hurry. For those who keep mentioning the burden of equippment, I did not see the hunter going any faster when he is carrying just one rifle at the first place.
3. There are also problems with the damage system. For the smart Zzabur dude who asks me to shoot the chest, I seriously doubt whether he has played the game through. Shooting the lung in this game, as I can remember, never gives a 100% score (unless you use a larger bullet which devastates your integrity score). Shooting spine and head remain the most reliable instant kill to me compared to heart (However he can be a master who can hit the heart everytime, then that is my fault). The frustrating thing is than when you slightly miss the brain the animal literally runs away like nothing happened. Clearly you can see they have been hit to the ground by the impact of bullet, the cerebral concussion should make them barely able to move yet they run as normal.
These are problems I found, they are not so obvious when you just shoot random animals and have fun. But when you are aiming for high socre or trying to complete some missions, such problems will pop out.

A few difficulty spikes (one in particular - grr) are the only things that I'd complain about with this rather hidden gem.
The 3rd person shooter gameplay from minute to minute is solid if a touch clunky at times, but mostly works well. Firefights are satisfactory on the whole with a good balance between player power and AI challange. Enemies appear to move, shoot and behave intelligently on the whole, occasionally flushing you from cover with a well aimed grenade! Cover is plentifal however, and generally affords good protection. The levels are fairly linear but usually there are several routes available in a confrontation, allowing you to flank the enemy and gain the advantage while your teammates provide covering fire.
Where the game really surprises is in the story. What appears at first to be very standard disenguage-brain fodder, quickly heads in a darker and more surprising direction. It complements the atmospheric visuals well and lends a menacing overtone to the whole environment. Suffice it to say it is one of the few game stories where I really wanted to find the outcome, and then to replay to find all the alternative endings.
Overall this is a real surprise. A solid 3rd person military shooter with a dark and enguaging story that will hook you in and drive you through the campaign.
