This game has great progression and a variety of utility options.  There are many design strategies for buildings you can think of, or find online.  I really enjoyed learning about the mechanics and materials, and playing with a massive amount of people that can vary from friendly to kill-on-sight.  Each play session is different because you'll always have different encounters, whether it's accidentally stepping on territory owned by a clan, running out of supplies and dying by nature, or unexpectedly running into a bear.
The downside of this game for me was when I finally learned pretty much everything, and I realized something: there is virtually no way to fully protect your gear and home from other players.  There is always a way for people to find a way to either destroy, or infiltrate your base.  Whether its C4, or even rocket launchers-- any wall, any door, can be broken.  So you can never really rest assured that your gear is safe.  That reason alone makes this game a whole lot harder later.  You have to be prepared to lose everything at any point, and the only exception to that is if you join a large group/clan.
Solo/duo gameplay is fun, but only if you don't care about sustainabililty.  Server hosts understand that this is a thing, so most servers are wiped clean every week or two.  Basically, this game isn't about long-term progression.  If that's what you want, this isn't for you.  Honestly, I think this game would be more interesting if it did something like survival of the fittest, starting with a set amount of players, and if you die you're kicked off the server until the next cycle.  That way the game fully embraces its short-term playstyle.  Instead, you're given this false sense of security with elaborate building possibilities and extensive upgrading, which is essentially all pointless if someone passes by your house with a few C4 explosives on hand, which unfortunately is common.
All this being said:  this game is fun.  Is it worth checking out?  Yes.  Is it a game you can sink endless hours into?  Yes.  Do I recommend it? ..Yes.
Just don't get the wrong idea.  You won't live long.  You're never safe.  Don't get attached to your accomplishments.  Cause odds are you'll log back in tomorrow and you'll be either raided, or dead.

On one edge of the Nuketown 2025 multiplayer map, there is a small greenhouse, with plants being watered by a sprinkler system that moves along a track on the ceiling, never ceasing its back-and-forth movement through the entirety of the match. It's little touches like this that draw you into the Call of Duty franchise's most fully-realized world to date. Ever since CoD 4 changed the industry forever, Treyarch is the studio that has been taking all the chances, leaving Infinity Ward to continue making only minor improvements every two years. But it's not the creativity Treyarch put into its dark vision of the near future that makes Black Ops II the best entry in the controversial series. It's that it is the biggest, most thoughtful, and most innovative installment since 2007's Modern Warfare. The innovations begin with the campaign. Black Ops II's single player is hand-down the best the series has to offer. More open battlefields allow for some degree (however small) of player freedom, which is amplified by the player's ability to choose their loadout before each mission. In addition to presenting more options in combat, it's strangely humorous to bring an M8 to a 1980s gunfight. And then, of course, there is the franchise debut of nonlinear storytelling. Based on various choices made by the player throughout the thoroughly compelling narrative, no fewer than six different endings are available upon completion of the game. All this, and I haven't even mentioned the multiplayer. Treyarch did an excellent job of building each map with a minimum of camping spots, almost managing to make untouchable snipers a thing of the past. And then there's the brilliant Pick 10 system, forcing every player onto the same level, twitch skill notwithstanding. And for the sake of not letting this entry run rampant, I'll gloss over the addictive Zombies mode, which became so popular that it even spawned its own self-contained narrative. The most expansive and consistently fun installment so far, Black Ops II is the quintessential Call of Duty experience.
SCORE: 9.75/10

I simply love this game.  Mostly the zombies, but I love the rest of the game, too.
The campaign alternates between Alex Mason, and his son, David, and hops between the 80s and 2025 time wise.  Every 4-5 missions, there's a RTS-style mission, where you are the commander of a group to defend a point, which I'm stuck on. Last but not least, zombies, my favorite.  You start off with 4 maps, the most without DLC since WaW.  There are also 3 gamemodes: Survival, Grief (two teams of 4 survive as long as possible, last team standing wins) and CoD's trump card, Tranzit;  craft items to save points, and build yourself the power and PaP, and some cross-playthrough keepsakes, like the locker for your guns, and vault for your points.  It's possible to get around 15K in less that 10 seconds!
All in all, Black Ops 2 is one of the best games of all time, and now that I have the Season Pass, there's more BLOPS2 to go around starting this month!

With a superb story, great soundtrack, and multiple difficulties Spec Ops The Line is easily one of the best third person cover shooters around. Although the story is great, the game play is even better. It says a lot when a game can get you to play through it multiple times on different difficulties just for the challenge of it. While my original experience was a spectacle of story and gameplay the subsequent playthroughs were heightened by the sheer level of enemy difficulty. The increased difficulty changes play a lot. You have to start eliminating targets from afar; and setting yourself up with plenty grenades, quality guns, and ammo before the next checkpoint becomes a must. There are no incredibly lofty achievements tied to this game besides "MFWIC" which requires you complete the game on the dreaded FUBAR difficulty. That experience was as frustrating as it was rewarding. It should also be noted that there are no achievements linked to multiplayer in this game. This is a wonderful game with some less common plot themes.

Spec Ops: The Line...
Starting my review with commenting on how good of a story this game had (IMO).
Dramatic twists of events. Taking choices you wouldn't want to. Going through a deep slow path of insanity by each chapter.
I'm usually not amused by any type of story an army game has to offer and I must admit in my eyes most of them are more or less the same.
However out of the bucket of clichés and reused material Spec Ops: The Line stands out.
The fictional concept told here is so well blended that it kept my interest through the whole time from start to end.
I even did 4 runs of the game itself in order to experience all 4 different endings.
Can't say it is original, after the amount of movies and games that have been out so far, there's hardly anything new to be served in militaristic games. However it is the way the content is served that makes the difference in this type of games, this one right here gets the cookie for me.
The game is very very well directed. The way the story is balanced through action sessions, intense cutscenes, sweet environmental designs, and impressive musical options.
All combined so smoothly with some of the very best voice acting I've seen for an action shooter.
Neatly scripted on Unreal Engine 3, the game has sweet physics and sandstorm and smoke dynamics. Of course there have been titles a lot more famous for their graphics for 2012.
But for the experience offered, Spec Ops: The Line's graphics are just perfect and it's lacking major bugs or issues.
Very easy and comfortable to handle. Ammo and amount of weapons is just about right.
Destructible environment (just a few details here and there) add a good taste on the style of the shooter experience and of course not missing the ability to take cover and using commands to make your crew help you dynamically in various situations.
Difficulty makes a difference from the easiest to the hardest mode and it gets more and more challenging, sometimes kinda too hard in the hardest difficulty level.
The music used in the game is AMAZING.
Not only the acoustic backrgound is very good, but you will also hear a brilliant collection of songs through the game, every single one very accurately put in each situation like a glove.
Cool environmental and battle effects that seem about right at any moment of the game. No problems with blending music or voice acting.
Considering that this game was implemented by a very small team and the studio itself is not even famous for having any other major titles around the market (Yager Development only have one other game implemented which is very old)
It was freaking amazing. With a story that has a beginning, a peak, and an end.
Well made, balanced, satisfying, with good action and even a well done multiplayer and co-op modes.
Considering how shallow other a lot more famous games from bigger studios have ended up being, Spec Ops: The Line is by the full meaning of the phrase 'a job well done'.
And for the asked price, this title is pure gold!
Do get it. 100% recommended!

Beautiful hunting game that's hit and miss
There are a very games that manage to recreate the beauty and complexity of nature as well as TheHunter Call of the Wild. Games like Farcry, Tombraider, Ghost Recon come to mind with each their own style. But for me CotW captures more than pretty graphics; and that is feeling. A sense of immersion, of actually being there. A sense of lonelyness. The lighting, the amazing colors of the leaves on the trees, the reflection of a waterpuddle, the heatshimmer over a cornfield, the swaying of trees and bushes in the wind, the distant overhead humm of an airplane. The game also manages to create a sense of curiosity: "I wonder whats over that ridge. Or behind that bend in the road. Whats over there by that water?" All this is very well done and thought out.
But at the same time the game also has some major flaws in that same design: while the re-use of the same type of trees, bushes, rocks and grass is not that bothersome and still manages to create a beautiful environment, the re-use of the exact same models for outposts, lookout towers, abandoned barns and hiking shacks soon becomes a distracting annoyance. These locations where you can re-stock your supplies and buy new items or rest to advance the time, are very static and feel very empty. Some of those locations offer even no interaction at all.
The hunting mechanic is very well done, with realistic animal behavior and animations and your presence in the environment accurately impacts how the wildlife reacts.
There are a few options in the menu that allow you to adjust what is visible in the HUD, such as blue outlines around spotted animals for example, but its still hard to find a good middlepoint between Arcade and hardcore simulator. There are too few adjustible options in my opinion.
The mission-system is also not very strong in this game. There is a somewhat decent storyline to guide players towards new areas to explore and animals to hunt, but some of the missions are tedious or outright annoying. The "take a photo of two bears" type missions can be a serious headache and being sent out to down a red fox with a bow, way before the player is able to unlock the small animal Caller is very frustrating.
The slow pace of the game unfortunately soon becomes a grind. Prices in the shop for equipment and ammunition are outrageous and earning experience points for Skills and Perks takes forever. Some of those skills or perks have minimal or no impact on actual gameplay which is not very rewarding.
The game is still actively being developed with new patches or DLC very few weeks or so. The fact that some items like an ATV and tents and blinds that should have been part of the base game were added in as a paid DLC, and that sit not very well with the majority of players.
These patches are desperately needed because the game still has a ton of bugs like graphic glitches, sounds cutting out, missing items from the gameworld or inventory, wildlife spawn issues etc. etc. Eventhough the game is playable the buglist is huge.
But all in all this is a very enjoyable and pretty virtual world to walk around in. I hope the developers focus on what needs to be fixed in the current game, before adding any new stuff.

I've had some fun, but the game is riddled with bugs and it's aggravating. I don't recommend buying this unless you get it on sale. The same goes for the DLCs.
And not just things like "animals get stuck" or weird AI, but absolutely trivial UI bugs. Things that any UI programmer (not just gaming) has to deal with. Bad scrolling in the store. Stats on items switched around. Clicks not registering. Menus registering in-game clicks and doing things after they've been dismissed.
There are bug reports in the discussions section dating back to February (it's July as I write this) that are just stupid, fundamental mistakes that any remotely-competent UAT or QA/QC process should have caught, and yet they're still not addressed.
On top of those fundamental UI problems, the game does indeed also have problems with the core gameplay. Crouching in blinds puts you too low (can't see out over the half-wall), but when standing your head is too high (can't see the skyline, only the terrain right near the blind). Animals getting spooked by a gunshot, but then within a couple minutes returning to the same exact place, even right next to the carcass of the animal just shot. You can literally take down an entire herd without moving. Kill one, call them back, wait a minute, and repeat. Or if you shoot them from 250+ ish yards, they won't run away at all... like they didn't even notice one of the herd just dropped dead.
Some areas are grossly overpopulated (20+ Elk within 100 yard diameter circle), others are virtually deserted. When you combine the this with the AI issue above, it becomes apparent that the best way to gain money and XP is to find those good spots and just farm them dry.
Meanwhile there has been 2 paid DLCs (which are also buggy). It's not hard to see that the developer isn't particularly concerned about quality.

This game is full of fun experiences, and definitely worth the money.
You can wander from different regions and find a whole different range of animals, the times can change how many animals there are wandering, the wind directs your scent which can cause the animals to smell you.
For a person that has never gone hunting, this gave me an experience more than I could of wished for.
But theres alot to talk about that could be added, or is a problem in the game.
First off, the game could have a larger range of animals, seeing as within the first 10-15 hours of playing the game, I had experienced, sighted, tracked and killed nearly every single animal in the game, even the hardest like the European Bison.
If there was a different weather system in a different region, like a snowy biome, or a desert biome, because these different biomes could have a different range of animals from thing such as polar bears to arctic rabbits, and kangaroo's to camels. This would bring a whole new experience to this game which would intrigue you to play more, and would be a big part of the game.
although 50 square acres is alot of space for the maps, it gets very repetitive, and would help if you could change up from different biomes and weather systems.
The Multi-player could do with some re-works seeing as 2 different players are sometimes not synced, with sounds and animal locations, and the progression has to be done by the host, and the host only which limits where the 2nd player can spawn/fast travel causing it to be hard work to be able to explore more of the map together.
Conclusion: The whole game as it stands is amazing, and a really good hunting simulator, but on the other hand it could have more maps and animals to be less repetitive, and multiplayer could do with some fixes and reworking.

I didn't think restarting a game a multitude of times would be fun. Then again, the oldest games out there are fun just because you keep trying to beat your old high score.
This game begins as one of your fore fathers goes into a castle and tries to battle his way through. I'll be honest, I didn't pay attention to the story line I just wanted to start playing. The game works as so : every generation (or every time you die) there is a new line of blood that comes to challenge the castle. This new blood line comes in many forms, some have ADD, some are colorblind (to the point where your screen is colorblind), some generations are smaller or larger than usual with different classes (mage, paladin etc...), some are dyslexic (to where your screen is as well) and some are far sighted. Mixing up classes (or choosing to stay the same) is a nice feature. As you progress and collect coins you are able to unlock different sort of classes and even upgradable classes (or upgrade your HP, mana etc...). You can save your coins instead and spend money on new armor or weapons. These require the player to unlock "blue prints" before such purchases can be made. The short version:
Do you have friends? Do you enjoy the company of those friends? If you answered yes to both of these questions, you should buy this game.
The longer version:
This is a great Co-Op (and even single player, though it's less challenging and not quite as fun by yourself) game that really shines when you have a party of people that you can play with. The classes work well on their own for the most part, but a few really shine when they have the support of teammates, where they are somewhat lackluster on their own. For instance, playing the assassin is great fun, though it tends to be difficult for solo-ing large groups of enemies, requiring a bit of kiting and creative play to fully use the assassins' skillset. With friends on the other hand, you can play the assassin relatively worry-free, letting your more durable friends take care of distracting them, while using your sniper rifle and some range to support them from afar.
On the other hand, if you want to run in guns blazing and slash every enemy up like a raging psycho, you're more than welcome to do that in the assassin, or any other class for that matter, every class can do every role, though some are better at one than the other, it's not impossible (and sometimes even fun) to run around sniping people as a gun-crazy midget, or dive into melee as a prepubescent girl, whatever you choose to do, you can. But it'll always be more fun with friends.

If you only recently heard from this game you have to know that in 2009/10 it was not only one of the few survival games (letting zombies out here) that were on the market it was also a really promising approach to use the Arma II engine to make a reallistic survival game.
For that time it was really good and we had much to hope for in fact it was received from the players so well that it ignited into one of the most viewed games on twitch for a very long time (talking years) and some streamers could even build up a whole carreer on the attention this game got.
In the time when DayZ was not seperated from Arma II you would run this game as a mod... it got many players to buy Arma II and it's Addon wich includes me and it ran so poor for the first couple of years that many folks decided to buy whole new hardware bundles to be able to produce 30 FPS also including me.
But all the success this game got brought a very dark and deadly idea into the minds of the upper management of many game publishers... it was the beginning of the EARLY ACCESS era of gaming industry.
Seeing the attention and money this game generated while it was not even finished and produced low budget, it got many publishers to overthink there marketing strategies. As a result we now have Triple A studios releasing games in early access wich in my eyes is a really bad and shameless thing to do.

Spec Ops: The Line...
Starting my review with commenting on how good of a story this game had (IMO).
Dramatic twists of events. Taking choices you wouldn't want to. Going through a deep slow path of insanity by each chapter.
I'm usually not amused by any type of story an army game has to offer and I must admit in my eyes most of them are more or less the same.
However out of the bucket of clichés and reused material Spec Ops: The Line stands out.
The fictional concept told here is so well blended that it kept my interest through the whole time from start to end.
I even did 4 runs of the game itself in order to experience all 4 different endings.
Can't say it is original, after the amount of movies and games that have been out so far, there's hardly anything new to be served in militaristic games. However it is the way the content is served that makes the difference in this type of games, this one right here gets the cookie for me.
The game is very very well directed. The way the story is balanced through action sessions, intense cutscenes, sweet environmental designs, and impressive musical options.
All combined so smoothly with some of the very best voice acting I've seen for an action shooter.
Neatly scripted on Unreal Engine 3, the game has sweet physics and sandstorm and smoke dynamics. Of course there have been titles a lot more famous for their graphics for 2012.
But for the experience offered, Spec Ops: The Line's graphics are just perfect and it's lacking major bugs or issues.
Very easy and comfortable to handle. Ammo and amount of weapons is just about right.
Destructible environment (just a few details here and there) add a good taste on the style of the shooter experience and of course not missing the ability to take cover and using commands to make your crew help you dynamically in various situations.
Difficulty makes a difference from the easiest to the hardest mode and it gets more and more challenging, sometimes kinda too hard in the hardest difficulty level.
The music used in the game is AMAZING.
Not only the acoustic backrgound is very good, but you will also hear a brilliant collection of songs through the game, every single one very accurately put in each situation like a glove.
Cool environmental and battle effects that seem about right at any moment of the game. No problems with blending music or voice acting.
Considering that this game was implemented by a very small team and the studio itself is not even famous for having any other major titles around the market (Yager Development only have one other game implemented which is very old)
It was freaking amazing. With a story that has a beginning, a peak, and an end.
Well made, balanced, satisfying, with good action and even a well done multiplayer and co-op modes.
Considering how shallow other a lot more famous games from bigger studios have ended up being, Spec Ops: The Line is by the full meaning of the phrase 'a job well done'.
And for the asked price, this title is pure gold!
Do get it. 100% recommended!

Best Movie Based game I have played. It is open world game. Max can go anywhere he can reach do whatever he wants. Gameplay mostly involves winning back territory from gangs. Imagine a global map with sectors that all have a threat ratings. Some sectors have friendly camps were you can talk to local leaders about tasks, food, ammo and support. But sectors are mostly full of enemy strongholds. As you take out strongholds, sectors become less violent and you win the trust of the friendly camps. In this regard, the game feels like a lot of other games I have played like FarCry (3).
Graphics are excellent, voice acting and music are top notch.   Combat comes in two forms: Melee and Car combat.  Melee bulls down to timing parries and car combat includes grinders, flame throws, rocket launchers and harpoons. Once the car is upgraded with a rocket launcher, taking out enemy convoys is very fun.
Negatives include combat redundancy and the lack of choices in the storyline.  Melee combat is pretty boring. It bulls down to watching for the parry icon and hitting mouse 2 when you see it and then spamming mouse 1.  There... you just mastered melee. And it would have been nice if Boss Stronghold fights involved learning a custom melee tactic for each boss. But no, once you learn the tactic needed to beat the first boss, you just reuse the same tactic on every other boss in the game.
The story is good. characters are memorable, voice acting is excellent.  But you dont get any say in what Max does or says or how he reacts to the various people he meets. This bothered me at times since Max is ... crazy .  I'm used to controlling the protagonst both in where they go, how they fight AND what they say.  The fact that this game gives you no dialogue choices makes it feel more like an interactive movie Even FarCry gave you a choice at the end which resulted in 2 different endings. This game has exactly 1 ending and zero replay value.
That said, it was a good story and the single playthrough was worth it.  (At least as good if not better than most the movies). Get it on sale if you can. I know I did and I dont regret it.

If you liked Far Cry 3-4 and the movie Mad Max: Fury Road, BUY THIS GAME. Like the Farcry games, it's setup like an open world RPG divided into strongholds, though it's a bit heavier on vehicle racing and combat (mostly combat). Instead of FPS combat, you mix it up with Arkham-style brawling. Like the movie, there's just enough story to hold it all together without getting too dramatic or involved; there's never so much plot that you feel like you can't take the time to explore and complete side missions. The art is fantastic. The level design is stellar. Audio is spot on. I only encountered a few glitches, but they were all with crazy physics, which is pretty much unavoidable these days. Take note, gamers and game developers alike: THIS is how you make an open world RPG.

A solid 9/10 for me. Delivered (almost) everything I wanted from a Mad Max game.
Pros:
-	Super pretty skyline and environment (even if it is a lot of… wasteland, they did a bang up job making it something worth looking at)
-	Hand to hand Combat is solid (Arkham styled if you didn’t know already, but don’t fix what isn’t broken and that system is good to begin with)
-	Car combat is intense, satisfying, and cinematic. I especially loved taking out convoys!
-	Upgrading the toggling the Magnum Opus (Max’s car) offers lots of options to fit your needs
-	Exploring the wasteland and what it had to offer was genuinely fun (to me), and collecting History Relics offers a glimpse into how things used to be prior to the world descending into madness, diving into the Mad Max lore and world
-	Raiding camps felt awesome, particularly breaking in by destroying the camp’s defenses.
-	Collecting things outside the car made the wasteland much more terrifying. This is something I see listed as a negative a lot, having to get out of the car and manually collect scraps and such things, but I appreciated it. It was a risk getting out of the car to collect that stuff, knowing a War Boy party could be just over the horizon
-	The story makes for an excellent prequel to the 2015 film, even if they’re not officially (source needed?) linked by any means
-	Chum Bucket
-	The desert storms were legitimately terrifying, both in appearance (hard as hell to navigate do to SAND and lightning strikes) and in sound (roaring winds)
-	LOTS of stuff to do. I dumped nearly 60 hours into the game clearing regions of threats and doing the main story. That doesn’t even include all the side stuff you can do.
Cons:
-	Water, food, and gasoline hardly matter much. Ideally, the theme of it being a harsh wasteland should be felt more strongly through the scarcity of such things, but they’re easy to come by even early on in the game and only become more common to the point of being irrelevant later
-	Getting hit by a car or a boss? Pshaw. Bring it on. Getting punched by a War Boy? OW FUDGE THAT HURTS.
-	Second to last final boss difficulty was insane. Final boss was way too easy (cool, but easy).
-      Top Dog "bosses" could use more variety
-	Thunderpoon makes car combat WAY too easy toward the end game.
-	Searching for Insignias and Scrap piles within a location, camps in particular, could be one of the most obnoxious chores at times
-	Crow Dazzle’s noise wagon
-	Disarming Minefields was an overly tedious chore that required the use of Chum Bucket’s MEDIOCRE buggy and the dog’s (annoying) barking
-	Auto aim of the sniper rifle. I could not for the life of me figure out how to turn it off. Granted I didn’t google it, so there might be a way. If there is, then ignore this.
Overall for me, it’s a great game. Not GOTY material in my opinion, but an incredible game for those wanting to delve into the Wastelands of Max’s world and experience it for themselves or even a fan of sandbox style games.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game about morality and introspection. An action/adventure title which grips you with just above average game-play mechanics. Along side that, there is profound situational scenarios that forces an analytical and emotional side from you, with every decision. It may seem like you start as, just, another soldier given, just, another mission. Although, as you act in what seems to be an orderly manner, you begin to question the authenticity, or integrity of such orders. You begin to question because of the veracious nature of these orders. It becomes difficult and even, regretful, when you persist to just 'follow orders.'
It is a game which for the most part of the story, is confusing. Your distaste by all the violence you do as this character, I don't want to give any spoilers but there are some really deep philosophical questions that the game provokes from you, after these unfortunate situations. All that thought, accumulates into a severe confusion and doubt about where this is all going. Why so much pain? So much death?...Well, the ending holds a powerful question, the question is what will you do?
In regards to the game-play mechanics, they're inherently superficial and refined. This allows for the player to not completely focus on just the action, but the scenery, the sounds, the presentation of a doomed Dubai. There were many breathtaking scenes, in which I have numerous images for.
There is only one reason one should purchase this game, it is if you are looking for a intellectually provocative game. Take head tho, there is alot of filler action. Seemingly useless scenes of violence. Furthermore, I would like to add, that discussing such an issue, as this game does, with such a small script, was impressive. I hope the studio is working on the next of the series, maybe one that jumps further deep into the monstrous acts of war, and the repercussions of those wars.

As many other reviews have already mentioned: the shooting is pretty basic, even boring at certain times, and only the story and the great scenery (with lots and lots of great details) kept me going. The story isn't even that great actually, but the important thing is that it tells a different story than most other shooters. There are a few emotionally challenging points in the game, which is always good and should be implemented in games way more often, and near the end there are many (fourth wall breaking) lines and quotes which seem to be directed more to the player than the ingame characters. This is what makes this game truly unique at this moment and therefor a must play for anyone even remotely interested in games as a serious medium next to film, music and literature. The questions it raises about war and gaming continued to be on my mind even a few days after finishing this game, and this is something not many games or works of art in general can do.

Undertale is renowned for its notorious fanbase; a reason for my initial aversion to the idea of playing the game. My sister was an avid fan, and eventually she convinced me to give the game a try. I purchased it on sale and sat down to see what all the hullabaloo was about this fairly cheap, low-graphics game. At first, I simply couldn't see what made Undertale so special - it didn't help that I didn't necessarily enter the game completely blind. That being said, there were a few things about it that surprised me, even things I had previously been informed of before witnessing them in-game. The story is simple, yet incredibly complex at the same time. The characters can be compelling, and some of them even inspiring. I felt like I was able to play the game the way I wanted to while still being able to achieve the perfect ending - an ending where no one dies! Games where there are minimal to no casualties are few and far between these days (I'm looking at you, Final Fantasy XV, Hyper Light Drifter, Fallout 4, etc.).
That being said, I would not give this game a perfect 10/10. My main reason for deducting points can be summed up in one sentence: this game is CREEPY. There are moments, characters, and histories presented in the game that are simply and absolutely terrifying. The game's own self-awareness only contributes to the stand-offish horror that Undertale manages to bring to the table. If that sort of unsettling element is what you like, then you would probably adore this game without inibition. The graphics also deserve a small mentioning, but that eventually contributes a sort of charm to the game.
Essentially, Undertale is an unorthodox deconstruction of the RPG genre. The story is immersive and comes about full circle. It's short, sweet, and to the point. There's no sex, drugs, or extreme language, and the game only gets violent if you choose to play it that way. Not many games give you that freedom. Another unique attribute is that Undertale tests your own character, and it utilizes its own self-awareness to leave an impact on how you perceive your actions. Undertale is unsettling to be certain, but it was rewarding at the same time, and it leaves a good message in the end: if you are determined, and if you choose the right, you will find your happy ending, and you might even bring others (many, many others) happiness along the way.

This game is simply spectacular. It has it all: unforgettable characters, an interesting battle mechanic, a true choice-based story where your decisions have real consequnces, an amazing soundtrack, and a world that entices you to discover every one of its many, many secrets. It has elements of puzzle games, but it doesn't really fit neatly into one: at it's core it is an unorthodox RPG, but it's very accessible and enjoyable even if you are not a fan of RPGs (like me).
Like many others, I cannot really say much more because it would spoil it. But what I will say is that the game is more than the sum of its parts. Whatever you've heard about the game, from how it plays, to the characters, to the central theme of the game's mechanics, none of them really capture what the game IS all on their own. It really is something that must be experienced. Don't be deterred by the (admittedly intimidating) fanbase, and don't let anyone tell you the game has to be played any certain way. Buy this game, and see it for yourself; you will not regret it.

Mad Max is a fantastic game, though it does have it's shortcomings.
First the great:

Graphics: 9/10 - Wow the scenery is very convincing of a post apocalyptic dehydrated desert landscape. With the graphics maxed out (GTX970 2560x1080) the environment is near photo-realistic at times. There are some truly exquisite and sometimes subtle touches that really add to the visual impact.
Sound: 10/10 - Sound is fantastic. From the blowing wind to the sound of bones breaking it is all very immersive.
Game Play: 8/10 - The game play is very enjoyable especially for the first half of the game. After 40 hours of play though the game does tend to suffer from a lack of variety. It does at times become a repetitive grind. This may have something to do with my style of play. My play through was about 130 hours but I pretty much completely cleared all areas to 0 threat before I entered gas town and I only used fast travel a few times when a glitch got me stuck. Gasoline was a just a wasted mechanic since I never came close to running out of fuel. The Magnum Opus damage model was also weak. I could flip off any cliff I cared to and damage was minimal. It sort of removed some of the effectiveness of the terrain.
The bad:
Story: 4/10 - The story is incredibly thin. I'd say Trojan Bearskin Condom thin. I wont ruin what little these is here. The first two hours of play had some story elements as did the last six or so hours. That is 8 out of 130 hours. The war boys and even the level bosses has the personality of cardboard cut-outs. This was a really poorly executed aspect of the game and a missed opportunity. Just a few more cut scenes and some more build-up would have gone a long way to make each territory more exciting.  As it stands the game quickly becomes a shooting gallery. Max was fully maxed out for skills less than half way through the game and scrap became a moot point about the same time with a balance of 20k or higher for the rest of the game.
Conclusion:
Great game. It entertained me to one degree of another for over 130 hours and that makes it wholly worth the money especially since I picked this up on a steam sale.  If you can forgive the lack of story and enjoy the scenery this is a great time killer.

While mechanically the game is a rather average to mediocre cover shooter, the true strength of the title is the story that delves into the psyche.  True to its dual inspirations, this is a decent into apocalyptic darkness.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game about morality and introspection. An action/adventure title which grips you with just above average game-play mechanics. Along side that, there is profound situational scenarios that forces an analytical and emotional side from you, with every decision. It may seem like you start as, just, another soldier given, just, another mission. Although, as you act in what seems to be an orderly manner, you begin to question the authenticity, or integrity of such orders. You begin to question because of the veracious nature of these orders. It becomes difficult and even, regretful, when you persist to just 'follow orders.'
It is a game which for the most part of the story, is confusing. Your distaste by all the violence you do as this character, I don't want to give any spoilers but there are some really deep philosophical questions that the game provokes from you, after these unfortunate situations. All that thought, accumulates into a severe confusion and doubt about where this is all going. Why so much pain? So much death?...Well, the ending holds a powerful question, the question is what will you do?
In regards to the game-play mechanics, they're inherently superficial and refined. This allows for the player to not completely focus on just the action, but the scenery, the sounds, the presentation of a doomed Dubai. There were many breathtaking scenes, in which I have numerous images for.
There is only one reason one should purchase this game, it is if you are looking for a intellectually provocative game. Take head tho, there is alot of filler action. Seemingly useless scenes of violence. Furthermore, I would like to add, that discussing such an issue, as this game does, with such a small script, was impressive. I hope the studio is working on the next of the series, maybe one that jumps further deep into the monstrous acts of war, and the repercussions of those wars.

As many other reviews have already mentioned: the shooting is pretty basic, even boring at certain times, and only the story and the great scenery (with lots and lots of great details) kept me going. The story isn't even that great actually, but the important thing is that it tells a different story than most other shooters. There are a few emotionally challenging points in the game, which is always good and should be implemented in games way more often, and near the end there are many (fourth wall breaking) lines and quotes which seem to be directed more to the player than the ingame characters. This is what makes this game truly unique at this moment and therefor a must play for anyone even remotely interested in games as a serious medium next to film, music and literature. The questions it raises about war and gaming continued to be on my mind even a few days after finishing this game, and this is something not many games or works of art in general can do.

Undertale is renowned for its notorious fanbase; a reason for my initial aversion to the idea of playing the game. My sister was an avid fan, and eventually she convinced me to give the game a try. I purchased it on sale and sat down to see what all the hullabaloo was about this fairly cheap, low-graphics game. At first, I simply couldn't see what made Undertale so special - it didn't help that I didn't necessarily enter the game completely blind. That being said, there were a few things about it that surprised me, even things I had previously been informed of before witnessing them in-game. The story is simple, yet incredibly complex at the same time. The characters can be compelling, and some of them even inspiring. I felt like I was able to play the game the way I wanted to while still being able to achieve the perfect ending - an ending where no one dies! Games where there are minimal to no casualties are few and far between these days (I'm looking at you, Final Fantasy XV, Hyper Light Drifter, Fallout 4, etc.).
That being said, I would not give this game a perfect 10/10. My main reason for deducting points can be summed up in one sentence: this game is CREEPY. There are moments, characters, and histories presented in the game that are simply and absolutely terrifying. The game's own self-awareness only contributes to the stand-offish horror that Undertale manages to bring to the table. If that sort of unsettling element is what you like, then you would probably adore this game without inibition. The graphics also deserve a small mentioning, but that eventually contributes a sort of charm to the game.
Essentially, Undertale is an unorthodox deconstruction of the RPG genre. The story is immersive and comes about full circle. It's short, sweet, and to the point. There's no sex, drugs, or extreme language, and the game only gets violent if you choose to play it that way. Not many games give you that freedom. Another unique attribute is that Undertale tests your own character, and it utilizes its own self-awareness to leave an impact on how you perceive your actions. Undertale is unsettling to be certain, but it was rewarding at the same time, and it leaves a good message in the end: if you are determined, and if you choose the right, you will find your happy ending, and you might even bring others (many, many others) happiness along the way.

Borderlands 2 like its predecessor is a role playing shooter. You begin your adventure as the victim of train sabotage by Handsome Jack. And awaken from catastrophe relatively unscathed at the feet of Claptrap. Claptrap eventually leads you to resistance against Handsome Jack, led by the original four characters from Borderlands. The story has seen improvement over the original. The quality writing as a whole has drastically increased from first insulation, but it’s made not for story structure but in the dialog as well. From the dialog alone, I predict that Handsome Jack will start appearing top 10 favorite villain list over the internet sometimes soon. He has a great personality, his funny human and ultimately very very evil.
The journey will rack you-in over 30 hours to complete the main quest line. That’s if you don’t do any side missions, go off exploring, team up with friends and their games. Borderlands 2 is a time enthralling but I mean the most enduring way possible. No matter if you catch the game on sale or if you pay full price, you will get your money’s worth. It’s jam packed with quality content from start to finish. If I use the term “finish” likely because once you complete the main quest, you can play thru the entirely game again against harder and more diverse enemies that drop more elaborate guns and gear pushing you seemingly temporary cap of level fifty.
In that regard, Borderlands 2 is like an MMO but one you only experience with friends and strangers if you want to. Teaming up with your friends and strangers is as easy as flickering on light switch. Cooperative gameplay not only exponentially increases the fun factor with your friends, but it also causes the game to spawn tougher enemies and better loot. There are plenty of bad♥♥♥♥♥awards, permanent perks for performing various in-game task that can only be achieve with help from your friends.
Graphically, Borderlands 2 has seen a significant facelift over the original but still uses the same art style. I ran on several different graphics but somehow hard time pushing few of the games more fantastic effects when there was tons of actions on the screen. But all in all, I am very pleased that way the game performed. I experienced very few crashes and my connectivity issues were hammered out by the third day of gameplay. The varied locations grade from deserts, to rocky mountain ranges, to green steps, to snowy wastelands, to urban environments and industrial complexes located in the world’s harshest terrain. You’ll be fighting classic enemies like skag, rakk and pyscho but there is also nice variety of new beast, malcontents and machines.
Getting from point A to Z in Borderlands 2, can be done either by foot, car or fast travel stations. Considering the massive size of the entire world, you’ll be happy for any type of transportation after a particularly grew some firefight session. It is important to note that driving cars on PC, takes some getting used to. But most of all, I am slightly disappointed to see that enemies clearly have air superiority over you with transforming robots and buzzard drop ships. This isn’t necessarily negative mark against Borderlands 2 or a side note. I really really want to fly those buzzards around in the available areas within Pandora.

Despite everything I love about Borderlands 2, it definitely has an ugly side to it. Unfortunately, it comes from the multiplayer. Joining cooperative games which I haul hardly recommend on doing. You can miss entire chunks of the storyline and game important unlocks by hopping on with players who are only few levels ahead of you depending where you are in the game. This game has great progression and a variety of utility options.  There are many design strategies for buildings you can think of, or find online.  I really enjoyed learning about the mechanics and materials, and playing with a massive amount of people that can vary from friendly to kill-on-sight.  Each play session is different because you'll always have different encounters, whether it's accidentally stepping on territory owned by a clan, running out of supplies and dying by nature, or unexpectedly running into a bear.
The downside of this game for me was when I finally learned pretty much everything, and I realized something: there is virtually no way to fully protect your gear and home from other players.  There is always a way for people to find a way to either destroy, or infiltrate your base.  Whether its C4, or even rocket launchers-- any wall, any door, can be broken.  So you can never really rest assured that your gear is safe.  That reason alone makes this game a whole lot harder later.  You have to be prepared to lose everything at any point, and the only exception to that is if you join a large group/clan.
Solo/duo gameplay is fun, but only if you don't care about sustainabililty.  Server hosts understand that this is a thing, so most servers are wiped clean every week or two.  Basically, this game isn't about long-term progression.  If that's what you want, this isn't for you.  Honestly, I think this game would be more interesting if it did something like survival of the fittest, starting with a set amount of players, and if you die you're kicked off the server until the next cycle.  That way the game fully embraces its short-term playstyle.  Instead, you're given this false sense of security with elaborate building possibilities and extensive upgrading, which is essentially all pointless if someone passes by your house with a few C4 explosives on hand, which unfortunately is common.
All this being said:  this game is fun.  Is it worth checking out?  Yes.  Is it a game you can sink endless hours into?  Yes.  Do I recommend it? ..Yes.
Just don't get the wrong idea.  You won't live long.  You're never safe.  Don't get attached to your accomplishments.  Cause odds are you'll log back in tomorrow and you'll be either raided, or dead.

Mad Max is a fantastic game, though it does have it's shortcomings.
First the great:

Graphics: 9/10 - Wow the scenery is very convincing of a post apocalyptic dehydrated desert landscape. With the graphics maxed out (GTX970 2560x1080) the environment is near photo-realistic at times. There are some truly exquisite and sometimes subtle touches that really add to the visual impact.
Sound: 10/10 - Sound is fantastic. From the blowing wind to the sound of bones breaking it is all very immersive.
Game Play: 8/10 - The game play is very enjoyable especially for the first half of the game. After 40 hours of play though the game does tend to suffer from a lack of variety. It does at times become a repetitive grind. This may have something to do with my style of play. My play through was about 130 hours but I pretty much completely cleared all areas to 0 threat before I entered gas town and I only used fast travel a few times when a glitch got me stuck. Gasoline was a just a wasted mechanic since I never came close to running out of fuel. The Magnum Opus damage model was also weak. I could flip off any cliff I cared to and damage was minimal. It sort of removed some of the effectiveness of the terrain.
The bad:
Story: 4/10 - The story is incredibly thin. I'd say Trojan Bearskin Condom thin. I wont ruin what little these is here. The first two hours of play had some story elements as did the last six or so hours. That is 8 out of 130 hours. The war boys and even the level bosses has the personality of cardboard cut-outs. This was a really poorly executed aspect of the game and a missed opportunity. Just a few more cut scenes and some more build-up would have gone a long way to make each territory more exciting.  As it stands the game quickly becomes a shooting gallery. Max was fully maxed out for skills less than half way through the game and scrap became a moot point about the same time with a balance of 20k or higher for the rest of the game.
Conclusion:
Great game. It entertained me to one degree of another for over 130 hours and that makes it wholly worth the money especially since I picked this up on a steam sale.  If you can forgive the lack of story and enjoy the scenery this is a great time killer.

I understand that 8.7 hours is all I have on record with Day Z. I also understand that 8.7 hours is very little compared to other players in the community. However, 8.7 hours was all that I could take. Yes, I understand DayZ is still in alpha. Yes, a beta is being promised soon. I am not holding my breath. With that out of the way, let's begin.
I bought the game expecting a different experience than what I received. There was next to no loot around the map. I searched entire small villages, on several occasions, to walk out with maybe a can of soda, box of matches and three different colors of the same plaid shirt. Melee weapons are everywhere. Honestly I should say that nearly anything you pick up can be used as a melee weapon. This I have no problem with. However, when I would find a gun it would have no ammunition. When I found ammunition it was rare for it to be for any gun I had. Food and water are scarse. With no real loot to rely on, I starved to death or dehydrated. Stack these issues with 99.5% of the DayZ community being shoot on sight (whether you have gear on you or not), made the learning curve unbearable. When I complained, I was told to search Youtube for answers to my survival. I did. Basically I was directed to stop relying on loot I could find and to craft things instead. I now find myself on the beach, spamming my keyboard in search of a sharp rock to use as an improvised knife. I find myself spamming my keyboard at trees looking for apples... Seriously?
The game is about the zombie apocalypse and survival. It feels like a gardening simulator paired with zombies and highly disgruntled, armed neighbors. A simple text based instructional system for new players, or at least a tab to click in the menu that would provide a quick text based tutorial would be helpful. Loot is either non-existant or, when you do find loot, very repetitive. The community that still plays appears to be small. Small and hostile. Small and hostile like little rabid Yorkie pups heat. If you are a player of the game and are enjoying yourself, by all means carry on sir. If you are contemplating purchasing this game, I would recommend against it. At least until this Beta is released.

I have played many indie games in my time since I have downloaded a few for my Xbox 360, and I think it is a great community. I say this because it allows developers to showcase their talent and creativity without the worries of advertising, merchandising, or profit making. A lot of these indie games I have played are fantastic in their own way.
Limbo was great because its unique artstyle was like no other. Braid was great because its puzzle designs were engaging and genius. Super Meat Boy was great because it played great. Shovel Knight was great because it was an 8-bit throwback that any player would have wanted.
But, Undertale is something else!
I have never played anything like Undertale. It is just simply a work of art that excludes itself from other video games to become a mastercraft. Its quality can even be compared to some of the best AAA games ever made.
So, what is it about Undertale that makes it stand out? Is it the wonderfully weird cast of characters? Is it the unique bullet hell shooter combat system? Or could it be the thoughtful story that this game holds? In my experience, it is all of those. But the real reason why I love Undertale is because... it affected me emotionally.
Undertale made me realise that there are no bounds to human genius, that there is hope, and that even the most vague of decisions cannot bring the most positive outcomes. But Undertale is one of those games that does need to be played so that you can understand why it is getting the amount of praise it deserves.
If you have not played this game, you like Indie games, and you would like the best experience possible, then I could not recommend this game enough. If it is the pixelated graphics or perhaps the fandom that is often considered as cancerous putting you off, don't let it put you off this beautiful, incredible, outstanding experience like no other.
Undertale will remain in my heart for years to come. Play this game, and you will see why everyone is filled with DETERMINATION.

This game is a rogue-like platformer that's pretty fun for a while.  This game has three phases, I feel.
First, it's frustratingly difficult, where you are just getting slaughtered by surprising and unforgiving rooms.  The procedurally generated nature of the game means that you can't practice until you master it.  You also lose all your gold with every playthrough, so if you ALMOST could afford that tiny health upgrade but fell short, you'll be eagerly looking for cheat codes.
Then, you have enough health to make some money, you now keep half your money each playthrough, you can take out the bosses, and you don't want to run as soon as you see something big.  You graduated to big boy pants... HIGH FIVE!
Finally, you get through new game +X and you realize you are only playing this to finish off your upgrades, grinding for those few stat bonuses... and you took out those special hard versions of the bosses (the ones that gave you infinite attempts to beat).  At this point, the game is no longer fun.  But I guess this is where the game ends.
It's just that... I still play other rogue-likes that I've mastered because the game presents a fun challenge.  Rogue Legacy is a grind all the way through, but it's a fun grind... for a while.

Rogue Legacy is yet another indie roguelite metroidvania, another in a long indie gaming fad of making roguelite metroidvanias. In Rogue Legacy, each character you play only lives once. While playing, you collect gold and artifacts which you then can use in future playthroughs, by spending gold on levelling up your stats, unlocking new classes, or unlocking new items. Slowly but surely, your character scales upwards in strength. You'll also unlock new weapons, armor, and other things through finding them in the castle or defeating bosses.
Without getting super deep into the details, Rogue Legacy is a satisfying gameplay experience, with a bit of a weird learning curve. Initially, when you start, you'll struggle with making much progress. Especially since you cannot carry gold between castle runs, and because you can sometimes roll multiple useless characters in a row, you'll sometimes just be unable to progress. Eventually, you'll have a huge run, make tons of gold, and break through the threshold, but it can be a bit frustrating to wait until that moment.
I enjoyed my time with Rogue Legacy, and I still sometimes boot it up to replay the castle a few times. Once you beat the final boss, you can either continue on in New Game+ infinitely (I've seen people at New Game +++++++!) or you can wipe your slate clean and start fresh.
Ultimately, I feel like Rogue Legacy is a satisfying experience and a worthy entry to the long line of Roguelite Metroidvanias that we can't seem to escape. The closest cousin to this game would be Spelunky, although Spelunky is definitely a much more razor-thin cutthroat kind of game.

A masterpiece, Spec Ops: The Line is no ordinary third person shooter; it is about the human condition and of morality that questions what it really means to be a soldier. This game is up there with and comparable to The Last of Us as both titles really do explore the true journey into the darkness of ourselves. Gameplay-wise is also great with easy controls, fun cover base combat that allows teammate commands, a good variety of weapons and enemies to takedown. I highly recommend that you watch Francis Ford Coppola's 1979 classic Apocalypse Now (preferably the Redux edition) before you play Spec Ops which has very similar themes to the film for the ultimate Heart of Darkness experience.

A meaningful psychological thriller following a mostly linear path of story telling.  Experience the truely rare immersion that  many shooters lack in an intense and fast-paced style of tactical shooting and squad-commanding.  You ARE the protagonist as YOU make the choices that shape your character and the story.  Your choices have everlasting affects on the progression of the story with sometimes severe repercussions, and the morality of these choices are constantly questioned by characters throughout the game.  A memorable gaming experience with a very powerful story that will make you reflect on the game a good deal of time after the 12 hours it takes to complete the story.  If you are looking for a story- and character-driven game with strong immersion qualities and challenging tactical gameplay, and hope to enjoy a meaningful story in a decent amount of time... then this is the game for you!

The Line is at once one of the best military games I have ever played and one of the darkest experiences I've encountered. Definitely worth playing through at least once through the entire game, and repeat the last 2 levels to experience all 4 endings.
- Mature, engaging storyline, one of the few around.
- Solid shooting mechanics.
- Solid, if light, squad mechanics.
- Variety, especially in set pieces.
- Challenging, 'just right' difficulty (on normal).
- With the exception of the very detailed character models, graphics are mostly plain and serviceable.
- Squad AI can occasionally be a bit wonky.
- Only ran accross a couple of bugs, but both were gamebreakers and required a checkpoint reload.
- Short game. Over in roughly 5 hours, a solid gamer on easy could probably clear through this in 4.
Definitely worth playing through for the storyline. It takes a bit to get going (

When it comes to Early Access games, Prison Architect and their team does it right.
- Scheduled Updates, with explanations of what has been changed and how it impacts your gameplay.
- Interaction with community, as you can spend a bit extra to be immortalized in the game.
- Consistent improvement to the game mechanics.
- Timely addressing of known issues (Within reason. Some programming issues take time to resolve properly. Better a cure than a band-aid)
- Addition and removal of game features to deepen the experience.
- A friendly and light-hearted dev team who keep you in the loop.
Most importantly, having purchased this game over a year ago, I have seen it steadily improve month after month, getting easier, then harder, then easier again. New features are added that increase the challenge. Mechanics are tweaked to make it manageable.
For me, the great "Litmus test" of a good early access game is simple:
If I walk away from this game for 6 months and come back, has the gaming experience changed?
Answer: Yes.
Is this change an improvement?
Answer: Yes
The beauty of supporting an Early Access release game (other than supporting starving game devs) is that you get to see the game evolve over time, and the game experience itself changes. With Honoured Mentions to "Towns", in no Early Access Game have I had such a positive experience in coming back to a game I had put on the shelf for a few months and seen it changed enough to be full of new tweaks and features I have to wrap my head around and incorporate into my game while staying true to the simple mechanic and gameplay that drew me to the game in the first place.
Even though the updates have broken my prison on more than one occasion, it was never so frustrating as to destroy my desire to just sell it and build a new one (Especially since I remember when they added that feature in an update and I not only made a cool $500,000, but "Fixed" my broken workshop and other prison design flaws by rebuilding.)
If you like builders, sims, prison, violence, or just generally being an iron-fisted prick in charge or other people, this game is a must have.
If you are a game developper with a game you hope to release in Early Access, for the sake of your reputation and the success of your game, take notes on how Prison Architect has been released and updated and follow their formula as best you can.
There will always be negative reviews and gamers who complain about everything your game isn't. What is important is in focussing on what your game IS and staying true to that identity and concept throughout.
Introversion does that brilliantly in this title, and the results are astounding.

Rust is the closest I’ve ever come in a videogame to feeling like I was living in The Most Dangerous Game or any of those pursuit-and-survival classics that we read every year in school. Every player you meet is potentially a mortal threat or a potential ally, which is common enough for a survival multiplayer game, except that Rust also functions a bit like a social experiment. It’s like someone gave Stanley Milgram a private island, a private army, and an endless supply of willing prisoners and said, “See what you can make happen here.
Every few hours in-game, a cargo plane flies overhead and makes a supply drop that draws players from all around the map into a highly charged, dangerous confrontation over the mere possibility of treasure. There might be nothing very special in those supply drops… but there might be advanced gear that would be difficult or impossible to craft yourself.
Alternately, an attack helicopter sometimes appears to hunt down and kill any players that it manages to see, and its appearance is as chilling as it is unexplained. It’s existence is contrived, like everything else in Rust’s deserted, semi-industrial wilderness, but still unsettling. It’s something that forces me to consider what Rust looks like from above, as a bunch of half-naked, violent, and greedy people try and create peace and security for themselves in a setting of profound anarchy.

This is probably my favorite game on Steam. If it looks interesting, just get it, because this game is just as good (if not better) than it looks. I guess one potential con is that it can be sort of repetative, but it is a rogue-like/rogue-lite (if you didn't get that from the name).

A hard thing to do in upgrade type games is to manage the fine balance between making the game too quick, and making the game feel grindy. This game manages this AWESOMELY. You do not compile all your money. You work your way through the dungeon, and however much gold you get, that's what you can use to purchase things (character upgrades, equipment, and abilities). You then lose your gold the next time you go in (the cost can be reduced to 50%, but the element remains in the game). This means that the game might get to that easy point, but that just means you can last longer in the dungeon. It will always be difficult to get enough coins to upgrade what you want. This means there is a grinding aspect to it, but it's not easy, mindless, or annoying. The game never feels grindy. It gives you a great sense of accomplishment when you're able to buy that big upgrade, because you actually earned it by getting an awesome dungeon run, rather than just committing enough time to grinding. This is an excellent aspect to the game, that works absolutely perfectly.
As for the gameplay. The dungeon being different every time you enter makes it always interesting. The regular game is fun, and a bit challenging, then you get the remix bosses that are completely insane and difficult, which gives more hardcore players a good challenge. The combat system is a lot of fun, and the way you customize your characters based on what heir you get is a lot of fun. You can get an assassin, and then tweak him/her out with gear and abilities that match that class, or you could get a barbarian, and completely change your tactics.
It's a really unique spin on the classic platformer genre. Totally worth it. Honestly one of my favorite games, and I'm hoping they make a second one.

This game features a different mechanic to the Rogue-Like Genre:
Dying doesn't end the game.
It follows a system in which you enter the castle, fight to your final breath, and then use the riches and items you found in the castle so that your kin can continue your families quest to defeat the evil within the castle. The catch? You lose all of your gold upon entering the castle, as the gatekeeper won't let you pass without paying with everything you own. Every character has their own little perks. Some are color blind (Meaning all gameplay is in black and white), are clumsy (Everything you move past is destroyed), have ADHD (Move faster) among many, MANY other perks your heir can have. The game, due to the special mechanic that the castle changes with each heir, lets players choose when they want to farm and when they should go after bosses.
Overall, you can play this game for hours on end with no completion in sight. You have to become good at the game to actually be able to finish. Enemies, unlike some other games, can still deal damage. Early on in the game, depending on your class, you can actually get one-shot if you venture too far out from the proper path. Learning the quirks and patterns of enemies is key to beating the game, which requires foresight, concentration, and attention to detail.
This game is worth every penny you spend on it.

Mad Max was a pretty suprisingly amazing game considering I bought it on sale as a spur of the moment. Runs incredibly smooth, looks fantastic and handles well with mouse and keyboard. I've sunk a good amount of time into this, as of this review haven't collected every upgrade and what-not but I got close enough that I felt satisfied.
The combat was enjoyable, vehicular combat in particular was a blast. The ground combat was competent and felt pretty satisfying, as someone who hasn't played any of the Arkham style combat games I didn't have any issues with 'seeing it again', as it was my first real introduction to it.
There is quite a bit of repetition in this game, but most of it is optional. Though I do say 'optional' lightly, as to get most of the upgrades for your car you have to spend quite a bit of time doing these repetitive tasks in order to unlock them, which is probably one of my bigger gripes with the game, as well as them locking upgrades behind story quests and your character level.
I do recommend the game despite the story being kind of♥♥♥♥♥ mainly because the rest of the game is pretty damn enjoyable.
However the story lacked and the ending outright sucked in my opinion, here's why:
!!! SPOILER BELOW DON'T READ UNLESS YOU DON'T CARE ABOUT HAVING THE STORY SPOILED. !!!!
So I don't know about you guys but I felt the story sucked massive♥♥♥♥♥especially in the conclusion. I wasn't all that invested in the story to begin with but they really killed it for me. First off, the concubine... soon as I saw her the game basically screamed "oh look, it's the love interest/replacement wife and daughter". I felt as if both her and her daughter could've been left out of the game entirely and it would've made for a better story, but let's just accept that she's here.
The game gave me zero reason to feel invested in Hope (the concubine) throughout the entire game other than "look, walking bewbs". How much 'screen time' did this character even get? I feel it was less than 5minutes easily, with barely any dialogue either.  Yet nearing the ending of the game Max feels compelled to help her, which is pretty obvious why going back to "replacement wife/daughter". Okay fine so you help her out and rescue her daughter, daughter has some backstory in the 'bio' but if you weren't to read that then you'd have little reason to be attached to the character. And then a skip and a jump across the wasteland and Max refuses Hopes' offer of 'being a family' and both Hope and her daughter are killed while Max is off chasing Chumbucket.
So why does Max suddenly care? He's got the magnum opus ready for his journey yet he chases down Scrotus for the showdown. First off, there were many ways to orchestrate a showdown between Max and Scrotus without the inclusion of Hope, so the incentive wasn't really needed. Secondly Max sacrifices Chumbucket to not even kill Scrotus? I mean Chumbucket was probably the ONLY character that was interesting and I got overly attached to and that Max should've been attached to, but ok yep he's dead too. While a 'happily ever after' ending with Hope, Chumbucket and Glory (glory is the daughter) would've been a bit♥♥♥♥♥♥ I would've preferred it over the one we got. As this is how it spoke to me
"Oh hey look, Max is gonna be happy again with all this rebuilding with Griftah (spirtual guide) and Chumbucket (a friend) and Hope & Glory (Family). But wait a sec, we can't do this because that'd make him 'not mad' anymore oh♥♥♥♥♥♥quick can it all! Kill all of the characters! heh heh... no worries guys! He's still Mad Max, we wouldn't dare encroach on anything bold like having an outcome for him as that'd 'ruin' the canon and upset people, look he even has more reason to be Mad! Got his car back too, anyway bye!"
Anyway it just seemed tacked on for me, like 'we'll construct something that seems like a story but by the end of it, it was actually all for nothing'. Because it was, Max lost all development made and you basically achieved nothing other than killing a crapton of morons and a couple bigger morons, the game basically says this by giving him the car back and having the outro the same as the intro, pic of his daughter/wife, black on black car and open road.... so what did we just do again?
I love the story of Mad Max and have watched all the movies, but I felt as though they could've been a bit more ambitious with the story instead of giving us a very unsatisfying conclusion, as you don't really feel Max as a character got anything out of it... because he didn't.

Right from the beginning you have an awesome action sequence, then, for anyone that has seen the movies, we see Max try to recover everything he has lost and succeed on the different challenges set for him. There are many characters that accompany him, some minor like Jeet and others that are major, like Chumbucket. It may take some time to learn their stories, but they are definitely worth the time and give great insight into the world of Mad Max. Combat is fluid, upgrades are easy to get, there is little difficulty in obtaining scrap to get most, if not all of them, so that was a downside for me, I wanted to struggle to get the materials needed. Similarly, by the end game, there is little fear in combat, Max can easily beat tens of enemies at the same time, same with the Magnum Opus. My only complaint was that the last battle felt anticlimactic, it could have been much better definitely and more symbolic.

This is a game that should not be played for the fun of it, or because it can be a fun way to kill time, but should be played for the experience. This game really got to me and instilled feelings of actual physical sickness and distress, as well as captivating me with a frighteningly detailed story. The latter is something most developers of similar titles push aside in order to squeeze in more reasons to shoot arabs, russians and other non-americans. Play this if you want a different experience and want to take part in a story that is a bit deeper and more personal than the typical "shoot-all-brown/slavic-people" nonsense that we have up to our ears these days. The gameplay itself can be a bit tricky since you're not as much of a bullet-sponge like in many others, and your squaddies become fairly special-ed if you give them orders other than the ones each of them specialize in. Remember when games used to be about fun and finishing levels as fast as possible, and were so stupid that one could laugh at them no matter what happened in-game?

I bought this game for my 4yo newphew, so he and I could play it together.  And, he loves it!  So, if you're buying it for kids who love cars/trucks, then read no further -- just buy it.
As for what *I* think about the game:  I was immediately impressed by the detail and the graphics.  It's a solid game and it performs very well (plus, I haven't ever experienced any bugs, which is nice).  You can set up the controls to be as realistic or as simple as you like, but a big rig can be hard to control even with the easiest control settings.  As someone who is used  to playing games like grand theft auto, it certainly took me some time to get used to the VERY realisitc driving physics in this game -- I was running into objects A LOT.  It gave me a new-found respect for big truck drivers.
The level of detail in this game is pretty great too:  there are pedistrian drivers who obey road laws and you get fines for disobeying them yourself (no cops, just automatic fines).  One negative comment about the game would be that (although it is a HUGE open world) it suffers from classic game "invisble wall" syndrome which keeps your from driving your big rig off into majestic fields.  Oh well.  You'll just be limited to your thousands of kilometers worth of roads.  *sigh
I can't comment much on the "actual" gameplay,  because all I do is drive around wherever my newphew wants until my trucking company goes bankrupt, and then I start a new game.  Heh.
If you like simulators and to drive trucks. This is the perfect game.
