Readers looking for an in-depth review of Black Ops II’s multiplayer, I’m sorry to disappoint. My knowledge in that area is minimal and as far as I’m concerned, nothing’s changed since the last iteration (save for some new weapons and maps). It’s still a fun and solid experience rivaled only by few others, but my true qualifications as a reviewer lie mainly in single player.
Despite Black Ops II’s static multiplayer component, the game still shows effort to break new ground through its ambitious campaign. As usual, the plot involves some conspiracy to incite global warfare, but this time, it’s one worth revisiting even after the credits have rolled. Since the first Black Ops, Treyarch (one of three Call of Duty developers alongside Infinity Ward and Sledgehammer Games) has shown a knack for storytelling. Their talents are still clearly visible here through their complex narrative cleverly woven together by events of the Cold War and Treyarch’s vision of the year 2025.
For the first time in Call of Duty history, the campaign offers branching storylines that are shaped by missions with multiple endings (determined by whether or not objectives were achieved) and choices made by the player. In the case of the later, decisions don’t boil down to choosing from a list, but are made with gameplay mechanics, be it interacting with the environment or choosing which limb to shoot. Often times, you’ll play through these moments without even realizing that alternate options existed and that’s what makes Black Ops II great - it encourages players to reconsider their actions. Ultimately, the secrets found and choices made will determine which of the five ways the game can end.
Also new is a tower defense-like mini game in which the player must direct troops against waves of enemies in bird’s-eye view. At any moment, the player may assume first person control of a friendly unit on the battlefield and play as normal. These missions, known as Strike Force missions, serve as supplements to the main story, unlocking themselves when certain conditions are met. They’re a welcomed addition and help immensely to vary the gameplay.
As proud as I am of Treyarch, especially for their contributions to the single player, there’s still plenty of room for improvement. In vehicle segments, handling feels extremely sluggish and the unrealistic physics breaks all immersion. The script is filled with clichés and the absurdity of some missions should have been toned down. Stages set in 2025 introduce several game-changing gadgets with promising potential that never reappear. But the biggest culprit of all is the fact that Black Ops II feels like a glorified game of Whack-a-Mole where enemies repeatedly pop out for you to shoot.
Multiplayer and single player aside, there’s still the topic of Zombie Mode. The new features here are a separate campaign and a new 8 player game type. While Treyarch’s efforts are appreciated, the final product is all but satisfying. The “campaign” merely consists of ordinary survival maps strung together by cutscenes and fighting zombies with an army makes an already dull experience even duller.
It’s refreshing to see a developer cater to the single player fans for a title with a track record for being predominantly multiplayer. In doing so, Treyarch has raised the bar for first person shooter narratives. Regardless of what comes from Infinity Ward next year, I can honestly say that I eagerly await Treyarch’s next release, knowing very well that they aren’t one to shy away from being different.
Grade: 4/5

Treyarch has a weird history with me. I was an Infinity Ward fangirl for quite some time as I adored Call of Duty 1, 2, and 4. I absolutely despised the 3rd installment for the series (mainly because I hate shooters on console), and WaW just didn't do it for me. Ever since Modern Warfare 2, I've loathed the next slapped together installment of IW's take on Call of Duty. And then Treyarch swooped in and showed me the light. Treyarch really tries, and it blossoms in both Black Ops 1 and 2. Sure, Black Ops 2 has its fair share of moments where it seems slow, or where something could have been done differently to make the player feel more engaged, but Black Ops 2 is still my personal favorite Call of Duty title. The campaign is excellent, the story is good, and the multiplayer has been ironed out to make it more fair, more fun, and more skilled based. I highly recommend Black Ops 2 to anyone looking for a decent 8 to 9 hours to kill (and replay it for the different branching story-lines) and a multiplayer that's quick and easy to jump into.

Borderlands 2 like its predecessor is a role playing shooter. You begin your adventure as the victim of train sabotage by Handsome Jack. And awaken from catastrophe relatively unscathed at the feet of Claptrap. Claptrap eventually leads you to resistance against Handsome Jack, led by the original four characters from Borderlands. The story has seen improvement over the original. The quality writing as a whole has drastically increased from first insulation, but it’s made not for story structure but in the dialog as well. From the dialog alone, I predict that Handsome Jack will start appearing top 10 favorite villain list over the internet sometimes soon. He has a great personality, his funny human and ultimately very very evil.
The journey will rack you-in over 30 hours to complete the main quest line. That’s if you don’t do any side missions, go off exploring, team up with friends and their games. Borderlands 2 is a time enthralling but I mean the most enduring way possible. No matter if you catch the game on sale or if you pay full price, you will get your money’s worth. It’s jam packed with quality content from start to finish. If I use the term “finish” likely because once you complete the main quest, you can play thru the entirely game again against harder and more diverse enemies that drop more elaborate guns and gear pushing you seemingly temporary cap of level fifty.
In that regard, Borderlands 2 is like an MMO but one you only experience with friends and strangers if you want to. Teaming up with your friends and strangers is as easy as flickering on light switch. Cooperative gameplay not only exponentially increases the fun factor with your friends, but it also causes the game to spawn tougher enemies and better loot. There are plenty of bad♥♥♥♥♥awards, permanent perks for performing various in-game task that can only be achieve with help from your friends.
Graphically, Borderlands 2 has seen a significant facelift over the original but still uses the same art style. I ran on several different graphics but somehow hard time pushing few of the games more fantastic effects when there was tons of actions on the screen. But all in all, I am very pleased that way the game performed. I experienced very few crashes and my connectivity issues were hammered out by the third day of gameplay. The varied locations grade from deserts, to rocky mountain ranges, to green steps, to snowy wastelands, to urban environments and industrial complexes located in the world’s harshest terrain. You’ll be fighting classic enemies like skag, rakk and pyscho but there is also nice variety of new beast, malcontents and machines.
Getting from point A to Z in Borderlands 2, can be done either by foot, car or fast travel stations. Considering the massive size of the entire world, you’ll be happy for any type of transportation after a particularly grew some firefight session. It is important to note that driving cars on PC, takes some getting used to. But most of all, I am slightly disappointed to see that enemies clearly have air superiority over you with transforming robots and buzzard drop ships. This isn’t necessarily negative mark against Borderlands 2 or a side note. I really really want to fly those buzzards around in the available areas within Pandora.

Despite everything I love about Borderlands 2, it definitely has an ugly side to it. Unfortunately, it comes from the multiplayer. Joining cooperative games which I haul hardly recommend on doing. It can have some massively negative repercussions to your single player experience. You can miss entire chunks of the storyline and game important unlocks by hopping on with players who are only few levels ahead of you depending where you are in the game. Even though Borderlands 2 offers a system to counter this possibility, it’s not 100% effective. And sadly, there is no Replay Mission option available which could potentially resolve this issue entirely.
I love Borderlands 2 and truly love it. Certainly, there are few dense in the hall but all in all its exemplary experience from start to finish whether you play along or with friends. I can easily say one of the best cooperative games I’ve played this generation and easily one of my favorite first person shooter as well.

I wish I could run the game, but it continues to crash on start up, on Windows XP. I've tried out several fixes suggested by others running into similar issues, such as running it windowed, disabling the steam client overlay, updating NVIDIA and Physix drivers and downloading a DLL.
Furthermore upon each launch it generated log files at around 700 MiB each(!!!), until my system drive was filled out which forced me to investigate the issue and found out about the log files, and where they are. Specifically they are in MyDocuments/MyGames/SpecOps-TheLine/SRGame/Logs if anyone else experience the same thing.
Edit:
When I updated to Windows 7 I did manage to get it to work, so here are some more thoughts:
The game has a very restricted feel, not being able to go back to where you were, not being able to jump except at very specific predetermined places and several controversial decisisions not being your own choices, which made me less emotionally vested. And at the same time the intel ask you to explore within the extremely narrow space you're given, which forces you to clearly notice all the limitations if you hadn't already, which is a bit strange. I also dislike the combat-mode vs. non-combat that magically triggers when hostiles are near or not near, which removes a lot the suspense. Long loading times even when you die in an area and need to respawn there. I would assume it would be possible to retain a lot of the data (the area) in memory and thus reload faster, but alas.
A few times I did manage to backtrack a little for ammunition, but all weapons had magically disappeared. And then there's that guiding arrow constantly as if it isn't linear enough already, and AFAIK it cannot be disabled.
...and all the help text everywhere (relevant because otherwise you assume you can't do something that would logically be possible) makes it feel like the whole game is a tutorial.
Anyway, as for the message the story conveys which is perhaps more war skeptical than many shooters, I fully agree with it, and think it is a refreshing, welcome deviation from the norm.

I can't recommend this game enough. Must have if you like shooting other people with assault rifles.

This game is a charming, endearing masterpiece - I cannot wait to see what Toby Fox might come out with next (assuming he has plans to make other games).
The simple, pixelated visual style harkens back to the age of the SNES and arcades, as does the original musical score, both of which make it an incredibly charming and somewhat nostalgic play for someone like me who grew up playing games like Super Mario, Kirby, Pac-Man and Tempest.
Better than these things though is the story, or stories, the game provides. Seemingly taking a page out of the book of games like Ib, Mad Father, The Crooked Man and The Witch's House, depending on choices you make as you explore the world of Undertale and interact with its peoples determines what ending you get, giving it wonderful replay value.
The combat system is both simple and amazing, combining turn-based combat similar to the Final Fantasy series that most expect from a pixelated game while also incorporating a wholly unique dodging system that presents obstacles to avoid unique to each enemy you encounter; it also presents an attack system I personally had never seen before, making landing a powerful hit into something of a timing based mini-game, all of which makes it an incredibly engaging RPG adventure game. Instead of simply selecting options from a menu and then watching the animation/result, which can get a bit boring and static, it goes out of its way to stay engaging at all times, something that I, personally, think more games of its type could do with.
The characters in the world are well-thought out, well rounded and well designed. It's incredibly easy to get attatched to them, even if the interaction is remarkably brief, which speaks volumes to the writing skills of Toby and his team. Moreover, some characters have intricacies that aren't revealed without playing through the game multiple times and fully exploring all the endings available - or for those like me who have tender hearts, looking it up and reading about it online.
All in all, I feel like this is a game that everyone should play at least once for themselves, or at the very least watch someone else play through at least once - it is a truly memorable expeirence.

This is a revised version of the first game, Freestyle: Street Basketball (released in 2004).
Freestyle 2 (2014) is an updated game featuring a very high skill cap, emphasis on teamwork, and mind games.
Visual indicators are now introduced to alleviate the problem of not knowing how effective the shots are going to be.
This makes FS2's mechanics absolutely rock-solid compared to FS1 (which felt RNG-based as a result).
Being an online game with twitchy and responsive controls, having a low ping is MANDATORY or you will see issues with catching rebounds and to other players, you will be de-syncing (teleporting). What this means is that the player with the lowest ping will be able to react to the timing needed to perform the rebound faster than the player with the higher ping. Most people get by at around 100ms, and some players compensate by diverting attributes to those areas if they feel they are being outplayed due to the difference in ping. Of course, this isn't limited to rebounds and other actions also rely on it.
While this game does feature a cash shop, it is not as pay-to-win as most people think it is since "premium characters" are given out in events for free, and the extra attributes advantage they possess is extremely minimal due to the strict and increasing diminishing returns on ranking up your attributes. You get about 40 points worth so when the diminishing returns ramps up by a factor of 2 points for every 5 points invested, you could only realistically and effectively pump several off-stats" instead with it or take the sliver of an upgrade in your main attributes.
If you intend on playing ranked matches seriously, be prepared to spend $20 on extra skill slots, which gives you a definite competitive advantage ONLY at the pro level (referring to the actual in-game channel where skilled players congregate). This is due to both the level requirements to unlock the endgame skills, and the long grind needed to get there which makes picking the optimal skill loadout more necessary than having more overall skills than the opposition. Even if you never will buy skill slots, rare (and I mean RARE) yearly events do hand them out.
Even if you miss those events, you can still effectively compete but will have to keep any mistakes to an absolute minimum.
Regarding the game's current meta, a 3v3 team composition of two PFs (Power Forward) and a main scorer (Point Guard is very popular for this composition) is both top-tier and easy to play.
The PFs should setup isolation play (iso) and the PG should duel his facing opponent while utilizing the PFs effectively.
For offense, the PFs can be always be brought in at opportune times to provide scoring assistance.
And to really abuse the isolation play setup, PFs should optimize for 3 pointer shots and long-range lay ups to increase the offensive power ten-fold.
For defense, the PFs already provide huge coverage using box-out to force opponents away from key areas, and their massive height allows easier rebounds and shot blocks while the PG goes for the diving ball catches from blocked shots to increase turnovers in your favour.
That being said, you can break the meta easily since the skill cap is high enough.
You just can't expect to win as often since PF-PF-PG is very simple to play optimally with better overall match ups and more overall opportunities to score.
Make no mistake, this is an incredibly skill-based alternative to the NBA2K franchise that comes with the famous Korean-level MMO grind, and an inversely incredible amount of dumb players. This next topic is actually worth exploring because if you're playing to win, as with any online game, you will eventually encounter someone who just wants to play a basketball game. It's not the same game as you're playing, since he's abiding by a different set of self-determined rules.
Example #1:
You're completely open and can make a scoring attempt without any penalties to your accuracy.
The other player has the ball.
He will generally not pass to you and will look to have fun by outplaying both his current facing opponent and the "big guy" guarding the paint (Center or Power Forward).
He may actually pass to you, but he would like the ball back immediately.
Example #2:
You realize he wants to attempt plays even if it's completely sub-optimal or just plain dumb, and so you avoid passing to him.
He will eventually get frustrated that he's not playing his game and when he does get the ball, he won't pass it out for fear of not getting the ball back.
This leads to a 3v1 where he will still try to make a play and ends up losing the ball as expected.
This street does go both ways, so you will end up smashing teams who have but a single selfish player, which leads me to my next point...
Always make sure to queue up with 2 of your friends for an absolute blast!
Alternatively, you can join a clan or if you still insist on soloing, just get out of the "Rookie" channel as fast as you can.
In any case, the game is free, so you might as well try it out and get wrecked!

I held out for so long wondering over whether to buy Mad Max. After seeing it in a few 'Games of the Year' lists, I decided, why not? Well, there's a few very good reasons why not, as it turns out.
Let me be clear when I say that the core of the game is solid. I like driving, I like post-apolcalyptic gameplay, I even don't mind QTE-style combat. But this game is immensely frustrating. There's no thought in the details.
Want to sneak into an enemy camp? Great news, you can! Except that if you die, your own car will magically spawn outside their front door, alerting all the guards you snuck past and forcing you to reload an earlier save or get instantly firebombed/shot to death over and over again. And you WILL die. Unless you have been practising some kind of quick-time-event-based religion for the past thirty years, you will miss a button at some point during a camp. from there, it's pot luck - sometimes you'll get away with a single hit, sometimes the enemies will juggle you from punch to punch until you fall over. The difficulty spikes between missions seems sometimes vast and sometimes non-existent; enemy vehicles seem significantly faster and more powerful when driven by enemies and magically slow down why you hop in, and so on.

At first I wasn't sure about this game. Sure, I liked Roller Coaster Tycoon when I was a kid, but only with unlimited funds. Knowing this was an early access game, I went in skeptical and after the introduction wasn't very clear on how to actually start your prison I looked up a tutorial video on YouTube. After that, I was hooked. I stopped halfway through the tutorial to start making my own decisions on how to run the prison.
It didn't go well at first, a lot of prisoners had serious complaints and started rioting. Some guy died due to an overdose. I realised I had to start making some serious changes in my prison, I started doing a lot of grants (Sort of quests to make your prison better) and in no time my prisoners were well-fed and said they were being treated well. At this point I started worrying if I hadn't made my prison a hotel, but I was content.
It is, however, clear that this is an early access game. There are occasionally some bugs and some features are missing. I would really like to place some "sketch-objects" where you plan your objects themselves. Sure, you can place object-tyles in planning but I often forget which ones they were in the long run. At the very least, I'd like to annotate my planning.
All in all, I really do like this game. It's a great timewaster. Even though it has it's fair share of bugs and lacking features it makes up for it's in-depth gameplay, and it will only get better because it's still in early access. I would reccomend this game.

]You are here, because you want to feel something, you are not... A hero!
Can a game put a blame on player for his actions? Can it mock the whole industry of so called "Military Realistic Shooters"? Can a game present main protagonist as not a player but his\her personality and deconstruct everything we knew about shooters so far?
Spec Ops: The Line proves that it can be done! First of all, if you looking for fun in this game -- FORGET IT! There is no fun, this game has zero fun, and it feels right. that how this game should be; with both main hero and player, game gives both cognitive dissonanse and WTF feeling... Game puts blame on player, but also educates him. It hard to talk about this game without spilers, and I do not wish to spoil this expiriense for you.
Know this, game communicates with player. And main hero represent not what you would expect. It build to deconstruct genre and gamers belives. Or maybe just the other way around, in embrasses player and his\her principles and gives a tool to stand a ground supporting second personality?
Let's just say, that imagine if you would go into a strip club or bar, expecting to have fun! But the moment you enter, something starts to feel wrong, but at the saame time right -- like this is how it is supposed to be. You sit throug routine, when suddenly before closing, something rewealing strikes. And afterwards you expereinsing something that you never experienced before, of rarely. Think about it, like you want, choose the fate of main protaganist and yourself.
But at the end, playing Spec Ops: The Line is like diving into a void, that sucks all good, leaving only darkness, pain and misery.

Awesome side-scrolling game with RPG stat elements. You run, jump, swing a sword, and occasionally throw a fireball against enemies who'd likely see you dead. When your characters dies, their descendants inherit their wealth they recieved from the dungeon exploring, which they used to upgrade their stats and buy equipment (stats and equipment carry over thankfully) but you have to spend ALL of it right then because you're not allowed to carry that wealth into the dungeon (unless you get a veeery expensive skill and even then it can only be graded up to 50% of ya monies) so the trick then becomes making as much gold as you can before you ultimately die.

Congratulations to Rogue Legacy for missing the entire point of Rogue.
Rogue and its derivatives were one of the very few games where leveling systems made sense by virtue of using it as a resource that you needed to manage and by taking away your levels when you lost. Rogue Legacy manages to bork it up by making the leveling system not only PERMANENT, but completely external to the game play itself. There is no level resource to manage in each playthrough. Your equipment is set in stone from the beginning of each game. And each time you die, you get a little stronger.
So the way you succeed in this game is by DYING. What you learned from each death is much less important than the permanent +1 to strength you're going to get when you do. In fact, this makes dying DESIRABLE.
Hey game, if you're going to give me all these classes and levels eventually anyway, why are you making me go through the work of unlocking them? And while we're at it, how about you just set the difficulty to a reasonable level from the very start?
Oh yeah, that would violate the sacred tenet of gaming known as the "leveling system."
On top of that, the level layouts will deny you things by virtue of you having brought the wrong runes or by what random traits your new character has. Then when you pick those things you need, the RNG can just as easily not require them of you. What's the lesson here? "♥♥♥♥ you," apparently.
But unfair BS is kind of the name of the game. You'll be put into plenty of unfair situations simply by virtue of how far you can see on your screen. You'll be put into expansive rooms where everything has projectile weaponry and fires at you all at once, but the game thinks this is okay because it has this mess of off screen indicators for you to try to parse. Is the high or low bullet going to enter the screen from the left first? Oops, never mind, that one top indicator was actually a stack of four arcing bullets indicators coming from an enemy you haven't yet seen. And god help you if your character views the world upside down.
You will spend hours and hours of unnecessary grinding in this game for no reason, and when you do succeed, you have no idea how much was your own improvement and how much was just the fact that your stats are so much higher than when you first started. It's especially weird that the developer thinks this is somehow related to Rogue. Rogue isn't the best game in the world, but it works because there is no permanent progression. Rogue Legacy reverses that, and tries to convince you it's because it wants everyone to beat the game eventually. But if you want to make a game where everyone wins, then just making losing impossible. Don't give me more stats until I win and then pretend it was me all along.
Rogue Legacy makes you grind out thousands of deaths to reach the difficulty level you should've had in the first place. It gives you so many crutches and helping hands along the way that by the end, it's patently obvious to you that your win has been gift-wrapped with a big red bow. And when the game tries to come back at the end to give you a pat on the back for doing such a good job... it's pretty disingenuous. Downright insulting, really.
If this was to be Rogue's legacy, I'd advocate for more birth control.

At this point I started worrying if I hadn't made my prison a hotel, but I was content.
It is, however, clear that this is an early access game. There are occasionally some bugs and some features are missing. I would really like to place some "sketch-objects" where you plan your objects themselves. Sure, you can place object-tyles in planning but I often forget which ones they were in the long run. All in all, I really do like this game. It's a great timewaster. Even though it has it's fair share of bugs and lacking features it makes up for it's in-depth gameplay, and it will only get better because it's still in early access. I would reccomend this game.

First of all this game is not for people who are impatient and who want to do some run and gun.
This game is for people who like walking through a beautiful virtual nature with all of its sounds and atmosphere.
I played TheHunter Classic for a long time, now I discovered The Hunter Call of the wild and I bought it.
At first I thought about getting a refund for it because it looked blurry and flickering.
I am sensitive for flickering and flickering makes me feel sick.
So I tried reshade (just google it) which adds various effect to the game. With this I added some effects and managed to minimize the blur and flickering and I decided to give the game a chance.
I played the game 3 hours at a time until I had to stop. This game is so amazing and looks amazing. I did really not expect this.
At first I was stunned by the beautiful virtual nature. It looks amazing and it sounds amazing.
I just stood still and listened to all the noises around me. You can hear any kind of noise which you can hear when you go into the forest (animals, wind, rain, rustle of the undergrowth, crunchy stones...).
Second there is a great weather system. The weather keeps changing from foggy, to sunny, to rainy or to stormy.
When you see dark clouds appearing in the sky then you can be sure that it will soon start raining.
There is also a day/night cycle and the game feels totally spooky during night. You can hear owls in the distance and bats flying around. I played a lots of survival games and during nights it always feels like zombies or mutants would appear xD.
I know that this is a hunting simulation but the simulation of the wilderness is just amazing.
When you want to hunt down some animals then this is not a easy job. The animals can hear you, smell you and see you. You always have to be very careful or the animal will just run away (like it happened to me a lot :D).
You can lure them by using varios lures or you can track them by following their calls or tracks.
But do not expect that there will be an animal every 5 minutes. You need to be patient an careful.
I have been waiting for about 30 minutes in a hideout until a deer appeared. This was not boring for me, it was thrilling for me.
Even when you spot an animal, you have to be patient. You cannot just shoot easily on 100 meters at the beginning of the game.
It needs to come closer until you can shoot it. But even when it is close enough it is not easy to shoot it.
You need to hold your breath and then you have to aim carefuly for the zones where you want to hit it. You cannot just shoot the foot and then it dies. There are different zones where you should hit it.
If you do not hit the deadly zones then it will bleed and run away and then you have to trace it. This process takes a lot of time so you should better be patient and hit the correct zone.
I also like the sounds of the weapons. They sound quite real. Everything is quiet, then you aim and... boom... a shot breaks the silence. This feels really great and also contributes to the atmosphere.
This game is a real hunting simulation and I really like it.
I did not find any bugs or technical issues yet but I hope the developers will add more options for graphics so that you do not have to use reshade to make the game look great.

Congratulations to Rogue Legacy for missing the entire point of Rogue.
Rogue and its derivatives were one of the very few games where leveling systems made sense by virtue of using it as a resource that you needed to manage and by taking away your levels when you lost. Rogue Legacy manages to bork it up by making the leveling system not only PERMANENT, but completely external to the game play itself. There is no level resource to manage in each playthrough. Your equipment is set in stone from the beginning of each game. And each time you die, you get a little stronger.
So the way you succeed in this game is by DYING. What you learned from each death is much less important than the permanent +1 to strength you're going to get when you do. In fact, this makes dying DESIRABLE.
Hey game, if you're going to give me all these classes and levels eventually anyway, why are you making me go through the work of unlocking them? And while we're at it, how about you just set the difficulty to a reasonable level from the very start?
Oh yeah, that would violate the sacred tenet of gaming known as the "leveling system."
On top of that, the level layouts will deny you things by virtue of you having brought the wrong runes or by what random traits your new character has. Then when you pick those things you need, the RNG can just as easily not require them of you. What's the lesson here? "♥♥♥♥ you," apparently.
But unfair BS is kind of the name of the game. You'll be put into plenty of unfair situations simply by virtue of how far you can see on your screen. You'll be put into expansive rooms where everything has projectile weaponry and fires at you all at once, but the game thinks this is okay because it has this mess of off screen indicators for you to try to parse. Is the high or low bullet going to enter the screen from the left first? Oops, never mind, that one top indicator was actually a stack of four arcing bullets indicators coming from an enemy you haven't yet seen. And god help you if your character views the world upside down.
You will spend hours and hours of unnecessary grinding in this game for no reason, and when you do succeed, you have no idea how much was your own improvement and how much was just the fact that your stats are so much higher than when you first started. It's especially weird that the developer thinks this is somehow related to Rogue. Rogue isn't the best game in the world, but it works because there is no permanent progression. Rogue Legacy reverses that, and tries to convince you it's because it wants everyone to beat the game eventually. But if you want to make a game where everyone wins, then just making losing impossible. Don't give me more stats until I win and then pretend it was me all along.
Rogue Legacy makes you grind out thousands of deaths to reach the difficulty level you should've had in the first place. It gives you so many crutches and helping hands along the way that by the end, it's patently obvious to you that your win has been gift-wrapped with a big red bow. And when the game tries to come back at the end to give you a pat on the back for doing such a good job... it's pretty disingenuous. Downright insulting, really.
If this was to be Rogue's legacy, I'd advocate for more birth control.

The game is arguably transversable art moreso than a game.
The game is most fun when you’re smashing through or bringing down pillars/towers and driving off cliffs from various driving POV, otherwise it truly feels like a wasteland and a great pause-able vehicle driven game... or a waste of time after a while.
The audio/dialogue is lacking, idc if it is a wasteland, either add more than a few audio lines for your compatriot, or a wasteland radio or audio player of some kind. These are vehicles, hearing nothing but the same roar of the engine, wind, then to have it be interrupted by "Its' dinky dee" or some other quote every few minutes gets to the point of debating on whether or not 1 should mute the game and play some music when driving.
Combat is easy, both vehicle and melee after a short while, especially if you’re a completionist. Tear tires and armor off of vehicles... even vehicle combat becomes a chore due to how repetitive it is.
The wasteland has the aesthetic of being one, and the size of one, with an abundance of resources... thus one gets to drive absurd distances hearing every one of the few lines your compatriot can say... whilst rarely having to refuel or drink (heal).
I ultimately should have gave this game a thumbs down since there are so may thumbs ups for a $60 game that is going for $12 bucks elsewhere, has repetitive in gameplay as well as model usage by quite a bit, and lacks a variety audio one would expect for the pricepoint, albeit the world is beautiful, followed by the vehicles, which is probably where most of the budget went... but I did enjoy this game for the time I put into it, thus the clause on pricepoint.
If you can pick it up for $5-$10 bucks and expect 1-2 hours of enjoyable gameplay per buck spent, you probably will get your money’s worth, otherwise I recommend against this game.

What is DayZ?
DayZ is a hardcore survival game developed by Bohemia Interactive. Originally it was a mod for Arma 2 and its DLC, Operation: Arrowhead that was extremely popular and would later lead onto the development of the standalone. The standalone Alpha was launched on December 27 2013 on Steam and has been in early access development since.
I remember when I first heard of DayZ. It was mid 2013 and the mod was getting more popular than ever. Some of the largest names on Youtube’s gaming community were making videos on it. I was instantly intrigued by the game and wanted to know more. I quickly found out there was going to be a standalone release later on that year. However, I didn’t get the game until earlier this year and I think I got it at the best possible time.
When I got DayZ, Bohemia Interactive were gearing up to release 0.62 a.k.a the visual patch, so I was able to catch the end of 0.61 making it easy to compare and contrast the two versions.
The goal of the game is to survive, this means looting, hunting and killing, over and over again until someone does the same to you.
There are plenty of mechanics in game to ensure the survival of your character such as taking a bladed weapon like an axe or a knife to a tree and cutting off some branches and some bark so you can create a fire to stay warm or to cook food. Almost every item in the game has a use to ensure survival or bring you or another player an inch closer to death. Do not expect the game to be easy. The learning curve in this game is harder than a punch from Superman. A player could have several hundred hours of playtime and still be learning new mechanics. That is the type of learning curve this game has.
The gameplay revolves around what type of player you are. Are you a survivor gathering whatever supplies you can? Are you a bandit killing and stealing from everyone you see? Are you a hero hunting down the bandits and helping out fresh spawns? The game feels different depending on how you, the player, interacts with the world. It’s almost like each playstyle is a different level of difficulty, with banditry being normal, heroism being hard and survival being realistic. I’m not saying that to play this game you should devolve to banditry to get a foothold of how the game plays, but rather choose how you play and learn, DayZ is what you make of it.
There is no direct story or an objective that you have to follow, there is just, you, Chernarus and every other person in it. Whether you want to kill everyone you see is up to you. There are two tips I give to new players, don’t ever expect that you’re alone and don’t make a mistake, otherwise the game will punish you.
How Has DayZ changed?
Since DayZ was released in early access there were some drastic changes to the game. One of the biggest changes was the game engine. Initially the game ran off a modified version of the Arma 2 engine and was scheduled to hit beta in 2015. However the development team realised the engine was not powerful enough, so they spent about a year making a new engine called the “Enfusion Engine” and rewriting all of the code to be compatible with it. This delay annoyed many fans of the game causing a negative stigma around this game being in “development hell”.
Now how has the Enfusion Engine changed the game? Well the new user interface is faster and more accessible. The new engine makes the game world have a bit more of a splash of color, giving it a far more vibrant and appealing look while still reminding the player they’re in a zombie apocalypse. The player controller was also slightly changed so that it was easier to play while still staying as advanced as it is.
Even with all these changes and revisions the community is still more split than firewood. One side hates the game and want it to be more like the mod, and the other side love the game and while being able to criticize its flaws. This causes the community to be in a big yelling match, with one side yelling about how bad the game is and the other side defending the game. Some people state the game is “dead” and that the developers have “abandoned” the game. However that is simply not true, as the development team have been making their presence known and that the beta version is only around the corner. This beta version aims to completely revamp the game by adding in a new player controller, an improved and more in-depth base building system, a new stamina system, new road textures, a new camera, a new damage system and the biggest thing of all, modding, and this is only some of what’s to come.
Another huge change is the development team. As of recent the development team has been very vocal about the progress of 0.63 and how passionate they are for its release. They have also been far more connected to the community, regularly holding events for content creators, making a working playable demo version of 0.63 to be played at Gamescom and EGX. Popular Twitch streamer M1NDR (pronounced min-der) has stated that at EGX the dev team were extremely excited about what they were working on. If it weren’t for this passion this game would be “dead” and “abandoned”.

Borderlands 2 is an incredibly addictive First-Person Shooter Co-Op RPG. It features procedurally generated guns that are like crack. Guns! More guns! MORE GUNS!
The writing is hilarious, and the characters are great, the classes are interesting and surprisingly unique, the guns and the combat are very satisfying, and it's just an all around fantastic experience (especially when playing with friends). The replayability is good, since the game features a New Game+ mechanic that increases the level of everything and even introduces new types of enemies on latter playthroughs. I'd recommend getting the GOTY edition, because the DLCs are incredibly good and absolutely worth the extra money.
The level scaling is a bit weird at times. It's very easy to suddenly find yourself grossly overleveled because you've done every sidequest. I'd prefer it if the game scaled a bit more aggressively, because the game can get frustratingly easy if you're a completionist. On the other hand, if you want to stand a chance against some Raid Boss type encounters, you'll either have to be 5+ levels over the intended level, or have a group of four unless you wanna get blasto'd. It would be cool if the Raid Bosses were realistically doable (but still extremely challenging) without cheesing or exploiting when playing in a group of two or even solo if you're super good. Then again, maybe we're just really bad at the game.
Anyway, it's great. BUY TORGUE.

Note: Spoilers below.
The problem with this game, is that the "twist" is that you end up attacking civilians unknowingly.
This works fine if the player always attacks everything they see without a second thought, but it's absolutely possible to only engage attackers *after* they attack you first, since the narrative specifically tells you that you cannot tell friendly from hostile on sight.
If the player chooses the cautions route, and only attacks people who attack them first, then the "twist" moment doesn't work, because the game arbitrarily decides, in a cutscene, that you attack someone without knowing if they *are* hostile. This dissonance completely breaks the supposed "message" of the game. Since the "message" is the main selling point of the game, this causes the entire game to be basically worthless if you're not a mindless killing machine.

Assuming one has a Nvidia (PhysX) rig (or hacked drivers for AMD) that can run it (I have a Nvidia and AMD rig, I’d have gotten tired of the game much sooner if it weren’t for the particle systems I got with Nvidia (PhysX))… those dust storms are fun. The game is arguably transversable art moreso than a game.
The game is most fun when you’re smashing through or bringing down pillars/towers and driving off cliffs from various driving POV, otherwise it truly feels like a wasteland and a great pause-able vehicle driven game... or a waste of time after a while.
The audio/dialogue is lacking, idc if it is a wasteland, either add more than a few audio lines for your compatriot, or a wasteland radio or audio player of some kind. These are vehicles, hearing nothing but the same roar of the engine, wind, then to have it be interrupted by "Its' dinky dee" or some other quote every few minutes gets to the point of debating on whether or not 1 should mute the game and play some music when driving.
Combat is easy, both vehicle and melee after a short while, especially if you’re a completionist. Tear tires and armor off of vehicles... even vehicle combat becomes a chore due to how repetitive it is.
The wasteland has the aesthetic of being one, and the size of one, with an abundance of resources... thus one gets to drive absurd distances hearing every one of the few lines your compatriot can say... whilst rarely having to refuel or drink (heal).
I ultimately should have gave this game a thumbs down since there are so may thumbs ups for a $60 game that is going for $12 bucks elsewhere, has repetitive in gameplay as well as model usage by quite a bit, and lacks a variety audio one would expect for the pricepoint, albeit the world is beautiful, followed by the vehicles, which is probably where most of the budget went... but I did enjoy this game for the time I put into it, thus the clause on pricepoint.
If you can pick it up for $5-$10 bucks and expect 1-2 hours of enjoyable gameplay per buck spent, you probably will get your money’s worth, otherwise I recommend against this game.

What is DayZ?
DayZ is a hardcore survival game developed by Bohemia Interactive. Originally it was a mod for Arma 2 and its DLC, Operation: Arrowhead that was extremely popular and would later lead onto the development of the standalone. The standalone Alpha was launched on December 27 2013 on Steam and has been in early access development since.
I remember when I first heard of DayZ. It was mid 2013 and the mod was getting more popular than ever. Some of the largest names on Youtube’s gaming community were making videos on it. I was instantly intrigued by the game and wanted to know more. I quickly found out there was going to be a standalone release later on that year. However, I didn’t get the game until earlier this year and I think I got it at the best possible time.
When I got DayZ, Bohemia Interactive were gearing up to release 0.62 a.k.a the visual patch, so I was able to catch the end of 0.61 making it easy to compare and contrast the two versions.
The goal of the game is to survive, this means looting, hunting and killing, over and over again until someone does the same to you.
There are plenty of mechanics in game to ensure the survival of your character such as taking a bladed weapon like an axe or a knife to a tree and cutting off some branches and some bark so you can create a fire to stay warm or to cook food. Almost every item in the game has a use to ensure survival or bring you or another player an inch closer to death. Do not expect the game to be easy. The learning curve in this game is harder than a punch from Superman. A player could have several hundred hours of playtime and still be learning new mechanics. That is the type of learning curve this game has.
The gameplay revolves around what type of player you are. Are you a survivor gathering whatever supplies you can? Are you a bandit killing and stealing from everyone you see? Are you a hero hunting down the bandits and helping out fresh spawns? The game feels different depending on how you, the player, interacts with the world. It’s almost like each playstyle is a different level of difficulty, with banditry being normal, heroism being hard and survival being realistic. I’m not saying that to play this game you should devolve to banditry to get a foothold of how the game plays, but rather choose how you play and learn, DayZ is what you make of it.
There is no direct story or an objective that you have to follow, there is just, you, Chernarus and every other person in it. Whether you want to kill everyone you see is up to you. There are two tips I give to new players, don’t ever expect that you’re alone and don’t make a mistake, otherwise the game will punish you.
How Has DayZ changed?
Since DayZ was released in early access there were some drastic changes to the game. One of the biggest changes was the game engine. Initially the game ran off a modified version of the Arma 2 engine and was scheduled to hit beta in 2015. However the development team realised the engine was not powerful enough, so they spent about a year making a new engine called the “Enfusion Engine” and rewriting all of the code to be compatible with it. This delay annoyed many fans of the game causing a negative stigma around this game being in “development hell”.
Now how has the Enfusion Engine changed the game? Well the new user interface is faster and more accessible. The new engine makes the game world have a bit more of a splash of color, giving it a far more vibrant and appealing look while still reminding the player they’re in a zombie apocalypse. The player controller was also slightly changed so that it was easier to play while still staying as advanced as it is.
Even with all these changes and revisions the community is still more split than firewood. One side hates the game and want it to be more like the mod, and the other side love the game and while being able to criticize its flaws. This causes the community to be in a big yelling match, with one side yelling about how bad the game is and the other side defending the game. Some people state the game is “dead” and that the developers have “abandoned” the game. However that is simply not true, as the development team have been making their presence known and that the beta version is only around the corner. This beta version aims to completely revamp the game by adding in a new player controller, an improved and more in-depth base building system, a new stamina system, new road textures, a new camera, a new damage system and the biggest thing of all, modding, and this is only some of what’s to come.
Another huge change is the development team. As of recent the development team has been very vocal about the progress of 0.63 and how passionate they are for its release. They have also been far more connected to the community, regularly holding events for content creators, making a working playable demo version of 0.63 to be played at Gamescom and EGX. Popular Twitch streamer M1NDR (pronounced min-der) has stated that at EGX the dev team were extremely excited about what they were working on. If it weren’t for this passion this game would be “dead” and “abandoned”.

As you can tell by my playtime in this game, I enjoyed it. The developers are constantly updating and improving the game and are charging the game for a reasonable price.
However, what I absolutely HATE about this game is that there are "server wipes", which are basically what they sound like: Resetting server data. This means that all of your hard work in a particular server is all wiped and reset, so you have to rebuild and restart all over again.
There are two kinds of wipes: Mandatory wipes and server-based wipes. Mandatory wipes are enforced by the developers every month (for reasons I cannot recall as of now) while server-based wipes are resets performed by the owner of each server where wipe schedules are up to their discretion. Usually, server-based wipes happen every week to two weeks. I don't know about you, but I get kinda nostalgic over losing all of my stuff.
Anyways, other than that, this game is a lot of fun to play, especially with friends. I would only recommend buying this game if you have friends who (will) play it as well.

First let me get this out of the way. I don’t really like shooters, be the first or third person. I’ve never enjoyed modern military games or sci-fi military. I think it’s because I’m not an American so military prowess and firearms aren’t as celebrated in my culture. Now with that being said:

It’s rare when a shooter gets you thinking and tells a story that makes really question the purpose of modern military. In Yager’s Spec Ops: The Line you play as Captain Walker as he and his squad travel through Dubai to find Konrad (who also has a military designation but I can’t remember it) and if that name sound familiar it’s probably because you have a good taste in literature.
The inspiration behind The Line is the movie Apocalypse Now, which follows Captain Willard’s journey up a river in Vietnam during the Vietnam War to apprehend a rogue military agent, Col. Kurtz. Once you change the names and the locations you get the same skeleton behind The Line (except there isn’t a fat Marlon Brando); but the inspiration doesn’t stop there! Like Apocalypse Now Spec Ops: The Line also draws heavily from Joseph Conrad’s novella Heart of Darkness, though more in the thematic area than the plot of the game.
What  Apocalypse Now and Heart of Darkness set out to do is make the audience stop and think about the atrocities that we, as a society, ask every day men and women to commit and then to walk away unaffected. Spec Ops: The Line is continuing on that path, updating a classic story for a modern age. Like other modern you get to play with cool military gadgets but then when you do, or make a no win decision, the game kicks you when you’re down.
What’s nice about The Line is that you don’t get the sense that the game is trashing the military but instead is trying to drive home the point that war is hell and perhaps modern society shouldn’t glorify the military as much as we do. I picked up Spec Ops: The Line on Steam as part of their midweek sale and I highly, and fully, recommend that you give it a try.

However it is  almost totally ruined by poorest movementfunctions  I've seen lately. Never know whether I am going to actually "use" cover or leap over headlong into a thousand rounds. Dual use functions are the worse I've seen. Impossible to correct with keyboard mapping because you can't split out functions ( an artifact of console controllers?) . I suggest developers quit trying to reinvent the wheel and screw it up as badly as this and simply use the STALKER series controls which are the best, most intuitive  FPS/TPS move/shoot controls I have seen. And don't dual use commands, period. PC's have lots of keys:we are not limited like consoles.
Sound could have been better, most sounds reminded me of my first firing sessions many years ago when my ears were deafened and everything sounded muffled. That lasted only a short time, and never in my years of firing did weapons sound muffled, nor did flat loud cracks of rounds passing near.

To put it out at the start, I love this game. As a new recruit to the Mad Max universe after watching all 4 movies (Yes even Thunderdome) I knew this game would help quench my thirst for more, and that it does.
The developers created the Australian wasteland beautifully with a post-apocolypes feel. The car segments are hands down the best part of the game for me as you have many options of attack; blast apart fuel tanks with your trusty quad barreled shotty, or tear off tires with you harpoon.
With all this in mind the game is nowhere near flawless.
My largest hate for this game is the autosave system. Imagine this...
In the middle of a heated death race where you come to a segment full of sharp corners and a steep cliff surrounded by AI whose only purpose is to knock you off the road when suddenly, you get that hated autosave icon and your game locks for a second, or at least, your controls and screen do. You're thrown off the road and have to restart the race once again thanks to the way the autosaves are coded where the game locks up for a second to write the data onto your disk, only solution, SSD.

No, I haven't finished the game. I do not expect the rest of it to be the complete opposite of what I've seen, and by some miracle change every single facet of itself. No game has had a fantastic second half only. Even if it did, being forced to play such an awful game for so long to get nowhere is enough to turn me off of it.
Many reviews I've seen say to "ignore the hype, just get the game and
". What experience? This is the least immersive game I've ever played. COD has more depth than this. How can one enjoy the experience, when the game does everything it can to annoy you?
The visuals are awful, and while most would think that graphics do not matter, this is entirely different than what you are thinking. The main character must be intentionally ugly, how could a developer look at that and say "yep, this is good. That's relatable, and not at all the ugliest array of pixels to ever be created"?  NPCs? Just as bad, they look like they were drawn in MS paint, then pixelated so that it could pass off as an art style. Just becuase it's pixelated doesn't mean it's OK for it to be so goddamn misshapen and disgusting. And don't even get me started on color selection. A dark, gloomy castle? What color should that be? That's right, good old 255-0-255 burn-your-eyes-out purple. But it doesn't stop there. There is absolutely no need to use such bright color. It's bad enough that I have difficulty just looking at this thing without getting a headache.
Heard of this amazing story its got? Well that's just bull. 90% of the writing is just bad puns; I am not even joking, it's not just an excess, almost all of the dialog is devoted to the lamest excuse of comedy I've ever seen. I like puns, they can be legitimately funny. But that's clearly not how these were intended to be funny. As far as I can tell, the only joke is that somebody was so incredibly unique and unusual as to make a pun. And they don't let up, all of the characters have no depth or interest to them at all, they are just another conduit to make the most generic image of uniqueness ever made. This game is unique. But not in any way good or refreshing at all. It looks and feels like it was made by a 12 year old, not just because of how awful it is, but the kind of humor right down to the "drama" is immature, naive, and underdeveloped. Choices impact the story, but don't give you anything worth seeing. The whole lore seems complex enough, though beyond boring. It's very difficult to take the story seriously, because the characters themselves hardly ever become serious themselves. When they do, it is with identical personality and writing style used to tell those awful jokes.
The game mechanics aren't actually that bad. It is evident that the creator attempted to keep it interesting by throwing in new mechanics and events, but there is only so much you can do. I eventually found the non-boss fights too repetitive to pay attention to, and just got them over with so I could leave to the next area (even the boss fights got like this eventually. Instead of depth, just throw in another gimmick). But for what? More god-awful story and dialog? That fantastic new type of eye-searing neon colors? Honestly, this is by far the worst game I have ever played, and I've seen them pretty bad. It has no redeeming qualities. It actively repels me in every aspect. I have lost all hope that this game is anywhere near deserving of getting on steam, let alone the popularity it has seen.

A heartfelt tale that continues the Life is Strange franchise and Chloe's story. Quality writing; several amazing moments and plenty heart-breaking ones that are emphasized by the original game. The characters are perfect; especially our two main protagonists, including the new characters which are just as memorable as the returning cast. I give full props to Deck Nine as it had me enthralled from the get go and captured the original developer’s passion for the franchise, even as far to say that they go balls out on some issues that DontNod was slightly apprehensive about.
The games focus on Chloe’s relationship with Rachel is very well portrayed and shows how events surrounding the pair shaped them leading up to LiS. Bring tissues.
Don’t be off put by the different voice actors; they do a marvellous job, with my only gripe that maybe a couple of the background roles could have used a little work, but I feel the same was true in the original. It doesn’t detract from the story in any way though.
There are a couple of bugs in the game at this time such as voice lines being cut off and buggy saves/scenes but hopefully that will be ironed out in when the final episode is finished.
Overall I would hightly recommend, even if you havent played the first game!

Was surprised at how well done the single player campaign is.
Was expecting a constant max-extremeness level throughout the whole campaign, but it was paced quite well with some slower stealthy parts, and I enjoyed the story more than BLOPS 1 and in fact every other call of duty so far. The motion captured animation and facial animation has a big part to play in this. The dialogue was also a big improvement.
I think the real reason why I liked this was the believably "semi" futuristic setting and technology. I got a definite Deus-Ex:Human Revolution  vibe from this game. The gunplay was solid/snappy, and the perks/modification system featured throughout the campaign, which lets you play missions with the weapons you want.
Another improvement was that there weren't any more infinitely spawning enemies, There never was a moment where I grew frustrated merely from being overwhelmed by numbers or explosive spam, which was common in previous COD SPs.
Graphically this game is really a step up, and there is a huge noticeable difference. They dont shy away from color, and the game looks very nice and detailed. I also thought the music was pretty decent. However, a lot of the guns sound the same (a bit tinny).
The MP has been disappointing so far; Most weapons are simply too accurate and powerful, which boils down to highest rate of fire/mag capacity usually winning. Some of the perks and attachments are easily exploitable. The maps are also a bit too porous and very easily campable, and the spawning system is not ideal. It is very clear that this is a casual shooter designed so that anyone can easily get a lot of kills, and the skill cieling is not very high.
There is no server browser and the UI doesnt map well to PC in many parts. You cant see your ping, and servers are joined through matchmaking or partying. Half the servers I have joined have recurring lag spikes every 2 seconds, and I am not the only one experiencing this. Sensitivity settings are not fine-grained and low enough, and FOV is capped at 90. However, there is greater weapon, perk and build variety.
Overall this game has an engaging single player, but the multiplayer is lacking. If you are a fan of futuristically themed SPs, give it a try. However, if you are looking for a solid competitive FPS, you are better off looking elsewhere.

Unlike all the other COD titles, Black Ops 2 tries to mix it up a bit. I’ll start with the single player which is still horribly short. This time however, Treyarch have provided choices for the player to make that changes the ending of the game. I believe there are about 6 different endings to the single player campaign. Additionally you can customize your loadouts before beginning missions and even have the choice of taking part in Special Ops missions. These missions are more strategy based than shooter based and I personally didn’t find them interesting at all. I don’t want to manage, I want to enjoy a quality cinematic experience that the COD games are known for.
By comparison to the Modern Warfare series, the story in Black Ops falls short. It always seems more about the characters rather than the events unlike the Modern Warfare games which are more about the events and the effects they have on the characters (if you know what I mean). Every pivotal moment in Black Ops 2 storyline didn’t have the same impact on me because I found it difficult to understand the reasoning behind the antagonist and the seemingly random escalation of conflict and violence. I do enjoy the flashbacks between the 80’s and the future levels though. That’s a nice way of changing things up, using different technology, different characters etc.
The multiplayer is quite different as well. No more camping thanks to a lack of the Ghost perk, and a much more in depth customization system for your classes. The perks have all been nerfed to allow for more than three to be used at the same time. You can literally choose to have hundreds of different loadouts now.  Three attachments on a primary gun, different camos on your secondary gun, more than one lethal piece of equipment, even potentially six perks! The combat is as you would expect from a COD multiplayer experience, not much change (apart from being a bit faster paced). Map design is decent although most levels feel too small considering how fast some players can move. The spawn system needs to be worked on because players can literally traverse the entire map and spawn camp enemies. It’s quite annoying on certain smaller levels. Overall I really am enjoying the multiplayer though, it’s refreshing and changed for the better in my opinion.
The final mode, Call of Duty Zombies is back and better than ever! There are several starting maps that you can choose from now, rather than just one map for you to get sick of really quickly. There are 2 new game modes in addition to the classic survival mode. Tranzit is a very complicated mode in which you travel by bus across all of the starting maps in one BIG map. There are things that you can craft and all sorts of future and cold war era weapons to get your hands on. There are even new zombies to blast apart. No, I haven't finished the game. I do not expect the rest of it to be the complete opposite of what I've seen, and by some miracle change every single facet of itself. No game has had a fantastic second half only. Even if it did, being forced to play such an awful game for so long to get nowhere is enough to turn me off of it.
Many reviews I've seen say to "ignore the hype, just get the game and
". What experience? This is the least immersive game I've ever played. COD has more depth than this. How can one enjoy the experience, when the game does everything it can to annoy you?
The visuals are awful, and while most would think that graphics do not matter, this is entirely different than what you are thinking. The main character must be intentionally ugly, how could a developer look at that and say "yep, this is good. That's relatable, and not at all the ugliest array of pixels to ever be created"?  NPCs? Just as bad, they look like they were drawn in MS paint, then pixelated so that it could pass off as an art style. Just becuase it's pixelated doesn't mean it's OK for it to be so goddamn misshapen and disgusting. And don't even get me started on color selection. A dark, gloomy castle? What color should that be? That's right, good old 255-0-255 burn-your-eyes-out purple. But it doesn't stop there. There is absolutely no need to use such bright color. It's bad enough that I have difficulty just looking at this thing without getting a headache.
Heard of this amazing story its got? Well that's just bull. 90% of the writing is just bad puns; I am not even joking, it's not just an excess, almost all of the dialog is devoted to the lamest excuse of comedy I've ever seen. I like puns, they can be legitimately funny. But that's clearly not how these were intended to be funny. As far as I can tell, the only joke is that somebody was so incredibly unique and unusual as to make a pun. And they don't let up, all of the characters have no depth or interest to them at all, they are just another conduit to make the most generic image of uniqueness ever made. This game is unique. But not in any way good or refreshing at all. It looks and feels like it was made by a 12 year old, not just because of how awful it is, but the kind of humor right down to the "drama" is immature, naive, and underdeveloped. Choices impact the story, but don't give you anything worth seeing. The whole lore seems complex enough, though beyond boring. It's very difficult to take the story seriously, because the characters themselves hardly ever become serious themselves. When they do, it is with identical personality and writing style used to tell those awful jokes.
The game mechanics aren't actually that bad. It is evident that the creator attempted to keep it interesting by throwing in new mechanics and events, but there is only so much you can do. I eventually found the non-boss fights too repetitive to pay attention to, and just got them over with so I could leave to the next area (even the boss fights got like this eventually. Instead of depth, just throw in another gimmick). But for what? More god-awful story and dialog? That fantastic new type of eye-searing neon colors? Honestly, this is by far the worst game I have ever played, and I've seen them pretty bad. It has no redeeming qualities. It actively repels me in every aspect. I have lost all hope that this game is anywhere near deserving of getting on steam, let alone the popularity it has seen.

Borderlands 2 is an incredibly addictive First-Person Shooter Co-Op RPG. It features procedurally generated guns that are like crack. Guns! More guns! MORE GUNS!
The writing is hilarious, and the characters are great, the classes are interesting and surprisingly unique, the guns and the combat are very satisfying, and it's just an all around fantastic experience (especially when playing with friends). The replayability is good, since the game features a New Game+ mechanic that increases the level of everything and even introduces new types of enemies on latter playthroughs. I'd recommend getting the GOTY edition, because the DLCs are incredibly good and absolutely worth the extra money.
The level scaling is a bit weird at times. It's very easy to suddenly find yourself grossly overleveled because you've done every sidequest. I'd prefer it if the game scaled a bit more aggressively, because the game can get frustratingly easy if you're a completionist. On the other hand, if you want to stand a chance against some Raid Boss type encounters, you'll either have to be 5+ levels over the intended level, or have a group of four unless you wanna get blasto'd. It would be cool if the Raid Bosses were realistically doable (but still extremely challenging) without cheesing or exploiting when playing in a group of two or even solo if you're super good. Then again, maybe we're just really bad at the game.
Anyway, it's great. BUY TORGUE.

In my opinion the Borderlands series is one of the best game-series ever, not only in gameplay or story! When it comes to funny games Borderlands is, again in my opinion, at the very top (in case of dialogues).
First off i want to mention that it is a Action-Shooter-RPG-lootsplosion thingy, which basicly means that you have classes, a leveling system and items (loads and loads and loads of loot) evolved around action-rich shooter gameplay.
But i want to specify on Borderlands 2, the second game in case of relese date but not in case of story development (The Pre Sequel plays inbetween Borderlands 1 and 2).
You get attached to not only the friendly but also the villain characters.
Smutty language, endless jokes and eastereggs combined with the great Storyline make it a good game even for just one playthrough, and i promise: even if you dont enjoy the start too much, you will still have a pretty good time throughout the game!
The game does not end after you beat it, you can still do all remaining quests and DLC's + you unlock the next mode called the "True Vault Hunter Mode" or simply TVHM which increases the level of your enemies, the items you receive and raises the difficulty to provide an bigger challenge that in quite some cases requires a bit of tactical playwise instead of just running and shooting.
The endgame gameplay is based around farming bosses or specific DLC arenas, i guess people who dont like playing without real quests or farming wont enjoy that state of gameplay too much.
You can have a really good time in the different DLC's which, luckily, keep the same endlessly overdone humour the rest of the game has.
I have played trough normal mode and TVHM and it didnt get boring even the second time, actually i really wanted to play it again after beating it for the first time because i lungered for more.
Off the DLC's i reccomend playing "Tiny Tina's Assault On Dragon Keep" the most, but only after you're done with the story because it does contain some major spoilers!
Borderlands, especially Borderlands 2, has grown to be my favourite game in the past few days and i couldnt reccomend it more.

Pros:

Cons:
♥♥♥♥♥hole of a main character.  Sick of game devs doing this, thinking it's cool or something?
-Repetition aplenty

-♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending
-Adding game time by forcing you to clear zones to progress

This game has a lot of potential of being much, much better...  Not to say it isn't a good game, but it seems as if it is sooooo close to being a great game.  The combat is fun, a la Batman style, though it can be a bit annoying at times.  I've had my character flat out refuse a button input to block (and actually do other things on occassion, like getting out of a vehicle about to blow up.  The animation started, then he stopped and wouldn't move), and, just like Batman, you can get "chain combo'd", going from full to 1/3rd your health with just a few well timed enemy swings, and a few off-timed blocks from the player.  Bit frustrating.
The driving is pretty fun, although it is annoying in its' own rights sometimes.  You have a vast amount of upgrades, requiring many mundane tasks to unlock them all, though...  So if you want to just blow through the game, chances are you'll never see the "Magnum Opus" at it's prime.  Getting nudged by an enemy vehicle can send you spinning, which is mostly infuriating during the Death Races.  In fact, during the Death Races, your enemy AI don't even care about the objective and will go out of their way to ruin the race for you if you get within 5 feet of you, which makes sense, but they will drive 30 feet off the race track, basically say "♥♥♥♥ the race", and do their utmost to keep you pinned.  The handling is a bit wonky at times, but hey, sand, so I get this...  Though I'll admit that the tires specifically made for sand grip are a bit underwhelming.
Challenges are a-plenty, and you'll complete the majority of them by just playing through the game, making the final achievement a bit easier... But no less tedious!  I was at the highest Wasteland rank by about the fifth mission?  I went out of my way to 100% this game, of course, but it was a bit too easy to get that rank.  Ended up finishing at Road Warrior level 188.
The characters are pretty good, with the exception of the main character.  Max is a prick.  He's just rude to everyone, and yeah, I get his situation, but seriously?  He can't even say thank you every now and then?  He's an♥♥♥♥♥HOLE.  Lord.  The rest of the game is filled with your typical wasteland people... Survivors, slaves, warlords, etc.  I'd have to say Chumbucket is the most interesting character by far.
Overall, the game isn't bad...  But like I said, it could be better.  They really had a nice formula, and delivered most of it pretty well.  You can do it better next time, Warner Bros.  I believe in ya.

You have games like Pokemon (which I LOVE, don't get me wrong), where grinding eventually has to happen for you to get stronger, and it, after time, becomes a chore. When I was grinding to get stronger in Rogue Legacy, because of the randomized layouts and the randomized traits at the start of each new run, I never ONCE felt bored. Re-reviewing this great little game. A top down Prison building/management simulation. You build a prison (duh) along with it's many amenities, then hire various staff, research upgrades, set routines for the inmates, thwart escape attempts, rehabilitate, treat and occasionally, fry these tiny misunderstood orange clad bodies with your custom built electric chair. You also have to keep the rest of the less troublesome inmates happy too, otherwise general dissent has a way of quickly escalating into a full blown riot. Leaving you with lots of blood (definitely hire cleaners) and lots of tiny orange guys with red holes in them, courtesy of your riot police. So build a morgue. Or keep them happy of course.
The thing is, the more dangerous prisoners tend to give approximately zero f*cks about your agenda, since they all have their own little backstory and plans for the future. Some of the scum, sorry, inmates, think they're starring in the lead role of Prison Break and others appear to believe they're in The Longest Yard. I have a large morgue.
Overall a fun engaging title. The best prison building/management game I've played, which admittedly isn't saying much considering the competition in this area. Being an early access game, official content is still relatively light on the ground and the game has little depth if you're an old hand at building/management simulations, but it does have a solid little Steam Workshop community going on. This is one of the few early access games actually worth coming back to from time to time.

9/10. It's pretty good, one of the better games I've played honestly. My biggest criticism is the abysmally short length of the game, a normal playthrough of the game can be as short as just over 2 hours even if you weren't going particularly fast. That said it has huge replayability due to the different endings, all of which have additional variants as well, meaning if you really wanted to get every possible piece of dialouge possible you would have to play through the game a multitude of times. Storywise, I don't generally care much about a game's plot but this one certainly has a good one with a lot of powerful underlaying themes. The game play is pretty fanatastic in my own opinion as I love turn based games and at the same time find them a bit repetitive and boring, Undertale is turn based but the active way you dodge enemy attacks and how each enemy has different attack patterns it makes the gameplay much more engaging. The graphics aren't by any means 'modern' they are very pixely and I believe they are intentionally retro, I love them but if you're looking for modern HD stuff you won't find it here. It can be really serious at times and pretty funny at others. Also one last thing, and this is probably the only time I will ever even mention a games soundtrack as I find it extremely irrelevant, the music during the genocide path's final battle is amazing.
