Borderlands 2 is a FPS (First Person Shooter) that immerse you in an imaginary post-apocaliptic world.
I have to say that I became bored of FPS's but, thanks to my friend EdW, I gave it a try.
I can't compare with previous Borderlands because I didn't play it, but in general I can say that this one is awesome.
Everything is carefully designed for making you to feel like if you were really the character you are playing, and the world looks like if it is alive itself.
What I liked most of this game, aside from the great story, is that the AI is excellent. Enemies won't attack you if they don't see you, or will keep attacking the area where you were seen last time... or if there are several factions fighting in an area, they will attack each other ignoring you if you stay quiet.
Without any kind of doubts, you should try the game.

It feels like Kingdom of Amalur in firt person, with guns. It has a very MMO feel, but it's only co-op. There is tons of loot and most of it is junk. Some of the random weapons combos are interesting, but the constant need to get new weapons to handle the constant enemy scaling makes this minigame seem tedious. The gunplay is closer to being on the level with AAA fps', but feels a little clunky. Enemies always feel like bullet sponges. There are some cool mechanics like shooting someone in the foot and they'll fall, or if they're shot in the groin the collapse cradling their jewels, etc etc.
I wouldn't recommend this game. I don't like the insubstantial feel everything has. The minigames seem to overtake the main gameplay too much of the time. I do like the banter from the characters and that's what kept me interested in this game the most. I've tried to play through this game several times, both on the 360 and PC, I have a lot of friends that love this game. I just can't force myself to keep going through the campaign, there's no skill involved and the story isn't interesting enough to keep me onboard. If you like co-ops, in first-person, with an MMO feel and squishy combat you might like it.

Having played this game for quite some time this is how I feel about it:
Positive:
+ It's fun: Seriously, the game is really fun.
+ Has a nice mixture of simplicity and complexity: The game is easy to get into, the controllers are kind of basic but it has a high skill cap, it's hard to master them.
+ Character Costumization: It's really nice.
+ The game has tons of features to keep you entertained: Bingo, My Ball, Freestyles, Challenges, etc.
+ It's rewarding to play: The achievement system combined with Bingo, My Ball, Freestyles, etc. makes you feel like a winner even when you're losing, so there's some reward in actually playing the game, even if you're not that good at it and just like playing it for the sake of having fun.
+ MVP: MVP rewards the player that contributes more for the team instead of the one that just scores all the time. Maybe it could be a bit more balanced, but it's nice to see the game reward team play.
Ofcourse there are negative points too.
Negative:
- Paying actually makes you better: Or atleast makes you seem like you are. Paid characters, like Ginger, for example, WILL punish you if you make a mistake, they are deadly because of the bonus they are given. Maybe in higher levels of gameplay that becomes less noticeable, but in lower levels it's really noticeable, they barely miss. And also there are skill slots unlockable by paying, and that gives more options to people that pay to unlock them, giving them an advantage over free plays. I'll put this on capslock: THE GAME IS NOT FULLY PAY TO WIN. That's not what I'm saying here! What I'm saying is the feeling that I got, that if you're a free player and paying against a paid character in a similar player skill level it's more likeable that he will easily punish your mistakes thanks to the character he has than you are likely to punish is, since you don't have as much stats and special bonus as he has.
- Matchmaking is... weird: I dont know how matchmaking works on this game, but more than a few times I got to play against players that you could see by the skills they were using that they were atleast 10 levels above the players on my team. And I also felt the reverse on some games, that I was being matched with people levels below. Most of the time it felt fine, but I think it was like 80/20, so I thought it would be worth to mention.
- Menus: Menus can be a bit confusing for newer players, since they are presented with a huge BOOM of stuff.
- Clarity: The game isn't very clear on some stuff. For example, I had to go google for quite a bit of time why I couldn't level any stat after putting 5 points into it and the game doesn't tell you what keys to use on your controller, so even if it supports it, it's kind of better to play on the keyboard. That kind of stuff.
Overall it's a good and fun game. I recommend it, even if you don't like basketball that much, give it a shot and try to bring your friends to play it with you, only makes it more fun. I'm curious to see the game evolve, since It's kind of new, from what I've read.

Black Ops 2 is the second Call Of Duty yet to try something different and I really enjoyed this game. I am mainly a campaign guy and this Call Of Duty is possibly the best Call Of Duty yet. Black Ops 2 takes place in the future with some scenes being flashbacks to the 80s and the storyline was fantastic. Surprisingly the voice acting was excellent too with the famous actors lending their voices such as Micheal Rooker, Sam Worthington, Micheal Keaton and of course Nolan North and Troy Baker. This Call Of Duty changed the HUD, the guns, the sounds, the story, the gore, the soundtrack, and how open the game was with multiple endings. The environments for this game sometimes felt massive. There was one scene in the desert where you had to defend a small area but you had to go around this massive level and complete multiple objectives. Scenes of this scale felt epic. Another thing that they added was finding multiple ways to get through the level easier such as exploring a little bit and finding extra areas with weapons and robots that you can use to your advantage. You can also set up your class/weapons you spawn with at the beginning of every level. I loved the campaign in this game and you already know how the multiplayer is since it hasn't really changed a whole lot but the Zombies is better than ever with a campaign like mode and much more open environment. This game also uses DX11 and isn't too demanding but I did have some issues running it on a couple computers. I had issues running it on a i7 3770K with a 560 Ti and an i5 2410M with a 560M but the game ran perfectly on an i7 2600 with a Nvidia 660 Ti and an AMD 5600 APU with a Nvidia 650 Ti. I don't know why but the game's performance seems more inconsistent than your average game, so be careful if you have a lower end rig because it may not run well. The graphics and sounds were nice, and they were both pretty big improvements since last time. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good FPS.

This is one of the best hunting games I ever played, but..... there are some issues. If you are willing to overlook them, then this game is for you. As for the issues...
- Bow hunting can be very frustrating. The wind had such an extreme effect on the arrow, it's rediculous. This could be fixed eventually, but currently most people avoid the bows all together.
I'm a controller user so...
- Controller support? Hardly. Sure you can play the game with a controller to a degree, but there are some issues that WILL effect gameplay. One major issue is they have mapped the (holding breath) button to the same analog stick that makes your character move/walk. Trying to hold your breath for a shot only to ACCIDENTLY start walking and causing your scope to sway all over is rage worthy. What's worse is they offer no button remapping, so you either put up or shut up. Another issues is the crouch button is the same as the stand up button and it's bugged. Numorous times I've tried to conceal my position from an approaching animal only to immediately stand back up. It's happens if your crouched to and try to stand, your character would automatically revert back to the previous stance position. (button remapping? non-existent). Driving the ATV with a controller might seem like the way to go, but unlike mouse/KB, there is an auto center camera on controllers that limits the ability to look around while driving around. There are other controller bugs that can be found in the bug report section of the forums, but these are some of the more pressing bugs.
I'm sure these bugs will be worked out eventually, but they have other bugs that take priority position. I keep coming back after every patch to read the patch notes, but controller support just isn't a top priority.

The Hunter: Call Of The Wild is a gorgeous game with a great hunting experience.  I really enjoy tracking and hunting animals in these enormous and stunning maps of the Pacific Northwest/ Europe.  It is more polished then other hunting games such as Cabela's or Hunting Simulator but is not without it's faults.  I have spent many hours hunting or riding my quad around just looking at the beauty of this title.  I find myself just looking at the valleys or mountainous terrain getting lost in the scenery.  This is not the most replay able game atm in my opinion.  There are missions of hunt this animal, or find a hiker, or get a picture of some animal.  It does get repetitive with the grinding for these unreasonably expensive weapons/ bullets/ callers etc.  After hunting and looking across the maps or riding an atv, or shooting at the range it is bland.  In all at this moment I would recommend this title at the steam summer sale price of $20 price point.

PROS

Gorgeous scenic views of two amazing places on Earth
Amazing Immersion when the wind is blowing through the trees or rain on the lake coming down sideways
Driving across the map just relaxing
The thrill of the hunt and tracking animals
Playing with others to take down animals or shooting at the range
Realistic AI with the animals while hunting , tracking, using a caller or spray

CONS

The settings changing without your consent, the audio changing back to (Vanilla) randomly
The VSYNC is terrible and does not work and needs attention and an apply button
The FPS is not so great even with my setup which I would get 80-100 FPS on Ultra maxed out settings cannot achieve this because VSYNC is not switch able
Issues with screen tearing, and blue hue randomly throughout gameplay
Audio is great and the soundtrack is amazing, but it does randomly cut out and go silent and cut back in for no reason
The amount of animals is very minimal and needs to be more realistic.  The rabbits and squirrels are there but not relevant and cannot be killed and taken.  The real forest has hundreds of animals, birds, fish etc. but you do not feel this or see this in this game.  It is immersion breaking with the lack of wildlife in the game. Deer, Bear, Moose, Coyote, Wild Boar, Elk,  Red Fox, Bison.

Conclusion

All in all this is a fun game and if you use the $1 per hour of gameplay then yes it is worth the money.  Do keep in mind it is a hunting game so it gets repetitive and not much substance in the way of completing missions or variety.  It is very beautiful and a great place to relax and just get lost in the game.  It is a relaxing way to wind down at the end of a hectic day for me and lets me just zonk out.  The animals are great at acting normal but there are bugs where some will run in circles while you put 100 rounds into them but not very often.  You can spend your earned money on things but all the rifles are placeholders until you get the 7MM or .338 Lapua.  The other weapons shotgun, pistol are useless in the big scheme of the game, and the bow is a taste thing.  The bow is more of a different play style than the rifle where you can just shoot from 500 meters out over and over without alerting other animals.  The bow is a whole new way of hunting slowly and quietly very up close and personal.  After hunting for 30-40 hours it gets stale with the same missions over and over just hunting at night is the only variation.  The devs seem to listen to the community and seem to care about criticism and helpful ideas but in my case do not listen and care to help.  It does have updates which are hit and miss because the issues are still there on some tech issues.  It is better than an early access STEAM ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t game which is nice but does have its pitfalls.  I hope this helps someone and gets more people into the community to keep the game moving in the right direction.

Our whole family spent the better part of two weeks taking turns playing (and replaying) Rogue Legacy together. Way too much fun!
Good.

Good music, learning curve, etc.
Although its leveling system makes you grind a bit for boosts, it wasn't as bad as I expected - you can grind in some runs and when you're comfortable you can just rush to the boss. In other rogue-likes, rushing to the boss can be nearly impossible, so you end up grinding every single run for items anyway (I'm looking at you, original Binding of Isaac). It also decreases the luck factor, since you don't get to find an OP item and do a easy run or vice-versa, all that matters is your HP and mana.
The only thing I didn't like was the endgame (as in, after completing the game a few times). As the enemies get to the highest level, the game starts looking like an impossible bullet hell and the rooms get too painful to clear, in my opinion.
In the end, still very worth it.

This is going to be a bit deep and emotional, so if you are not interested i will put the short version here:
This game has perfect idea, but terrible developement.
Long story:
December 2013 (@peak 45k players ingame): I bought this game. I knew the idea from original ArmA MOD and I was furious to see this idea put by professional game developement studio instead of 1 community modder of ArmA. The original creator of mod - was even involved into developement! What can go wrong, right? In early stages, everything looked reasonable, there were some bugs, usually also hotfixes or fixes in reasonable time by game updates. Then somewhere game struggled, some bugs were persisting for a longer period of time, community put some pressure. No response. For like a year or two dayZ received only ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of useless content like clothing, not usable/decorative items. It ended up in a ridiculous state where you could find 30 different useless items in one house. Core bugs still persisting. Developer decides in a mid-run they need a new engine, meanwhile, playerbase did drop to 10k peak players (April 2016), just before the 0.60 version, with brand new Enfusion engine was released. I have to admit, the 0.60 brought quite a refresh to the old engine, game looked better, sounds got better, some mechanisms were introduced etc.. It even woke players that lost faith - bringing game back to life peaking almost 30k players. Actually no. Everyone wanted to see, if after 3 years the game stepped up after tons of promises. 3 months later, game is back to dead state - 8k peak players, 4k avg (last 30 days its 2k players in average). Developers introduced beta version on Gamescom few weeks earlier, but I don't see anything is going to change dramatically. I'd like to see if there is a defending mechanism for consumers on Steam, because this is literally a ripoff, somebody took more than he can handle. They received everything from fat capital generated by EA revenue from milions of copies sold, they have got fairly big playerbase actively reporting bugs on tracker. It's 4 years now since EA release and if you check developement of reviews here, you may find that this game and idea is being killed by developers, sadly (did I mention that even the original creator of Mod had to quit developement team?). TL;DR: perfect format and ideas ended in wrong hands, I don't see a chance that this will change, I believe that BI (developers) got enough professionals to take care of this game but I feel like they've learned their lessons on DayZ and changed their focus to their new game - Escape from Tarkov (subjective speculations). Don't buy it, i'd wait until final release, check the final game state and then consider buying, now you are going to hate this game in a day.

The PF position is way overpowered. Even aside from Big Joe. The PF position is stronger than every other position by a huge amount. They'll almost always dunk over a Center. This game assumes that every single PF in the entire ♥♥♥♥ing world is LeBron James, which just isn't the case.
If you're a C or a PF or a SF, you'll never hit 3s no matter how open you are. I understand that those position aren't usually used for 3s anyway, but you know how to make it so it's actually fair? When you shoot, there's an accuracy bar as in every basketball game really. You have to get the slider into the green position to get a good shot. On these positions, there isn't a green section. Make there be a green section, but make as tiny as my♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ There's no reason for the game to say, "Hey, you're not supposed to be taking those kinds of shots, so you're just gonna automatically miss it."
When you get a "perfect shot" after hitting the green on the slider (hit the green, nobody guarding you, full shot quality), it'll almost certainly miss. Either take out the little "PERFECT SHOT!" graphic or actually make it hit.
The game has Pay2Win features. You CAN win without paying, but people who pay money for cards are just bound to have better stats.
There's a Skill called box out that can be placed on PF and C. If you don't know what boxing out is, it's basically guarding the basket to get a rebound. This skill needs a big tweek job in the game. If you even touch somebody while they're boxing out, your character will get stuck for like a second as they back up. It's enough to have the space to get a rebound against somebody, but making that person freeze for a second just for bumping into them is stupid as ♥♥♥♥. Anybody who has the box out skill is always going to get the rebound.

If this happens to you, you won't be able to start a match again until the readied players unready and ready back up.
Some problems with the community: Why the ♥♥♥♥ even press the "ready" button if you're just gonna go AFK as soon as the ♥♥♥♥ing game starts? You serious? Way too many people do this. If you're not ready, don't press the "ready" button. It's not hard.

This is one game that truly surprised me in a very good way.  It seems so commonplace for themes and dialogue in games to be lazy, sloppy, and/or tailored toward tweens.  Frequently I find myself cringing at cheesy derivative dialogue in otherwise decent games.  Even with stunning visuals and otherwise well thought out plots, the dialogue and thematic presence can be disappointingly weak in many titles.  Fortunately, this game does not suffer from those shortcomings.  While it may seem like the developers were trying a bit too hard to be edgy and shocking, most of their work was effective and poignant.  I found myself witnessing the fictionalized, but nearly true-to-life, horrors of war in a very succinct and surreal way.  Some scenes will have their intended purpose - to make you cringe.  Others caused me to look introspectively and question whether I was doing more harm than good.  Are there such things as good guys and bad guys or are the lines much more blurred?
The adult and heavy dialogue is punctuated with bits of cheesy humor and the overall narrative is very well voice-acted.  The action, however, is fairly bog-standard third-person fare.  It is a cover-shooter in every sense of the term.  That's not a complaint, but don't expect much more than that.  There are some strategic elements and team commands that can be useful, though.  If you run out into a firefight with your arms flailing you will quickly meet your demise.  However, if you order your team to throw a flashbang, then pick off the blinded enemies your chances will tend to go up dramatically.  I'm a FPS gamer at heart, so I don't have the most experience with TPS's, but I would expect that even veteran TPS gamers found this game challenging.  The damage model is brutal and swift.  A few rounds and you're dead.  The same goes for your enemies.  Some parts felt unusually cruel as far as difficulty, but overall it was decently balanced and I managed to complete the campaign in about 6 hours.  Yes, that's very short, but it was an impactful experience.
In a catalogue of mediocre "been there, done that" shooters, this title distances itself from that group.  The combat may seem like you've seen it all before, but allow this game's story and atmosphere drive you on to the next chapter.  For me, it was definitely worth it.

First thing I want to say before writing this review is that if you dislike strong political statements or anything that breaks the 4th wall you should not play this game. Spec Ops: The Line is set in Dubai after the Country was destroyed by sandstorms. You are a 3 man Delta force unit sent in to find out what happened to a US army 33rd Battalion. Sooner rather than later you find dead American soldiers scattered around and are attacked by an unknown enemy foce that will be revealed later into the game.
After the first encounter with the enemy insurgents you are met with a radio broadcast that signals you to US soldiers who have been captured by the enemy. You don't get there in time however and two of the soldiers are executed. One soldier remains who is slowly bleeding out and tells you about the 33rd battalion. Your unit moves into the city and it's all gone to hell.
The story of this game is absolutely magnificent and the way that the developers played it out made it even better. The length of the story was perfect and if they played it out anymore than they did it probably would have been boring and would have seemed to be dragged out. It's short, with about 6 hours play time but it has some replayability with the achievements and the unlockable difficulty.
There are multiple things to destroy in this game that makes sand smash everything which can be quite hilarious. There are also choices that the player needs to make which can effect what happens with the story and the direction the game is going in. There are also multiple endings which I will leave you to find out. When facing these decisions the player will go through and question themselves when choosing which one to do. There are also a lot of dead bodies in this game, a lot. There are also a lot of burning bodies and burned bodies.
Graphics on this game are great, the scenery is very nice and even though most of it is sand and destroyed buildings it still looks great. Even though I played on medium settings it still looked good so if you have it on High with AA turned to the highest it would look amazing.
Overall this game is a 9/10 and I highly recommend it to anyone who likes third person shooters which are different and want a bit of variety.

This game starts out very close to any other military shooter you've played but even at the start you know something is off and a little unsettling. Maybe it's the chaos of the post apocolyptic Dubai that the game takes place in or the American soldiers that you are constantly mowing down because they shot at you first right? If the main character, the hero, of the game thinks it's what is necesarry and good then it must be! Then you hit the half-way point of the game. If you didn't realize something was going on by now then prepare to be thrown out of your comfort zone into one of the most disturbing acts that you will ever have to commit in a video game. After this point you'll start to wonder why you are here? The original mission was recon not rescue or revenge. You were to radio in for evac if you discovered any sign of survivors but if your mission is completed why were you still fighting your way to the heart of the city? This game will make you feel like a horrible person. It will make you question why you even enjoy shooters it will throw atrocities of war into your face and point blank ask you if you are having fun yet. If you are enjoying what you have done. It will ask if you don't enjoy this then why are you still playing and it will carry this. It will call you a horrible person who loves to see suffering and throw it on until the very end. Now enough with the story and lets talk about the gameplay which is not nearly as great as the story. It is very standard third person shooter controls you can spring and take cover the aiming works well gunplay feels tight and the action is all there nothing much to write home about. There is some "strategy" and by that I mean there is a single button dedicated to giving your two A.I. companions orders. Short of taking people out silently when you don't have a silenced gun you won't really be using this button. I'm not exactly sure how to wrap this review up but I seem to have forgotten any form of comedy while writing it. Oh well. Rating: did you actually read this whole thing? Prison Architect is a game about creating a prison (well duh). You must build all of the offices, all of the cells, water and electricity lines, and hire staff! The game at first may not seem complicated, but when you first play it... wow do things change! You start out with a clever tutorial that puts you in the place of a prison that is already built, but you must build an execution building. There is a short storyline to the tutorial, but it does not transfer over to the normal game after.
As of the time writing this review you are given eight different options when creating your prison.
Steam Workshop is integrated. I have not personally tried it, but I have heard that it is fantastic and has a great modding community!
You can build your prison however you like it! I'm not going to tell you what you can or cannot do, as that is part of the fun of the game! Look up prison architect timelapse videos to see what you are able to do in the game!
Every prisoner has their own status. Some require drugs, others just want freedom and wanting to talk to family. Some want to just play games, eat, sleep, or exercise. You can fulfill all of these. You can choose to keep your prisoners happy or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. If they get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, then they may try to smuggle spoons or forks out from the cafeteria. They may start fights when in the yard or when taking a shower. Some may try to escape, attacking your staff. You'll have to call a riot police if things get out of hand.
When building your prison you are given several materials to build with. You can make concrete and brick buildings. There are a variety of different floors you can build with. You have different objects like Staff Door, Large Prison Door, Prison Door, TV, Bed, Table, Chair, and even more (There's a plus button on the menu to show more items). You have to hire your own staff. You start out with the Warden, Chefs, Guards, and Builders. To unlock more staff, your warden must research other people, who then may research other people. An example would be the warden researching the foreman. Then the foreman would research the janitor. Now you can clean up your grimy floors. Electricity and water don't come from no where, you must connect the power consuming objects to power supplying utilities. You start out with one power generator and one capacitor, which increases the amount of power you can supply to your prison. You use electric cable underground to connect different parts of your prison together. Water supplies are also fulfilled by a water pump, large pipes, and small pipes. There is also a planning function, which will allow you to sketch on your prison and get an idea on how your prison will look. This is a very important feature if you want to make sure your prison works good.
While this game is very fun, it is still in Alpha! There are quite a few glitches and bugs that may make your game unplayable. The things for me have been builders not wanting to build things, the game saying there is no route to the object they are in fact able to get to, and prisoners getting stuck in solitary. I do have a working save, however, and it is very fun.
I highly recommend this game, as it has so much to offer! And with it being in Alpha, there are many new features to come! Look past the bad side of the game, and enjoy it!

Truly a strangely addictive game that manages to get fun out of prison management and construction. It's fun, it's enjoyable, it's got steam workshop intergration and it's well made. Just buy it. It's worth what ever you decide to pay for it. Within my first day of owning it I easily got of 6hrs of straight playtime and I was just messing around with the standard features, trying to see what you could do.
The game just works and gives you a sense of acheivement whenever your prison makes a profit (Though I rarely see it) and your prisoners are satisfied. The challenge to make your prison "Perfect" is high and requires you to really plan out how it is going to work in the end and is not as shallow as "Build something anywhere and prisoner is happy".
Though it is fun and well made, there are still some annoying issues which are excusable because it is in early access. The most annoying issue I had was that I accidently set out some foundations that were to small to have an inside and thus couldn't use an entrance making it unable to become a biulding or be destroyed. Another issue is that the A.I. have to be micromanaged all the time and some don't do anything at all on their own most of the time (doctors) and some can't be sent to where their needed at the time (Janitors and Workers). There are a few placement issues (Fridge which can't be placed against a side wall.
Apart from those issues I faced in the game, I would say that Prison Architect was more or less packed game which even in its early access stage gives you hours of entertainment. It's definitely worth a buy.

At first I wasn't sure whether I liked this game or not.  Early on Chloe is a bit of a c u next Tuesday, and I was getting much of the same vibe from the original Life Is Strange where it felt like a game of telephone where someone from Japan was trying to tell a story about American teenagers.
That all changed about halfway through when you start getting into the relationship between Chloe and Rachel, which is unbearably cute, but melancholy when you've played the first game and you know how it's going to end.  The choices are actually kind of hard to make at times, and feel like an exchange of advantages and disadvantages rather than just lip-service flavor you get in other games *cough* Telltale *cough*
The second episode started out with a bit of the same degenerate behavior as the first but flipped my expectations when you get to the performance of the Tempest.
The whole "smack-talk" mechanic is... a little weird.  It's a little Japacheesy.  If you talk like that to someone in the U.S. it won't work out.  As a game mechanic, it's a minigame and it's interesting and original.  I don't dislike it.
OTW I really like this game.  I can't wait for Episode 3.  Highly recommended for people who enjoyed the original and like these kinds of games.  If you didn't like the original, or you don't care about story, or you get an aneurysm from occasional cringe-y writing, then don't.

Rogue Legacy is a game about risk, chance, and a little bit of luck. It harkens back to the days when Simon Belmont could only take four hits before succumbing to sweet oblivion, or when Arthur's armor burst off his body upon simply touching a defiled zombie. Modern conventions and some wacky characteristics keep Rogue Legacy feeling fresh despite its old-school charm, though these sources of intrigue can prove a bit frustrating at times.
Following a short prologue and introduction to death, Rogue Legacy tasks you with exploring a castle with four distinct areas, dispatching bosses as you proceed towards the ultimate goal of defeating the final evil locked behind a gold door. There's a little bit of story told in journal entries scattered about the environment, but mostly this is a tale about killing monsters and gathering loot, and the game is better for it. We didn't need much explanation back in the NES days other than, "Dracula has risen, now go kill him good!" With the recent glut of cutscenes and dialogue in today's big-budget AAA world, Rogue Legacy comes across as a breath of fresh air with its focused and directed nature. "Explore the castle, get stuff, and power up" are reasons enough to scour the corridors of this huge deathtrap.
Rogue Legacy takes advantage of a distinct 16-bit graphical palette that adds to its old-school charm. Your on-screen avatars are pixelated and slightly deformed, holding his/her sword awkwardly as they run through the castle on short, stubby legs. Giant skeletons, headless horses, robed mages, and various other nefarious creatures attempt to halt your progress with colorful attacks and old-timey patterns requiring a great deal of memorization. Rogue Legacy isn't going to blow anyone away with amazingly intricate environments. You have a castle area, a forest area, and dungeon-y areas. Familiar almost to a fault, you'd be forgiven in thinking that this game is quant and simple... until you actually play it and get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you.
I died on the second room on my first castle run. This was my first real death, and there were many (...many) more before I finally started to get my bearings and understand the mechanics at play. Enemies hit hard and fast, barely giving you any time to figure them out before they fill the screen with large area-based attacks ranging from fireballs to ice blasts and everything in-between. Controlling your character feels almost too precise and tight for this type of game. You can easily change direction mid-jump, and you'll probably overcorrect and hurt yourself if you grew up with the Belmonts. Within an hour, though, the controls feel great and really open you up to pulling off some intense maneuvers and stunts, though the downward strike necessary for some traversal mechanics never feels quite right.
I didn't really understand Rogue Legacy when I first started playing and grew frustrated quickly as a result. Dying so early without any real progress felt odd, and I was rolling my eyes with some of the "gotcha" moments with spike traps and large enemies hitting me immediately after a screen transition. Death, however, reveals the wonderfully modern conventions of RL that make it stand out amongst a sea of "old-school" games released during this massive indie boom in the industry. Every time you die, you select a new character from a list of three, and then you get the opportunity to spend your ancestor's hard-earned loot on upgrades for your family. These range from the ability to lock the randomly designed castle into its previous incarnation to new character classes and stat boosts. Better still, Rogue Legacy incentivizes you to spend all of that money because you go back down to zero upon reentering the castle. Leveling your family yields huge results that fundamentally changes the way you play the game and perceive death. Dying results in initial disappointment, followed by the joy of selecting skills and stats, and then finally a return to the castle to find more loot. It's truly wicked game design, provoking you to play just one more character before turning the game off. You're almost always unlocking new pieces of gear or abilities, and you even get to tailor your play style with runes and special skills. Maybe you like to focus on double jumping, or perhaps you want to lower the level of your enemies but receive reduced rewards as a result. Rogue Legacy feels deeply personal and meticulously constructed, never coming across as a tedious affair.
Character selection quickly becomes the driving force when you venture into the castle. The classes all perform differently and most are best suited for certain situations. The speedy, hard-hitting ninja makes regular enemies feel like a joke, but he is probably too squishy for some of the more terrifying bosses. The miner gets a huge boost to gold pickups, making him an essential part of your family's economy. Still, some classes feel a bit useless if you haven't invested enough of your family's fortune into their chosen stat. My mages felt horribly underpowered, making some runs more frustrating than others. This becomes truly detrimental when trying to tackle one of the game's bosses. I waited nearly six generations before finally getting a paladin capable of taking out the last boss, which proved more aggravating than exhilarating. Sure, I was able to power level a bit, but I wanted to get something done, and it's hard to break from that line of thought when you die waiting to accomplish a goal. This was the one time Rogue Legacy frustrated me, but that comes with the randomization of both the castle and your family tree.
Nearly every selected character brings along some kind of trait to liven up the gameplay a bit. One guy might be colorblind, leading to a black and white screen, while another character may have irritable bowel syndrome, resulting in a great deal of fart noises coming from your speakers. Usually, these traits provide little more than entertainment and a bit of individual flavor for each excursion, but they can sometimes prove beneficial or outright disastrous to your forward momentum. I was never a fan of getting characters who are giant, for example, as this made them an easy target for some of the nasty projectile attacks enemies like to spam.
Rogue Legacy makes a lot of really smart decisions to keep it feeling fresh while maintaining some pretty old-school game design. "Hard but fair" usually comes to mind whenever you finally fall victim to the onslaught, but randomness brings both variety and some frustration to the proceedings. You have to go with the flow and understand that maybe you won't get the right class for a given situation, that some people just aren't meant to vanquish evil. Some of your offspring may be simple cannon fodder, while others are little more than accountants looking to build up your future heroes. Death is almost a reward in a way, and perhaps more designers should look to keep things fresh and interesting even when the dreaded "Game Over" finally appears on screen.

Want to drive a truck but you can't real life? This is the perfect game for you! You can drive various of European trucks with hours of roads to drive through. From the UK to Poland, from Sweden to Italy, you can drive, maybe not everywhere in Europe but in most of it.
Where the road begins...
Pick your starting city, you can choose one of the hundreds of cities included in the game. You can start virtually at any city, from the historical Berlin, Paris, the city of love and the iconic London.
Where does the road end?..
There is no end! You can drive until your PC breaks! The game will never let you stop driving, so if you want to have a quick 30 minute drive, or a massive 5 hour long haul, then no problem, you can play to your heart's content.
Truck is love, truck is life...
There are 13 trucks available, another one is soon to come and I know a lot more will be in the future. They are all licensed thus they will feature real-life badges, so the realism in terms of trucks, are spot on! But when you buy a truck, you won't stop there! There are a lot of things you can add to your trucks, from the door handles, to the paint and from the cabin to the interior you can customize your truck to your needs and no one can stop you!
Scenery, scenery everywhere!
Everywhere you look is stunning, everywhere you go to, you must take a screenshot. Especially if you have the North and East Expansion Pack DLCs, then the scenery will totally blow your mind.
Are there any cons?..
Unfortunately, the AI traffic is not the best, they can sometimes be too aggresive, and sometimes they will block off the whole highway for you to merge in. There are also some minor things that I would like personally to get improved upon, like for example; the rain, the physics and the detail are too light, I mean, the wipers doesn't leave any lines on the window which you would get in real life and the rain physics when the cabin moves is unrealistic, if you suddenly turn left, then all of the rain drops will suddenly move to the right, but they don't, they are in a fixed position, they only move down.
Things missing from the game...
Just the ability to get out of the truck and get a cup of coffee would be amazing, when you stop over at a gas station and you have to manually get out of the truck and fill up the truck yourself rather than turning the engine off and pressing and holding ENTER and when trying to get in a ferry, you need to get a ticket in the office and all of other things real life truckers do outside their trucks. Emergency and law enforcement services are also one thing that I would like added, especially a feature where you would yield(or give way) to emergency vehicles passing by, and also getting pulled over by police and getting to answer some questions the cops ask.
Conclusion...
Overall the game is amazing, it has so many things to it that you guys must try out. The trucking is amazing and the amount of good things about this game surpass the amount of bad things found in the game. I would totally recommend this game to anyone who is willing to take my opinion. The game is awesome and I solute SCS Software for this game and for ATS(Which I still need to play myself).

Prison Architect is a game about creating a prison (well duh). You must build all of the offices, all of the cells, water and electricity lines, and hire staff! The game at first may not seem complicated, but when you first play it... wow do things change! You start out with a clever tutorial that puts you in the place of a prison that is already built, but you must build an execution building. There is a short storyline to the tutorial, but it does not transfer over to the normal game after.
As of the time writing this review you are given eight different options when creating your prison.
Steam Workshop is integrated. I have not personally tried it, but I have heard that it is fantastic and has a great modding community!
You can build your prison however you like it! I'm not going to tell you what you can or cannot do, as that is part of the fun of the game! Look up prison architect timelapse videos to see what you are able to do in the game!
Every prisoner has their own status. Some require drugs, others just want freedom and wanting to talk to family. Some want to just play games, eat, sleep, or exercise. You can fulfill all of these. You can choose to keep your prisoners happy or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. If they get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, then they may try to smuggle spoons or forks out from the cafeteria. They may start fights when in the yard or when taking a shower. Some may try to escape, attacking your staff. You'll have to call a riot police if things get out of hand.
When building your prison you are given several materials to build with. You can make concrete and brick buildings. There are a variety of different floors you can build with. You have different objects like Staff Door, Large Prison Door, Prison Door, TV, Bed, Table, Chair, and even more (There's a plus button on the menu to show more items). You have to hire your own staff. You start out with the Warden, Chefs, Guards, and Builders. To unlock more staff, your warden must research other people, who then may research other people. An example would be the warden researching the foreman. Then the foreman would research the janitor. Now you can clean up your grimy floors. Electricity and water don't come from no where, you must connect the power consuming objects to power supplying utilities. You start out with one power generator and one capacitor, which increases the amount of power you can supply to your prison. You use electric cable underground to connect different parts of your prison together. Water supplies are also fulfilled by a water pump, large pipes, and small pipes. There is also a planning function, which will allow you to sketch on your prison and get an idea on how your prison will look. This is a very important feature if you want to make sure your prison works good.
While this game is very fun, it is still in Alpha! There are quite a few glitches and bugs that may make your game unplayable. The things for me have been builders not wanting to build things, the game saying there is no route to the object they are in fact able to get to, and prisoners getting stuck in solitary. I do have a working save, however, and it is very fun.
I highly recommend this game, as it has so much to offer! And with it being in Alpha, there are many new features to come! Look past the bad side of the game, and enjoy it!

Pros:
- easy to get into with a bit of basketball knowledge

Cons:
- ..but that nearly never happens, toxic community, lot of ego players, who only spam "pass me the ball" and never pass back and insult you anyway

- lags are a huge issue, a lot of players warp around the court and score or rebound or get lose balls without the game even showing anything. it just happens.

Summary:
It really has a lot of potential and could be fun, but the issues and the community are just to bad to keep playing it for longer.

Rogue Legacy is an expertly crafted game with a confusing title.
The rogue-like is an obtusely defined genre of games focused around permanent death, random environments and unforgiving mechanics. There have been suggestions for better descriptors, including the Procedural Death Labyrinth (or
) which I personally prefer, but with Rogue prominently featured in the title I guess there's no denying that this
a Rogue-like, Rogue-like-like or Rogue-like-lite.
The player character is tasked with conquering a magical castle filled with devious traps and dangerous monsters and he/she
fail and die horribly.
Luckily your character had the foresight to leave behind a legacy and you'll cheerfully head back into the castle as one of your character's children.
The castle changes each time you enter it though, so even though you will get the benefit of knowing the types of things it can throw at you you won't be able to memorize the castle's layout and breeze through it.
Why would this next generation have a better shot than the ones that came before it? Because you get to buy upgrades before heading in using the gold your ancestor found in the castle.
These are permanent improvements that will usually influence your character and always influence your offspring. Things like increased strength or armour, but also unlocking new classes for your children to be. Each time you choose a new character you have a choice of 3 randomized character classes, and upgrading in such a way that you unlock more of them keeps the game varied and helps to make the castle easier to overcome.
Your basic warriors will soon diversify into wizards, barbarians, rogues and a handful of other classes that I don't feel like spoiling. They all have their place in the game and I never felt that a class didn't have any use (though I definitely had my favourites). Each classes can also be upgraded to get a unique ability, warriors become paladins that can expend MP to block any attack with their holy shield and along the same lines you'll get Barbarian Kings/Queens, Assassins and all sorts of colourful characters.
As if that wasn't variety enough, each character has up to two randomly assigned traits (on top of their gender, class and spell) to differentiate them. These range from the comical (being bald, occasionally passing gas when jumping or being stereo-blind which will flip each sprite Paper Mario style when it turns) to the useful (remembering where enemies are, not triggering spike traps, getting MP by destroying furniture) to the hindering (colour blindness, dyslexia, being short sighted).
These are all charming and often funny traits that will help set each character apart, and you'll go through a lot of them. Over my course of playing the game (and its extra challenging New Game+ mode) I went through 138 generations of characters, and even though I wouldn't be able to recall any of them specifically I never felt that two consecutive runs were similar.
The castle you explore is divided in four different regions, which all have their own look, set of enemies and imposing boss at the end. The Castle area (you start here), the Maya high among the castle's towers, the Forest to the east and the Dark, deep below in its cellars. Beat all four bosses (in any number of runs, this is one of the things that
carry over between runs) and the large door in the foyer that you've run past dozens of times will slowly swing open allowing you access to the game's final boss.
This is not a perfect game though, even though almost all parts of it are excellent, my main gripe with it is that it can get quite grindy. The main aspect to blame here is the gatekeeper, Charon. To enter the castle you have to give him all the gold you have left over after buying upgrades / equipment. This means that, as you get the cheaper upgrades and gear, you'll soon get to a game state where you'll need a minimum amount of gold from a run to be able to afford
upgrades and it can sometimes feel like you've 'wasted' a run.
(There is a late-game upgrade that somewhat mitigates this problem by convincing Charon to only take 50%-90% (depending on upgrade level) of your gold).
Overall though, this is an amazing game and definitely one where you're vulnerable to "one more try" situations turning into gaming sessions lasting deep into the night.
As long as you can stomach that not every run will contribute to your progress through the castle and you feel like playing an excellent 2D platformer, this is definitely a game to pick up.

I finished Spec Ops: The Line at 6 am, on the hardest difficulty. I left my secluded room for the first time in almost ten hours in a daze. My mother was watching the ending of Howl's Moving Castle in the living room. The only way to describe how I felt at that moment was with a single thought that stuck with me for the rest of the day. "I'm a terrible, terrible person."
Spec Ops: The Line, though hindered by mediocre combat and cut-and-dry mechanics of the industry saves itself (though you wouldn't know it from the Call of Duty-esque trailers) in its story and attention to detail. Just a quick Google search for the minor details that evolve throughout the game will give you a sense of the devotion the dev team put into it.
It's hard to describe what makes this game absolutely amazing without ruining the story, but in short it will make you feel like a terrible person. Inspired by Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now, you take the role of a Delta Force fireteam leader tasked with entering a post-apocalyptic Dubai and locating the commander of a rogue unit of US soldiers.
Throughout the game you will be faced with a) vs. b), and sometimes c) short-term choices that will have you question your morality. Even entire objectives with apparently obvious justifications turn into nightmares as you realize the true nature of what you took for granted, and cannot undo.
Each choice to be made has an achievement to it, so after one complete play-through (which I strongly advise everyone to do) you can see everything you did. There is only one choice towards the end that can be called "good", and you'll know it when you reach it. But the delivery is so subtle and abrupt that it'll take you a minute to catch on.
Strong side characters, good dialog, mind-blowing setpieces, and oppressing atmosphere all combine to deliver a psychological journey into the dark recesses of your mentality only a videogame, which pins the responsibility directly on you, can make you experience.
8/10 - I did what I had to.

It's impossible to give a true review of this game without spoiling everything, but here's the best I could come up with: This is a very well written game with visuals that range from good to creepy to absolutely terrifying, with really great characters and some really great music in its home-made soundtrack (they're not all winners, however, but there's some real good ones in there). There is however, 3 major problems holding it back.
One is that the game gets too wrapped up in its message that it takes glee in punishing you through tedium and disappointment than through actual pain, which is what you do feel until you get to the end and the much better punishment for your misdeeds are wiped away, however this is healed somewhat by the ending.
Second is that the game does a very poor job of communicating what it expects from you, maybe because as I say above, it wants you to fail, but that isn't fair, I mean, its not done in a way like spec ops is, where its a throughful deconstruction, this tries to be a thoughtful deconstruction, but your choices are not properly presented in front of you. Also, the way it expects you to solve problems for maximum ending is very linear and obscure/doesn't really make sense.
Third, this game really tests your patience. It just does. I almost quit after the first playthrough (this game is meant to be played through twice (~5 hours each playthrough), but I urge you, have DETERMINATION and do things right, the ending is worth it, but boy will you hate this game after your first playthrough
But all in all, its worth it, its a good game and I like it, its just not a perfect game, but what is, really?

Dayz Standalone is currently in development, but don't let that make you think it is a bad game. All of the people hating on it do not understand how game development works, especially for a game with as many core functions as Dayz. Let's look at the current hot pot of a game, PUBG. PUBG has been out for only a short time but is currently more complete then Dayz. That isn't because Bohemia is lazy or the devs abandon it, actually quite the opposite. PUBG does not have any survival mechanics other than the other players so all that needs to be focused on is the guns and the vehicles. PUBG also outsources all of the modeling, and uses a premade engine. (Unreal) They also have gotten help from Epic Games to raise the player cap. (A company they are trying to sue) Dayz is currently rebuilding a brand new engine based on the Arma engine, as well as making their own models, animations, scripts, and is also just a branch of Bohemia. In its current state, it seems underwhelming how little is complete in the time, but many don't understand how long it actually takes to make something this massive from scratch.

Note: I bought this game at 66% off during the winter sale of 2015, and so I'm reviewing this as a $20 game, not a $60 game.
Not the perfect Mad Max game; a lot of the systems are too limited, and it can be very grindy. Obviously a product of the general formulaic insert-open-world-here game that Ubisoft and WB have perfected, with the likes of the Arkham, Shadow of Mordor, and Assassin's Creed franchises, among others. It's a huge collect-a-thon, with towers that reveal bits of the map, and a few plug-n-play activities and mostly forgettable characters.
But for all that, it excels at being a really GOOD plug-n-play open world game. Max Max might just be a setting, but it's a really good setting, and it's a lot of fun. The core of what you do is driving around, and that core is entertaining.
The main thing that stands out is the brutality of this game, in comparison to a lot of other AAA games - the amount of blood and gore is kind of astonishing at times, and some of the in-game events had me truly taken aback. Hardly a Spec Ops: The Line, but considerably more likely to stay with you than a standard CODBLOPS-thing.

All-New Characters and All-New Classes: Four all new playable classes including the Siren, the Commando, the Gunzerker and the Assassin. I finished Spec Ops: The Line at 6 am, on the hardest difficulty. I left my secluded room for the first time in almost ten hours in a daze. My mother was watching the ending of Howl's Moving Castle in the living room. The only way to describe how I felt at that moment was with a single thought that stuck with me for the rest of the day. "I'm a terrible, terrible person."
Spec Ops: The Line, though hindered by mediocre combat and cut-and-dry mechanics of the industry saves itself (though you wouldn't know it from the Call of Duty-esque trailers) in its story and attention to detail. Just a quick Google search for the minor details that evolve throughout the game will give you a sense of the devotion the dev team put into it.
It's hard to describe what makes this game absolutely amazing without ruining the story, but in short it will make you feel like a terrible person. Inspired by Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now, you take the role of a Delta Force fireteam leader tasked with entering a post-apocalyptic Dubai and locating the commander of a rogue unit of US soldiers.
Throughout the game you will be faced with a) vs. b), and sometimes c) short-term choices that will have you question your morality. Even entire objectives with apparently obvious justifications turn into nightmares as you realize the true nature of what you took for granted, and cannot undo.
Each choice to be made has an achievement to it, so after one complete play-through (which I strongly advise everyone to do) you can see everything you did. There is only one choice towards the end that can be called "good", and you'll know it when you reach it. But the delivery is so subtle and abrupt that it'll take you a minute to catch on.
Strong side characters, good dialog, mind-blowing setpieces, and oppressing atmosphere all combine to deliver a psychological journey into the dark recesses of your mentality only a videogame, which pins the responsibility directly on you, can make you experience.
8/10 - I did what I had to.

SO:TL is dark. Don't be fooled by the sun reflecting off Dubai's sand dunes, this game pulls no punches in bringing the horrors of war to you.
The game plays like a standard 3rd-person cover-based shooter, but all the interesting aspects of the game simply use that as the foundation. You control a small squad as they search for what happened to the American troops that were sent to help evacuate Dubai, and slowly uncover the truth. Its all brought home by some stunning environments and incredible sound design, and the story itself challenges the player to maintain their own humanity when there's none left around them.
The campaign is quite short, but I played it through on FUBAR difficulty as I enjoyed the game so much. There are a couple of scenes where the difficulty spikes (the "Freebird" scene being the main offender!) but for most of the game it is fairly well paced.
There are plenty of twists and lots of clues as to what is going on, just sit back and enjoy the ride. Anyone who enjoys modern shooters owes it to themselves to complete this game at least once.

Note: I bought this game at 66% off during the winter sale of 2015, and so I'm reviewing this as a $20 game, not a $60 game.
Not the perfect Mad Max game; a lot of the systems are too limited, and it can be very grindy. Obviously a product of the general formulaic insert-open-world-here game that Ubisoft and WB have perfected, with the likes of the Arkham, Shadow of Mordor, and Assassin's Creed franchises, among others. It's a huge collect-a-thon, with towers that reveal bits of the map, and a few plug-n-play activities and mostly forgettable characters.
But for all that, it excels at being a really GOOD plug-n-play open world game. Max Max might just be a setting, but it's a really good setting, and it's a lot of fun. The core of what you do is driving around, and that core is entertaining.
The main thing that stands out is the brutality of this game, in comparison to a lot of other AAA games - the amount of blood and gore is kind of astonishing at times, and some of the in-game events had me truly taken aback. Hardly a Spec Ops: The Line, but considerably more likely to stay with you than a standard CODBLOPS-thing.

In short yes I reccomend this game despite it's many flaws.
Long version, I still feel a lot of disapointment towards this game.  The hand to hand combat in paticular was a big let down for me.  It's a good foundation, but the overall lack of moves and the fact that knives are single use consumables and bats break after about five strikes makes it overly simplistic, not very engaging, and sometimes outright frustrating.  This is compunded by the fact that the counter button is the same button used to aim the shotgun, sometimes causing me to clam up and draw in the middle of a fist fight only to be pummled by a right hook coming towards my jaw.  Why can't I be a knife fighter like the enemy characters?  Why can't I carry a nail bat all the time if I want?  It seems like theres a whole melee combat system and branching weapon skill trees that is just missing from the game.  Weapon degredation can be made to work, so the fact that it's limited in such an arbitrary way just makes it feel lame.  I wanted Snowpiercer and got Desert Boxing sim 2015.
The car stuff is the only thing that kept me around, which is more immersive engaging and exciting, but also not without flaws.  The cars don't require any finesse to handle, and theres no ability to drift or pull complex maneuvers.  Just forwards, backwards, and a hand brake j turn that results in being t boned 100% of the time if used during combat.  There's a ram function used for side by side attacks which is implemented well, and the grappling hook is nice touch and when everything comes together it looks pretty damn cool. Disclosures: I have no ties with the developer, and purchased this game myself.
Rogue Legacy, the first big production from Cellar Door Games, places you into a unique situation for a Rogue-like game. You start by invading a castle in the tutorial. Ultimately, you meet your gory end there. The remainder of the game has you taking the role of each new heir who madly delves the castle to find the truth of what happened.
Each time you die, you are presented with three different randomly generated characters. The characters have a class, a spell, and often one or more odd traits. These traits can both help and hinder your progress through the castle. As you explore the castle, you fight through randomly arranged and spawned rooms versus a variety of enemies, with the ultimate goal being to take down 5 bosses. Each boss has their own wing of the castle save the final one, whose door you pass as you first enter the castle. The wings are generically always in the same locations, though how to access them changes each time the castle respawns.
Upon death, you take any collected gold, item plans and runes with you back to your family home, which serves as an upgrade screen. You are able to build new rooms that grant you access to new classes, more health, stronger attacks and special skills like death avoidance. Once you step out as your new heir, you can then forge new gear and buy runes. As you progress, you eventually can even lock the castle design if you have a little gold left. This feature is useful if you are attempting to run through the bosses. Once you re-enter, a percentage of your gold is taken depending on how you've upgraded your castle, and you repeat the process.
The gameplay itself is punishing but fair. Enemies aren't extremely varied, but that's a good thing. You need  to learn your opponents well to make the best use of each heir to gain the most gold and items possible. While the random levels can create issues, typically because at times enemies will spawn too near an entrance to kill without receiving damage, there is rarely a time you will feel that the randomness has screwed you over.
Featuring platforming elements, melee combat and magic use in a 2-D side-scroller, the game can be hours of fun, as each run has real progress, even if only to gain a bit more gold for that next upgrade. The bosses themselves are challenging, and the game also features hard-mode versions you can unlock via finding in-game items. And once you're finished, you really aren't. Featuring a new game plus mode that drastically ups the difficulty, you get to once more challenge the castle to see if you can find out what happened so many generations ago.
Overall, it's a game well worth the price of admission, and a great first effort as far as a full release game goes. If you enjoy Rogue-likes with progression, pick this one up today.

It's impossible to give a true review of this game without spoiling everything, but here's the best I could come up with: This is a very well written game with visuals that range from good to creepy to absolutely terrifying, with really great characters and some really great music in its home-made soundtrack (they're not all winners, however, but there's some real good ones in there). There is however, 3 major problems holding it back.
One is that the game gets too wrapped up in its message that it takes glee in punishing you through tedium and disappointment than through actual pain, which is what you do feel until you get to the end and the much better punishment for your misdeeds are wiped away, however this is healed somewhat by the ending.
Second is that the game does a very poor job of communicating what it expects from you, maybe because as I say above, it wants you to fail, but that isn't fair, I mean, its not done in a way like spec ops is, where its a throughful deconstruction, this tries to be a thoughtful deconstruction, but your choices are not properly presented in front of you. Also, the way it expects you to solve problems for maximum ending is very linear and obscure/doesn't really make sense.
Third, this game really tests your patience. It just does. I almost quit after the first playthrough (this game is meant to be played through twice (~5 hours each playthrough), but I urge you, have DETERMINATION and do things right, the ending is worth it, but boy will you hate this game after your first playthrough
But all in all, its worth it, its a good game and I like it, its just not a perfect game, but what is, really?

Disclosure - I am British, non-gun user, non-hunter and have no desire to ever do this IRL.
This version of the franchise has been getting a bit of flack from buyers, especially after the first DLC, due to it seemingly straying away from it's original purpose which was to provide an alternative to those who are wouldn't be the most out of the pay per season model of the original game.  I brought the game as this wave of negativity started, and it might have been justified in parts, there seemed to be a slightly cynical way in which the DLC was being put out.  But, since then, personally I feel the Devs have been excellent in listening to feedback, adjusting the sale strategies and the regular patches have been coming in to get rid of the wrinkles and creases.
PROS:
Beautiful to look at
Good implimentation of multiplayer
Plenty to do for someone who dips in and out
Has a good balance between sim and less serious game.
CONS:
Some missions can be a bit of a chore
Make a few assuptions on only being played by people who already know about hunting
The animal types in the two maps are quite similar in style (minus the bears).
It's been nice to wander around a take a shot at antlered beasties every now and then, I feel like it's making a very bad user of mouse and keyboard get ever so slightly better without the pressure that most FPSs would have.  I even feel a bit more confident going into a PUBG game after warming up on here for a bit (that feeling lasts about one round).
I get why there are some criticisms of the DLC, but I think that is being addressed, and for me the price of adding these packs is minimal to what I have happy sunk into games like Destiny etc.  I am not saying the method they are using is perfect but it's not bank breaking and I think a few some who are being the most vocal about this stuff are probably being a bit over the top considering the very transistional period the games industry seems to be lumbering through.
For me, the biggest negative has been sticking points with some of the missions.  It's perfectly possible to just play without them but they have been good to show me some of the different things in the game to do (I would have never tried night hunting otherwise).  But there are some early missions that are exceptionally challenging to complete without items that take a considerable amount of time to level up enough to buy.  There is still plenty to do while you wait but for me I just wanted to fire up the game, do a mission and the get back to work, playing something else.  Once I unlocked a new more powerful rifle though this became less of an issue, mainly due to opening up the larger animals as sandbox prey.
Future maps with a bit more landscape and animal variety would be the icing on the cake - as there were 2 included with the £25 pound base game I think an extra £7 for each would be fair for new ones but we'll have to wait an see.

Rewriting my previous negative review as stability issues have largely been resolved.
It's tough to do, but I still wouldn't recommend this game. I've played it a lot, and I've had a lot of fun, but it's a running joke in the Rust community just how much this game will make you hate life.
I'll rate each gameplay element, but for the TL/DR, skip to "Community" at the end.
There is no PvE; the only ultimate point of this game is PvP.  You raid bases, you kill other players.  I love PvP, so this suits me just fine.  I won't say PvP is broken, but it's often ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and/or pointless.
To me a great PvP game means A) 1v1 fights are fairly even and mostly decided on skill, rather than luck or gear, and B) a great player can take on 2 or even 3 average players with some skill and luck.
In Rust, 80-90% of your PvP deaths will be someone you didn't see headshotting you from behind and you instantly dying.  I'm not sure that's even a "fight"; the most important PvP skill in Rust is watching out for other players.  Gear decides most of the rest as any player with a gun will kill anyone without one 98% of the time.
PvP is almost mathematically decided by:
- Who got the jump on who?
- Who has a (better) gun?
- Who has more people?
Since those disparities represent most encounters in this game, it makes actual PvP fights mostly pointless since you already know who will win.  Or, you're just instantly dead from that headshot from behind.  (Running or hiding are not effective strategies either, you will be hunted down)
The learning curve is also quite steep.  That said, it's still real fun when you get into an actual fight, and it's decently balanced (between people who have guns).
Do you like farming and crafting?  This game is really fun for that!  Except that when you're farming you make a lot of noise and will be killed a lot (see "Headshot from behind", above).
Crafting and base building in this game are very solid and very fun, and devs keep things fresh by changing things up with experimenting with various blueprint systems etc.
The only downfall is that there are monthly server wipes.  Which means every base, craftable item, weapon, and (sometimes) blueprint you made is gone.  Now on the one hand, that keeps the game fun...there are so many games where you build a base and then it's done and there's no reason to keep playing.  You get to build a new base every month.
The problem is that week before the wipe.  Why bother playing?  Everything you do will be gone in X days.  It's just waiting for that next Thursday to hit to go do it all over again.
The other problem with base building/crafting is that cyclical nature.  About 3-6 days into a wipe when other players get the ability to bust down your doors, you WILL be raided when you're offline, no matter what you do, and you will lose everything.  All the hours you spent farming (and dying), all the rare items you found you were so excited to survive to make it back and keep...yeah.  All gone.  It's basically "Hardcore" mode at all times.
When raiding becomes commonplace the server population drops ~80% as everyone logs in, sees all their stuff (sometimes including their base itself) gone and rage quits.  The server devolves into a war zone of abandoned bases, nakeds with rocks, and clans with massive sprawling bases and crazy advanced weaponry.
Cancerous.  I have never seen such a group of hostile, racist, homophobic, trolling, griefing, immature, set of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in a community ever.  EVER.  Facepunch says they monitor official servers but that's a lie.  You will see painted swastikas, racial slurs, comments about racial violence/slavery, sexual assault jokes and violent threats literally constantly.  PS -- This is playing on a Canadian server (!!!).
There are no friendly players, you will be killed on sight.  The only groups are clans of 10-30 players who are unstoppable due to sheer numbers, get a huge lead on gear and then 6v2 you in case it might have been remotely fair.  You will be doorcamped.  People will lurk around your base for hours.  You will be killed for no reason when you have a rock and they have an AK.  Your base will be griefed and/or stolen.  When other players know you're in your base, a common tactic is for them to scream profanities/threats/unintelligibly into the mic to taunt you into coming out.
The especially shocking/tragic thing about this is the number of very young players.
