I've already wrote a brief review of this title on reddit, but I'll expand more on here...
---
Mad Max is probably one of the most optimized PC games. Lots of graphical options to tune, and maintains a nice fps in nearly any setup. A thing to note is that under Audio there's a setting to turn on Fury Mode, which amps all the sounds in the game. It's not so that it's louder but everything's much more furious and raspier, as the mode is named with. I'd recommend trying it out as it gives the game a much more grittier feel.
In terms of looks the game looks stunning. It's a treat to even drive around the region. And those sandstorms - they're pretty intense! It's even crazier than FO4's rad storms!
In terms of gameplay it's a little repetitive. I'd compare it to JC3 because in Mad Max you're basically reducing Scrotus' and Stank Gum's influence in each region, much like in JC3 where you reduce the DRM's influence. However Mad Max does it a bit better because there's a number of ways to reduce influence, whether it's taking down oil wells, removing scarecrows, or removing convoys off the map.
Other stuff you can do is take out scarecrows, take out snipers, blow up Buzzard lairs, find high-value cars (for some reason these aren't explicitly tracked), build Archangels (basically special variants of your main car that require certain upgrades to build), do Death Runs (sort-of like races but with twists), and so on. Basically there's a lot of stuff to do. As of this review I'm still not done. So in terms of replayability there's a good amount. But I doubt I'll be repeating another playthrough, as the story itself is very linear.
Vehicular combat isn't very common in games these days, but Mad Max gets it right. Eliminating convoys for example are surprisingly lots of fun. And you have plenty of tools to take them out, like the Harpoon or the Thunderpoon (aka a rocket launcher). Outside of convoys you'll run into War Boys or Stank Gum itching for a fight, but sometimes they won't even chase you, either because you're too fast or they won't bother. These guys don't seem to provide very much loot, so it's better to ignore them.
Speaking of combat there's also on-foot combat. That means that you can upgrade Max, so you can spend your Scrap on more skills or better gear. Now onto combat: It's a bit like Batman, but isn't. Meaning there's no actual flow to it. Max can enter Fury which boosts his attacks, but it doesn't introduce anything jaw-dropping. There's also different archetypes of enemies which spices things up but you still throw the same punches. Top Dogs act as bosses but they all seem to have the same moveset and weapon.
I honestly thought there was gonna be combat where Max would get out of his car, climb onto the roof and fend off the guy next to him. A bit like in the movie Fury Road. Abit disappointed there wasn't one.
The story is good but not groundbreaking or anything. Max himself is almost like a silent protagonist and takes favors as long as he gets something in return. There's also Wasteland missions but those are basically fetch quests. The characters you meet are interesting (like Gutgash) but they aren't that developed (however their respective Wasteland Missions expand on their intent). The history relics you find in the world tell sad tales of the past and how it became as it is now. Max commentating on the relics are a nice touch (some of what he says are surprisingly profound).
There's also Wasteland encounters you find when you explore the wasteland. Most of those are just jargon that you already knew, but some of them can provide Intel to help in taking a difficult camp. But there's the odd encounter or so that made me pretty depressed, really bringing out that it's really the end of the world.
Much of the upgrades in this game don't seem very worth it, especially the Griffa tokens. Mostly because the game is inherently easy. Though once you unlock the northen region the game gets much tougher, while the southern region is exceptionally easy.
Plus in spite of being a post-apocalyptic game there aren't many hardcore or survival aspects. Max doesn't get hungry or thirsty, so eating food or drinking your canteen only heals you. And fuel is plentiful and declines slowly enough to not worry about (there is a weapon that uses fuel though).
Each region has a Stronghold that houses the main guy of that region, like Jeet or Deep Friah, as well as their followers. You can improve these places by setting out and finding project parts to construct Water Storages or Maggot farms. These projects provide Max instant full water or instant full ammo when you enter the Stronghold, as well as improving the looks of the place. While the projects do make searching for water or gas redundant, bear in mind that there's a time limit after you get your stuff, so it kinda forces you to go out and find more sources. Of course that only affects the Stronghold you've entered. Additionally some projects are unavailable until you've done the main guy's Wasteland missions.
The game's "currency" is Scrap, and you find it pretty much anywhere. You can earn them through clearing camps, so allies can populate 'em to deliver you Scrap every once of a while. You can also find them in places that you can loot, off of cars you take out, and so on. There's even a project in the Strongholds that adds Scrap when your game is off! Essentially it doesn't really run out. Of course you spend the Scrap on upgrades or improving Strongholds. However a lot of the upgrades require prerequisites to be done first. This can be like doing Wasteland missions or achieving a certain level.
Speaking of levels, you can gain more levels by completing Challenges. I don't personally track 'em but getting upgrades that require a certain level take some time. Fortunately the bulk of the Challenges come pretty naturally so they don't become a huge chore.
All in all Mad Max is a great PC title that's optimized and has pretty engaging gameplay. In terms of story I'd say it's decent but it isn't Undertale or anything.
If you want a nicely optimized PC title, yes.
If you want good vehicular combat, yes.

I'm only a casual fan of rogue-style games, and have only played a few kinds like that.  However, Rogue Legacy is definitely the most fun rogue thing I have ever played. Castlevania, and Dark Souls.
You are a noble hero who is entirely over comfident setting out on a quest to find out what is going on with this castle. Should you die... (you totally will) your descendant will take on the burden. Every time you enter the castle Charon who looks like death will take all your milk money. The objective is to spend the money updating your castle and character gear before you ask him to let you in the castle. These updates give you characters higher health, mana, and much much more. The castle itself has four areas which each have a boss. Once one of the four bosses is defeated it unlocks part of the seal on the main boss door. If your character dies that boss remains dead. If you beat all four bosses and the final one you move onto new game plus. You should also find chests and horde in lots of gold while searching for runes and blueprints.
The castle upgrades and different character classes add good variety to the game. The castle being randomly generated aids in this as well. The armors have different pros and cons depending on your play style. Finding blue prints and runes by completing challenge rooms adds once again. The clown games and the guess the chest game are a nice distraction. With everything you rarely realise that you are essentially grinding for gold as a micro goal to upgrade enough to beat the bosses. The art style great as well as deceptive because it looks like an easy mode phone game, but behaves more like a 2D Dark Souls. The game is also highly addictive with a I just want to upgrade my castle, but before you know it you already paid Charon and are on a run.
The game is not for the faint of heart difficulty wise. There is not a ton a variations to the combat. They use a ton of the same exact character model reskinned. These and more examples are ways you can tell the developers were on a major budget and only spent like 15k on developement. Even the bosses are really just basically large versions of normal enemies. They do at least change up the attacks, but much of the time they are just super enlarged versions of the attack or more of it. The dungeon itself is very small which is both a good and a bad thing.
I bought this game for $2.99 not expecting much. I was horribly wrong considering how addicted I soon became to it. I am currently on New Game ++ and have taken down three of the five remix bosses. I am at this point burnt out on it though. The lack of a combo system and variety of enemies eventually catches up with the game so I hope Rogue Legacy 2 has some extra features when it comes out in the next few years.
This game is easily worth the $15 not on sale price if you can handle the difficulty.

I know I've barely scratched the surface of what's possible with this game - and I know that a lot more will be added - but I thought it would be good to post a little review just to say that my one major concern before playing Prison Architect was that it would too heavily trivialize the rather awful incarceration model of criminal justice, but that fear was unwarranted.
It's still a game, so it's not a perfect simulation and doesn't address every single issue, but it's also still very much in development, and every change made (via the changelogs, not from first-hand experience) has made the game more humane, thoughtful and carefully balanced.
I love that my policy of humane treatment and blanket ban on solitary confinement or armed guards is being rewarded with positive results, and I love that those positive results all flow naturally both from the game systems and real-world causation.
Put all that care in a package with tools to tweak, build, and design infrastructure, structure, and policy, and this game fits perfectly alongside Banished, Galactic Civilizations II, and Civ V as an incredible time sink and deeply absorbing simulation.

Borderlands 2… Where to begin? From appearances only, it is a very good-looking game, with it’s comic style art, splash intros, and of course, explosions. The amount of weaponry is truly staggering: grenade mods, relics, shields, class mods, and so, so, so many guns. I have logged a substantial amount of time in each class, and I have never gotten the same gun twice, except from missions. And speaking of classes, you truly have a choice for every playstyle. Zer0, the enigmatic assassin, excels in sniping and backstabbing. Gaige the Mechromancer, is able to summon a partner, Deathtrap, who can shoot lasers, clap explosively, and “sparkle” with the element of your choice. If that wasn’t enough, Gaige also has a system called Anarchy, in which your aim gets worse as your damage increases, which proves to be quite the challenge once the stacks grow into the 100s. Axton the Commando is somewhat like a discount Gaige, throwing down a turret, or two if you upgrade him enough. I don’t have any experience with Salvador or Kreig, but both are very much a “rush in guns blazing” type. Maya, the Siren, armed with an (elemental) SMG and phaselock, preferably with co-op partners, is a force to be reckoned with. Speaking of, co-op is truly worth the slightly tougher enemies, and makes the game less tough and more fun, with duels and multiplayer-based vehicles. So, why should you buy it? Surely there are newer, better games that cater to this playstyle, right? I beat the story more times than I care to count, but why? Borderlands 2, like it’s counterparts, just has an indescribable quality that draws you in. The combination of quirky characters, thoughtful story, gameplay, and trademark sense of humor just stick with you for a long time. The story is often heralded as a fun romp through Pandora, but it goes much deeper. No spoilers, but the story has a lot more depth and emotion that you can’t help but empathize with, and I will admit, I was a little misty eyed at certain points. However, the humor is all it’s cracked up to be, no doubt, wether you’re shooting your way through midgets, or getting one of Moxxi’s vibrator guns. All in all, Borderlands is a great experience, and the DLC just makes it even better.

With almost one hundred hours invested into this game its safe to say its one of my favorite games I’ve ever played. This is the first ever prison management and creation game I’ve ever played, really this is the first prison game I’ve ever played. When this game first really caught my attention and gave me a urge to buy it was in alpha 18. Before I had heard and watched some playthroughs and the many bugs and lack of interesting features turned me away from purchasing the game. But now in alpha 28 there is no issue about not having enough interesting features. From door controls, to cctv cameras, the game has it all. One surprisingly strange thing that thought I would forever hate is the graphics. While the graphics aren’t particularly amazing there’s a strange enjoyment with the graphics. I find myself actually liking what the game looks it just seems to fit perfectly with the style of the game. Another thing I thought I was going to never play the game for was all the bugs, and to be honest in the beginning I really didn’t play much of the game, because of the bugs. Now they dedicate whole alphas on just strictly fixing bugs which is nice but, it doesn’t eliminate all the bugs. Really once they did the first bug fixing alpha and got rid of the very major bugs everything was fine for me sure every so often you get a little annoyed because something is broken or not working but, really its not that bad. Another thing we need to keep in mind is we are buying a game in alpha so we can’t expect it to be perfect. One very nice thing I like about the alpha system is every month they release a new alpha with new features, bug fixes, and what not. I find myself always interested because I know next month I’m going to get to play with new features. It’s almost like playing a whole new game each month but with the same principle in mind. The alpha system that they have has been the reason that I’ve played for so long. Really it keeps you interested in the game. I would one hundred percent reccomend this game to anyone and everyone. While the bugs can be annoying its only in alpha and it continues to get better and better as time goes on.
- ChrisTheCritic

So after owning the game a month, and almost 100% the game, I feel like I should re-write my review.
So to start, I should state, this game is my personal favorite release of 2015.
So lets get the negatives out of the way. Honestly the most obvious is the repetitiveness of the levels. The bosses are basically the same over and over just switched color scheme and voices.
Another major negative is the climax of the story, not going to spoil it, but it ends with a few things that should have been handled differently.
Other than those negatives, here a few nuetral items, that dont really effect my opinion on the game. One is the on foot combat system. Its simple, a little too simple. But its not bad in any way, it honestly reminds me of Arkham Asylums combat. The only other nuetral thing to me is the tedious scrap collecting. You remember Lego Star Wars, Batman, Indiana Jones etcs. minikit and stud/true hero collecting system? Its the same in this game in the case of its a time consuming process trying to get everything, and is kinda annoying if your trying to 100% the whole game [like me].
Now on to the positives.
This game didnt just get game of the year for nothing!
Honestly its really enjoyable, because of the feel of the enviroments, the graphics and atmosphere, and the story and voice actors. The Wasteland really feels straight from the movies in the sense of apocalypse and survival. The graphics are just plain amazing, I only have a I3 and a 760, and can run it on high! For how good the looks are its surprising I could even run it. The car combat is fantastic. Simply stated. The explosions are the best I have ever seen in a video game. The characters are really fleshed out well. As for technical stuff, I have experienced absolutely no bugs, or FPS issues.
In short: Mad Max is game of the year because it does such a great job of capturing the cinematic feel of the movies, it is a strong 9/10, for being a great open world third person survival/action game. Now finally the price tag. Is it worth it? Hell yeah! Especially if your thinking of buying Black Ops 3 or Battlefront, just do not even go there, buy this! And if its on sale, its definetly a steal!

Game preferences are personal things. So the things I hate, someone else will love.
Mad Max is like a reverse of Rage. That had first-person exploration and combat, 3rd person driving. This has first-person driving (once you search the Internet for how to switch to it), 3rd person exploration and combat. For me the ideal game would be a combination of both, with the option for 1st or 3rd person in each case, depending on what the player likes.
Pros
+ 1st person driving
Cons
- 3rd person exploration/fighting. I'd read articles which said things like: "And yes, you can also play the game in first-person while on foot."
Turns out you can't. There's no obvious reason why they didn't include that option. The world would be more immersive. The 3rd person combat is a boring system of pressing the RMB when told, then clicking LMB a few times, and would work just as well in 1st person. Think of the way combat works in Dark Messiah, Mirror's Edge, Zeno Clash, Riddick ... far more exciting than the telegraphed system here. At the very least they could have offered 1st person on-foot exploration as an option, even if it reverted to 3rd person for the fisticuffs.
- The world is overpopulated to a silly level - drive for 30 seconds and there's another camp. It doesn't feel like the huge, deadly, sparsely populated world we saw in any of the films.
- You can't turn off the map, the popup messages, the continuous notifications. I like to find my way around myself, not have blobs floating on the horizon always telling me where to go. A key element of surviving in a wilderness is getting lost. That's impossible in Mad Max. There's always a navigation pointer, a map with coloured routes and icons.
- The game claims you're a tough, self-reliant road warrior - then it holds your hand every step of the way. I've already mentioned the maps and pointers and so on to make sure you can't get lost. But it takes away your freedom and choices again and again. I picked up a knife - but the game wouldn't let me fight with it. I could only use it when it flashed a message on screen. Likewise the game puts up big icons to tell you when to block or dodge. It even tells you when to climb, and won't let you climb or jump up any other ledge, even teeny low ones. You have to be given permission to climb by the post-apocalyptic Health & Safety committee. I'm surprised he's allowed to drive without a helmet. That's probably why the game saddles you with an annoying Golem-like companion who does everything for you, tells you where to go, and can't be dumped.
- You know, the notifications annoyed me enough to mention another aspect. You aren't allowed to search the bodies of your foes. Instead the game pops up an icon above the bodies that have something on them. You already know which ones to search, and what they have on them (e.g. one shotgun shell). You're not allowed to experiment or try things out yourself. It just tells you "Nope, leave that body, nothing on it, but this one does." These constant ways in which the game undercuts player agency, takes away the feeling of surviving. It even tells you when you have found all the nearby scrap, some crazy sixth sense combined with nagging to "move on now, there's nothing else to see".
- Unskippable logos every time you load.
- It kept failing to run offline, requiring an Internet connection. A friend told me it is because it uses some DRM called Denuvo that requires online connections. Incredibly frustrating that Steam doesn't warn you about it, I try to never buy games that require online connections beyond Steam (which is why I prefer GOG if the game is available there).
I really wanted this game to be immersive. I pictured exploring in the first person (as was implied in early articles); climbing and jumping and exploring and getting lost and having crazy adventures and feeling that I was on my own, because I was Mad Max. I didn't get that feeling at all due to the way the game is built around nagging and hand-holding and notifications and repetitive grinding for minor boosts.
This is why I'm annoyed that most publishers don't do demos any more. They promise the world, and because you can't try it out first in a demo your only option is to believe them; then you download 25GB (!), play the game and realise it's full of annoyances where they decided you had to play it their way, rather than how you want to play, and they refuse to implement player choices.
This game is beast

Hmmmm. This is a difficult review to write.
There is no question the game is a little bit janky.  Max's animations can be poor.  His interaction with "the world" leaves a lot to be desired.  You have the standard sort of problems....You can't step up onto a rock where you think you should be able to step up....Your feet disappear into the floor....You have to stand at "exactly the right point" to get the action button prompt sometimes which led to me circling round a camp more than once trying to find the thing I needed to activate.
BUT.
The world is superbly realised.  It feels dirty, hostile, scary and dangerous.  The graphics are stunning and I had a constant 60FPS even in the heat of the largest vehicular battles with explosions, fire and cars everywhere.
There is an addictive gameplay loop around going into the world and collecting "scrap", use scrap to upgrade your car and add more moves to Max's combat arsenal and ultimately make it easier to complete the "challenges".  The challenges earn you "griffa" tokens which let you improve Max's base skills (max health, punch power, etc).  Link your "scrap" collecting missions with the various stronghold requirements and you have a very nice progression loop which absorbs the hours without you getting bored while you're playing, planning  what to do next and where to go next and....
HOWEVER.
When you stop playing and take a look at the big picture you suddenly realise things aren't too rosy.  I've spent 20-odd hours in the game and I've only cleared the progression missions in around 1/4 of the map......I've enjoyed it, but there's no way I want to spend another 60 hours in this game doing the same stuff......There are still a ton of car upgrades I haven't even unlocked.  There are skills I haven't seen yet.  There are missions I can't start because I haven't got the requisite "influence" level down low enough and, to be honest, I don't care.
It's a nice game, well worth a few quid to play for 20-odd hours, but I can't imagine anyone completing it.  Progression is far too slow and, ultimately, there is too much game here for the variety of content.  Get rid of half the map and the game would be a different proposition.  If I was in the final 25% of the game instead of the first 25% I would be rating this MUCH higher, but as it is, I just can't see myself sticking with it to complete the rest of the map.  Meh.
Shame.  It is a LOT of fun and the car combat is beginning to get interesting but there are so many other games.....

Before you buy the game, consider the following:
- This game has been in development for many years, from the day I owned it, it would be 4 years. And yet with its 126 million $ revenue it has not managed to keep it on schedule.
- The updates come slowly and some nice features have been removed briefly, but have been re-introduced later.
So, why do I recommend this game? I don't recommend it, because that is my opinion. I am here to give you solid facts and discoveries that me and my friends had while playing this game.
First of all:
- I got a global ban from the BattlEye service on this account. I don't know what happened, might have been something with the server. But it will get raised by December.
- I liked the game so much, even though I got banned, I bought the game again on another account. This would be against steams rules, but I really enjoyed it at the time, and I would not want to stop playing it.
The game itself is nicely structured, the devs have done a wonderful job underlining the smallest of detail on the map. It has always been a pleasure to play it with friends, you can achieve stuff together, plan raids on looting spots which are kept secure by hostiles. Even though this game is more multiplayer based, any actual proper DayZ player can say that they love the game. It is a big game and progress takes some time, you have to deal with it. But when progress is made, it is very rewarding to the players.
I remeber the day the new render update came, it was a wonderful feeling. The game ran smoothly and there were no problems with graphics up to this day ever again.
Now. An important question. Is this comparable to Arma 2 DayZ mod or Arma 3. Not really. Even though Arma 2 DayZ mod was the basis of the game, there have been amazing changes to performance and other in-game logic systems such as the physics engine. As an example, you can roll wheels down a hill.
This might be a small part of the whole picture, but it's the craftsmanship that went into the game. No proper game is made in a year. And with the small team that they have at Bohemia Interactive working on DayZ they have achieved so many nice things.
For a team their size, I love the devs, they have managed to build up a full fetched game from a basis older mod for one of their previous games. Somehow, this small team managed to satisfy me so much, that I can't even believe how far they have come.
The big Beta update is coming soon, and I am genuinly excited for it.
Everything in short:
- Great fun
- Upates come slow, but steadily
- Amazing for multiplayer, long game sessions
- Absolutely lovely community
I have read some comments that were posted in September, 2017. I am a bit shocked. I can see that people are inpacient. I know that the devs haven't been up-to-date all the time! But the game turned out to be great!
And for those newbies out there. Don't expect to be the best player in the game the first time you log-on a server. Because you are not. You got to learn to play the game. So, if you get shot in the first 10 minutes of the game, analyse what you did and what you think went wrong. That's how you learn to play the game.
So... Overall? What would I say?
Buy it. It's that simple. Just do. If you don't like it, ok. Fine, uninstall it, and then someday come back to it later. If you like a peaceful game with amazing graphics and nice scenery, buy it. You can make amazing looking screenshots in the game.
If the devs are reading this, here is a message from me to you guys there:
*"Thank you so much for this wonderful game, it fits very well to LAN Party scenarios and is not just A game. Even though you got to walk for a while to find something, it's a social game. It's nice to play it with someone, socializing with them. Talk about the most random stuff. It's fun. It can be frustrating sometimes, but so is life in general. In this game I learnt not to run away from things, but to solve them head on. When I first bought the game, I never went near walkers (zombies) without or with a gun, I was scared that I would die and have to start again. That's what I did. It helped me in-game, and in life."*
Thank you developers for this amazing experience.

The Game is the most brutal survival game I've ever played. The Needs system is A-1 , the crafting system is lit. I play this on a completely survival based theme though. Hunting, fishing, farming, and the occasional kidnapping. overall the negative even provide a reason beyond the "boohoo so much money so much time" excuse. All in all the game will be great when released and if you want to support a game that , as stated earlier, is the most comprehensive survival game out there . then give this a shot. Oh , and don't drink the gasoline.
Pros:
Persistent Characters
Perma Death
Deep Survival Mechanics
Plenty of Server Options : Role Play, PVP, Low Pop
Global Loot System : People complain about loot but , what do you expect, its back country Russia in the middle of an apocalyptical pandemic. If you do make it to a military base, you are most certainly guaranteed some gear. IF you  make it.
Crafting : You can craft anything from an improvised knife, to a mid-tier backpack (A civilian backpack can hold 28 Slots, the improvised messenger back has 20 and the Improvised backpack 28)
Customization: You know that game Escape from Tarkov? the one EVERYONE is drueling over the gameplay of? Yea that's a watered down DayZ SA. You can turn your One AK-47 from a Long range rifle , to a Silenced CQB Variant. All from finding gun parts.
More Pros, but let's just leave it at that.
Cons:
Walking Simulator 5000 Complete with Thirst and Hunger so you can never make a beeline North.
UI is Ok , very clunky and manual. For example You need to open your Inventory menu to turn on the flashlight on your Handgun, or Bind the flashlight to a hotkey , then turn it on , then put it back on your gun.... <--- Very Big CON. Be prepared to take calculated risks to loot a person you just killed. P.S - If you usually play on LOW POP servers you don't need to worry as much, but transferring items to your inventory is manual and time consuming.
Vehicles : they are hard to come by ( Same as in Vanilla DayZ) (DayZ Mod server owners used to manually add more vehicles to their maps)- When you do find a vehicle. Its usually missing a part. Or some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ got it stuck. Overall on the subject of vehicles: be prepared to just walk, you may get lucky with a vehicle but if you enjoy nature and landscapes, then walking isn't that bad ( seriously , the game is beautiful)
KOS Players: This isn't necessarily a Con or a Pro , but in a game where death is almost always certain and guaranteed some players kill others on sight. Like I said it isn't a bad thing but overall It can suck the life out of the game. I tend to play on servers that have minimal players, the reason being is that I rather face the environment and all its grueling obstacles instead of dealing in death to other people , don't get me wrong there is an entire community of players who strictly PVP on this game, but as I stated in the Pros, you have a slew of options when it comes to what you want your server to be : PVP, RP, PVE.
Early Access: This is a CON because I feel that the majority of the Negative light being shown on this game is due to the player base going from a almost Complete MOD from an OLD GAME, to a NEW STANDALONE rendition of that IDEA. The devs then proceeded to share that with the community and ask them to participate in the dev process in the form of EA. The players then went from an almost COMPLETE MOD OF AN OLD GAME, to a NEW STANDALONE RENDITION of the IDEA in its most basic form. On top of that you combined an anxious veteran player base of this IDEA and make them wait 5+ years before they see this IDEA come to fruition.
--------------------------------------------------------
CONCLUSION
--------------------------------------------------------
If you really want to support this Idea then get this EARLY ACCESS version of the game
If you are on the fence about it then get it when its RELEASED.

Sometimes the game was actually a lot of fun, and I'll be the first to sing the game's praises on its personality and character. To illustrate, at one point you run into a dude named Face McShooty who loudly demands you shoot him in the face. Talk to him and he'll give you a quest, where the objective is to…shoot him in the face. Complete this objective, and you get an achievement.
The hybrid FPS-RPG thing was also a great touch and I loved seeing my character grow stronger over time while still retaining the player-skill-based challenge that is the FPS genre. So…why the average score from me?
The developers of this game do NOT understand how to make a game challenging. Instead, they know how to make the game frustrating. For one, shields in the game do precisely jack. There's a problem when I walk into a zone with enemies 20+ levels below me and a standard mook can still take out my shield in 1-2 hits. And after that, they can deplete my life marginally slower. And then, when I go into Fight For Your Life mode, they run away so I can't hit them for a Second Wind. Finally, when I respawn, an annoying voice appears to taunt me on dying when I couldn't do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥about it.
The major boss battles all have adds. Example: at one point you fight a giant flying robot with mounted cannons, and he's pretty tough. But what really makes the fight annoying is the infinitely respawning mook robots that harass you as you're running around, avoiding the boss's attacks, while trying to shoot him. A great way to do that fight is to hide inside the bunker and take potshots…which makes the fight long, tedious, and not challenging. So my choices are (1) run outside and fight an annoying infinite army of respawning robots or (2) stay inside and potshot the boss to death. Great design, guys.
I fought the raid boss just to see what the fuss was about. The raid boss has a lot of HP and pretty damaging attacks, and that was fine. The raid boss can also one-shot you by knocking you off the cliff that you fight him on and you can do…hmm…jack♥♥♥♥♥♥about that unless you stand in a specific spot where he can't do that and then chip away at his health until he dies. Are you seeing a trend here?
Look, there are ways to make a game hard without making it frustrating and unfair. I mean, I could design a game that's unfair too, where the maximum damage you can do is 99 and the weakest enemy in the game that can one-shot you 20 times over has a minimum of 568925782085709468029580 health. It wouldn't be a fun game, and neither is dying repeatedly to cheap one-shots while having to avoid adds.

I love this game, it is probably my favorite dungeon crawling Rogue-lite. The goal of the game is to explore a castle, clear rooms full of enemies and defeat 4 bosses with each of their own zones, defeating the four bosses gives you access to a fifth and final boss. Thankfully it saves the bosses that you've already defeated so you can progress no matter how many times you die, AND YOU WILL DIE without a doubt. With each time you die you choose one of three children that make up of different classes with their own advantages and disadvantages, this is the 'legacy' mechanic, and every character is unique because they can have different traits that can make the game easier or harder for the player or not effect the gameplay at all, for example you can have the color blind trait, everything is black and white which can make it difficult to identify colored variants of enemies that have different attacks or dwarfism that reduces the size of your hitbox and grants you access to secret tunnels. It has a level up system with a huge variety of upgrades and unlockable classes or upgradable versions of classes that give them special abilities, although it seems that a lot of the upgrades make such a miniscule effect on the gameplay that it forces you to grind for money to be able to level up those upgrades so they actually have an effect, mind you all your money is taken away every time you enter the castle so this makes grinding for skills that are more expensive a bit more difficult. There is also equipment and runes that you can collect throughout the castle that can effect your movement, damage, gold bonuses, and abilities that range from double jumping to making enemies weaker but have less gold and vice versa. But to be able to use any of these you would need to both pay gold and find them in challenge chests or normal chests, and for runes the amount of gold you need to pay increases with how many you buy. There are also random challenge rooms where you have to acheive an objective like shoot 8 targets with throwing daggers and you have 10 chances or give 25% of your gold and choose one of three chests to triple the amount of gold you put in. There may be some details I might have missed or forgot to explain but that just says something for how much depth in the gameplay this game has, if there's one thing in this game that I don't like it would have to be how there is so much forced grinding in it, even though it can be eased with items and perks that help with gold gain but there is still a lot of grinding involved to just get those items and perks and gold is absolutely needed to be able to progress with the enemies and bosses.  In conclusion, it's a challenging game with a lot of depth to the gameplay, a lot to do and a genious legacy mode that brings a new experience every time but with a grinding issue.

I agree with the people who say to go into this game blind. I did back in 2015 shortly after it came out and have kept away from outside influences and it's been one of the best gaming experiences of my life. You need to pay attention from the get go and get into a "video game way of thinking" to experience the whole story as it should be experienced on your first go, which granted, not everybody will do. But I feel like the people who don't pick up on the clues in the game and/or get immersed in the world and the story won't be the ones to get the neutral ending first and then make an effort to play it from the beginning to get the whole story. Which is fine.
But if you can go into this game fully intent on experiencing it the way it wants to be experienced then you're going to have a great time. I understand the problems with the fandom, at one point the fans of the game almost managed to alienate even me, someone who played this game before I even knew about the hype, because it can make you feel like the game itself thinks it's so smart. It really doesn't. It just wants to tell you a story.
What it does is it builds a world with dozens of humorous, interesting NPC's, tell dozens of tiny stories and one grand story of love, humanity, friendship, and family in a way that is both inventive and reminiscent of where the RPG genre originates from. The music is absolutely beautiful, the references and jokes are amazing, every corner of the world is radiating personality, the structure and pacing are narratively brilliant, and it just has so much heart, it will send you on an emotional rollercoaster all the way throughout.
I don't know how many times I've played through it (only got it on Steam recently) and every time I tear up at the same parts and get that excited and nervous shaking in my stomach during the climax of the story. And as for the genocide route, that's some A+ meta there, it takes a jokeful jab at gamers, let's players, people who watch let's players, cheaters, other games of the same genre, the karma system format, it's really just a triumph of video game making.
I have so much love for the kind of games that make me feel like home every time I start another playthrough, and the fact that after so much time spent in the game I still find new things and jokes (and puns! so many puns!) just adds to the experience.
Definitely recommended for everyone who cares to be immersed in a beautiful, full of heart story.

Overall a great game, here are some quick pros and cons...
Pros:
-Great Storyline
-Some of the characters are hilarious
-The combat looks boring, but it's actually quite fun, especially the bosses
-Music is great and really fits the game
-You can run this game on a toaster with no lag
Cons:
-EVERYTHING IS PIXELATED (Horrible graphics, I literally ran it with no graphics card installed on  my computer...)
-Parts of the game can be incredibly confusing, and you kind of are forced to turn to the internet for help...
-Genocide run breaks your game, and you are forced to reinstall it if you want to do another normal run
-Some bosses can get grindy
-Doing genocide weighs heavily on your conscience
-Reseting the game is a crucial part of the storyline, but it can be hard to leave what you've finished, especially leaving True Pacifist for Genocide
I think my favorite thing about Undertale is that it has multiple timelines, and you really have to play the game 4 (technically 3) times to really experiance the game. There are technically 3 routes: Neutral (Killing some and befriending others), True Pacifist (Befriending everyone), and Genocide (Seeking out every possible  monster and killing them all). I also did No Mercy, which is killing everyone you meet but not seeking them out, but this produces the same ending as a neutral run. The first game you do cannot be true pacifist. That aside, I love the story of Undertale, the fights are fun (RIP Sans) and the music is absolutely awesome! (My only complaint about the music is that it's all pixelated...) Definetly worth the $10.
EDIT: Someone had told me you can't do True Pacifist on your first run, but they were wrong. You can do any route your first time, but I would say it probably makes the most sense if you do Neutral first...

UPDATE: The review below reflects the singleplayer game only. Some additional testing in multiplayer since this review was written, even after patch 1.91, has multiplayer as a broken mess. At least 2 critical errors showed immediately. No phone appears for new players and this makes tracking etc. impossible. The second fault was being unable to claim outposts/towers/lookouts essentially made the game unplayable without first going into singleplayer to unlock them.
If you
want to play singleplayer then read on because it remains a fair and honest appraisal.
************************************************
Silky: Oh, the view. This is gorgeous. Many have said they spend more time shooting photos than animals. Weather effects are very special.
Rough: Bugs. Ugghh. Some of the AI is also just plain silly. But... they're polishing so with that said....
222 hours and despite enduring multiple bugs, some very serious ones at release, and with many still left unfixed (they vary in severity), EW has certainly shown they're prepared to make this title one of the best hunting pseudo-sims out there.
Now I say pseudo-sim because it's not strictly a knock-down, drag-me-around simulation. In order to appeal to a more casual audience, this title leaps over a few of the "realities" of hunting to allow the fun factor to stand out. (For those wanting more serious, if you have the coin, try theHunter Classic, EW's flagship).
The number of animals and the area to work in is quite staggering when you consider what we see. There are other sims out there with more animals and reserves but sorry, the environment quality is just not there. If EW add more reserves and animals to the core of what they have, then this will surpass the competition for a long time yet.
The shooting is pretty darn good. If I can put a projectile into the back of a head at 400m, exactly where I expected it to go, and repeatedly, then no-one can argue the accuracy of the weapons. There's a reasonable variety of them, graded to match species, and utlising a low calibre weapon on a large beast will leave you tracking a wounded beast for an inordinate amount of time. Some might say that we should be able to kill a moose with a .223 but you know, despite the game essentially making sure you wouldn't, we wouldn't in RL either. The converse is also true. You could use a 7mm to shoot a roe deer but unless you like your meat tenderised before it goes under the knife.... you wouldn't.
And the bonus system ensures you won't either.
- We have a "quick kill bonus" tied to downing the animals cleanly and quickly.
- We have the "integrity bonus" to make sure we select the appropriate weapon for the size of the prey.
- Lastly we have the "consecutive harvest bonus" which ensures that you don't leave your bad shot left hobbling around wounded. You need to initially shoot 5 beasts for the 100% but you then need to follow up on all shootings to maintain it.
(The other 2 are independent bonuses tied to weapon selection and the quality of the shot so are essentially redeemable at every shoot).
Sure, you can ignore all the bonuses and just blaze away for the payout but I guarantee, the minute you realise you missed a "Diamond" trophy red deer due to the cowboy in you, you'll change your practices.
Tracking can be difficult but it is a case of practice. The tracking directions and visual clues like broken foliage (a later skill), droppings etc. prior to the shoot and during wounded tracking (if you should mess up your shot) are predictable and intuitive - once you're used to it.
Perks and skills are acquired during play to a skill maximum of 60. Some are passive, meaning you have them at all times, some are active and you may chose to deploy your one skill/perk depending on the shoot. (eg: I use the scope zeroing skill mostly because I do a lot of long range shooting, while others might prefer windage detection for bow shooting... etc.)
Among those skills and perks are ambush and stalker specialities as well as skills that improve your visibility, noise and scent, all of which are monitored and displayed in the lower right, along with compass, wind and any active skill.
At the time of writing there a couple of cosmetic free DLC's, the shooting range DLC, 2 paid DLC's (tents and an ATV) and a willing bunch of devs listening to our requests for more.
As I mentioned earlier, the view is divine in the 2 supplied maps and the weather effects are special. It can also be quite frustrating if you get a thunderstorm, replete with strong winds, driving rain and thunder when you're desperately trying to listen to a fox in the undergrowth you've been calling in for the perfect bow shot.
I could go on about the goodness this title brings and I could even spend some more time on the bugs but there's a list of them on the forum already, they are working on it and well, many of them are cosmetic and more inconvenient than actually game breaking.
Overall, it's just a great hunting game. Play singleplayer, and I think you'll find, apart from the occassional hiccup, some most likely self-generated, you'll enjoy this title immensely, if only to go walking around in.
An easy 9/10 and if they get some real polish on it... it'll go 10.

For as much as Spec Ops: The Line does exceedingly well it failed in one very key area: gameplay. That combined with questionable marketing and tacked on multiplayer doomed this gem to be a commercial flop.
But what a gem it is underneath that fatal flaw. You'll be hard pressed to find a better story in the video game genre, particularly among shooters. At numerous points throughout the game I found myself stopping to simply admire the scenery. The voice acting, motion capture and script were all impressive. The audio, too, caught my attention in a positive way with some engrossing sound effects (I could practically feel the buffeting winds of the game's sandstorms) and a killer soundtrack that is creatively woven into the narrative with the Radioman character.
I don't want to give any plot points away but let me caution that this is a dark, twisted journey that is not for the faint of heart. And you won't be just a spectator throughout. You'll be forced to make decisions that stain your conscience and leave you wondering where the line between good and evil is.
There are some interesting articles out there commenting on how the gameplay was purposely made to be a distasteful slog through a seemly endless supply of faceless enemies. This is meant to impress upon the player that war isn't fun and that a killer's rationalizing mindset ("I had to do it") may be easier to arrive at than we realize. As much as I respect the effort to add depth with this kind of game design, I think that good gameplay is too important to compromise for the sake of making a point that many people won't even notice.
Before closing I'd like to note that this is a fairly short game. My total playtime for 2 playthroughs and unlocking 48/50 achievements was 12 hours. Roughly 6-7 hours first time on normal difficulty, 2 hours on achievements and 3-4 hours playing it again on easy just for the story. I didn't touch the multiplayer.
While the average score for Spec Ops: The Line is not very impressive I strongly recommend looking passed that. It is a game worth experiencing, one that I won't soon forget and one of the better games I've played in recent years.

READ FIRST: I finished this game originally on a console before but bought It again on Steam because I'm primarily a PC gamer. I finished this game twice to make sure I got the facts and the story straight.
INTRODUCTION:
Do you feel like a hero yet?, this is tag line that will haunt you all throughout the story of Spec Ops the Line.
At first glance this game looks like your average American Action War Hero game much like most modern day military shooters but it's not, its something else.
PROS:
+ Great story and unexpected plot: -Most games glorifies war and conflict but this game oddly focuses (in a good way) on the horrors of it. It takes unexpected twist that makes you question all the decision's you've made through the game. Gameplay wise (see Cons) you can call it generic, the thing that carries this game however, is the story.
+ Graphically pleasing: -Given that most games right now has stunning visuals, this is unique in it's own right, adding small details such as sweat, grime and atmosphere makes into a nice experience.
+ Sound : -Very nice voice acting that draws you into the story.
+ Healthy Game Time: -Not too long, not too short, it doesn’t overstay it's welcome but long enough to make the price tag reasonable.
CONS:
- Gameplay: -Aside from the added "sand" feature, it's a generic 3rd person cover based shooting game much like Gears of War.
- AI (both allies and enemy): -Some parts of the game, your allies act like real Special Forces, but in some parts they act like a clueless kid playing a multiplayer match. The game artificially increases the challenge by enemy numbers and bullet damage, but does nothing to improve the enemy AI's survivability. Would have been nice if they properly used cover and flanking moves (like FEAR 1).
Conclusion:
GREAT GAME for someone looking for a good story and plot, Spec Ops The Line has that movie "Apocalypse Now" feel to it.
NOT for people who are looking for a Gung Ho, Rambo, "look at me I'm the best" storyline. For that I can recommend something else.

Mad Max... A good story, and a great sandbox experience. The story is enjoyable, despite the repeating challenges and objectives. The combat is very well made, but seeing every Top Dog boss doing the exact same was kind off a let-down.
The story (as mentioned earlier), lives up to its needs. Yet I can’t help to dislike its general ending, it has been bothering ever since I finished the main story.
The car handling was also some-what uneasy to control, it seemed to have a 0.5  second delay upon pressing the ‘turn left & turn right’ keys. And some cars/trucks were seriously hard to control.
I did enjoy the storms that occurred now and then. They were seriously enjoyable, and sometimes even hilarious to witness.
The landscape was scares but there was a lot to explore, even after 70 hours, I still haven’t seen it all. The intel off every enemy along with its information was also very well made, as you don’t see this being done in other games.
So to summarize my opinion:
-	Great story
-	Huge map
-	Customizable vehicle
-	Enjoyable combat moments

Just a simple kind of fun.

UPDATE: The review below reflects the singleplayer game only. Some additional testing in multiplayer since this review was written, even after patch 1.91, has multiplayer as a broken mess. At least 2 critical errors showed immediately. No phone appears for new players and this makes tracking etc. impossible. The second fault was being unable to claim outposts/towers/lookouts essentially made the game unplayable without first going into singleplayer to unlock them.
If you
want to play singleplayer then read on because it remains a fair and honest appraisal.
************************************************
Silky: Oh, the view. This is gorgeous. Many have said they spend more time shooting photos than animals. Weather effects are very special.
Rough: Bugs. Ugghh. Some of the AI is also just plain silly. But... they're polishing so with that said....
222 hours and despite enduring multiple bugs, some very serious ones at release, and with many still left unfixed (they vary in severity), EW has certainly shown they're prepared to make this title one of the best hunting pseudo-sims out there.
Now I say pseudo-sim because it's not strictly a knock-down, drag-me-around simulation. In order to appeal to a more casual audience, this title leaps over a few of the "realities" of hunting to allow the fun factor to stand out. (For those wanting more serious, if you have the coin, try theHunter Classic, EW's flagship).
The number of animals and the area to work in is quite staggering when you consider what we see. There are other sims out there with more animals and reserves but sorry, the environment quality is just not there. If EW add more reserves and animals to the core of what they have, then this will surpass the competition for a long time yet.
The shooting is pretty darn good. If I can put a projectile into the back of a head at 400m, exactly where I expected it to go, and repeatedly, then no-one can argue the accuracy of the weapons. There's a reasonable variety of them, graded to match species, and utlising a low calibre weapon on a large beast will leave you tracking a wounded beast for an inordinate amount of time. Some might say that we should be able to kill a moose with a .223 but you know, despite the game essentially making sure you wouldn't, we wouldn't in RL either. The converse is also true. You could use a 7mm to shoot a roe deer but unless you like your meat tenderised before it goes under the knife.... you wouldn't.
And the bonus system ensures you won't either.
- We have a "quick kill bonus" tied to downing the animals cleanly and quickly.
- We have the "integrity bonus" to make sure we select the appropriate weapon for the size of the prey.
- Lastly we have the "consecutive harvest bonus" which ensures that you don't leave your bad shot left hobbling around wounded. You need to initially shoot 5 beasts for the 100% but you then need to follow up on all shootings to maintain it.
(The other 2 are independent bonuses tied to weapon selection and the quality of the shot so are essentially redeemable at every shoot).
Sure, you can ignore all the bonuses and just blaze away for the payout but I guarantee, the minute you realise you missed a "Diamond" trophy red deer due to the cowboy in you, you'll change your practices.
Tracking can be difficult but it is a case of practice. The tracking directions and visual clues like broken foliage (a later skill), droppings etc. prior to the shoot and during wounded tracking (if you should mess up your shot) are predictable and intuitive - once you're used to it.
Perks and skills are acquired during play to a skill maximum of 60. Some are passive, meaning you have them at all times, some are active and you may chose to deploy your one skill/perk depending on the shoot. (eg: I use the scope zeroing skill mostly because I do a lot of long range shooting, while others might prefer windage detection for bow shooting... etc.)
Among those skills and perks are ambush and stalker specialities as well as skills that improve your visibility, noise and scent, all of which are monitored and displayed in the lower right, along with compass, wind and any active skill.
At the time of writing there a couple of cosmetic free DLC's, the shooting range DLC, 2 paid DLC's (tents and an ATV) and a willing bunch of devs listening to our requests for more.
As I mentioned earlier, the view is divine in the 2 supplied maps and the weather effects are special. It can also be quite frustrating if you get a thunderstorm, replete with strong winds, driving rain and thunder when you're desperately trying to listen to a fox in the undergrowth you've been calling in for the perfect bow shot.
I could go on about the goodness this title brings and I could even spend some more time on the bugs but there's a list of them on the forum already, they are working on it and well, many of them are cosmetic and more inconvenient than actually game breaking.
Overall, it's just a great hunting game. Play singleplayer, and I think you'll find, apart from the occassional hiccup, some most likely self-generated, you'll enjoy this title immensely, if only to go walking around in.
An easy 9/10 and if they get some real polish on it... it'll go 10.

Undertale is something that words can't just put together. During the entire game there's this weird feeling of curiosity and wonder that just can't be described. Don't even get me started on the OST and the sound design, they're beyond perfect. The game also manages to be really self aware, but still keeping the seriousness of every situation. The game is so full of meaning, and i just can't describe my experience with this game well enough to describe this masterpiece. Almost 2 years after playing it UNDERTALE still has an everlasting mark on me, and i don't think any game would ever be capable of meaning more for me than UNDERTALE does.
Overall, the game hit me like nothing did before, and i consider it beyond perfect.
I HIGHLY recommend UNDERTALE, it's something everyone deserves to experience.

For as much as Spec Ops: The Line does exceedingly well it failed in one very key area: gameplay. That combined with questionable marketing and tacked on multiplayer doomed this gem to be a commercial flop.
But what a gem it is underneath that fatal flaw. You'll be hard pressed to find a better story in the video game genre, particularly among shooters. At numerous points throughout the game I found myself stopping to simply admire the scenery. The voice acting, motion capture and script were all impressive. The audio, too, caught my attention in a positive way with some engrossing sound effects (I could practically feel the buffeting winds of the game's sandstorms) and a killer soundtrack that is creatively woven into the narrative with the Radioman character.
I don't want to give any plot points away but let me caution that this is a dark, twisted journey that is not for the faint of heart. And you won't be just a spectator throughout. You'll be forced to make decisions that stain your conscience and leave you wondering where the line between good and evil is.
There are some interesting articles out there commenting on how the gameplay was purposely made to be a distasteful slog through a seemly endless supply of faceless enemies. This is meant to impress upon the player that war isn't fun and that a killer's rationalizing mindset ("I had to do it") may be easier to arrive at than we realize. As much as I respect the effort to add depth with this kind of game design, I think that good gameplay is too important to compromise for the sake of making a point that many people won't even notice.
Before closing I'd like to note that this is a fairly short game. My total playtime for 2 playthroughs and unlocking 48/50 achievements was 12 hours. Roughly 6-7 hours first time on normal difficulty, 2 hours on achievements and 3-4 hours playing it again on easy just for the story. I didn't touch the multiplayer.
While the average score for Spec Ops: The Line is not very impressive I strongly recommend looking passed that. It is a game worth experiencing, one that I won't soon forget and one of the better games I've played in recent years.

READ FIRST: I finished this game originally on a console before but bought It again on Steam because I'm primarily a PC gamer. I finished this game twice to make sure I got the facts and the story straight.
INTRODUCTION:
Do you feel like a hero yet?, this is tag line that will haunt you all throughout the story of Spec Ops the Line.
At first glance this game looks like your average American Action War Hero game much like most modern day military shooters but it's not, its something else.
PROS:
+ Great story and unexpected plot: -Most games glorifies war and conflict but this game oddly focuses (in a good way) on the horrors of it. It takes unexpected twist that makes you question all the decision's you've made through the game. Gameplay wise (see Cons) you can call it generic, the thing that carries this game however, is the story.
+ Graphically pleasing: -Given that most games right now has stunning visuals, this is unique in it's own right, adding small details such as sweat, grime and atmosphere makes into a nice experience.
+ Sound : -Very nice voice acting that draws you into the story.
+ Healthy Game Time: -Not too long, not too short, it doesn’t overstay it's welcome but long enough to make the price tag reasonable.
CONS:
- Gameplay: -Aside from the added "sand" feature, it's a generic 3rd person cover based shooting game much like Gears of War.
- AI (both allies and enemy): -Some parts of the game, your allies act like real Special Forces, but in some parts they act like a clueless kid playing a multiplayer match. The game artificially increases the challenge by enemy numbers and bullet damage, but does nothing to improve the enemy AI's survivability. Would have been nice if they properly used cover and flanking moves (like FEAR 1).
Conclusion:
GREAT GAME for someone looking for a good story and plot, Spec Ops The Line has that movie "Apocalypse Now" feel to it.
NOT for people who are looking for a Gung Ho, Rambo, "look at me I'm the best" storyline. For that I can recommend something else.

One of those rare third person shooter game with great visuals, great narration, great voice actors and incredibly well written story.
Spec Ops The Line never attempts to be great at gameplay. In fact, it tries to be as simple, as streamlined and straightforward as possible. What you need aside of shooting enemies (well , this is third person shooter game after all), is to make a good cover of yourself using environment as a shield. The game literally forces you to hide all the time, and only come out to make a progress. When in battle, AIs force you to hide like 95% of the time and they do a great job at it. There's no upgrades, skill trees, side quests, open world or anything your regular gamers want from today's games. Learning curve is minimal at worst, at best it is no curve at all.
This simplicity, however, what makes the game good. It really fits with the game's linearity and storyline that challenges your moral/ethic code.
You control Walker, one protagonist, and go on a simple rescue and evacuate mission. During the process, there's many background stories that develop into more complicated moral-driven situations. Throughout the game, I was forced to make some decisions I would not have made in real life - where I have the options, where I have the luxury to do many things I want.. during peace. In a war, all is different. The atmosphere made in game is just perfect depicting that condition - you feel yourself in Walker's shoes - see and think in his perspective. Very rarely does a game try to do that.
That said, the game also has stunning visuals where I have no complaints at all. You see a detailed landscape of post-apocalyptic Dubai, along with the occasional sandstorms. Graphic optimization is also great, I've got no problem running this maxed on my laptop rig that's mediocre at best.
Audio wise, it's more than enough to accompany the visuals. When fighting, it feels realistic. The sound of guns, explosions, environment sounds are well made make you feel the tense and heat of the battle. Furthermore, with decent voice actors, it makes game's narration just perfect - each characters' dialogues are performed with heart.
Game's pretty short, 7 hours should net you almost everything. Nevertheless, as a whole, Spec Ops The Line is a great experience that all gamers should feel themselves. A game that starts great with great end.

This review reflects an early stage of development. Nevertheless it is already a great game!
Essentially, it is a chaotic and awesomely funny beat 'em up game. It has good controller support for I think up to four players, but I had the opportunity to play with only one other player yet. For beginners, you can take control by just pressing random buttons at a high rate, which results in accidental roundhouse kicks and arbitrary mayhem - it seems to be intended to do so in this game. Some more controlled movements like grabbing, lifting and throwing someone (over the edge) also work for me now. Overall, the game appears to be balanced through the physics involved.
This leads me to the highlight I want to share in this review. I don't remember any other game constantly rendering ragdoll physics. It is usual to have ragdoll physics during uncontrolled drops or while being "unconscious". In Gang Beasts you always control your plastic and somewhat clumsy body. It makes the characters look ridiculous and fits well into the theme of the game. The developers did a good job to still give you the feeling of having the control. I wonder if once the game will qualify to have official championships.
While it is possible to play one of the two game modes 'survival' (co-op) as a single player, the game is clearly intended to be played with friends. Perhaps further modes will be implemented in the future - I would appreciate that.
A few drawbacks are there at present:
- Probably because of the physics the game does not run so smoothly on my machine. You will need a bold processor to be able to enjoy smooth punches to the chin.
- The standard controller binding has a quick exit key, which is accidently pressed every five minutes in game due to beginners randomly pressing buttons. A confimation dialog would help here.
- There are some blind areas where the camera is not able to follow you. Perhaps this is an intended wickedness - very well.
As a conclusion I fully recommend the game if you have people to play with. The price tag gives rise to some expectations for the final game.
